Discussion
The chromosome 7q11.23 region is widely recognized 
because it contains the critical genes leading to Williams 
Beuren microdeletion and microduplication syndromes 
[10, 11]. It is flanked by 3 main clusters of low-copy 
repeats (LCR) named proximal (LCR-P), central (LCR-
C), and distal (LCR-D), and it encompasses many and 
highly transcribed genes. Indeed, its gene density and 
transcriptional rate are significantly higher when com-
pared with other segments of chromosome 7 [12]. To 
date, the genes between LCR-P and LCR-C have been 
marked as causative of these two disorders. The region 
involved in rearrangement is 1.4–1.5  Mb in length, 
encompassing about 26 to 28 genes, between the NSUN5 
gene on the centromeric end and GTF2IRD2 gene on 
the telomeric end [10, 13, 14]. Notable genes include 
ELN, coding for elastic fibers, in connection with con-
nective tissue abnormalities and cardiovascular disease; 
and NCF1, in connection with the risk of hypertension. 
Less than 100 cases of 7q11.23 microduplication syn-
drome have been described in the literature. Although 
the clinical phenotype of individuals with dup7q11.23 
syndrome is not completely delineated, it is agreed that 
it is associated with milder and less distinct clinical fea-
tures than its reciprocal microdeletion syndrome .[10, 
13, 14]. Common clinical features of 7q11.23 duplication 
include delayed speech and developmental delay, learn-
ing difficulties, variable cognitive functions (from normal 
to intellectual disability), autism, characteristic facial fea-
tures (broad forehead, high, broad nose, short philtrum, 
thin lips), growth issues (head size, height), congenital 
malformations (heart defects—PDA, subaortic stenosis, 
and aortic dilatation, renal anomalies, undescended tes-
tis, brain malformations), and epilepsy [3, 10, 15–18].
Most dup7q11.23 syndrome cases are diagnosed in 
childhood or adulthood due to language impairment, 
intellectual disability, mild facial dysmorphisms and con-
genital malformations [19]. However, very little prenatal 
information has been collected. A report by Dang et al. 
described two fetuses with dup7q11.23 syndrome car-
rying a typical 1.4–1.5  Mb duplication. One case with 
dup7q11.23 syndrome presented with lateral ventriculo-
megaly and polyhydramnios, while the other one showed 
choroid plexus cyst by prenatal ultrasonography [19]. 
Marcato et  al. reported a fetus with dup7q11.23 syn-
drome, manifested with increased NT, absence of nasal 
bone, inversion of the “a” wave of the ductus venosus, 
and mild bilateral ventriculomegaly, lissencephaly-type 
abnormality [21]. Various congenital malformations were 
reported in the postnatal literatures, including many mal-
formations which we assume that could be detected in 
prenatal ultrasonography, such as heart defects (subaor-
tic stenosis and aortic dilatation), brain malformations 
(ventriculomegaly, agenesis of corpus callosum, poste-
rior fossa cysts and cerebellar vermis hypoplasia), renal 
anomalies, cleft lip and/or palate [16–18]. Among fetuses 
diagnosed with 7q11.23 microduplication syndrome in 
our case series, the following intrauterine phenotypes 
were identified: ventriculomegaly (42.9%, 3/7), low-lying 
conus medullaris (42.9%, 3/7), dilated ascending aorta 
(28.6%, 2/7), cleft palate (14.3%, 1/7), hyperechogenic 
aortic valve (14.3%, 1/7), anencephalus (14.3%, 1/7), 
severe hydronephrosis of the left kidney with dilatation 
of the left ureter (14.3%, 1/7). In addition, fetal short long 
bones in Case 2 were suspected to be caused by the de 
novo pathogenic variant in COL2A1, which was associ-
ated with hypochondrogenesis type 2.

The structural malformations observed prenatally in 
our research were consistent with those reported in the 
literature. The ventriculomegaly was the most common 
sonographic feature observed in our case series, and was 
also reported in previous prenatal studies [20, 21]. The 
ventriculomegaly on brain imaging has been reported in 
several affected children and adult cases of dup7q11.23 
syndrome as well [3, 16, 22, 23]. The ultrasound images 
of the fetus 2 showed a median cleft of the hard palate. It 
is a common congenital anomaly that has been reported 
in several affected children and adults [3, 17, 23]. Case 3 
has severe hydronephrosis of the left kidney and dilata-
tion of the ureter, which is consistent with two affected 
children in previous reports [10]. In our case series, there 
were three cases suspected of aortic disease. Case 1 had 
hyperechogenic aortic valve, Case 6 and 7 were MCDA 
twins with dilated ascending aorta (z-scores for the aorta 
were 1.95 and 2.09, respectively). Congenital cardiac 
defects have been reported in many pediatric and adult 
cases as well [16, 19], especially patent ductus arterio-
sus and aortopathy. Since patent ductus arteriosus is a 
postnatal diagnosis, it could not be identified prenatally. 
Parrott et  al. presented a series of eight children and 
one adult with 7q11.23 microduplication syndrome, all 
of them had aortic dilation. The dilated ascending aorta 
was a rather specific abnormality repeatedly observed in 
pediatric and adult cases, and also in our prenatal cases. 
Moreover, three fetuses in our study showed a low-lying 
conus medullaris (CM). The CM position is important 
and abnormal position is associated with tethered cord, 
characterized by walking difficulty and sensory dysfunc-
tion in infants. Detection of a low-lying CM is essential 
in prenatal evaluation [24, 25], and we should stay alert 
if the CM below the L3 level after 23 weeks of gestation. 
In Fetus 2, the CM located at the L4 level at 24 weeks of 
gestation, but the fetus was aborted due to multiple mal-
formations and no follow-up was available. Fetus 6 and 7 
were MCDA twins both found low-lying CM at 24 weeks, 
the CM ascend to L2-3 at 32  weeks, and follow-up to 
1 year old showed no associated symptom.
The ELN gene is considered the most critical and 
extensively explored gene in WBS. It encoded elastin 
protein (Elastin), which is a major component of the 
elastic fibers that strengthen connective tissue through-
out the body. Its haplo-insufficiency is reported to 
cause supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS) in patients 
with WBS. The comparison have been made to the 
apparent opposite phenotypes caused by the 7q11.23 
deletion and duplication, including opposing dysmor-
phic features and the relative strength/weakness in 
expressive language [17]. Moreover, SVAS was com-
monly observed in WBS, and aortic dilation was usually 
identified in individuals with 7q11.23 microduplication 
syndrome [17]. Here in our case series, this phenom-
enon was also found in prenatal cases (Case 6 and 7). 
While the SVAS in WBS has been attributed to ELN 
deletion, we postulate that a gene dosage effect of ELN 
may be the underlying cause for the prenatal dilated 
ascending aorta in these patients with the microdupli-
cation. However, the exact cause of aortic dilation in 
these patients remain unknown at this time.
Phenotype of 7q11.23 microduplication syndrome 
could be variable in the family series, ranging from 
apparent normal phenotype to delayed speech, autis-
tic spectrum manifestations, intellectual disability, 
and cardiac abnormalities [26]. In the prenatal genetic 
counseling of 7q11.23 microduplication, it may not be 
accurate to predict the postnatal performance of off-
spring based on the symptoms of other positive mem-
bers of the family. In our study, Case 6 and 7 were 
MCDA twins, and their 7q11.23 microduplication were 
inherited from their asymptomatic mother. They had 
typical facial features, dilation of the ascending aorta, 
and mild ventriculomegaly by the age of one year, fol-
low-ups (cardiac, neural) on annual basis is onging. 
There was another pair of MCDA twins with 7q11.23 
microduplication in our study, Case 4 and 5, but their 
prenatal progress were different: Case 4 diagnosed with 
anencephalus as early as 12  weeks of gestation, while 
Case 5 showed no apparent abnormality up to 20 weeks 
on labor induction. However, the prenatal phenotypes 
of case 6 and case 7 were consistent, including ven-
triculomegaly, low-lying CM, dilated ascending aorta 
at 24 weeks. Previous studies indicated that phenotypes 
of 7q11.23 duplication syndrome may vary significantly 
within a family, and this study further suggests that pre-
natal findings may be variable even for MCDA twins.
One limitation of our case series is that not all cases 
underwent exome sequencing to rule out additional 
molecular lesions. Case 2 is an example of how the short 
bones may have been erroneously reported as a potential 
association. We will conduct a thorough investigation to 
avoid potentially erroneous associations in our subse-
quent research.
Conclusions
In summary, prenatal ultrasound findings of dup7q11.23 
cases are diversified, with ventriculomegaly and low-lying 
conus medullaris being the most common intrauterine 
phenotypes. As frequently observed in adults and chil-
dren cases, cleft palate, dilated ascending aorta, and renal 
abnormalities were also observed in the present prenatal 
cases, and should be pay attention to in subsequent stud-
ies. These findings may provide important clues for pos-
sible prenatal diagnosis of dup7q11.23 syndrome.

title: Skeletal Dysplasia: A Case Report.
abstract: This paper presents a rare case of fetal hydrops detected at just 23 weeks of gestation in a 22-year-old woman’s first pregnancy. The fetal ultrasound revealed severe skeletal anomalies, craniofacial deformities, and thoracic abnormalities, suggesting a complex and severe skeletal dysplasia, potentially type IA Achondrogenesis—a lethal autosomal recessive condition marked by ossification delay. This case highlights the significance of advanced genetic testing, such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), in diagnosing and understanding skeletal dysplasias. Skeletal dysplasias represent a group of genetic disorders that affect osteogenesis. The prevalence of this condition is 1 in 4000 births. Sadly, 25% of affected infants are stillborn, and around 30% do not survive the neonatal period. There is a wide range of rare skeletal dysplasias, each with its own specific recurrence risk, dysmorphic expression, and implications for neonatal survival and quality of life. When skeletal dysplasia is incidentally discovered during routine ultrasound screening in a pregnancy not known to be at risk of a specific syndrome, a systematic examination of the limbs, head, thorax, and spine is necessary to reach the correct diagnosis. Prenatal diagnosis of skeletal dysplasia is crucial for providing accurate counselling to future parents and facilitating the proper management of affected pregnancies. An accurate diagnosis can be a real challenge due to the wide spectrum of clinical presentations of skeletal dysplasia but advances in imaging technologies and molecular genetics have improved accuracy. Additionally, some of these skeletal dysplasias may present clinical overlap, making it especially difficult to distinguish. After the 11th revision of genetic skeletal disorder nosology, there are 771 entities associated with 552 gene mutations. The most common types of skeletal dysplasia are thanatophoric dysplasia, osteogenesis imperfect, achondroplasia, achondrogenesis, and asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy. Keywords: skeletal dysplasia, hydrops, hypomineralization, micromelia

title: Prenatal whole-exome sequencing in fetuses with increased nuchal translucency.
label_reason: Increased NT fetuses with karyotype, CMA and WES.
abstract: Increased nuchal translucency (NT) is associated with an increased risk for genetic disorders. The aim of this study was to investigate the value of whole‐exome sequencing (WES) in detecting genetic abnormalities for fetuses with isolated first‐trimester increased NT. After the exclusion of aneuploidies and pathogenic copy number variants (CNVs) by quantitative fluorescent polymerase chain reaction (QF‐PCR) and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), WES was performed on 63 fetuses with isolated first‐trimester increased NT (≥3.5 mm). Overall, WES yielded a 4.8% (3/63) diagnostic rate for fetuses with isolated increased NT. Pathogenic variants were identified in 37.5% (3/8) fetuses that developed additional structural anomalies later in gestation, and no pathogenic variants were detected in increased NT that resolved or remained isolated throughout the pregnancy. This study provides powerful evidence to offer prenatal WES for increased NT only when additional abnormalities are present. Early detailed ultrasound to detect emerging anomalies can help physicians offer prenatal WES to fetuses with a greater likelihood of diagnosis. Keywords: chromosomal microarray analysis, genetic counseling, increased nuchal translucency, prenatal diagnosis, whole‐exome sequencing

Prenatal whole‐exome sequencing in fetuses with increased nuchal translucency

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Nuchal translucency (NT) is an ultrasound measurement of the maximal thickness of the subcutaneous translucency between the skin and subcutaneous soft tissue overlying the cervical spine in a mid‐sagittal view of the face of a fetus at 11–14 weeks' gestation (Nicolaides et al., ). Increased NT is defined as a measurement ≥95th percentile by crown‐rump length‐adjusted percentiles (crown‐rump length range 45–84 mm) in accordance with the standards of the Fetal Medicine Foundation (Wright et al., ). Increased NT (≥3.5 mm) is associated with genetic disorders, which can result in adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as miscarriage, intrauterine fetal death, congenital heart disease, extensive skeletal dysplasia, and intellectual disability (Bilardo et al., ; Grande et al., ; Hellmuth et al., ; Nicolaides et al., ). Identification of the etiology of increased NT is essential to assist in genetic counseling, inform prognosis, establish recurrence risk, and direct clinical care. Chromosomal abnormalities can be identified in approximately 30% of increased NT by combining karyotype and CMA (Bardi et al., ; Bilardo et al., ; Stuurman et al., ). However, fetuses with negative results on karyotype analysis and CMA are still at high risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, which indicates some as‐yet‐undiscovered underlying causes (Bilardo et al., ; Ghi et al., ). In clinical practice, when karyotype and CMA are normal, couples are routinely recommended to await the fetal anatomy survey and echocardiogram to rule out structural abnormalities in the second trimester. In occasional cases with an increased NT and normal CMA, there is still a risk for genetic conditions even though no other abnormalities are detected in pregnancy (Yang et al., ). In consideration of the increased parental anxiety during the long wait before the second‐trimester scan, and the limitations of prenatal ultrasound for diagnosing childhood‐onset genetic diseases, a more efficient diagnostic assay is warranted to detect underlying disease‐causing variants in fetuses with isolated increased NT and negative results on karyotype analysis and CMA. With decreases in costs and increases in the speed of bioinformatics analytical pipelines, exome sequencing has been increasingly used in the prenatal diagnosis of Mendelian diseases. Many studies on prenatal exome sequencing have successfully identified genetic diagnoses in fetuses with structural abnormalities, but diagnostic rates differed greatly in different phenotypic subgroups (Chen et al., ; Drury et al., ; Kucińska‐Chahwan et al., ; Lord et al., ; Petrovski et al., ; Sparks et al., ; Vora et al., ; Zhang et al., ). Exome sequencing studies focused on isolated increased NT obtained diagnostic rates ranging from 0% to 21% (Chen et al., ; Daum et al., ; Drury et al., ; Lord et al., ; Mellis et al., ; Petrovski et al., ; Sparks et al., ; Xue et al., ; Yang et al., ). The substantially different diagnostic rates challenge the clinical application and cost‐effectiveness of WES. In this study, we determined the diagnostic yield of WES and explored factors that influence diagnostic rates in isolated first‐trimester increased NT.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
MATERIALS AND METHODS Ethical compliance This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Maternal and Child Healthcare Hospital. Study design and participants Between June 2018 and December 2020, 169 singleton pregnancies with increased NT (≥3.5 mm) at 11–14 weeks' gestation were screened in Urumqi Maternal and Child Health Hospital. Among these fetuses, 23 (13.6%) presenting additional ultrasound abnormalities, including cystic hygroma, were excluded from this study. All couples who agreed to participate in the study provided written informed consent. At the time of enrollment, we carefully reviewed family and past obstetrics histories and conducted expert examinations of each couple. Fetal samples were collected by chorionic villus sampling (chorionic villi) or amniocentesis (amniotic fluid) according to the gestational age at the time of the invasive prenatal diagnosis. Parental blood samples were routinely collected at the time of the prenatal diagnostic procedure. For genetic testing, samples first underwent rapid aneuploidy testing using QF‐PCR. When QF‐PCR detected aneuploidy, no further testing was done. Samples with normal QF‐PCR results were arranged for CMA. DNA of cases with normal CMA was sent for trio WES with parental samples. The WES results and a formal report were provided directly to couples at the time of diagnosis with a turnaround time of 4–8 weeks. All pregnancy outcomes were followed up twice, at 6 and 18 months, respectively, after the expected date of birth. Ultrasound examination Ultrasound examination was performed by physicians qualified for prenatal ultrasound diagnosis. An E8 Voluson (GE) ultrasound system with a 3.5–5 MHz ultrasound probe was used. The procedure of prenatal ultrasound diagnosis was conducted according to the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology practice guidelines (Salomon et al., ; Salomon et al., ). Chromosomal microarray analysis DNA was extracted from both fetal and parental samples with a DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Catalog No. 69504, Qiagen) following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA concentrations and quality were determined with a NanoDropOne spectrophotometer (Life Technologies, Thermo Fisher Scientific). DNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis. CMA was performed on a CytoScan 750K platform (Applied Biosystems, Affymetrix). Briefly, 250 ng DNA was required, and the experiment was conducted following the manufacturer's protocol. Aberration analysis was performed with ChAS (Affymetrix). CNVs were categorized according to the joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Clinical Genome Resource (Riggs et al., ). Parents of fetuses with pathogenic or likely pathogenic copy number variants (CNVs) subsequently underwent CMA to determine whether the CNVs were de novo or inherited. Whole‐exome sequencing An Agilent SureSelect Human ALL Exon V6 Kit was used for whole‐exome DNA library construction. A HiSeq 2500 sequencer (Illumina) with 100 bp paired‐end sequencing mode was used to sequence the genomic DNA of the family. Raw image files were processed with CASAVA v1.82 for base calling and generation of raw data. Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19/GRCh37) with the Burrows–Wheeler Aligner tool, and PCR duplicates were removed with Picard v1.57 (http://picard.sourceforge.net/). The third‐party software GATK (https://software.broadinstitute.org/gatk/) was used for variant calling. Variant annotation and interpretation were conducted by ANNOVAR (Wang et al., ). Variants analysis targets coding exons and splicing regions for all putative disease‐causing genes curated from Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, including candidate genes. Genes associated with RASopathies, inborn errors of metabolism, skeletal dysplasia, neurodevelopment disorders, generalized lymphatic dysplasia, cardiomyopathies, mitochondrial mutations, etc., were carefully analyzed. The clinical significance of variants was classified according to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Richards et al., ). Pathogenic variants, likely pathogenic variants, and novel variants of uncertain clinical significance were shortlisted as candidate variants. Any variants considered disease‐causing were verified by Sanger sequencing. Family members, including proband, if available, were also examined by Sanger sequencing to test the origin of the variants. WES data were re‐analyzed based on prenatal and/or postnatal phenotypic changes, and linked to the latest ClinVar, ClinGen, OMIM, and Human Gene Mutation Database. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were done with SPSS (version 22.0). The two‐tailed Fisher's exact test was used to compare rates of diagnostic genetic variants between sub‐groups, and p < 0.05 was considered as significant difference.

RESULTS
RESULTS The workflow of this study was presented in Figure . During the study period, 146 cases with isolated first‐trimester increased NT were screened out, among which aneuploidies were detected (17 cases of trisomy 21, 5 cases of trisomy 18, 3 cases of Turner syndrome, 1 case of 47, XYY syndrome, and 5 cases of monosomy X mosaicism) in 31 cases, and pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNVs in 8 cases (Table ). For case 4 in Table , two pathogenic CNVs originated from one derivative chromosome, which were confirmed to be inherited from father with a karyotype of 46, XY, t(16;18)(p13.3;p11.2). Combination of QF‐PCR and CMA obtained a diagnostic rate of 26.7% (39/146). CMA had an incremental detection rate of 5.5% (8/146). Flow chart of this study. CMA, chromosomal microarray analysis; CNVs, copy number variants; NT, nuchal translucency; QF‐PCR, quantitative fluorescent polymerase chain reaction; WES, whole‐exome sequencing. For the remaining 107 cases with normal CMA, 41 couples declined WES and 3 cases were excluded because of poor‐quality fetal DNA. DNA samples of 63 fetuses and matched parents were sent for trio‐WES. Pathogenic variants were detected in three cases (see Table ), yielding a 4.8% (3/63) overall diagnostic rate. Case 8 had a de novo missense variant NM_002834.3:c.236A>C(p.Gln79Pro) in PTPN11 (OMIM: *176876), which was associated with the autosomal dominant disease Noonan syndrome 1 (OMIM: #163950). The fetus presented with pulmonary valve stenosis on second‐trimester ultrasound. Case 9 had a de novo missense variant NM_006912.5: c.270G>T(p. Met90Ile) in RIT1 (OMIM: *609591), which was associated with the autosomal dominant disease Noonan syndrome 8 (OMIM: #615355). Second‐trimester ultrasound of the fetus revealed atrial septal defects, which are common prenatal ultrasound findings for Noonan syndrome 8. Case 10 had a de novo missense variant NM_007373:c.4A>G(p.Ser2Gly) in SHOC2 (OMIM: *602775), which was associated with the autosomal dominant disease Noonan syndrome‐like with loose anagen hair 1 (OMIM: #607721). The fetus presented with mitral valve dysplasia and atrial septal defects on second‐trimester ultrasound. Validation results using Sanger sequencing for all three variants were shown in Figure . Among the 63 fetuses with isolated first‐trimester increased NT, additional abnormalities were detected in 8 cases (12.7%) later in gestation, with a diagnostic rate of 37.5% (3/8). For the 5 cases with additional abnormalities and negative findings, phenotypic features were listed in Table . In fetuses without other abnormalities later, no diagnostic variants were detected. There was a significant difference in diagnostic rate between increased NT with additional abnormalities and those resolved or remained isolated throughout the pregnancy (37.5% vs. 0%, Fisher's exact two‐tailed test; p < 0.01). Furthermore, five variants of unknown significance (VUS) were detected in genes with an autosomal dominant manner (Table ). There was no sufficient evidence and/or the prenatal phenotype was not specific enough to classify the variants as (likely) pathogenic. All these five cases present normal postnatal ultrasound scan at birth, and normal physical and neurobehavioral development at 18 months of age. Among the 23 cases with additional ultrasound abnormalities at the NT scan, 7 opted for termination of pregnancy (TOP) without further testing, 6 with aneuploidies opted for TOP, 1 developed intrauterine death, 9 born alive and follow‐up results were normal. Among the 44 fetuses that declined WES or with poor fetal DNA quality, 3 developed structural abnormalities later in gestation and opted for TOP, 1 with pulmonary sequestration continued pregnancy and underwent surgery after birth, 40 born alive and follow‐up results were normal. Among the 63 cases received WES, 4 (including 3 with pathogenic variants) opted for TOP, 2 with isolated cardiac defects continued pregnancy and underwent surgery after birth, 57 born alive, and follow‐up results were normal.

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION The aim of this study was to gain more insight into the diagnostic use of prenatal WES in fetuses with isolated increased NT and normal QF‐PCR and CMA and explore factors that influence diagnostic rates. Studies using QF–PCR as a first‐line test showed that about 30.2%–51.3% of fetuses with NT >3.5 mm had common aneuploidies (Pan et al., ; Sinajon et al., ). This study yielded a diagnostic rate of 21.2% (31/146). The relatively low diagnostic yield in this study may partially be attributed to the exclusion of cases with additional ultrasound abnormalities in the first trimester. The low cost, rapid turnaround time, ability to detect significant abnormalities, and the high incidence of aneuploidies make QF‐PCR an ideal initial test prior to additional testing (Chitty et al., ; Langlois et al., ). Practice guidelines have recommended CMA as first‐tier test when a fetal anomaly has been detected by ultrasound or other fetal imaging and is rapidly becoming the preferred diagnostic test for fetuses with structural malformations (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, Society for Maternal–Fetal Medicine, ; Committee on Genetics, Society for Maternal–Fetal Medicine, ). Most recently, Mastromoro et al. () performed a systematic review of the literature and meta‐analysis, to calculate diagnostic yields of genetic testing in fetuses with increased NT and cystic hygroma. They established that the incremental CMA detection rate was 4.1% for isolated increased NT (≥3.5 mm). The percentage of pathogenic findings in this study was 5.5%, which is, therefore, in line with most other studies (Mastromoro et al., ). In this series of 63 pregnancies with isolated first‐trimester increased NT (≥3.5 mm), WES identified pathogenic variants in three cases, yielding an incremental diagnostic rate of 4.8%. This discrepancy in diagnostic rate between this and previous studies may be attributable to different cohort sizes, cohort ascertainment, cut‐off for increased NT, and criteria for variants interpretation (Mastromoro et al., ). In certain studies, such as one from Petrovski et al. (), did not distinguish increased NT with or without structural abnormalities, leading to a high diagnostic rate in those with structural abnormalities. Some studies, such as one from Daum et al. (), used 3.0 mm rather than 3.5 mm as the cut‐off for increased NT, leading to a relatively higher likelihood of diagnosis in the larger increased NT group. Among studies focused on isolated increased NT in the first trimester and used the 99th percentile (≥3.5 mm) as the cut‐off for increased NT, Yang et al. obtained a 5.5% (4/73) increase in diagnostic rate over CMA using medical exome sequencing (Yang et al., ); Mellis et al. obtained a diagnostic rate of 9.0% (14/155) using prenatal WES (Mellis et al., ). The recent systematic review and meta‐analysis by Mastromoro et al. established an overall 2.44% diagnostic yield for exome sequencing in fetuses with isolated increased NT (≥3.5 mm) (Mastromoro et al., ). The great discrepancy in diagnostic rate questions the application of WES in fetuses with isolated increased NT. We observed a high diagnostic rate (37.5%) for increased NT with additional abnormalities later in gestation, which was consistent with Mellis et al.'s analysis (37.5% vs. 32.4%, Fisher's exact two‐tailed test; p = 1.00) (Mellis et al., ). We did not obtain any (likely) pathogenic variants for cases with isolated increased NT that resolved or remained isolated later in gestation, whereas Mellis et al. obtained a diagnostic rate of 1.8% (2/111). Note that one of the findings was chromosome 15 uniparental disomy, which was presumed to have been detected on prenatal SNP‐array analysis. Therefore, in Mellis et al.'s analysis, the diagnostic rate of WES may be as low as 0.9% (1/111). These low diagnostic rates for isolated increased NT without additional abnormalities are consistent with an existing body of evidence indicating that, after exclusion of chromosomal abnormalities, if a detailed ultrasound examination in the second trimester demonstrates resolution of the increased NT and absence of any major abnormalities, then the prognosis is likely to be good and the chances of delivering a baby with no major abnormalities are more than 95% (Bilardo et al., ; Bilardo et al., ; Souka et al., ). In this study, among the eight fetuses with additional abnormalities later in gestation, only three were detected with diagnostic variants, which indicates that there are still underlying etiology undiscovered by prenatal WES. Sequential testing that CMA followed by WES is unable to detect certain types of variations, such as noncoding single nucleotide variants, small CNVs that affect single or few exons, and balanced structural rearrangements. Choy et al. evaluated the feasibility of applying genome sequencing (>30‐fold) in prenatal diagnosis for 50 fetuses with increased NT, and yielded a twofold increase in diagnostic yield (32.0%, 16/50); moreover, they identified two cryptic insertions and two inversions; follow‐up study further demonstrated the potential pathogenicity of an apparently balanced insertion that disrupted gene BMPR2 at the insertion site (Choy et al., ). Whole‐genome sequencing is a holistic approach for comprehensive detection of the disease‐causing genetic variants with a low input‐DNA requirement (≈100 ng) and a rapid turnaround time (18 ± 6 days) compared with that (31 ± 8 days) of the CMA plus WES sequential strategy, and it is proposed to be beneficial in prenatal diagnosis (Saunders et al., ; Talkowski et al., ; Willig et al., ; Zhou et al., ). However, it is still not revealing all the causative variants and relevant clinical studies in prenatal diagnosis are limited. Compared with WES, whole‐genome sequencing would yield a larger number of VUS, which prevents the value of the clinical application. Increased NT was the most common phenotypic expression in fetuses with RASopathies (Stuurman et al., ), and was associated with a 10% risk of Noonan syndrome, a disorder belonging to the RASopathies or RAS/MAPK syndromes (Ali et al., ). Prenatal exome sequencing studies have implicated many genes of the Ras‐MAPK pathway in increased NT (Chen et al., ; Drury et al., ; Fu et al., ; Lord et al., ; Mellis et al., ; Petrovski et al., ; Sparks et al., ; Yang et al., ). In this study, all three genes (PTPN11, RIT1, and SHOC2) with diagnostic variants are those of the Ras‐MAPK pathway, which confirms that increased NT is associated with a high risk for RASopathies (Sinajon et al., ). Given that WES currently remains relatively costly and time‐consuming, and there is inevitably VUS and secondary findings which complicate data interpreting and results report, the RASopathy gene panel testing could be considered as an alternative detection method. Literature showed that, for cases with NT ≥3.5 mm and associated anomalies, the frequency of RASopathies, 7.69%, appears to be higher than in apparently isolated cases, being only 1.44% (Mastromoro et al., ). It was recommended that, after a normal CMA, RASopathy prenatal testing should be offered when any prenatal ultrasound finding suggestive of lymphatic dysplasia (cystic hygroma, increased NT or nuchal fold, hydrops, effusions, other lymphatic anomalies) or suggestive congenital heart disease (like valvular dysplasia and/or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) is found alone or in association, except for isolated increased NT below 6 mm or isolated increased nuchal fold (Scott et al., ). However, since the RASopathy gene panel does not cover all genes associated with increased NT, there is a risk of missed diagnosis. Patients should be completely informed of advantages and limitations of each testing strategy before testing is ordered, and adequate genetic counseling should be provided in clinical practice. WES can significantly improve the yields of diagnostic variants, it also increases the chance of detecting VUS, secondary findings, and incidental findings (Westerfield et al., ). The limitations of fetal phenotyping especially complicate the interpretation of VUS for their pathogenicity in the prenatal setting. It is of great significance to expand the knowledge base on fetal phenotyping–genotyping relationships and establish a public database to document this growing knowledge to assist in accurate data interpretation and genetic counseling in future clinical practice. Secondary findings (SFs) are genetic variants, unrelated to the primary presentation and actively sought in genes that are part of a defined list. The SFs list includes a total of 73 genes on the SF v3.0 version and is updated on an annual basis by the ACMG Secondary Findings Maintenance Working Group (Miller et al., ). Incidental findings are pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants identified in genes unrelated to the test indication that are not part of the ACMG SFs gene list. ACMG has suggested that, in the prenatal setting, laboratories should consider reporting VUS in genes that fit the fetal phenotype, especially in autosomal recessive conditions if the VUS is found in trans with a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant; if the patient consents to SFs analysis, variants identified in the ACMG SFs genes should be reported; highly penetrant incidental findings, but known to cause moderate to severe childhood‐onset disorders, are recommended to be reported; SFs and incidental findings should be discussed with the patient as part of the pre‐test counseling and informed consent process with an opt‐out option of the reporting of these variants (Monaghan et al., ). The development of next‐generation sequencing technology expands the content of sequencing tests, including multigene panels, exome sequencing, and genome sequencing, leading to ever larger amounts of variants to be identified on patient samples. As evidence on variants evolves, previous classifications may later require modification. For example, the discovery of new relationships between diseases and genetic variants may make the reinterpretation of variants to be necessary, the availability of variant frequency data among large populations has led many uncertain significance variants to be reclassified as benign, and testing additional family members may result in the reclassification of variants. Interpretation of prenatal WES results is especially complicated as the characteristic phenotypes of many disorders may not be present at this stage, which highlights the importance of periodical reanalysis of sequencing data based on phenotypic changes, as well as the changes of variant knowledge. It is recommended that laboratories suggest periodic inquiry by health care providers to determine whether knowledge of any variants of uncertain significance, including variants reported as likely pathogenic, has changed (Richards et al., ). The health care provider, clinical laboratory, patient, and family may share the responsibility of re‐contact. These expectations should be explicitly delineated as part of the informed consent process before the sample is obtained. Regarding the responsibility of re‐contact and the informed consent process, see the ACMG policy statement on patient re‐contact after revision of genomic test results (David et al., ). WES can greatly increase the diagnostic yield in fetuses with structural abnormalities and those initially presenting with non‐isolated increased NT (Chen et al., ; Drury et al., ; Emms et al., ; Lord et al., ; Petrovski et al., ; Sparks et al., ; Yang et al., ). Thus, in this study, we excluded initially non‐isolated cases, and only focused on those initially isolated, which could greatly reduce the detection rate in this study. One limitation of this study is the limited sample size. Future prospective studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to draw useful conclusions regarding the value of WES in fetuses with isolated increased NT. In conclusion, the present data support the application of WES for increased NT only when additional structural abnormalities are present. Early detailed ultrasound to detect emerging anomalies can help physicians offer prenatal WES to fetuses with a greater likelihood of diagnosis.

title: Pregnancy outcomes and genetic analysis for fetal ventriculomegaly.
label_reason: Fetal ventriculomegaly cohort with karyotype and CNV-seq.
abstract:
Introduction: Fetal ventriculomegaly (VM) is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, partly caused by genetic factor. 
 Methods: To systematically investigate the genetic etiology of fetal VM and related pregnancy outcomes in different subgroups: IVM (isolated VM) and NIVM (non-isolated VM); unilateral and bilateral VM; mild, moderate, and severe VM, a retrospective study including 131 fetuses with VM was carried out from April 2017 to August 2022. 
 Results: 82 cases underwent amniocentesis or cordocentesis, of whom 8 cases (9.8%) were found chromosomal abnormalities by karyotyping. Meanwhile, additional 8 cases (15.7%) with copy number variations (CNVs) were detected by copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq). The detection rate (DR) of chromosomal abnormalities was higher in NIVM, bilateral VM and severe VM groups. And CNVs frequently occurred in NIVM, bilateral VM and moderate VM groups. In the NIVM group, the incidence of chromosomal aberrations and CNVs in multiple system anomalies (19.0%, 35.7%) was higher than that in single system anomalies (10.0%, 21.1%). After dynamic ultrasound follow-up, 124 cases were available in our cohort. 12 cases were further found other structural abnormalities, and lateral ventricular width was found increased in 8 cases and decreased in 15 cases. Meanwhile, 82 cases underwent fetal brain MRI, 10 cases of brain lesions and 11 cases of progression were additionally identified. With the involvement of a multidisciplinary team, 45 cases opted for termination of pregnancy (TOP) and 79 cases were delivered with live births. One infant death and one with developmental retardation were finally found during postnatal follow-ups. 
 Discussion: CNV-seq combined with karyotyping could effectively improve the diagnostic rate in fetuses with VM. Meanwhile, dynamic ultrasound screening and multidisciplinary evaluation are also essential for assessing the possible outcomes of fetuses with VM.

Pregnancy outcomes and genetic analysis for fetal ventriculomegaly

Introduction
Introduction Fetal lateral ventricular width, usually 7.6 ± 0.6 mm from 15 to 40 weeks of gestation, is a routine examination parameter in prenatal ultrasound screening. Fetal ventriculomegaly (VM) is defined as the width of one or both sides of the lateral ventricles ≥10 mm according to ultrasound diagnostic criteria (), with a prevalence of 0.3‰–1.5‰ (). Fetal VM can be classified into different subtypes: mild (10–12 mm), moderate (13–15 mm), severe (>15 mm) VM (); unilateral and bilateral VM; isolated VM (IVM) and non-isolated VM (NIVM) indicating plus other multi-system abnormalities. It has been reported that 7.9% fetuses with mild IVM may have neurodevelopmental retardation, and the prevalence of adverse outcomes may increase to 38%–90% in fetuses with severe IVM or hydrocephalus (; ; ). Therefore, it is pivotal for clinicians to predict the possible prognosis of the affected fetuses. The outcomes of fetal VM can be influenced by a variety of factors such as chromosomal abnormality, viral infection and progression in utero. Hence, it makes prenatal counseling more challenging for clinicians. The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) recommends that clinicians should perform a comprehensive evaluation for fetuses with VM, including detailed fetal structures, invasive prenatal diagnosis for genetic etiology, and a workup for fetal infections (). Compared with traditional karyotyping, copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) based on next-generation sequencing has outstanding advantages of high resolution, high throughput and whole genome coverage. In recent years, it has been widely applied in the field of prenatal diagnosis (). In this study, we focused on analyzing the value of genetic analysis, dynamic ultrasound screening, and multidisciplinary evaluation for the purpose of improving perinatal management in fetuses with different types of VM.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study subjects In this retrospective study, 131 fetuses diagnosed with VM by prenatal ultrasound were enrolled at the prenatal diagnosis center of Xuzhou Central Hospital from April 2017 to August 2022. Patients with underlying diseases or high-risk factors were ruled out, such as hypertension, immune diseases, trauma, twin or multiple pregnancy, etc. All pregnant women received prenatal counseling and provided written informed consents for further examinations. 82 cases underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis for karyotyping, and 51 cases simultaneously underwent CNV-seq (). 124 cases were further evaluated by dynamic ultrasound examination and 82 cases further underwent fetal brain MRI (). Our study has been approved by the ethics committee of Xuzhou Central Hospital (XZXY-LJ-2017- 0626-003). Flow chart of clinical management procedures. Flow chart of imaging diagnosis pathway. Ultrasound examination and MRI Prenatal ultrasound scanning was performed by ultrasound physicians using a 2.5∼5 MHz transabdominal transducer and color doppler ultrasound instrument (GE Voluson E8, American) according to the guidelines of the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) (). Fetal VM was diagnosed as the width of lateral ventricles ≥10 mm at the level of the choroid plexus perpendicular to the ventricular cavity (). Fetal MRI was performed by experienced operators using a 1.5T scanner (Infineon, Philips Medical Systems). The transverse diameter of the trigones of both lateral ventricles was measured and any additional central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities should also be carefully examined (). The results were then compared with ultrasound findings. Karyotyping and CNV-seq 51 amniotic fluid samples and 31 cord blood samples were collected by ultrasound-guided amniocentesis or cordocentesis. These samples were then subjected to the following procedures: in situ cell culture, harvesting, G-banding, and result judgment. All karyotyping reports were interpreted in line with the International System for Human Cytogenetic Nomenclature at the level of 300–400 bands (). Fetal genomic DNA extraction and library construction were conducted following laboratory standard operating procedures. The following massive whole-genome sequencing (0.1x) in parallel was carried out using the NextSeqCN500 platform (Illumina, United States). 50 ng fetal DNA from each prenatal sample was used for CNV-seq. The sequencing data were analyzed by GISTIC 2.0 with reference to the human reference genome sequence version GRCh37/hg19, the standards of the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) (; ), and related databases such as Database of Genomic Variants (DGV). For the cases with abnormal CNVs, parental peripheral blood samples were also suggested to further verify whether it was inherited or de novo. Follow-up of pregnancy outcomes An experienced multidisciplinary team (MDT) from many departments, including ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), prenatal diagnosis and neurology, worked together to assess the possible prognosis of fetuses with VM. Pregnancy outcomes were recorded by postpartum telephone and electronic medical record system. Neonates and infants were followed up from 6 months to 2 years after birth and comprehensively assessed in terms of neurodevelopmental outcomes by experienced pediatricians. Statistical analyses The data were analyzed by SPSS software (version 26.0, IBM, Armonk, NY, United States). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and independent sample t-test was used for comparison between groups. Enumeration data were expressed as frequency, and chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test was used to compare the rates between groups (p < 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant).

Results
Results Basic characteristics of study subjects 131 fetuses with VM were included in our study, including 50 cases with IVM and 81 cases with NIVM. The basic characteristics were listed in . The mean maternal age (MA) was 28.76 ± 4.91 years, 20 (15.3%) were in advanced age (≥35 years old); the mean gestational age (GA) was 26.75 ± 4.31 weeks; nulliparas accounted for 45.0%. Five pregnant women had histories of adverse pregnancy: 2 induced labor due to hydrocephalus, 2 fetal cardiac anomalies, and 1 fetal cervical hygroma. No obvious statistical differences were observed in MA, GA and parity (p > 0.05). The percentages of mild, moderate and severe VM were 74.0%, 19.1% and 6.9%, respectively. There were 58.8% fetuses with unilateral VM and 41.2% with bilateral VM. Except 7 cases (5.3%) lost to follow-up, 79 cases (60.3%) were delivered and 45 cases (34.4%) opted for termination of pregnancy (TOP). Significant differences were found between IVM and NIVM groups in the degree of VM (mild: 88.0% vs. 65.4%; moderate: 10.0% vs. 24.7%; severe: 2.0% vs. 9.9%), lateral of VM (unilateral: 72.0% vs. 50.6%; bilateral: 28.0% vs. 49.4%) and pregnancy outcomes (delivery: 88.0% vs. 43.2%; TOP: 8.0% vs. 50.6%; Lost to follow-up: 4.0% vs. 6.2%) (p < 0.05). Abnormal karyotypes in different subtypes of fetal VM Chromosomal abnormalities were found in 8 cases (9.8%) by karyotyping, including trisomy 21 (n = 3), mos46,XX [43]/46,XY [57], mos47,XXY [21]/46,XY [79], 46,XY,inv (9) (p12q21.1), 46,XX,del (5) (q14), and 46,XX,del (1) (p36) (, ). Although no significant differences were observed in the subtypes (p > 0.05): IVM and NIVM groups (3.2% vs. 13.7%); unilateral and bilateral VM groups (6.0% vs. 15.6%); mild, moderate and severe VM groups (9.2% vs. 9.1% vs. 16.7%), we found that abnormal results mostly occurred in NIVM, bilateral VM and severe VM. CNVs in different subtypes of fetal VM 11 cases (21.6%) with CNVs were detected by CNV-seq in the 51 subjects, including pathogenic CNVs (P) (n = 4; dup (21) (q11.1q22.3), del (5) (q14.3q15) associated with Bosch-Boonstra-Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome (BBSOAS), del (1) (p36.33p36.22) associated with 1p36 microdeletion syndrome, del(X) (p22.13p22.12) associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 2 and retinoschisis 1), likely pathogenic CNVs (LP) (n = 3; del (16) (p11.2) associated with 16p11.2 deletion syndrome (n = 2), dup (11) (q25)), and variants of uncertain significance (VOUS) (n = 4; del (1) (p36.32p36.21), del (16) (p13.11), dup(X) (p22.12), dup (6) (q23.3)) (; ). 3 cases were consistent with karyotyping results, while the remaining 8 (15.7%) were additionally revealed by CNV-seq, indicating that CNV-seq could effectively make up for the deficiency of karyotyping. Furthermore, the DR of CNVs was higher in fetuses with NIVM than those with IVM (27.3% vs 11.1%), bilateral VM than unilateral VM (22.7% vs 20.7%), and moderate VM than mild VM (40.0% vs 18.4%). However, no statistical differences were shown in the above three groups (p > 0.05). Correlation between chromosomal aberrations and indicators for NIVM In the NIVM group, 51 cases underwent the molecular genetic test, including 30 single system anomalies and 21 multiple system anomalies (). Although the DR of both chromosomal abnormalities and CNVs were higher in multi-system anomalies (19.0%, 35.7%) than in single system anomalies (10.0%, 21.1%), no significant differences were observed between the two groups (p > 0.05). It suggested that chromosomal abnormalities are the ones that increase the risk of NIVM. What’s more, cardiovascular system abnormalities were mostly found in multi-system anomalies. 25.0% (3/12) abnormal karyotypes and 25.0% (2/8) CNVs were revealed when combined with cardiovascular abnormalities. Follow-up outcomes After dynamic ultrasound screening, 124 fetuses with VM were available in the cohort (). 12 cases were further found other structural abnormalities, and lateral ventricular width was also found increased in 8 cases and decreased in 15 cases. Meanwhile, 82 cases underwent fetal brain MRI, and 21 were inconsistent with ultrasound findings, including 10 brain lesions with poor prognosis (agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) (n = 8), Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM) (n = 1), cerebral cortical growth retardation (n = 1)) and 11 cases of lateral ventricular width progression. It suggested that fetal brain MRI can improve the diagnosis of additional CNS anomalies and monitor the degree of VM. Finally, 79 (63.7%) cases continued the pregnancy and 45 (36.3%) opted for TOP (), most of whom followed the recommendations of MDT. The latter 45 cases included mild VM (n = 21), moderate VM (n = 15) and severe VM (n = 9). In the mild VM group, 6 cases were terminated due to chromosomal aberrations (Case 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 14); 11 cases complicated with other malformations (ACC (n = 3), DWM (n = 2), cerebral cortical growth retardation (n = 2), holoprosencephaly (HPE) (n = 1), cerebellum dysplasia (n = 1), myelomeningocele (n = 1), bilateral polycystic kidneys and oligohydramnios (n = 1)); 4 cases progressed to severe VM. In the moderate VM group, 4 cases were terminated due to chromosomal aberrations (Case 5, 11, 13, 15); 8 cases complicated with other anomalies (ACC (n = 2), HPE (n = 1), HPE and cleft lip and palate (n = 1), choroid plexus papilloma (n = 1), polyhydramnios and bilateral renal pelvis separation (n = 1), cerebral cortical growth retardation (n = 1), atrial and ventricular septal defect (n = 1)); 3 cases progressed to severe VM. Moreover, 9 cases were terminated in the severe VM group, including chromosomal XX/XY mosaicism (Case 1); isolated severe VM (n = 1); 7 cases complicated with other abnormalities (posterior fossa widened (n = 2), ACC (n = 2), septo-optic dysplasia, HPE and ventricular septal defect (n = 1), spina bifida (n = 1), aqueductal stenosis and encephalomalacia (n = 1)). Flow chart of follow-up outcomes. 79 cases continued the pregnancy, including 5 premature babies and 74 full-term babies (51 boys and 28 girls). 5 cases were found chromosomal aberrations (Case 2, 6, 9, 12, 16). The prognosis of the 5 fetuses was predicted to be relatively good by MDT based on imaging and genetic information. Postnatal follow-ups were performed in 59 subjects from 6 months to 2 years after birth. One infant without genetic test died at 6 months due to progressive VM and ACC. One infant with mild unilateral VM and normal karyotype was found speech and motor retardation at 2 years old. No abnormalities were found in the remaining 57 children.

Discussion
Discussion Fetal VM may increase the risk of neurodevelopmental abnormalities after birth, such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy (; ; ). Our study highlighted the importance of genetic etiology in fetal VM, and indicated that karyotyping together with CNV-seq can effectively improve the detection rate of fetuses with VM. Previous studies have shown that chromosomal abnormalities occurred in 5%–20% of fetuses with IVM, and pathogenic CNVs are also common causes accounting for about 4.20% (; ; ). In our study, 9.8% cases with VM were found chromosomal abnormalities by karyotyping, meanwhile, additional 15.7% CNVs were detected by CNV-seq (; ). Some are recognized as microdeletion or microduplication syndromes, including BBSOAS, 1p36 microdeletion syndrome, and 16p11.2 deletion syndrome. The DR of chromosomal aberrations in fetuses with VM was higher by CNV-seq than by traditional karyotyping, regardless of single or multi-system anomalies. It suggested that CNV-seq can effectively improve the DR of fetuses with VM over karyotyping (). It is not hard to see that fetuses with NIVM, bilateral VM or moderate-to-severe VM have a higher risk of chromosomal abnormalities or CNVs. Therefore, more attention should be paid to the above fetuses, to effectively avoid birth defects with genetic factors. In fetuses with NIVM, the DR of chromosomal aberrations in multi-system anomalies was higher than that in single system anomalies (), which is consistent with the findings of Chang (). It suggested that chromosomal abnormalities are the ones that increase the risk of NIVM. Thus, when fetal VM combined with multiple malformations, especially cardiovascular system, we should be more aware of the possibility of chromosomal aberrations. From our point of view, karyotyping combined with CNV-seq should be recommended to rule out genetic abnormalities, especially for fetuses with NIVM, bilateral VM or moderate-to-severe VM. It is often difficult to reveal fetal phenotypes at a certain point in time by prenatal ultrasound due to the limitations of the fetal position, gestational age, and amniotic fluid volume. In our study, during dynamic ultrasound screening, additional structural abnormalities in 12 patients and an increase or regression of lateral ventricular width in 23 patients were revealed. Therefore, dynamic ultrasound follow-up is of great significance to avoid under/overdiagnosis and assess the possible prognosis to facilitate better management for the affected fetuses. In addition, 10 cases of fetal brain lesions with poor prognosis were detected by MRI but missed by ultrasound, and 11 cases with lateral ventricular width progression were also detected. Therefore, fetal brain MRI can act as an effective complementary tool to confirm the diagnosis and reveal additional CNS anomalies. Based on the above strategies, multidisciplinary consultation should be recommended for couples on whether to continue or terminate the pregnancy, especially in the late second or third trimesters, which might comprehensively provide better perinatal management for fetuses with VM. Regarding pregnancy outcomes, 79 cases continued the pregnancy with live births including 5 cases diagnosed with genetic etiology (a low proportion of sex chromosomes mosaicism (20% 47, XXY and 80% 46,XY), inversion of chromosome 9, microdeletion in 1p36.33p36.22 inherited from the mother, microduplications in Xp22.11 and 11q25). From our experience, the involvement of MDT, as well as parental persistence, contributed to the continuation of pregnancy. Postnatal follow-ups from 6 months to 2 years showed 1 neonatal death at 6 months, and 1 speech and motor retardation at 2 years old. A large population-based study explained that even in apparent IVM, there was a significant risk of postnatal additional structural anomalies and neonatal death (). Hence, even for mild, isolated VM, we cannot leave out the possibility of poor results. It is pivotal for MDT to carefully evaluate fetuses with different types of VM both prenatally and postpartum. In our data, TOP was chosen in all cases with severe VM. When VM is the only abnormal finding, the parents make decisions mostly based on the severity of VM, as the poor outcomes increase with the degree of VM aggravated. Whether the degree of VM can act as an independent risk factor to judge fetal prognosis needs to be further explored through larger sample sizes. It is also the responsibility of MDT to carefully make a recommendation for TOP after comprehensive consideration. There are still some limitations in our study that need to be improved. First, fetal brain MRI has been proven as a useful tool to identify additional CNS anomalies, such as ACC associated with poor outcomes (), but not all cases in our study received the examination. Secondly, tests for pathogenic microorganisms such as cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis should be performed to rule out infectious factors (). Last but not least, the follow-up time and sample size were not sufficient to find neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the children. Longer follow-ups and more cases will be enrolled in the future to explore the outcomes of fetal VM. In short, CNV-seq could effectively improve the diagnostic rate of fetal VM, over karyotyping. Meanwhile, dynamic ultrasound screening and multidisciplinary evaluation are also essential for better management of fetuses with VM.

title: The challenges in the interpretation of genetic variants detected by genomics techniques in patients with congenital anomalies.

abstract: Despite the efforts that have been made to standardize the interpretation of variants, in some cases, their pathogenicity remains vague and confusing, and sometimes their interpretation does not help clinicians to establish clinical correlation using genetic test results. This study aims to shed more lights on these challenging variants. In a clinical setting, the variants found from 81 array CGH and 79 whole exome sequencing (WES) in patients with congenital anomalies were interpreted based on American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines. In this study, the interpretation of the disease‐causing variants and the variants with uncertain clinical significance detected by WES was far more challenging than the variants detected by array CGH. The presence of unreported clinical symptoms, incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, parents' reluctance to analyze segregation in the family, and the limitations of prenatal tests, were among the challenging factors in the interpretation of variants in this study. A careful study of the pedigree and disease mode of inheritance, as well as a careful clinical examination of the carrier parents in diseases with autosomal dominant inheritance, are among the primary strategies for determining the clinical significance of the variants. Continued efforts to mitigate these challenges are needed to improve the interpretation of variants. Keywords: array CGH, challenges, congenital anomaly, variants interpretation, whole exome sequencing

The challenges in the interpretation of genetic variants detected by genomics techniques in patients with congenital anomalies

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Congenital anomalies (CA) are among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in 2%–4% of live births, 20% of infantile death, and 21% of prenatal deaths., Therefore, genetic investigations are very important to diagnose the cause of these anomalies. In 2011, the International Standard Consortium for Cytogenomic Array (ISCA) reported a consensus statement on the use of chromosomal microarray as a first‐line diagnostic test in the evaluation of individuals with developmental delay and/or congenital anomalies. While in recent years whole exome sequencing (WES) has shown a higher diagnostic rate than array CGH in these patients., , Recently, the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) recommended whole exome sequencing/Whole Genome sequencing as the first‐tier or second‐tier diagnostic tests (e.g., after array CGH or targeted gene testing) for patients with congenital anomalies and intellectual disability/developmental delay. However, interpretation of some variants resulting from these tests are challenging and vague. In this article, we tried to describe the challenges we have encountered in the interpretation of the variants found in patients with congenital anomalies.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
MATERIALS AND METHODS The current study is part of a congenital anomaly's cohort approached between April 2019 and February 2022 as illustrated in Figure , a stepwise approach was implemented to ensure that individuals suspected to have genetic CA were included in the study. Stepwise illustration of study design. Selection of patients with major congenital anomaly(ies); elimination of patients with exclusion criteria; WES, array CGH or both testing in patients; result; diagnosis and interpretation challenges; number of family and variants with challenging interpretation. The number of tests and their resulting variants are written in parentheses. CNV, copy number variation; LP, likely pathogenic; P, pathogenic; VUS, variant of uncertain significance; WES, whole exome sequencing. Initially, patients with at least one major anomaly that was determined based on the criteria provided by the National Birth Defects Prevention Network (NBDPN) using the 2017 update were selected. Next, patients proved to be caused by non‐genetic factors such as infections during pregnancy (TORCH), amniotic bands, and teratogenic exposure during pregnancy, were excluded. In total, 136 affected cases (54 aborted fetuses and 82 dead or alive patients) were selected for further analysis by WES or array CGH, or both. This study was approved by the ethics committee at Tehran University of Medical Sciences (Ethics code: IR.TUMS.MEDICINE.REC.1399.1278). DNA extraction Chromosome microarray analysis and whole exome sequencing were performed on the genomic DNA extracted from peripheral blood or tissue using E.Z.N.A. DNA Blood and Tissue kit (Omega Bio‐Tek) following the manufacturer's protocol. Chromosome microarray analysis Patient and control DNA samples were cut into fragments and then labeled with cyanine 3 or cyanine 5 dyes using Agilent's sure tag DNA Labeling Kit (Agilent Technologies). The labeled samples were mixed in equal proportions and hybridized using a SurePrint G3 ISCA v2 8X60K array (Agilent Technologies, Inc) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Microarrays were scanned using a dual‐laser scanner (INNOPSYS ‐ InnoScan Microarray Scanners‐InnoScan 900). The fluorescence intensity of each probe and the aberration patterns of the CGH microarray profiles with respect to the human reference genome (GRCh37/hg19 collection) were performed in the extracted images using Agilent Cytogenomic software (v4). The detected copy number variations (CNV) were interpreted according to the published guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG). Whole exome sequencing Extracted DNAs after targeted enrichment using Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon V7 (Agilent Technologies, Inc.), were sequenced by IlluminaNovaSeq 6000 (Illumine Inc.). Evaluation and analysis of raw data generated using the GenAP Genome Analysis Platform (Cimorgh Medical IT solutions Inc.)., For maximum sensitivity and reducing the number of variants that require labor‐intensive specialized investigation, genotype‐driven and phenotype‐driven analyses were used in filtering. With the genotype‐driven analysis strategy, almost all variants that may have sufficient evidence to be classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, including quality control (QBase <20), candidate gene identification, previously reported pathogenic variants, and Loss of function variants, were captured. Then, a comprehensive investigation of potential variants associated with the anomaly(ies) observed in the patient was done with the strategy of phenotype‐driven analyses. Also, in the investigation of candidate variants, if even a part of the symptoms matched the disease reported in the OMIM database or literature review, the variant was considered for further investigation. On the contrary, the possibility of phenotypic expansion, variable expressivity, incomplete penetrance, or the possibility that additional syndromic features of the disease were not identified clinically were considered. Finally, bioinformatics tools, including SIFT, Polyphen‐2, and MutationTaster were performed to evaluate the pathogenicity of the variants. Finally, the interpretation of variants was managed according to the ACMG guideline for the interpretation of sequence variants. All candidate variants were checked in Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) as in silico confirmation. Confirmation of candidate variants Confirmation of candidate variants and segregation studied were done when indicated by Sanger sequencing for variants detected by WES and qRT‐PCR for CNVs detected by array CGH.

RESULTS
RESULTS In this study, detection rate of CMA and WES tests were estimated for pathogenic/likely pathogenic and variant of uncertain significance (VUS) variants in prenatal and postnatal case are listed in Table . CNVs from array CGH analysis were found in 14 families that could be considered causative, and of these, we faced challenges in interpreting 1 pathogenic CNV and 8 CNVs of uncertain clinical significance. Also, in this study pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and VUS variants, were identified in 71 families by WES. We faced challenges in the interpretation of VUS variants in 17 families and also pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants in 13 families, which are shown in Figure . These challenges included reluctance to perform segregation studies، mutations in genes with incomplete penetrance or variable expression, patients with more than one disease‐causing mutation, novel symptoms associated with certain potential disease‐causing variants and interpretations that differ from the current ACMG consensus criteria.

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION Array CGH and WES have revolutionized clinical genetics practice and many previously unexplained patients have gotten to a diagnosis. However, there are challenges in interpretation of pathogenicity of many rare variants. Here, we discuss some of the challenges we faced with variant interpretation in few families with congenital anomaly(ies). Reluctance to perform segregation studies, especially in the VUS variants A major challenge in applying WES and array CGH is the interpretation of VUS variants. Although segregation study is a crucial step to overcome this challenge, it was refused by some families due to financial costs, which created uncertainty in the variant's interpretation. In this study, only one out of nine CNVs with uncertain clinical significance detected by array CGH (Table ) in seven cases was investigated in the parents. The results showed that the asymptomatic mother carries the same CNV. As a result, the classification of CNV in patient MCA‐13 is changed from VUS to likely benign. Unfortunately, the remaining eight CNVs in six cases has remained unsolved. This challenge was more prominent in WES test results where 45 VUS variants were identified in 32 families, but the segregation study was performed in 24 families only (Table ). Since all WES tests were performed solo in the proband only, due to the high cost, family segregation had to be performed to determine the inheritance status and pathogenicity of variants. For example, segregating VUS variants in genes with autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance in the patients ICA‐31 and ICA‐32 could help with a definitive diagnosis, but the families were reluctant to do so. As another example, the unwillingness of the F‐MCA‐27 patient's family to perform segregation analysis for the LP and VUS variants found in the DONSON gene caused the pathogenicity of these variants to remain unknown. Meanwhile, in a study by Reynolds et al., it was shown that these variants in cis with other pathogenic variants of the DONSON gene cause disease with somehow similar symptoms. Mutations in genes with incomplete penetrance or variable expression Another challenge was the interpretation of variants in genes with autosomal dominant inheritance when inherited from asymptomatic parents, which can be due to incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, or mild clinical manifestations. Precise clinical examinations and investigations of carrier parents might be helpful in such circumstances. For example, Noonan syndrome is associated with variable expressivity, and its manifestations are often delicate and in fact, many affected adults remain undiagnosed until their affected infants are born., In this study, two pathogenic variants in the SOS1 and RIT1 genes, both causing Noonan syndrome, were detected in a 7‐day‐old baby with multiple anomalies (Web naked, UDT, Macrosomia, hyperpigmentation, hydrocephaly, ASD‐2, PDA, low set ear) (ref art). The first variant was Glu433Lys in the SOS1 gene, inherited from the healthy mother (with short stature), and the second was Ser217* in RIT1, inherited from the father with slurred speech and a history of developmental delay. Interestingly, the symptoms observed in this patient were a combination of symptoms reported from both genes. To the best of our knowledge, there are no reports of hydrocephalus associated with the SOS1 gene, but one study has reported an association of hydrocephalus‐induced macrocephaly with the RIT1 gene. Additional challenges arise when VUS variants in genes with incomplete penetrance are inherited from asymptomatic parents. We also experienced this situation with variants in the CUX2 and CIC genes with the patient ICA‐10, FOXP1, and RERE genes in patient ICA‐27, GRIN2A gene in patient ICA‐29, RERE gene in patient MCA‐12, ZMIZ1 gene in patient ICA‐56 and EFTUD2 gene, in patient ICA‐72 (Table ). Considering the 50% probability of transmitting these variants to the children in subsequent pregnancies, genetic counseling for these families can be challenging and it might be difficult to decide on prenatal diagnosis (PND), preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD), or other fertility options. Importance of precise clinical investigations of patients and their family members The importance of precise clinical evaluation of patients and their family members following genetic investigation was acknowledged in previous studies. Here in patient MCA‐11, the variant c.546G>C (VUS) in the FLNA gene inherited from an asymptomatic mother was detected. Mutations in the FLNA gene result in periventricular heterotopia. Investigations showed that due to unclear penetrance of the FLNA gene, transmissive parents of non‐LOF variants might have nodules detectable by brain imaging in neurologically asymptomatic individuals. Fortunately, the mother's brain MRI did not indicate any evidence of nodules, and her periventricular heterotopia was ruled out. Therefore, it seems unlikely that the mentioned variant is the cause of the disease, and this variant was considered likely benign in the present study. Patient with more than one disease‐causing mutation In some patients, more than one pathogenic variant was diagnosed, of which only one might be the cause of the observed phenotype. For example, two pathogenic variants (NM_005210:c.72del in the CRYGB gene and NM_001244008:c.821C>T in the KIF1A gene) were detected in the same patient, which respectively, explain unilateral congenital cataract and primary ataxia in this patient. The patient's father also presented with a history of cataracts, ataxia, cerebellar atrophy, and walking difficulty and a variant in the CRYGB was inherited from the father. Novel symptoms associated with certain potential disease‐causing genes We identified several genetic variations that are associated with certain phenotypes but are not reported in the OMIM database and the existing literatures. For example, myelomeningocele that we observed in fetus with multiple anomalies (Spina bifida, Clubfoot, skull deformity, Hydrocephaly, compressed cerebellum, and myelomeningocele) has been reported in patients with a mutation in the BBS9 gene. In this fetus, a homozygous pathogenic variant (deletion of exons 11–20) in the BBS9 gene was detected. In accordance with this finding, Shobi Velley et al. have shown that the complete failure of neural tube closure and hydrocephalus occur as the consequence of bbs9 gene deletion in the zebrafish. Similarly, we reporting for the first time microcephaly, club foot, and cleft palate in patients harboring pathogenic variants in the ST3GAL3 gene (NM_174964.4:c.846del), the JUP gene (NM_002230.4:c.201dup), and the ENTPD1 gene (NM_001164178.1:c.822_823del), respectively. Moreover, several genetic mutations have been found to be associated with phenotypes in a few case studies that are not reported in the OMIM database. For instance, microcephaly has not been reported in the OMIM database in patients with Branched‐chain keto acid dehydrogenase kinase deficiency (MIM # 614923). However, it has been reported in patients with BCKDK deficiency,, and we have also observed it in patient with Microcephaly, abnormal brain MRI, DD, who has a likely pathogenic homozygous variant in BCKDK gene (NM_005881.4:c.1128C>A). Accordingly, increased NT, club foot, VSD, microcephaly, renal agenesis, and hypospadias were observed in patients with the causative variants in genes TRIP11 (NM_004239.4:c.4432_4433del),, SCN4A (NM_000334.4:c.1107C>A),, ANKS6 (NM_173551.5:c.907+2T>A), GALC (NM_000153.4:c.658C>T),, CHD7 (NM_017780.4:c.6217C>T),, and GJA1 (NM_000165.5:c.561C>A), respectively. We believe that it worth to note these findings because it could help to identify them as disease‐causing genes/variants by OMIM if observed by others, too. All the symptoms observed in patients with pathogenic findings in array CGH were consistent with known syndromes except one patient. In this patient who has a 46,XX karyotype, array CGH revealed the presence of p11.32p11.2 region of Y chromosome (arr[GRCh37], Yp11.32p11.2 (1354749_3356137)x1, containing the SRY gene). The thing is that this finding can only explain the patient's ambiguous genitalia but not her syndactyly. Although there are few reports of skeletal anomalies in patients with 46XX DSD (Disorders of Sex Development), syndactyly has not reported to be associated with gain of Yp11.32p11.2. Interpretations that differ from the current criteria Despite guidelines published for the interpretation of sequence variants by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), the degree of subjectivity and uncertainty allowed by the guidelines can lead to inconsistent variable classification in clinical laboratories and evaluation. In the present study, the interpretation of the three variants was challenging. The first was a novel heterozygous variant (frame‐shift insertion) in the MSL3 gene (c.299dupA) in a 1‐year‐old girl (ICA‐41) with hydrocephalus and brain atrophy. According to the ACMG criteria, the variant should have been classified as likely pathogenic. However, considering the X‐linked dominant inheritance nature of this gene and the presence of an asymptomatic hemizygous father, this variant may not be the cause of the disease or may be influenced by yet‐to‐be‐identified modifier genes. So this variant was reported as VUS in this study. Further studies are required to verify this finding. The second case was related to an affected fetus (F‐MCA‐16), where the homozygous variant c.829G>T in the MYOD1 gene was diagnosed. According to the ACMG criteria (null variant and no report of this variant in population databases), this should have been classified as likely pathogenic, while the variant was identified as homozygous in the asymptomatic father. Therefore, this variant probably cannot be the cause of observed anomalies in this patient and was considered VUS in the current study. As earlier described, a homozygous pathogenic variant (loss of exons 11–20) was identified in the BBS9 gene, which could explain the symptoms observed in this patient. The third variant was diagnosed in a family with a history of miscarriage and infant death with skeletal anomalies and short rib dysplasia (F‐ICA‐45). Since the sample of the first aborted fetus was unavailable, ES analysis was performed in the mother and the heterozygous variant c.9749A>G in the DYNC2H1 gene was identified. As this variant is more frequent than expected (0.00286) in population databases and 11 homozygous individuals have been observed in populations (gnomAD), it should be classified as a benign variant according to the ACMG criteria. However, this variant has been reported in the ClinVar database as a variant of uncertain clinical significance in short rib polydactyly syndrome. According to data in her pedigree, her sister had a history of two miscarriages and two infants deceased with clinical suspicion of short rib dysplasia too, of which no sample was available. Both sisters had consanguineous marriages and their husbands were far related. This variant was found in a heterozygous state in couples and their unaffected child. This variant was used for prenatal diagnosis of this couple's future pregnancies. In the first pregnancy afterward, the fetus carries this variation in a homozygous state. The short rib phenotype was confirmed by ultrasound in the fetus, and the termination of pregnancy was decided by the parents. This mother again became pregnant and her fetus was heterozygous; fortunately, a healthy baby was born. Collectively, this variant may be causative according to the above‐mentioned evidence. However, it may be affected by modifier genes that have not been identified so far. Limitations with prenatal testing In addition to the widespread utilization of WES and array CGH analysis in postnatal cases, there is increasing evidence of the use of WES for fetuses with possible genetic disorders in the clinical setting. However, there are at least three major concerns regarding the application of WES and array CGH in the prenatal period in Iran. First, the legal time for pregnancy termination in Iran is prior to the 4th month of gestation (before 19 weeks)., , Second is the turnaround time (TAT) required to issue the reports in Iran is 6–8 weeks for WES and 1–2 weeks for array CGH. Third, the presence of incidental findings and the challenging interpretation of VUS variants can create confusions and anxiety for both healthcare providers and the families. Due to these concerns, array CGH is offered in the first and second trimesters when congenital anomaly or increased nuchal translucency is detected in the fetuses. Therefore, it is presently unlikely for ES to become a 1st and 2nd‐trimester clinical test and it might take some time and rationale to achieve this.

CONCLUSION
CONCLUSION Although the ACMG guidelines have been developed to allow consistent and reliable interpretation of variants, classification discrepancies and potential inaccuracies exist across clinical laboratories. However, a careful study of pedigree and type of disease inheritance, as well as a detailed clinical examination of carrier parents in diseases with autosomal dominant inheritance, are among the strategies to determine the accurate classification of variants. In conclusion, despite the numerous challenges in the interpretation of variants in genomic tests, this field continues to progress, and these challenges, in addition to the above, are overcome through collaboration, updating and integrate data, and the use of advanced technologies.
