Application of Whole‐Exome Sequencing in the Prenatal Diagnosis of Foetuses With Central Nervous System Abnormalities

Introduction
Introduction The prevalence of central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities is 0.14%–0.16% among live births and is as high as 3%–6% among stillbirths (Onkar, Onkar, and Mitra ; Sun et al. ; Huang et al. ). Causes of foetal CNS abnormalities vary. In addition to environmental factors, CNS abnormalities in foetuses are frequently associated with chromosomal aneuploidy, copy number variants (CNVs) and pathogenic sequence variants in developmental genes. CNS abnormalities can be manifested by a series of neurologic and neurodevelopmental variations, such as intellectual disability and epilepsy (Griffiths et al. ). With the development of prenatal ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), an increasing number of CNS abnormalities have been found in utero, and the diagnostic sensitivity of prenatal US for CNS abnormalities has increased to approximately 90% (Paladini et al. ). However, the situation that CNS abnormalities are detected by prenatal US performed when the affected structure of the foetus has not yet fully developed can pose a clinical dilemma, hence the necessity of search for more convenient means of diagnosis. Current practice guidelines recommend karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) as first‐tier test when a foetal abnormality has been detected by US or other foetal imaging (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists'Committee on Practice Bulletins‐Obstetrics et al. ; Committee on Genetics and the Society for Maternal‐Fetal Medicine ). These tests are able to detect aneuploidy, chromosomal rearrangements, or CNVs in a total of 30%–40% of pregnancies studied (Wapner et al. ; Breman et al. ; Shaffer et al. ; Hillman et al. ). Using CMA, pathogenic CNVs can be detected in 10.9% of foetuses that are diagnosed with CNS abnormalities with or without other associated abnormalities (Sun et al. ). However, while the karyotype and CMA results are negative, the truth the cause underlying most CNS abnormalities is due to the fact that many of these abnormalities are monogenic, caused by numerous variants in a multitude of different genes. The growing incorporation of next‐generation sequencing (NGS) techniques into widespread clinical use is revolutionising the diagnostic path for many families with monogenic disorders (Yang et al. ; Stranneheim and Wedell ). WGS involves evaluating both coding and noncoding regions of the genome, Exome sequencing (ES) examines the 1%–2% of the genome that encodes proteins and harbours around 85% of known disease‐causing genetic variants, and can be applied in practice as a whole ES (sequencing or analysing all exons), medical/clinical ES (sequencing or analysing only the exons of known Mendelian disease genes), or targeted ES (applying ‘virtual’ gene panels to ES data to limit analysis to genes of interest for a specific phenotype) (Mellis et al. ). A prospective study, systematic review and meta‐analysis of monogenic conditions and central nervous system anomalies have analysed 30 studies (N = 1264 cases). The incremental yield with prenatal exome sequencing (pES) (included whole, clinical, targeted ES or whole‐genome sequencing (WGS)) for any CNS anomaly was 32% (Blayney et al. ) A study of 28 cases of CNS abnormalities tested by WGS, primary genetic diagnosis was achieved in 16 cases, including three cases of chromosomal abnormality, one case of microdeletion and 12 cases of single‐nucleotide variants (SNVs) (Liao et al. ). Another study of CNS abnormalities tested by WGS, 162 foetuses with 11 common CNS anomalies were enrolled. Primary diagnosis was achieved in 62 cases, with an overall diagnostic rate of 38.3%. Causative variants included 18 aneuploids, 17 Copy number variations (CNVs), three small CNVs and 24 SNVs (14.8%) (Yang et al. ). All 105 foetuses with structural anomalies were categorised into 12 phenotypic groups tested by CES/MES. A definitive diagnosis was achieved in 19% (20/105) of the cases, with the diagnostic yield in the brain structural abnormalities (25%) (Chen et al. ). The other MES study was conducted by Hu Tan et al. who identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in five of 11 cases of CNS abnormalities (Tan et al. ) detected prenatally. There were three studies of WES for foetuses with CNS abnormalities. One was conducted by Rechs et al. who identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in five out of seven cases of CNS abnormalities (Reches et al. ). The detection rate in the study was 71.4%. In an expanded review of two previously published prospective cohort studies, the foetuses with CNS abnormalities diagnosed by US were recruited to be subjected to the UK PAGE10 and US CUIMC11 for foetal exome sequencing studies. Among 268 foetuses with CNS abnormalities that underwent sequencing, a total of 37 (13.8%) were found to have pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants that were considered causative of the foetal phenotype (Baptiste et al. ). In another study, 86 CMA‐negative cases were analysed using WES, which detected P/LP sequence variants in 38/86 (44%) (Yaron et al. ). In all of the studies, NGS improved the detection rate to varying degrees. WES and WGS in particular are often used as the tools for diagnosis of structurally abnormal foetuses in the United States. The targeted ES is rarely used for prenatal diagnosis because the phenotype of foetal remains unclear. Medical/clinical ES that involves sequencing or analysing only the exons of known Mendelian disease genes, and not including genes of unknown clinical significance, has been used less recently. While WGS may provide more information due to its scope, it requires more data analysis and is not routinely used in clinical testing. In contrast, WES not only analyses the coding sequences of known disease‐causing genes (clinical exons) but also includes genes of unknown clinical significance. It is generally less costly and easier to interpret than WGS, making it the current choice for the evaluation of foetuses with structural abnormalities. In this paper, we describe our experience in using WES to diagnose CNS abnormalities detected by prenatal US of foetuses from both termination of pregnancy (TOP) and ongoing pregnancy from 149 families. We aim to evaluate the proportion of foetuses with CNS abnormalities that had identifiable variants in genes associated with developmental disorders detected by WES. The study represents a real‐world setting in the genetic counselling service, where a mixture of various indications of WES were encountered. WES was performed for clinical purposes and paid for by families.

Materials and Methods
Materials and Methods In this study, all the samples were from the cases who were treated at the Prenatal Diagnosis Center of Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital from December 2016 through October 2022. They were all Han nationality, nonconsanguineous couples and received genetic counselling and detailed clinical evaluation at the above‐mentioned centre. All foetuses were ultrasonically evaluated by dedicated neurosonographic examinations, performed by a senior experienced sonographer. These US examinations were standardised, including biometry of the foetal head, measurement of the posterior horn of the lateral cerebral ventricles, visualisation of the cavum septum pellucidum and measurement of the transverse cerebellar diameter. All foetuses were assessed for cortical development by an experienced brain sonographer. All foetuses that were found to be with CNS abnormalities by prenatal US examination, such as ventriculomegaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and microcephaly, with or without other abnormal US findings, were enrolled from TOP and ongoing pregnancies. Due to the multifactorial inheritance pattern of nonsyndromic neural tube defects and the contribution of environmental factors, cases with isolated open neural tube defects were excluded (ACOG Committee on Practice Bulletins‐Obstetrics ). Where there was a discrepancy between the MRI and US findings, the MRI findings were used for classification. To evaluate the effect of the type of foetal CNS abnormalities detected by US on WES referral and diagnostic yield, we classified the foetuses into three phenotypic groups (Table ). Single and isolated CNS abnormality (e.g., isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum). Multiple CNS abnormalities (e.g., Agenesis of the corpus callosum along with cerebellar vermis dysplasia). CNS abnormalities along with other organ system abnormalities (e.g., ventriculomegaly along with skeletal deformities). For single and isolated CNS abnormality, the solitary choroid plexus cyst (CPCs) was excluded. When isolated CPCs were found, counselling confirmed that the prognosis was favourable (DiPietro et al. ). We defined a head circumference more than −3 SD and less than or equal to ≤−2 SD as small head circumference, and a head circumference smaller than the mean by three standard deviations as foetal microcephaly (Gelber, Grünebaum, and Chervenak ; Chervenak, Jeanty, and Cantraine ). This is because a head circumference of −2 SD is associated with 10% incidence of intellectual disability, whereas a head circumference of −3 SD is associated with a 50% incidence of severe intellectual disability (Mighell, Johnstone, and Levene ). Ventriculomegaly was classified based on the lateral ventricular diameter as mild (10–15 mm) or severe (hydrocephalus) (> 15 mm) (Scelsa et al. ). The mild ventriculomegaly is not typically considered a CNS structural anomalies and is often classified as a soft marker for aneuploidies. However, the rate of molecular diagnoses with CMA has already been demonstrated to be higher than other soft markers and is indeed comparable to that of a structural anomaly (Mastromoro et al. ), so the mild ventriculomegaly is classified as CNS structural anomalies in our study. Cases with multiple CNS abnormalities were then reviewed by a paediatric neurologist to ensure that our categorisation was accurate. For example, a foetus with microcephaly and delayed sulcal appearance initially categorised as having multiple CNS abnormalities was re‐categorised as having isolated and single microcephaly since the delayed sulcal appearance was a feature of microcephaly. Similarly, mild ventriculomegaly and agenesis of the corpus callosum were also re‐categorised as an isolated and single finding. However, since the agenesis of the corpus callosum and abnormal cerebral sulcation were two independent phenotypes, a foetus with them was categorised as having multiple CNS abnormalities. Markers of aneuploidy (echogenic intracardiac foci, etc.) were not regarded as extra‐CNS abnormalities. However, oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios, foetal growth restriction (FGR) was considered as extra‐CNS abnormalities, so was a nuchal translucency more than or equal to 3.0 mm. Further US reports and clinical information of all foetuses in late pregnancy were reviewed; nonetheless, the initial findings were used to categorise cases. All the foetuses underwent karyotype and chromosomal microarray (CMA) and their results were normal or noncausative. Foetal DNA was extracted from amniotic fluid, umbilical cord blood, villi or foetal material taken during the termination of pregnancy (TOP) procedure and was stored for genetic testing. All TOPs were approved by the institutional committee. Parental DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples. WES was performed as a clinical service which was paid for directly by the families, and the final WES report was issued by the performing lab. Both parents provided written informed consent for the clinical WES after they had received an explanation regarding the benefits and limitations of the test. All WES tests were performed in the Medical Genetics Center Laboratory of Shenzhen Maternal and Child Health Hospital, and data were analysed by two experienced data analysts. Whole‐Exome Sequencing The WES testing and interpretation were performed at the medical genetics centre laboratory of SHEN ZHEN Maternal and Child Healthcare Hospital. The genomic DNA from blood, amniotic fluid, umbilical cord blood or other tissue sources were extracted by QIAGEN blood mini kit. The Berry nano‐WES chip was used to capture and enrich the DNA sequence in exons and flanking intron sequence of ~20,000 genes. The illumina novaseq platform was used for sequencing. Sequencing data were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh37/hg19. Bioinformatics analysis was performed by using Seqmax software. Disease‐causing variants were searched by using pipeline created by our laboratory. Variant classification was performed according to ACMG guidelines (Richards et al. ). The P and LP variants which can explain the foetal phenotypes were reported. The VUS variants were discussed by a multidisciplinary team to decide whether to report or not. All pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants detected by WES were validated by Sanger sequencing. For statistical analysis, we used Pearson chi‐square or Fisher's exact test (two‐sided), as appropriate. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results In this study, WES was performed on 149 foetuses with CNS abnormalities detected by US and their mothers and fathers (Trio‐WES). In addition to US, out of the 149 families, foetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was carried out for 80 families. The average age of the mothers of the foetuses was 30.4 years old (these mothers' ages ranged between 20 and 41 years old). These pregnant women were at an average gestational age of 25+6 weeks (their gestational ages ranging between 12 weeks and 37 weeks) at the time of undergoing WES. WES was performed on 24 foetuses (16.1%) from TOP and 125 foetuses from ongoing pregnancy (83.9%). Sixty‐nine cases were classified as having single and isolated CNS abnormality, 49 as having multiple CNS abnormalities and 31 as having CNS abnormalities along with other organ system abnormalities. Overall, Of the 149 fetuses tested, 43 were found to possess pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants that met the criteria for molecular diagnosis, yielding a diagnostic rate of 28.9%. Among these, 29 exhibited autosomal dominant inheritance, one was attributed to paternal inheritance, two to maternal inheritance, and the rest were due to de novo mutations. Additionally, among the 43 diagnosed monogenic disorders, nine cases exhibited autosomal recessive inheritance, and eight resulted from inheritance by both parents. Notably, one particular case of autosomal recessive inheritance was found to have two variations: one was a de novo mutation, while the other was inherited from the mother (Table ). Sixty‐nine foetuses had single and isolated CNS abnormalities, including mild ventriculomegaly, abnormal cerebral sulcation and microcephaly (Table ). Causative pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in 12 (17.4%). The most common isolated finding was isolated mild ventriculomegaly which was found in 17 foetuses, of which three (17.4%) were found by WES to have pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. WES had the highest detection rate in isolated hydrocephalus (lateral ventricle width more than or equal to 1.5 cm); three out of seven foetuses (42.9%) with such abnormality were found by WES to be with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (L1CAM, CCDC88C and PTCH1). The PTCH1 gene variation was inherited from the foetus' father who was diagnosed with basal cell nevus syndrome, and had no symptoms of hydrocephalus but had surgery for a mandibular cyst 10 years ago. Besides, three out of eight (37.5%) of the foetuses had isolated microcephaly. The ASPM gene variation was found in two foetuses, but there was no finding of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in eight foetuses with small head circumferences. Of seven foetuses with abnormal cerebral sulcation, two were found to have pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, a detection rate of 28.6%. Both of the two foetuses were found to have NSD1 gene variation. The TUBA1A gene variation which is associated with Lissencephaly 3, was also found in two foetuses. One of them showed isolated cerebellar dysplasia when WES was performed at 24 weeks, but developed cortical malformations and ventriculomegaly at 31 weeks. The other one had a range of US phenotypes, notably mild ventriculomegaly, dysgenesis of the Sylvian fissure and a delayed sulcal appearance at 25+4 weeks, and was categorised as having multiple CNS abnormalities. There were 49 foetuses with multiple CNS abnormalities, of which 14 (28.6%) had P/LP findings (see Table ). There were three foetuses with schizencephaly along with other CNS abnormalities. WES revealed one likely pathogenic variant in the COL4A2 gene and two pathogenic variants in the COL4A1 gene. The TMEM237 gene was associated with Joubert syndrome, and among the 14 foetuses, two with the same CNS abnormalities had pathogenic variants in TMEM237 gene, which were of autosomal recessive inheritance from both parents. Seventeen of 31 (54.8%) foetuses with CNS abnormalities along with other organ system abnormalities had P/LP variants. There were five foetuses with craniosynostosis and other organ system abnormalities, for which the detection rate of the WES was 100%: four were found by WES to have FGFR2 variants, and one have FGFR3 variants. In two foetuses with ventriculomegaly (bilateral), developmental retardation of the cerebral sulcus and gyrus along with other organ system abnormalities, pathogenic variants in the NFIX gene associated with Marshall–Smith syndrome were found. One foetus with cerebellar dysplasia and FGR but having negative CMA results was found by WES to have a 30.244‐kb deletion of 21 (q22.11). This deletion region contains exons 3–12 of the SON gene which has a haplodose deficiency sensitivity score of 3 in the ClinGen database, and novel truncated variants of this gene were reported in several patients with intellectual disabilities (Kim et al. , Tokita et al. ). We used Pearson chi‐square or Fisher's exact test (two‐sided) for statistical analysis. It is suggested that different groups have different effects on the results, and there is a certain correlation between them (χ 2 = 14.613, p = 0.001). Cramer's V = 0.313, indicating that there is a medium degree of correlation between the grouping and the result. In this study, the frequency of positive observations in the groups of abnormalities in multiple organ systems, including the CNS (17), is nearly twice the expected frequency of 8.9, with an adjusted standardised residual of 3.6. This difference is statistically significant, indicating that the groups of CNS abnormalities along with other organ system abnormalities are more inclined to be positive.

Discussion
Discussion In our study, we evaluated the detection rate of WES for CNS abnormalities of foetuses in a nonselective cohort from both terminated and ongoing pregnancies who had normal or nonpathogenic karyotyping and CMA results for the main purpose of clinic diagnosis instead of research; all the WES testing were fully paid for by families in question. Therefore, the study represents a real‐world situation in terms of the practicality of prenatal counselling, where the diagnosis was performed due to clinical need of the hospital rather than research purpose, demonstrating clinical experience and practice within a tertiary maternal and child health care hospital in China. The total rate of pathogenic findings in foetuses with CNS abnormalities by WES was 28.9%, the detection rate of WES in our cohort was lower than that small sample sizes study, which was 71.4% (5/7) (Reches et al. ), the detection rate of WES in our cohort of nonselective foetuses also was lower than that in a cohort of selective foetuses consists of highly selected cases that were severe enough to warrant termination of pregnancy, which was 44% (38/46) (Yaron et al. ). Thus, the conclusions may not apply to all brain anomalies. The detection rate of WES in our cohort was higher than that in a cohort of nonselective foetuses for scientific research purpose which was 13.8% (Baptiste et al. ). And the detection rate of WES was comparable to the systematic review and meta‐analysis of central nervous system anomalies in 2023 by Gillian V. Blayney, 30 studies were included (n = 1264 cases). The incremental yield with pES for any CNS anomaly was 32% (Blayney et al. ) (Table ). Just as other studies have demonstrated, our study also showed foetuses with multiple CNS abnormalities and multi‐system abnormalities had a higher rate of LP/P variants than the foetuses with single and isolated CNS abnormality; in our study, 54.8% foetuses with CNS abnormalities along with other organ system abnormalities were found to have LP/P variants. Our findings highlight the importance of performing WES even for a single and isolated CNS abnormality, such as mild ventriculomegaly, a common abnormality detected by prenatal ultrasound that affects 0.4–1:1000 livebirths (Scelsa et al. ). The developmental prognosis for isolated mild ventriculomegaly is usually good, with 78%–100% of cases showing no neurological deficit. However, studies on long‐term outcomes, particularly those assessing mild neurobehavioural problems are limited (Scelsa et al. ; Pagani, Thilaganathan, and Prefumo ; Perlman et al. ; Malinger, Lev, and Lerman‐Sagie ). We discovered that 17.4% (3 out of 17) of the cases presenting with isolated mild ventriculomegaly (1.0–1.5 cm), were identified through Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) to possess pathogenic variants, yielding rates comparable to those from a study of 268 cases. The yield rate was 13% (3/23). However, mild ventriculomegaly was not included in other studies mentioned above. The three pathogenic variants were in the SOS1, YY1 and AHDC1 genes. The SOS1 variants were de novo variants associated with Noonan syndrome 4. Patients with Noonan syndrome are mainly characterised by short stature, special facial features and congenital heart abnormalities. Compared with the general Noonan syndrome patient population, patients with SOS1 mutations are more likely to develop pulmonary artery stenosis and curly hair. NT thickening and polyhydramnios are common prenatal abnormalities. Progressive hydrocephalus is not a rare complication of Noonan syndrome, as it has been observed in three out of 62 such patients (Henn et al. ). The YY1 variants associated with Gabriele‐de Vries syndrome were also de novo variants. Gabriele et al. reported 10 Gabriele‐de Vries syndrome‐unrelated patients, ranging in age from 1 to 39, with a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by delayed psychomotor development and intellectual disability. Among the 10 patients, five had nonspecific abnormal brain imaging showing delayed myelination, frontal gliosis, white matter abnormalities, and/or enlarged ventricles (Gabriele et al. ). The AHDC1 gene variants cause mental retardation and autosomal dominant 25, which is characterised by hypotonia and delayed psychomotor development with a deficiency in or poor expression of language. Structural brain abnormalities include corpus callosum abnormalities, mild cerebral atrophy, ventriculomegaly, diffuse cerebral atrophy and a small pituitary (Xia et al. ; Ritter et al. ). The high rate of monogenic conditions in foetuses with mild ventriculomegaly is a finding of utmost importance. Therefore, foetuses with isolated mild ventriculomegaly may have monogenic disease for which WES testing needs to be considered which can provide more evidence for counselling regarding foetal lateral ventriculomegaly. The yield for cases of isolated severe ventriculomegaly was 42.9% (3/7). A systematic review and meta‐analysis of diagnostic yield of exome sequencing in prenatal severe bilateral ventriculomegaly has been conducted (Mustafa, Sambatur, et al. ). A total of 28 studies included 1988 prenatal exome sequencing analyses performed following negative CMA results for various prenatal phenotypes, which included 138 cases with prenatal bilateral severe ventriculomegaly. Thirty‐five percent (11/33) of cases with isolated severe ventriculomegaly had LP/P variants, which is comparable to our study despite the big samples. We found that two out of seven (28.6%) foetuses with isolated abnormal cerebral sulcation had pathogenic variants in the NSD1 gene which is associated with Sotos syndrome and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. The three main features of Sotos syndrome are distinctive facial appearance, learning disability and overgrowth. Other signs and symptoms of Sotos syndrome include autism spectrum disorder, hypotonia, poor feeding, neonatal jaundice, scoliosis, cardiac and renal abnormalities, joint laxity and cranial imaging abnormalities. Such patients have an increased risk of developing neoplasms, especially in adulthood (Cohen Jr. ). The above‐mentioned features have generally been found in postnatal individuals. A retrospective study of eight pregnancies with foetal Sotos syndrome caused by NSD1 gene mutations found no specific sonographic finding in the affected foetuses (Zhang et al. ). The two foetuses in our study had no other syndrome except isolated abnormal cerebral sulcation manifested by delayed development of parieto‐occipital sulcus, calcarine sulcus, insula and sylvian fissure compared with the corresponding gestational age. One of the foetuses was terminated, while the other had macrocephaly, frontal bossing, a pointed chin, large hands and mild language retardation during the follow‐up at 26 months after birth. Therefore, foetuses with such abnormalities can be tested by WES. The sonographic finding of abnormal cerebral sulcation can be characteristic of Sotos syndrome and should be further confirmed. Our cohort included 25 foetuses with agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC), among which three (12%) were found to have no pathogenic variant and were considered to have isolated ACC. Among the 22 nonisolated ACC foetuses, 22.7% (5/22) were found to have P/LP variants. In contrast, in a study of 65 foetuses with agenesis of the corpus callosum, 15% of foetuses with isolated ACC were found by WES to have pathogenic variants, while 42% of foetuses with nonisolated ACC were found by WES to have pathogenic variants (Heide et al. ). A Systematic Review and Meta‐analysis included 267 prenatal agenesis of corpus callosum (ACC) cases tested by WES, 43% had positive P/LP variants. The highest yield was observed for ACC with extracranial anomalies (55%), followed by ACC with other cranial anomalies (43%), and then isolated ACC (32%) (Mustafa, Barbera, et al. ). Isolated ACC cases had a small proportion in our study and were found to have no pathogenic variants. This may be because isolated ACC was defined more precisely in our study after a detailed assessment of cerebral cortical development. Previous studies on using WES to diagnose CNS abnormalities have focused on postnatal individuals with unexplainable neurodevelopmental disorders, including intellectual disability/developmental delay and epilepsy. To date, hundreds of genes have been found to be responsible for such disorders (Vissers, Gilissen, and Veltman ; Mei et al. ). These individuals may also show one or more types of malformations of cortical development, including lissencephaly, polymicrogyria, schizencephaly, focal cortical dysplasia and periventricular nodular heteropia (Parrini et al. ), for which the detection rate of WES is 20%–30% (Vissers, Gilissen, and Veltman ; Mei et al. ). Compared with the prenatal foetus, the clinical phenotypes of post natal individuals can be well‐described. Since accurate genotype–phenotype correlation is the basis for variant filtering by WES, prenatal WES is faced with special challenges, as well as numerous ethical issues to be contemplated and addressed (Chandler et al. ). This is especially true for foetuses with CNS abnormalities because CNS development continues throughout pregnancy and after delivery and thus it is challengeable to give a detailed phenotypic analysis of neurological changes before birth. Development and growth of the brain and other parts of the CNS are not completed until after birth (Van den Veyver ). Many phenotypes of CNS abnormalities cannot be detected until the third trimester of pregnancy or even after the birth of the foetus, which poses a challenge to clinical consulting. Trio‐WES can serve to identify the genetic aetiology in these affected foetuses, and help clinicians to make a more precise prognosis and offer better management for these foetuses, and it would be a key factor for the parents to make a choice between continuing and terminating the pregnancy with the permission of the law. In our study, it was found that 13 out of a total of 43 (30.2%) genetic variants detected were inherited, with three being autosomal dominant inheritance, nine being autosomal recessive inheritance, and one being X‐linked recessive inheritance and de novo P/LP variants accounting for 69.8%. The detected results may be valuable for prenatal diagnosis and even preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) as well as for genetic counselling regarding recurrence risks in subsequent pregnancies and reproductive options. Therefore, WES is an important tool in the prenatal evaluation of foetuses with CNS abnormalities, but having negative results in karyotyping and chromosome array. WES may also be of beneficial for isolated CNS abnormalities. But of course, it is very important to confirm the imaging findings of CNS abnormalities before WES is performed. Strengths and Limitations This study includes 149 families with unselected CNS abnormalities that underwent WES, representing a real‐world situation in terms of the practicality of prenatal counselling, where the diagnosis was pursued due to a clinical need and not for a research purpose. The limitations of this study are that the sample size of each specific abnormality was small, which limits the generalisability of our findings. The study includes novel variants that have been neither previously reported nor found in the databases. Restricted by time and budget, no functional analysis at the molecular level was conducted for our cases. Thus, segregation of the variant in other family members was crucial to support the diagnosis. In light of these limitations, we cannot definitely exclude the possibility that some of the molecular diagnoses are false positives. In the future, more and more cases of diagnosing foetal CNS abnormalities by WES will be collected in prenatal diagnosis. Functional analysis of novel variants, both at the molecular level and in animal models, will gradually be applied in clinical practice.

title: Agenesis of the Ductus Venosus and Its Association With Genetic Abnormalities.
label_reason: Fetuses with ductus venosus agenesis tested by CMA/ES.
abstract: To investigate the association of agenesis of the ductus venosus (ADV) with genetic abnormalities using genetic studies—Chromosomal Microarray Analysis (CMA) and Exome Sequencing (ES). Retrospective study of all fetuses diagnosed with ADV between January 2013 and December 2022 in a tertiary center. ADV was diagnosed in 33 fetuses. The diagnosis was made at a mean gestational age of 21.2 ± 8.4 weeks. Conventional karyotype was applied in a single fetus (3.0%), CMA was applied in 21 fetuses (66.7%), and five fetuses (22.8%) were additionally tested with ES. ADV was isolated in eight fetuses (24%), whereas in 25 (76%) it was associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, including increased nuchal translucency (NT), intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and variable structural malformations, mostly cardiac (42%) followed by central nervous system (CNS) and skeletal malformations (24%). Genetic abnormalities were found in six fetuses out of 22 investigated (27%), of which 3 were detected by ES, 3 by CMA and 1 by conventional karyotype. A higher incidence of genetic aberrations was evident among ADVs associated with abnormal ultrasound findings. Genetic abnormalities were indicative of Prader Willi/Angelman syndrome, Noonan syndrome, CASK related disorder, 16q24.3 microdeletion syndrome and Trisomy 21. ADV associated with abnormal ultrasound findings is commonly correlated with genetic abnormalities and consequently unfavorable pregnancy outcomes. Our study emphasizes the value of genetic studies chiefly among cases associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, enabling early diagnosis of fetal pathologies associated with ADV, and providing better parental counseling.
text:
Agenesis of the Ductus Venosus and Its Association With Genetic Abnormalities

Background
Background The ductus venosus (DV) is a unique fetal vascular structure constituting one of the three pivotal physiological shunts through which oxygenated blood circumvents the fetal portal system to enter the heart []. Agenesis of the DV (ADV) is a rare congenital anomaly, with a variable prevalence of 0.04%–0.6% []. With ADV, blood flows from the umbilical vein through an aberrant vessel that may be extrahepatic, bypassing the liver, or intrahepatic via the portal venous system [, , ]. ADV is known to be associated with an increased risk for genetic abnormalities, fetal malformations [], and adverse perinatal outcomes including fetal growth restriction (FGR) and stillbirth []. However, genetic abnormalities associated with ADV are hypothesized to be underdiagnosed using conventional cytogenetic studies [, ]. In recent years, advancements in genetic testing, namely Chromosomal Microarray Analysis (CMA) and Exome Sequencing (ES), have allowed for comprehensive analysis of the fetal genome, enhancing the prenatal diagnosis of genetic abnormalities associated with ADV. Despite the potential of genetic techniques in the research of ADV, there is a paucity of genetic studies addressing ADV cases in the literature. A recent case series regarding the genetic abnormalities associated with ADV in the exome era was reported [] in which ES was used in a single case. Our study aimed to investigate genetic abnormalities associated with ADV with the integration of CMA and ES into clinical practice.

Methods
Methods A retrospective cohort study of all fetuses diagnosed prenatally with ADV between January 2013 and December 2022 in our tertiary center. Study Population All pregnancies who attended the routine screening were considered eligible. Inclusion criteria were the availability of the first (11–14 weeks) and second (17–22 weeks) trimester ultrasound scan results, including the DV assessment, and the pregnancy outcome. Pregnancies without follow‐up or those with incomplete files were excluded. Data Collection Medical records were extracted from the hospital's computerized database. Evaluation of the DV is performed in all women as part of routine anatomical screening, in both low‐ and high‐risk pregnancies; as well as during targeted anomaly scans, for women referred to our ultrasound unit for targeted scans. When ADV was diagnosed in our unit, a full anatomical scan was performed by fetal ultrasound specialist and, in addition, an echocardiogram was made by a pediatric cardiologist. All were referred to genetic consultation, and genetic studies were recommended in all cases, including conventional karyotype, CMA and ES. We extracted data on gestational age at ADV diagnosis, obstetrical complications, associated abnormal ultrasound findings or genetic findings, pregnancy outcomes as well as complications—namely termination of pregnancy, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm delivery, and mode of delivery. Statistical Analysis Statistical analysis was performed using SAS software version 34.0 (SAS Corp., Cary, North Carolina, USA). Descriptive statistics are presented by number and percentage for categorical variables and mean and standard deviation for continuous variables. Ethics The study was approved by the local Institutional Review Board (049–20‐RMC). Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective design of the study.

Results
Results ADV was diagnosed in 33 fetuses. Mean gestational age at diagnosis was 21.2 ± 8.4 weeks (range 12–38 Gestational weeks). In 23 cases (70%) ADV was identified as part of routine anatomy screening, while in 10 (30%) at targeted fetal anomaly scan due to other suspected malformations. The epidemiological and clinical background are presented in Table . Isolated ADV Versus ADV Associated With Abnormal Ultrasound Findings ADV was isolated in eight cases (24%), whereas in 25 cases (76%) it was associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, including increased NT above 3 mm (24%, n = 6), IUGR (36%, n = 9) and/or structural malformations evident in 17 fetuses (85%). Cardiac anomalies were diagnosed in 15 fetuses (88%) with ventricular septal defect (VSD) being the most common malformation within this category, as detected in five cases (29%). The abnormal ultrasound findings are listed in Table . No chromosomal or monogenic disorders were found among isolated ADV cases that proceeded to genetic testing. ADV Associated With Genetic Abnormalities Of the 33 cases of ADV in our study, 22 women (67%) underwent invasive prenatal genetic testing, 17 (77%) by amniocentesis (AC), and 5 (23%) by chorionic villus sampling (CVS). Overall, one fetus (5%) was tested with conventional karyotype, while 21 fetuses (95%) were tested with CMA. Of them, 5 (24%) were additionally tested with ES (Table ). Among the eight cases of isolated ADV, 6 (75%) were tested with CMA without any genetic abnormalities detected. Out of these six cases, one (17%) continued for ES without genetic abnormalities detected. Among the 25 cases of ADV associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, 16 (64%) underwent genetic studies. 15 (94%) were tested with CMA, of which two fetuses (13%) had abnormal CMA, revealing genetic abnormalities corresponding with genetic syndromes: 15q11.2‐q13.1 microdeletion (Case 1) and 16q24.3 microdeletion (case 2). Of the 13 fetuses (81%) with associated ADV and normal CMA, four cases (31%) continued for ES, of which 3 (75%) revealed genetic aberrations. One fetus was diagnosed with RIT1 likely pathogenic (LP) variant (Paternally inherited) (case 3), and one with BRAF pathogenic (P) variant (de novo) (case 4), both known as RASopathies corresponding to a phenotype of Noonan/Cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome. A third fetus was found with an LP variant in the CASK gene (Case 5) ‐ compatible with microcephaly with Pontine and Cerebellar Hypoplasia (MICPCH) and X‐Linked Intellectual Disability (XL‐ID) with or without nystagmus, which was de novo in the fetus. Trisomy 21 was detected in one fetus with associated ADV (6%) using a conventional karyotype (case 6). Overall, 6 out of 22 genetically analyzed cases (27%) in our study were diagnosed with genetic aberrations, all with associated abnormal ultrasound findings. The genetic findings are summarized in Table . Pregnancy Outcomes In our study, 18 live births (54%) were recorded: six cases (33%) of isolated ADV and 12 (67%) with associated abnormal ultrasound findings; Termination of pregnancy (TOP) opted in nine cases (27%)–eight cases (40%) were among ADV associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, compared with a single case (8%) in the group of isolated ADV. In the group of associated ADV were also recorded, one case of stillbirth (4%) and one (4%) late spontaneous abortion before 22 gestational weeks. Among the 18 women who had a live birth, 14 deliveries (78%) were at term and 4 before term (22%), ranging between 29 + 3 to 30 + 6 gestational weeks. The mode of delivery was vaginal delivery in 11 women (61%) and cesarean delivery in 7 women (39%) (Figure ). Pregnancy outcomes in cases of isolated and non‐isolated ADV.

Discussion
Discussion Our study aimed to investigate the association of ADV with structural and genetic abnormalities, focusing on genetic testing (CMA and ES). Among 33 cases of ADV, 8 were isolated, while 25 were associated with abnormal ultrasound findings, including increased NT, IUGR and multiple structural malformations. Advances in genetic techniques have improved our ability to assess genetic abnormalities in cases of ADV undetectable by conventional testing modalities such as conventional karyotype. However, previous studies lacked data related to the application of prenatal genetic studies of genetic abnormalities associated with fetal ADV [, ]. Moaddab et al. [] published a systematic review of the literature in 2015 describing 259 fetuses with ADV associated with genetic abnormalities as detected by conventional karyotyping performed in 154 cases (59.4%). In 38 fetuses (24.7%), chromosomal abnormality was detected: monosomy X (n = 11, 28.9%), trisomy 21 (n = 10, 26.3%), chromosomal deletions (n = 7, 18.4%), trisomy 18 (n = 6, 15.8%), Robertsonian translocations (n = 2, 5.2%), trisomy 22 (n = 1, 2.6%) and trisomy 13 (n = 1, 2.6%). Pacheco et al. [] published in 2017 the largest literature review from publications spanning 25 years. The study included 410 fetuses with ADV, of which 70 (17.1%) were isolated and 340 (82.9%) were associated with other abnormalities. Conventional karyotype was performed in 141 cases (41.4%) of which 48 (34%) were abnormal. However, none of these studies included either CMA or ES genetic evaluation. McBrien et al. [] had the only publication incorporating CMA and ES into the genetic workup of ADV. They described their experience in a small retrospective series of 14 cases in 2020. Only 8 fetuses (57.1%) were tested by conventional karyotype, CMA, or ES. All had associated genetic or structural anomalies. In total, six cases of those tested (75%) were found to have genetic abnormalities. Only two cases of those tested (25%) had aneuploidy, 3 (38%) had single gene variants, of which two were detected by gene panel testing for Noonan syndrome and one was diagnosed through ES (RASA1). Remarkably, in our study, CMA was the standard of care and was employed in all but one instance of ADV in which prenatal genetic testing was performed. Genetic testing enabled the identification of genetic syndromes not listed elsewhere in the literature as associated with ADV, and which would not be detected by conventional karyotyping alone—15q11.2‐q13.1 microdeletion and chromosome 16q24.3 microdeletion syndromes—rare chromosomal abnormalities associated with variable developmental delay, facial dysmorphism, seizures and autistic spectrum disorder [, ]. Trisomy 21, which we also identified in our study, is already described in the literature as ADV‐associated []. Moreover, we report three cases (14%) among the 21 analyzed with CMA, in which CMA was reported normal, and the LP/P variants were detected only by ES, emphasizing the importance of enhanced genetic studies []. Using ES allowed the diagnosis of MICPCH and XL‐ID—a rare syndrome characterized by microcephaly, pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia, postnatal growth retardation, low weight for length, severe intellectual disability and marked motor retardation []. To the best of our knowledge, vascular malformations as demonstrated in the fetus (porto‐systemic shunt and ADV) were not previously reported as a part of CASK related syndromes. Therefore, it appears to be an incidental finding that does not explain the fetal phenotype []. BRAF [] and RIT1 P/LP variants correlated with Noonan syndrome/CFC syndrome (Rasopathies), previously described in recent studies in the context of ADV [], and were also detected in our study using ES. In our cohort, all the cases diagnosed with a genetic disorder had associated ultrasound findings. Therefore, non‐isolated ADV should be offered extended genetic testing. Non‐isolated ADV is associated with genetic disorders, mainly aneuploidy and RASopathies. Widespread use of advanced genetic testing will diagnose these conditions but may also identify other diseases not yet linked to ADV. This could expand current knowledge about the connection between this finding and additional genetic diseases, as possibly suggested by our sample. In our cohort, 25 fetuses with ADV (76%) were diagnosed with associated abnormal sonographic findings. Among this population, we found variable structural malformations to be associated with ADV, of which cardiac anomalies exhibited the highest prevalence. This finding is also supported by larger studies addressing ADV‐associated structural anomalies [, ]. We also found that prenatal diagnosis of non‐isolated ADV is linked to less favorable pregnancy outcomes and a high rate of pregnancy termination. This may be due to the presence of associated fetal anomalies, which impacts parental decision making and is similar to previous studies [, , , ]. Of note, the prognosis for fetuses with isolated ADV is generally favorable, with a lower risk of detecting genetic aberrations. The mean time of ADV diagnosis in our study was during mid gestation, as part of routine prenatal screening and/or targeted fetal anatomy scans in cases where earlier findings of structural abnormalities were evident. This is in accordance with previous studies [] reporting a mean GA of 22.9 ± 6.9 weeks at the time of ADV diagnosis. It is worth mentioning, however, that larger studies demonstrated the ability to detect ADV already earlier in gestation during the first trimester when systematically evaluated []. However, data in the literature on the efficiency of first trimester screening in diagnosing ADV is sparse, and the prevalence of the anomaly is not clear []. The late diagnosis was also probably because our ultrasound unit is a tertiary center where women are referred for dedicated anatomical scanning following the routine anatomical scan in community centers [, , , , ]. The strength of our study is the meticulously selected population of cases with ADV, of which most had genetic testing. In addition, pregnancy follow‐up by multidisciplinary staff, including specialized ultrasound obstetricians, clinical geneticists, pediatricians and other specialists in our center, helps to evaluate the cases better. The primary limitation of our study lies in its retrospective nature, which may introduce referral bias. It is plausible that we did not capture all instances of ADV within our population, potentially missing cases that remained undiagnosed. Another significant limitation is the small study size, particularly those cases tested by ES. Furthermore, some of our patients chose not to undergo genetic testing despite the high risk of chromosomal or monogenic disorder due to multiple structural findings. This could lead to probable underestimation of genetic conditions. Further studies with a larger number of participants are needed to confirm our results. ADV is, however, a rare finding, and therefore a multi‐center study may be a better approach in the future.

Conclusion
Conclusion We demonstrated that 75% of cases of ADV were identified with additional abnormal ultrasound findings, including increased NT, IUGR, and other structural fetal abnormalities. Isolated ADV in our study was not detected with genetic aberrations, whereas ADV with abnormal sonographic findings displayed a 37.5% incidence of genetic conditions with various phenotypes. It is, however, worth mentioning that only 1 of 8 fetuses (12.5%) in the isolated ADV group was analyzed by ES, compared with 4 of 25 fetuses (16%) in the group of ADV associated with abnormal ultrasound findings. Several genetic abnormalities in cases with ADV cannot be detected using CMA or conventional karyotype alone, emphasizing the diagnostic yield of ES. As ADV is subsequently linked with unfavorable pregnancy outcomes, early identification of fetal pathologies affiliated with ADV may provide better parental counseling.

title: Is intermediate risk really intermediate? Comparison of karyotype and non-invasive prenatal testing results of pregnancies at intermediate risk of trisomy 21 on maternal serum screening.

abstract: The purpose of this study was to assess the additional contribution of karyotyping compared with genome‐wide non‐invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for pregnancies at intermediate risk for trisomy 21 (T21), calculated using the maternal serum screening without major structural anomalies detected through sonography. Karyotype results of all pregnancies undergoing invasive prenatal diagnostic testing between January 2013 and March 2022 were obtained from a large hospital‐based laboratory. Pregnancies with no major structural anomalies on ultrasound (including soft markers) and an intermediate risk for T21 on maternal serum screening were included in this study. The additional contribution of karyotyping for abnormal karyotype results was calculated after excluding results that could theoretically be identified with genome‐wide NIPT. Among the 511 pregnancies analyzed, 13 (2.54%) were found to have abnormal karyotype results, 9 (1.76%) of which could theoretically have been detected with genome‐wide NIPT. Within the cohort, 6/263 (2.28%) of women aged 35 years and older, and 3/248 (1.20%) of women younger than 35 years had results that could have been detected with genome‐wide NIPT. After excluding results detectable using genome‐wide NIPT, the additional contribution of karyotyping was found as 4/502 (0.79%) for the entire cohort, 2/257 (0.77%) for women aged 35 years and older, 2/245 (0.81%) for women younger than 35 years. Of the 511 examined pregnancies at intermediate risk for T21 by maternal serum screening, genome‐wide NIPT would have failed to detect 4 of 13 abnormal karyotype results. The findings hold importance in guiding couples' informed decision‐making processes regarding their choice of genetic screening and diagnostic testing in case of intermediate risk for T21. Keywords: intermediate risk, karyotype, non‐invasive prenatal screening, prenatal diagnosis

Is intermediate risk really intermediate? Comparison of karyotype and non‐invasive prenatal testing results of pregnancies at intermediate risk of trisomy 21 on maternal serum screening

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION In general, chromosomal abnormalities are observed in an incidence of 1 in 150 live births (Nussbaum et al., ). Trisomy 21 (T21) is the most common chromosomal anomaly among neonates occurring in 1 of 660 live births worldwide (Jones, ). Prenatal screening is performed because T21 is associated with significant intellectual disability and various medical impairments. Prenatal diagnosis allows women options including preparing for the birth of an affected child or termination of pregnancy. Since the identification of cell‐free DNA (cfDNA) of fetal/placental can be performed in the maternal circulation, NIPT has been successfully used for fetal chromosomal aneuploidy screening such as T21, trisomy 18 (T18), trisomy 13 (T13), and the sex chromosome aneuploidies (SCAs) in clinical practice since 2011 (Agarwal et al., ; Lo et al., ). NIPT is currently the best non‐invasive method to assess the risk of T 21, T18, and T13 (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’ Committee on Practice Bulletins—Obstetrics; Committee on Genetics; Society for Maternal‐Fetal Medicine, ). In a meta‐analysis conducted by Gil et al. () the detection rates were found as 99.7%, 97.9%, and 99.0% for T21, T18, and T13, respectively, and the rate of false‐positive results was 0.04%. Further advances in NIPT technology have shown that rare autosomal trisomies (RATs), recurrent microdeletion/microduplication syndromes, and even genome‐wide copy‐number variants could be detected. An expanded NIPT includes recurrent microdeletions (such as 1p36.3‐1p36.2, 4p16.3‐4p16.2, 5p15.3‐5p15.1, 15q11.2‐15q13.1, and 22q11.1.2 deletions) and genome‐wide NIPT usually detects deletions and duplications greater than 5 Mb (Chen et al., ; Hu et al., ; Wapner et al., ). To screen for common trisomies in the general population, NIPT can be used as a first‐line screening method or depending on the results of the combined test performed at 11 and 13 weeks of gestation (contingent NIPT screening; Gil et al., ). Contingent NIPT screening is a strategy with a much higher detection rate and significantly lower cost compared to the use of NIPT as a first‐line screening method (Kagan et al., ). This strategy also offers the advantages of correct gestational age calculation, ultrasound examination for the early detection of several major fetal defects, and first‐trimester biochemical testing (Nicolaides, ). Different cut‐off values classified as intermediate risk have been used in contingent NIPT screening (1 in 100 or 150 and 1 in 1000–2500; Chitty et al., ; Gil et al., ; Miltoft et al., ). In a study, Miltoft et al. found that an invasive test offered to women who had risk of ≥1 in 100 in the first‐trimester screening test, and contingent NIPT screening offered to women who had a risk of 1 in 100 to 1 in 1000 had the same sensitivity for T21, T18, and T13 compared with offering an invasive test to all women who had a risk of ≥1 in 300 in the first‐trimester screening test. The false‐positive rate was found as 1.2% in the two‐stage model, whereas it was 3.0% in the conventional approach (Miltoft et al., ). In Turkey, prenatal care is provided both by public and private sectors. In the public health system, prenatal care is free of charge which is predominantly performed by family practice providers and obstetricians. According to the Ministry of Health Prenatal Care and Management Guideline, all pregnant women should receive at least four sessions of prenatal care during their pregnancy, as the first one takes place within 12 weeks of gestation. Additionally, all pregnant women should be routinely offered prenatal screening as a part of their prenatal care (Guide, ). Traditional screening tests applied in Turkey are first‐trimester screening (nuchal translucency measurement and measurement of serum analytes) between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation, triple/quad screening (measurement of maternal serum analytes) between 16 and 20 weeks of gestation, and fetal anatomic ultrasound survey between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation. Despite NIPT is currently available through private providers, it is not yet available in publicly funded prenatal services. Pregnancies with abnormal serum screening (at the threshold of 1:250–300) or with sonographic anomalies are referred to the tertiary fetal medicine centers for further invasive prenatal diagnostic testing (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis, or cordocentesis). Moreover, the invasive tests are also financed by government in the pregnancies of mothers aged 35 years and older, the parental chromosomal rearrangements, past history of a fetus or infant with T21, and intermediate risk for T21 at the parents' own discretion. Prenatal invasive procedures are generally performed by the fetal–maternal medicine team, while both pre‐ and posttest counselings are done by clinical geneticists. Last but not least, maternal serum screening tests and karyotype analysis are generally performed in in‐house laboratories. The national prenatal screening strategy (current practice) in Turkey is illustrated in Figure . The National Prenatal Screening Strategy For Trisomy 21 in Turkey. The performance of NIPT in pregnancies at intermediate risk for T 21 has been defined in large cohorts (Gil et al., ; Kagan et al., ; Nicolaides et al., , ); however, there is limited evidence showing the comparative results of NIPT and karyotyping data in this group. In our study, we aimed to assess the additional contribution of karyotyping compared with genome‐wide NIPT for pregnancies at intermediate risk for T21 based on a large karyotyping cohort that had no major structural anomalies.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
MATERIALS AND METHODS This retrospective cohort study was based on the database of the Center of Genetic Diagnosis, Akdeniz University Hospital (Antalya, Turkey). After obtaining approval from the Akdeniz University Faculty of Medicine Clinical Research Ethics Board (Number: 326, Date: 15.05.2022), we retrospectively assessed the karyotype. Results of all pregnancies who underwent invasive prenatal diagnostic testing at the outpatient clinic of Perinatology, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Akdeniz University Hospital between January 2013 and March 2022. Eligibility criteria included: (1) pregnancies undergoing diagnostic testing due to intermediate risk for trisomy 21 by maternal serum screening with normal ultrasound and (2) accompanied with or without the soft markers. Pregnancies with multiple fetuses or sonographic anomalies (including structural anomalies, nuchal translucency over 3 mm, polyhydramnios, or intrauterine growth restriction) were excluded from the study. The risk of T21, calculated using the combined first‐trimester screen, ranging from 1/101 to 1/1000, is classified as intermediate risk as proposed by Nicolaides et al. (Chitty et al., ). Demographic characteristics of patients, antenatal screening methods (double, triple, and quadruple test), presence of minor markers in ultrasonography, gestational weeks, and the invasive method technique applied (chorionic villus biopsy, amniocentesis, and cordocentesis) were recorded. The karyotyping results were categorized as normal or abnormal, and abnormal results were further divided into subgroups based on the type of abnormality. Abnormal results were analyzed according to the type of abnormality and whether they could be detected through genome‐wide NIPT. Non‐mosaic T13, T18, T21, or SCAs, recurrent microdeletions (1p36.3‐1p36.2, 4p16.3‐4p16.2, 5p15.3‐5p15.1, 15q11.2‐15q13.1, and 22q11.1.2 deletions), and deletions and duplications greater than 5 Mb were considered detectable with genome‐wide NIPT (Hu et al., ). Deletions and duplications smaller than 5 Mb, as well as any form of mosaicism, were considered non‐detectable with genome‐wide NIPT. The additional contribution of karyotyping for abnormal results was calculated by excluding results that could be detectable via NIPT. Subgroup analysis was performed for pregnancies with an advanced maternal age (i.e., aged 35 years and older) versus younger women. The Chi‐square test with Yates's correction was used to compare the detection rates between subgroups. A P‐value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

RESULTS
RESULTS During the study period, karyotype analyses were performed on 3217 prenatal samples in a genetic laboratory. Among them, 518 were found to be pregnancies with intermediate risk for T21 by maternal serum screening. After excluding 7 cases with multiple fetuses and sonographic anomalies (including structural defects, nuchal translucency over 3 mm, polyhydramnios, or intrauterine growth restriction), 511 pregnancies were included in the study. Among 511 analyses, 263 were performed in women aged 35 years and older and 248 in younger than 35 years (Figure ). Flow chart describing the karyotyping detection rates in pregnancies with intermediate risk for T21 by maternal serum screening and the contributions of karyotyping after excluding theoretically genome‐wide NIPT detectable findings. NIPT, non‐invasive prenatal test; T21, trisomy 21. Regarding the prenatal invasive methods used, 500 patients underwent amniocentesis, 7 underwent chorionic villus biopsies, and 4 underwent cordocentesis. The mean maternal age was 33.5 ± 2.7 years. The mean gestational age at CVS, amniocentesis, and cordocentesis was 12.2 ± 5, 18.1 ± 2, and 21.6 ± 1 weeks, respectively. There were no procedure‐related miscarriages among the 511 patients. Soft markers were detected in eight patients, including pyelectasis in five, choroid plexus cyst in two, and a hyperechogenic bowel in one patient. Of the 511 patients who underwent prenatal invasive procedures, 13 cases (2.5%) were found to have abnormal karyotype results. Among them, 8 (3%) were in women aged 35 years and older, whereas 5 (2%) were in women younger than 35 years. Regarding the distribution of the anomalies, T21 was the most frequent abnormality at 46.1% (6/13), followed by mosaicism at 23% (3/13), unbalanced structural abnormalities (deletion, derivative chromosome, and isochromosome) at 23% (3/13), and balanced structural abnormalities (translocation) at 7.6% (1/13). Table and Figure summarize abnormal karyotype results in the examined cohort. Theoretically, 9 of 13 abnormal karyotype results (69.2%) could have been detected using genome‐wide NIPT. Among them, six were T21 (47,–,+21) cases, one was Turner syndrome with isochromosome X (46,X,i(X)(q10)), while one was a deletion (46,–,del(18p11.23) dn) case, and one was a derivative chromosome case (46,–,der(22)t(Y;22)(q12;p11.2) pat). The percentage of results detectable using genome‐wide NIPT was 9/511 (1.76%) for the entire cohort, 6/263 (2.28%) for women aged 35 years and older, and 3/248 (1.20%) for women younger than 35 years. When results detectable using genome‐wide NIPT were excluded, the additional contribution of karyotyping was 4/502 (0.79%) for the entire cohort, 2/257 (0.77%) for women aged 35 years and older, and 2/245 (0.81%) for women younger than 35 years. The difference was not significant (p > 0.05). Additional contributions of karyotyping are summarized in Table .

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION Our study reveals that genome‐wide NIPT would have missed 4 abnormal karyotype results out of 13 abnormal results, as per the karyotyping results of 511 pregnant women in the intermediate‐risk group for T21 who had no major structural anomalies. After excluding results detectable using genome‐wide NIPT, the additional contribution of karyotyping for abnormal karyotype results was found to be 0.79%. This additional contribution was 0.81% for women younger than 35 years and 0.77% for women aged 35 years and older. Considering the contribution of karyotyping, if NIPT had been used as the first‐line screening method for patients in the intermediate‐risk group, it would have missed three mosaic results (mosaic trisomy 21, mosaic tetraploidy, and mosaic deletion) and one balanced structural anomaly (balanced translocation) although it would have detected six T21 results and three unbalanced structural anomalies (derivative chromosome, deletion, and isochromosome). Despite low‐risk NIPT results significantly reducing the aneuploidy risk, it does not guarantee a normal karyotype. The notable residual risk was demonstrated in different groups for clinically significant chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) results after excluding NIPT results. In a study by Maya et al. (), the residual risk for clinically significant copy number variants in low‐risk pregnancies with normal serum biochemistry was 0.68% for the entire group, 0.82% for women older than 35 years, and 0.5% for women younger than 35 years after excluding genome‐wide NIPT results. In another study, 21 clinically significant abnormalities were found in CMA among 559 amniocentesis cases performed due to abnormal maternal serum screening results. The residual risk for CMA findings was 2.0% after theoretically normal NIPT results (Sagi‐Dain et al., ). In another retrospective cohort study, among 122 clinically significant CMA results from 8605 pregnancies with normal ultrasound results (including abnormal serum biochemistry and soft markers), the additional contribution of CMA following omission of genome‐wide NIPT detectable findings was 0.91% for the entire cohort, 1.01% for women older than 35 years, and 0.61% for women younger than 35, whereas it was 1.74% for pregnancies with abnormal serum biochemistry and 0.95% for the soft marker group (Maya et al., ). The frequency of fetal chromosome abnormality detection depends on clinical indications (Nishiyama et al., ). In our cohort, the incidence of chromosomal abnormalities was 2.5% with 61.5% (8/13) of chromosomal abnormalities detected in women aged 35 years and older, and 38.5% (5/13) detected in women younger than 35 years. T21 (46.6%) was the most frequent trisomy for both age groups. These results appear to be consistent with the previous studies reporting that the incidence of chromosomal anomalies and T21 ranged from 2.9% to 3.6% and 36.9% to 61.9%, respectively (Han et al., ; Mademont‐Soler et al., ; Ocak et al., ). This finding may be significant when offering prenatal genetic counseling to patients in the intermediate‐risk group for T21. Fetal mosaicism was detected in three of the abnormal karyotype results in our study (mosaic trisomy 21, mosaic tetraploidy, and mosaic deletion). Postzygotic mitotic errors lead to chromosomal mosaicism in approximately 1–2% of chorion villus samples (Hahnemann & Vejerslev, ). The source of cell‐free DNA is apoptotic cytotrophoblasts secreted from placental chorionic villi to maternal blood. The cytotrophoblast layer of chorionic villi does not always represent the fetus because it is derived from the trophoblasts of blastocysts, whereas the fetus comes from the inner cell mass. Cytotrophoblasts, mesenchymal nuclei, and fetal karyotypes may differ (Bianchi et al., ). If abnormal cells are limited to the cytotrophoblast layer, they are classified as confined placental mosaicism (CPM) type 1. In CPM type 2, abnormal cells are limited to the mesenchyme. In CPM type 3, abnormal cells are present on both layers of the chorionic villi but absent in the fetus. True fetal mosaicism is associated with a normal karyotype in cytotrophoblasts while the fetus itself has an abnormal karyotype and is classified as true fetal mosaicism type 5 (TFM 5; Grati et al., ). In a review, it was reported that CPM was the cause of 32% of all false‐positive cases in NIPT, and TFM type 5 was the cause of 92% of false‐negative cases (Hartwig et al., ). Due to limited reports on mosaic results detectable via NIPT, the accurate detection rate remains unclear (Brison et al., ). In our study, we also considered mosaic results as detectable only by karyotyping. In our study, balanced structural anomaly (balanced translocation) was detected in one of the abnormal karyotype results. Balanced translocations are chromosomal rearrangements consisting of components where two different chromosomes change segments without genetic material gain or loss, with a frequency of 0.08%–0.3% in the general distribution (Zhang et al., ). In patients carrying balanced reciprocal translocations, mispairing of translocated chromosomes during the first meiotic division can lead to different forms of segregation, which can result in balanced, unbalanced, normal gametes of the translocated chromosomes and may cause the transmission of chromosomal abnormalities to their offspring (Pourjafari et al., ). CMA is recommended as the first‐line test in cases of fetal structural anomalies and/or stillbirth, and it replaces the need for karyotyping in most cases. However, it is not able to identify balanced translocations or inversions. Karyotyping remains an important method in prenatal diagnosis of balanced translocations (Sparks & Dugoff, ). In prenatal series, the estimated prevalence of microdeletions included in extended NIPT is 1: 5000 (such as 1p36.3‐1p36.2, 4p16.3‐4p16.2, 5p15.3‐5p15.1, 15q11.2‐15q13.1, and 22q11.1.2 deletions; Srebniak et al., ). Although the majority of pathogenic microdeletion/ duplication syndromes cause miscarriage in the first trimester of pregnancy or present as abnormal ultrasound findings during routine developmental checks, some are potentially viable to term and result in developmental and/or physical disorders (Chen et al., ). No cases of microdeletion/microduplication were detected in our study. This may be due to the inclusion of pregnancies with normal ultrasound and the small sample size in our study. Therefore, microdeletion/duplication screening in our cohort would not have altered results. In our study, there were no procedure‐related miscarriages among the 511 patients. A meta‐analysis performed in 2019 suggested that the procedure‐related risk of pregnancy loss after amniocentesis and CVS was lower than the risk currently quoted to women and it might be 1/300 at the most (Salomon et al., ). There is evidence highlighting the fact that the risk of miscarriage from invasive procedures is related to the skill and experience of the operator (Bakker et al., ). The fact that the results of our study were obtained from a specialized fetal medicine center and thus all procedures in the study were either undertaken or directly supervised by fetal medicine specialists may have contributed to the avoidance of fetal loss. Indeed, both the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) emphasize the importance of both pre‐ and posttest counseling as essential components of prenatal genetic testing (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’ Committee on Practice Bulletins—Obstetrics; Committee on Genetics; Society for Maternal‐Fetal Medicine, ; Dungan et al., ). The purpose of pre‐ and postgenetic test counseling is to ensure patient‐informed consent and autonomous decision‐making (Rink & Kuller, ). In fact, in Turkey, no standard procedure is currently applicable for genetic counseling regarding prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for T21 during antenatal care. The primary obstetrical provider (obstetrician and family practice provider) is the initial source of information for patients about genetic testing. There are no special training and/or certificate programs for genetic counseling by non‐physicians. Clinical geneticists (with the addition of a medical genetic residency or pediatric genetic fellowship training after pediatric residency) are employed in the tertiary genetic centers as ‘Genetic Counselors’. Furthermore, most pregnant women in Turkey meet genetic counselors, when they are diagnosed as “high‐risk for T21.” This timing is too late to counsel couples about prenatal genetic screening and diagnostic testing. Studies from Turkey affirm that women do not have enough knowledge to be able to make an informed decision concerning prenatal screening and diagnostic testing (Seven et al., , ). In fact, there are no national guidelines/policies for NIPT in Turkey. Self‐financed NIPT is offered by obstetricians as either a first‐line screening test or pregnancies at intermediate risk of T21 after first‐ or second‐trimester screening test results through private clinics and NIPT performance does not require genetic counseling. Therefore, the couples are not exposed to the information and understanding of the limitations of NIPT which potentially compromises the couple's autonomy in prenatal decisions. There are several limitations of this study. First, the study cohort is biased selectively due to the retrospective analysis of pregnancies at intermediate risk of T21 that had undergone diagnostic testing. Second, the specific maternal serum screening risk was not determined through a standard test but through first‐trimester tests, triple tests, and quadruple tests. Another limitation was the lack of CMA results for pregnant women at intermediate risk for T21 which could detect critical anomalies not detected in karyotyping and could impact neonates in the future. The theoretical definition of NIPT‐detectable findings may be inaccurate because this technique has false‐negative and false‐positive rates. In addition, some pregnancies with NIPT‐detectable aberrations may result in miscarriage prior to amniocentesis. Unfortunately, data on later prenatal and postnatal follow‐up were not available. Finally, additional factors could potentially influence the residual risk such as ethnicity, maternal weight, or paternal age. Given these limitations and considering the biases of the cohort with diagnostic testing, the results may not be generalizable to general population at intermediate risk for T21. A randomized clinical trial in a larger cohort is needed to objectively evaluate the additional contribution of karyotyping in pregnancies at intermediate risk for T21. Nevertheless, our results show that in pregnancies at intermediate risk for T21 without major structural anomalies detected in sonography, low‐risk NIPT results still carry a residual risk of chromosomal abnormalities detected by karyotyping. This knowledge is important for the patients, obstetricians, and genetic counselors to facilitate informed decisions regarding prenatal testing and screening options.

title: Callosal Injuries in Cytomegalovirus Fetopathy: A Neurosonographic Study.
label_reason: 72 CMV fetuses with US brain anomalies (ventriculomegaly, callosal), all had CMA/exome (negative) and amniotic CMV-PCR; per-case table.
abstract: Among the fetal brain anomalies described in cases of congenital infection, callosal insults are rarely cited in medical literature. The aim of this study was to describe the rate and pattern of callosal injury in cytomegalovirus (CMV) fetopathy. This retrospective study included fetuses with confirmed CMV-PCR, assessed in a single center. Demographic data including maternal seroconversion info were collected. Dedicated US including neurosonography was performed, with high frequency probes, using TV route whenever feasible. Fetal brain biometry including callosal length and the corpus callosum (CC)/OFD ratio was performed. Length below the 5th centile or morphological abnormalities were considered abnormal. Brain and body morphology were thoroughly assessed, and any abnormal finding reported. Seventy-two patients were included in our cohort. In 76% infection occurred in the 1st T or periconceptional. In 12 patients, the exact time of infection was inconclusive, including two cases of secondary infection. In 34.7%, a callosal anomaly was observed and it was never isolated. CNS abnormalities included: periventricular hyperechogenicity (PVHE) 55.5%, calcifications 52%, ventriculomegaly 33%, periventricular pseudocysts 31.4%, occipital cysts 22.2%, echogenic ganglionic eminence 30.5%, lentostriatal vasculopathy 26.4%, sulcation abnormalities 22.2%, cerebellar findings 18% and HC below −2 SD 18%. In 19 cases, the CC was short with calcifications in four. In one case, the insult was severe and in another the CC was absent. The most common association with CC insult was PVHE (56%) and calcifications (52%). Although not referred as a classic brain structure affected by CMV infection, the CC was injured in one-third of our patients, including cases of late infection. The mechanism of disease and the prenatal patterns of callosal involvement in these cases appear to be different from the postnatal patterns and are not reversible. The presence of a callosal injury would imply a worse prognosis and significant increment to the risk of neurodevelopmental impairment.
