title: Inherited Unbalanced Reciprocal Translocation with 18p11.32p11.21 Tetrasomy and 9q34.3 Trisomy in a Fetus Revealed by Cell-Free Fetal DNA (cffDNA) Testing: Cytogenetic and Cytogenomic Characterization in Prenatal Diagnosis.
label_reason: Pelvic kidney on US; fetal karyotype after NIPT.
abstract: Background/Objective: Balanced reciprocal translocations are structural chromosomal anomalies that involve a mutual exchange of segments between two non-homologous chromosomes with a consequent 50–80% risk of conceiving fetuses with unbalanced chromosomal anomalies. This study describes a 37-year-old woman, at 13 + 5 weeks of gestation, who is a balanced reciprocal translocation 46,XX,t(9;18)(q34;q11.2) carrier, with a high-risk non-invasive prenatal screening test, NIPT, for chromosome 18 aneuploidy. Methods: The highlighted aneuploidy was characterized with cytogenetic, FISH and SNP-array techniques. Results: Cytogenetic analysis, performed on flask-cultured amniocytes, indicated a 48,XX,+2mar karyotype on 50 metaphases. SNP array analysis showed a 15.3 Mb duplication of chromosome 18p (arr[hg19]18p11.32-p11.21(12,842-15,303,932)x4), consistent with a partial tetrasomy 18p, and a 926 kbp duplication of chromosome 9q (arr[GRCh37]9q34.3(140,118,286-141,044,489)x3), consistent with partial trisomy 9q. FISH analysis with a 9q34.3 probe was performed on flask-cultured amniocytes’ metaphases, highlighting the presence of a third signal on one of the two marker chromosomes (18p11.32-p11.21). Conclusions: The evidence of such partial aneuploidies suggests that different mutational events may be possible at meiotic segregation or probably post-meiotic segregation. The results obtained highlight the high sensitivity of the screening test, NIPT, with massive parallel sequencing, and the usefulness of cytogenetics, cytogenomics and molecular biology techniques, in synergy, to characterize and confirm positive NIPT results. Keywords: inherited unbalanced reciprocal translocation, non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), prenatal diagnosis, SNP-array analysis
text:
Inherited Unbalanced Reciprocal Translocation with 18p11.32p11.21 Tetrasomy and 9q34.3 Trisomy in a Fetus Revealed by Cell-Free Fetal DNA (cffDNA) Testing: Cytogenetic and Cytogenomic Characterization in Prenatal Diagnosis

1. Introduction
1. Introduction Reciprocal balanced translocations (RBT) are structural chromosomal anomalies characterized by two breaks on two non-homologous chromosomes and by the mutual exchange of the affected segments, without loss or gain of genetic material. The RBT carrier is a phenotypically normal individual; however, the carrier may manifest a pathological phenotype if the translocation breakpoints involve a dominant gene or interfere with the expression of immediately neighboring genes []. Indeed, birth defects and/or neurodevelopmental disorders and mental disorders have been observed in approximately 27% of patients with de novo RBT [], and all individuals with RBT are at risk of reproductive problems. Balanced reciprocal translocations have a frequency of 1/500 (approximately 0.5–0.2%) in the general population. They are diagnosed due to infertility, multiple abortions (RPL), stillbirth, or the presence of congenital anomalies and unbalanced karyotype at birth [,]. In 6.6% of couples with multiple abortions, one of the two members of the couple is a carrier of RBT [,,]. The frequency of RBT is ~1.3% in infertile males [,]. Meiotic segregation of a balanced reciprocal translocation can produce balanced and unbalanced gametes as a consequence of five possible types of segregation. At meiosis I, after the gametogenesis, to achieve the pairing of homologues, the chromosomes arrange themselves forming a quadrivalent which undergoes segregation through five possible modes: alternate, adjacent-1, adjacent-2, 3:1 or 4:0 []. Alternating segregation produces balanced gametes. Adjacent-1, adjacent-2, 3:1, and 4:0 segregations produce unbalanced gametes. It is not easy to predict how an RBT will segregate because many factors are involved, including: (a) the type of chromosome involved and its size; (b) the size of the segments involved in the translocation; (c) the position of the breakpoints; (d) the genetic content; (e) the patient’s sex and other aspects []. It is likely that many segregation events that produce chromosomal imbalances may not be detected if they cause infertility or early embryonic death. RBT carriers produce approximately 10–20% euploid embryos [,]. Several studies [] on meiotic segregation patterns have identified different elements that can influence the imbalances of reciprocal translocations, such as the sex and age of the carrier, the location of breakpoints, the type of chromosome and the quadrivalent structure [,,,,]. Some studies have analyzed meiotic segregation in blastocysts using comprehensive chromosome screening (CCS) [,,], demonstrating that segregation in blastocysts could be influenced by the presence of acrocentric chromosomes and terminal breakpoints, rather than the carrier sex [], suggesting that, in the female group, there was a higher percentage of blastocysts with an unbalanced rearrangement than males. A 3:1 segregation appears to be more frequent in the female group and in the presence of an acrocentric chromosome (Acr-ch) []. In support of this observation, studies on gametes and embryos have highlighted that the sex of a carrier can influence the various modes of meiotic segregation and that the male carrier has a higher percentage of alternating segregation [,]. However, literature data reported that the proportions of adjacent-1, adjacent-2 or 3:1 segregations were significantly different in male and female carriers, while for alternating segregation, no difference was observed [,,,,]. Although prenatal diagnosis can highlight the imbalances obtained from the malsegregation of a balanced translocation, the risk of miscarriage associated with these procedures cannot be excluded []. Imbalances in these translocations can also be detected by cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA)-based screening (NIPT) as reported in several studies [,,]. In these cases, the result is a partial deletion and duplication. Recently, Flowers et al. presented their experience on screening pairs of RBT carriers, analyzing whole genome cell-free DNA-based non-invasive prenatal screening (gw-NIPS) []. Here, we describe a prenatal case with unusual structural chromosome rearrangements evidenced by NIPT and characterized with cytogenetic and cytogenomic techniques.

2. Materials and Methods
2. Materials and Methods 2.1. cffDNA Isolation from Plasma and NIPT Analysis For NIPS analysis, streck blood collection tubes were used to collect about 10 mL of peripheral blood from the pregnant women. Firstly, the blood sample was centrifuged at 1600× g for 10 min at 4 °C to separate the maternal plasma from peripheral blood cells. Then, 900 μL of plasma was used to extract cell-free DNA using the QIAamp DNA Blood MiniKit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol. NIPT analysis was performed using the VeriSeq NIPT Solution v2 pipeline (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) according to which the pregnant woman can choose to have the results as Basic, with reporting for common autosomal trisomies and sex chromosomes aneuploidies (SCA) (if selected), or as genome-wide analysis if the detection of the genome-wide fetal anomalies were included (including rare autosomal aneuploidies and partial deletions and duplications ≥ 7 Mb) [,]. Sample results were classified using the VeriSeq NIPT Solution v2 Assay Software (https://emea.support.illumina.com, accessed on 15 November 2021) (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) and analysis of “raw data” was performed, as reported previously [,]. 2.2. DNA Extraction, QF-PCR and Karyotype Analysis Genomic DNA was extracted from the amniocyte using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany)). The quantitative fluorescent polymerase chain reaction test for rapid aneuploidy detection was performed, using the Devyser Compactv3 QF-PCR kit (QF-PCR; Devyser Compactv3, Devyser, Stockholm, Sweden) as previously described []. GTG-banding analysis of amniotic fluid was performed in established cell culture following standard laboratory protocols. Then, 50 metaphases were analyzed with the CytoVision software (CytoVision Version 7.6, Leica Biosystems, Richmond, IL, USA CytoVision). Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) was performed on flask-cultured amniocytes’ metaphases. An RP11-644H13 FISH Probe (GRCh37/hg19: 140535110-140719726, Empire Genomics Green) (9q34 locus-specific probe, labelled in red), was used to highlight the partial trisomy 9q34.3). FISH slides were examined by using the LEICA DM5500 B fluorescent microscope (Tokyo, Japan) and analyzed with the CytoVision software (CytoVision Version 7.6, Leica Biosystems, Richmond, IL, USA CytoVision). Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP array) analysis was performed using the HumanCytoSNP-12v12.1 kit following the manufacturer’s protocol https://emea.support.illumina.com/, accessed on 25 November 2021). Stained BeadChips were scanned using a HiScan (Illumina, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). GenomeStudio and Bluefuse Multi Software v.4.5 (Illumina, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) were used to perform, respectively, the generation of data and analysis of the results. All CNVs > 100 Kb were interrogated. All results were reported according to GRCh37 (hg19) assembly.

3. Case Report and Results
3. Case Report and Results A 37-year-old Caucasian woman came to the attention of the Ames Laboratory for NIPT testing at 13 + 5 weeks of gestation. The pregnant woman reported a history of multiple miscarriages in the maternal branch and that her brother, with a cleft palate and left preauricular appendix, died a few days after birth due to cardio-respiratory failure. Moreover, her mother had two miscarriages for unknown causes. The pregnant woman and her husband, following a repeated abortion, performed a constitutional karyotyping at another genetic laboratory. The husband’s karyotype was normal, while the woman’s karyotype highlighted a balanced reciprocal translocation involving the long arm of chromosome 9 and the long arm of chromosome 18: 46, XX, t(9;18) (q34;q11.2). The pregnant woman had a first pregnancy, which terminated in IVG, because of an unbalanced t(9;18), and a second pregnancy ended in a miscarriage. The couple had a healthy child with a balanced reciprocal translocation t(9;18), completely similar to the maternal one. For the pregnancy described, the first-trimester ultrasound findings, at 12 + 4 weeks, were normal with a nuchal translucency (NT) of 1.9mm. Threats of abortion were reported in the first few weeks and treated with progesterone therapy for a month. The woman decided to perform the NIPT screening test for previous miscarriages. NIPT analysis showed a high risk for duplication on chromosome 18: dup(18)(p11.32q11.2) and a fetal fraction of 7% (A). In addition, the observed LLR scores for trisomy 18 in the “raw data” were lower than expected in the chromosomes 18 with trisomy 18 (internal validated data) and the case was considered a complex chromosomal abnormality. In light of this result, the woman decided to confirm the aneuploidy T18, undergoing amniotic fluid sampling at 16 + 0 weeks. QF-PCR for the trisomies 13, 18, 21 and sex chromosomes’ aneuploidies showed partial trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 18. (A). NIPT results: WISECONDOR plot showing the abnormal NIPT result with a duplication of the short arm of chromosome 18. (B). GTG banding on amniotic fluid cultured cells’ metaphases showed a 48,XX,+2mar karyotype. Red arrow indicates the two markers. The fetal G-banding karyotype analysis, performed on flask-cultured amniocytes, highlighted a karyotype 48,XX,+2mar on 50 metaphases (B). Cytogenomic characterization was thus performed to define the nature of the markers using the SNP-array test. SNP array analysis on uncultured amniocytes showed a 15.3 Mb duplication of the chromosome 18p (arr[hg19]18p11.32-p11.21(12,842-15,303,932)x4) consistent with a partial tetrasomy 18p and a 926 kbp duplication of chromosome 9q (arr[GRCh37] 9q34.3(140,118,286-141,044,489)x3) consistent with a partial trisomy 9q (A). FISH analysis was performed on flask-cultured amniocytes’ metaphases and highlighted the presence of a third signal on one of the two marker chromosomes (18p11.32-p11.21) (B). (A). SNP-array analysis on uncultered amniocytes showed a 15.3 Mb duplication of the chromosome 18p (arr[hg19]18p11.32-p11.21(12,842-15,303,932)x4) and a 926 kbp duplication of chromosome 9q (arr[GRCh37]9q34.3(140,118,286-141,044,489)x3). Stained BeadChips were scanned using a HiScan System (Illumina). (B). FISH analysis was performed with the RP11-644H13 FISH Probe (GRCh37/hg19: 140535110-140719726, Empire Genomics Green) on flask-cultured amniocytes’ metaphases. A positive 9q34.3 green signal indicated by the arrow is found at the terminal segment of one of the two marker chromosomes (18p11.32-p11.21) (LEICA DM5500 B fluorescence microscope) and analyzed with the CytoVision software (CytoVision, AB Imaging). An ultrasound scan, performed at 19 weeks, showed an empty right renal lodge with a kidney located in the ipsilateral pelvis. After the genetic counseling, the couple decided to terminate the pregnancy at 19 + 4 weeks. Unfortunately, no autopsy was performed on the fetus.

4. Discussion
4. Discussion Reciprocal translocations are the most common structural chromosomal abnormalities resulting from the mutual exchange of non-homologous chromosome segments. They are present in 0.14% of the neonatal population and in 0.6% of infertile couples [,]. Carriers of a balanced reciprocal translocation are at risk of producing unbalanced gametes which, after being fertilized, can lead to the formation of an embryo with an unbalanced karyotype due to the presence of partial trisomies and/or monosomies []. In the present study, we described a fetal karyotype, following a high-risk NIPT test for trisomy 18, with a partial tetrasomy 18p and a partial trisomy 9q, originating in part from malsegregation of a balanced maternal reciprocal translocation (t(9;18)(q34; q11.2)) and whose evidence suggests that different mutational events may be possible. Meiotic segregation of a balanced reciprocal translocation can lead to the formation of balanced and unbalanced gametes, as a consequence of five possible types of segregation: alternate, adjacent-1, adjacent-2, 3:1 or 4:0 (both at meiotic segregation) []. In light of the results obtained in our case, it is conceivable to hypothesize that the gametogenesis of the female carrier of the balanced reciprocal translocation t(9;18) occurred with 3:1 segregation. We hypothesize that during 3:1 maternal segregation, a gamete with 24 chromosomes could be formed, due to the presence of an additional chromosome marker: der(18)t(9;18)(q34;q11.2). In our case, the maternal gamete, fertilized by a presumably normal paternal gamete, generated a zygote with 47 chromosomes with an additional chromosome marker: der(18)t(9;18)(q34;q11.2). Consequently, it may follow that the zygote thus formed should have a partial trisomy 18p11.32p11.21 region and 9q34.3 region. FISH analysis with the 9q34 telomeric probe highlighted the presence of a signal on the terminal segment of one of the two marker chromosomes, identified as 18p. From the tests performed and possible at the time of the genetic investigations, however, it was not easy to find proof of the origin of the second marker, der(18)(p11.32p11.21), also given the difficulty of being able to further study the biological samples of the two parents. Therefore, it is only conceivable that: (a) a nonallelic homologous recombination (NAHR) may have occurred during maternal meiosis; (b) a mitotic non-disjunction in the embryo with subsequent NAHR; (c) a possible gonadal mosaicism, both maternal and paternal. In a study, meiotic segregation modes of structural rearrangements highlighted in blastocyst biopsies, obtained from individuals carrying balanced reciprocal and balanced translocations, obtained by PGT, were analyzed, and it was seen that there is a greater incidence of 3:1 segregation in the translocations in which there are involved acrocentric chromosomes [], which was consistent with studies from the Lim [] and Ye [] groups. The authors also take into consideration the importance of an interchromosomal effect (ICE) which could disturb the correct pairing and disjunction of other chromosomes during meiosis I and, as a consequence of this, could lead to chromosomal numerical anomalies which are not present translocation []. This study demonstrated that non-translocated chromosomal abnormalities were significantly higher in translocations not involving acrocentric chromosomes compared to translocations with acrocentric chromosomes, suggesting that ICE may be influenced by the chromosome types involved in the translocation. What the authors report could help us interpret and explain the presence of the second chromosomal marker in the fetal karyotype. In almost all the cases described in the literature, tetrasomy 18p was derived from an additional isochromosome of the short arm of chr18, (i(18p)), whereas our case presents a partial tetrasomy of the short arm of chromosome 18 (p11.3p11.2). Tetrasomy 18p syndrome (OMIM#614,290) is a very rare chromosomal disorder with a prevalence between 1/140,000 and 1/180,000 [] and affects both sexes equally. Most tetrasomy 18p cases are “de novo” and maternal meiosis II nondisjunction [] origin of trisomy 18p is a rare condition [,,,]. Individuals with tetrasomy 18p clinically present developmental delay, cognitive impairment, microcephaly, hypertonia, strabismus, and scoliosis/kyphosis []. The prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of tetrasomy 18p syndrome is difficult due to the absence of specific morphologic features. Therefore, ultrasound examination in synergy with a prenatal genetic test is an effective method for the diagnosis of tetrasomy 18p. In the case we are describing, amniocentesis was performed to confirm the positive NIPT result. Actually, the woman, as a carrier of an apparently balanced reciprocal translocation, should have chosen an invasive genetic test, but due to her personal and family history of repeated miscarriage, she preferred a non-invasive prenatal screening test, NIPT, despite being aware of the problem of fetal-placental mosaicism that this test may present. However, the ultrasound performed during the second trimester of pregnancy did not highlight any clinical signs attributable to chromosomal aneuploidy, perhaps due to the early gestational age or the limitations of ultrasound. Furthermore, the ultrasound examination did not reveal any signs relating to partial trisomy 9q34. Indeed, individuals described with dup 9q34 present with mild psychomotor retardation, low birth weight, normal length at birth and poor initial feeding and growth, joint contractures, long thin limbs, evident arachnodactyly, abnormal thumb implantation, increased space between the first and second toes and an excess of digital creases, erythema and heart murmurs, ptosis and strabismus, dolichocephaly, facial asymmetry, narrow horizontal palpebral fissures, microphthalmia, prominent nasal bridge, small mouth, thin upper lip with downturned corners, and mild retrognathia [,,,]. Other reports of cases of trisomy 9q34.1qter were the result of unbalanced segregation of reciprocal translocations and therefore associated with some other chromosome imbalance [,,,,,]. In light of the results obtained and after genetic counselling the woman decided to terminate the pregnancy. Unfortunately, no autopsy was performed on the fetus; thus, we cannot add partial phenotype to this report. The NIPT test, despite being a screening test, in the case described, proved to be highly sensitive, highlighting the possible presence of an aneuploidy of chromosome 18, confirmed by the cytogenomic results. In addition to trisomy 13, 18 and 21, NIPT can detect structural chromosomal abnormalities, such as deletions and duplications [,], although in our case, the 926 kbp duplication was not identified by NIPT due to size limitations. Our case confirms the high sensitivity of NIPT, based on genome-wide massive parallel sequencing for chromosome 18, in that a triplicated p-arm (four copies) of chromosome 18 corresponding to an NCV of approximately 40% increased in respect to the fetal fraction of DNA compared to that of a full trisomy 18, giving significant risk for chromosome 18 aneuploidy by NIPT. Chromosomal microarray and FISH on amniocytes confirmed that the increased NCV for chromosome 18 was due to fetal tetrasomy 18p and not to maternal mosaicism. In addition, a 926 kbp duplication of chromosome 9q was found, which suggests that different mutational events may be possible, probably at segregation or post-meiotic time. The use of the cytogenetics, cytogenomics and molecular biology techniques, in synergy, helps to characterize and confirm the positive NIPT results.

5. Conclusions
5. Conclusions In this case report, we present a fetus with an unexpected structural chromosomal abnormality suspected by routine basic non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) including trisomy 13, 18 and 21 in a high-risk first-trimester pregnancy. The evidence of such partial aneuploidies suggests that different mutational events may be possible, at meiotic segregation and/or perhaps post-meiotic time. This case confirms the high sensitivity of NIPT, based on genome-wide massive parallel sequencing for common aneuploidies, as well as for the detection of sub-chromosomal abnormalities. The use of the cytogenetics, cytogenomics and the molecular biology techniques, in synergy, help to characterize and confirm the positive NIPT results.

title: Prenatal ultrasound assisted diagnosis of de-novo terminal 7q deletion syndrome: A case report with literature review.

abstract: Terminal 7q deletion is a rare chromosomal anomaly resulting from partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7. 7q terminal deletion syndrome results in variable clinical phenotypes, such as microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, craniofacial abnormalities, sacral hypoplasia, etc. We report a case of prenatal diagnosis of this syndrome with multiple abnormalities including holoprosencephaly and other craniofacial anomalies seen on ultrasound seen at NT scan. Pregnancy was terminated and chromosomal microarray showed ∼5.5 MB deletion in chromosome 7 spanning the 7q36.2-36.3 region. In addition, a literature review was done to enlist the various prenatal ultrasound features of this rare syndrome.
text:
Prenatal ultrasound assisted diagnosis of de-novo terminal 7q deletion syndrome: A case report with literature review

Introduction
Introduction Terminal 7q deletion or distal 7q monosomy is a rare chromosomal anomaly worldwide resulting from partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 []. Due to the small number of cases documented in the literature, the precise incidence of the illness is unknown. Holoprosencephaly (HPE), microcephaly, intrauterine growth retardation, sacral dysgenesis, cranial-facial abnormalities, and other traits are among the key hallmarks of the widely diverse phenotype of the condition []. We present a case of several prenatal ultrasonography abnormalities seen during the NT scan. After the pregnancy terminated, the abortus underwent chromosomal microarray (CMA), which revealed a ∼5.5 MB deletion in the 7q36.2-36.3 region of chromosome 7. We also reviewed the literature to compare the different prenatal ultrasonography characteristics of this uncommon disease. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of terminal 7q deletion syndrome from the Indian subcontinent that has been documented. Furthermore, our case is unique in that the ultrasound abnormalities were identified at the time of the NT scan.

Case report
Case report A 27-year-old primigravida visited our ultrasound center at 12 weeks 6 days of gestation for an NT scan. The patient was a nonsmoker, and nonalcoholic. She was overweight with a body mass index of 28.9. There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, or thyroid disorders. There was no history of any prior abortion. Marriage was nonconsanguineous without any family history of any structural abnormalities. Her viability scan showed a single live embryo with a normal heart rate at 7 weeks. At NT scan the ultrasound showed a singleton fetus with alobar holoprosencephaly (, ), subcutaneous edema over the upper body () with NT measuring 1.7mm corresponding to 48th centile, hypotelorism (), cleft palate (), absent nasal bone, and single umbilical artery (SUA). Trisomy 13 was suspected based on sonography. (A) Ultrasound transthalamic view of the fetal head shows monoventricle (white arrow) with absent anterior falx and fused thalami (yellow arrow). (B) Ultrasound transventricular view of the fetal head shows monoventricle (white arrow) with absent anterior falx and fused echogenic choroid plexus (yellow arrow). Fig 1 ( Ultrasound axial view of the fetal head shows subcutaneous edema (white arrow). Fig 2: Ultrasound coronal view of the fetal face shows hypotelorism with closely placed orbits. Fig 3: Ultrasound mid-sagittal view of the fetal face shows a defect in the hard palate, maxillary gap sign (white arrow) with absent nasal bone (orange arrow). Fig 4: The patient opted for termination of pregnancy. A fetal autopsy () was performed which showed multiple craniofacial abnormalities including holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and cleft palate, low-set ears, largemouth, and single umbilical artery. Chromosomal microarray () was also performed on the product of conception which showed ∼5.5 MB deletion in chromosome 7 spanning 7q36.2-36.3 region. Parental karyotyping done to exclude balanced translocation was normal. Anterior and posterior profiles of the delivered fetus. Fig 5: Karyoview of the CMA analysis showing ∼5.5 MB deletion in chromosome 7 spanning 7q36.2-36.3 region. Fig 6:

Discussion
Discussion A partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 causes the rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome known as terminal 7q deletion syndrome, also known as distal 7q36 monosomy. The syndrome's highly variable phenotype includes holoprosencephaly, developmental delay, growth restriction, facial abnormalities, ocular abnormalities, and other congenital malformations. Cardiopathies have also been described seldom []. Patients with terminal 7q deletion syndrome have been documented in the literature, along with descriptions of their variable phenotypes. Nonetheless, the majority of case reports describe the diseases that are discovered after birth without a prenatal ultrasound diagnosis. Only a few cases describing the antenatal ultrasound features associated with terminal 7q deletion syndrome have been reported. Following a thorough review of the literature on PubMed, 5 examples documenting the prenatal ultrasound characteristics of this syndrome were found. provides a summary of the cases. At 23 weeks gestation, Song et al. [] reported a case of 7q deletion with an isolated ultrasonography finding of hemivertebra causing scoliosis in the lower thoracic spine. No other ultrasound abnormalities were seen and the patient chose to terminate the pregnancy. In a case of 21 weeks gestation, Zhao et al. [] reported intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), subcutaneous cystic mass in the neck, congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), cleft lip, cleft palate, and HPE on prenatal ultrasonography. Pregnancy was terminated and genetic testing showed a loss at 7q32.3qter. Chen et al. [] reported a case of 7q35 deletion associated with IUGR, tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), and microcephaly at 22 weeks of gestation on prenatal ultrasonography. Hallmark craniofacial abnormalities such as HPE or cleft lip/palate were absent. Prenatal ultrasound signs of HPE, proboscis, cyclopia, and IUGR were reported at 23 weeks in a case with partial trisomy 3p and monosomy 7q, according to a case report by Chen et al. []. At 15 weeks of gestation, Chen et al [] reported a case of distal 3p duplication and terminal 7q deletion which was associated with nuchal edema, HPE, and cyclopia in a fetus seen on antenatal ultrasound. The antenatal ultrasound findings of this syndrome at an NT scan have only been documented in our case. This suggests that severe anomalies like HPE, cleft palate, and absent nasal bone can be detected as early as 12-13 weeks of pregnancy. Thus, our example demonstrates that anomalies related to this defect can be found on prenatal ultrasound at 12-13 weeks of gestation, allowing for prompt care and well-informed decision-making. The most frequent ultrasonography abnormality in the 6 cases, including ours, was holoprosencephaly, which was detected in 4 (67%) of the cases, followed by IUGR in 3 (50%) cases, cleft palate in 2 (33%) cases, and cyclopia (33%) in 2 cases. In our case, there was just 1 umbilical artery and no nasal bone, which have not yet been documented in the literature. It is our novel observation that terminal 7q deletion syndrome shows overlapping ultrasound features with Trisomy 13 or Patau syndrome []. Both can present with HPE, cyclopia, hypotelorism, cleft lip and palate, CDH, SUA, and IUGR. In our instance, hypotelorism, cleft palate, and alobar HPE were the overlapping features. To distinguish between the 2, fetal autopsy or invasive testing is required.

Conclusion
Conclusion In summary, our case exhibited both novel features—such as a missing nasal bone and a single umbilical artery—and the conventional ultrasound characteristics of 7q syndrome, such as holoprosencephaly, cleft palate, and hypotelorism, thereby extending the phenotypic of 7q- syndrome prenatal ultrasonography. Our results and the literature research show that HPE and craniofacial abnormalities are the primary ultrasonography characteristics of 7q- syndrome. There may be traits that overlap with Trisomy 13, thus the differential needs to be taken into account. The abnormal findings can be picked up as early as an NT scan. For patients with abnormal prenatal ultrasound results, genetic analysis must be carried out to expeditiously guide management and decision-making.

Patient consent
Patient consent A written and informed consent was obtained from the parents for publication of this case report.

title: Bilateral ulnar longitudinal deficiency with oligodactyly in newborn.
label_reason: Postnatal newborn ulnar deficiency case.
abstract: The objective of this study was to report a case of bilateral ulnar longitudinal deficiency with oligodactyly in a male newborn. A full-term male newborn, born following an uncomplicated gestation with no abnormalities detected on prenatal ultrasounds, presented upper limb malformations described as shortening of the left forearm and absence of three digits bilaterally upon neonatal physical examination. Diagnostic investigations including X-rays, abdominal ultrasound, head ultrasound, echocardiogram, and karyotype analysis were conducted, facilitating detailed identification of the malformations and exclusion of other anomalies, thereby suggesting the diagnosis of congenital longitudinal deficiency of the ulna. Discharge planning encompassed supportive care and rehabilitation as per the patient’s needs. Ulnar longitudinal deficiency is a rare congenital upper limb malformation, whose estimated incidence is 1:100,000 newborns. It is believed to be related to the Sonic Hedgehog gene, and the upper limb anomalies vary according to the ulnar involvement. The early diagnosis is not routine, being more common at the first physical examination with the aid of imaging tests. Keywords: Malformations, Upper limbs, Hemimelia, Genetics, Hand deformities
text:
Bilateral ulnar longitudinal deficiency with oligodactyly in newborn

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Ulnar longitudinal deficiency (ULD) is a rare and sporadic congenital malformation of the upper limbs, characterized by partial or complete ulnar absence. Also known as “ulnar club hand,” “congenital ulnar hemimelia,” or “postaxial longitudinal deficiency of the upper limb,” the ULD is probably related to an interruption of the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene, responsible for the ulnar-sided forearm structure formation, thought to occur during weeks 4 and 5 of fetal development. , Usually, ULD is an isolated condition and is rarely associated with internal organs malformations or systemic syndromes. Although other skeletal malformations are frequently seen, such as congenital short femur, phocomelia, fibular hemimelia, congenital scoliosis, and digital abnormalities. The patient’s hand is normally hypoplastic, and 90% of cases have missing digits, but other conditions like syndactyly, thumb abnormalities, rotated metacarpals, and hypoplastic tendons and muscles can appear. , In addition to the clinical findings, the diagnosis might be confirmed with a radiological study of the affected body parts. There are two relevant classifications for ulnar longitudinal deficiency: the modified Bayne’s system to describe forearm and elbow deformities, and, for hand ones, the most accepted classification is from Cole and Manske. , The treatment can be surgical or conservative, depending on how severe the involvement of the arm is, including the elbow and forearm anomalies classification, as well as hand position and presence of digital abnormalities.

CASE REPORT
CASE REPORT A male newborn was delivered by cesarean section at 40 weeks due to fetal distress. Mother was 25 years old and had three other children, all healthy and without any abnormalities. Mother was up to date on vaccinations and took iron and folic acid supplements during the current pregnancy. She denied addictions or a family history of malformation. She attended eight prenatal visits without complications, with all her serologies negative, no risk of maternal-fetal blood incompatibility, and no abnormalities found on the morphological ultrasound. Through neonatal physical examination at birth, the neonatologist noticed malformation of both hands and left forearm, described as absence of three fingers on both hands and shortening of the left forearm (). Further investigation with X-rays confirmed left ulnar absence along with a deformed radius, dislocation of the elbow joint, and bilateral absence of the third, fourth, and fifth digits and metacarpi. Karyotype, echocardiogram, abdominal and head ultrasounds, and computed tomography (CT) of the head and spine were normal. (A) Newborn with upper limbs malformations. (B) Right upper limb. Forearm with preserved flexion and absence of three fingers on the right hand. (C) Left upper limb showing shortening and rotation of the left forearm, ulnar deviation of the left hand, and the absence of three fingers. These malformations demonstrate ULD’s characteristics and exhibit one of the most common dysplasias of the ulna: the Ulnar Club Hand. The set of clinical findings and radiological results found in the case determined the diagnosis of ulnar longitudinal deficiency, and, after 4 days of care, the mother and the infant were discharged. As management, the newborn was referred to a neurologist, a geneticist, and an orthopedist for follow-up, showing expected development for his age currently.

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION Ulnar longitudinal deficiency (ULD) is one of the rarest malformations of the upper limbs, which has the radial longitudinal deficiency (RLD) as the most common deficiency. ULD has an estimated incidence of 1:100,000 newborns, four to ten times less usual than RLD. Previously known as ulnar club hand, this condition is marked by underdevelopment or absence of the ulna bone. Common clinical findings during a physical exam are shortening of the forearm and ulnar deviation of the hand. ULD is generally isolated, and systemic findings are unusual. However, it can be associated with other skeletal malformations, such as digital abnormalities. ,, Congenital limb defects can be divided into two categories: transverse and longitudinal defects. Longitudinal limb deficiencies refer to hypoplasia or the complete absence of a bone — or several bones — parallel to the axis of the limb. Radial and Ulnar Longitudinal deficiencies are the most common types of congenital limb defects. , ULD represents a set of abnormalities that affect the ulnar margin of the upper extremity, in which upper arm and forearm deformities follow the ulnar longitudinal axis, although structures of the radial margin can be affected as well. About 70% of the ULD presentations are unilateral, mostly right-sided, and incomplete, with a common presentation including a shortened forearm, ulnar-sided hand deviation, radial head subluxation, and fixed flexion deformity of the elbow joint. , Usually, the hand is hypoplastic, and about 90% of the patients have absent fingers. The etiologies of congenital limb malformations are frequently related to the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene pathway, responsible for the anteroposterior developmental axis. Embryologically, disrupting the production of SHH from the zone of polarizing activity posteriorizes the developing limb, and the SHH deficiency explains the finger anomalies that may occur in cases of ULD. Since the SHH is also responsible for developing four ulnar-sided digits, its lack of function causes digit loss. ULD can appear isolated but can also be associated with other skeletal malformations. Differential diagnoses include Holt-Oram syndrome, Aase-Smith syndrome, Thrombocytopenia and absent radius syndrome (TAR), Levy-Hollister syndrome, Weyers ulnar ray-oligodactyly, Femur-fibula-ulna complex, Ulnar hypoplasia-split foot syndrome, Cornelia de Lange Syndrome, and Ulnar-mammary syndrome (). - However, due to the predominantly syndromic nature of these pathologies, they can be ruled out in the reported patient’s case. Genetic counseling and molecular genetic testing could be useful for excluding these syndromes, though the ULD’s diagnosis is mostly clinical and confirmed by a radiological study. The early diagnosis of ULD and other upper limb differences is not usual. Even though fetal ultrasound is a crucial tool for prenatal diagnosis of fetal anomalies, studies show that the overall sensitivity for detecting them is low. , Therefore, ULD is usually suspected by birth at the first physical examination. The main exam to confirm the diagnosis of ULD is the X-ray of the arm, forearm, and hand, where it will be possible to observe any anomalies present, including malformations or even the absence of one or more bones. There are two classifications used to differentiate the types of ULD: Bayne’s classification and Cole and Manske’s classification. ,, Bayne’s classification divides ULD into four different types: type I is the ulnar hypoplasia with normal epiphysis, type II has partial ulnar aplasia, and this is the most common type of ULD. Type III corresponds to complete ulnar absence plus carpal and digital anomalies. Type IV is related to radiohumeral synostosis. , On the contrary, Cole and Manske’s classification is divided into six types, in which type 0 represents a normal ulna with hand anomalies, type I hypoplastic ulna with the presence of both epiphyses, type II distal ulnar aplasia, type III complete ulnar aplasia, type IV radiohumeral synostosis, and type V proximal ULD. In the reported case, the left upper limb corresponds to Bayne’s classification IV and Cole and Manske’s classification C. Meanwhile, the right upper limb corresponds to Bayne’s classification 1 and Cole and Manske’s classification C (). (A) X-ray of the right upper limb corresponding to Bayne’s classification 1 and Cole and Manske’s classification C. (B) X-ray of the left upper limb corresponding to Bayne’s classification 4 and Cole and Manske’s classification C. Managing ULD cases can be complex and should be highly individualized. Operative or nonsurgical approaches could be chosen, depending on how severe the ulnar involvement is and the classification of the elbow and arm anomalies. Therefore, management includes referral to a geneticist, orthopedic, and plastic surgeon. Surgical intervention is employed as necessary to enhance limb functionality. In cases involving the hand, corrective procedures for syndactyly and reconstruction of the first commissure are conducted if required. For forearm issues such as hyperpronation or angular deformities, radial osteotomy is considered. In instances of distal ulnar absence, the option of constructing a single bone may arise. However, caution is advised against dissecting the radial head, as it could potentially destabilize the elbow.

title: Autosomal recessive renal tubular dysgenesis: antenatal ultrasound scanning and molecular investigations.
label_reason: Fetuses with ultrasound findings (oligohydramnios, renal) had WES, Sanger, CMA.
abstract: This study aimed to elucidate the fetal ultrasound characteristics, pathology, and molecular genetic etiology of autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia. This retrospective study examined four fetuses with autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia (ARRTD) from two pregnancies, utilizing ultrasound evaluations and fetal renal pathology. Whole-exome sequencing-copy number variation analysis was employed to identify gene mutations. We present for the first time renal vascular resistance in fetuses with ARRTD, characterized by increased renal blood flow resistance and reversed diastolic blood flow, indicating fetal renal insufficiency. This is the first report of a nonsense mutation (C.571C>T) found in the angiotensinogen gene. ARRTD disease should be strongly suspected when ultrasound examinations reveal increased renal blood flow resistance, oligohydramnios, and inadequate bladder filling, regardless of the presence of renal abnormalities. Keywords: angiotensinogen mutation, antenatal ultrasound, autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia, oligohydramnios
text:
Autosomal recessive renal tubular dysgenesis: antenatal ultrasound scanning and molecular investigations

Introduction
Introduction Autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia (ARRTD) is a rare and severe condition that primarily impacts fetal kidney development. This disorder is characterized by early-onset persistent anuria, which can result in oligohydramnios, intrauterine fetal death, or early neonatal death (; ; , ). The histopathological hallmark of ARRTD is the absence or hypoplasia of the proximal renal tubules (, ). Oligohydramnios causes compression of the fetus within the womb. This compression results in reduced intrauterine mobility, which can lead to facial deformities, joint deformities, limb movement defects, and lung hypoplasia. The fetus may be stillborn in utero, or the newborn may die from anuria and respiratory failure after birth (; , ). The genetic basis of ARRTD is attributed to mutations in genes that are integral to the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS). The RAAS is a hormonal system that plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure, extracellular volume, and renal blood flow and function. Key components of this system include angiotensinogen (AGT), renin (REN), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), and the angiotensin II receptor 1 (AGTR1). Among these components, mutations in the ACE gene are the most common cause of ARRTD (). Regardless of the specific genetic mutation involved, the severity of the disease remains consistent, suggesting that the RAAS system is pivotal in maintaining fetal blood pressure and renal blood perfusion. Given the severity of ARRTD disease, early detection of this condition is essential for effective prenatal diagnosis. By utilizing clinical assessments, ultrasound scans, and molecular genetic testing, we can identify ARRTD disease at an early stage, facilitating timely prenatal diagnosis and reproductive counseling. In this report, we present the prenatal ultrasound findings, genetic results, and pathological testing of four patients from two families. Our findings provide valuable insights into the prenatal diagnosis and management of ARRTD.

Methods
Methods Patients Family 1 A 27-year-old woman with a history of two unsuccessful pregnancies due to oligohydramnios visited our hospital (Fig. ). In her first pregnancy, at 30 weeks, oligohydramnios led to termination. An ultrasound examination revealed oligohydramnios, slightly enlarged fetal kidneys with increased echogenicity, and an unclear fetal bladder. The amniotic fluid index (AFI) was measured at 3.5 cm, with an amniotic fluid volume of 1.2 cm (Fig. ). Umbilical cord blood puncture was performed for karyotyping, microarray analysis, cytomegalovirus and rubella virus testing, and whole-exome sequencing (WES). The second pregnancy exhibited similar signs at 23 weeks, prompting another termination. An ultrasound examination revealed normal-sized fetal kidneys; however, there was increased cortical echogenicity, a blurred corticomedullary boundary, and an absent bladder. The AFI had decreased to 0.93 cm (Fig. ). An umbilical cord blood puncture was performed, and following delivery, fetal kidney pathology testing was conducted (Fig. ). Fortunately, her third pregnancy resulted in a healthy male baby delivered at full term. (a) A pedigree illustrating individuals from family 1 with a homozygous AGT deletion, indicated by filled black symbols. (b) Schematic diagram of the c.830-619_1242 + 243delinsTTGCCTTGC mutation in the AGT gene. This mutation results from the deletion of nucleotides from c.830-619 to c.1242 + 243, which are replaced by nucleotides TTGCCTTGC. (c) Illustration of the deletion of AGT by WES-CNV: a homozygous deletion of the AGT gene in the fetus, while the couple is heterozygous for this deletion. (d) A 2870 bp deletion with a 9 bp insertion (indicated by the dashed box) was detected by Sanger sequencing in individual II-1, while individual II-3 does not carry the deletion. (e) pathological examination of II-2 revealed that the number of proximal convoluted tubules was small and poorly developed. AGT, angiotensinogen; CNV, copy number variation; WES, whole-exome sequencing. Prenatal ultrasound images of the fetus (II-1, II-2, and II-3) in family 1. Fetus II-1 with ARRTD at 30 weeks gestational age (wGA) shows slightly enlarged fetal kidneys with enhanced echogenicity, an underfilled bladder, and an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 3.5 cm, with a depth (AFV) of 1.2 cm. Fetus II-2 with ARRTD at 23 weeks gestational age reveals normal-sized fetal kidneys; however, there is enhanced cortical echogenicity, a blurred corticomedullary boundary, and an absent bladder. The AFI was measured at 0.93 cm. Fetus II-3 at 23 wGA shows normal kidneys and a full bladder. The AFI is 16.09 cm, with a depth (AFV) of 4.75 cm. ARRTD, autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia; AFV, amniotic fluid volume. Family 2 A 22-year-old woman, pregnant with her first child, presented at 24 weeks of gestation with oligohydramnios (Fig. ). The ultrasound findings were similar to those observed in family 1’s pregnancy (Fig. ). After conducting umbilical cord blood tests, the couple decided to terminate the pregnancy due to the risks associated with oligohydramnios. In her subsequent pregnancy, she again encountered issues related to oligohydramnios. At 27 weeks of gestation, an ultrasound examination revealed that the fetal bladder was not fully dilated, indicating oligohydramnios. Although no obvious abnormalities were noted in the morphology or structure of the kidneys, increased renal blood flow resistance and reversed blood flow during full diastole suggested potential fetal renal insufficiency (Fig. ). Additionally, the fetus exhibited a small amount of pleural effusion. (a) A pedigree illustrating individuals from family 2 with compound heterozygous AGT mutations is represented by filled black symbols. (b) A schematic diagram of the compound heterozygous mutation in the AGT gene. This mutation results from a deletion of nucleotides ranging from c.830-619 to c.1242 + 243, which is replaced by the nucleotides TTGCCTTGC (indicated by the dashed box) in the AGT gene. Additionally, there is a heterozygous C.571C>T (p.Gln191Ter) mutation, represented by the red triangle, also within the AGT gene. (c) Illustration of the deletion of the AGT gene as detected by WES-CNV and Sanger sequencing: a heterozygous deletion of the AGT gene is present in both the fetus and the father, while the mother does not carry the deletion. (d) A heterozygous C.571C>T (p.Gln191Ter) mutation (indicated by a red triangle) was detected by Sanger sequencing in both the fetus and the mother, while the father does not carry the mutation. (e) A three-dimensional structural diagram of wild-type and mutant (C.571C>T) AGT proteins. Fetus II-1 with ARRTD at 24 weeks gestational age (wGA) shows normal kidneys, an unclear bladder, and an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 2 cm, with a depth (AFV) of 1.3 cm. Fetus II-2 with ARRTD at 27 weeks gestational age (wGA) revealed normal kidneys, an underfilled bladder, and an AFI of 5.3 cm, with a depth (AFV) of 1.6 cm. There was increased renal blood flow resistance and reversed blood flow during full diastole. AFV, amniotic fluid volume. AFV, amniotic fluid volume; ARRTD, autosomal recessive tubular dysplasia. Clinical whole-exome sequencing and direct Sanger sequencing The fetuses underwent Trio whole-exome sequencing (Trio-WES) following normal or nondiagnostic karyotype and chromosomal microarray results. Fetal DNA was extracted from umbilical cord blood, while parental DNA was obtained from peripheral blood samples. Both parents provided written informed consent for the clinical WES after receiving a comprehensive explanation of the benefits and limitations of the test. Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAGEN Blood Mini Kit. The Berry Nano WES chip was utilized to capture and enrich the DNA sequences in exons and adjacent intronic regions of approximately 20 000 genes. Sequencing was performed using the Illumina NovaSeq platform. Bioinformatics analysis was conducted using SeqMax software. Disease-causing variants were identified through a pipeline developed by our laboratory. Variant classification was performed in accordance with ACMG guidelines. All pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants detected by WES were confirmed through Sanger sequencing. Pathological tissue sections Hematoxylin–eosin staining method After paraffin sectioning, the tissue is dewaxed, and the nuclei are stained with hematoxylin and eosin. This is followed by dehydration and sealing. The nuclei appear blue, whereas the cytoplasm and interstitial spaces are stained pink.

Results
Results Family 1 experienced two pregnancies, both of which presented with oligohydramnios. An umbilical cord blood puncture was performed. Initially, the karyotype, microarray, and WES revealed no pathogenic or suspected pathogenic variants consistent with the observed phenotype. However, the pathological examination of the fetal kidneys raised several concerns. The kidneys displayed a lobulated shape, and in certain areas, the boundaries between the cortex and medulla were indistinct. The glomeruli were located deep within the medulla; although the glomerular structure was discernible near the renal hilum, it was not fully developed. Furthermore, the number of proximal convoluted tubules was limited and poorly formed, with no evidence of tubule dilation (Fig. ). These findings suggest that the fetus may have experienced renal insufficiency or other renal-related issues, which could have contributed to the observed oligohydramnios. In conjunction with the clinical history, ARRTD disease was considered, and the WES data of the two fetuses were reanalyzed. The WES-copy number variation (CNV) analysis revealed a homozygous deletion of exons 3 and 4 of the AGT gene in the first child. This deletion was subsequently confirmed by qPCR and Sanger sequencing, identifying it as a homozygous mutation in the AGT gene (NM_001384479.1) with a specific deletion and insertion pattern (c.830-619_c.1242 + 243 delinsTTGCCTTGC). This mutation results in a deletion of approximately 2870bp and an insertion of 9bp, affecting intron 2, exons 3 and 4, and intron 4 of the AGT gene. The mutation is predicted to result in the absence of 292 amino acids in the protein encoded by the AGT gene (Fig. ). The couple is heterozygous for this mutation. In the second pregnancy, qPCR confirmed that the second fetus also carried a homozygous deletion of exons 3–4 of the AGT gene (data not shown). This finding explains the renal abnormalities observed in the pathological examination of the fetal kidneys. Fortunately, in the third pregnancy, the amniocentesis results indicated no abnormalities in the karyotype or microarray, and no mutations in the AGT gene were detected (Fig. ). Inspired by the previous case, the WES test of both fetuses from family 2 revealed two potential pathogenic variants in the AGT gene, which were subsequently confirmed through Sanger sequencing. These variants include a heterozygous deletion of exons 3–4 in the AGT gene and a heterozygous mutation in the AGT gene designated as C.571C>T (p.Gln191Ter) (NM_001384479.1) (Fig. ). These mutations were inherited from the fetus’s father and mother, respectively. The WES-CNV analysis further confirmed the heterozygous deletion of exons 3–4 in the AGT gene. Sanger sequencing validated this deletion as a heterozygous mutation in the AGT gene (c.830-619_c.1242 + 243 delins TTGCCTTGC) (Fig. ). Notably, the C.571C>T (p.Gln191Ter) mutation in the AGT gene has not been reported previously, making it a novel mutation.

Discussion
Discussion ARRTD is a rare and fatal disorder that affects fetal kidney development. This condition is characterized by the absence or poor differentiation of proximal convoluted tubules, severe arterial hypotension, pulmonary hypoplasia, and anuria, leading to an exceptionally high mortality rate. Nearly all patients succumb to the disease either in utero or within the first few days of life, primarily due to refractory hypotension and/or pulmonary hypoplasia (; , ). ARRTD is associated with mutations in genes that encode components of the RAAS. Key components of the RAAS include AGT, REN, ACE, and AGTR1 (; ). Mutations in the genes encoding these RAAS components are believed to contribute to tubular dysplasia and ARRTD, likely due to impaired renal perfusion. Mutations in the RAAS are believed to contribute to tubular dysplasia and ARRTD, likely due to impaired renal perfusion. ARRTD specifically impacts renal tubular development during prenatal stages, often presenting as hyperechoic kidneys on ultrasound, which may be accompanied by increased renal size (). A histological hallmark of this kidney disease is the lack of differentiation or a reduced number of proximal tubules, resulting in densely packed glomeruli (). Identifying these RAAS mutations is essential for prenatal diagnosis, genetic counseling, and the development of potential therapeutic interventions aimed at correcting or compensating for defective RAAS function. Monitoring renal perfusion and blood flow resistance during prenatal ultrasonography can facilitate the early detection and management of ARRTD, potentially improving outcomes for affected fetuses. The AGT gene, located on chromosome 1q42, encodes the AGT protein, a key component of RAAS. Mutations in the AGT gene can lead to alterations in the function of the RAAS, potentially resulting in diseases such as renal tubular dysplasia (RTD) and other related renal disorders. In the two families with ARRTD described in this article, oligohydramnios was observed at 23–24 weeks of gestation, with similar clinical courses and severity. Prenatal ultrasound imaging in the first family revealed hyperechoic kidneys in two fetuses, and renal pathology confirmed RTD. In contrast, no hyperechoic kidneys were observed in the children of the second family. At 27 weeks of gestation, although no obvious abnormalities were noted in kidney morphology and structure, renal blood flow resistance increased, and reverse blood flow occurred during diastole, suggesting fetal renal insufficiency. This increased renal blood flow resistance is indicative of fetal renal perfusion injury. In two families affected by ARRTD, mutations in the AGT gene were identified. In family 1, a homozygous mutation, c.830-619_c.1242 + 243 delinsTTGCCTTGC (exon 3–4 deletion), was discovered. This mutation is a deletion that targets exons 3 and 4 of the AGT gene, leading to the skipping of these exons during transcription. As a result, a truncated protein is produced that lacks the serpin domain, which is critical for the interaction of AGT with REN, a key enzyme in the RAS. The deletion mutation disrupts this interaction, resulting in decreased levels of angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor and mediator of the RAS. In family 2, heterozygous mutations were identified, including deletions of exons 3 and 4, as well as a missense mutation designated as C.571C>T (p.Gln191Ter). Similar to the deletions observed in family 1, these deletions result in exon skipping and the subsequent production of a truncated protein. The missense mutation, on the other hand, causes a change in a single amino acid residue, resulting in a premature stop codon that terminates protein translation. This leads to the production of a shortened and potentially nonfunctional protein. Computer modeling studies suggest that this mutation weakens the interaction between AGT and REN, further emphasizing its potential pathogenicity. Notably, the C.571C>T mutation has not been reported previously. The identification of novel C.571C>T mutation provides further insights into the genetic basis of renal diseases and may lead to the development of more effective therapeutic strategies. The deletion of exons 3 and 4 in the AGT gene has been identified in multiple studies as a causative mutation for ARRTD. These cases have demonstrated the severity of the mutation, with most affected individuals experiencing severe renal dysfunction and high mortality rates. The carrier rate for this deletion variant in Taiwan stands at a significant level of 1.2% (). The two families we reported are both from the Chaoshan area. During the Ming and Qing Dynasties, some immigrants from the Chaoshan area migrated to Taiwan. CNVs are a significant component of genetic variation, often exceeding 1 kilobase (kb) in length and affecting approximately 12% of the genome. These large-scale genomic rearrangements can be challenging to detect, particularly when dealing with smaller CNVs. While karyotyping, microarray analysis, and CNV-seq are commonly used methods for CNV detection, they have limitations, especially in identifying smaller variants (). Therefore, it is crucial to prioritize the CNV analysis of genes that are strongly implicated as potential disease-causing agents based on the phenotype. In the two families we reported, CNVs were excluded through microarray analysis. Due to the small fragment size of the CNVs, the deletion initially went undetected. WES is an invaluable tool for the genetic diagnosis of rare diseases. Recent technological advancements have facilitated the accurate and sensitive detection of CNVs from WES data, thanks to sophisticated bioinformatics tools (; ). A study involving 920 patients who underwent WES found that among 454 unresolved cases, the application of a WES-CNV algorithm resulted in the identification of pathogenic CNVs in 40 patients. This significantly increased the diagnostic yield of WES from 50.7 to 55% (). These exon-level CNVs cannot be detected by traditional methods, making them a critical focus in genetic analysis. It is essential to consider these variations when investigating suspected genetic diseases, particularly when concentrating on highly implicated genes based on phenotype. The ability to detect and analyze CNVs, especially exon-level variants, from WES data offers valuable insights into the genetic architecture of rare diseases and can significantly enhance diagnostic yield. Conclusion In summary, we reported on patients with ARRTD based on ultrasound scans and fetal kidney pathology. We performed WES-CNV analysis to identify mutations in disease-related genes. For the first time, we clarified the renal vascular resistance during the prenatal period, noting increased renal blood flow resistance and reverse diastolic blood flow, which indicate fetal renal insufficiency. Additionally, this is the first report of the nonsense mutation (C.571C>T) identified in the AGT gene. By utilizing prenatal ultrasound, fetal kidney pathology, and WES methods, we successfully elucidated the molecular genetic etiology of the ARRTD fetus. We are confident that our findings will significantly enhance prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling efforts.
