Sequential prenatal diagnosis of fetal skeletal dysplasia: A cohort study

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Skeletal dysplasia (SD) is a prevalent structural malformation, occurring in approximately 5 per 1000 fetuses. This congenital disease impacts the composition and structure of bone and cartilage tissue. Clinical manifestations of SD include various abnormalities in skeletal tissue growth and development. Additionally, this condition may co‐occur with malformations in other systems and organs., , In severe cases, abnormal skeletal development in fetuses can lead to fetal death. Survivors may face disabilities due to skeletal malformations, and in some instances, various degrees of intellectual disability, severely affecting patient quality of life. Therefore, early detection through prenatal screening and diagnosis is crucial for timely clinical intervention. Although prenatal lethal or severe structural abnormalities in the fetus can usually be detected by ultrasound, the symptoms of SD fetuses overlap significantly, making a definitive diagnosis difficult. Current research indicates that fetal SD is linked to multiple factors, including genetics, infection, and radiation. Among these, genetic factors are considered primary contributors. Nosology of genetic skeletal disorders has identified 771 types of hereditary bone diseases, divided into 41 groups involving 552 genes. Molecular diagnosis is essential in genetic counseling and in assessing the risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies and has thus become a valuable complement to ultrasonography. SD is not only related to chromosomal abnormalities, but also a significant proportion of it is caused by monogenic abnormalities which are usually caused by point variations., Therefore, the current first‐line prenatal diagnosis techniques, karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) of amniotic fluid exfoliated cells, may not fully meet the needs of clinical prenatal diagnosis. Whole exome sequencing (WES) encompasses 1–2% of the genome yet includes about 85% of known disease‐causing genetic variants. The detection rate of fetal structural abnormalities by WES varies greatly among different research teams (10%–80%)., Additionally, a meta‐analysis of 66 studies and 72 reports underscored the significant value of WES in prenatal detection. This study found that for fetuses with structural abnormalities, the detection rate of WES was 31% higher compared with CMA or karyotyping. Notably, the detection rate for SD was the highest (53%). However, current clinical studies on fetal SD are insufficient and the sample size is extremely limited. Therefore, the application of WES in prenatal diagnosis of SD has both great potential and many challenges, especially the ability and skills of clinicians in genetic counseling. The aim of this study is to explore the effect of WES on the prenatal diagnosis of SD fetuses through a large fetal SD cohort, aiming to provide guidance for clinicians to make accurate prenatal consultation and prognosis.

MATERIAL AND METHODS
MATERIAL AND METHODS Subjects A total of 147 pregnant women who were diagnosed with fetal SD by ultrasound in Changzhou Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital, Suqian First People's Hospital, and Lianyungang Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital from January 2019 to May 2024 were selected. Ultrasound diagnostic criteria (simultaneously meeting the following two conditions): ① the long bones of the limbs, the length of the femur (FL), and the length of the humerus (HL) were lower than the 5th percentile of the fetus at the same gestational age; FL/AC (abdominal circumference) ratio ≤1.6; ② abnormal ultrasound findings of bone morphology, such as long bone bending, angulation, fracture, “telephone receiver” changes, thoracic dysplasia, bone mineral density changes, etc. Prenatal diagnostic methods Genetic counseling and sample collection After suspected SD detected by prenatal ultrasound, 117 pregnant women chose prenatal diagnosis voluntarily, and 30 pregnant women refused amniocentesis and chose termination of pregnancy (TOP) because of other severe structural malformations or pregnancy complications after genetic counseling and informed consent. In China, TOP can be carried out for fetuses with severe structural malformations or congenital diseases at gestational ages less than 28 weeks after verification and issuance of corresponding certificates by professional doctors. The fetal tissue of TOP was collected for CMA or WES detection after the informed consent of the couple. TOP causes include SD combined with cardiac dysplasia, hydronephrosis, brain dysplasia, and other systemic malformations. The study design and protocol were reviewed and approved by the ethics committee of Changzhou Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital (2017 [3]). CMA After taking 10 mL of the amniotic fluid or abortive tissue, genomic DNA was digested, linked, amplified, purified, fragmented, labeled, hybridized, washed, and scanned by Affymetrix CytoScan™ 750 K(Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) chip assay. The data were analyzed by ChAS software. Analysis and judgment of genome‐wide copy number variants (CNV) properties in reference online public related database, for example, DECIPHER (http://www.sanger.ac.uk, PostGenomics, DECIPHER), OMIM (http://www.omim.org), and DGV (http://projects.tcag.ca/variation). Sequence analysis was performed according to the ACMG (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics) joint ClinGen expert consensus on chromosome copy number variation. WES Genomic DNA was extracted according to the instructions of the Kit (MagPure Buffy Coat DNA Midi KF Kit, MAGEN), and the genomic DNA of the sample was interrupted, end repaired, adapter ligated, amplified, and purified to complete the library construction. Hybridization and capture were performed with the use of custom probes (KAPA HyperExome, ROCHE). Capture libraries were sequenced using a high‐throughput sequencer DNBSEQ‐T7. LUSH_Aligner software was used to evaluate the quality of Raw reads, and then low‐quality and contaminated reads were removed. The obtained clean reads were aligned with the hg19 (GRch37: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001405.13/) using LUSH_Aligner software for sequence alignment. Subsequently, SNV (single nucleotide variant) and Indel (insertion and deletion) queries were performed using LUSH_BQSR and LUSH_H software to generate results on base polymorphisms in the target region. Furthermore, multiple databases including NCBI dbSNP v147, dbNSDP v2.9.1, ESP6500 v2 HapMap, the 1000 human genome dataset, and the database of 100 Chinese healthy adults were compared to identify suspicious variations. BGI's proprietary algorithms were then used for annotation and screening purposes. The exomeDepth variation analysis software was utilized to target exon CNVs, and the detection of CNVs larger than 1 m was successfully accomplished using the CNV kit. The pathogenicity of variants was assessed based on the ACMG guidelines, incorporating data from ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), OMIM (https://www.omim.org/), HGMD (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/), and other disease databases. The ExpansionHunter software was employed for the identification of dynamic variations within the genome. Sanger sequencing For all point variations found, primers were designed upstream and downstream of the fragment in which they were located. Then, PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing were performed. The results were compared with the standard gene sequence to verify the results of high‐throughput sequencing. Genetic counseling and follow‐up After genetic testing, all cases received genetic counseling to decide the next step of pregnancy management. After 6 months, all cases were followed up by telephone, and the data collected included delivery information, presence of other malformations, surgical treatment, etc. If related system abnormalities are found, timely specialist follow‐up consultation is recommended. Review of the literature on the detection of WES in SD fetuses Literature source Searches were conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for articles published from 2014 to 2023. Search strategy This involved using a combination of subject terms and keywords. (1) For English subject terms: ‘skeletal dysplasia’ was represented by ‘skeletal abnormalities’, ‘SD’, ‘SKA’, ‘SDs’, and ‘skeletal dysplasia's’. Similarly, “whole exome sequencing” and “WES” were used to refer to “exome sequencing.” (2) Additionally, references from identified literature were reviewed to locate other relevant studies. (3) Finally, two researchers independently conducted and evaluated the literature search. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria: (1) SD fetuses, with or without additional abnormalities. (2) Prospective or retrospective cohort studies. (3) Prenatal WES including exome sequencing (ES), targeted exome sequencing (TES), or SD panel, for diagnosing SD fetuses. (4) Cases where CMA results were negative or not diagnostic, and where numerical, structural, and copy CNVs of chromosomes were ruled out. (5) Full‐text reports available in the English language. Exclusion criteria: (1) Literature types such as reviews, case reports, reader letters, animal studies, expert opinions, conference papers, etc. (2) Studies that did not use exome sequencing. (3) Studies where data could not be extracted. Study selection Following the removal of duplicate content, two investigators independently examined titles and abstracts. For abstracts deemed potentially relevant, full texts were scrutinized based on predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any disagreements between the investigators were resolved through discussion. To prevent data duplication, only studies with the largest or most recent sample sizes were included. Statistical analyses SPSS 26.0 software was used for statistical analysis. The count data were expressed as rates or percentages (%), and the chi‐square test or Fisher's exact probability method was used for comparison between groups. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

RESULTS
RESULTS Clinical description A total of 147 SD fetuses were included in this study, and all the enrolled fetuses underwent detailed ultrasound examinations during pregnancy. After suspected SD fetuses were detected by prenatal ultrasound, all patients received genetic counseling. Gestational age at diagnosis ranged from 12+1 to 31+6 weeks, with a mean of 23.4 weeks. The proportion of SD fetuses with short long bones (SLBs), foot varus, and long bone curvature is relatively high: 36.7% (54/147), 24.5% (36/147), and 7.5% (11/147), respectively. After amniotic fluid or abortive tissue was taken, 147 cases were tested by CMA, followed by WES in 58 of the CMA‐negative cases, as shown in Figure . SD fetuses undergoing WES were highly selected for monogenic etiology after evaluation by genetic experts based on ultrasound results. Flow chart for sequential prenatal diagnosis of skeletal dysplasia fetuses suggested by ultrasound. CMA, chromosomal microarray analysis; CNV, copy number variants; SD, skeletal dysplasia; VOUS, variants of uncertain significance. Prenatal diagnosis results CMA results of 147 SD fetuses: a total of 23 cases were reported to have chromosomal abnormalities, and the rate of chromosomal abnormalities was 15.6% (23/147). As shown in Table , 9 cases had chromosome aneuploidies, including 2 cases of T21, 5 cases of T18, 1 case of T13, and 1 case of Turner syndrome. 14 fetuses were reported to have pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNV, mainly involving chromosomes 16, 4, 15, and 22. There were 10 cases (71.4%, 10/14) of deletion, 3 cases (21.4%, 3/14) of duplication, and 1 case (7.1%, 1/14) of deletion combined with duplication. The size of the fragment ranged from 427.522Kb to 93.1 Mb. 16p11.2 microdeletion syndrome and 22q11.2 were the most common pathogenic CNV. WES was performed in 58 cases with negative results of CMA, and 21 cases were reported to have pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants. The rate of abnormal prenatal WES was 36.2%(21/58). 21 genes with pathogenic/likely pathogenic 23 variants were detected in 21 cases, including FGFR3 (n = 11), COL1A1 (n = 2), COL1A2 (n = 1), RUNX2 (n = 1), COL2A1 (n = 1), LMX1B (n = 1), GLI3 (n = 1), DYNC2H1 (n = 1), ALPL (n = 1), and SHOX (n = 1) (Figure ). FGFR3 had the highest detection rate of 52.4% (11/21), of which 7 cases (case28‐34) had the same variant site c.742C>T(p.Arg248Cys), accounting for 63.6% (7/11) of FGFR3. COL1A1 accounted for the second highest proportion of genes detected, which was 9.5% (2/21). The proportion of genes with pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants detected in 21 of 58 skeletal dysplasia fetuses. Among the 21 SD fetuses, 18 cases (85.7%, 18/21) had an autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance pattern, 2 cases (9.5%, 2/21) had an autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance pattern, and 1 case (4.8%, 1/21) was unknown. Among the 21 detected SD fetuses, 9 (42.9%, 9/21) were de novo variants, 7 (33.3%, 7/21) inherited variants from their parents, and 5 (23.8%, 5/21) had not been tested for genetic origin. In addition, we found a novel SD‐related variant, c.105C>G(p.Tyr35*), in the SHOX gene (Table ). Comparison of detection rates of SD fetuses in subgroups As shown in Table , among the 147 cases of SD fetuses, 91 cases (61.9%, 91/147) were isolated SD, and 56 cases (38.1%, 56/147) were SD combined with other system abnormalities. In the isolated SD subgroup, there were 19 cases (20.9%, 19/91) of isolated SLBs and 5 cases (5.5%, 5/91) of isolated short and curved long bones. Among the 54 cases of SLBs, 19 cases (35.2%, 19/54) were isolated SLBs, and 35 cases (64.8%, 35/54) were non‐isolated SLBs. Among the 35 cases of non‐isolated SLBs, 16 cases (45.7%, 16/35) were SLBs with other skeletal abnormalities, and 19 cases (54.3%, 19/35) were SLBs with non‐skeletal abnormalities. The detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities, the detection rate of monogenic abnormality, and overall detection rate were compared among the SD subgroups. The detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in isolated SD fetuses was 7.7% (7/91), which was lower than that in SD fetuses combined with other system abnormalities (28.6%, 16/56), and the difference was statistically significant (p = 0.001). The detection rate of monogenic abnormality in isolated SLBs (21.1%, 4/19) was significantly lower than that in isolated curved short long bones (80.0%, 4/5) (p = 0.028). In addition, FGFR3 was detected in 2 of 4 isolated SLBs and in four fetuses with isolated curved short long bones with monogenic abnormality. The detection rate of monogenic abnormalities in SLBs combined with other skeletal abnormalities was 62.5% (10/16), which was higher than that in SLBs combined with non‐skeletal abnormalities 10.5% (2/19), and the difference was statistically significant (p = 0.003). The detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in SLBs with other skeletal abnormalities (6.3%, 1/16) was lower than that in SLBs with non‐skeletal abnormalities (21.1%, 4/19). The overall detection rate of SLBs combined with other skeletal abnormalities was significantly higher than that of SLBs combined with non‐skeletal abnormalities (68.8%[11/16] vs. 31.6%[6/19]; p = 0.044). Specific clinical features are provided in Table . Follow‐up Of the 147 cases, 141 cases (95.9%, 141/147) were successfully followed up, and 6 cases were lost to follow‐up. Among the 141 cases with successful follow‐up, 95 cases had adverse pregnancy outcomes, including 86 cases of TOP, 4 cases of embryo arrest, 2 cases of death after birth, and 3 cases of developmental delay after birth. The remaining 46 cases were live births. Among the 86 cases who chose to terminate pregnancy, 30 cases chose to terminate pregnancy without amniocentesis because of other severe structural malformations or pregnancy complications after the initial ultrasound examination suggested fetal SD, 32 cases chose to terminate pregnancy after CMA or WES detected pathogenic or likely pathogenic abnormalities, and 24 cases with no abnormality in prenatal diagnosis terminated pregnancy in the third trimester because of a severe SD phenotype or other severe structural malformations. Among the 44 cases with abnormal results detected by CMA and WES, 42 cases (95.5%, 42/44) terminated pregnancy, and 2 cases (case 21 and case 44) were born alive. Case 44, whose father had clinical symptoms of polydactyly and carried the same variation, was detected to have a likely pathogenic GLI3 variant associated with polydactyly by WES. After prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling, the couple chose to continue the pregnancy and delivered a girl at 37 weeks of gestation who had polydactyly and syndactyly on her fingers and toes, respectively. In case 21, a likely pathogenic CNV was detected by CMA. After prenatal genetic counseling, the couple chose to continue the pregnancy and delivered a baby with low birth weight and growth retardation at 36 weeks of gestation. Among the cases with TOP after WES diagnosis, case 40 and case 45 had natural pregnancy again, and the WES test after amniocentesis showed no abnormality, and they continued the pregnancy. In case 46, the couple tried genetic diagnosis before embryo transfer after genetic counseling. Of the 103 SD fetuses with no abnormalities detected by CMA or WES, 44 (42.7%, 44/103) couples chose to terminate the pregnancy due to spinal deformity, hydronephrosis, brain dysplasia, and other malformations. Among these 54 cases of SLBs, CMA or WES detected 23 cases of abnormalities, of which 22 cases (95.7%, 22/23) chose to terminate the pregnancy. In the remaining 31 cases with no abnormalities detected, 25.8% (8/31) chose to terminate the pregnancy because of severe SD phenotype or other severe structural malformations. Among the 17 fetuses with SLBs born alive (including 1 case with likely pathogenic CNV detected by CMA and 16 cases with no abnormality), we tracked the changes of long bone in 12 fetuses during the whole pregnancy. CMA and WES did not detect any abnormalities in these 12 cases, of which 2 cases reached the normal range of long bone length before birth, and the remaining 10 cases had short long bones at birth. Retrospective analysis of the application of WES in SD fetuses in different studies By searching the databases of PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, 18 published reports on WES in SD fetuses from 2014 to 2023 and this study were retrospectively analyzed. The inclusion criteria, sequencing methods, number of cases included in the study, and detection rate of each study were extracted (Table ). Inclusion criteria varied from the broad indication of SD on ultrasound to the narrow requirement for measurement of fetal long bone and femur length. The sequencing methods are different, including WES, TES, SD panel, etc. The number of cases included in the studies ranged from 8 to 94, of which two reported studies had higher sample sizes than the present study, which were 94 and 65 cases, respectively. The detection rate of exome sequencing in SD fetuses ranged from 15.4% to 89.1%, and three studies had lower detection rates than our study (10%, 15.4%, and 23.5%, respectively).

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION CMA can identify the greater genetic chromosome abnormality, so CMA testing for diseases caused by point variants has limitations, and WES can identify these variants. In this study, only 15.6% (23/147) of SD fetuses were definitively diagnosed by CMA. By WES, the molecular etiology detection rate of SD was 36.2% (21/58) in a subgroup of CMA‐negative fetuses. This result is consistent with the results of previous studies of selected SD fetuses (diagnosis rate from 15.4% to 89.1%) (Table ). Therefore, prenatal WES can significantly improve the additional detection rate of fetal abnormalities and find more pathogenic variants compared with the current prenatal CMA. WES can clarify the molecular etiology related to SD fetuses. In this study, 23 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 21 genes related to SD fetuses were identified by WES. Variants in FGFR3 were detected in 52.4% (11/21) fetuses, highlighting that pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in FGFR3 are the most common genetic cause of SD, consistent with the findings of Bai et al. Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), one of four different transmembrane tyrosine kinases, plays an important role in bone development as a high‐affinity receptor for a variety of fibroblast growth factors., Pathogenic variants in FGFR3 cause achondroplasia (ACH) and thanatophoric dysplasia (TD), the more common fatal skeletal disease., In this study, the FGFR3 gene was detected in 2 of the 4 isolated SLB fetuses and in four fetuses with isolated curved short long bones with monogenic abnormalities. Therefore, FGFR3 is closely related to SLBs and long bones that are short and curved. In addition, variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2, which are present in approximately 90% of osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) individuals, were detected in three cases. TD (42.9%, 9/21), ACH (33.3%, 7/21), and OI (14.3%, 3/21) were the most common diagnoses in this cohort, which is consistent with Krakow et al.'s study. We also identified a de novo variant c.105C>G(p.Tyr35*) in the SHOX gene in case 48 with short femur and humerus, which has not been reported previously, and will expand the variant spectrum of skeletal‐related abnormalities. In subgroup analysis of isolated SD phenotype, the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in isolated SD (7.7%, 7/91) was significantly lower than that in SD combined with other system abnormalities (28.6%, 16/56) (p = 0.001). Therefore, fetuses with SD combined with other system abnormalities are more likely to carry pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNV. The detection rate of monogenic abnormality in isolated SLBs (21.1%, 4/19) was significantly lower than that in isolated long bones with short and curved (80.0%, 4/5) (p = 0.028). Therefore, fetuses with short and curved long bones are more likely to carry SD‐related pathogenic genes. Subgroup analysis showed that the overall detection rate of isolated SLBs (31.6%, 6/19) was lower than that of non‐isolated SLBs (48.6%, 17/35), but there was no statistical significance (p = 0.228), which was consistent with the conclusion of Tse et al. The overall and monogenic detection rate of SLBs combined with other skeletal abnormalities (femoral bending, spinal dysplasia, equines deformity, etc.) was significantly higher than that of SLBs combined with non‐skeletal abnormalities (increased cervical transparency, tricuspid regurgitation, cerebellar dysplasia, polyhydramnios, etc.) (68.8%[11/16] vs. 31.6%[6/19], p = 0.044; 62.5%[10/16] vs. 10.5%[2/19], p = 0.003), the finding consistent with the study by Huang et al. However, the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in SLBs with other skeletal abnormalities (6.3%, 1/16) was lower than that in SLBs with non‐skeletal abnormalities (21.1%, 4/19), which showed that fetuses with SLBs combined with other skeletal abnormalities were closely related to skeletal‐related monogenic disorders. Therefore, when fetal long bones are shown to be short on prenatal ultrasound, the length of their long bones should be measured and a thorough skeletal evaluation should be performed to determine if other skeletal morphological abnormalities are present. In addition to genetic diagnosis, long‐term follow‐up was performed to assess the prognosis of SD fetuses. Among the 17 SLB fetuses, the long bone length was successfully tracked throughout pregnancy in 12 fetuses, and two of them reached the normal range prenatally. Therefore, fetuses with slightly SLBs may develop to the normal range in the uterus. It is suggested that fetuses with SLBs do not need to terminate pregnancy immediately, and continuous attention should be paid to the changes in fetal long bones during pregnancy. Among the detected cases by WES, 16 cases were tested by trio‐WES and 9 cases had de novo variants. De novo variants are generally associated with a 1% risk of fetal abnormalities in a subsequent pregnancy. However, the possibility of reproductive mosaicism still needs to be considered in the next pregnancy, and invasive prenatal diagnosis is recommended in the next pregnancy. The parents of the other 7 cases carried the corresponding pathogenic variants, and the risk of recurrence was as high as 25%, so prenatal diagnosis or preimplantation genetic diagnosis was still recommended for the next pregnancy. Case 44 was identified to have a GLI3 variant associated with polydactyly by WES. The father had clinical symptoms of polydactyly and carried the same variant. After prenatal genetic counseling, the couple chose to continue the pregnancy and delivered a baby girl at 37 weeks, who had polydactyly and syndactyly on her fingers and toes, respectively. Among the cases with TOP after WES diagnosis, case 40 with a pathogenic COL1A2 variant detected from the mother and case 45 with likely pathogenic DYNC2H1 variants detected from both parents had natural pregnancy again. WES testing after amniocentesis showed no abnormality, and the pregnancy was continued. Likely pathogenic variants of ALPL originating from both parents were detected in case 46, and the couple tried genetic diagnosis before embryo transfer after genetic counseling. Prenatal WES can not only provide guidance for the management, prognosis, and treatment of the current pregnancy but also provide recurrence risk assessment based on the molecular etiology for the next pregnancy to provide a personalized prenatal diagnosis plan. The differences in detection rates can be explained by differences in samples. The summary of cohort studies on the application of WES in fetal SD in recent years showed that the fetal detection rate was affected by many factors, such as cohort size, study inclusion criteria, detection method, and so on (Table ). So far, SD fetuses included in studies tend to be in small cohorts highly selected for monogenic etiology after evaluation by genetic experts, and highly selected monogenic disorders may translate into higher detection rates. For the detection of fetal SD by WES, our sample size was only lower than that of 2 reported studies and was the largest among the studies reported in recent years (Table ), covering a more abundant phenotype. Therefore, our results are relatively objective and reliable in the diagnostic yield of fetal SD compared with other small sample studies. However, the study has some limitations. Firstly, considering family economic status, only 16 families were tested with trio‐WES. Secondly, sample selection may be biased. Some couples refused prenatal diagnosis after the initial ultrasound examination suggested fetal SD. As a result, some SD fetuses were not included in the prenatal diagnosis management system, resulting in sample selection bias. In the study, a variety of measures were taken to reduce the bias of sample selection as much as possible, such as combining multi‐center studies, strict inclusion criteria for research subjects, unified experimental methods, strict quality control, and so on. In addition, prenatal WES faces ethical challenges which should be paid attention to. In clinical practice, it is difficult to provide genetic counseling for variants of uncertain significance, secondary findings and incidental findings detected by WES. The genetic counselors should fully inform the couple of these findings and its significance as part of informed consent. In addition to severe genetic diseases and fatal diseases, the retention of embryos with “non‐severe genetic diseases” has been controversial. Therefore, in clinical practice, genetic counselors should ensure that prospective parents fully understand the ethical issues raised by the potential findings of prenatal WES and reproductive decisions before and after WES testing. The interpretation of WES results should actively cooperate with multidisciplinary teams to provide the most comprehensive information for pregnant women and their families, and their choices should be weighed with fully informed consent. When necessary, the ethics committee should be initiated to discuss the decision. In 2020, ACMG issued “the Statement on the Clinical Application of Fatal exome Detection Technology in prenatal Diagnosis,” which recommended that WES should be considered when both CMA and karyotype analysis failed to confirm the diagnosis. The results of this study show that prenatal WES provides a higher additional detection rate compared with prenatal CMA for fetuses with SD indicated by ultrasound. Therefore, the combination of WES and CMA should be used in the sequential prenatal diagnosis of SD fetuses.

CONCLUSION
CONCLUSION SD is mostly caused by monogenic abnormalities. Prenatal WES has significantly improved the detection rate of SD fetuses. The prenatal WES can be used as an important molecular genetic testing method combined with CMA in the sequential prenatal diagnosis of SD fetuses. Accurate molecular diagnosis will provide more scientific genetic counseling for the recurrence risk of pregnancy, prenatal diagnosis, pregnancy management, and intrauterine treatment.

abstract: Congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT) are one of the most common sets of congenital defects. Bilateral renal agenesis is a severe presentation of the CAKUT spectrum. We report on two families who presented with recurrent pregnancies affected with bilateral renal agenesis and negative family histories. Likely pathogenic variants in the GREB1L gene were identified in the affected pregnancies and subsequently in their asymptomatic fathers. The first familial variant was identified by a multi-gene CAKUT panel and the second by whole exome sequencing. Renal ultrasound showed the father in family 1 had asymptomatic unilateral pelvic kidney and the father in family 2 had no apparent renal anomalies. Recent identification of genes responsible for CAKUT allows for genetic testing of affected families. Identification of the genetic etiology of CAKUT cases has multiple benefits including accurate risk assessment and reproductive options. Genetic counseling around CAKUT is challenging due to the extreme variability in presentation of the disorders.
text:
Challenges in genetic counseling for congenital anomalies of the kidneys and urinary tract (CAKUT) spectrum

Introduction
Introduction Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) include a wide spectrum of structural malformations resulting from defects in the morphogenesis of the kidney and of the urinary tract []. CAKUT range from complete renal agenesis to renal hypodysplasia, multicystic kidney dysplasia, duplex renal collecting system, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, horseshoe kidney, hydronephrosis, megaureter, and posterior urethral valve [, ]. The most commonly used classification is based on anatomical characteristics (the segment of the urinary tract involved), with ureteropelvic junction obstruction being the most frequent observed phenotype (20%). Altogether, CAKUT are one of the most common sets of congenital defects, affecting 3–7 out of 1,000 live births and represent more than 20% of birth defects. CAKUT are responsible for 40–50% of pediatric and 7% of adult end-stage renal disease worldwide []. It is estimated that bilateral renal agenesis occurs at a frequency of 1/3,000–1/5,000, while unilateral renal agenesis occurs more frequently in up to 1/1,000 births []. CAKUT are commonly detected with prenatal sonography; however, many cases remain undiagnosed until adulthood and represent a large spectrum of diseases with highly variable grades of severity and outcome. Moreover, CAKUT can appear as an isolated feature or as part of a syndromic condition with extra-renal manifestations, making diagnosis and clinical classification even more challenging []. The etiology of the CAKUT spectrum is complex and multifactorial involving genetic and non-genetic factors [, ]. In recent years, alterations in more than 75 genes have been shown to cause isolated or syndromic CAKUT, in an autosomal dominant or, less frequently, recessive mode of inheritance []. In addition, copy number variations have been widely associated with CAKUT spectrum [, ]. Despite recent advances, genetic diagnosis of CAKUT is still challenging due to their genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity as well as incomplete penetrance. Consensus guidelines on genetic evaluation of CAKUT is currently lacking. GREB1L was identified as a CAKUT-susceptibility gene in 2017 [, , ]. It has been reported as a target of retinoic acid signaling, a pathway that is crucial for renal development. Dysregulation of this pathway has been proposed as a causative mechanism for urinary tract malformations []. Mutations in GREB1L have been associated with a form of renal hypodysplasia/aplasia (RHDA3) (OMIM#617805), which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and presents as early as fetal life. The phenotype is characterized by high variability within and among families, as well as incomplete penetrance. Bilateral renal agenesis, as seen in our families, is typically associated with perinatal demise, either prenatally due to complications of severe oligohydramnios, or postnatally due to pulmonary and metabolic issues related to absence of normal renal function. Individuals with this genotype, however, may instead have unilateral agenesis that is compatible with life, or milder manifestations, such as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Female mutation carriers may also have uterine or ovarian abnormalities ranging from uterine agenesis with bilateral renal agenesis to milder defects such as unicornuated uterus and unilateral ovarian and fallopian tube agenesis []. In a study of 183 unrelated families affected by various forms of CAKUT, 16 (8.7%) heterozygous pathogenic or suspected pathogenic variants in GREB1L were identified, 12 of which were found in 54 cases (25.8%) with bilateral renal agenesis in this cohort []. In another study of 612 individuals affected by renal agenesis and hypodysplasia, 17 (2.8%) heterozygous pathogenic or suspected pathogenic variants in GREB1L were identified [].

Case presentation
Case presentation History of family 1 Family 1 first presented to genetic counseling with a pregnancy found to be affected with fetal bilateral renal agenesis at 16 weeks gestation (). The fetal bladder was not visualized though branched umbilical arteries were seen on color flow in the region of the bladder. Echogenic fetal bowel was seen. Inquiry of the couple’s reproductive history revealed a previous pregnancy also affected with fetal bilateral renal agenesis, in addition to clubfeet, single umbilical artery, non-visualized fetal bladder and anhydramnios; these anomalies were identified at 20 weeks 5 days gestation. The previous pregnancy was electively terminated at 21 weeks gestation due to poor prognosis; no kidney tissue was identified on gross examination of the products of conception. Chromosomal microarray of the products of conception revealed a normal female genotype. In addition, the couple’s reproductive history included a healthy male offspring, spontaneous abortion of a twin pregnancy at 8 weeks gestation due to an unknown etiology, as well as a chemical pregnancy. The couple both denied any personal and family histories of CAKUT, although the father did report that one of his siblings was stillborn due to an unknown etiology (). Ultrasound images of proband of family 1. (A) Anhydramnios and absent renal fossae. (B) Anhydramnios. (C) Absence of renal artery blood flow from aorta. Pedigree of family 1. The pregnancy was terminated at 17 weeks gestation due to poor prognosis. Based on its recurrence, the bilateral renal agenesis was suspected to have a genetic etiology. A CAKUT multi-gene panel was performed on the products of conception of this second affected pregnancy. A likely pathogenic variant, c.5356_5357del (p.Gln1786Valfs*13), was identified in GREB1L. This sequence variant was predicted to result in a frameshift and premature protein termination. This variant had not been reported previously but was expected to be pathogenic. Fetal chromosomal microarray revealed a normal female genetic complement. Targeted analysis of the GREB1L variant was subsequently performed on the parents; the father was found to carry the variant, while the mother was negative. Although the father previously denied any personal history of CAKUT, his abdominal/pelvic ultrasound revealed a unilateral pelvic kidney. The mother’s renal ultrasound was normal. The couple’s son had targeted analysis of the likely pathogenic variant in GREB1L and was negative. Although he had not had postnatal renal evaluation, his prenatal ultrasound had been unremarkable. At the time of writing this manuscript, the patient was nearing the end of a new pregnancy, achieved via conception after ovulation induction, resulting in diamniotic-dichorionic female twins. The couple was offered both 1st trimester and 2nd trimester prenatal diagnostic testing for the GREB1L mutation but declined, since they had decided they would not consider pregnancy termination or selective reduction based solely on the fetuses’ genetic statuses, given the variable expression seen within their own family. An early fetal structural ultrasound at 16 weeks gestation demonstrated no evidence of genitourinary anomalies in either twin, and subsequent ultrasounds into the third trimester demonstrated normal anatomy, including the urinary systems, in both fetuses (). History of family 2 Family 2 was referred to genetic counseling due to suspected recurrence of bilateral renal agenesis. The couple had two previous female pregnancies affected with bilateral renal agenesis that resulted in preterm neonatal death. The couple’s reproductive history also included an unaffected son (not tested) and one early miscarriage. For the current pregnancy, a detailed fetal anatomic survey performed at 17 weeks 5 days showed a smaller sized fetus measuring 16 weeks 1 day, right renal agenesis, a very small and suspected nonfunctional left kidney, absent stomach, absent bladder, small thorax, an echogenic intracardiac focus, and anhydramnios (). Placental biopsy was performed for genetic studies prior to termination of pregnancy. Results of chromosome microarray analysis showed a normal female complement. Whole exome sequencing trio results showed a variant in the GREB1L gene, c.5622T>A (p.Cys1874X), which was classified as likely pathogenic. This variant had not been previously reported but was predicted to introduce a premature termination codon in the GREB1L protein, which was predicted to result in truncation or loss of the GREB1L protein via nonsense mediated decay. The variant was also detected in the father. The couple denied any personal or family history of CAKUT (). The couple also reportedly had normal renal ultrasounds. Ultrasound images of proband of family 2. (A) Transverse views of fetus that show empty renal fossa bilaterally and normally oriented heart. (B) Anhydramnios and absence of fluid filled stomach and bladder. (C) Placental biopsy. Pedigree of family 2. At the time of writing this manuscript, the couple had experienced a subsequent pregnancy of a male fetus with anhydramnios, and suspected bilateral renal agenesis based on absence of the fetal bladder and inability to see fetal kidneys and renal arteries at 19 weeks 6 days gestation. The couple elected to undergo termination of this pregnancy due to poor prognosis. Prenatal diagnosis was declined because the option of placental biopsy was unavailable locally.

Discussion
Discussion The identification of CAKUT genes is changing the practice of prenatal diagnosis for families with a history of renal anomalies. Prenatal chromosomal microarray analysis has been a standard recommendation for evaluation of all major fetal structural abnormalities including renal agenesis (ACOG 682). Our experience suggests that when renal agenesis is identified, testing for CAKUT genes should also be considered especially when chromosomal microarray results are non-diagnostic. A number of studies in the mid-2010s demonstrated that targeted panels had a diagnostic yield of 6–10% in patients with isolated CAKUT [, ]. The diagnostic yield is likely higher as mutation panels are updated when new genes are identified. In addition, as the list of defined syndromes grows and the cost of sequencing declines, whole exome sequencing or genome sequencing will likely emerge as the preferred primary diagnostic modality []. In recent studies, the diagnostic yield of whole exome sequencing has been reported to be as high as 14.5% in isolated CAKUT cases, and higher in syndromic cases [], [], []. When renal agenesis is diagnosed in the second and third trimester and oligohydramnios does not allow for amniocentesis, prenatal diagnosis via placental biopsy can allow for a genetic diagnosis. In cases where prenatal diagnosis is not possible due to technical factors or parental choice, genetic testing after delivery is appropriate. The CAKUT in both of the families appeared to be autosomal recessive on initial clinical evaluation, with affected female probands who are sibs and reportedly negative family history. However, genetic testing proved the conditions to be autosomal dominant in both families. In family 1, an asymptomatic CAKUT (unilateral pelvic kidney) was discovered in the mutation-carrier father on subsequent renal evaluation; this exemplified the condition’s variable expressivity. In family 2, the carrier father had normal imaging studies of the renal and urinary system, which demonstrated the condition’s reduced penetrance. Based on our experience, due to CAKUT’s incomplete penetrance and intra-familial variable expressivity, apparently sporadic cases may in fact be familial, with additional affected family members yet to be diagnosed. Autosomal dominant inheritance should be considered even when the known affected individuals are within the same sibship and inheritance may appear to be autosomal recessive. For the same reasons, clinical evaluation of the genitourinary system should be considered in apparently asymptomatic first degree relatives, including parents and siblings. If a clinically significant variant for an autosomal dominant condition is identified in the proband, testing first degree relatives for the variant should be considered to establish inheritance pattern in the family. In addition, genetic testing of unaffected family members, including parents and siblings, is appropriate to help establish disease penetrance in the family and allow for more accurate genetic counseling to other at risk individuals in the future. In the majority of reported cases where GREB1L variants were identified in patients with bilateral renal agenesis, the mildly affected or unaffected mother is the carrier. This observation led to the hypotheses that the GREB1L gene is imprinted, with specific expression of the maternal allele during kidney development (paternally imprinted gene) or that GREB1L variants would affect male fertility, explaining the low rate of paternal inheritance []. Our cases do not support these hypotheses. Identification of the genetic etiology of renal agenesis helps define recurrence risks, allows for early prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing (PGT), and informs subsequent diagnosis and follow up of family members and pregnancies that are at risk for CAKUT. The anomalies seen in CAKUT spectrum are greatly variable, and as such, the time for detection by ultrasound is variable as well. Serial ultrasonography in at risk pregnancies (e.g., pregnancies with a positive genotype and at-risk pregnancies where prenatal diagnosis was declined) would be advised, as CAKUT findings may not be detectable until later in pregnancy or post-natal life. Although the aforementioned genetic and clinical evaluations provide many benefits, challenges remain in genetic counseling for CAKUT especially in the prenatal setting. The variable expressivity and reduced penetrance pose significant difficulties for clinicians to provide prognostic information on mutation-positive fetuses that have yet to demonstrate clinical signs of the condition. The extremely broad prognosis makes it difficult for prospective parents to make decisions regarding continuation or termination of a genetically affected pregnancy. Identification of additional genetic and environmental modifiers of the CAKUT phenotype can potentially help with these remaining challenges.

title: Prenatal diagnosis of ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting syndrome ‒ a case report with literature review.

abstract: The ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting (EEC) syndrome is a rare genetic anomaly described as ectrodactyly (hands and feet), ectodermal dysplasia, and facial cleft with an incidence of around 1 in 90,000 in the population. This syndrome belongs to the TP63 gene’s mutation family. Ectrodactyly is described as the absence of the central toes or fingers or parts of these appendages. Ectodermal dysplasia usually includes changes in the skin, teeth, hair, nails, endocrine glands, nasolacrimal ducts, genitourinary system, conductive hearing loss. This is a unique case of a 40-year-old second gravida, suspected of having a sporadic form of EEC syndrome. Routine transabdominal ultrasound at 14 weeks of gestation revealed malformation of the limbs. The two-dimensional and three-dimensional ultrasound at 16 weeks showed a fetus with ectrodactyly of right hand and foot and cleft palate presence. Diagnostic amniocentesis was performed at 17 weeks of gestation. A molecular genetics test using the Sanger sequencing method from amniotic fluid was performed by scanning TP63 gene sequences and revealed a heterozygous pathogenic variant in TP63. The patient decided on feticide. The heredity of the syndrome is autosomal dominant with high variable expression. More than 300 clinical cases of this syndrome are described in the literature, including both sexes, but the actual etiology is unknown. text:
Prenatal diagnosis of ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting syndrome ‒ a case report with literature review

Introduction
Introduction The ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting (EEC) syndrome consists of symptoms that include ectrodactyly and syndactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, and cleft lip or/and palate. There are two types of this syndrome: syndrome of the TP63 gene’s mutation called EEC3 syndrome and syndrome EEC1 due to changes in the 7th chromosome []. The heredity of both types of the syndrome varies from partial to complete penetrance [, ]. Using sonography, limb buds can be seen transvaginally at eight weeks of gestation, and at 11–12 weeks joints of upper and lower limbs, fingers and toes are visible. Distal limb congenital malformations can be observed either as isolated anomalies involving hands and feet or in the setting of specific syndromes or chromosomal aberrations. Diagnosis of EEC consists of typical phenotype changes and detection of mutations in the TP63 gene or chromosomal abnormalities. Commonly the EEC is one at least of six overlapping syndromes and is determined by the mutations of the TP63 gene. The EEC inheritance is autosomal dominant. However, de novo cases can occur in 70% of TP63-related diseases []. There are three major phenotypes of TP63 pathogenic variants: ectodermal dysplasia, orofacial clefting, and split-hand/foot malformation []. Heterozygous pathogenic TP63 variants are associated with five different syndromes with overlapping phenotypic features: ectrodactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, cleft lip/palate syndrome (EEC), ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate (AEC) syndrome, Rapp–Hodgkin syndrome (RHS), acro-dermo-ungual-lacrimal-tooth (ADULT) syndrome, and limb-mammary syndrome (LMS) also rare TP63 variants are causative for Orofacial Cleft syndrome (OFC8) and non-syndromic split-hand/foot malformation type 4 syndrome (SHFM4) []. This is a case of EEC syndrome diagnosed at the 16th week of pregnancy after ultrasound evaluation showing fetus with classic hand, feet and face malformations and confirmed with molecular genetic testing.

Case presentation
Case presentation A 40-year-old gravida 2, para 2 patient was administered to the Hospital of the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences (LUHS) Kaunas Clinics, Outpatient department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology for prenatal ultrasound screening because of suspicions of fetal limb anomalies. The first routine ultrasound was performed at a primary health care centre at 14 weeks of gestation, and transabdominal ultrasound revealed malformation of the limbs. The patient and her partner had no other illnesses and family history of hereditary diseases. 10 years ago, from a different partner, she delivered a female newborn with left kidney hypoplasia. Two and three-dimensional ultrasound was performed at 16 weeks of gestation and ectrodactyly in the right hand () and foot (), left kidney pyelectasis. A lip/palate defect () was diagnosed. Biometry results matched gestational age. Diagnostic amniocentesis was performed at 17 weeks of gestation with the resulting karyotype 46, XY. EEC syndrome. Two-dimensional ultrasound demonstrates the lobster-claw hand. EEC syndrome. Three-dimensional ultrasound in rendering mode demonstrates the lobster-claw foot. EEC syndrome. Two-dimensional ultrasound demonstrates the cleft lip. A molecular genetics test using the Sanger sequencing method from amniotic fluid was performed by scanning TP63 gene sequences (TP63: E05, E06, E07, E08, E13, E14). According to the manufacturer’s instruction, genomic DNA was isolated from amniotic fluids using a QIAmp DNA blood mini kit. DNA amplification was performed using AmpliTaq Gold 360 PCR mix (6.25 μL), forward and reversed primers for TP63 exons E05, E06, E07, E08, E13, E14 (1 μL), genomic DNA (1 μL), and deionised water (4.25 μL). Primers were designed using Primer3 software. The PCR conditions were: initial denaturation step at 95 °C for 10 min followed by 15 cycles (denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s, annealing at 55 °C for 30 s, elongation at 72 °C for 1 min) and final elongation at 72 °C for 10 min. For Dye-terminator sequencing, BigDye Terminator v3.1 mix and universal sequencing primers M13 were used. Product separation was performed with Applied Biosystems 3500 Genetic Analyzer; the results were obtained and analysed using SeqPatient and NovoSNP software against the reference sequence. The sequence analysis revealed a heterozygous pathogenic variant in TP63 (NM_003722.4): c.727C>T (p.Arg243Trp), which is causative for EEC3 syndrome (). This gene encodes transcription factors of p63 and is essential in cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis. p63 protein is crucial in early ectodermic tissue development []. Sanger sequencing electropherogram of TP63 gene at position 727 shows a pathogenic variant. The patient decided on feticide at 22 weeks of gestation. Stillbirth was induced with misoprostol. The patient delivered a male stillborn with multiple dysplasias: absence of the second, third, and fourth fingers on the right hand (), presence of the fusions between the first and the second, the third and the fourth toe on the right foot (), cleft lip and palate (). No other abnormalities were observed, but continued examination was made difficult because of the prematurity of the fetus. No further test was performed at the request of the parents. EEC syndrome. Stillborn right-hand demonstrates cleft hand. Stillborn foot demonstrates fusion with the first and second toe. Stillborn face demonstrates cleft lip and palate.

Discussion
Discussion Ectrodactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, and cleft lip/palate syndrome is known by various names, including a split hand-split foot–ectodermal dysplasia–cleft syndrome or split hand, cleft hand, or lobster claw hand/foot. This dysplasia contains more than 170 syndromes []. In 1970 Rudiger et al. [] were the first to describe the ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting syndrome. Thurman was the first scientist who described a clinical case of this dysplasia in 1848 [], but the term ‘ectodermal dysplasia’ was first introduced in 1929 []. Ectrodactyly, with or without syndactyly, usually affects central toes or fingers []. Face dysplasias, for example, maxillary hypoplasia, can manifest in nose abnormalities, such as broad nasal tip, choanal atresia, the abnormally long groove between the nose and the upper lip. The outer part of the ears can be malformed, resulting in tiny ears []. Ectodermal dysplasia affects exocrine glands (sweat, sebaceous, salivary glands), skin, teeth (hypodontia) and hair. Abnormal activity of the salivary glands causes mouth dryness. Lacrimal duct abnormalities can cause increased tearing and vision impairment due to increased risk for eye infections, such as conjunctivitis. Other effects on the eyes can manifest by photophobia, blepharitis, keratitis, corneal ulcerations. Di Iorio et all describes limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) as the major cause of ocular morbidity. P63 gene plays a key role in corneal epithelia and explains why mutations might lead to defective limbal stem cell function and progressive keratopathy []. Due to sweat glands dysfunction and reduced ability to sweat, fever or heat intolerance can occur. Individuals with EEC syndrome often have dry, discolored, itchy skin, dysplastic nails, hyperkeratosis, coarse, thin, slow-growing hair. They could have no or skinny eyebrows and eyelashes []. Endocrine abnormalities can also occur. Some individuals have underdeveloped thymus and hypopituitarism. Glandular abnormalities can result in somatotropin deficiency. The intellectual development of children with EEC syndrome is usually unhindered []. Affected individuals may have genitourinary anomalies. Symptoms can include renal agenesis, urethral atresia, and obstruction of the ureters resulting in hydronephrosis. The thin lining of the bladder epithelium that is atrophic or dysplastic can cause dysuria []. The EEC inheritance is autosomal dominant and is determined by the mutations of the TP63 gene. TP63 gene is localised in the long arm of the 3rd chromosome (3q27–q29). This gene encodes proteins necessary for limbs and ectoderm development. TP63 gene spans 267 kb, contains 16 exons, encodes a large number of p63 isoforms. But pathogenic variants are found on two TP63 – the TAp63α and the ΔNp63α isoform (which is shorter and has an alternate N-terminal TA domain (TAΔN)). The full-length TP63 gene consists of transactivation (TA), DNA binding (DBD), oligomerisation (OD), C-terminal sterile alpha motif (SAM), C-terminal transcription inhibitory (TI) domains []. The DNA binding domain is present in all splicing isoforms of p63. All EEC-causing pathogenic TP63 variants are almost exclusively found in this domain, resulting in abolishing the DNA binding fully or partially in all p63 isoforms that affect the protein’s TA capacity. In contrast, AEC-causing pathogenic variants are found in the SAM or TI, or TAΔN domains []. TP63 gene has been found to have around six isoforms, with their prime function being modulating gene expression []. As it was mentioned above, there are five syndromes reported in the literature caused by mutations in the TP63 gene and have overlapping phenotypic features. For example, split-hand/foot malformation/syndactyly is the common feature for all TP63 related syndromes except orofacial cleft eight syndromes (OFC8), meanwhile, Cleft lip/palate is not characterised for ADULT and SHEM4 syndromes []. Antenatal diagnosis is feasible using molecular genetic testing, and samples are obtained using chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, which should be performed if there is suspicion on fetal ultrasound. Afterbirth diagnosis consists of evaluating phenotype, patient history, and a variety of examinations and tests. For example, X-ray for abnormalities of face and limbs, the ophthalmological exam for potential eye complications, kidney ultrasound, skin biopsy. Molecular genetic testing can also be performed after birth []. Molecular analysis, conducted by sequencing coding regions, identifies from 75 to 99% of all pathogenic variants of TP63 mutations. If a mutation is not found, it is possible to perform a deletion/duplication analysis to test for rare cases. Nearly 90% of all EEC3 syndrome cases account for missense mutation, causing arginine substitution in exons 6, 7, 8 disrupt DNA binding []. In rare cases, frameshift mutation is found in exon 13. Moreover, the location of the pathogenic variants, which commonly are as amino acid substitutions, in the TP63 gene determines the phenotype in overlapping syndromes: AEC syndrome is caused by mutations in exon 13, and 14 (82% in SAM domain and 18% in ΔNp63-specific N-terminal domain) [], in ADULT syndrome pathogenic TP63 gene variants are found in the DNA binding domain, also in ΔNp63α (an alternative TA domain), in TAp63α isoform between the TA and DNA binding domains [], in LMS syndrome pathogenic missense variants are located between the transactivation (TA) domain and the DNA binding domain (p.Gly115, p.Ser129, p.Gly173 residues in TAp63α isoform) or by truncating variants in the SAM domain [], in ORF8 syndrome pathogenic TP63 variants (as large deletion) are found in the DNA binding domain []. The treatment of the EEC syndrome is very individual, depending on each patient and the type of the dysplasias. The most of the treatment is symptomatic and sometimes palliative. It is focused on surgical correction of facial and limb deformities. Postnatal problems may involve abnormalities of the tear duct, which can cause corneal damage, as well as anomalies of the hair, teeth, skin, and nails. Because of the great variability in clinical expression, the management of cases of EEC syndrome requires multidisciplinary action. A team of various specialists should participate, including pediatrics, surgeons, plastic surgeons, orthopedics, dentists, speech therapists, ophthalmologists, audiologists, dermatologists, geneticists, psychiatrists, and psychologists []. Early interdisciplinary therapy could allow the patients for better social integration.

Conclusions
Conclusions Accurate diagnosis of skeletal anomalies can be challenging in the first or sometimes even in the second trimester in the absence of relevant family history. Ultrasound features and fetal karyotyping with molecular genetic testing are the keys to correct diagnosis of EEC syndrome. Molecular genetic testing takes time. Its performance as early as possible, preferably in the first trimester, could allow for the appropriate patient counselling in the second trimester. The case demonstrates the importance of ultrasound screening for detecting fetal anomalies prenatally.
