title: Umbilical artery aneurysm without aneuploidy and delivery of a live neonate.
label_reason: Single case with prenatal US cord aneurysm; karyotype 46,XX done on the same infant after delivery. Borderline since test was postnatal.
abstract: Umbilical artery aneurysm, a rare structural anomaly of the umbilical cord, is frequently associated with fetal aneuploidy, fetal growth restriction and fetal demise. At present there are no definitive protocols or guidelines for the surveillance and management of this condition. The index case is an 18-year-old primigravida who had an ultrasound at 35 weeks and 5 days gestation due to lagging symphysio-fundal height measurement. The ultrasound scan revealed a normal fetus with estimated fetal weight that was appropriate for gestational age. There was a cystic structure with internal echoes originating from the placenta at the point of the umbilical cord insertion, which was determined to be a 1.9 × 1.8 cm umbilical artery aneurysm on 3D and Doppler imaging. On follow up imaging the aneurysm had increased in size and measured 3.06 × 1.79 cm. The patient subsequently had a cesarean section delivery of a live female. Karyotyping subsequently revealed 46 XX. A total of 15 cases of umbilical artery aneurysm have been reported in the literature to date, of which there were 5 live born infants with normal karyotype. The remaining 10 cases were intra-uterine fetal demise or trisomy 18 with subsequent neonatal deaths. When monitoring the aneurysms with ultrasound, change in size and Doppler indices play a pivotal role in helping to determine time and mode of delivery and thus allow for a favorable perinatal outcome.
text:
Umbilical artery aneurysm without aneuploidy and delivery of a live neonate

Introduction
Introduction Umbilical artery aneurysm is a rare structural anomaly of the umbilical cord and is frequently associated with fetal aneuploidy, fetal growth restriction and fetal demise []. Umbilical artery aneurysm has been found to be associated with trisomy 18 syndrome and is due to the abnormal placental vasculature seen in these pregnancies []. Euploid fetuses with umbilical artery aneurysms have high rates of demise occurring between 26 and 34 weeks gestation. It is quite difficult to ascertain the exact etiology and predict the timing of greatest risk of intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD) []. Technological advances with higher resolution images and detailed prenatal evaluations have revolutionized the diagnosis of umbilical artery aneurysm []. At present there are no definitive protocols or guidelines for the surveillance and management of this condition. Important clinical parameters such as the influence of size and location of the aneurysm on perinatal outcomes, appropriate timing and mode of delivery are yet to be fully elucidated []. Such information would certainly facilitate better patient counseling and plan for more comprehensive allow for better counseling of patients and for a more comprehensive multidisciplinary team involvement including perinatology, neonatology, and the medical genetics team. Here we report a case of umbilical artery aneurysm diagnosed in the third trimester and subsequent delivery of a live neonate with normal karyotype and will highlight aspects of management reviewed in the literature.

Case presentation
Case presentation The index case is that of an 18-year-old primigravida who was referred to the antenatal testing center for a growth scan at 35 weeks and 5 days gestation, due to lagging symphysio-fundal height measurement. She had no significant past medical history, and her antenatal course was uncomplicated. A detailed ultrasound scan was done and revealed a normal fetus with estimated fetal weight that was appropriate for gestational age, normal amniotic fluid index and a posterior placenta with a 3-vessel umbilical cord. There was a cystic structure with internal echoes, originating from the placenta at the point of the umbilical cord insertion, which was determined to be a 1.9 × 1.8 cm umbilical artery aneurysm on 3D and Doppler imaging (). On subsequent imaging 3 days later at 36 weeks and 1 day, the aneurysm was noted to measure 3.06 × 1.79 cm, an increase in size from prior measurement. Umbilical artery Doppler studies were within normal limits (). The middle cerebral artery peak systolic volume calculated was 1.04 MoM, which was at the higher end of the normal range. Fetal echocardiogram was done and revealed normal cardiac evaluation, with no abnormality detected in the ductus venosus velocimetry. Umbilical artery aneurysm on 3D and Doppler imaging. (A) Cystic structure near cord insertion to the placenta. (B) 3D ultrasound representation of the aneurysm. Color (A) and pulse wave (B) Doppler flow through the umbilical artery aneurysm. Due to the increase in size of the aneurysm over a short interval, the patient was counseled regarding the risks of intra-uterine fetal demise and was transferred to the labor and delivery unit. Fetal monitoring via non-stress test revealed fetal tachycardia, with a baseline heart rate above 165 bpm and regular uterine contractions. Her calculated Bishop score was 2, she was remote from delivery with a category 2 tracing, and a potentially compromised fetus. The decision was then made to proceed with cesarean section delivery. A live female infant was delivered weighing 2,850 g; Apgar scores were 7 at 1 min and 9 at 5 min. The baby was admitted to the special care nursery for observation due to transient tachypnea. The newborn hemoglobin was 15.8 g/dL. Karyotyping subsequently revealed 46 XX. On pathological examination, the placenta was ovoid in shape with an eccentrically inserted 22 cm long 3-vessel edematous umbilical cord (). There was a 2.5 × 2.4 × 1.2 cm dilated intact vessel containing a soft dark red blood clot, approximately 0.4 cm from the base of the umbilical cord (). Surrounding the blood vessel was a 7.0 × 6.0 cm ovoid pale tan area. The umbilical artery aneurysm was confirmed at the point of insertion onto the placental disc. Microscopic and macroscopic chorionic pseudocysts were also noted. Aneurysmal area near the cord insertion measuring 2.5 × 2.4 × 1.2 cm. Showing thrombus within the aneurysmal vessel. (A) Umbilical artery aneurysm with a thrombus in the dilated vessel. (B) Histopathologic representation of clot within aneurysm (formed prenatally).

Discussion
Discussion A total of 15 cases of umbilical artery aneurysm have been reported in the literature to date, of which there were 5 live born infants with normal karyotype []. Our case represents the sixth live born infant with normal karyotype. The remaining 10 cases were IUFD or trisomy 18 with subsequent neonatal deaths. From the reported cases 53% of patients with umbilical artery aneurysm had a single umbilical artery, 23% had trisomy 18 and an IUFD risk overall of 47% [, ]. Typically, umbilical artery aneurysms are seen at the insertion of the cord, close to the placental insertion (as was noted in this case) or close to the fetus []. Four other cases of umbilical artery aneurysm affecting structurally normal fetuses with a 3-vessel umbilical cord and without aneuploidy have been highlighted in the literature. The site of the aneurysm in relation to the cord was noted to be in the middle in 2 cases [, ]; 3 cm from the fetal end in one case [] and at the placental site insertion in the other case []. In terms of overall prognosis, one fetus with the aneurysm located in the middle of the cord ended in an IUFD [], therefore including this case, four structurally normal fetuses, without aneuploidy and a 3 vessel umbilical cord ended in live births. It has been proposed that the poor fetal outcome associated with umbilical artery aneurysm is likely as a result of hemodynamic changes related to compression of the rest of the cord by the aneurysm, thrombosis or rupture []. The underlying etiology surrounding the development of an umbilical artery aneurysm is unknown but may be related to congenital thinning of the arterial wall, or a degeneration of the normally protective Wharton’s jelly, which would normally protect the vasculature and prevent the formation of an aneurysm []. The fetal and placental sites of cord insertion therefore represent points of weakness for aneurysmal formation. Microscopic and macroscopic pseudocysts are often seen associated with umbilical artery aneurysm and likely represents degeneration of Wharton’s jelly [] and was also noted on pathologic evaluation of the placenta in this case. In previously published case reports, the sizes of the reported umbilical artery aneurysms have ranged from 1.9 cm to 8 cm []. The impact of size may be more important in cases where only a single umbilical artery is present, as the aneurysmal vessel can potentially cause significant compression of the umbilical vein. In addition, the aneurysm may well lead to increased vascular resistance to flow in the umbilical artery and thereby increase systemic pressure, culminating in severe intra-uterine growth restriction or cardiomegaly []. The index patient was delivered at 36 weeks and 1 day after noting an increase in size of the aneurysm over a short interval, in conjunction with a category 2 fetal heart rate tracing. Other authors have proposed delivery as soon as fetal lung maturity is achieved, or even as early as 32 weeks if the diagnosis of umbilical artery is made early [, ]. Understandably such measure would likely decrease the risk of IUFD, as only three live births at 36 weeks or above have been reported including this case. Timing of delivery however still remains controversial with no uniformly generalized consensus. In keeping with current guidelines, antenatal corticosteroids administration is a reasonable consideration for patients expected to deliver prior to 37 weeks gestation and is definitely recommended for those less than 34 weeks []. The patient in the index case was delivered expeditiously by cesarean section prior to completion of the antenatal steroid course as she had a category 2 fetal heart rate tracing, on the background of an increase in size of the umbilical artery aneurysm. Interestingly, in the last five reported cases, elective cesarean section was the mode of delivery chosen and whilst this seems to be the trend more data is required to make a generalized recommendation []. Although this patient was delivered by primary cesarean section due to the possibility of a ruptured expanding aneurysm, it is unclear whether this mode of delivery as a whole would improve fetal outcome. However, due to the higher risk of fetal demise, shared decision making should be employed, and all available data presented to the patient. The theory that an expanding aneurysm may possibly rupture when the umbilical cord comes under tension due to fetal descent during a vaginal delivery is quite reasonable and may be related to the size of the aneurysm. Two cases of aneurysmal rupture have been reported, with sizes of 6 and 9 cm, both cases ending with cesarean section deliveries. One baby had mild anemia and thrombocytopenia and had an uneventful neonatal course; whilst the other baby developed severe anemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and later died [, ]. In fact, Matsuki and colleagues went on to suggest cesarean delivery for aneurysms greater than 5 cm in diameter, further specifying that a classical cesareans section or a transverse uterine fundal incision be considered []. Such recommendations may be prudent due to lack of robust clinical evidence to suggest otherwise at this time. In this case the aneurysm was less than 5 cm (approximately 3 cm) and was noted to be intact on pathological evaluation. Each case of umbilical artery aneurysm should have its management individualized to facilitate a safe outcome for both mother and baby as there is no great wealth of current evidence to guide definitive management. Such optimization should therefore include very close fetal surveillance via (1) ultrasonography, including Doppler studies to detect early signs of fetal anemia, which may indicate rupture of the aneurysm or thrombosis. (2) Non-stress testing twice weekly as part of assessment of fetal wellbeing. (3) Multidisciplinary team approach with relevant stakeholders including neonatology team so that early planning and co-ordination may improve neonatal outcomes. (4) Timing of delivery as determined by clinical parameters; with reasonable consideration at 32 to 36 weeks gestation if the aneurysm remains stable in size and no evidence of fetal compromise and (5) consider delivery via cesarean section if the aneurysmal diameter is greater than 5 cm due to increased risk of rupture. While there are no specific pathognomic or characteristic features on cardiotocography related to an umbilical artery aneurysm; identifying any abnormal fetal heart rate patterns in these fetuses would certainly raise concern for the obstetric team to implement the necessary management options accordingly.

Conclusions
Conclusions Umbilical artery aneurysm is a rare structural anomaly of the umbilical cord. Recommendations for adequate interval of fetal monitoring and surveillance require further studies with more reported cases to inform prudent management guidelines. When monitoring the aneurysms with ultrasound; change in size as well as Doppler indices play a pivotal role in helping to determine time and mode of delivery and thus allow for a favorable outcome as was seen in this case.

title: The new frontier: a case for whole exome sequencing with multiple fetal anomalies.
label_reason: Multiple fetal anomalies, karyotype/CMA/WES done.
abstract: Standard genetic testing can fail to identify an underlying genetic etiology in pregnancies affected by multiple fetal abnormalities. Recently, whole exome sequencing (WES) studies have shown promise in recognizing genetic diagnoses where standard genetic testing does not yield answers. A 35-year-old G1P0 healthy female found at anatomy scan to have multiple fetal anomalies, including severe bilateral ventriculomegaly, renal pyelectasis, and short long bones. Karyotype and microarray were normal. Whole exome sequencing showed the fetus was compound heterozygous for likely pathogenic variants in the ROBO1 gene. In the presence of multiple fetal anomalies with normal karyotype and microarray, whole exome sequencing should be considered to not only provide answers for the affected parents, but also aid in future pregnancy planning. Keywords: fetal anomalies, genetic counseling, ultrasound, whole exome sequencing
text:
The new frontier: a case for whole exome sequencing with multiple fetal anomalies

Introduction
Introduction Fetal abnormalities are identified in 2–5 % of pregnancies, and pregnancy outcome and prognosis can vary greatly depending to the types of abnormalities detected, whether they are isolated or multiple, and if there is an underlying genetic etiology []. Using established cytogenetic and molecular techniques, prenatal genetic diagnosis identifies an underlying genetic etiology in around 40 % of fetuses with structural anomalies, leaving the majority of cases undiagnosed [, ]. Several prenatal whole exome sequencing (WES) studies, including a recent systematic review and meta-analysis, have identified genetic diagnoses in fetuses with structural abnormalities when standard genetic testing was not diagnostic [, ]. In these cases, WES can add clinically relevant information that can assist not only current management of a pregnancy, but also future pregnancy planning. We present a case of a patient with multiple fetal anomalies who had normal karyotype and microarray, and the decision to pursue WES not only yielded important information for the future, but also provided closure for the current pregnancy.

Case presentation
Case presentation A 35-year-old Caucasian female G1P0 presented for routine obstetric care. Her spontaneously conceived pregnancy was complicated by advanced maternal age, for which she had a low risk noninvasive prenatal screening and normal Smith-Lemli-Opitz and neural tube defect screening. Her expanded carrier screening showed she was a carrier for factor XI deficiency, otherwise negative for 421 diseases. The father of the pregnancy was 33-years-old and in good health; he was not a carrier for factor XI deficiency. The patient’s father and sister were affected with factor XI deficiency, but otherwise she had an unremarkable family history. She had a normal first trimester ultrasound with nuchal translucency measurement of 2.68 mm. At her anatomy ultrasound at 20w1d, there was notable bilateral ventriculomegaly measuring up to 15 mm, dangling choroid plexus, dilated third ventricle, heart with left axis deviation, and femur length measuring in the 5th% percentile (). There was also marked left renal pyelectasis measuring 1.1 cm with a dilated left ureter and hydronephrosis. Following genetic counseling, an amniocentesis was performed which showed 46, XY karyotype and normal microarray. Cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, and parvovirus IgM and IgG titers were all negative. Of note, the patient did have L1CAM testing included in her carrier screening which came back negative. 20-week anatomy ultrasound findings compared to 22-week follow-up ultrasound. Transabdominal ultrasound images showing severe bilateral ventriculomegaly (A), renal pyelectasis (B), and short femur (C) length at time of 20-week anatomy ultrasound (left) and worsening in severity at a follow-up 22-week ultrasound (D–F, respectively) (right). The patient subsequently had a fetal brain MRI which corroborated these findings, showing marked dilatation of the lateral ventricles measuring 18–20 mm in diameter. A follow-up ultrasound at 22w0d showed worsening bilateral ventriculomegaly measuring 20 mm, femur length in the 2 % percentile, and worsening left renal pyelectasis with suspected ureteropelvic junction obstruction (). Whole exome sequencing was performed, and the trio analysis (proband and parents) showed the fetus was compound heterozygous for a likely pathogenic variant and a variant of unknown significance (VUS) in the ROBO1 gene (). The paternally-inherited variant of ROBO1, c.583C>T, is predicted to result in premature stop codon of arginine. This is a nonsense variant and predicted to be pathogenic. The maternally-inherited variant, c.1021G>C, classified as a VUS and results in amino acid substitution from alanine to proline. However, there is an absence of conclusive functional and genetic evidence. Both variants have not previously been reported in literature. The parents opted to terminate the pregnancy. Surgical pathology confirmed the head and kidney findings seen on ultrasound.

Discussion
Discussion ROBO1 (roundabout guidance receptor 1) is a protein coding gene that encodes an integral membrane protein that functions in axon guidance and neuronal precursor cell migration. The receptor itself is activated by SLIT-family proteins that have a repulsive effect on glioma cell guidance in the developing brain [, ]. Clinically, variants in ROBO1 have been reported in individuals with developmental disorder, language impairment, epilepsy, and autism [], [], []. ROBO1 variants have also been reported in association with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) []. In one family, there were reported compound heterozygous variants in ROBO1 in two fetuses also affected by CAKUT, with both fetuses found to have kidney agenesis, genital hypoplasia, hypoplasia of the halluces, intestinal malrotation, and anteriorly displaced anuses []. In our case report, each parent carried a recessive allele of the ROBO1 variant. Given the previously described integral role of ROBO1 in neuronal migration of the developing brain, it is plausible the combination of the two variants were associated with the structural CNS anomalies seen on ultrasound. It is likely the fetus would have been at significant risk for cognitive defects as previously described in literature [], [], []. It is also possible the ROBO1 variants contributed to the renal anomalies. The parents were counseled that given the mutations appear to be functioning as recessive alleles, the recurrence risk for future offspring is 25 %. Future pregnancy planning options discussed include prenatal testing via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, or in vitro fertilization with preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) for monogenic/single gene conditions to select against ROBO1. They were also counseled that other family members could be carriers of the ROBO1 variants and should be informed of this information and that genetic screening is available. When karyotype testing and chromosomal microarray fail to determine the underlying cause of a structural anomaly, whole exome sequencing can add clinically relevant information that not only can impact management of the current pregnancy, but also affect future pregnancies. Of note, before jumping to WES, there are specific target gene panels that can identify sets of monogenic disorders if a specific phenotype is known. If there are multiple anomalies or incomplete phenotypic ascertainment, however, the prenatal utility of such panels can be limited, and WES should be considered []. Next generation WES provides much greater resolution than standard genetic testing techniques, down to the single base-pair level. WES has been studied in the clinical setting only in the past few years, but studies so far have already demonstrated a diagnostic yield of 25–30 % in post-natal testing in cases undiagnosed with established methods [, ]. More recent studies have suggested that diagnostic yields for prenatal WES are higher in fetuses with multiple anomalies or in cases preselected following genetic review [, ]. In a prospective cohort study by Petrovski et al. using prenatal WES trio sequence data at a large academic center, diagnostic genetic variants were identified in 10 % of cases affected by a structural anomaly on prenatal ultrasound []. The PAGE cohort study by Lord et al. found that the overall detection rate of diagnostic genetic variants in a prospectively ascertained cohort was lower than previously suggested and recommended careful case selection to maximize clinical utility []. Accurate fetal phenotyping is key in ensuring highest yield for WES. He et al. found that WES especially added value in genetic diagnosis for abnormal fetuses with skeletal diseases with normal karyotype and microarray []. In another study looking specifically at Jewish families, WES yield was relatively higher (42.9–60 %) among families with involvement of brain, renal or musculoskeletal ultrasound findings, especially with a positive family history []. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis by Mellis et al. showed diagnostic yield was significantly higher for cases pre-selected for likelihood of monogenic etiology and ranged significantly between phenotypic sub-groups, with highest for isolated skeletal abnormalities at 53 % []. Multidisciplinary review may be useful in determining if a monogenic cause is likely and optimizing the expected diagnostic yield of cases. It is important to note that while WES can improve detection of clinically important variants, it will also increase detection of incidental findings and variants of uncertain significance which can be challenging to interpret. In one study, up to 15 % of abnormal fetuses with normal karyotype and microarray who underwent a WES were found to have VUS []. WES also has a lengthy turnaround time, high cost, and requires analysis by a multidisciplinary team of perinatal practitioners, geneticists, and laboratory specialists which presents feasibility challenges. Insurance coverage is challenging especially if the pregnancy has been terminated. Prohibitive costs and challenges with insurance can cause resistance to obtaining WES, which impedes its utilization. In our case, coverage was only approved after extensive peer-to-peer review, and ultimately the findings helped the family immensely for future pregnancy planning. We hope that as the technology improves and the clinical importance of WES becomes more widely recognized, it will be more universally offered and utilized. Given the high potential for clinical utility in the presence of multiple fetal anomalies with normal karyotype and microarray, whole exome sequencing should be strongly considered in these cases. The whole exome sequencing trio analysis in this case afforded the results needed to bring closure for the parents and aid in future pregnancy planning.

title: Whole Genome Sequencing in Prenatal Diagnostics: The Danish Approach to Guideline Formation and Implementation Within Public Healthcare.
label_reason: Guideline description, no fetal cases.
abstract: To describe the implementation of whole genome sequencing (WGS) in prenatal diagnostics and outline the national guideline system facilitating this. Clinical guidelines for WGS in prenatal diagnostics were developed and implemented by the Danish Fetal Medicine Society. Guidelines were developed by expert consensus following a review of 75 studies. Diagnostic yield served as a key factor in prioritizing WGS for various phenotypes, improving diagnostic accuracy and informing clinical decisions. Phenotypes for WGS include nuchal translucency ≥ 6.0 mm, multiple anomalies, skeletal dysplasia, neuromuscular diseases, non‐immune hydrops fetalis, central nervous system malformations, congenital diaphragmatic hernia and severe fetal growth restriction (< 3 SDs not explained by placental insufficiency). Small regional variations exist in indications, bioinformatics, and funding, but WGS is now routinely used nationwide for these indications. The Danish Fetal Medicine Society's guideline development, emphasizing diagnostic yield and gradual implementation, has supported the relatively uniform integration of WGS into prenatal diagnostics. Keywords: clinical guidelines, Denmark, diagnostic yield, genomic medicine, prenatal diagnostics, prenatal screening and diagnostic technologies, public healthcare system, whole genome sequencing

Whole Genome Sequencing in Prenatal Diagnostics: The Danish Approach to Guideline Formation and Implementation Within Public Healthcare

Introduction
Introduction The integration of prenatal trio exome/genome sequencing (WES/WGS of the fetus and both parents) into prenatal diagnostics is gaining traction globally, particularly when conventional methods such as karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) return normal results. This trend is reflected in various guidelines and expert statements, such as those from the International Society for Prenatal Diagnosis [] or American College of Medical Genetics []. However, guidelines are often contested and applied inconsistently, influenced by differing clinical practices, individual efforts, and financial constraints. Moreover, many of these documents offer limited guidance on how to prioritize patient groups as the demand for genomic testing grows. The Danish Context Since 2004, all pregnant women in Denmark have been offered tax‐paid prenatal diagnostics [], which include: (1) The first‐trimester ultrasound scan (US1) including a risk calculation for trisomy 21, 18, and 13 based on the Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF) algorithm and incorporates NT measurements and maternal serum analytes (free β‐hCG, PAPP‐A). Women with a risk above 1:300 for trisomy 21 or 1:150 for trisomy 13 or 18 (∼5% of all pregnancies) are offered an invasive test and CMA or non‐invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) []; (2) The second‐trimester ultrasound scan (US2) includes a detailed scan and assessment of the fetal organs and growth assessment to detect signs of disease or malformations. Approximately 95% of all pregnant women attend both scans []. In roughly 3% of Danish pregnancies (EUROCAT data, Funen 2022), one or more structural anomalies are detected, ranging from minor defects to fatal multisystem malformations. If US2 indicates a risk of/a condition associated with chromosomal abnormality, the woman is offered invasive testing. Up to 2013, the standard test was a cytogenetic chromosome analysis of invasively obtained material, which identified a chromosomal cause in an average of 14% of cases with fetal malformations []. In 2013, Denmark implemented CMA as the standard test for prenatal invasive procedures for fetal malformations [, ]. The need to supplement this with a WES/WGS guideline was suggested and decided by the Danish Fetal Medicine Society (DFMS) in 2019, developed in 2020, and the first guideline was issued in 2021. In 2021, a previous guideline introduced Whole Exome Sequencing or WGS as an option for pregnancies with for example, severe malformations with normal CMA [, ]. A significant milestone in advancing genomic medicine in Denmark was the donation of DKK 1 billion from the Novo Nordisk Foundation. This funding led to the establishment of two national genomics centers and the ambitious project to sequence 60,000 genomes offered to 17 patient groups, including critical fetal indications. This allowed WGS to be implemented without any sequencing costs before Q3, 2024 and fast‐forwarded the WGS implementation over WES. This paper describes the development and gradual implementation of guidelines for this new diagnostic test in a healthcare system committed to equal access. A challenge has been gradually scaling up this labor‐intensive analysis with diagnostic yield serving as the key tool for triaging patient groups.

Methods
Methods Obstetric Guideline Developments in Denmark The Danish Health Authorities outline maternal care, but below this there are multiple national guidelines to assist clinical decision‐making. These guidelines are developed collaboratively by medical specialties through voluntary contributions from members of medical societies [, ]. Every year, Danish fetal medicine experts, geneticists and FMF‐certified sonographers discuss and adopt common guidelines on topics identified at the previous meetings. The preparatory work is crucial. Groups composed of members from diverse geographical locations and experienced and early‐career professionals that thoroughly review the literature and present well‐founded guideline proposals at the meetings. The proposals are distributed to all participants well in advance of the meetings. A moderator, who is not part of the preparatory group, ensures that decisions can indeed be made in the full forum. Often, voting is used as a way to decide on whether new guidelines are ready for implementation. After each meeting, the proposals are revised according to the discussions and published on the societal websites within a few months of the meeting (www.dsog.dk, www.dfms.dk). While no formal mechanism exists to verify adherence to the guidelines, data from national registries and the obstetric community quickly highlight significant deviations. Implementation of WES/WGS in Prenatal Diagnostics The first guideline on prenatal use of WES/WGS was issued in 2021. This initial 2021 guideline recommended annual updates to adapt to new technology (then WES) and patient requirements. The guideline with 2023 and now 2024 revisions (now WGS) followed this approach: Preparation: Comprehensive literature review and assessment of diagnostic yield for various phenotypes. Original search 2021/2023 in Medline: (((“Exome”[MAJR]) OR (“Exome Sequencing”[MAJR])) AND (“Genetic Counseling”[MeSH Terms])) AND (“Prenatal Diagnosis”[MeSH Terms]). 2021: After review this included 31 papers. Update 2023: After review and removal of duplicates and additional chain search there was a total of 45 papers. Update search October 2024: (((“Exome Sequencing”[MAJR]) OR (“Whole Genome Sequencing”[MAJR])) AND (“Prenatal Diagnosis”[MeSH Terms])) AND (English[Language]) AND (“2022/01/01”[Date ‐ Publication]: “3000”[Date ‐ Publication]) identified additional 30 papers, leaving a total of 75 refences. Proposal and Discussion: Presentation, discussion (January 17, 2024) and acceptance (March 31, 2024) of the current WGS guideline []. Revision and Integration: Revision of guidelines based on feedback and gradual integration into clinical practice hereafter.

Results
Results Diagnostic Yield and Clinical Decision‐Making The decision to implement WGS in prenatal diagnostics is driven by the diagnostic yield for specific phenotypes. Key findings include (for details see Table ) [, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. High diagnostic yield for multiple anomalies (29%; 33%) [, ]‐ skeletal dysplasia (53%) [] and neuromuscular diseases (37%) [], non‐immune hydrops fetalis (22%; 37%) [, ], central nervous system malformations (17%) [] and severe fetal growth restriction without placental insufficiency (11%; 11%; 42%) [, , ]. Moderate diagnostic yield for congenital heart disease (11%) [] and isolated urogenital anomalies (9%) []. Low diagnostic yield for gastrointestinal and thoracic malformations, guiding selective use of WGS. Explicit Recommendations From the Guidelines Based on the diagnostic yields, the current Danish 2024 guideline provides specific recommendations for the use of WGS in prenatal diagnostics. Phenotypes recommended for WGS include nuchal translucency ≥ 6.0 mm, skeletal dysplasia, neuromuscular diseases, non‐immune hydrops fetalis, central nervous system malformations, and multiple anomalies. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia if postnatal surgery is planned and severe fetal growth restriction if unexplained by placental insufficiency are also included (Table ). Next in line for WGS is heart and kidney malformations (9%; 11% diagnostic yield). Guideline Contents on the Clinical Implementation of WES/WGS Besides ensuring the gradual implementation by diagnostic yield, the Danish WES/WGS guideline describes the expected everyday practice. Pretest counseling should be offered by specialists or trained personnel and include: likelihood of significant genetic findings, expected timeline for results, and only likely pathogenic (class 4) and pathogenic (class 5) variants according to ACMG classifications [] explaining the phenotype of the fetus are reported. A written consent form is completed, including patient preferences on the reporting of incidental and secondary findings. After the raw sequencing data are generated and processed at one of the two national genomic centers, vcf and cram files are transferred to the clinical genetics departments for filtering, interpretation, and reporting. Here variants are analyzed in a trio‐format according to local preferences. No department limits analyses to specific extensive gene panels; instead, a genome‐wide approach is applied. Add‐on gene panels individually tailored to each case are analyzed if needed with strong inspiration from Genomics England (https://panelapp.genomicsengland.co.uk/panels/). Variant of unknown Significance (VUS) are generally not reported in pregnancy with exceptions for relevant VUS in autosomal recessive cases with a pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant on the other allele. Monthly national meetings with prenatal clinical geneticists and laboratory geneticists address potential general differences in variant filtering and interpretation. All regions practise multidisciplinary team (MDT) clinics on difficult variants. Post‐test counseling is provided to the couples, including information on recurrence risk and future pregnancy options, with written documentation in the patient's health record.

Discussion
Discussion The Danish guideline system has effectively and relatively quickly integrated advanced genomic technologies into prenatal diagnostics by focusing on diagnostic yield. This approach aligns well with a gradual capacity expansion. Key challenges include capacity, funding, and concerns about secondary or incidental findings. However, MDT‐clinics (fetal medicine specialists and geneticists) have facilitated these processes in daily practice in a case‐by‐case manner. Furthermore, geneticists from each region hold bi‐monthly videoconferences to discuss and align implementation. We acknowledge that focusing on diagnostic yield may overlook broader clinical implications in everyday clinical scenarios. In everyday practice, individual considerations significantly influence individual patient management and are controlled through MDT‐clinics. For example, in Denmark, patients undergoing postnatal surgery for major congenital heart disease or omphalocele may have pWGS performed even though this is not stated in the guidelines for congenital diaphragmatic hernia. These cases remain relatively few for now but underscore how clinical utility is implicitly recognized alongside diagnostic yield in practice. Abnormal biometries have always been a challenge since this heterogenous group among others includes skeletal dysplasias, with high diagnostic yield, as well as growth anomalies caused by placental insufficiency or infection with a low diagnostic yield. As a clinical guideline, we recommend WGS when the phenotype clearly indicates skeletal dysplasia or in case of severely abnormal biometries (< 3 SD) where typical findings of placental insufficiency or infection have been ruled out. Further, it is important to know that the diagnostic yield from Table serves as the foundational metric, while other indications are included or excluded based on emerging data and clinical feedback as this guideline gets revised yearly. As mentioned, a significant milestone in advancing genomic medicine in Denmark was the donation of DKK 1 billion from the Novo Nordisk Foundation. This funding led to the establishment of two national genomics centers and the ambitious project to sequence 60,000 genomes, including critical fetal indications The decision to prioritize WGS over WES in Denmark was primarily driven by these funding opportunities. Specifically, the National Genome Center (NGC) offered genomes free of charge, whereas the regions expected the usual payments for exomes. Consequently, exomes were phased out within a short period of time. The National Genome Center (NGC) now serves as a central hub for genomic data collection (FASTQ‐files), analysis, and storage. Some may wonder why comprehensive gene panels, despite their utility, were not incorporated into the guidelines, or why CMA is performed before WGS, even though WGS has a higher diagnostic yield. Both decisions are influenced by diagnostic delays and the Danish rules for pregnancy termination, which currently limit the procedure to below GA 23 + 0 (viability). Given this legal framework, the time interval between ultrasound suspicion of a condition and the need for a confirmed diagnosis is often less than 2 weeks. CMA is typically feasible within this timeframe, whereas WGS also requires approximately 2 weeks, making it a tight fit in urgent situations. Comprehensive gene panels, with a turnaround time of approximately 3 weeks, are generally not practical in the Danish context. We are now transitioning toward a model where WGS is performed directly on prenatal samples without prior CMA. International Perspective The Danish guideline aligns well with the ISPD statement [] regarding setup, indication, and recommendations. As a Danish adapted guideline, it may be more prescriptive and binding in daily practice in public healthcare in Denmark and local adaptations facilitate implementation and awareness. Guidelines help ensure that every doctor can provide high‐quality, evidence‐based care to all patient groups, and easy digital access to these guidelines supports their use also in less familiar areas. They also help prioritize resources and may reduce overmedicalization. A significant drawback is the significant workload involved in creating and updating guidelines, often done in people's spare time. Another possible downside is reduced individualization of treatment, though intentional non‐adherence can be justified if properly documented. Limitations and Challenges in the Guideline Development Process The process of developing and implementing guidelines for whole genome sequencing (WGS) in prenatal diagnostics is not without its limitations. One significant challenge lies in the variability in study quality and differences in the definitions of diagnostic yield across the literature. These inconsistencies make it difficult to establish universal thresholds or draw direct comparisons between studies, as some include variants of uncertain significance (VUS) or secondary findings, while others do not. Additionally, achieving consistency in a consensus‐driven process involving multiple stakeholders presents its own challenges. The multidisciplinary nature of the effort, while critical for inclusivity and broad applicability, can lead to differences in interpretation and prioritization of evidence. Aligning diverse perspectives requires ongoing dialog and iterative revisions, which may compromise stringency but ultimately strengthen the everyday robustness of the guidelines. Looking ahead, addressing these limitations through systematic reviews, increased reliance on high‐quality multicenter studies, and streamlined consensus methodologies may improve the process further. By continually reflecting on and refining our approach, we aim to enhance the accuracy, reliability, and clinical utility of these guidelines.

Conclusion
Conclusion The Danish approach to developing clinical guidelines and integrating whole genome sequencing (WGS) into prenatal diagnostics underscores the value of a structured, national, and evidence‐based system aimed at improving diagnostic yield. WGS has contributed to better diagnostic accuracy and more informed clinical decisions, with further data collection planned. Insights from the experiences of other public healthcare systems in developing and implementing WGS guidelines would be beneficial.

The PreGen Research Program: Implementing Prenatal Genomic Testing in Australia—A Commentary

Introduction
Introduction The introduction of prenatal exome and genome sequencing (ES/GS) for fetal structural anomalies (FSA) has been shown to achieve a significantly increased diagnostic rate compared with karyotype and microarray []. Despite this, prenatal genomic testing is not available uniformly across Australia for families with high‐risk pregnancies. Approximately 2%–5% of pregnancies will have an FSA detected on ultrasound [], and more than 80% of these have a genetic aetiology []. The prenatal diagnostic rates for conventional testing (prior to next‐generation sequencing) are 8%–10% for karyotype [] and 6% for microarray []. The overall ES diagnostic rate for FSA has been estimated to be 31% []. Early diagnosis of a genetic disorder in pregnancy may benefit families by decreasing costly and time‐consuming diagnostic odysseys [] and enabling the development of tailored perinatal management plans and patient counselling []. Prenatal diagnoses can also facilitate reproductive modulation []. Even an uninformative result may be helpful in providing reassurance for families as the residual risk of a Mendelian disorder may be reduced. PreGen (https://pregen.neura.edu.au/) is a 5‐year translational research program that aims to implement prenatal genomic testing for FSA in the Australian population and to better understand how to care for patients and families undergoing genomic testing in pregnancy. As PreGen has progressed, we have identified significant barriers to the implementation of prenatal genomic testing in Australia. These include access to funding, the availability of genomic testing, access to termination of pregnancy services and the availability of specialist genomic centres and support services.

Access to Funding
Access to Funding In Australia, prenatal ES trio testing costs approximately $3200. There is no uniformity of genomic testing budgets within the public hospital system. There are gaps in funding for some locations which may lead to referrals being made to laboratories with the lowest costs even if in a different state. ES trio costs are prohibitive for many patients to self‐fund, further compounding the inequity of service provision. In the context of FSA, some maternity hospitals and genetic units without specific funding for ES trios may offer to fund less expensive alternatives with a lower diagnostic rate such as limited gene panels []. The PreGen program provides funding for prenatal genomic testing for families with an identified FSA who may then also take part in psychosocial and health economic assessments. The PreGen inclusion criteria are listed in Table . A requirement of referral to PreGen from a public hospital is that a funded genomic test would otherwise be available if the patient does not wish to take part in PreGen. This was an ethical consideration to reduce the risk of undue influence on patients invited to participate in the research program. This requirement for “safety net” funding has already highlighted that alternative funding options for prenatal genomic testing do not exist in some locations. Alternative funding pathways were required to be established by some referring hospitals to enable PreGen enrolment for their patients. The absence of uniform local funding could be resolved with a federal MBS item number for prenatal genomic testing.

Availability of Testing
Availability of Testing There are currently only three laboratories accredited for prenatal ES testing in Australia, meaning that patients from several states require samples to be transferred to interstate laboratories. This can increase the turn‐around time for results as well as the chance of sample loss. The urgency of prenatal genomic samples also impacts every laboratory's resources to process local samples, both urgent and non‐urgent. Ideally, each state should have an appropriately sized provider of prenatal genomic testing, which could be facilitated through a federal MBS item number. In addition to sample processing arrangements, families who reside in areas that are distant from metropolitan hospitals may experience delays in diagnosis, as well as financial burden and logistical complexity. Rural and regional patients may be required to have multiple appointments in city hospitals or stays in a metropolitan area to access prenatal genomic testing. Some patients may need to rely on family members to look after other children while they attend multiple appointments. Other patients may not have this option, leading to additional logistical and financial burdens related to childcare arrangements. Each state also has different travel and accommodation benefits available for families. Unexpected costs and complex claims processes can impact patients financially at a time when they are under immense psychological pressure. The PreGen program is examining how the area of residence impacts families' experiences when accessing prenatal genomic testing with a view to improving the model of care and reducing inequity for rural and regional families.

Access to Termination of Pregnancy Services
Access to Termination of Pregnancy Services Access to termination of pregnancy after diagnosis of FSA varies across Australia. The termination of pregnancy laws also vary state by state (Table ). In Australia, women routinely have a detailed morphology ultrasound examination at 18–20 weeks gestation. The earlier 11–14 week ultrasound scan confirms fetal number, gestation and viability and is used to screen for common forms of aneuploidy (trisomies 21, 18 and 13) [], but most FSAs are currently detected later in gestation []. Given the restrictions placed on the termination of pregnancy in some states, families may have limited opportunity to decide on the outcome of a pregnancy if a genomic diagnosis occurs after 20 weeks gestation. Faster and more accurate means of testing pregnancies for genetic conditions could facilitate broader choices regarding pregnancy management for families. A federal MBS item number for prenatal genomic testing could improve access, reduce turnaround times and promote discussion in legislative bodies regarding the discrepancies in termination of pregnancy laws around Australia. Examining some state‐specific laws to harmonise the time required for families to access testing and facilitate reproductive decisions may be beneficial to improve equity of access to termination of pregnancy.

Availability of Specialist Genomic and Support Services
Availability of Specialist Genomic and Support Services While each state has maternal‐fetal medicine teams, they are not all integrated with genetic services with ready access to clinical geneticists and genetic counsellors. Access to counsellors trained in providing prenatal genetic counselling is required for the best patient outcomes [, ] and patients also seek genetic counselling prior‐ and post‐termination of pregnancy for FSA [, ]. Patients often want rapid answers following the termination of pregnancy to understand recurrence risk in future pregnancies []. Inadequately resourced genetics units have long wait times for appointments, limiting timely access to genomic testing for families planning future pregnancies. Collaboration between maternal‐fetal medicine teams and clinical genetics units is integral to the referral process and appropriate perinatal management [, ]. Patient services are maximised when teams work cohesively to counsel patients about ultrasound findings, arrange the most appropriate testing and provide genetic counselling in a timely manner [, ]. The extent to which collaborative management is achievable is often dependent on locality‐specific resourcing which is not uniform across Australia. Local solutions are therefore required for best‐practice patient management []. Multiple studies have highlighted the importance of support services being made available for families who have a diagnosis of an abnormality in pregnancy []. This can include social work support, experienced perinatal loss midwives and in‐hospital psychology services []. Unfortunately, access to these services is not equal across Australia or even within states. Despite the existence of best‐practice guidelines in perinatal loss, management pathways are heavily dependent on which facility identifies the FSA []. Some tertiary hospitals can provide access to all these support services however in other centres the perinatal loss midwife performs the role of social worker as well as mental health professional. Support services need to be available to all patients diagnosed with an FSA or experiencing pregnancy loss.

Next Steps
Next Steps There is a clear need for adequate public funding to be provided for pregnant women seeking prenatal genomic testing for FSA to achieve best practice and equitable care for all patients across Australia. The PreGen program's evaluation of the impact of prenatal genomic testing on decision making for patients and healthcare providers is providing valuable insights on how to address the current barriers to equitable access. PreGen has been well‐received by families to date. Comprehensive data from the psychosocial sub‐study will identify the psychological impact of PreGen, including perceived benefits and any associated challenges. The results of PreGen will be used to design best‐practice prenatal genomics management guidelines inclusive of psychosocial support and resourcing for required turn‐around times for test reporting. The aim is to facilitate the provision of a federal item number for prenatal genomic testing to increase equitable test availability, promote the use of local resources and reduce delays to diagnoses by making them in pregnancy. The introduction of prenatal genomic testing will remove the need for low‐yield diagnostic interventions while emphasising personalised patient management and family support.

title: Arachnoid cyst found in fetal ultrasound: A case report.
label_reason: Fetal arachnoid cyst on ultrasound/MRI; karyotype normal.
abstract: Arachnoid cysts are rare, fluid-filled cavities within the arachnoid membrane of the central nervous system. While typically asymptomatic in postnatal cases, their prenatal detection on ultrasound poses diagnostic and prognostic challenges. We report a case of a fetus diagnosed with an arachnoid cyst during routine second-trimester ultrasound. High-resolution ultrasound and fetal MRI confirmed the presence of an isolated, noncompressive arachnoid cyst. Genetic testing, including karyotyping, and serological evaluations revealed no chromosomal abnormalities or associated structural anomalies. This case underscores the importance of accurate prenatal imaging and multidisciplinary care. Isolated arachnoid cysts generally carry a favorable prognosis, yet regular monitoring is essential to detect potential complications. Management includes detailed prenatal counseling, delivery planning, and postnatal evaluation to assess the need for surgical intervention. Prenatal diagnosis of arachnoid cysts facilitates early counseling and comprehensive management planning. Further research is needed to enhance diagnostic accuracy and optimize management protocols for these rare lesions.
text:
Arachnoid cyst found in fetal ultrasound: A case report

Introduction
Introduction Arachnoid cysts are benign sacs filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that arise between the brain or spinal cord and the arachnoid membrane. They are estimated to occur in approximately 1% of the general population, and most cases diagnosed incidentally in adulthood. Prenatal diagnosis is extremely rare, but is becoming more common with the widespread use of advanced imaging technologies such as high-resolution ultrasound and fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) []. This article highlights a case of an arachnoid cyst identified during routine fetal ultrasound at 24 weeks of gestation. The purpose is to provide information on the diagnostic process, imaging features, potential fetal and neonatal outcomes, and the available management strategies for healthcare providers and expectant parents []. Case presentation A 30-year-old primigravida underwent a routine second-trimester anomaly scan at 24 weeks of gestation. The pregnancy had progressed uneventfully to this point, with no history of maternal illness, exposure to teratogenic agents, or a family history of congenital anomalies. During the ultrasound examination, performed using a Voluson S6 ultrasound machine, an abnormal fluid-filled structure () was observed in the fetal cranial region. The lesion appeared as a well-circumscribed, anechoic, and nonvascular area, measuring approximately 15.1 mm in diameter ( and ). Based on these characteristics, the differential diagnosis included an arachnoid cyst, porencephaly, intracranial cystic tumor, or congenital malformations such as Dandy-Walker malformation. Ultrasound image showing a well-defined fluid-filled arachnoid cyst. Fig 1: Measurements of cyst diameter, confirming its size as 15.1 mm. Fig 2: Comparative imaging of adjacent brain structures, which shows no significant mass effect. Fig 3: Genetic testing was performed, including amniocentesis for karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis, to exclude chromosomal abnormalities. The results confirmed a normal karyotype, effectively ruling out common genetic conditions such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21. Additional maternal serological tests for infections such as toxoplasmosis and cytomegalovirus were also negative, eliminating infectious causes of intracranial abnormalities. These findings supported the diagnosis of an isolated congenital arachnoid cyst with a favorable prognosis. The absence of structural or genetic anomalies suggested that the lesion was unlikely to have a significant impact on fetal development. Postpartum confirmation and follow-up imaging Postpartum evaluation of the neonate included both clinical assessment and imaging studies to confirm the prenatal diagnosis. Within the first week after birth, a cranial ultrasound was performed, revealing a well-circumscribed, anechoic lesion in the same cranial region initially identified at 24 weeks of gestation. To further delineate the characteristics of the cyst, a neonatal MRI was subsequently obtained. This MRI confirmed the presence of a nonenhancing, fluid-filled cyst with smooth margins, consistent with an arachnoid cyst. These findings are in agreement with the literature, which highlights that prenatal identification of an isolated arachnoid cyst is reliably confirmed postpartum through ultrasound and MRI imaging. The absence of associated structural anomalies on postpartum imaging corroborated the initial diagnosis and supported the favorable prognosis suggested by the prenatal findings.

Discussion
Discussion Arachnoid cysts are cerebrospinal fluid located between the brain or spinal cord and the arachnoid membrane, one of the meninges that cover the central nervous system. Their aetiology is largely attributed to developmental abnormalities, specifically tearing, duplication, or malformation of the arachnoid membrane during embryogenesis []. These malformations can disrupt the normal flow of cerebrospinal fluid, leading to the formation of cysts. Arachnoid cysts are classified as primary (congenital) or secondary (acquired). Primary cysts are developmental in origin, while secondary cysts result from trauma, infection, or surgery. In this case, the absence of maternal or fetal infection history, normal genetic test results, and no significant environmental risk factors strongly support the diagnosis of a primary congenital arachnoid cyst []. The mechanisms driving the formation of primary arachnoid cysts remain incompletely understood. Research suggests that defective remodeling of the meningeal layers during early gestation may contribute to their development. Genetic factors may also play a role, although no specific gene mutations have been conclusively linked to isolated arachnoid cysts. More studies are needed to elucidate the molecular and genetic pathways involved in the formation of arachnoid cyst formation []. The prognosis of arachnoid cysts identified prenatally depends on several factors, including size, location, and potential impact on adjacent brain structures. Isolated arachnoid cysts, as observed in this case, generally have a favorable prognosis, particularly when they do not exert a significant mass effect, interfere with cerebrospinal fluid circulation, or compromise brain development. Long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in such cases are typically normal, and most children experiencing no neurological deficits []. However, larger cysts or those located in critical areas of the brain, such as the posterior fossa, can be associated with complications, such as hydrocephalus, brain compression, or disruptions of normal brain function. In such cases, the prognosis can vary and early intervention may be required to mitigate the risk of long-term neurological sequelae. The lack of additional structural or chromosomal abnormalities in this case further supports the likelihood of a positive outcome. The management of prenatally diagnosed arachnoid cysts is centered around careful monitoring and multidisciplinary collaboration. Serial ultrasounds are essential to track cyst growth, assess the development of complications such as hydrocephalus, and assess any impact on surrounding brain structures. These follow-up evaluations provide critical information to guide counseling and delivery planning []. Delivery in a tertiary care center equipped with advanced neonatal care and access to specialists in neonatal neurology and neurosurgery is strongly recommended. This approach ensures that immediate postnatal imaging and clinical evaluation can be conducted to confirm the diagnosis and guide further treatment. Postnatal imaging, typically with MRI or CT, provides more detailed anatomical information about the cyst and its relationship to adjacent structures. For cysts that cause significant symptoms postnatally, surgical interventions, such as fenestration (creating a small opening in the cyst wall to allow cerebrospinal fluid drainage) or shunting (placing a catheter to divert fluid), may be necessary. In most cases involving isolated, asymptomatic cysts, conservative management with regular monitoring is sufficient and invasive interventions are not required []. Although high-resolution ultrasound remains the primary modality for the prenatal diagnosis of arachnoid cysts, it has inherent limitations. Distinguishing arachnoid cysts from other intracranial anomalies such as porencephaly, intracranial cystic tumors, and Dandy-Walker malformation can be challenging due to overlapping imaging features. The precise characterization of cysts often requires complementary imaging modalities, such as fetal MRI. However, in resource-limited settings where MRI is not readily available, diagnostic accuracy is highly dependent on the expertise of the sonographer and the quality of the ultrasound equipment. Another limitation lies in the inability to assess the functional implications of the cyst prenatally. Although structural imaging can provide detailed anatomical information, it cannot predict with certainty the impact of the cyst on postnatal neurological development. Therefore, prenatal findings must be interpreted cautiously, with an emphasis on postnatal follow-up to confirm diagnosis and monitor developmental milestones []. This case underscores the need for more research into the natural history of arachnoid cysts detected prenatally. Larger longitudinal studies are necessary to better understand the factors that influence cyst growth, the risk of complications, and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Furthermore, research into advanced imaging techniques and biomarkers that can improve diagnostic specificity and prognostic accuracy would greatly enhance the management of these cases. Genetic studies can also reveal potential hereditary or de novo mutations associated with congenital arachnoid cysts, paving the way for targeted diagnostic and therapeutic approaches []. From a clinical perspective, early detection of arachnoid cysts allows for informed decision making, including counseling for expectant parents about potential outcomes, risks, and treatment options. Clear communication about the likely benign nature of isolated cysts, as well as the importance of postnatal follow-up, can alleviate parental anxiety and help set realistic expectations. Collaborative care with obstetricians, radiologists, genetic counsellors, and pediatric neurologists is essential to ensure complete evaluation and management []. In conclusion, this case highlights the diagnostic and prognostic considerations associated with the prenatal identification of an isolated arachnoid cyst. Although the limitations of prenatal imaging must be acknowledged, ongoing advances in diagnostic modalities and a multidisciplinary approach provide an optimistic outlook for affected pregnancies.

Conclusion
Conclusion Arachnoid cysts are rare findings in fetal ultrasound, and their detection requires careful evaluation to determine their potential impact on fetal and neonatal health. Multidisciplinary management involving obstetricians, radiologists, genetic counsellors, and neonatologists is crucial to provide comprehensive care. More studies are needed to establish standardized guidelines for the prenatal diagnosis and treatment of arachnoid cysts.
