title: Second Trimester Ultrasound Diagnosis of External Hydrocephalus in Two Fetuses with Noonan Syndrome-Case Report Series.
label_reason: Two fetuses with ultrasound anomalies, WES found SOS1 and PTPN11 variants.
abstract: Background: Noonan syndrome (NS) is a relatively common RASopathy that can be associated with a variety of phenotypic and genotypic variations and potential long-term health consequences. Its most described prenatal ultrasound features in the first trimester are thickened nuchal translucency (NT) and dilated jugular sacs; while heart defects, polyhydramnios and facial dysmorphisms are its known manifestations in the second and third trimesters. Methods: We present two cases of NS with the prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of external hydrocephalus (EH) in the second trimester. Results: Case 1 had a normal first trimester scan and showed mild polyhydramnios, an echogenic intracardiac focus (EIF) in the left ventricle and pyelectasis in the second trimester in association with the EH. The whole exome sequencing (WES) confirmed a pathogenic variant in the SOS1 gene. Case 2 showed increased NT, agenesis of the ductus venosus (DV), single umbilical artery (SUA), an EIF in the right ventricle and an abnormal prefrontal space ratio (PSFR). By the 19th gestational week, EH appeared. The ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns were also slightly widened. The WES revealed a PTPN11 gene variant. Conclusions: The most reported sonographic features of NS are either non-specific or difficult to integrate into routine screening, requiring substantial experience. In our two cases, we detected EH in the second trimester, which is rarely described as a prenatal ultrasound diagnosis. To our current knowledge, this is the first case reported of EH in NS caused by an SOS1 gene variant and these are the first cases reported with the prenatal sonographic diagnosis of EH in NS.
text:
Second Trimester Ultrasound Diagnosis of External Hydrocephalus in Two Fetuses with Noonan Syndrome—Case Report Series

1. Introduction
1. Introduction Noonan syndrome is a relatively common RASopathy associated with a variety of phenotypic and genotypic features. Its prevalence is estimated to be 1:1000–2500, but in mild cases might be higher [,] and, therefore, more common than Edwards or Patau syndrome []. It is named after Jacqueline Noonan, an American pediatric cardiologist who published a paper in 1963 describing nine patients with pulmonary valve stenosis and various other coexisting conditions []. NS is mainly inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and in about 50% of the cases due to a variant in the PTPN11 gene (176876). Other known gene variations that lead to NS are NS3 (609942), KRAS (190070); NS4 (610733), SOS1 (182530); NS5 (611553), RAF1 (164760); NS6 (613224), NRAS (164790); NS7 (613706), BRAF (164757); NS8 (615355), RIT1 (609591); NS9 (616559), SOS2 (601247); NS10 (616564), LZTR1 (600574); NS11 (618499), MRAS (608435), NS12 (618624), RRAS2 (600098), NS13 (619087) and MAPK1 (176948), while the autosomal recessive form of Noonan syndrome is caused by NS2 (605275), LZTR1 (600574), NS14 (619745) and SPRED2 (609292) [,,]. Noonan syndrome is characterized by typical facial dysmorphism, skeletal anomalies, webbed neck and congenital heart defects []. Following Down syndrome, Noonan syndrome is the second most common genetic disorder associated with heart defects, typically with pulmonary stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy []. The prenatal diagnosis of Noonan syndrome is often challenging due to variability in the phenotypic presentation and occasionally mild and non-specific signs [,]. In NS, the most frequently reported prenatal ultrasound findings are increased NT, cystic hygroma, dilated jugular lymphatic sacs, thickened nuchal fold, cardiac defects, kidney malformations and polyhydramnios [,,,]. In those cases in which the fetus does not show the typical signs associated with Noonan syndrome, the detection rate remains low and, due to the often non-specific findings, the diagnosis might be delayed or missed even in postnatal life [,]. External hydrocephalus is defined as enlarged subarachnoid spaces detected on imaging modalities with normal or mildly dilated ventricles []. In the presented cases, the authors used the depth of the Sylvian fissure to determine the width of the subarachnoid spaces, based on the normal value database published by Alonso et al. []. In this paper, we report two cases of prenatally confirmed Noonan syndrome showing the rare sonographic finding of external hydrocephalus in the second trimester.

2. Case Report Series
2. Case Report Series We present two cases of Noonan syndrome with external hydrocephalus in the second trimester in the presence of the variations of the SOS1 and PTPN11 genes. To our current knowledge, this is the first paper describing the association of prenatal external hydrocephalus in Noonan syndrome caused by a variation of the SOS1 gene, and these are the first cases reported with a second trimester sonographic diagnosis of EH in NS. This case report is structured according to the CARE guidelines. We defined external hydrocephalus on the level of Sylvian fissure: measure over 95 percentile was defined as EH. 2.1. Case 1 2.1.1. Patient Information and Obstetric History The 46-year-old pregnant woman first presented for the first trimester screening at the gestational age of 12 weeks and 5 days. The mode of conception was IVF from oocyte donation (donor is under 25 years of age). She previously had a missed abortion at the 7th gestational week. She had a medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome, hypothyroidism and insulin resistance, her regular medications were metformin, levothyroxine, liothyronine, progesterone, escitalopram in combination with clonazepam, and enoxaparin. No family history of genetic disease was known. Body mass index (BMI) was in the normal range. 2.1.2. Ultrasound Findings The first trimester extended ultrasound scan (NT, nasal bone, DV, tricuspid valve regurgitation, early cardiac and intracranial scan) revealed no anomalies. The thickness of the nuchal translucency was 2.4 mm, representing 85 percentile based on the measured CRL of 69.9 mm, which was 3 days greater than the calculated gestational age according to the IVF. In the second trimester, a mild polyhydramnios was found (deepest vertical pocket: 9.3 cm, amniotic fluid index: 21 cm). BPD (52.2 mm) and HC (191.1 mm) were above the 90th percentile, all other biometric data were in the normal range. The diameter of the posterior horn at the atrium of the lateral ventricle was 9 mm. The ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns appeared slightly dilated (), and the Sylvian fissure measured 10.5 mm, which was above the 95th percentile (a). In addition, a mild hypertelorism (outer-to-outer distance: 35 mm, inner-to-inner distance: 16 mm), an echogenic intracardiac focus (EIF) in the left ventricle and mild bilateral pyelectasis were detected. An echocardiogram was performed by a pediatric cardiologist, which revealed no cardiac anomalies. Fetal ultrasound follow-ups were performed at the 27th, 31st and 34th gestational week. Mild-to-moderate polyhydramnios was confirmed throughout the pregnancy. BPD and HC increased steadily, with both above the 99th percentile by the 27th gestational week. The ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns remained enlarged and the subarachnoid spaces widened. At the 27th gestational week, the depth of the Sylvian fissure measured 17.4 mm, which is high above the 95th percentile (b) and the external hydrocephalus became evident also in the cranial views (). AC was measured at the 98th percentile at the 27th week, with an estimated fetal weight at the 97.9th percentile. These biometric data were maintained throughout the pregnancy. A mild dilatation of the right kidney remained with a diameter of 8 mm measured at the 34th week of pregnancy, while the width of the right kidney pelvis was normalized. 2.1.3. Genetic Studies A cf-DNA test was performed in the first trimester with normal results. An amniocentesis was performed following the second trimester scan. No chromosomal anomalies were confirmed by G-band analysis of the amniotic cell culture (46XY). The array CGH confirmed a 2 Kb heterozygous microdeletion affecting the RAB6C (OMIM: 612909) and SMPD4 (OMIM: 610457) genes. The following whole exome sequencing ruled out any compound heterozygosity and revealed a heterozygous pathogenic variation in the SOS1 gene (NM_005633.4:c.1644T>A, p.Ser548Arg) that confirmed Noonan syndrome 4 (Phenotype MIM number: 610733, location: 2p22.1, Gene/Locus MIM number: 182530). 2.1.4. Perinatal and Postnatal Outcome After detailed genetic counselling, the pregnant woman decided to proceed with the pregnancy. The baby was born by caesarean section in the 38th gestational week, with a birth weight of 3530 g, Apgar 9/10. The routine neonatal screening tests for vision and hearing were normal. The newborn underwent regular cardiological follow-up, which revealed mild supravalvular pulmonary stenosis with no progression during the follow-up period to date. The last check-up was at age 2, requiring no intervention and annual follow-ups. A cranial ultrasound at 7 weeks of age did not report any anomalies. The neurodevelopmental examination revealed minimal whole-body hypotonia and moderately delayed psychomotor development. Complex (motor, mental, speech) rehabilitation was recommended with a follow-up examination in 1 year. 2.2. Case 2 2.2.1. Patient Information and Obstetric History The 32-year-old pregnant woman was referred to our clinic with her spontaneously conceived second pregnancy. She had a previous normal vaginal delivery at the 39th gestational week following an uneventful pregnancy. Her only chronic medical condition was hypothyroidism that required no treatment. No family history of hereditary disease was known and BMI was in the normal range. 2.2.2. Ultrasound Findings The first trimester screening was performed in another clinic, NT was measured 3.2 mm and an agenesis of the DV was suspected; therefore, she was referred to our center. We confirmed an NT of 3.4 mm, representing 99 percentile according to the CRL of 70.6 mm, a DV agenesis, an SUA, an EIF in the right ventricle and frontally depressed cranial bones. A follow-up ultrasound scan at the 16th gestational week confirmed these anomalies and the DV agenesis (intrahepatic portosystemic shunt). A fetal echocardiogram performed by a pediatric cardiologist showed no evidence of major cardiac malformation; however, a small subaortic ventricular septal defect (VSD) with a suspected septal membrane aneurysm was reported. At the 21st week, in addition to the previously described anomalies, an abnormal PFSR and heart ventricular hypertrophy were confirmed. At the 19th week, a dilated Sylvian fissure of 8.0 mm was found along with an otherwise normal neurosonography. At the 22nd gestational week, the depth of the Sylvian fissure was measured 10.8 mm (). Both of these measurements represent values above the 95th percentile. The expansion of the subarachnoid spaces and Sylvian fissures was also remarkable in the coronal plane (). 2.2.3. Genetic Studies No cf-DNA test was performed. An amniocentesis was performed, and the results of the karyotyping and the SNP microarray revealed no pathologic findings. The whole exome sequencing found a heterozygous variation in the PTPN11 gene (c.124A>G, p.Thr42Ala; chr12-112884189 A>G, NM_002834.5, rs397507501), confirming Noonan syndrome 1 (Phenotype MIM number: 163950, Location 12q24.13, Gene/Locus MIM number 1768762.2.4). 2.2.4. Perinatal and Postnatal Outcome Following detailed genetic counseling and receiving comprehensive information, the pregnant woman decided to terminate her pregnancy.

3. Discussion
3. Discussion NS is a common genetic disorder, with a high variability in both genotype and phenotype. Due to the diversity of the syndrome, prenatal and even postnatal detection is often challenging []. Although NS can be detected by various genetic testing modalities such as targeted Noonan panels, WES and even cf-DNA tests, screening tests are not available routinely in all countries and might be a significant financial burden for patients, while diagnostic tests are carried out only based on a proper indication. Therefore, sonographic markers that could raise suspicion of this condition are playing an important role in providing effective prenatal screening and improving the detection rate []. Noonan syndrome is suspected mainly due to increased NT in the first trimester [,]. However, access to first trimester screenings might be influenced by the patient’s socioeconomic status and personal preferences [,,]. In a review published in 2024, Tangshewinsirikul et al. found increased NT to be the most frequently detected prenatal ultrasound anomaly in 105 cases of Noonan syndrome, occurring in 71% of the cases, followed by various body fluid collections (59%) and polyhydramnios (50%) []. Although in a study of 151 children with NS, only 12.5% of the echocardiograms were normal and 62% of the abnormalities were pulmonary stenosis. In the 105 fetuses with NS, the most commonly reported ventricular hypertrophy was found in 33% of the fetuses and pulmonary stenosis in only 13% [,]. The intracranial manifestations of NS have been described mainly in children or young adults and include hydrocephalus, Chiari I malformation, diverticular enlargement of the foramen of Luschka and cerebrovascular aneurysm [,,]. Helenius et al. reported a 22-week-old fetus with enlarged extracerebral CSF and delayed operculisation in addition to a hypoplastic vermis on prenatal MRI in a case of NS with RAF1 variation []. A widening of the subarachnoid spaces was described by Gripp in children with SHOC2 and Zarate in a case with the RAF1 variants, along with other extra- and intracranial abnormalities in individuals affected by NS. Mastromoro et al. described an MRI diagnosis of EH in the 27th gestational week following the genetic diagnosis of NS caused by a variation in the PTPN11 gene. In their case, the corpus callosum and the cerebellar vermis were measured under the 10th percentile []. The prenatal MRI diagnosis of EH has previously been described in some disorders such as Snijders Blok–Campeau Syndrome and benign external hydrocephalus [,]. Baron et al. reported 21 cases of macrocephaly diagnosed by ultrasound, all of which had a fetal MRI, which confirmed the presence of EH in 77% of the cases []. In postnatal life, the enlargement of the subarachnoid fluid spaces was reported in connection with RASopathies []. A postnatally described central nervous system anomaly in the presence of the SOS1 gene variation was a corpus callosum agenesis with severe developmental delay []. Another case report described spinal lesions resembling plexiform neurofibromas in NS caused by a variation in the SOS1 gene []. The involvement of the two gene variants we identified, SOS1 and PTPN11, in the development of the central nervous system has been previously reported. The PTPN11 gene encodes the Shp2 protein and in NS it has a gain-of-function variation. In mice, Shp2 reduces the axon myelination and increases the density of the neurons but decreases the astrocyte density within the forebrain and the hippocampus. SOS1 stimulates the nerve growth factor, which is expressed in the cortex of the newborns, and activates the Ras-MAPK pathway NMDA receptors in the neonatal cortex [,]. Whether these genes play a role in the development of EH in NS, and if so, via what exact pathway, requires further research. In our two cases, EH occurred in the second trimester without any other significant central nervous system (CNS) anomaly and was confirmed ultrasonographically by measuring the depth of the Sylvian fissure in the axial plane. To our present knowledge, Case 1 is the first case of external hydrocephalus with an otherwise normal CNS in the presence of the SOS1 gene variation. Furthermore, these are the first cases of NS with a second trimester ultrasound diagnosis of EH. Neurosonography and MRI are complementary modalities in fetal diagnostics. According to the ISUOG guidelines, a fetal MRI is indicated in 7–15% of cases following a well-performed neurosonography []. In our experience, ultrasound examination alone was adequate for evaluating the subarachnoid spaces, offering better cost-effectiveness, faster diagnosis and lower human resource requirements compared to MRI. Despite the two cases presented, it must also be taken into account that EH may have developed independently of NS in both cases. However, since external hydrocephalus is a known phenomenon in children suffering from NS, it is reasonable to assume that the prenatal finding is related to the syndrome [,,]. Examination of the subarachnoid spaces is currently not part of routine screening, and this may presumably contribute to undetected cases of external hydrocephalus. In the authors’ opinion, the measurement of the depth of the Sylvian fissure may be a suitable tool for a second trimester prenatal diagnosis of external hydrocephalus, and as an additional marker, could contribute to the timely implementation of genetic testing, which can be beneficial in some regions due to the legal regulation of termination. The application of Sylvian fissure depth measurement in this context requires further studies, but as its technical performance does not require the acquisition of new skills, it could be easily integrated into routine screening.

title: The hidden causes of pregnancy loss: a closer look.
label_reason: Fetal losses grouped by US anomaly, CNV-seq and WES on POC.
abstract: Unexpected pregnancy loss can be a traumatic experience for fertile couples. The aim of the study was to assess the nature and type of chromosomal variants involved in early and late pregnancy loss and provide couples an explanation on the cause of their pregnancy loss. Investigations were conducted on 2928 pregnancy loss cases where products of conception (POC) samples could be retrieved for genetic analysis. Chromosomal variants were detected by low pass copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq). In first-trimester miscarriages, 1272 of POC (60.4%) samples had a chromosome abnormality. Autosomal aneuploidy and monosomy X were the predominate variants (73.2%), followed by autosomal and sex chromosome mosaicism (10.7%), triploidy (9.6%), pathogenic CNVs (6.2%) and haploidy (0.3%). The chromosomal variants were similar in type and frequency regardless of whether the fetus had normal or abnormal ultrasound findings. In second trimester pregnancy loss where there was either a structural or non-structural ultrasound anomaly, only 15.3% of POC samples had a chromosome abnormality, involving mainly the smaller autosomes and monosomy X (55.7%), autosomal and sex chromosomal mosaicism (11.5%), triploidy (4.1%) and pathogenic CNVs (28.7%). Chromosomal variants contribute to fetal demise in almost two thirds of pregnancy losses. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-025-06678-x.
text:
The hidden causes of pregnancy loss: a closer look

Background
Background The incidence of fetal loss in implantation positive pregnancies is approximately 10–20%, occurring mainly in the first trimester []. Unexpected fetal loss is a traumatic experience and can have lasting psychological issues for the woman and their families [, ]. Many factors, such as chromosomal abnormalities, structural uterine abnormalities, autoimmune disorders, endocrine disorders and even poor lifestyle choices contribute to pregnancy loss [–]. Among these factors, numerical and structural chromosomal abnormalities detectable by either karyotyping, arrays or next generation sequencing (NGS) are the most common causes, reportedly accounting for around 50% of losses [–]. Copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) via NGS, with a resolution down to 0.1 Mb [, ], has become a useful technique for the rapid detection of copy number variants when investigating clinical samples. CNV-seq analysis of products of conception (POC) from failed pregnancies has revealed that whole chromosome aneuploidies, mosaic aneuploidies and CNVs are the predominant genetic variants [–]. More recent analysis of large sets of sequencing data [] and whole exome sequencing data from specific cohort studies [, ] has suggested that single nucleotide variants (SNVs) found in developmental genes may also play a role in sporadic miscarriage. Currently, there are no expansive studies reporting the type of chromosomal genetic abnormalities in the context of pregnancy loss and developmental fetal ultrasound findings. In this retrospective study, we analyzed 2928 POC samples by CNV-seq to ascertain the contributions of different chromosomal variants in early and late stage pregnancy loss.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study design Between January 2019 and October 2023, a total of 2928 POC were collected from women experiencing first time pregnancy loss (Fig. ). Early loss in the first trimester was broadly defined as fetal absence or fetal death in utero without any history of adverse events such as a car accident or serious falls. In contrast, late pregnancy loss (weeks 14–26) was defined as the loss of an ongoing pregnancy either due to spontaneous miscarriage or medical termination. POCs were washed and fetal tissues dissected to reduce misdiagnosis commonly caused by maternal contamination. Chromosomal variants were detected and characterized by low pass copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq). The genetic report was sent to the patients doctor and counseling was offered to all couples. This retrospective study was approved by the Zhengzhou University Ethics Committee (Approval No. 2019-KY-418). Study design. CNV-seq outcomes for early and late pregnancy loss samples are shown. US: ultrasound; POC: products of conception; TOP: termination of pregnancy; SM: spontaneous miscarriage; WES: Whole exome sequencing Fetal ultrasound During early pregnancy (6–10 weeks), gestational age was estimated by examining the head hip diameter of the fetus and determining the Crown-Rump Length (CRL). Fetal development was assessed using the ultrasonic diagnostic instrument Voluson 10 (GE Company). Routine check-up included gestational sac size, fetal bud, fetal heart, singleton or twin, CRL, limb development, fetal heart rate and the umbilical cord attachment position. Retrieval of products of conception (POC) Abortion specialists in the outpatient department (early pregnancy) or in the obstetric ward (late pregnancy) performed manual suction after fetal demise. POCs were fully flushed with PBS to remove blood clots and maternal decidua and immediately delivered to the prenatal center for analysis. For early gestation POCs, the villi tissues (clusters of the stem villi and floating villi) were picked from the disc-shaped chorion membrane. For late gestation POCs, fetal skin or digit tissue was isolated. All fetal tissue from early and late POCs was thoroughly washed in PBS to remove any residual maternal cell contamination (MCC). Assessment of maternal cell contamination in POC samples Quantitative fluorescent PCR (QF-PCR) was performed using the Goldeneye®DNA Identification System (Base point Cognitive Technology (Beijing) Co., LTD) 20 A to measure levels MCC in POC samples and to aid detection of triploidies such as 69,XXY and 69,XXX []. Polymorphic markers included D2S1338, D3S1358, D5S818, D6S1043, D7S820, D8S1179, D12S391, D13S317, D16S539, D18S51, D19S433, D21S11, AMEL, CSF1PO, Penta D, Penta E, TH01, TPOX and vWA. QF-PCR products of each marker were resolved by Genescan analysis on the GeneMapper® ID-X platform. Samples passed QC test for CNV-seq analysis if MCC was < 10%. Testing of POC samples for genetic variants Copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) was performed as previously described []. Briefly, genomic DNA from POC samples were extracted using the DNAeasy Kit (Qiagen, Germany). Following DNA fragmentation and library construction (ChroSure kit, Berry Genomics, Beijing), barcoded libraries underwent massively parallel sequencing on the NextSeq CN500 platform (Illumina). Approximately 3 million mapped reads were binned and 24-chromosome copy number plots generated. Trisomic or monosomic mosaics were defined as having a level of mosaicism > 10% and < 90%, whereas complex mosaics were defined as having one or more mosaic chromosomes. Identified CNVs were evaluated for pathogenicity according to guidelines outlined by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines [] and queried against public databases such as DGV, Decipher, OMIM, ClinGen, UCSC and PubMed. For reporting, CNVs were classified as either pathogenic, likely pathogenic or variant of uncertain significance. Whole exome sequencing (WES) for identification of pathogenic SNV/indel variants was performed as previously described []. Statistical analysis A chi-square or Fisher’s exact test was applied to analyze differences between groups for the frequency of different types of chromosomal abnormalities (P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant).

Results
Results First trimester pregnancy loss The 2928 pregnancy loss cases were divided into four main groups based on the timing of fetal demise and ultrasound (US) findings (Fig. ). Following pregnancy US scans between 6 and 10 weeks gestation, 1611 women were identified with a fetal US anomaly (Group A) and 1317 women had a normal fetal US (Group B). In Group A, 1020 conceptions (63%) involved an anembryonic pregnancy where the fetal sac was > 25 mm with no fetus, 562 conceptions (35%) had fetal demise and a missed abortion and 29 conceptuses (2%) had a fetal heart but were either underdeveloped or had other gross US abnormalities. In contrast, while Group B women all had normal fetal US findings, 496 women (Group B) experienced fetus demise post US and before the end of the first trimester. To identify chromosomal abnormalities, CNV-seq and STR analysis was used to test all POC samples of the 2107 first trimester fetal losses. A total of 1272 (60.4%) POC samples had chromosomal abnormalities and the frequency of chromosomal abnormalities was significantly higher in pregnancies with US anomalies compared to those with no US anomalies (62.8% versus 52.6%, P < 0.0001). The contribution of the different types of chromosomal abnormalities detected is shown in Table . Overall, for all first trimester fetal chromosomal abnormalities, whole chromosomal aneuploidies (WCA) were the most common (73.2%), followed by whole chromosomal mosaics (WCM) (10.7%), triploidy (9.6%), pathogenic CNVs (pCNVs) (6.2%) and haploidy (0.3%). For triploidy, 69,XXY was more common than 69,XXX (1.8:1.0; P < 0.0001). More detailed analysis of the type and nature of WCA,WCM and pCNVs found in Group A and Group B first trimester miscarriages is shown in Fig. . In group A, WCA predominately involved trisomies of all chromosomes and monosomy X (except chromosome 1). Amongst the trisomies, trisomy 16, 22, 15, 21 and 13 were the most common. WCM was observed for nearly all of the autosomes with the exception of chromosomes 10 and 11. Overall, the majority of WCM had levels of mosaicism exceeding 50% with the most prevalent type being mosaic monosomy X. For pCNVs, there were fetuses with microdeletions, microduplications and double CNV abnormalities involving almost all chromosomes with the exception of chromosome 15 and 20. In group B, trends in WCA were similar to Group A, although the proportion of sex chromosome abnormalities (mainly monosomy X) was significantly higher in Group B than in Group A (27.6% versus 9.8%, P < 0.0001). In addition, the profile of the top 5 trisomies in Group B (trisomy 16, 21, 22, 18 and 13) was different to Group A (trisomy 16, 22, 15, 21 and 13), although similar in the actual chromosomes involved. Mosaicism typically involved chromosome X, although chromosome 16 mosaicism was observed in group A at nearly the same level with some smaller chromosomes also evident in a mosaic state. pCNVs were found genome-wide, (except for chromosome 19) in both Group A and Group B with a similar distribution of microdeletions, microduplications and double CNV abnormalities. Nature and distribution of chromosomal variants associated with first trimester miscarriage. (I) and (III): Group A—pregnancy US anomalies; (II and IV): Group B—no pregnancy US anomalies For the 600 Group A and 235 Group B patients where no chromosomal abnormalities were revealed (Fig. ), a WES test was offered to identify any alternative genetic cause of the miscarriage. In all cases, patients declined any further genetic investigation into the cause of their pregnancy loss. Second trimester pregnancy loss There were 821 women with viable pregnancies at the end of the first trimester who experienced PL in the second or early stage of the third trimester (Fig. ). Fetal developmental US performed between 11 and 14 weeks gestation, identified 796 women (97.0%) with an US structural anomaly (Group C) and 25 women (3.0%) with no detectable US anomalies (Group D). Group C was further divided on the type of US anomaly, either structural (Group C1) or non-structural (Group C2). In the majority of cases (98%), based on the fetal abnormalities revealed by US and CNV-seq findings, parents elected medical termination of the pregnancy. In 16 cases (2%), medical termination was not chosen, but all fetuses spontaneously miscarried, either late in the second trimester or early third trimester. Likewise, for Group D patients, all 25 fetuses spontaneously miscarried, also either late in the second trimester or early third trimester. For Group C with US anomalies, the chromosomal abnormalities associated with second trimester pregnancy loss are summarized in Table . Within Group C1 with structural anomalies, there were 76 of 513 (14.8%) fetuses with chromosomal abnormalities comprising 39 (51.3%) with WCA, 30 (39.5%) with pCNVs, 6 (7.9%) with WCM and 1 (1.3%) with triploidy. Similarly, in Group C2 with non-structural anomalies, there were 46 of 283 (16.3%) fetuses with chromosomal abnormalities comprising 29 (63.0%) with WCA, 8 (17.4%) with WCM, 5 (10.9%) with pCNVs and 4 (8.7%) with triploidy. In Group D with no US anomalies, there were only 1 of 25 (4%) with chromosome abnormalities (Fig. ), involving a trisomy 20/monosomy X double aneuploidy. There were some similarities and differences in the type and nature of the chromosome abnormalities in Groups C1 (structural anomalies) and C2 (non-structural anomalies (Fig. ). WCA spectrums were relatively similar, with vast majority of autosomal aneuploidy involving trisomy of the smaller chromosomes, with trisomy 18, 21 and 13 being the most common. SCA was predominately due to monosomy X in both groups. However, WCM spectrums were quite different, with Group C1 involving most of the larger autosomes and chromosome X, whereas Group C2 involved only a few of the autosomes as well as chromosome X. Overall, levels of mosaicism tended to be higher in Group C1 compared to Group C2. For pCNVs, Group C1 had a higher proportion of microdeletions than Group C2, but was not significant (73.5% versus 62.5%, P = 0.66). In addition, pCNVs in Group C1 involved a broader range of autosomes than Group C2. Nature and distribution of chromosomal variants associated with second trimester pregnancy loss. (I) and (III): Group C1—pregnancy US structural anomalies; (II and IV): Group C2—no pregnancy US structural anomalies Within Groups C1, C2 and D, there were 437 of 513 (85%), 237 of 283 (84%) and 24 of 25 (96%), respectively, where no chromosome abnormalities were found in the POC sample by CNV-seq. These patients were offered further genetic testing by WES, however, only a small proportion (67 of 437, 15%) of Group C1 patients agreed on taking a second test. Of the 67 POCs tested by WES, 34 (50%) had positive results for a pathogenic variant (Fig. , Supplementary Table for details). The most common genes involved in the fetal structural anomalies were FGFR3, COL1A1, DYNC2H1, L1CAM, PIEZO1 and COL2A1 with minor contributions from 14 other genes (Fig. A). In terms of origin of the pathogenic variants (Fig. B), the majority (53%) were de novo (autosomal dominant), followed by autosomal recessive inheritance (32%), X-linked inheritance (9%) and autosomal dominant inheritance (6%). Whole exome sequencing findings in 34 fetuses with structural ultrasound anomalies. AD: autosomal dominant; AR: autosomal recessive; XLR: X-linked recessive

Discussion
Discussion In this study we explored the genetic basis of first and second trimester pregnancy losses. First trimester pregnancy loss was mainly due to abnormal embryonic development or fetal demise, and a chromosome abnormality was found in 60.4% of cases. For the ongoing pregnancies that survived the first trimester, the majority of couples elected medical termination due to the presence of an US anomaly and, in these cases, the association with a chromosomal abnormality was 15.0%. Taken together, first trimester pregnancy loss was predominately due to chromosomal aneuploidy, with significant contributions from mosaicism, triploidy and pCNVs. Overall, almost two thirds of fetal loss was attributed to a chromosomal variant. Previous genetic studies of first trimester miscarriage have consistently reported that chromosome abnormalities are present in approximately 50% of POCs [, , –]. In a recent study of 1,222 POCs where a bias was noted towards female fetal miscarriages, initial findings also identified 50% of the fetuses with a chromosome abnormality []. However, after adjustments were made for the effect of maternal contamination, the true contribution of chromosomal abnormalities to early miscarriage was 62%. In our study using CNV-seq and in a recent study using SNP based haplarithmisis [], the rate of chromosomal abnormalities in first trimester miscarriages was 60.4% and 67.8% respectively. The slightly higher gain of chromosome abnormalities using haplarithmisis was due to the increased resolution enabling detection of CNVs < 0.1 Mb in size. The types of chromosomal abnormalities found in early POCs are consistent with those found in the early embryo []. Consistent with previous reports [], the first trimester chromosomal abnormalities identified in this study were mainly whole chromosome aneuploidies followed by triploidy. Autosomal trisomy involving both the larger and smaller chromosomes and monosomy X were the dominant abnormalities seen in fetuses with or without an US anomaly. Whole chromosome mosaicism was also detected in a small proportion of POC samples, involving almost all the autosomes, with levels ranging from low (> 10%) to high (> 50%). Autosomal and monosomy X mosaicism were both dominant, with the later more prevalent in miscarriages with no US anomalies. In addition, a range of genome-wide pCNVs, including both duplications and deletions were also found at a rate of 8%. Our study findings support previous CNV-seq reports [, ] where a similar prevalence of mosaicism and pCNVs in early miscarriage samples was observed. There is increasing evidence for mosaicism and CNVs as more than a casual link to miscarriage. In a detailed investigation of POC samples where the mesoderm and extra embryonic tissue were compared, mosaicism was found almost exclusively in the mesoderm, suggesting that the mosaicism detected in miscarriage samples is predominately true fetal mosaicism and not confined placental mosaicism. Recently, in another study of biopsied POC samples, it was found that mosaicism, either uniform or localized, was associated with first trimester miscarriages []. In addition, from transfer studies of mosaic blastocysts, mosaic embryos tend to have a higher miscarriage rate compared to euploid embryos []. Taken together, trisomy and trisomic mosaicism are by far the largest contributors to early miscarriage. In regard to pCNVs, the vast majority found in early miscarriage samples were largely sporadic and there was no uniform pattern of specific genes or microdeletion/microduplication syndromes involved. This finding agrees with a previous study [], where deeper analysis showed that the CNV intervals specifically perturbed expression of genes important for normal fetal development. Further studies are still needed to investigate the mechanisms of miscarriage in the context of mosaicism and pCNVs and, potentially SNVs in genes important for fetal development. The increased diagnostic yield provided by CNV-seq testing of POC samples can potentially provide more couples experiencing pregnancy loss with an explanation for the loss of their fetus. Unexpected pregnancy loss can cause grief and blame, leading to guilt and despair. Counseling is particularly helpful for the couples to come to terms with losing their pregnancy, particularly if there is a genetic cause identified. In addition, the genetic information will help guide decisions about a future pregnancy attempt, either by natural conception or by assisted conception combined with preimplantation genetic testing, which can select a euploid embryo with a higher chance of establishing an ongoing viable pregnancy. Further, from the study findings, couples need to be advised that a normal pregnancy ultrasound at 6–10 weeks gestation does not preclude the possibility of a later miscarriage due to a fetal chromosomal abnormality. As demonstrated in this study, CNV-seq combined with an adjunct maternal cell contamination test is an efficient approach that can detect the main types of chromosomal abnormalities in POCs such as aneuploidy, mosaicism, polyploidy and CNVs and provides an alternative to current array-based methods. However, there are limitations of CNV-seq and array based methods including the inability to detect SNVs/indels, small CNVs below 0.1 Mb in size, low levels of mosaicism (< 10%), as well as balanced translocations, inversions or other types of complex chromosomal rearrangements. The key question now remains as to whether these other types of genetic variants missed by the current technologies also contribute to miscarriage.In a recent study using next generation variant exon screening (ngVES) to detect genetic causes of skin diseases [], it was possible to analyze the sequencing data with a series of algorithms and call both intergenic and intragenic CNVs as well as the standard SNVs/indels. In our limited WES investigation of fetuses with a structural anomaly where no chromosome abnormalities were found, approximately 50% of these fetuses were further tested by WES revealed a pathogenic SNV/indel in genes previously implicated in fetal structural development. Unfortunately, due to lack of patient consent for a further WES test, an opportunity was missed in this study to investigate whether POC samples with no fetal chromosome abnormalities had pathogenic SNVs/indels in specific genes that might explain the basis of their early unexpected fetal loss.

Conclusion
Conclusion Using CNV-seq as the diagnostic tool, examination of a large collection of POC samples retrieved from 2928 cases of pregnancy loss found that almost two-thirds had a chromosomal variant. From this study, however, it is evident that some other genetic causes of miscarriage are not being observed by our CNV-seq approach.Further research is also needed to assess other potential causes of pregnancy loss such as epigenetic, inflammatory or environmental factors in the subgroup of patients where no obvious genetic causes were found. Such studies will eventually shed more light on the relative contributions of different genetic and non-genetic factors to miscarriage and help individual patients come to terms with their experience of miscarriage and provide guidance for planning and management of a future pregnancy.

abstract: The L1CAM gene encodes an axonal glycoprotein belonging to the immunoglobulin supergene family that plays a crucial role in nervous system development. In this study, we reported a novel disease-causing mutation in the 3′ splice site of L1CAM and provided some insight into fetal X-linked hydrocephalus. We obtained ultrasound images and collected samples from a couple and their fetuses. Fetal samples were acquired through amniocentesis, followed by extraction of genomic DNA. We conducted copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), karyotype analysis, and whole-exome sequencing The mutation site of the L1CAM gene was verified using PCR and Sanger sequencing, with splicing effects analyzed by bioinformatics analysis via BDGP, MaxEntScan and SpliceAI, as well as in vitro research via minigene assays. The variant c.1380-1G > A in the first male fetus, located in the intron11 3′ splice site of L1CAM (chrX:153868728), led to malfunction and hydrocephalus by aberrant mRNA splicing. The ultrasound examination of the fetus revealed the presence of hydrocephalus and partial agenesis of corpus callosum. In the subsequent pregnancy, the second male fetus exhibited no mutation in L1CAM as identified by Sanger sequencing, and the ultrasound results were within normal limits. No significant findings were observed in their CNV-seq and karyotype analysis. The second fetus was delivered uneventfully and no report of hydrocephalus through the telephone follow-up for 12 months. This study identified the variant c.1380-1G > A in L1CAM as new pathogenic mutation for the first time according to ACMG/AMP (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology)-based guidelines, which caused severe fetal X-linked hydrocephalus and partial agenesis of corpus callosum. This discovery expands the mutational landscape of L1CAM -associated disorders, highlights the diagnostic utility of integrating WES into prenatal workflows for unresolved fetal anomalies, and provides actionable insights for genetic counseling in families at risk of X-linked hydrocephalus. Identification and functional characteristics of a novel splice site variant in L1CAM caused X-linked hydrocephalus

Introduction
Introduction X-linked recessive hydrocephalus constitutes the predominant congenital form of hereditary hydrocephalus among congenital anomalies, with epidemiological studies estimating its prevalence at ∼4.65 cases per 10,000 live births (). In prenatal diagnosis, when a fetus with hydrocephalus or other ultrasound anomalies fails to obtain a definitive diagnosis through CNV and karyotype analysis, ACMG recommends WES as the further genomic testing to yield more diagnostic information of the cases (). Clinical data reveal a significant gender disparity, where 2%–15% of male neonates with congenital hydrocephalus exhibit this X-linked subtype (). Molecular pathogenesis studies have identified deleterious mutations in L1 cell adhesion molecule (L1CAM) gene as the primary etiological factor underlying X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders (; ). The L1CAM gene, mapped to chromosomal region Xq28, spans 29 exons with its initial exon functioning as a noncoding regulatory element (). The encoded L1CAM glycoprotein (1,257amino acids) represents a key component of the immunoglobulin superfamily, characterized by its transmembrane structure and cell adhesion properties (). Functionally, this molecule plays a pivotal role in neurodevelopment through multiple interaction modalities: homophilic binding with adjacent L1CAM molecules, heterophilic associations with other Ig family members, and integrin-mediated adhesion via both RGD-dependent and -independent pathways (). Pre-mRNA splicing constitutes a critical regulatory mechanism in gene expression, wherein sequence variations frequently induce aberrant transcript formation (). Notably, splicing dysregulation in L1CAM underlies the phenotypic spectrum of L1 syndrome - encompassing X-linked hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis (HSAS, OMIM #307000), MASA syndrome (OMIM #303350), SPG1, and corpus callosum agenesis (OMIM #304100) (; ). The clinical heterogeneity of these disorders correlates with varying degrees of molecular dysfunction (). The splicing machinery involves conserved sequence elements (5'/3′splice sites, polypyrimidine tracts, branchpoints) and regulatory motifs (splicing enhancers/silencers), with structural RNA features further modulating spliceosome assembly (). NM_000425.5: c.1379 + 5G>A, a mutation near the 5′splice site of intron 11, has been linked to aberrant splicing and hydrocephalus (). In contrast, mutations at the 3′splice site of intron 11 remain unreported. Pathogenic 3′splice site variants may induce diverse splicing errors including exon skipping, intron retention, pseudoexon incorporation, and cryptic splice site activation (). While direct RNA analysis from affected neural tissue remains the gold standard for splicing variant characterization, practical limitations in tissue accessibility often necessitate alternative approaches (; ). Computational predictive tools offer preliminary insights into splicing impacts, though their clinical application requires rigorous experimental validation through functional assays (). Current ClinVar database document 84 pathogenic and 62 likely pathogenic L1CAM variants (last accessed 30 April 2025), exhibiting a broad spectrum of molecular alterations: 37 of them are missense, 45 of them are nonsense, and 34 of them are splice site variants. Our study documents a novel splice site variant (NM_000425.5:c.1380-1G>A) identified through whole-exome sequencing, supported by bioinformatics predictions and prenatal ultrasonographic findings. Following ACMG/AMP guidelines (), we propose a provisional assessment of its pathogenicity classification based on cumulative evidence from molecular and clinical analyses.

Material and methods
Material and methods Sample collection The blood samples of the parents and the amniotic fluid of fetuses collected by amniocentesis were kept at −80°C. Bioinformatics analysis Bioinformatics analysis was carried out to predict the splicing effect of the variant. The analysis of BDGP (available at http://www.fruitfly.org, score cut off 0.4) and MaxEntScan (available at http://hollywood.mit.edu/burgelab/maxent/Xmaxent.html) was done to determine the potential effects of variation on classic 3′acceptor consensus sites and to predict the generation of new sites (; ). SpliceAI (https://spliceailookup. Broadinstitute.org/, accessed on 21 February 2022) was also used to predict possible splicing outcomes (). The three-dimensional (3D) structural models of the proteins were obtained from AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (available at https://alphafold.com/) () and AlphaFold 3 (), displayed with PyMOL Molecular Graphics System. CNV-Seq and karyotype analysis CNV-Seq was performed as previously reported (). In brief, the workflow of CNV-seq included extracting genomic DNA, constructing a library, quality control, pooling, sequencing, bioinformatics analysis and interpreting the results. Karyotype harvest and analysis were conducted following previously established protocols (). Amniotic fluid was cultured in 3 mL of BIO-AMF-3 complete medium (Biological Industries, Cromwell, United States) and incubated at 37°C in a Thermo 3111 CO2 incubator (Thermo Fisher). Subsequently, amniocytes were harvested for G banding after culturing for 9–14 days. For each sample, 20 metaphase images were captured and counted using a Zeiss automatic karyotyping scanning system (Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany). Karyotypes were described according to ISCN 2024 guidelines. WES 1 μg genomic DNA was extracted from 200 μL peripheral blood, using a Qiagen DNA Blood Midi/Mini kit (Qiagen GmbH, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol. 50ng DNA was interrupted to 200bp around by fragmentation enzymes. The DNA fragments were then end repaired, and the 3′end was added 1 A base. Secondly, the DNA fragments were ligated with barcoded sequencing adaptors, and fragments about 320bp were collected by XP beads. After PCR amplification, the DNA fragments were hybridized and captured by WES according to the manufacturer’s Protocol. The hybrid products were eluted and collected, and then subjected to PCR amplification and the purification. Next, the libraries were quantified by qPCR. Finally, Novaseq6000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, United States), with 150 bp pair-end sequencing mode, was used for sequencing the genomic DNA of the family. Raw image files were processed using CASAVA v1.82 for base calling and generating raw data. Sequencing depth ≥30×, target coverage >95%, and Sanger sequencing validation of L1CAM variant with 100% concordance. The sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg38/GRCh38) using Burrows–Wheeler Aligner tool and PCR duplicates were removed by using Picard v1.57 (http://picard.sourceforge.net/). Verita Trekker® Variants Detection System by Berry Genomics and the third-party software GATK (https://software.broadinstitute.org/gatk/) were employed for L1CAM variant calling. Variant annotation and interpretation were conducted by ANNOVAR () and the Enliven® Variants Annotation Interpretation System. Minigene assays Minigene assay was preformed as previously reported (). Genomic DNA of the fetus and the mother were used to amplify the minigene regions spanning exon 11–12 and intron 12 of the L1CAM gene respectively, employing primers with EcoRI restriction sites ().The amplified products were cloned into the pSPL3 exon trapping vector by using ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The wild-type plasmid and the mutant plasmid were validated respectively by Sanger sequencing. The selected plasmids were prepared for further transfection. HEK293T cells were cultivated in DMEM medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum, penicillin (100 U/L), and streptomycin (100 mg/L) at 37°C in a 5% CO2, respectively. HEK293T cells were transfected with recombinant plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Total RNA was extracted from cells cultured for 48 h with TRIzol reagent (Cowin Biotech Co.). Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was conducted with a forward primer SD6 (F: 5′‐TCT​GAG​TCA​CCT​GGA​CAA​CC‐3′) and a reverse primer SA2 (R: 5′‐ ATC​TCA​GTG​GTA​TTT​GTG​AGC‐3′). PCR fragments were evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis, and isoforms were identified through Sanger sequencing. Assays performed in triplicate with wild-type and mutant. Minigene assay for L1CAM c.1380-1G > A mutation and schematic diagram of the splicing pattern. (a) The construction of a Minigene vector. (b) Results from gel electrophoresis of RT-PCR demonstrated the presence of bands for wild-type and mutant-type. The agarose gel electrophoresis results showed that the PCR product of pSPL3-WT exhibited a band at 546 bp, whereas pSPL3-MT displayed a band at 379 bp. (c) Analysis of the minigene product through sequencing. The wild-type minigene formed a normal mRNA, but the c.1380-1G > A substitution of L1CAM caused a splicing abnormality, which eliminated the Intron 11 canonical splice site, leading to lack of the Exon12. (d) The schematic diagram showed the splicing pattern of wild-type and mutant-type.

Results
Results Clinical features and identification of a novel L1CAM mutation in a prenatal case A 27-year-old nulliparous woman was referred to our prenatal diagnosis unit at 17 weeks and 3 days of gestation due to the detection of fetal hydrocephalus via ultrasound (). Comprehensive medical and family history assessments did not reveal any significant findings. To investigate the underlying genetic etiology, amniocentesis was performed, and amniotic fluid samples were subjected to copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) and G-banded karyotyping. CNV-seq and karyotyping results were prioritized to exclude common aneuploidies such as trisomy 13/18/21, and large structural rearrangements, focusing subsequent analyses on single-gene disorders. Pedigree of the X-linked hydrocephalus family. Circles denote female family members, squares denote male family members, triangles with slash denote aborted fetuses, blank symbols denates people without X-linked hydrocephalus, solid symbol subjects with X-linked hydrocephalus, core symbol denote carrier with X-linked hydrocephalus. The arrow indicates the proband. Both analyses yielded normal results (). However, follow-up ultrasound at 21 weeks and 2 days of gestation revealed progressive hydrocephalus with lateral ventricles measuring 15 mm and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum (). Given the severe and irreversible nature of these findings, the couple elected to terminate the pregnancy at 22 weeks of gestation. The ultrasound scan. (a) The ultrasound scan of hydrocephalus fetus (Ⅲ.1) in 21+2 weeks of gestation; (b) the ultrasound scan of normal fetus (Ⅲ.2) in 23+2 weeks of gestation. Post-termination genetic analysis included whole-exome sequencing (WES) on both maternal and fetal DNA samples. This analysis identified a novel hemizygous splice site mutation in intron 11 of L1CAM, specifically NM_000425.5:c.1380-1G>A. Sanger sequencing confirmed the maternal heterozygous carrier status and the fetal hemizygous mutation (). This variant has not been previously reported in population databases, including the 1000 Genomes Project, ExAC, EVS, or gnomAD (last accessed 26 April 2025). Sanger sequence chromatogram of L1CAM gene. Sanger sequencing showed that c.1380-1G > A was heterozygous in the mother (Ⅰ.2) and was semi-homozygous in the hydrocephalus fetus (Ⅱ.1, the proband), and was not detected in the normal fetus (Ⅱ.2). In their subsequent pregnancy, the couple opted for invasive genetic testing during the second trimester. Amniocentesis at 18 weeks and 6 days of gestation revealed a normal male karyotype, and both Sanger sequencing and CNV-seq confirmed the absence of the L1CAM c.1380-1G>A mutation (). Ultrasound monitoring throughout the pregnancy did not detect any structural abnormalities (), and the male infant was delivered at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery. At 1-year follow-up, the child exhibited normal development without signs of hydrocephalus. Functional analysis of the L1CAM splice site mutation To elucidate the functional consequences of the c.1380-1G>A mutation, a minigene assay was employed. This involved constructing a pSPL3 vector containing both wild-type (WT) and mutant (MT) L1CAM DNA fragments (). Following transfection into HEK 293T cells, RT-PCR and agarose gel electrophoresis demonstrated a significant reduction in the size of the PCR product from the MT construct, from 546 bp in WT to 379 bp in MT (). Sanger sequencing confirmed that this size difference was due to the complete skipping of exon 12 in the MT mRNA, resulting in a 167 bp deletion (). These findings indicate that the mutation disrupts normal RNA splicing, leading to the exclusion of exon 12 from the mature mRNA (). Bioinformatic analysis and pathogenicity classification Bioinformatic analysis with BDGP and MaxEntScan demonstrated that splice site variant c.1380-1G>A reduces the score of the WT 3′ splice site from 0.94 to NA, 9.42 to 0.67 and, respectively (). And SpliceAI indicated that there is a 99% probability of acceptor loss and a 93% probability of a new acceptor gain on 1 nt downstream (). Moreover, MES predicted the same acceptor gain that shift 1 nt downstream, which might lead to p.Trp460CysfsTer51, with the score rising from −2.67 to 5.28 (). A predicted new splice site would lead to p.Trp460CysfsTer51, a frameshift mutation and truncation of the immunoglobulin (Ig) domain 5, which is crucial for its adhesive and signaling functions (). The L1CAM c.1380-1G > A mutation resulting in abnormal protein structure. (a) Locations of c.1380-1G > A in the L1CAM gene and protein structure. Red arrows indicate the positions of the mutation. (b) Predicted wild-type L1CAM protein. Red region represents a truncated protein from Ig5 domain to the end (p.Trp460Ter). The splicing pattern of the minigene indicated that splice site variant c.1380-1G>A induces exon 12 skipping, which possibly result in p.Trp460Ter, a truncation from Ig5 domain of L1CAM. Three-dimensional protein structure prediction by Alphafold3 further demonstrated the structural disruption caused by a truncated protein from the Ig domain 5, disrupting ‘FnIII-like repeats’ conformation critical for structural stability of protein extracellular regions and interactions with other partners, which the absent region highlighted in red (). These data demonstrate that the variant c.1380-1G>A induces splicing disorders, causing a nonfunctional L1CAM protein due to a frameshift mutation from the Ig5 domain (p.Trp460CysfsTer51) or a truncation from the Ig5 domain (p.Trp460Ter). Based on the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) guidelines, the variant was classified as pathogenic (PVS1 + PM2 + PS3 + PP4). The PVS1 criterion was met due to the mutation affecting a canonical splice site, PM2 due to the absence of the variant in population databases, PS3 due to in vitro validation of minigene assay, and PP4 due to fetus’s phenotype and family history is highly specific for X-linked hydrocephalus with L1CAM genetic etiology.

Discussion
Discussion This case report underscores the pivotal role of whole-exome sequencing (WES) and detailed molecular analysis in identifying rare genetic variants associated with prenatal hydrocephalus. The identification of a novel L1CAM splice site mutation, NM_000425.5: c.1380-1G>A, not only contributes to the understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying X-linked hydrocephalus but also highlights the importance of comprehensive genetic testing in prenatal care. The mutation was identified in a heterozygous state in the mother and hemizygous in the aborted male fetus, leading to marked dilation of the cerebral ventricles and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, which are characteristic features of L1CAM-related disorders. Bioinformatics analysis predicted that this mutation impairs the acceptor site at the 3′splice site of intron 11, leading to splicing disorders. Although the results of the bioinformatics analysis were not completely consistent with those of the minigene experiment, both approaches indicated that the mutation causes exon 12 skipping, resulting in a frameshift truncation of the Ig5 domain (p.Trp460ProfsTer742) or a truncation from the Ig5 domain (p.Trp460Ter). This mutation is expected to disrupt the structure and function of the L1CAM protein, particularly the Ig5 domain, which is crucial for its adhesive and signaling functions. The L1CAM gene encodes a transmembrane glycoprotein that belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily and plays a critical role in neuronal migration, axon growth, and synaptic formation. The extracellular region of L1CAM is composed of six Ig domains and five fibronectin type III domains, which form a functional “horseshoe” structure essential for its activity. Deletion or truncation of the Ig5 domain, as seen in this case, has been associated with severe clinical manifestations, including hydrocephalus and corpus callosum agenesis. Consistent with these findings, previous reports have demonstrated that mutations affecting the Ig5 domain result in L1 syndrome, characterized by intellectual disability, adducted thumbs, and spastic paraplegia. Although this specific variant has not been previously reported, similar splice site mutations in intron 11, such as NM_000425.5: c.1379 + 5G>A, have been shown to cause abnormal splicing and result in hydrocephalus (). Other L1CAM splice site mutations, including c.1267 + 1G>A and c.1704-75G>T, have also been classified as pathogenic (; ; ; ). Splice site mutations in L1CAM account for over 16% of reported pathogenic variants and are known to cause exon skipping, activation of cryptic splice sites, or intron retention (; ). The pathogenicity of this variant was further supported by ACMG/AMP guidelines, which classified it as pathogenic (PVS1+PS3+PM2+PP1+PP3) (). The extracellular region of L1CAM is comprised of 6 Ig domains and 5 FNⅢ domains of 11 tandem immunoglobulin-like folds, which is effective at driving homophilic and heterophilic protein-protein interactions (). They can fold into the region shaped as a horseshoe, which is a functional unit of the protein that is equipotent with the full-length extracellular region in vitro (). A report has shown that an individual with NM_000425.5: c.1380G > C transversion leading to a p.Trp460Cys substitution was diagnosed with adducted thumbs, hydrocephalus, and dysmorphic corpus callosum (). Besides, a 40th week of gestation male fetus who carried the nonsense variant (c.1380G > A; p.Trp460X) result in truncation of Ig5 domain, performed pyramid hypoplasia, hydrocephalus and complete corpus callosum agenesis (). The L1-6D mutant mice, which are homozygous for a deletion that removes the Ig6 domain of L1CAM, revealed typical hydrocephalus (). Moreover, the activity of the horseshoe can be regulated by Ig5 and Ig6 stabilizing the horseshoe structure (). According to the previous study, Ig5-6 are critical for interaction with contactin (), which have roles in the development and function of tissuesby controlling processes of neurite extension, axon guidance, synapse formation, myelination, and axo-glia domain assembly (; ; ). In conclusion, currently available evidence displays the pathogenicity of this variant which splice site variants affecting structural key amino acids would disturb protein proper function (36). The expression level of the L1CAM was notably low in amniotic fluid cells (37), remaining amniotic fluid samples was insufficient to conduct effective RNA analysis for verifying splicing in vivo. While HEK293T cells, derived from human embryonic kidney tissue, inherently lack neural-specific splicing factors, their use in functional assays remains a common surrogate for initial validation of splice site variants. This is because they retain core splicing machinery components and can recapitulate aberrant splicing patterns observed in neurodevelopmental disorders when ectopically expressing neural genes. However, the absence of neuron-specific regulators may underestimate the complexity of tissue-dependent splicing regulation. We complemented HEK293T assays with in silico predictions (SpliceAI, MaxEntScan) and structural modeling, which aligned with the in vivo consequences of exon 12 skipping. This multimodal approach strengthens confidence that the c.1380-1G>A mutation directly drives pathogenic splicing disruptions relevant to L1CAM-associated hydrocephalus. Additionally, further cases are needed to provide more robust evidence for the clinical and molecular findings observed in this study. In summary, this study identifies a novel L1CAM splice site mutation and provides insights into its pathogenic mechanisms. The findings emphasize the importance of WES and detailed molecular analysis in prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling for X-linked hydrocephalus. The identification of this mutation expands the mutation spectrum of L1CAM-related disorders and may aid in the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for this and other L1CAM-associated conditions.

title: Compound Heterozygous Loss-of-Function Variants in CCM2L in a Fetus With Tetralogy of Fallot.
label_reason: Fetus with TOF and exome sequencing.
abstract: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. However, our current understanding of the genetic etiology for TOF is limited. Whole exome sequencing (WES) and Sanger sequencing were applied to a family trio diagnosed with TOF by fetal prenatal ultrasound examination. A minigene assay was performed to confirm the splicing defects. We identified compound heterozygous variants in the cerebral cavernous malformation 2‐like ( CCM2L ) gene, namely the paternally inherited nonsense variant NM_001365692.1 :c.741G>A p.(Trp247Ter) and the maternally inherited splice‐site variant NM_001365692.1 :c.1263+2T>A in a fetus with TOF featuring a ventricular septal defect associated with overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis. Minigene assay showed that the c.1263+2T>A variant led to skipping of CCM2L exon8 during RNA splicing, which is thought to result in frameshift and premature termination of translation. Both variants were absent from the public population databases (Genome Aggregation Database [gnomAD], 1000 Genomes [1000G], Clinvar) and classified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG guidelines (PVS1 + PM2 level evidence). To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of biallelic loss‐of‐function variants in human CCM2L . Our findings suggest a potential association of human CCM2L with TOF. Keywords: CCM2‐like, cerebral cavernous malformation, congenital heart disease, variant
text:
Compound Heterozygous Loss‐of‐Function Variants in CCM2L in a Fetus With Tetralogy of Fallot

Introduction
Introduction Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a severe form of congenital heart disease (CHD) and affects around one in 3600 live births (Shinebourne et al. ). TOF requires early surgical intervention to reduce morbidity and mortality. Timely and accurate prenatal diagnosis of TOF is important for perinatal management of affected newborns (Dib et al. ). However, our current understanding of the genetic etiology for TOF is limited (Althali and Hentges ). The human cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) family of genes has four members: CCM1 (OMIM: * 604214), CCM2 (OMIM: * 607929), CCM3 (OMIM: * 609118), and the later identified CCM2‐like (CCM2L) (HGNC: 16153) (Cullere et al. ). Causal relationships between the three CCM genes (CCM1, CCM2 and CCM3) and cerebral cavernous malformations are supported by the fact that loss‐of‐function variants of each of the three CCM genes have been identified in familial cases with autosomal dominant inheritance (Chaussenot et al. ). Previous mechanistic studies have shown that the CCM pathway characteristic of three adaptor proteins—CCM1 (Krit1), CCM2 (Osm), and CCM3 (PDCD10) forming a signaling complex, acts as a positive regulator of vessel stability; whereas CCM2L, a paralogue of CCM2, functions as a negative regulator of CCM2‐mediated stabilizing signals (Zheng et al. ). Despite these findings, little is known to date about the gene‐disease association of CCM2L. Here we report the identification of novel compound heterozygous variants CCM2L [NM_001365692.1:c.741G>A p.(Trp247Ter)];[c.1263+2T>A] from a fetus with ultrasound‐indicated TOF. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of biallelic loss‐of‐function variants in the human CCM2L gene.

Materials and Methods
Materials and Methods Ethical Compliance This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Hunan Provincial Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital (No. EC20180319). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants involved in the study. Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) We used a Trio‐WES strategy to prioritize the candidate variants in the present study. Genomic DNA was extracted from parental peripheral blood and fetal tissue samples using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen GmBH, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer's protocol. To construct sequencing library, an amount of 50 ng DNA was fragmented to 200 bp around by enzyme methods. The DNA fragments were then subjected to end repairing and addition with deoxyadenosine at the 3′ ends. Next, the DNA fragments were ligated with barcoded sequencing adaptors. Fragments about 320 bp were collected using XP beads (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA). After PCR amplification, the DNA fragments were hybridized and captured by NanoWES V2.1 (Berry Genomics, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The hybrid products were eluted and collected, followed by PCR amplification and purification. The generated libraries were quantified by real‐time PCR, and size distribution was determined using an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Finally, Novaseq6000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, USA) with 150 bp pair‐end sequencing mode was used for sequencing. Raw image files were processed through CASAVA v1.82 for base calling and generating raw data with consensus coding sequence (CCDS) coverage ≥ 95% and depth ≥ 20. Burrows–Wheeler Aligner tool was used to map the sequencing reads to the human reference genome (hg19/GRCh37), and PCR duplicates were removed by Picard v1.57 (http://picard.sourceforge.net/). Variant call format (VCF) files were generated using the GATK software (https://software.broadinstitute.org/gatk/). The ANNOVAR tool (https://annovar.openbioinformatics.org/)was used for variant annotation and interpretation. Public databases or online tools were referenced for analysis of WES data in the study, including the human population databases such as gnomAD (http://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), the 1000 Genome Project (http://browser.1000genomes.org), and dbSNP (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/snp), the online prediction algorithms such as SIFT (http://sift.jcvi.org), FATHMM (http://fathmm.biocompute.org.uk), MutationAssessor (http://mutationassessor.org), CADD (http://cadd.gs.washington.edu) and etc., and the disease and phenotype databases such as OMIM (http://www.omim.org), ClinVar (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar), and HGMD (http://www.hgmd.org). The pathogenicity of the variant was assessed and interpreted according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines and the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation (SVI) expert group's recommendations. Minigene Assay The wild‐type sequence of CCM2L (GenBank: NC_000020.11) intron 7 (460 bp)‐exon8 (130 bp)‐partial intron8 (552 bp) was cloned by two rounds of nested PCR using human genomic DNA as initial template. The mutated sequence was generated by overlap extension PCR method using the wild‐type sequence as a template. The wild‐type and mutated sequences were then subcloned into the pcMINI vector using the BamHI and EcoRI sites to construct the pcMINI‐CCM2L‐wt and pcMINI‐CCM2L‐mut vectors, respectively. Upon Sanger sequencing conformation, the pcMINI‐CCM2L‐wt/mut vector was amplified and purified for transfection of each of the HeLa and 293T cell lines. The transfected cells were harvested at 48 h for total RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis using GeneJET RNA Purification Kit and SuperScript III First‐Strand Synthesis System (Thermo Scientific, USA), respectively, following the supplier's instructions. Next, the cDNA template and specific primers flanking the inserted minigene sequence were used for PCR amplification. Agarose gel electrophoresis was run to visualize the PCR products, which were retrieved for Sanger sequencing. Minigene assay was also conducted with the pcMINI‐C vector harboring the wild‐type/mutated intron7 (536 bp)‐Exon8 (130 bp)‐intron8 (575 bp)‐Exon9 (139 bp) sequence following the above mentioned strategy. Sanger Sequencing Co‐segregation analysis of variants in family members was performed by Sanger sequencing. Forward and reverse primers for PCR amplification were designed using the Primer3 program based on the human genome reference sequence GRCh38/hg38. The sequencing reactions were set up using the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) according to the supplier's instructions. The purified PCR product was loaded for capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3730XL DNA analyzer (ABI PRISM, Foster City, CA, USA).

Results
Results Clinical Presentation A 26‐year‐old woman presented at 22 weeks of gestation for her second pregnancy. Her first pregnancy ended in spontaneous abortion, and the course of the current pregnancy was unremarkable. The couple denied any family history of hereditary diseases. Fetal echocardiography revealed a ventricular septal defect associated with overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis (Figure ), suggestive of TOF. The couple decided to terminate the pregnancy after thorough prenatal counseling. With written informed consent, skin tissue from the aborted fetus as well as venous blood samples from the couple were collected for genetic testing. Fetal echocardiogram of tetralogy of Fallot showing a large ventricular septal defect with overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis. Genetic Analysis Since the parents did not have CHD, our analysis focused on fetal de novo pathogenic variants and parental recessive pathogenic variants. We ranked the top 30 candidate variants (Table ) based on phenotype relevance and variant pathogenicity using a gene prioritization tool Exomiser as previously described (Lillback et al. ; Smedley et al. ). After exclusion of variants with a benign/likely benign classification by ACMG guidelines/Clinvar database, a CADD score of < 15, or a gene expression or function that is not directly related to heart development, variants of two strong candidate genes, namely the de novo CTBP2 NM_022802.3:c.2287G>A p.(Val763Met) (;) c.2276G>A p.(Arg759Gln) and the inherited CCM2L NM_001365692.1:c.[741G>A p.(Trp247Ter)];[c.1263+2T>A] were further considered. Although CTBP2 (OMIM: * 602619) has been suggested as a pathogenic gene in 10q subtelomeric deletions associated with CHD (Glessner et al. ), the majority of missense variants of this gene are classified as benign/likely benign in ClinVar, and a literature search on PubMed yielded no reports regarding disease‐associated missense variants of the gene. Therefore, we determined the biallelic loss‐of‐function variants in CCM2L as the cause in this study. The compound heterozygous variants in CCM2L in the fetus, namely c.741G>A p.(Trp247Ter) and c.1263+2T>A of paternal and maternal origin, respectively, were further confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure ). The c.741G>A variant introduces a stop codon at position 247, producing a largely truncated protein [p.(Trp247Ter)] in contrast to the full‐length CCM2L protein consisting of 571 amino acid residues. The c.741G>A variant was thought to be lossoffunction and absent from the public population databases [Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), 1000 Genomes (1000G), Clinvar]. Therefore, the c.741G>A variant was classified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG guidelines (PVS1 + PM2 level evidence). The c.1263+2T>A variant has a T to A transversion at position +2 of the splice donor site in intron 8. A minigene assay based on the insertion of CCM2L intron 7‐exon 8‐intron 8 sequence into the pcMINI vector (Figure ) or intron 7‐exon 8‐intron 8‐exon 9 sequence into the pcMINI‐C vector (Figure ) showed that the variant led to skipping of exon 8 during RNA splicing, which theoretically results in frameshift and premature termination of translation (c.1134_1263del p.Asn379CysTer34). The c.1263+2T>A variant was not present in the public population databases including gnomAD, 1000G, and Clinvar. Based on the ACMG guidelines, the c.1263+2T>A variant was classified as likely pathogenic (PVS1 + PM2). Results of Sanger sequencing showing the parental origins of compound heterozygous variants in CCM2L. A minigene assay of the c.1263+2T>A variant in CCM2L. (A) The construction strategy of pcMINI‐CCM2L‐wt/mut vector. The wild‐type/mutated sequence of CCM2L (GenBank: NC_000020.11) intron 7 (460 bp)‐exon8 (130 bp)‐partial intron8 (552 bp) was inserted into the pcMINI vector. (B) Agarose gel electrophoresis showing the differential splicing of the wild‐type (a) and mutated (b) sequences in mammalian cell lines 293T and HeLa. (C) Schematic diagram showing the normal (a) and exon 8 skipping (b) splicing. (D) Results of Sanger sequencing for the normal (a) and exon 8 skipping (b) splicing.

Discussion
Discussion The phenotypes of individuals with naturally occurring loss‐of‐function variants in protein‐coding genes provide important information for interpreting the human genome and for understanding the pathophysiology of human disorders. In this study, identification of compound heterozygous loss‐of‐function variants in CCM2L in a fetus with TOF highlights a potential association between the disease phenotype and human CCM2L deficiency. Animal models are remarkably useful tools for revealing the genotype–phenotype correlation and the pathogenesis of human diseases (Chan et al. ). In mouse models, global or endothelial‐specific deletion of any one of the three Ccm genes caused early embryonic lethality due to severe defects in vascular development, whereas postnatal deletion for each of the three genes resulted in vascular lesions that mimicked the human CCM (Boulday et al. ). In contrast to the three Ccm genes, the phenotype of complete loss of Ccm2L in mice was not remarkable; and thus it is thought to be dispensable for cardiovascular development (Zheng et al. ). Notably, in zebrafish, knockdown of ccm2l by morpholinos injection into early embryos yielded a big heart phenotype featuring dilation of the atrium and inflow tract (Rosen et al. ). Though biochemical, cellular, and animal model studies have revealed the functional roles of the CCM family genes in controlling vascular stability and their interactions in the CCM pathway, there was no significant evidence to support a role of CCM2L in human heart development prior to this study. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of biallelic loss‐of‐function variants in human CCM2L, providing novel clues for the genetic causes of congenital heart diseases (TOF). Validation of CCM2L expression in fetal tissue during early pregnancy will further support a role of the gene in development of the human heart. Studies using microarray data show that CCM2L is marginally expressed in heart atrium compared its levels in spleen and adipose tissue, with a z score of 4.02 versus 12.38 and 5.72 in the public database BioGPS (http://biogps.org/, ID: 140706, accessed on May 14th, 2025), where a z‐score > 5 suggests that the gene is expressed in that tissue (Wu et al. ). However, this does not exclude a significant transient expression of CCM2L in human embryonic heart. In situ hybridization studies showed that mouse Ccm2L expression was strongest in the E10.5 heart, but not detected in the heart or elsewhere after E12.5 (Zheng et al. ). Whether CCM2L is expressed in an early stage of human cardiac development needs further evidence. In the present study, the fetus with TOF was conceived by a healthy, non‐consanguineous couple who were each heterozygous for a nonsense or splice‐site variant in CCM2L, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance of the gene. This finding is in contrast to the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern of the three CCM genes. However, interestingly, a “two‐hit” mechanism has been proposed for CCM formation, in which germline mutation in one allele and somatic mutation in the second allele of a given CCM gene might be involved (Riant et al. ). In this view, the inheritance pattern of CCM2L does not seem at odds with that of the three CCM genes. In conclusion, the findings of our study suggest a potential association of CCM2L with developmental anomalies of the heart. More evidence is required to prove a causal relationship between CCM2L deficiency and congenital heart defects. Our finding provides useful information for genetic counseling, prenatal diagnosis, and screening of fetal cardiac malformations.
