title: Occipital Cephalocele, Polymicrogyria, Ocular Anomaly and Vermian Dysplasia: Prenatal Markers for Knobloch Syndrome.
label_reason: Fetal CNS anomalies with prenatal trio exome.
abstract:
Knobloch Syndrome‐1 is a rare autosomal recessive disorder typically diagnosed postnatally and characterized by occipital encephalocele, high myopia, and vitreoretinal degeneration. We describe a fetus with a constellation of prenatal neuroimaging findings, including occipital cephalocele, vermian dysplasia, bilateral polymicrogyria, and ocular elongation, that prompted genetic investigation. Trio exome sequencing identified biallelic pathogenic variants in COL18A1, confirming the diagnosis of Knobloch Syndrome‐1. This case highlights how advanced fetal neuroimaging and prenatal exome sequencing can facilitate early recognition of syndromes like Knobloch, and underscores the importance of considering COL18A1‐related disorders when multiple central nervous system anomalies are detected prenatally.

What is already known about this topic? Knobloch Syndrome‐1 has been associated with neurodevelopmental delay and epilepsy. Postnatally, Knobloch Syndrome‐1 is associated with central nervous system abnormalities including occipital encephalocele, polymicrogyria, cerebellar abnormalities, and ocular anomalies. What does this study add? This case illustrates how advances in fetal neuroimaging and prenatal exome sequencing enable earlier diagnosis of syndromes such as Knobloch Syndrome‐1, which have traditionally been diagnosed postnatally. Recognition of the constellation of occipital cephaloceles, polymicrogyria, and cerebellar vermian abnormalities on prenatal imaging should raise suspicion for COL18A1‐related disorders and prompt comprehensive genetic evaluation.
text:
Occipital Cephalocele, Polymicrogyria, Ocular Anomaly and Vermian Dysplasia: Prenatal Markers for Knobloch Syndrome

Fetal Phenotype
Fetal Phenotype A 36‐year‐old G3P1A1 patient was referred at 23 + 4 weeks of gestation for further evaluation following non‐visualization of the cavum septi pellucidi (CSP) and the presence of a Blake's pouch cyst on routine anatomy scan. First‐trimester screening, including nuchal translucency assessment at 12 weeks of gestation, was normal. A detailed fetal anatomy scan and targeted neurosonogram demonstrated a fetus appropriate for gestational age with multiple intracranial anomalies, including a small occipital cephalocele, vermian dysplasia, and bilateral diffuse polymicrogyria predominantly involving the frontal lobes (Figure ). Amniocentesis was performed on the same day. Although fetal MRI was offered promptly after the diagnosis at 23 + 4 weeks, imaging was ultimately performed at 27 + 4 weeks due to patient factors, including ambivalence about pregnancy management decisions and logistical challenges related to travel distance from the imaging center. Fetal MRI confirmed the vermian hypoplasia and dysplasia, a membrane communicating with an occipital bone defect and cephalocele, ocular elongation, and bifrontal symmetric polymicrogyria (Figure ). A repeat neurosonogram was performed after the MRI to monitor the progression of findings and to assist with patient counseling regarding prognosis. The findings were again demonstrated on repeat neurosonogram (Figure ; Table ). Ultrasound images at (a) 23 + 4 weeks midsagittal section demonstrating dysplastic vermis with meninges (arrow) pulled into a small posterior cephalocele (arrowhead). (b) 23 + 4 weeks with bilateral frontal lobe polygyria (arrows) and premature appearance of the cingulate gyrus (arrowhead) (c) 27 + 4 with extensive bilateral frontal polygyria. Fetal MRI at 27 + 4 weeks. Sagittal (d) and axial (e and f) HASTE T2 demonstrating an enlarged posterior fossa, vermian hypoplasia, and dysplasia with cephalad rotation of the vermis. A thin membrane (black arrow) from the fourth ventricle to a midline bony defect (white arrow) with fluid extending posterior to the bone in the subcutaneous tissues (asterix). Elongated eye globes (e) and foreshortened frontal lobes with bilateral frontal polymicrogyria (f) (white arrows).

Diagnostic Method
Diagnostic Method Amniocentesis revealed a male fetus with a normal karyotype on quantitative fluorescent polymerase chain reaction (QF‐PCR) and a normal chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). Clinical trio exome sequencing was funded by the Ministry of Health. Using genomic DNA from the proband and parents, the exonic regions and flanking splice junctions of the genome were captured using Twist Bioscience Exome 2.0 (Twist Biosciences, South San Francisco, CA). Massively parallel (NextGen) sequencing was performed on an Illumina system with 150 bp paired‐end reads. Bi‐directional sequence reads were assembled and aligned to reference sequences based on NCBI RefSeq transcripts and human genome build GRCh37/UCSC hg19 using a custom‐developed analysis tool. Data were filtered and analyzed to identify sequence variants as well as most deletions and duplications involving three or more coding exons. Reported variants were confirmed, if necessary, by an appropriate orthogonal method in the proband and in selected relatives.

Diagnostic Results and Interpretation
Diagnostic Results and Interpretation Clinical trio exome sequencing identified biallelic variants in COL18A1 (NM_130445.2). Both variants were predicted to result in protein truncation or nonsense‐mediated decay in a gene for which loss of function is a known mechanism of disease and were classified as pathogenic (Table ). Both the maternally inherited variant, c.3024_3042del; p.(Pro1009LeufsTer*13) and the paternally inherited variant, c.2823dup; p.(Gly942ArgRfsTer*142) were previously published in individuals with Knobloch syndrome []. Neither variant was observed as homozygous in large population cohorts (gnomAD). No other variants were reported.

Pregnancy Outcome and Neonatal Findings
Pregnancy Outcome and Neonatal Findings Multidisciplinary counseling was provided by maternal‐fetal medicine specialists, paediatricians and clinical geneticists. The parents were informed about the significant structural brain abnormalities, including polymicrogyria and occipital cephalocele, associated with high risks of neurodevelopmental delay, seizures, and possible vision impairment. Although isolated cases of favorable neurodevelopmental outcomes have been reported in Knobloch Syndrome‐1, the severity of imaging findings in this fetus suggests a more guarded prognosis. In accordance with our institutional policies, termination of pregnancy is permitted up to 24 weeks, and thereafter requires an ethics review and multidisciplinary approval. Given the severity of the findings, termination of pregnancy at a later gestational age was approved. The patient was also offered consultation with pediatric neurology and pediatric neurosurgery, but elected to proceed with termination without further consultations, at 28 weeks and 2 days. No autopsy was performed at the parental request. Limited external examination at delivery revealed no overt dysmorphic features or external anomalies apart from the occipital mass consistent with a small encephalocele.

Discussion
Discussion Knobloch Syndrome‐1 is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the COL18A1 gene (OMIM *120328) on chromosome 21q22.3, which encodes collagen type XVIII α1. This non‐fibrillar collagen is ubiquitously expressed and plays a crucial role in brain development, ocular structure formation, and neural tube closure []. Although Knobloch Syndrome‐1 (KNO1) was first described by Knobloch and Layer in 1971, reports in the literature remain scarce, with fewer than 100 documented cases—none of which have been detected prenatally []. This rare autosomal recessive disorder is classically defined by a characteristic triad of pathognomonic features including high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, and occipital encephalocele. Although previous reports suggest favorable neurodevelopmental outcomes, most literature has focused on the syndrome's ocular manifestations [, ]. However, emerging studies have identified postnatal diagnoses of pachygyria, polymicrogyria, heterotopic gray matter, and cerebellar abnormalities, often associated with atypical neurodevelopmental trajectories and epilepsy [, , ]. While previous reports have described central nervous system abnormalities in Knobloch Syndrome‐1 diagnosed postnatally, prenatal imaging findings have been less well‐characterized [, , ]. This case illustrates that advances in fetal neurosonography, fetal MRI, and widespread availability of prenatal genomic testing now enable earlier diagnosis of syndromes traditionally recognized postnatally. Therefore, a constellation of occipital encephaloceles, polymicrogyria, and cerebellar vermian abnormalities on prenatal imaging should raise suspicion for COL18A1‐related disorders and prompt comprehensive genetic testing, including exome sequencing. Our findings reinforce the importance of detailed fetal neuroimaging and prenatal genomic analysis in fetuses with complex brain anomalies.

title: Chorionic Villus Sampling for Rapid Confirmation of High-Risk NIPT Results for Trisomy 21, 18, and 13.
label_reason: T13 fetuses with US anomalies had CVS QF-PCR/SNP array; counts reported.
abstract: International societies recommend amniocentesis (AC) after high‐risk non‐invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) because of potential inconclusive results from chorionic villus sampling (CVS) caused by placental mosaicism. Our study aimed to evaluate the necessity of confirmatory amniocentesis following CVS for trisomies 21, 18, and 13 with separate analysis of cytotrophoblast (CTB) and mesenchymal core (MC). We retrospectively analyzed the confirmatory cytogenetic results between April 2017 and December 2022. CTB and MC were separated and analyzed by QF‐PCR and/or SNP array, and karyotyping when needed. Among 338 cases, 70% (237/339) of women underwent CVS (70.5%) and 30% (101/338) underwent AC. Mosaic trisomy in MC requiring additional amniocentesis was detected in 13.5% (5/37) of cases referred due to trisomy 13, 2.5% (4/158) of cases of trisomy 21% and 0% (0/42) of cases of trisomy 18. A definitive diagnosis of CVS was achieved in 97.5%, 100%, and 86.5% of patients with high‐risk NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, respectively. Moreover, our clinical practice confirms that the majority of pregnant women (70%) opted for CVS as a quick confirmatory test. We conclude that both CVS and AC can be offered when preceded by pre‐test counseling on the risks of potential inconclusive results as calculated in this study. Keywords: amniocentesis, chorionic villi sampling, CVS, follow‐up test, NIPT, non‐invasive prenatal test, prenatal diagnosis
text:
Chorionic Villus Sampling for Rapid Confirmation of High‐Risk NIPT Results for Trisomy 21, 18, and 13

Introduction
Introduction Non‐invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) of cell‐free DNA in maternal plasma has revolutionized prenatal screening for the common aneuploidies (trisomy 21, 18, and 13) and is now offered in most countries around the world [, ]. Despite its excellent predictive values for common trisomies, discordant positive as well as negative results do occur [, , ], both having a biological origin in the majority of cases. Confined placental mosaicism (CPM), maternal chromosomal mosaicism, maternal tumor, maternal copy number variation, or vanishing twin often underlie a discordant positive result []. Therefore, it is recommended to confirm a positive NIPT result by invasive genetic prenatal testing, and many societies recommend amniocentesis (AC) to prevent inconclusive results when mosaicism is encountered in chorionic villi (CV) [, ]. As NIPT can be performed early in pregnancy, a major drawback of confirmation in amniotic fluid is its timing in pregnancy. AC is usually performed after the 15 + 0 weeks of gestation to prevent pregnancy complications []. This potentially means a long waiting time for the pregnant woman to receive a definitive cytogenomic result after early NIPT that may be performed at 10 weeks of gestation. We have previously shown, based on existing literature, that despite the phenomenon of CPM, chorionic villi sampling (CVS) can be reliably used for confirmation of NIPT positive for trisomy 21, 18, and 13 with an estimated 3% need of an additional confirmatory amniocentesis []. The only requirement is that both cell layers of the CV, cytotrophoblast (CTB) and mesenchymal core (MC), are separated as previously recommended [, ]. CVS was always the method of choice for cytogenetic testing in pregnancies with a high aneuploidy risk [] as rapid definitive results could be achieved from the 11th week of gestation. In the Netherlands, NIPT is offered as a first‐tier screening test in the general pregnant population since 2017 []. In our clinics, pregnant women are offered a choice between confirmation through AC (with the disadvantage of a longer waiting time until the test can be performed) or through CVS with a ca. 3% chance of an additional confirmatory amniocentesis if the mesenchymal core of CV shows a mosaic chromosomal aberration []. The aim of this study was to evaluate the frequency of an additional confirmatory AC for inconclusive CVS results after NIPT revealed a trisomy 21, 18, or 13 and to evaluate how often pregnant women chose CVS.

Material and Methods
Material and Methods NIPT was performed as part of the Dutch TRIDENT‐1/2 study []. Written informed consent was obtained from all participating women. In case of an abnormal NIPT result for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, a fetal medicine specialist counseled parents on follow‐up testing: AC or CVS. The cytogenetic follow‐up tests were performed as part of routine prenatal care and are covered by health insurance. Patients with a high‐risk result for trisomy 21, 18 or 13 were offered a choice between a CVS ≥ 11 weeks of gestation and an amniocentesis ≥ 15 weeks of gestation. During the pretest counseling, the estimated 3% chance of a mosaic result with a CVS, requiring an additional confirmatory amniocentesis, was highlighted, especially in cases of trisomy 13 for which the risk is estimated to be the highest []. In our department, the cytogenetic investigation in CV includes routine separation of the cytotrophoblast (CTB) from the mesenchymal core (MC) to enable the correct interpretation of mosaic results and, therefore, to reduce the need for subsequent amniocentesis. The CV sample was evaluated under a microscope and all maternal and other non‐chorionic tissues were removed. Subsequently, the sample was washed twice in PBS to remove blood contamination. After transferring to a new dish, the villi samples were incubated 1 h in Trypsin/EDTA (0.05%) in a CO2 incubator at 37°C. During the incubation, the CTB separates from the MC. After the material was carefully re‐suspended, the CTB cells were expected to remain in the cell suspension. The sample is then filtered, which allows the capture of the solid pieces of the mesenchymal core that can be transferred to a new dish and washed with PBS. The CTB cell suspension was then used for DNA extraction. Mesenchymal core pieces were transferred to a centrifuge tube and incubated with collagenase (Collagenase II 600 U/mL medium) for 1 h in a CO2 incubator at 37°C. The mesenchymal core suspension samples were then mixed and centrifuged for 10 min at 2000 rpm and the pellets were re‐suspended in a culture medium. The pellets were divided into three portions, two for DNA extraction and one for backup cell culture. Separation of the CTB and MC allows defining CPM types: type 1, where abnormal cell line(s) are only present in CTB, type 2 with abnormal cell line(s) present only in MC and type 3 with abnormal cell line(s) present in both CTB and MC. Rapid Aneuploidy testing by QF‐PCR was routinely offered and the results were available within 2 days. If the result revealed a full trisomy 21, 18 or 13 in the MC, irrespective of the CTB result, this was considered a definitive diagnosis of a fetal common trisomy, and karyotyping was performed in case of trisomy 13 and 21 to exclude an unbalanced translocation. In case of a normal or mosaic result, SNP microarray (Illumina Infinium GSA + MD‐24 with a testing resolution of 0.5 Mb) was performed on both DNA isolated from CTB and MC [] and the results are available from 72 h up to 6 working days. If the SNP array on the MC was normal, irrespective of the CTB result, this was considered a certain normal fetal result. If the SNP array or QF‐PCR on the MC showed mosaicism, this was considered an uncertain result requiring follow‐up diagnostic testing in amniotic fluid to distinguish between CPM and generalized mosaicism. Ethical Approval Here, we describe the cytogenetic follow‐up in fetuses with high‐risk NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13 identified in the TRIDENT‐1 study and the TRIDENT‐2 study in 2017–2022. Permission for the TRIDENT‐1 study was granted by the Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport (350010‐118701‐PG) on March 28, 2014. A license for the TRIDENT‐2 study was granted by the Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport in 2017 (1017420‐153371‐PG) on September 20, 2016. Additionally, the study in the general population was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Amsterdam UMC, VU University Medical Center (VUMC No.2017.165) on March 27, 2017. All women consented to their data being used for research.

Results
Results In 2017–2022, 393 women chose invasive testing after receiving a high‐risk NIPT result for trisomy 21, 18 or 13. One woman did not consent for research and her data were excluded. Sixty percent (237/392) women underwent CVS and 40% (154/392) underwent AC. To study patients' preferences for one or the other test, some patients were excluded: nine women who had an AC were referred with NIPT performed elsewhere, and we could not conclude whether the CVS was not performed because of late NIPT results or because these couples chose AC. Moreover, 44 cases of AC were excluded because NIPT was performed after 13 + 4 weeks of gestation, and therefore, the results were available at about 15 weeks, when AC is a more reasonable choice for follow‐up testing. Of the remaining 339 samples, 70% (237/339) were obtained via CVS and 30% (101/339) via AC. The mean gestational age when patients received NIPT results was 12 + 4 wk.d. in patients where NIPT was requested before 14 weeks of gestation. In 4.2% (10/237) cases, a mosaic result in MC was found. One fetus died intrauterinely during the diagnostic process in CV and the confirmatory test was performed on skin fibroblasts. In the remaining 3.8% (9/237) of the CVS cases an additional confirmatory amniocentesis was necessary due to mosaic results in the MC, whereas 97.5%, 100%, and 86.5% of patients with high‐risk NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, respectively, received a definitive result from CVS (Table ). The chance for a subsequent amniocentesis depended on the trisomy and was 2.5%, 0%, and 13% for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, respectively. In 3 out of these 9 cases with follow‐up in amniotic fluid, a (mosaic) trisomy 21 was confirmed in the fetus, the rest being normal (Table ). Because the positive predictive value of NIPT showing a high risk for trisomy 13 is the lowest of the common trisomies and more mosaic cases are expected, we present detailed follow‐up results for trisomy 13 separately in Figure . Of the 69 patients with a high risk for trisomy 13, 54% (37/68) chose CVS, while 46% (31/68) preferred amniocentesis (Figure ). In 12/37 cases with NIPT suggestive for T13 who had chosen CVS, ultrasound anomalies (UA) were detected. In all cases with abnormal ultrasound, the final diagnosis of Patau syndrome (n = 11) or confined placental mosaicism type 1 (trisomy 13 restricted to CTB) (N = 1) was made based on CVS results. Among all cases who chose CVS and showed no UA, 20% (5/25) showed mosaicism in the mesenchymal core. Five cases required an additional confirmatory amniocentesis and one died intrauterinely, and a confirmatory test was performed on a skin biopsy that showed normal results (CPM type 3). However, 80% (20/25) could receive a final diagnosis based on CVS. AC, amniocentesis; CPM, confined placental mosaicism; CVS, chorinic villi biopsy; mos, mosaic; T13, trisomy 13; VT, vanishing twin. Figure shows all the results in cases with NIPT suggestive of T13. One can appreciate that CPM type 1 was detected in 6/37 cases suspected for trisomy 13. If the CTB and MC were not investigated separately, all cases of CPM 1 would require additional amniocentesis as the results of not separated CV would show mosaic trisomy 13. In case of trisomy 13, the risk of additional amniocentesis would significantly rise from 13.5% (5/37) to 29.7% (11/37).

Discussion
Discussion Offering chorionic villi sampling (CVS) after abnormal NIPT results is not a common practice and is a subject of debate. Our current results confirm our previous evidence‐based recommendation on choices between CVS and amniocentesis (AC) depending on the chromosome aberration [] and are in concordance with recently published studies as well [, ]. Moreover, we show that the need for a confirmatory amniocentesis, after CVS shows an uncertain result, is not notably different in a general obstetric population (current data) as compared to a high genetic risk pregnant population (most karyotype data from the literature also used for our previous estimations []). To identify CPM type 1 cases that don't need follow‐up testing in amniotic fluid, and to distinguish them from potential fetal mosaic cases with mosaicism in the mesenchymal core (MC), we suggest analyzing the cytotrophoblast (CTB) and MC of chorionic villi (CV) separately. The presence of abnormal cell lines in MCs poses a risk of fetal trisomy because of their common embryonic origin (the inner cell mass of blastocyst). Therefore, detecting mosaic trisomy in MC necessitates follow‐up testing in amniotic fluid. If CTB and MC were not separated, all CV mosaic cases would likely require an additional confirmatory amniocentesis, and indeed, CV sampling would not be as beneficial as in the case of our protocol. Separate analysis of CTB and MC can pinpoint whether the abnormal cell line is present in the cytotrophoblast or mesenchymal core, or in both, with only the former not requiring additional confirmatory amniocentesis. Our current study shows that CVS can be offered as a valid alternative to amniocentesis for follow‐up diagnostic testing in case of high‐risk NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13. Based on the previous estimations in the literature, an additional confirmatory amniocentesis would be necessary in 3% of patients choosing CVS for this indication []. In the present study, we showed that an additional confirmatory amniocentesis was necessary in 3.8% of the patients. Our results are in line with a recent report by Scarff et al., who showed that 4.3% of CVS results were mosaic and required subsequent amniocentesis to clarify the fetal karyotype []. We do agree with Scarff et al. [] that due to the low frequency in which subsequent amniocentesis was necessary, CVS can be recommended in case of trisomy 21 and 18 regardless of the ultrasound findings. Trisomy 13 shows higher risks for mosaicism and the necessity for additional confirmatory amniocentesis. Although the presence of ultrasound abnormalities may be an important factor in decision‐making on the choice of prenatal diagnostic test (CVS or AC), in our settings, no routine ultrasound investigations were performed during counseling for CVS or AC. More research is needed to evaluate the role of early ultrasound in patients' choices, as only invasive testing is able to provide the final diagnosis. In our cohort, cases of trisomy 13 showed higher risks for mosaicism and the necessity for additional confirmatory amniocentesis. Especially in the absence of ultrasound anomalies, 20% of CVS patients needed follow‐up amniocentesis for a definitive diagnosis, whereas this was 0% when fetal anomalies were seen. Proper pre‐test counseling is crucial so that women can make an informed choice on prenatal diagnostic testing, and the data presented in this manuscript can be used as guidance. Our team (conform the Dutch approach) facilitates individual informed choices, so we offer pre‐test counseling by experienced fetal medicine specialists ensuring informed individual choices based on the data available from the literature and patients' attitudes toward CVS as a quicker option with a higher risk for uncertain results [, , , ]. In our experience, most patients (70%) value rapid diagnosis and are able to take the risk of an uncertain result from CVS if a mosaic aberration is found, which is in line with previous reports also showing that most women elect CVS for a prenatal diagnosis of T21 and T18 []. In our opinion, offering only AC in all cases of NIPT showing a high risk for a common trisomy could raise an ethical question—is delaying the confirmation of positive NIPT results and therefore prolonging the period of uncertainty in all patients justified? In cases where NIPT is performed after an early ultrasound at 13–14 weeks of gestation, this challenge may not be present; however, in settings where NIPT is offered from 10 weeks of gestation [], the diagnostic delay may notably increase the psychological impact of later terminations of pregnancy (TOP) [, ]. Also, the risk of complications after TOP increases with advancing gestational age []. Offering only AC as a confirmatory option does not support the reproduction autonomy of the patients. Reproductive autonomy means that the decision‐making is left to patients and not to authorities []. Therefore, we decided to include patients in the decision‐making on the follow‐up test in case of positive NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13 rather than offering AC in all cases. All mosaic cases receive individualized patient care. In cases that require a secondary AC, thorough genetic counseling is performed by a clinical geneticist specialized in prenatal testing, and patients have access to psychological support if needed. In this way, we minimalized the long waiting time for the majority of patients and safeguarded the proper care for a small percentage (3.8%) that will need an additional confirmatory AC. Study Limitations The main limitation of this study is its retrospective nature. Patients who did not undergo follow‐up in our region could not be included?

Conclusions
Conclusions Our study showed that CVS provided conclusive results for 97.5%, 100%, and 86.5% of patients with high‐risk NIPT results for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, respectively. Moreover, we showed that in clinical practice, because of the separate analysis of CV tissues, CVS was the preferred confirmatory test. We concluded that both CVS and AC can be offered when assisted by appropriate pre‐test counseling on risks for an additional confirmatory amniocentesis in cases of mosaicism that assures informed individual choices. We recommend giving choices on prenatal follow‐up tests to patients, which best serves the couples' reproductive autonomy.

title: Isolated Feet Edema in Turner Syndrome by Prenatal Ultrasonography - Case Report and Literature Review.
label_reason: Fetus with US anomalies; amniocentesis 45,X karyotype.
abstract: Turner syndrome (TS), also known as congenital ovarian hypoplasia syndrome, is a sex chromosome abnormality caused by a complete/partial absence of the second sex chromosome with complete X chromosome. The most common findings by prenatal ultrasonography of TS include thickened nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma, cardiovascular system abnormalities, urinary system diseases, and growth retardation. We present a unique case of TS with the ultrasonographic features of dorsal skin edema on both feet and a progressive slow growth of humerus length (HL) and femur length (FL) at the second trimester of spontaneous pregnancy. We performed an extensive review of prenatal ultrasound features of TS cases from MEDLINE (PUBMED) published in English between 2000 and 2024 to prove this case’s uniqueness. A 29-year-old pregnant woman with her second pregnancy after a previous missed abortion presented as the prenatal ultrasound exam for fetal structural anomalies at 24 +3 weeks gestation revealed an edema of the dorsal skin on both feet and a short long bone of both femur and humerus for gestational age. Nuchal translucency (NT) measurement at week 13 +6 was 1.3mm, and fetal echocardiography at week 24 +2 showed normal. There were no markedly abnormal findings in the results of non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT) cell-free fetal DNA (cff-DNA) at 14 +6 weeks. Then, amniocentesis was performed and the results confirmed Turner syndrome with a 45,X karyotype. The final review included 11 with a total number of 884 cases identified, among which central lymphedema such as increased nuchal translucency or cystic hygroma is the typical finding with TS by ultrasonographic examination. Peripheral lymphedema resulting in fetal substantial swelling in feet was reported in 3 cases. Fetal feet edema accompanied with growth retardation are extremely rare. Peripheral lymphedema such as feet edema accompanied with long bone-involved growth retardation is rare but recognized features by prenatal ultrasonography, which should be considered as an index of chromosomal abnormalities in fetus with TS.
text:
Isolated Feet Edema in Turner Syndrome by Prenatal Ultrasonography – Case Report and Literature Review

Introduction
Introduction Turner syndrome (TS), also known as congenital ovarian hypoplasia syndrome, is a sex chromosome abnormality due to the complete loss or partial deletion/structural abnormalities of the second sex chromosome. During early pregnancy, 99% of chromosomally abnormal embryos spontaneously miscarry at an incidence rate of 1 in every 2500 live-born girls. Only 1% of TS fetuses whose abnormal sex chromosome is mosaic pattern can survive till birth. With the technical innovations through the decades, the analysis of cell-free fetal DNA (cff-DNA) in maternal plasma and serum, which has been called the non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT), is the innovation in the field of prenatal diagnosis. The amniocenteses were performed for routine clinical indications (such as sonographic abnormalities or advanced maternal age). Ultrasonography, as a noninvasive screening modality, is useful in prenatal diagnosis of TS based on the findings including thickening of nuchal translucency (NT), cystic hygroma, cardiovascular anomalies, urinary system disorders, growth retardation etc. Lymphedema is a common finding in fetuses with TS, especially central lymphedema such as cystic hygroma, which is found to be strongly associated with cardiac defects. Peripheral lymphedema is rare, although not specifically associated with cardiac anomalies, can result in substantial swelling in the hands and feet. Here, we present a unique case of TS in the second trimester with dorsal skin edema on both feet and a less short HL and FL by ultrasound screening.

Case Presentation
Case Presentation Medical records of the patient were reviewed and reevaluated to write this case report. The patient gave written consent for publication of this case report and prepared a written account of her experience. A 29-year-old pregnant woman with no history of consanguineous marriage or infectious disease/genetic history denial. Neither the pregnant woman nor her husband had any chromosomal abnormalities. It was her second pregnancy after a previous missed abortion at 8 gestational weeks. The present pregnancy was natural conception. All the pregnancy-related laboratory tests reported normal except an abnormal glucose tolerance at week 23+6, and the initial treatment consists of diet and exercise to achieve glycemic goals. Nuchal translucency (NT) measured at 13+6 gestational week was 1.3mm. There were no markedly abnormal findings in the results of non-invasive prenatal test (NIPT) cell-free fetal DNA (cff-DNA) at 14+6 weeks. Fetal echocardiography at week 24+2 reported no evident abnormalities. The ultrasound examination for malformation screening at 24+3 weeks gestation was performed by both Dr. Jing Ma and Li Liang on GE Voluson E8 with probe RAB2-5-D and about 0.7 ~0.9 cm thickness of skin and subcutaneous soft tissue on the back of fetus’ feet was noted ( and ). The value of HL was 3.5cm, FL was 3.9cm. The two values were less than two standard deviations (SD) when compared with those of gestational age (). No other structural anomaly was found in the heart, lungs and kidneys. Amniocentesis was recommended for advanced karyotype analysis. While waiting for the karyotype results, a routine ultrasound examination at 29+3 weeks gestation reported a less short HL and FL with 4.2cm and 4.9cm respectively, which was about four and three weeks’ lower than what should be for the gestational age as indicated. The edema on the dorsal skin on the feet was severe and the thickness of the skin increased approximately to 1.0~1.08cm. Other biological measurements were in accordance with the normal reference value. Chromosomal karyotype analysis of the fetal tissue showed monosomy X (45, X) (). Then the couple decided to terminate the pregnancy. Autopsy data showed an obvious swelling on both feet (). Prenatal ultrasonographic images of the fetus. (a) Two-dimensional ultrasound revealed the dorsal foot edema of the fetus. (b) Three-dimensional ultrasonographic image. Growth curve analysis of FL/HL (a) FL/HL measured at 24+3 gestational weeks indicating the values were below the 5th percentile. (b) FL/HL measured at 29+3 gestational weeks indicating the value was below the 1st percentile. Chromosomal karyotype analysis and autopsy data of the fetus (a) Chromosomal karyotype analysis showed chromosome X monosomy (45X). (b) Autopsy data confirmed the edema of the dorsal aspect of both feet. We also performed a literature review to find similar cases because the peripheral lymphedema of fetus in lower extremities is extremely rare. It was based on the survey of data available in PubMed with the following terms: “Turner syndrome and prenatal diagnosis” or “Turner syndrome and ultrasound”. The case reports, case series, and cohort studies with at least one case report published between 2000.01.01 and 2024.01.31 were reviewed. Review and opinion studies were excluded as well as non-English manuscripts. For the literature review, a total of 11 records about TS with specified prenatal ultrasonographic features were included in the final analysis (). There were 6 single or double case reports, and 5 were single/multicenter-center case series, with the largest including 680 confirmed TS. presents all papers and extracted data.The database includes gestational age at diagnosis, maternal age, ultrasonographic features, chromosomal karyotype and pregnancy outcome. A total number of 884 cases were reviewed, but not all data were available for all cases. The gestational age of abnormal detections by US was before 25 weeks in most cases. Out of all cases, only 1.5% (13/884) were diagnosed during the third trimester. The latest gestational age at the time of diagnosis was 40 weeks of pregnancy. The range of maternal age based on the data available was from 16 to 45, most of the pregnant women were under 35. Among these 884 cases, the most frequent karyotype in TS was 45,X karyotype (780/884, 88.2%), mosaicism was found in 11.8% of cases detected by prenatal ultrasound. Central lymphoedema including the increased NT and cervical hygroma were the highest incidence of ultrasonographic features of TS ranging from 71.2% to 100% in those 5 single/multicenter-center case series. Followed by cardiac anomalies, the incidence was from 10.7% to 69.2% in each study. Only 3 cases with peripheral lymphoedema of fetal feet were reported. The presence of short femur suggestive of growth retardation was found in 19 cases. Except one study involved 47 cases did not report the fetal outcome, 54.4% of cases terminated the pregnancy after diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound. Spontaneous intrauterine death occurred in 14.7% (123/837) cases and 7.3% (61/837) cases chose to continue the pregnancy. In one case, that was born at 38 weeks and died. PRISMA flow chart of Medline Search.

Discussion
Discussion Ultrasonography has played an important role that suggests an increased likelihood of TS by image rendering, which was considered as the another common NIPT technologies. For example, increased NT in the first trimester is a strong marker indicating autosomal trisomy syndromes and also common in fetuses with TS. Amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling are two generally used prenatal diagnostic procedures, which have been considered as gold standards for prenatal genetic diagnosis. While these two methods are not routinely used as screening tests because their invasiveness may lead to a risk of miscarriage. To obtain complete fetal genetic information and avoid endangering the fetus, NIPT techniques such as cff-DNA through serological screening of mothers in the first and second trimester are usually used to find possible risks of chromosomal abnormalities, but this method is less sensitive and accurate because it needs a high efficiency separation technology to obtain the scarce fetal cells from maternal circulation. As we presented case, the test of cff-DNA reported no abnormal findings while subsequent abnormal ultrasonographic findings were presented. Given that the blood sample contains maternal DNA, the mother must also be considered as a source of the false positive result. Missed and delayed diagnoses of TS remain a major problem if no further abnormal structure was detected prenatally. Karyotypes might affect the disease phenotype especially the structural abnormalities in the fetus, which can be detected by prenatal ultrasound scanning. Karyotypes include 45,X and mosaics (for example, 45,X/46,XX; 45,X/47,XXX). Congenital anomalies were detected more frequently by sonography in 45,X cases than in mosaics. As reported by Baena N, the most frequent karyotype was 45,X (81.6%), followed by mosaicism (16.8%). Papp C reported similar findings that 45,X karyotype was found in 90.4% of cases detected by ultrasound; while mosaicism was found in 9.5% of cases detected by ultrasound. Our data of literature review revealed that 88.2% cases were 45,X karyotype and 11.8% cases were mosaicism karyotype in 884 cases of TS with abnormal ultrasonographic finding. Our reported case also confirmed a 45,X karyotype. Lymphoedema including the increased NT, fetal cervical lymphatic hygroma and systemic edema are important features of TS. The presence of cystic hygroma makes the diagnosis of TS more likely. Approximately a third of TS fetuses present with persistent lymphoedema at birth, leading to lymphedema sequence after birth. Central lymphedema in a TS fetus with hydrops is found to be strongly associated with cardiac defects, while peripheral lymphedema was not specifically associated with cardiac anomalies. Fetal manifestation of edema in the hands, feet, and back is extremely rare. Only 3 cases with edema of feet in the fetal period were reported. Two of them were presented as case report reporting single ultrasonographic finding of dorsal foot edema in a female fetus; and the other one was presented in a retrospective study as associated findings with omphalocele. Both short femur and humerus were also observed in the present case, which were characterized with a progressive slow growth with gestation weeks. Among 25 cases as five literatures reported,,,,, 21 cases reported the short femur. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of prenatal diagnosis of TS based on the ultrasonographic finding of dorsal foot edema and progressively slow growth of FL and HL in a female fetus. The occurrence of dorsal foot edema is very crucial, which prompts the expectant mother to make up her minds to undergo the chromosomal karyotype analysis via amniocentesis. The gestational age of diagnosing fetal feet edema by ultrasound was commonly during the second trimester. It was 21 weeks and 22 weeks documented in 2 case reports and one should be before 25 weeks. Ultrasonographic images of fetal foot could be easily obtained during the second trimester, especially after 18 weeks. The gestational age of our case was 24 weeks when routine mid-trimester fetal ultrasound scan was performed. Usually, the ultrasound scanning of fetal feet was consisted with two parts, one is to scan the plantar plane, the shape of the foot, the toes and their number are tracked and observed; the other is the longitudinal scan along the lower leg to track the positional relationship between the foot and the lower leg, and also observe the shape of the dorsal skin and the arch of the foot. The longitudinal scanning can screen out structural deformities such as strephenopodia and rocker bottom foot. There was no abnormal findings before 24 weeks. Edema of the fetal foot may have existed, but the ultrasound resolution is incapable of detecting the detailed structural abnormalities at a small gestational age, or maybe the edema of the foot could not develop as structural abnormalities detected by ultrasound until the second trimester. It should be noted that another case report about the edema of the dorsal aspect of both feet by fetal ultrasonography at 15 weeks of gestation is a primary congenital lymphedema type I, also known as Milroy disease. Because of the rarity of isolated edema, and when it is seen, the threshold for chromosomal abnormality should be lowered by the physician prompting for thorough and further evaluation. Prenatal screening of sex chromosomes has a large risk of missed diagnosis, and non-invasive prenatal screening has certain limitations. Ultrasound and maternal serum screening are not diagnostic, and to make a prenatal diagnosis of TS, karyotype confirmation is obligatory. While typical ultrasonographic findings such as feet edema combined or not combined with other abnormalities might be a potentially useful prenatal marker of TS. Milroy disease (hereditary lymphedema type I) also should be included in the differential diagnosis because it is characterized by lower-limb lymphedema when isolated feet edema was presented. Paying special attention to the fetal feet edema on pre-natal ultrasound in general, and in history of previous abortion, chromosomal abnormality, and in presence of bone shortening.

title: A cut-off value for nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome in cystic hygroma cases.
label_reason: Cystic hygroma fetuses with invasive test (karyotype) results evaluated.
abstract: The aim of this study was to determine a cut-off value for nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome in cystic hygroma cases. This study was designed retrospectively in the perinatology department of a tertiary hospital. All fetuses followed up with a diagnosis of cystic hygroma between 2019 and 2023 were included in the study. Demographic characteristics, prenatal ultrasound findings, non-invasive screening test results, invasive diagnostic test results, clinical management, and postnatal outcomes were evaluated. A total of 34 patients diagnosed with cystic hygroma by prenatal ultrasonography were included in the study. The 50th percentile nuchal translucency value of cystic hygroma cases was 5.2 mm. Cystic hygroma cases were divided into two groups as nuchal translucency <5.2 mm and ≥5.2 mm. A receiver operator characteristics analysis was performed to determine an optimal cut-off value of nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome. There were no statistically significant differences between the groups for chromosomal/structural abnormalities and fetal losses. Chorionic villus sampling was performed in 28 patients, and amniocentesis was performed in one patient; five patients did not accept any invasive procedures. Nineteen cases had a chromosomal abnormality in chorionic villus sampling, while nine had a normal karyotype. The result of the amniocentesis was trisomy 18. A cut-off value of 4.03 mm was found for nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome (76.3% sensitivity, 66.7% specificity). Composite adverse outcome seems to be more common in cystic hygroma cases with an nuchal translucency ≥4.03 mm.
text:
A cut-off value for nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome in cystic hygroma cases

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Cystic hygroma (CH) is a congenital anomaly of the lymphatic system with an incidence of 1 in 6,000 . CH is characterized by the presence of edema and fluid-filled spaces in the posterior neck and back of a fetus at sites where the lymphatic and venous systems connect. It can occur as an isolated finding or be associated with other abnormalities as part of a syndrome . Environmental, genetic, or unknown factors can cause CH. Chromosomal abnormalities are present in approximately 50% of cases . Chromosomal or structural anomalies are associated with a poor prognosis. In the first or early second trimester, this condition can be diagnosed by ultrasound, with the measurement of fetal nuchal translucency (NT) in the mid-sagittal plane. If CH is diagnosed, the fetus should undergo a thorough anatomical screening for other systemic abnormalities. Subsequently, invasive fetal karyotyping should be offered to parents to detect any chromosomal abnormalities . Should the proposal be accepted, an obstetrician will perform chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis (AS) to facilitate further diagnosis. Previous research has indicated that pregnancies involving fetal CH and associated aneuploidy have resulted in worse perinatal outcomes. However, our knowledge is limited regarding the impact of NT value on the adverse outcomes in CH cases. For this reason, the main objective of the present study is to determine a cut-off value of NT in predicting composite adverse outcome in fetuses diagnosed with CH.

METHODS
METHODS This study was designed retrospectively in patients followed up for CH in the perinatology clinic of Ankara Bilkent City Hospital between January 2020 and August 2023. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee with ­reference number E2-23-5193, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Demographic characteristics, prenatal ultrasound findings, noninvasive screening test results (combined test), invasive diagnostic test results, accompanying congenital anomalies, and postnatal outcomes in fetuses that reached delivery were evaluated. Combined tests including NT, pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A), and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), were used as the aneuploidy screening test for all cases. The risk assessment for aneuploidy was performed based on the combined test results. Apgar scores and neonatal intensive care admissions were assessed for babies born alive. All cases were evaluated by the same expert perinatologist (O.K.) using a Voluson E10 with a 2–9 MHz abdominal convex probe. The data were statistically analyzed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences SPSS 22 (IBM Corp., NY). The 50th percentile of NT was found to be 5.2 mm in the study population, and the cases were divided into two groups as NT<5.2 mm and ≥5.2 mm. Demographic features, clinical outcomes, fetal complications, and chromosomal ­abnormality rates were compared between the groups. Furthermore, a composite adverse outcome, which was defined as the presence of at least one adverse outcome like intrauterine fetal demise, chromosomal abnormality, hydrops fetalis, or fetal structural abnormality, was compared between the groups. A receiver operator characteristics (ROC) analysis was performed to determine the optimal cut-off value of NT in the prediction of composite adverse outcome. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was applied to test whether data distribution was normal. Means and standard deviations were used for values that were applied to continuous variables that had a normal distribution. Whereas, median and range values were utilized to display continuous variables with non-normal distribution. Categorical variables were presented as numbers and percentages. As the data were not normally distributed, the Mann-Whitney U test was conducted to compare median values between the groups. ROC analysis and the Youden index were performed to determine optimal cut-off values of NT in the prediction of composite adverse outcome. A p<0.05 was regarded as statistically significant.

RESULTS
RESULTS Thirty-four patients diagnosed with CH by prenatal ultrasonography were included in the study. The 50th percentile of NT value for CH cases was 5.2 mm. CH cases were divided into two groups as equal or above and below this value. The two groups were similar in terms of maternal age, gravidity, parity, gestational age at diagnosis, maternal age over 35 years, fetal gender, fetal hydrops, fetal cardiac anomaly, fetal chromosomal anomaly, and intrauterine exitus. Composite adverse outcome was statistically higher in NT≥5.2 mm group [n=15(75%) vs. n=23(95.8%), p=0.045], respectively (). The risk of chromosomal abnormality was found to be high in 16, intermediate in 10, and low in 8 patients, respectively. Thirteen fetuses were male and 21 were female. CVS was performed in 28 patients, and AS was performed in one patient. Five patients did not accept invasive procedures. CVS was performed in 28 patients. Nine were found to have a normal karyotype among the CVS cases. Seven of these patients had trisomy 21, eight had Turner syndrome, and four had trisomy 18. One case of trisomy 18 was identified through AS. Fourteen patients were terminated due to chromosomal abnormalities, including trisomy 18 (n=4), trisomy 21 (n=4), and Turner syndrome (n=4). One patient with a normal karyotype result was terminated due to preterm premature rupture of membranes. One patient without a karyotype analysis was terminated due to a major congenital anomaly. Of the remaining 20 patients, 5 resulted in missed abortion before the 20th week of gestation, 5 resulted in intrauterine death, and 10 pregnancies were ­delivered. Of the five fetuses that resulted in miscarriage, two were diagnosed with Turner syndrome, one with trisomy 21, and one with trisomy 18. One fetus was not diagnosed because the parents did not give consent to invasive procedures. Of the five fetuses with intrauterine death, three had a normal karyotype, one had Turner syndrome, and one could not be karyotyped. Eight of the live newborns were admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to pleural effusion (n=1), cardiac anomalies (n=1), omphalocele (n=1), skeletal dysplasia (n=1), hypoplastic left heart syndrome (n=1), respiratory distress syndrome (n=1), and preterm birth (n=2). Cardiac abnormalities were identified in 8 of 34 fetuses diagnosed with CH. The prevalence of cardiac anomalies was higher in fetuses with Turner syndrome. Diffuse hydrops was observed in 9 of 34 patients. Six patients had no chromosomal or structural abnormalities, nor fetal loss. A summary of ROC analysis demonstrating the optimal cut-off value of NT in the prediction of composite adverse outcome in the CH group is shown in . The optimal cut-off value was 4.03 (76.3% sensitivity, 66.7% specificity), respectively (). Receiver operator characteristics curve of optimal cut-off value of nuchal translucency in the prediction of composite adverse outcome in the cystic hygroma group. ROC: receiver operator characteristics.

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION The results of the present study revealed that although the rates of chromosomal/structural abnormality and fetal loss were similar between the groups, the overall composite adverse outcome was higher in cases with larger NT values. Moreover, an optimal NT cut-off value could be determined in predicting composite adverse outcome. Although, the rates of chromosomal abnormality, intrauterine fetal demise, and fetal structural abnormality were comparable between the groups. The composite adverse outcome rate, defined as the presence of at least one of the complications, was higher in the greater NT group. The main goal of maternal–fetal medicine is to provide a healthy neonate to the parents. Thus, combining all complications in a group represents the rate of adverse perinatal outcomes more objectively. In a retrospective study conducted with 193 patients with NT≥6.5 mm. Invasive procedures were performed in 115 (59.3%) cases. Fetal chromosomal results were abnormal in 81 (70.4%) cases, including 58.0% of Turner syndrome, 21.0% of trisomy 18, 11.1% of trisomy 21, and 3.7% of trisomy 13. In this study, septations were observed in all cases. Septation was identified as a unique risk factor separate from NT thickness. It appeared that the existence of septation should not be a major consideration in prenatal counseling. The study findings indicated that a significantly large NT poses a high risk of chromosomal abnormality, with no notable increase in risk based on the presence of septation or ultrasound malformations. The fetal structural abnormalities presented in the mentioned study were congenital heart defect, hydrops fetalis, omphalocele, and skeletal dysplasia . Similar to the mentioned study, composite adverse outcome was more common in cases with larger NT values in our study. However, our study did not investigate the impact of septation. Over a span of 10 years, a total of 944 fetuses with nuchal CH diagnosed through first-trimester ultrasound were included in a retrospective cohort study. Karyotype results were available for 729 fetuses, of which 329 (45.1%) were normal and 400 (54.9%, 95%CI 51–58%) were abnormal. The NT thickness showed a significant increase in 298 fetuses with an abnormal karyotype, ranging from 1.4 to 24.7 mm, and a median of 6 mm (interquartile range 2–16 mm). In comparison, 242 fetuses with a normal karyotype had a range of 1.6 to 14.4 mm, with a median of 4.1 mm (interquartile range 1.9–12 mm, p<0.001). The authors also reported that every 1 mm increase in the NT thickness was associated with higher rates of adverse outcomes like abnormal karyotype, major structural anomalies, and perinatal loss. The difference in median NT was found to be statistically significant based on karyotype (p<0.001). In both univariable and multivariable regression analyses examining the correlation between NT thickness and outcomes, higher NT thickness was linked to abnormal ­karyotype, major congenital anomaly, perinatal loss, and adverse outcome , . The results of this study were consistent with the findings of the present study. In a retrospective study including 64 patients, prenatal and postnatal findings were investigated. CH without septa was found in 39 (60.9%) and with septa in 25 (39.1%) patients. Chromosomal abnormalities were detected in 25 (39%) patients. The most common chromosomal abnormality in CH without septa was trisomy 21 (27.8%). However, the most common chromosomal defect in CH without septa was Turner syndrome (23.8%). Survival was worse in those with additional structural abnormalities. Nine (14%) of the infants were born alive and were followed up postnatally . In one study, 29 cases of CH were followed up in two centers over a 4-year period. Of the 27 fetuses that were diagnosed before the 30th week of pregnancy, only one survived to term. Out of 27 fetuses, 25 were aborted; 21 of these 25 cases had severe hydrops. Spontaneous regression occurred in the second trimester in two of the 27 fetuses, both with Noonan syndrome stigmata. Seventeen fetuses were successfully karyotyped, including nine without abnormalities, seven with 45 X, and one with trisomy 21. The incidence of polyhydramnios (0 vs. 67%), extra anomalies (12 vs. 67%), and consanguinity or history of abnormal pregnancies (0 vs. 89%) was lower in fetuses with atypical karyotypes. Only three fetuses survived in the mentioned study . On the other hand, in our study, approximately 20% of the cases had no composite adverse outcome, slightly higher than the mentioned research. The main strengths of the present study were the determination of a cut-off value for NT in predicting composite adverse outcome, a relatively high number of study parameters, and the evaluation of middle-term outcomes. However, retrospective design, single-center experience, and lack of information related to the long-term outcomes were the main limitations. In conclusion, CH cases with larger NT values had higher composite adverse outcome rates, and physicians should be more careful in the management of CH cases with NT≥5.2 mm values. Closer prenatal follow-up, comprehensive assessment for fetal structural abnormalities, and detailed antenatal counseling may be useful in the management of cases with NT values above this cut-off.

ETHICS APPROVAL
ETHICS APPROVAL This study was approved by the Local Ethics committee and the approval number is E2-23-5193.

title: Prenatally and postnatally sequential genetic etiology detection in corpus callosum abnormalities.
label_reason: Corpus callosum abnormality cohort with karyotype, CMA, WES.
abstract: To evaluate the clinical utility of genetic testing via karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and exome sequencing in cases with corpus callosum abnormalities (CCA). Here, 65 prenatal and 12 postnatal cases diagnosed with CCA via ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging examination were enrolled. All cases were divided into two groups: 21 (27.3%) isolated and 56 (72.7%) non-isolated CCA groups. Karyotyping and CMA were first performed in parallel, then followed by whole exome sequencing (WES) after negative karyotype and CMA results. Clinical outcomes were also followed up. Karyotype abnormalities were identified in 7 cases (9.1%, 7/77). Karyotype abnormality rates in the isolated and non-isolated CCA groups were 8.0% and 9.6%, respectively ( p >  0.05). Pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs were identified in 11 cases (14.3%, 11/77), including 2(9.5%, 2/21) and 9(16.1%, 9/56) cases in the isolated and non-isolated CCA groups, respectively ( p  > 0.05). WES identified P/LP diagnostic genetic variants in 8 (47.1%, 8/17) cases, including 2 and 6 cases in the isolated and non-isolated CCA groups, respectively. Additionally, 3 cases with variants of unknown significance were identified. Of the 65 prenatal cases with CCA, 31 (47.7%) were terminated, 1 (1.5%) was a miscarriage, 33 (50.8%) yielded live born babies; of these, 4(12.1%, 4/33) yielded babies with neurodevelopment disorders (NDDs). Of the 12 postnatal cases with CCA, all presented NDDs. Genetic causes of CCA are highly variable. Prenatal brain magnetic resonance imaging and systemic ultrasound examination should be performed to examine other anomalies when CCAs are detected via ultrasound. WES is also recommended following negative karyotype and CMA results. text:
Prenatally and postnatally sequential genetic etiology detection in corpus callosum abnormalities

Introduction
Introduction Corpus callosum is a white matter structure connecting the two hemispheres of the brain. Corpus callosum abnormality (CCA) is a relatively common craniocerebral malformation, accounting for approximately 1:4000 live births. CCA may be due to various genetic or non-genetic causes, including vitamin deficiency, alcohol exposure, intrauterine infections. The underlying genetic causes of CCA include karyotype abnormalities, copy number variations (CNVs), uniparental disomy (UPD), and monogenic diseases. Fetal CCA may occur alone or in combination with other central nervous system (CNS) or extra CNS anomalies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is commonly used owing to its advantage in comprehensively evaluating craniocerebral abnormalities upon fetal CCA detection via ultrasonography. Percentages of underlying CCA genetic causes identified via chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and whole exome sequencing (WES) following negative karyotype results are 12.5 and 47%, respectively. Mustafa et al. identified pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in 43% of 267 fetal ACC cases using WES. Due to the variable clinical and genetic heterogeneity, counselling for prenatal CCA cases can be challenging. Therefore, comprehensive genetic cause evaluation is vital for accurate prognostic analysis and genetic counseling. Exome sequencing has a higher genetic diagnostic rate of P/LP genetic variants than karyotyping or CMA in fetal CCA cases. In this study, we performed genetic testing of karyotypes, CNVs, and single gene disorders in 77 cases with CCA with or without other ultrasound anomalies (UAs) to investigate the genetic etiology of CCA.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Subjects and sample collection A total of 77 cases with CCA with or without additional UAs enrolled at a tertiary referral center (Prenatal Diagnosis Center, Fujian Maternity and Child Health Hospital, Fuzhou, Fujian) from December, 2018 to December, 2023 were included in this study. Written informed consent was obtained from each case. Prenatal samples were collected via invasive diagnostic procedures at different weeks of gestation, and postnatal samples were collected by drawing the peripheral venous blood, peripheral venous blood from the parents was also collected. Overall workflow of the genetic diagnosis of cases with CCAs is shown in Fig. . Workflow of the genetic diagnosis of cases with corpus callosum abnormalities. CNV copy number variation, Indel insertion-deletion, LOH loss of heterozygosity, P/LP pathogenic/likely pathogenic, SNV single nucleotide variant, SNP single nucleotide polymorphism, VUS variants of uncertain significance, WES whole exome sequencing. *When the cytogenomic results via karyotyping and array analysis can not explain the phenotypes of the affected cases, WES were further recommended to perform. Conventional karyotyping analysis Karyotyping was performed following the standard procedures in our center, and karyotypes were scanned using Leica GSL120. At least 20 metaphase cells were counted, and five karyotypes were analyzed. Abnormal karyotypes were named according to the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature 2020. Isolation of genomic DNA Next, CCA sample, prenatal 30–40 mL of amniotic fluid, or 2–5 mL umbilical cord blood or postnatal whole blood was obtained, and genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen Inc., Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Maternal cell contamination was ruled out using multiplex quantitative-fluorescent polymerase chain reaction (QF-PCR) Darui kit (Darui, Guangzhou, China). CMA CMA was performed using the Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K array (Affymetrix Inc., Santa Clara, CA, USA) in all cases, and data were analyzed using the Affymetrix Chromosome Analysis Suite Software (version 3.1.0.15), as previously described. The reporting threshold was set at loss ≥ 500 Kb, gains ≥ 1 Mb, and loss of heterozygosity (LOH) ≥ 10 Mb. CNVs were classified as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign, or benign according to the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines. WES and bioinformatics analysis To identify the potential P/LP single nucleotide variants (SNVs)/small insertion/deletions (Indels) variants, a total of 23 cases with negative karyotypes and negative/VOUS CMA results, including 11 prenatal and 12 postnatal cases, were subjected to trio-WES with informed consent. Six cases failed due to insufficient quality or insufficient DNA for WES analysis. Libraries of genomic DNA samples were prepared using the Agilent Sure SelectXT Human All Exon V6 kit (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Paired-end sequencing was conducted using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Coverage for samples was > 99% at a 20× depth threshold. All sequencing reads were mapped to the human genome reference sequence (hg19 build). All SNV/Indel variants were annotated using public population frequency databases, including PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), Genome Aggregation Database (http://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), 1000 Genomes Project (http://browser.1000genomes.org/), Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC, http://exac.broadinstitute.org/), HGMD (http://www.hgmd.org), ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (http://www.omim.org/), and the Human Gene Mutation Database (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/index.php), and other literature and disease databases, and the pathogenicity of the variants was evaluated according to ACMG guidelines. Suspected variants were verified using Sanger sequencing. All candidate variants were reviewed and assessed by a multidisciplinary team consisting of geneticists, obstetricians, fetal medicine physicians, neonatologists, bioinformaticians, and radiologists. Obstetric outcome and follow-up information For cases with CCA, we collected data related to basic information, imaging findings, genetic testing results, obstetric outcomes, and follow-up information. Perinatal outcome data were collected from electronic medical records or via telephone and face-to-face assessments, including postnatal physical examination, Gesell Developmental Scheduleneurodevelopmental assessment, and postnatal ultrasound and cranial MRI result. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was conducted by SPSS software version 22.0 (SPSS, Inc., Chicago, IL). Measurement data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, comparisons between groups were performed using χ2 test and the two-tailed Fisher’s exact test when less than 5, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
