Pregnancy outcomes Follow-up was successfully performed in all 77 cases with CCA (Tables , and ), including 65 prenatal cases and 12 postnatal cases (all had abnormal phenotypes). Among these, 47 (61.0%) were male and 30 (49.0%) were female. Of the 65 prenatal cases, 33 fetuses (50.8%, 33/65) were delivered, including 15 fetuses (78.9%, 15/19) in the isolated CCA group and 18 fetuses (39.1%, 18/46) in the non-isolated group. Thirty-one fetuses (48.1%, 31/65) were terminated, including 4 fetuses (21.1%, 4/19) in the isolated CCA group and 27 fetuses (58.7%, 27/46) in the non-isolated CCA group, and one case of miscarriage with pathogenic genetic variant. In the non-isolated CCA group, the rate of pregnancy termination was the highest in multisystem anomalies (100%, 14/14), followed by cardiac anomalies (50.0%, 1/2) and cranial anomalies (30.6%, 11/36). Of the 33 fetuses born, all underwent regular physical examinations at 1.0-2.5 years old. Of these, 29 (87.9%, 29/33) exhibited normal neurodevelopment and 4 exhibited abnormal phenotypes, including two (13.3%, 2/15) cases (both refused WES test: one with language delay and the other with epilepsy) in the isolated CCA group and 2 (11.1%, 2/18) cases (both refused WES test: one with mental retardation and the other with global developmental delay) in the non-isolated CCA group, with no significant difference (p > 0.05). Of the 9 fetuses with P/LP CNVs detected by CMA, all 9 fetuses were terminated. Of the eight cases with diagnostic genetic variants detected via WES, two prenatal cases were terminated/miscarriaged, six postnatal cases presented abnormal phenotypes including NDDs (Table ).

Discussion
Discussion The corpus callosum is a transverse bundle of nerve fibers connecting the two hemispheres of the brain, and it is an important structure to maintain the function of the brain hemispheres. Complete formation of the corpus callosum occurs at 18–20 weeks of gestation. CCA was detected by ultrasound combined with MRI prenatally. CCA is a congenital craniocerebral anomaly, which not only leads to attention disorders and memory difficulties after birth, but also causes epilepsy, blindness and developmental delay. Agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) occurs in 2-3% of children with neurological disorders. Therefore, early and accurate diagnosis of fetal CCA is of great significance. Currently, genetic testing, including karyotyping, chromosome microarray analysis (CMA) and whole exome/genome sequencing (WES/WGS), is recommended for fetuses with structural anomalies. Comprehensive genetic information can aid in the prognostic evaluation of fetuses with CCA, and facilitate optimization of clinical management plans and the recurrent risk assessment for future pregnancies. In our cohort, we present a cohort of 77 cases with CCA who underwent sequential genetic testing, including karyotyping, CMA, and WES. Various genetic causes, such as abnormal karyotypes, CNVs, and monogenic disorders, are associated with CCA. Currently, sequential testing for prenatal genetic disorders, such as CMA for genomic diseases and ES or genome sequencing for single-gene diseases, is widely implemented in many hospitals,. Compared to karyotyping, microarray analysis can detect additional submicroscopic CNVs and UPD in 0.4–1.7% of fetuses. Therefore, karyotype and microarray analysis were performed for all cases in our cohort. Various karyotypic abnormalities have also been reported in non-isolated CCA. Chromosomal abnormalities were found in 10.0-17.3% of children with absence of corpus callosum, with chromosome aneuploidy being the most common, among which trisomy 13 was the highest (15.6%), followed by trisomy 18 (13.8%), trisomy 21 (5.5%) and sex chromosome abnormality (2.8%),. In this study, seven cases of chromosomal abnormalities were detected, including one case of sex chromosome abnormality, one case of structural abnormality of chromosome 6, and 5 cases of other chromosomes structural abnormality, with an abnormality rate of 9.1(7/77)%, which is lower than the reported rate of 14.0%, the difference may be related to the size and the selection of samples, the afore mentioned chromosome aneuploidy were not found in our cohort. The application of array technology suggested that causal 8p rearrangement, 1q36 microdeletion, 1q42q44 microdeletion, 14q microdeletion and distal deletion of chromosome 6 were correlated with CCA. In our cohort, CMA analysis revealed 11 cases of P/LP CNVs, with an abnormality rate of 14.3%(11/77), which is slightly higher than the 12.5% reported by Tsai P, et al.. The penetrance of 1p36 microdeletion syndrome in CCA is about 5.8%, the patients of this syndrome may manifest as typical craniofacial features, developmental delays and intellectual disabilities, seizures, feeding difficulties, congenital heart defects, eye abnormalities, skeletal abnormalities, hearing loss, and genitourinary system malformationsand Ski gene in the 1p36 region, which has been a focus of research on CCA. In this study, case BL61427 with CCA was diagnosed with 1p36.33p36.32 microdeletion postnatally, the affected child with 1p36.33p36.32 deletion exhibited hypertonia, growth delay, motor delay, delayed speech and language development, intellectual disability, seizures, strabismus, gait disturbance, impaired continence and hyperactivity after birth, consistent with the afore mentioned reports. The other 8p rearrangement, as well as 1q42q44 and 14q microdeletions were not found in this study. Previous study has shown that distal deletion of 6p is associated with ACC, there were two sites related to ACC, located at 6q25 and 6q26q27 respectively. The affected patients present different phenotypes, including ventriculomegaly, Dandy-Walker deformity, periventricular nodular heterotopic disorder, multicerebellar gyrus malformation, facial malformation, mental retardation, cerebellar malformation, hydrocephalus and ACC. A few patients with ACC also had deletion of 6p25 and 6q26q27. In case R5713, the fetus with 6p25.3p22.1 microduplication as well as 6q27 microdeletion in our study exhibited ACC, cerebellar and vermis dysplasia, right lateral ventriculomegaly, VSD, thymus dysplasia, pulmonary artery and branch stenosis, dysossification of bilateral sacrococcygeal vertebral arch, also consistent with the afore mentioned literature reports. The karyotypes of the fetus and the mother were 46,XY, rec(6)(pter→q26::p21.3→pter)mat and 46,XX, inv(6)(p21.3q26), respectively. The pregnancy was terminated finally. Informed selection for preimplantation genetic diagnosis and invasive prenatal diagnosis are recommended in the next pregnancy due to chromosomal abnormalities in the pregnant woman. Due to the incremental yield in identifying monogenic diseases, trio WES was further recommended for fetuses with UAs following a negative karyotype and CMA according to the ACMG guideline,. The development of the corpus callosum is regulated by multiple genes. CCA associated with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive inheritance modes have been reported, such as Donnai-Barrow syndrome, Meckel syndrome, Hydrolethalus syndrome, Acrocallosal syndrome–Mowat-Wilson syndrome, Sotos syndrome–X-linked agenesis of the corpus callosum, and Andermann syndrome. In case P2546, the GTG-banding karyotype of amniocyte showed constitutive r(13) in 72% of the cells, and monosomy 13 in 28%, based on CMA allowed refinement of the breakpoint region of the affected chromosome 13 and was useful in determining the gene content within the deleted region. However, due to the nature of the chromosomal rearrangements, CMA identified only the microdeletion that comprised more than 30% of the mosaicism in the fetus. Monosomy 13 were absent in the CMA result due to its limitations for detecting low-level mosaicism, the formation of monosomy 13 (45,XX,-13) in chromosome mosaicism [mos 46,XX, r(13)(p11q32)/45,XX,-r(13)] mainly results from the instability of ring chromosome 13 or random mitotic loss, resulting in the complete absence of chromosome 13 in some cells,. The emergence of chromosome mosaicism reflects chromosomal dynamic abnormalities in early embryonic development. WES/WGS is a feasible technology for prenatal diagnosis of CCA following normal array results. She Q, et al. have shown that BDNF, SLC1A2, and PAX6 may be involved in the development of isolated CCA. Baptiste et al.further solidified the efficacy of WES in identifying P/LP diagnostic genetic variants in CCA. In our cohort, eight cases with P/LP SNV/indel variants were detected by WES, indicating a WES diagnostic rate of 47.1% (8/17), which is higher than the reported rates of 34% and 43%, but consistent with the reported detection rate of 47%. This difference may be closely related to the differences in the sample size and proportion of different types of CCA, as well as the interpretation of prenatal genetic variants. Recent studies have shown that 33% of fetuses with UAs are caused by monogenic diseases, and half of the variants are de novo,,. Of eight cases with diagnostic genetic variants detected in our study, five (29.4%, 5/17) cases carried de novo variants, our data showed that the importance of further molecular genetic testing for CCA following normal cytogenetics, even with a negative family history. CCA may be isolated or accompanied by other UAs, such as common ventriculomegaly and cerebellar developmental abnormalities. Of the 77 cases with CCA in our cohort, 25 (32.5%) had isolated CCA and 52 (67.5%) had non-isolated CCA (accompanied with other CNS and non-CNS anomalies), which agrees with the findings reported by Manganaro et al.. Of the 52 non-isolated CCA, 32 (61.5%) had cranial anomalies, 20 (38.5%) had extracranial anomalies, which is lower than the rate reported. Our results showed that once CCA is examined by ultrasound, further brain MRI is recommended to rule out other cranial anomalies owing to its advantage of multiplanar capability and contrast resolution,and further fetal level III/II ultrasound examination is also required to detect other UAs. Lei et al. identified diagnostic genetic variants in 43.8% of the fetuses with non-isolated CCA and 29.4% with isolated CCA via WES. In this study, the overall molecular diagnosis rates using WES in the isolated CCA group and non-isolated CCA groups were 2/2 (100%) and 6/15 (40%), respectively. Although the two postnatal CCA cases (cases BL54708 and BL66103) were isolated, the detection rate was high may due to their abnormal phenotypes after birth. Our findings also confirmed that even for isolated CCA, prenatal WES should be considered after excluding chromosomal aberrations. In our non-isolated CCA group series, the rate of P/LP SNVs/indels variants in cranial anomalies was the highest (44.4%, 4/9), which is comparable to the rate of 43% by Mustafa et al.followed by 40% (2/5) in the multi-systemic anomaly group. Our data also confirm that WES is further considered because of the high yield of positive P/LP findings if the karyotype and CMA are negativeespecially in fetal CCA associated with cranial and multiple anomalies, further research is required due to the small sample size of each subgroup. The neurodevelopmental prognosis of cases with isolated CCA remains unclear. Tsai et al. found that 70.0% (7/10) of the liveborn isolated CCA fetuses without genetic causes had a favorable prognosis in early childhood, and 28.8 − 50% of children with CCA have intellectual, social, and/or behavioral impairments. The prognosis of fetal CCA is variable and depends mainly on whether the condition is isolated, as well as whether there is a genetic cause. In isolated CCA, outcomes range from normal in 65% of cases to varying degrees of NDDs in 35% of cases. Approximately 66.6% of children with isolated complete ACC have favorable outcomesand 70% of isolated CCA cases might present subtle NDDs as the follow-up time increased. Non-isolated ACC has a limited prognosis concerning neurodevelopmental outcome. Fetuses with CCA accompanied by other structural UAs had a poorer prognosis compared to the isolated group. In our series, all 33 born infants underwent regular physical examinations; among them, at the time of submission for this study, 4(12.1%, 4/33) infants had abnormal phenotypic findings, including 2 (13.3%, 2/15) cases in the isolated CCA group and 2(11.1%, 2/18) cases in the non-isolated CCA group. Due to the small sample size, a larger population study is required. Interpretation of prenatal WES data is challenging owing to limited fetal phenotypes and the lack of relevant evidence-based medical evidence, especially for VUS variantswhich could increase the anxiety of affected pregnant couple. The detection rate of VUS variants via WES associated with fetal phenotypes was 17.6% (3/17) (cases PC7362, R3641, and BL67864) in our cohort. The clinical features of the single-gene diseases associated with these three variants of uncertain significance were all partially concordant with UAs, and the uncertain variation and heterogeneity of CCA make prenatal counseling a challenge. Additionally, a history of an undiagnosed fetus affected by recurrent similar structural malformations yielding a negative karyotype or CMA results in the current pregnancy was highly suggestive of a single-gene disorder, such as in case PC7362 in this study, and the fetus was finally terminated after multidisciplinary team evaluation. This study has some limitations. First, as this was a retrospective single-center study, the true prevalence may have been overestimated due to the small sample size; Thus, future study with larger sample sizes is required. Second, the follow-up period was not long, which may miss some abnormal phenotypes postnatally, especially NDDs; thus, further extension of follow-up time is needed in subsequent studies. Third, 49.2% (32/65) of fetuses could not be followed further due to pregnancy termination/miscarriage, which may have impacted the prognostic evaluation of CCAs. Finally, WES was performed in only 22.1% (17/77) of CCA cases, this may lead to missed diagnosis of some monogenic diseases. CCAs are relatively common brain anomalies. The genetic causes of CCA are highly variable, WES/WGS should be highly considered following normal karyotype and array in cases with CCA. Overall, our data expand the spectrum of CCA phenotypes and related genetic variants.

title: Genetic etiology of ventriculomegaly in 73 fetuses identified by High-Throughput sequencing.
label_reason: Ventriculomegaly fetuses with CNV-seq and WES.
abstract: To investigate the genetic etiology of ventriculomegaly (VM) in fetuses by analyzing chromosomal aberrations and genetic variations through high-throughput sequencing. Clinical data and samples (amniotic fluid or miscarriage tissue) were collected from fetuses with ventricular width >10 mm, diagnosed at Shanxi Children’s Hospital between 2020 and 2023. All samples underwent copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), and those with negative CNV-seq result were further analyzed by whole exome sequencing (WES) to identify single-gene variants. Chromosomal abnormalities and monogenic variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0, and pregnancy outcomes were tracked. Among 73 VM fetuses, 23 (31.5%) cases exhibited chromosomal aberrations via CNV-seq, including 4 aneuploidies, 12 pathogenic CNVs, 2 likely pathogenic CNVs, and 8 variants of unknown significance. The incidence of chromosomal abnormalities was significantly higher in non-isolated VM fetuses compared to isolated VM ( p  < 0.05). WES analysis of 33 CNV-negative cases identified single-gene defects in 16 (48.5%) fetuses, including SPATA5 , PDHA1 , TRIM71 , PIK3R2 , TUBB , CRB2 , PIDD1 , RTTN , FGFR3 , AIMP1 , POGZ , MYH7 , CNOT3 , MACF1 , and PURA gene, with 10 novel variants reported. Fetal VM is associated with heterogeneous neurodevelopmental outcomes, and genetic etiology plays an important role in its pathogenesis. WES enhances the efficiency of diagnosis, particularly for VM fetuses without detectable aneuploidy or CNVs. Identifying the genetic etiology of fetal VM is is crucial for informing birth defect prevention strategies and improving the overall health of the newborn population. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-06714-2.

Genetic etiology of ventriculomegaly in 73 fetuses identified by High-Throughput sequencing

Introduction
Introduction Central nervous system (CNS) anomalies are among the most concerning findings during prenatal screenings, with ventriculomegaly (VM) representing the most common sonographically detected CNS abnormality. VM, defined as dilatation of the cerebral ventricles, is closely associated with long-term cognitive impairment and psychomotor developmental delays. Prenatal diagnosis of VM relies on ultrasonography of the lateral ventricular width. While the normal range during the second and third trimesters (14–40 weeks of gestation) is approximately 5.4–7.6 mm, a width > 10 mm is considered the diagnostic threshold for VM. Based on ventricular diameter, VM is typically classified into 3 categories: mild (10–12 mm), moderate (12–15 mm), and severe (> 15 mm),. The primary pathogenic mechanisms of fetal VM include brain parenchymal loss, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obstruction, or excessive CSF secretion. In some cases, the development of VM can be associated with genetic factors, such as chromosomal aberrations and genetic variations, or maternal factors, including cytomegalovirus or toxoplasmosis infections during pregnancy. Fetal VM is clinically heterogeneous, with outcomes ranging from normal postnatal development to severe neurological impairment or even death. Notably, the presence of chromosomal aberrations or single-gene defects (SGD) has been strongly linked to adverse prognoses. In addition to traditional non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), genetic diagnostic examination is increasingly being utilized to detect abnormalities via karyotyping, copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), whole exome sequencing (WES), and trio-WES (simultaneous fetal-parental variant analysis). Combining genetic examination with clinical and neurologic imaging findings can improve predictive outcomes, refine VM classification, optimize patient-specific management strategies, predict neurocognitive outcomes, and stratify patients into treatment plans. Moreover, this combined approach may help identify possible VM genetic mutation sites, establish effective clinical management during pregnancy, provide guidance for prenatal counseling in high-risk families, reduce incidence of birth defects and provide guidance for subsequent pregnancies. However, few studies have combined CNV-seq and WES to investigate the genetic etiology of fetal VM. As such, We analyzed the genetic etiology of 73 fetuses with VM, searched for chromosomal aberrations and pathogenic genes associated with fetal VM, and evaluated the detection efficacy of different prenatal genetic diagnostic techniques. The fetal genetic etiology of isolated VM (IVM), non-isolated VM (NIVM) and ventricular widening was compared. Pregnancy outcomes of fetal VM were followed up to provide reference for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling.

Results
Results Of the cases meeting inclusion criteria (n = 73), 33 exhibited no detectable copy number variations (CNVs) by CNV-seq and subsequently underwent WES. Figure shows the flowchart and results of the genetic analysis for the cohort. Demographics, VM characteristics, and sequencing information are summarized in Table . The median maternal age was 29 (range: 22–42) years, and the fetuses were assessed at a median gestational age of 25 (range: 17–33) weeks. Flowchart and results of genetic analysis in cohort. Flowchart showing inclusion in study of fetal VM genetic testing, and findings of next-generation sequencing analysis. CNV, copy-number variant; CNV-seq, CNV sequencing; WES, whole-exome sequencing; P, pathogenic; LP, likely pathogenic; VOUS, variants of uncertain significance. Results of CNV-seq Of the 73 fetal samples that underwent CNV-seq analysis, 23 (31.5%) had chromosomal abnormalities with 26 CNV fragments were detected, including 4 cases of aneuploidy (5.5%) and 22 CNVs classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines: 12 pathogenic (P), 2 likely pathogenic (LP), and 8 variants of uncertain significance (VOUS). Of these, 3 patients harbored 2 CNV fragments (P11 and P65 exhibited both P and VOUS variants, while P38 carried both P and LP variants). A relatively high frequency of CNVs was observed on chromosomes 1, 15, 17 and 22 (Tables and , S1). Results of WES Of the 33 pregnancies that underwent WES analysis, 16 (48.48%) had positive results. In cases of identified SGD among 33 pregnancies, prenatal IVM samples (n = 6) revealed mutations in SPATA5, PDHA1, TRIM71, PIK3R2, PIDD1, and MACF1 genes, with 5 novel loci: SPATA5 c.544delA(exon5), PDHA1 c.273(exon3)T > A, TRIM71 c.1799(exon4)G > A, PIDD1 c.1855(exon11)A > G, and MACF1 c.18,597(exon74)_c.18,600(exon74)delCAAA. Furthermore, prenatal NIVM (n = 10) samples revealed mutations in PDHA1, TUBB, CRB2, FGFR3, RTTN, AIMP1, POGZ, MYH7, CNOT3, and PURA genes. with 5 novel loci: CRB2 c.3078(exon10)_c.3093(exon10)delGGCGCGGCCCCGGCCC, AIMP1 c.187(exon3)A > T and c.110(exon3)delT, POGZ c.3406dupG, and MYH7 c.3133(exon25)C > A. Moreover, patients P14 and P18 were found to have a pyruvate dehydrogenase E1-α deficiency (PDHAD) (Table , S2). Chromosome aberrations and gene variations in different fetal VM groups NIVM showed a significantly higher detection rate compared to IVM (43.2% vs. 19.4%, p < 0.05, Fig. ). No significant differences were observed in the detection rates of chromosome aberration or gene variation in different width of VM detected by CNV-seq and WES. In NIVM, the results showed that 58.3% (7/12) of chromosomal aberrations and 55.6% (5/9) of genetic variants are present in combination with skeletal system abnormalities (Table ). Results of genetic tests for different fetal VM types. Follow-up outcomes Postnatal follow-ups were performed for 3 months to 3 years after pregnancy. Among CNV-seq-positive cases, in 16 cases parents chose to terminate the pregnancy and in 7 infants were delivered alive. Of the live births, 6 had postpartum developmental delays and 1 had Klinefelter syndrome. Among WES-positive cases, 9 sets of parents chose to terminate the pregnancy and 7 infants were delivered alive. Live-born infants gradually exhibited the clinical phenotype associated with their corresponding SGD at postnatal follow-ups. Among CNV-seq-negative cases, 17 also had a negative result following WES, and 17 families declined further testing. Of these cases, 10 sets of parents selected to terminate pregnancy (including 1 miscarriage sample) and 24 infants were delivered alive without incident. Even in patients who tested negative for both CNV-seq and WES, there were 5 cases with a poor postnatal outcome, including 1 case of neonatal death and 4 cases of developmental delay. Detailed follow-up information on pregnancy outcomes was shown in Table , S2, S3.

Discussion
Discussion The aim of this study was to evaluate the contribution of genetic etiology in fetal VM. Among the entire VM cohort (n = 73), chromosomal aberrations were detected in 31.5% of cases (23/73), with 12 of these classified as pathogenic based on CNV-seq analysis. Furthermore, relatively high aberration frequencies were noted in chromosomes 1, 15, 17 and 22, including 1q21.1 recurrent deletion, Prader-Willi syndrome, Koolen-de Vries syndrome, and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. For the patients diagnosed with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (P11 and P28), both presented with moderate VM and cardiac abnormalities, which is consistent with previously reported phenotypes. In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (also known as DiGeorge syndrome and Velocardiofacial syndrome), multiple genes are affected, including the critically important TBX1 and DGCR8 genes. TBX1 gene encodes the transcription factor T-box and DGCR8 gene plays an essential role in microRNA biogenesis. Both genes are crucial for the normal development of multiple organ systems. During the development of the nervous system, loss or mutation of these genes leads to aberrant neural progenitor proliferation and differentiation, with subsequent neuronal defects affecting ventricular morphology and contribute to the pathogenesis of VM–. It is still unclear whether there are differences in chromosomal aberration detection rates when comparing mild, moderate, or severe fetal VM, but the risk of chromosomal abnormalities was much higher in NIVM compared with IVM (9.5–36% vs. 1.5–12.0%)–. Consistent with previous studies, the rate of chromosomal aberration in this study was significantly higher in NIVM than in IVM, thus further confirming that NIVM is associated with an elevated risk of chromosomal aberrations. We found 58.3% (7/12) of chromosomal aberrations and 55.6% (5/9) of genetic variants of NIVMs were accompanied by skeletal system abnormalities, thus, particular attention should be paid to the possibility of chromosomal aberrations and genetic variations when fetal VM is accompanied by skeletal dysplasias. However, when comparing detection rates between mild and moderate-to-severe VM, no significant difference was determined. These findings indicate that regardless of the extent of ventricular enlargement, families should be informed of the risk of chromosome aberration or gene variant, and advised further prenatal diagnostics. Recent studies have strongly suggested a closer relationship between VM and gene mutations,. With the rapid development of second-generation sequencing technologies, the diagnostic paradigm has shifted from low-depth CNV-seq analysis to WES. Furthermore, ACMG guidelines suggest that exome or genome sequencing is considered as a primary or secondary diagnostic tool in patients with congenital anomalies. WES, a high-throughput genetic platform, systematically interrogates coding regions across thousands of genes, enabling efficient identification of pathogenic variants linked to fetal VM. This approach not only enhances diagnostic accuracy but also supports informed decision-making in genetic counseling,. While using WES to assess fetal structural abnormalities isn’t new, most studies on fetal VM have been limited to case reports of SGD or cohort analyses focusing on karyotype and CNV findings. The strength of this study is that we combined CNV-seq with WES while categorizing each case. This approach enabled valuation of WES’s incremental diagnosis, identification of genotype-phenotype correlations across VM different widths and concurrent structural anomalies, and assessment of SGDs’ contribution to fetal VM. Herein, WES significantly enhanced the genetic diagnostic yield for VM fetuses, with 48.5% of SGD identified independent of CNV-seq. For the high detection rate of WES, in addition to the substantial contribution of genetic factors to fetal VM, we also attribute it to the following factors: Parents of fetuses with multiple system malformations or severe phenotypes were more inclined to pursue advanced testing, which increases the probability of identifying SGDs; Cases in the tertiary referral center (Shanxi Children’s Hospital) are likely to be concentrated in more complex cases, and the genetic diagnosis rate is naturally higher than in the general prenatal screening cohort. Fetal VM is manifested as part of a genetic syndrome in most cases. While SGDs causing IVM is uncommon, L1CAM, AP1S2, MPDZ, and CCDC88C genes have been previously recognized as causally related to VM, and TRIM71, SMARCC1, PIK3CA, PTEN, MTOR, FOXJ1, FMN2, PTCH1, and FXYD2 have been identified as VM risk genes. Among the 16 WES-positive cases in our cohort, VM was also mainly presented as one of the manifestations of SGD. Variants in SPATA5, TRIM71, PIK3R2, PIDD1, MACF1 and PDHA1 genes were discovered in the IVM group, and variants in TUBB, CRB2, FGFR3, RTTN, AIMP1, POGZ, MYH7, CNOT3, PURA and PDHA1 genes were discovered in the NIVM group. Few previous reports have focused on the prenatal diagnosis of these genetic variant-related disorders, and our study confirms that VM can serve as a prenatal manifestation of them, and provide case material for prenatal phenotyping studies of related genes. Meanwhile, we identified 10 novel variant loci, expanding the variant spectrum of related genes. Notably, the majority of WES-positive cases occurred in NIVM (10/20). Given the substantial cost of WES in many healthcare systems, prioritizing its use in NIVM cases with specific clinical indications (e.g., syndromic features or familial recurrence) is critical for cost-effective implementation. This targeted approach ensures optimal resource allocation while maximizing diagnostic yield in the population. Additionally, in the 2 patients with PDHAD (P14 and P18), one had moderate IVM and the other had severe VM combined with callosal dysplasia. The prenatal diagnosis of PDHAD is rarely reported, but 91.7% of the patients with available prenatal histories exhibit VM as a prenatal manifestation. These findings suggest VM may represent a cardinal prenatal manifestation of PDHAD, nominating PDHA1 as a candidate VM risk gene. This association warrants further investigation. Prenatal WES has demonstrated its value in identifying potential SGDs and guiding perinatal decision-making. However, it also introduces significant challenges, particularly in data interpretation and the analysis of genetic heterogeneity. The detection of variants of VOUS is especially problematic in the prenatal setting, as fetal phenotypes are often nonspecific. This uncertainty complicates genetic counseling, may lead to ambiguous clinical management, and results in heightened parental anxiety. While this study advances our understanding of fetal VM, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the relatively small cohort (n = 73) limits statistical power to detect rare genetic associations or phenotype-genotype correlations. Second, the absence of standardized parental phenotyping and genetic analyses introduces potential confounding, as undiagnosed parental mosaicism or mild syndromic features could remain undetected. Third, the limited resolution of conventional prenatal ultrasound hinders the detection of subtle neurological abnormalities, which may only become apparent postnatally through advanced neuroimaging or developmental assessments. Finally, the follow-up duration of 3 months to 3 years for postnatal neurodevelopmental evaluation falls short of the recommended 3–5 years required to reliably assess cognitive and motor deficits. To address these limitations, future studies will recruit larger cohorts with detailed phenotypic assessment of fetuses and parents. Additionally, the follow-up period will be extended in order to more accurately characterize neurodevelopmental outcomes in VM fetuses. In this study, the genetic etiology of 39 fetuses with VM were successfully identified by CNV-seq and WES, and prenatal counselling as well as guidance on reproduction was provided to affected families. Among these cases, 19 families chose to abort, when given the opportunity to make an informed decision regarding the potential for birth defects; those who chose to continue the pregnancy were receptive to the possible prognostic outcome, and the genetic test results subsequently helped doctors and parents to manage and treat children. In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of genetic etiology in fetal VM, and shows WES can effectively improve the diagnostic rate of fetal VM. Moreover, integration of genetic testing with neuroimaging findings within a multidisciplinary framework is essential for optimizing prenatal assessment, clinical management, and counseling in VM-affected pregnancies.

Methods
Methods Samples Second and third trimester fetuses with ventricular width >10 mm, as determined via routine ultrasound or fetal cranial MRI, were selected from the Shanxi Children’s Hospital between 2020 and 2023. Fetuses with VM that could be associated with environmental factors such as infection, drug toxicity, environmental radiation, or chemical exposure were excluded. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shanxi Children’s Hospital (IRB-KYHZ-2019-006). Informed consent for testing was obtained from the parents. All parents underwent genetic counselling and the risks and benefits of sample collection were also explained. All research was performed in accordance with the guidelines and regulations of the review board and the publisher to ensure the scientific and reliability of the research methodology. Clinical data for the study cohort (n = 73) were obtained, in 7 cases elective pregnancy termination took place following prenatal diagnosis by board-certified fetal medicine specialists. After hospitalisation and preoperative informed consent form signed, fetal skin-muscle (2 cm length) were retained as samples after abortion in the obstetrics and gynaecology department. The remaining 66 cases underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis. After genetic counselling, informed consent was signed and preoperative preparations were carried out, the placental position and amniotic fluid volume were assessed via ultrasound to determine the puncture site. Under aseptic conditions, 20 ml of amniotic fluid was collected via transabdominal amniocentesis. The samples were subjected to QF-PCR, and maternal contamination was excluded by detection of genetically marked short tandem repeats (STRs). Fetuses were divided into mild VM (10–12 mm) and moderate-to-severe VM (> 12 mm) groups, and further divided into two groups (IVM and NIVM) according to whether combined with other abnormal findings. All samples were routinely screened via CNV-seq and those with negative results were subsequently screened via WES. No additional samples were needed for WES. The pregnancy outcomes were followed by telephone and genetic clinic, including whether the fetus was born and whether any postnatal abnormalities were observed. Ultrasound examination and MRI According to the guidelines of the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG)prenatal ultrasound examinations were performed by experienced sonographers using a 2.5-5 MHz transabdominal transducer and a color Doppler ultrasound system (Voluson E8, GE Healthcare, USA) to assess the presence of VM. Fetal MRIs were performed by an experienced operator using a 3.0T scanner (Ingenia, Philips Medical Systems, Netherlands), with the transverse diameter of the ventricular triangle on both sides measured in addition to examining the CNS for other abnormalities. Extraction of genomic DNA and genomic DNA library Preparation TIANamp Micro DNA Kit (DP316, TIANGENBIOTECH, China) was used to extract DNA from fetal amniotic fluid or miscarried fetal tissues according to the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA purity and concentration were evaluated using Qubit 2.0 fluorimeter (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and electrophoresis with 0.8% agarose gel. A OD260/OD280 ratio of 1.8-2.0 was deemed pure and concentrations were determined to be between 50 and 100 ng/L. DNA library preparation was performed according to Supplementary Material, using Chigene Library Prep Kitas (Beijing Chigene, China) and prepared library should meet the following requirements: concentration (Qubit 2.0: 25 uL, > 15 ng/uL); effective molecular concentration (q-PCP: 25 uL, > 10 nM); DNA fragment (Agilent 2100 detection: main peak 430 bp, range 300–600 bp). Copy-number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) Sequencing was performed using DNBSEQ-T7 sequencer (PE150, MGI Techdocs, China) and approximately 5 million sequencing reads per sample were mapped to the NCBI Human Reference Genome (hg19/GRCh37) by Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) tool. Reads were assigned to a 20 kb sequencing bin for sliding at 5 kb. CNV fragments were analyzed and annotated using Decipher, OMIM, and ClinVar, with frequencies evaluated based on Database of Genomic Variants (DGV). CNV pathogenicity was then determined based on the ACMG guidelines using the following classifications: pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), variants of uncertain significance (VOUS), LB (Likely benign), and B (Benign). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) Protein-coding exome enrichment was performed using xGen Exome Research Panel v2.0 (IDT, Iowa, USA) that consists of 429,826 individually synthesized and quality-controlled probes, which targets 39 Mb protein-coding region (19,396 genes) of the human genome and covers 39 Mb of end-to-end tiled probe space. High-throughput two-end sequencing was performed using DNBSEQ-T7 sequencer with 150 bp paired-end reads, and not less than 99% of target sequence were sequenced. The raw data (fq/vcf format data) was imported through the Chigene Genetic Diseases Analysis Cloud platform, combined with major databases (dbSNP, ExAC, ESP, OMIM, HGMD, and ClinVar, etc.) for interpretation. Protein function was performed using Provean, SIFT, PolyPhen-2, and MutationTaster. Gene loci with higher combined scores were then classified according to the 2015 ACMG guidelines as described above. Follow-up of pregnancy outcomes A multidisciplinary team of sonologists, prenatal diagnostic departments, and pediatric neurology comprehensively assessed the prognosis of fetuses with CNS abnormalities to inform parents. Pregnancy outcomes were monitored through telephone and genetic clinic. If the fetus is delivered, the child undergoes follow-up evaluations from 3 months to 3 years post-birth. A comprehensive assessment, focusing on neurodevelopmental outcomes, was conducted by an experienced pediatrician. Details of pregnancy outcomes are shown in Table , S1, S2, S3. Statistical analyses Statistical analysis was performed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 26 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, IL, USA). Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies (percentages). Categorical variables are presented as frequencies (percentages). The total sample size in this study was ≥ 40, and the expectation in all cells of fourfold table were ≥ 5. Thus, comparisons between subgroups were performed using the Pearson χ² test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

title: A Prospective Evaluation of the Diagnostic Utility for Low-Coverage Genome Sequencing in Prenatal Samples: A Comparison With Chromosomal Microarray Analysis.

abstract:
The present study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of LC‐GS in detecting clinically relevant chromosomal abnormalities in comparison with conventional CMA within a prenatal context. We conducted a prospective study involving 200 amniotic fluid samples. All specimens were analyzed via LC‐GS and traditional tests, including CMA and karyotyping. LC‐GS was performed with 3X coverage to gauge its proficiency in identifying copy number variations (CNVs), aneuploidies, regions of homozygosity (ROH), and chromosome mosaicism. Data from both methods were compared to evaluate their sensitivity, specificity, and overall clinical utility. LC‐GS at a depth of 3X identified a total of 77 positive samples, yielding a detection rate of 38.5% (77/200). This included 17 cases of aneuploidy, 36 instances of CNVs, 20 cases linked to ROH, and 8 cases of chromosomal mosaicism. LC‐GS demonstrated high concordance with CMA in aneuploidy, CNVs, ROH, and chromosomal mosaicism, achieving a diagnostic yield of 21% (42/200), with additional benefits of reduced cost. Moreover, LC‐GS outperformed CMA in terms of resolution for identifying submicroscopic CNVs. LC‐GS presents a robust alternative to CMA for prenatal diagnosis, effectively identifying aneuploidies, CNVs, chromosomal mosaicism, and ROH. It delivers comparable sensitivity and specificity in the detection of a wide spectrum of genomic abnormalities.

What's already known about this topic? ◦ CMA is a gold standard for the analysis of CNVs in prenatal diagnostics. ◦ The effectiveness and clinical utility of NGS at lower depths (3–5x) for prenatal diagnosis have not been thoroughly investigated. What does this study add? ◦ Our investigation evaluated the feasibility of employing LC‐GS (3x) as a substitute for CMA in prenatal laboratory settings. ◦ Our study suggests that LC‐GS (3x) represents a viable alternative to CMA in the context of prenatal diagnostics.

A Prospective Evaluation of the Diagnostic Utility for Low‐Coverage Genome Sequencing in Prenatal Samples: A Comparison With Chromosomal Microarray Analysis

Introduction
Introduction Chromosomal abnormalities constitute a significant cause of pregnancy loss and congenital defects. It is estimated that over 50% of first‐trimester miscarriages are attributable to genetic defects []. Among newborns, approximately 0.6% exhibit aberrant chromosomal alterations, often leading to malformations, deformities, or developmental disorders [, ]. Consequently, the International Society for Prenatal Diagnosis, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics advocate offering prenatal genetic diagnosis to all pregnant women. Invasive prenatal diagnosis is recommended following positive noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) results, abnormal ultrasound findings, or high‐risk pregnancies. Standard methods for prenatal diagnosis include karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and chromosome microarray analysis (CMA). These techniques can be utilized concurrently or sequentially to facilitate comprehensive genetic analysis and facilitate family recurrence risk assessments. Among these methods, CMA is endorsed as the first‐line test for high‐risk pregnancies presenting with ultrasound abnormalities. However, CMA is constrained by its reliance on available data, incorporating probes targeting genes identified during its development phase. This renders the technology significantly dependent on the gene content accessible at that time and limits its throughput []. Over the past decade, low‐coverage/pass genome sequencing (LC‐GS/LP‐GS) has emerged as a promising approach for chromosome analysis of prenatal or postnatal samples. In 2016, Dong et al. validated the clinical utility of 0.25X LC‐GS for detecting pathogenic copy number variations (pCNVs) and chromosome mosaicism in a cohort comprising 198 miscarriages, 37 stillbirths, 149 prenatal samples and 186 postnatal samples []. Wang et al. further supported the application of 0.25X LC‐GS for pCNV detection by recruiting a total of 1023 women who underwent prenatal diagnosis []. Recently, the functional evaluation of LC‐GS has gradually shifted towards the detection of mosaic CNVs, low‐level chromosome mosaicism and regions of homozygosity (ROH), with the specific depth required for detection currently under investigation [, , ]. Ma et al. conducted a combined analysis of CMA and LC‐GS using 67 prenatal retrospective mosaic samples and reported that the mosaic levels defined by LC‐GS ranged from 6% to 92%, whereas those identified by CMA ranged from 20% to 72% []. Mighton et al. demonstrated high consistency between 5X LC‐GS and CMA in detecting CNVs and ROH in 49 retrospective prenatal samples []. However, prospective studies that comprehensively investigate the role of LC‐GS in detecting pCNVs, chromosome mosaicism and ROH are rare. Further prospective studies are needed to refine its clinical utility to replace CMA for prenatal diagnosis. Despite these advancements, prospective studies comprehensively investigating the role of LC‐GS in detecting pCNVs, chromosome mosaicism, and ROH remain scarce. In this study, we independently and simultaneously conducted LC‐GS (3X) and CMA analyses on 200 amniotic fluid samples to comprehensively assess the performance and reliability of LC‐GS in detecting various genetic variants. Our findings revealed that LC‐GS identified all positive cases detected by CMA and offered additional insights into submicroscopic CNVs, highlighting its potential as a valuable tool for prenatal diagnosis.

Methods
Methods Cohort Recruitment A total of 200 amniotic fluid samples were included in this prospective study from the Prenatal Diagnosis Center of Sichuan Provincial Women's and Children's Hospital between 2023 and 2024. Pregnant females were eligible if they met the following inclusion criteria: (1) High‐risk findings from NIPT, including suspected fetal chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 21,18 and 13, as well as other chromosomes). (2) Polyhydramnios, defined as amniotic fluid index (AFI) ≥ 25 cm or amniotic fluid volume (AFV) ≥ 8 cm. (3) Fetal growth restriction (FGR) with abdominal circumference (AC) < 10th percentile and estimated fetal weight (EFW) < 10th percentile for gestational age. (4) Fetal lateral ventricle dilatation, characterized by atrial width ≥ 10 mm measured in the standard transventricular axial plane. (5) Advanced maternal age (≥ 35 years). (6) Maternal request. Participants who had contraindications to prenatal diagnosis or who declined further testing after being adequately informed were excluded. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Sichuan Provincial Women's and Children's Hospital. Written consent was obtained from each participant. Karyotype Analysis Amniotic fluid (20 mL) was obtained from pregnant women during the gestational period of 18–30 weeks. The collected samples were subjected to cell culture following established cytogenetic procedures []. Subsequently, the cultured amniocytes were stained using the Giemsa banding technique to facilitate detailed chromosomal analysis, which was then followed by comprehensive karyotyping. Nomenclature was provided according to the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN, 2020). Chromosomal Microarray Analysis DNA samples were amplified, labeled, and hybridized via the Affymetrix Cytoscan 750k array platform (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Chromosome Analysis Suite v3.1 was used to analyze the obtained CEL files (GRCh37). When calling CNVs by CMA, the size cutoffs used are > 100Kb or a continuous sequence of 25 probes indicating a deletion, or a continuous sequence of 50 probes indicating a duplication. Public databases such as DGV (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/dbvar/), OMIM (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/omim), DECIPHER (http://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/), ISCA (https://www.iscaconsortium.org/), UCSC (http://genome.ucsc.edu), and PubMed (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/) were used for the interpretation of the results and to analyze genotype‒phenotype correlations alongside the local database. The CNVs were classified as benign (B), likely benign (LB), variants of uncertain significance (VUS), likely pathogenic (LP), or pathogenic (P) according to the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines. ROH/UPD was evaluated according to the ACMG statement. Low‐Coverage Genome Sequencing The DNA sample (100 ng) was fragmented via enzymatic digestion, and a PCR‐free library was subsequently constructed (end flattening and adapter ligation), purified, and quantitatively inspected with a specialized library preparation kit. The hybrid DNA library was subjected to pair‐ended sequencing on a NovaSeq 6000 instrument (Illumina, USA) with a 150 bp read length (PE150) at Be Creative Lab Co. Ltd. The clean reads of each sample were more than 60 million after quality control. All the samples were subjected to STR detection to exclude fetal triploidy and maternal cell contamination (MCC) to avoid sample errors. After quality control, the reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh37/hg19) via BWA. SAM tools were utilized for formatting and deduplication. Aneuploidy and CNVs > 50 Kb were analyzed with software constructed in‐house. CNVs were classified as pathogenic CNVs (P‐CNVs), possibly pathogenic CNVs (LP‐CNVs), CNVs of VUS, benign CNVs (B‐CNVs), or possibly benign CNVs (LB‐CNVs) by referring to ACMG guidelines. Scientific reports and the following public databases are also included as references: OMIM (https://omim.org), DGV (http://dgv.tcag.ca/dgv/app/home), DECIPHER (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/), UCSC (http://genome.ucsc.edu), ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), and PubMed (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/). Genomic polymorphism fragments are typically not reported. ROH Analysis A sliding window approach with a dynamic size, containing approximately 500 single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) per window, is employed to scan each chromosome. The proportion of completely homozygous SNPs within each window was calculated. If this proportion exceeds a predefined threshold, the window is classified as part of a homozygous region (ROH). To minimize the influence of genotype errors or noise, each sliding window allows for a small fraction of heterozygous SNPs, with their proportion not exceeding 5%. Ultimately, a genomic segment is designated as an ROH if the number of consecutive windows meeting the criteria exceeds a predetermined threshold of 10 windows or if the density of homozygous SNPs within these windows surpasses the expected frequency. Chromosome Mosaicism Analysis The log2 of the average CNV along each chromosome for each bin was plotted, where log2[1] indicates two copies (normal), log2[1.5] indicates three copies (duplication), and log2[0.5] indicates one copy (deletion). Trisomic mosaicism was defined as an average chromosome copy number between log2[2.05/2] (5%) and log2[2.8/2] (80%). Monosomic mosaicism was defined as an average chromosome copy number between log2[1.2/2] (80%) and log2[1.95/2] (5%). Data Analysis and Statistical Significance Statistical comparisons between the two groups were evaluated by Fisher's exact test. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results Cohort Characteristics The median maternal age was 29 years (range: 20–42 years), and the median gestational age (GA) was 24 weeks (range: 18–34 weeks); high‐risk results from NIPT (n = 80), polyhydramnios (n = 37), fetal growth restriction (n = 25), lateral ventricle dilatation (n = 13), advanced maternal age (n = 9) and maternal request (n = 36) (Table ). LC‐GS Outperforms CMA in CNV Detection Both LC‐GS (3‐fold) and CMA were successfully performed on all 200 amniotic fluid samples. The average number of clean reads for LC‐GS was 110 million (median: 104 million) (Figure ), with 97% of the bases achieving a high‐quality score of Q30 (Figure ). LC‐GS identified 77 positive cases, corroborated by CMA findings (Table ). Specifically, 53 samples (26.5%) presented with abnormal copy number variations (CNVs), 14 presented with aneuploidy, and 3 presented with aneuploidy alongside ROH (Figure ). Aneuploidies manifested mainly as T21 (41.2%, 7/17) and 47, XXY (29.4%, 5/17) (Figure ). In addition to aneuploidy, LC‐GS detected CNVs in 36 samples, comprising 16 deletions and 25 duplications. According to ACMG guidelines, 20 CNVs were classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP), with 13 CNVs (13/20, 65.0%) being submicroscopic CNVs (≤ 5 Mb) ranging from 93.985 Kb to 3 Mb, highlighting the sensitivity of LC‐GS for detecting submicroscopic pathogenic CNVs above 50 kb (Table ). Number of clean reads and percentage of high‐quality (Q30) bases in all samples. (A) Distribution of the number of clean reads, (B) distribution of the percentage of Q30 in 200 amniotic fluid samples. Overall variations detected by LC‐GS. (A) The detection rate and frequency distribution of chromosomal abnormalities by LC‐GS analysis for 200 samples. LC‐GS detected 17 aneuploidies, 8 mosaics, and 18 P/LP CNVs, (B) spectrum of 17 aneuploidies, (C) examples of representative pathogenic/likely pathogenic CNVs detected by LC‐GS and CMA, (D) LC‐GS revealed a 140.3 Kb duplication at 7p14.1. Figure illustrates the typical pathogenic CNVs detected consistently by LC‐GS and CMA. Fetal27, fetal31, and fetal40 showed variations in the 1q21.1, 15q11, and 22q11.21 regions, respectively, as indicated by NIPT (Table ). Notably, fetal27 exhibited a 500 kb duplication in the Xq28 region, encompassing the Xq28 recurrent region (int22h1/int22h2‐flanked), which includes the RAB39B gene, associated with Xq28 duplication syndrome (Figure , top panel). In another case, fetal48, derived from a 24‐year‐old mother, presented with fetal growth restriction (FGR) and oligohydramnios (Amniotic Fluid Index, AFI 6.2 cm) at 32+6 GA. LC‐GS revealed a 756.4 Kb deletion in the 16p11.2 segment of chromosome 16 involving 33 RefSeq protein‐coding genes, including PRRT2 and TBX6. This deletion spans the 16p11.2 recurrent region (proximal, BP4‐BP5) and is linked to 16p11.2 microdeletion syndrome, which is characterized by developmental delay. Four additional CNVs were identified by LC‐GS compared with CMA. However, when the current ACMG guidelines for the interpretation and classification of CNVs were applied, these variants were categorized as VUSs (Table ). Fetal 43 had a double superior vena cava and exhibited focal echogenicity in both ventricles. LC‐GS revealed a 140.3 Kb duplication at 7p14.1 (Figure ) encompassing exons 6–14 of the CDK13 gene (NM_003718) in this fetus. In contrast, the microarray lacked probes for this region. Heterozygous CDK13 mutations are linked to an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by congenital heart defects, dysmorphic facial features, and intellectual disability (OMIM: 603309). However, clinical follow‐up indicated that the infant was born at term, healthy, and without congenital heart disease. Thus, this variant of unknown significance (VUS) lacks clinical relevance. LC‐GS Has the Same Mosaicism Detection Performance as CMA Chromosomal mosaicism is a biological phenomenon in which two or more genetically distinct cell populations are present within a single embryo. It occurs as a result of mitotic errors during postfertilization cell division. The high‐throughput capabilities of next generation sequencing (NGS) technology allow for the detection of low‐level mosaicism. Among the 77 positive samples in this study, LC‐GS identified all 8 cases with chromosome mosaicism detected by CMA, comprising 4 deletions and 4 duplications. Five cases of X chromosome mosaicism and one case each for chromosomes 21, 15, and 13 were identified. The percentage of chromosome mosaicism ranged from 7% to 63% (Figure ; Figures ). The size and mosaic percentage of mosaicism detected by both LC‐GS and CMA were nearly identical (Table ). Notably, fetal21 had a low proportion of mosaicism, with a mosaic proportion of 7%, which was consistent with the karyotype results (Figure ). The fetus was from a 23‐year‐old pregnant woman who underwent amniocentesis because the NIPT result was high risk at 22+1 GA. Low‐level mosaicism of chromosome 13 characterized by LC‐GS and CMA. (A) LC‐GS identified a low‐level (7%) duplication on chromosme 13 in fetal21. In the genomic profile, green lines denote regions with a chromosome copy number of two, whereas red lines signify areas with low‐level amplifications. The image on the right provides an enlarged view of the region delineated by the dotted box, (B) CMA revealed the same mosaic pattern in fetal 21. The image on the right offers a magnified perspective of the area outlined by the dashed border. Red lines indicate regions characterized by subtle duplication, (C) karyotyping confirmed the mosaic chromosomal gain of chromosme 13. LC‐GS Reliably Detects ROH (> 5 Mb) ROH is a genomic alteration characterized by the presence of a long contiguous region of homozygous alleles on a chromosome. ROH detection is increasingly important for the diagnosis of specific imprinting disorders and rare Mendelian disorders caused by homozygosity. ROH can be a result of uniparental disomy (UPD). UPD means that an individual's homologous chromosomes or partial segments of chromosomes are inherited from only one of the parents. Consistent with the CMA, the LC‐GS detected ROH in 20 cases (Table ). In single‐chromosome ROH, the most commonly involved chromosome is chromosome X (n = 3) (Table ). Among them, fetal11 had ROH involving the entire X chromosome, thus increasing the risk of homozygous X‐linked recessive single‐gene diseases. The fetus was diagnosed with Klinefelter syndrome, and the study was terminated. Among the cases involving ROH on chromosome 6, fetal70's mother is 36 years old. Her previous fetus died a few hours after birth with abnormal development of external genitalia (short size), short upper limbs, and respiratory distress. LC‐GS revealed that fetal70 had a 12.9 Mb ROH at 6q13q14.3 (Figure ), which included 12 genes, including SLC17A5, COL12A1, MYO6 and other autosomal recessive inheritance (AR) disease‐related genes. Moreover, in the same sample, ROH segments exist in both 6p22.2p21.32 and 6q21q22.31 with sizes of 5.6 and 8.4 Mb, respectively. In fetal66, there was a region of ROH on chromosome 15 (Figure ). Methylation‐specific multiplex ligation‐dependent probe amplification (MS‐MLPA) was performed on the fetal sample and revealed no abnormal methylation (data not shown). The infant was born at 38 weeks of age, weighed 3725 g, and was healthy. In other single chromosomal cases, the ROH ranged from 6.4 to 18.17 Mb. Representative cases with ROH detected by LC‐GS. (A) Fetal70 is from a 36‐year‐old pregnant woman who underwent amniocentesis because her previous baby died at birth. Three segmental ROHs were observed in the chromosome 6, (B) A 11.9 Mb ROH was observed in fetal66 using LC‐GS, (C) A 16.3 Mb ROH in the 15q12q15.2 region was detected in fetal68. Among the multichromosomal ROHs, LC‐GS identified an additional 6.9 Mb segmental ROH on chromosome 9 in fetal61 (Table ). In the case of fetal68, whose parents were consanguineous couple, a 16.3 Mb ROH in the 15q12q15.2 segment of chromosome 15 was identified (Figure ), containing NSMCE3 (OMIM: 608243), FAN1 (OMIM: 613534), RYR3 (OMIM: 180903) and 20 other genes related to AR diseases. LC‐GS revealed an additional 4.5 Mb ROH on chromosome 15, whereas CMA revealed additional 6 ROHs (range: 3.1–4.67 Mb) on chromosomes 1, 6 and 7 (Table ). Further trio‐based whole‐exome sequencing also revealed multiple ROH segments, indicating third‐degree kinship, but no pathogenic gene mutations were identified (data not shown). The three other cases with multiple chromosomal ROHs had a history of adverse pregnancy and childbirth. Overall, LC‐GS was 100% consistent with CMA analysis for reporting cases with clinically significant ROH (> 5 Mb) (Figure ). The spectrum of ROH identified by CMA and LC‐GS in 20 samples. ROH regions identified by CMA were indicated by green bars in the inner circle and ROH regions identified by LC‐GS were indicated by blue bars in the outer circle across the genome. The reported size cutoff was set as 5‐Mb. Clinically Identifiable Syndromes Involved in This Study In this study, LC‐GS and CMA simultaneously detected 17 aneuploidies (8.5%), 18 (9%) cases with P/LP CNVs, and 7 (3.5%) cases with P/LP chromosome mosaicism, resulting in a diagnostic yield of 21% (42/200). Among the 6 main clinical indication groups, the subgroup with NIPT high‐risk had the highest diagnostic rate (30/80, 37.5%), followed by the subgroup with FGR (4/25, 16%) (Figure ). Figure shows the distribution of different kinds of variations in each subgroup. In addition to aneuploidy, 22q11.21 duplication syndrome was the most common clinically significant CNV in our study (n = 5, 2.5%, OMIM#608363). The second most common microdeletion syndrome was 15q11.2 microdeletion syndrome (n = 3, 1.5%, OMIM#615656). Other clinically significant CNVs include Leri–Weill Dyschondrosteosis SHOX deletion (n = 2, OMIM#127300), Int22h1/Int22h2‐mediated Xq28 duplication syndrome (n = 2), 15q11q13 duplication syndrome (n = 2, OMIM#608636), etc. (Figure ). Analysis of chromosome variations according to different indications. (A) Diagnostic rate in pregnancies with different indications. *, p < 0.05, (B) distribution of identified variants in each subgroup, (C) frequency distribution of the most common clinically recognizable syndromes encountered in this study.

Discussion
Discussion We conducted a prospective back‐to‐back study to evaluate the accuracy and additional yield of LC‐GS with the CMA as a reference. Our study revealed that sequencing‐based methods provide CNV detection resolution similar to that of chromosome microarray analysis (CMA). Among the 200 enrolled samples, LC‐GS at a depth of 3X detected a total of 77 positive samples with a detection rate of 38.5% (77/200), including 17 aneuploidies, 36 cases with CNVs, 20 cases with ROH and 8 cases with chromosome mosaicism. Eighteen cases of P/LP CNVs, with fragment sizes ranging from 93.985 Kb to 64.5 Mb, involved 22q11.2 duplication syndrome, Xq28 duplication syndrome, 15q11q13 microduplication syndrome, 16p11.2 microdeletion syndrome, etc. The diagnostic rates of LC‐GS and CMA were both 21% (42/200), which are higher than those reported by Qian (8.3%, 31/375) []. Furthermore, 4 additional CNVs were detected by LC‐GS. Compared with the probe design of the chip, LC‐GS provides better CNV detection (> 50 Kb) sensitivity and specificity because of the unbiased distributed/aligned reads. Chromosomal aneuploidy is a common chromosomal abnormality that accounts for approximately 50% of spontaneous abortions. Complete aneuploidy is lethal, except for trisomy 13, 18, and 21, which can survive to term. However, mosaic aneuploidy is present in 0.5% of live births and 0.1%–0.3% of fetal amniotic fluid [, , , ]. Mosaic aneuploidy is caused by two main mechanisms: postzygotic chromosome segregation errors and post zygotic trisomy/monosomy rescue of preexisting aneuploidy of meiotic origin. The identification of genetic mosaicism is important for diagnosis, assessment of recurrence risk, and accurate genetic counseling []. Next‐generation sequencing technology has been able to identify mosaicism at a level lower than that detectable by chromosome microarray analysis. Ma et al. used 67 prenatal retrospective mosaic samples to perform a combined analysis of CMA and LC‐GS and reported that the mosaic levels defined by LC‐GS ranged from 6% to 92% []. In this study, 8 cases of mosaic aneuploidy (4%) were detected in 200 fetuses. Chromosome mosaicism involves chr13,15,21, X, and Y chromosomes, with mosaic rates ranging from 7% to 63%. The results showed that ROH analysis via LC‐GS was highly consistent with that via CMA. LC‐GS also exhibited increased sensitivity in detecting low‐level mosaicism. There are three situations in which ROH occurs in prenatal samples: (a) UPD indication: ROH of ≥ 5 Mb (terminal chromosome segment) or ≥ 10 Mb (interstitial chromosome segment) is detected on only one of the imprinting disease chromosomes (6, 7, 11, 14, 15, 20). (b) Pedigree identity: ROH > 10 Mb appears on multiple chromosomes, indicating a close relationship between the parents (the closer the relationship is, the more ROH regions); (c) Common ancestral markers in the population. ROH < 5 Mb on one or several chromosomes. Combining the chromosomes involved in ROH and the corresponding segment sizes, this study identified a total of 20 cases of ROH with a size distribution from 5.2 to 155 Mb on the basis of the reporting threshold of 5 Mb recommended by the ACMG []. At this threshold, the LC‐GS was highly consistent with the CMA. Chaubey et al. estimated that an approximately 5‐fold depth of LC‐GS is required to reliably and accurately detect the ROH region. By analyzing ROH in 17 prenatal/postnatal samples that were previously confirmed by the CMA, Dong et al. showed that ROH analysis via 4X LC‐GS was highly consistent with that via CMA []. Using prospective prenatal samples, our study further revealed that the ROH detection sensitivity of 3X LC‐GS is comparable to that of CMA. A recent study has shown that algorithms specifically developed for ROH can detect ROH with ultralow depth (0.1X) []. These findings suggest that LC‐GS has great potential in ROH detection. In the current investigation, there was also a case with balanced structural rearrangement, whose karyotype was 46,XY,inv(9)(p12q13), involving an inversion of chromosome 9 with a breakpoint located in a highly repetitive sequence. Neither CMA nor LC‐GS detected it. By reanalyzing the structural variation via the Lumpy algorithm for inversions and translocations, no breakpoint information was detected (data not shown). This finding indicates that 3X LC‐GS still has limitations in detecting such balanced structural rearrangements involving highly repetitive sequences. This limitation is related to the principle of LC‐GS. LC‐GS has inherent limitations due to the use of large‐scale random sequencing, short reads, difficulty in aligning reads to the genome, comparisons between samples within a batch, and inconsistent bioinformatics algorithm models []. The accuracy of confirming breakpoints is limited, and detecting complex structural rearrangements such as reciprocal translocations and inversions is difficult. Because inversions involve the reversal of genomic fragments, the sequence direction of the region changes. However, traditional short‐read sequencing may have problems with sequence alignment in the inversion region, especially at the boundary of the inversion region. Therefore, inversions may not be easily identified using conventional short‐read sequencing methods. Our study has several limitations. First, this was a single‐center study, and incomplete follow‐up information may have led to an underestimation of the number of late‐onset adverse phenotypes. Second, in most cases, parental samples could not be used to determine the source of ROH, and no placental studies were performed; therefore, UPD could not be determined. In addition, the incidence of ROH in our cohort may be greater than that in the general population because we recruited women who underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis for various indications, including abnormal NIPT and advanced maternal age, who are generally at greater risk of fetal chromosomal abnormalities than the general population is, to evaluate the performance of LC‐GS for ROH. Finally, we utilized the Affymetrix Cytoscan 750k array platform in our research. The coverage range of Affymetrix Cytoscan 750k probes is limited, thus its detection capability is restricted. Short‐read NGS is changing prenatal genetic testing at an unprecedented rate []. Mighton et al. evaluated the possibility of LC‐GS replacing CMA in a prenatal setting and reported that 5X LC‐GS had good cost‐effectiveness []. Our study extends this evidence by demonstrating the feasibility of 3X LC‐GS for multiple tests, further supporting the transition from array‐based methods to sequencing‐based approaches. The declining cost of sequencing technology has been a driving force behind its widespread adoption. While CMA currently costs approximately $600 per test, Illumina's introduction of the NovaSeq TM 6000 v1.5 kit in 2020 reduced the cost of whole‐genome sequencing (WGS) at ∼30X coverage to the same price point [, ]. In 2022, the launch of the NovaSeq X Series further lowered the cost of ∼30X WGS to around $200, making LC‐GS an increasingly cost‐effective option. This reduction in cost significantly lowers the application threshold for LC‐GS, enhancing its accessibility and facilitating broader implementation in prenatal settings. LC‐GS offers several advantages over CMA, including lower costs, higher resolution, and unbiased genomic coverage. These features position GS‐based NGS as a promising alternative for detecting a wide range of genetic abnormalities, including aneuploidies, chromosomal mosaicism, and ROH. However, our study also identified four additional CNVs classified as VUS, which introduce interpretive challenges in clinical decision‐making and may complicate patient management and genetic counseling. It is important to note that while LC‐GS demonstrates significant potential, it currently has limitations. Specifically, our analysis pipeline cannot detect inversions or balanced translocations, and karyotyping remains the gold standard for these structural variants. Future work will focus on optimizing software tools to enhance the detection of such complex rearrangements. Additionally, the development of targeted algorithms for ROH detection will improve the sensitivity and expand the utility of LC‐GS in prenatal diagnostics.

Conclusion
Conclusion LC‐GS presents a robust alternative to CMA for prenatal diagnosis, effectively identifying aneuploidies, CNVs, chromosomal mosaicism, and ROH. It delivers comparable sensitivity and specificity in the detection of a wide spectrum of genomic abnormalities. Its advantages, including increased genome coverage and reduced costs, enhance its feasibility and accessibility in clinical practice.

title: The Ultrasound and Genetic Characteristics of Fetuses With Laterality Defects-A Prenatal Cohort in Asian Population.
label_reason: Fetal laterality defects on echo with CMA and trio ES.
abstract:
To investigate the distribution of laterality defects in fetuses, including situs inversus totalis (SIT) and situs ambiguous (SA), and to explore the potential genetic etiology of these laterality defects. Detailed fetal echocardiography and extracardiac structural evaluations were performed. Genetic testing, including chromosomal microarray analysis, and trio exome sequencing was conducted to identify potential genetic variants. The incidence of heart malformation was significantly higher in SA fetuses than in SIT group (30/31 vs. 2/36, p  < 0.001). The incidence of univentricular heart with single atrium was significantly higher in right isomerism compared with left isomerism (12/19 vs. 3/12, p  = 0.029), while the incidence of double outlet right ventricle was significantly higher in left isomerism (5/12 vs. 1/19, p  = 0.022). Genetic testing identified variation within candidate genes of cardiac development. Except for CFAP300 c.604delG and KMT2D c.16351T>C, which were rated as “likely pathogenic”, all other variants were categorized as variants of uncertain significance, with some fetuses having compound heterozygous variations. Fetuses with SA have a significantly higher likelihood of concurrent heart malformations compared with those with SIT. Genetic testing identified potential genetic variants that may play crucial roles in the mechanisms underlying normal fetal visceral positioning. Further studies are needed to explore the clinical significance of these genetic variants and to improve our understanding of the etiology and management of fetal laterality defects.

What is already known about this topic? ◦ Laterality defect includes situs inversus totalis (SIT) and situs ambiguous (SA). Fetuses with SA often have complex cardiac malformations and a poor prognosis. The etiology of laterality defects may involve genetic or environmental factors. What does this study add? ◦ Our results suggest that genes associated with cardiac malformations may harbor unrecognized roles in the development of laterality defects, such as CHD4. Our results also indicate CFAP300 and PKD1L1 might play complementary roles in the pathogenicity of laterality defects.

Fetuses with SA often have complex cardiac malformations and a poor prognosis. The etiology of laterality defects may involve genetic or environmental factors. What does this study add? Our results suggest that genes associated with cardiac malformations may harbor unrecognized roles in the development of laterality defects, such as CHD4. Our results also indicate CFAP300 and PKD1L1 might play complementary roles in the pathogenicity of laterality defects.
