The Ultrasound and Genetic Characteristics of Fetuses With Laterality Defects—A Prenatal Cohort in Asian Population

Introduction
Introduction The human body demonstrates left–right symmetry in external morphology. However, intriguingly, its internal architecture reveals a striking asymmetry, with nearly all visceral organs in the thorax and abdomen displaying a left‐right asymmetrical arrangement. The definition and classification of laterality defects in the human body are indeed intricate. Situs solitus represents the normal condition, where all organs in the thorax and abdomen are positioned as expected. Specifically, the majority of the liver, the superior and inferior vena cava, the right auricle, and the trilobar lung are situated on the right side of the body, whereas the stomach, spleen, left atrium and left atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, and bilobar lung are located on the left side. In contrast, situs inversus totalis (SIT) describes a condition where the normal organ positions are completely reversed, typically presenting as a mirror‐image transposition. Between the normal situs solitus and the completely reversed SIT, there exists a spectrum of situs ambiguous (SA), also termed heterotaxy, which is characterized by two forms: left isomerism (LI) and right isomerism (RI). This SA condition is frequently associated with multiple malformations in one or more organs, adding further complexity to the understanding and classification of laterality defects in the human body. The prevalence of laterality defects is very rare, with the incidence of SIT reported to be 1 in 10,000 livebirths []. The incidence of SA is estimated to be even lower than that of SIT (as reported to be 0.8 in 10,000 livebirths []). The etiology of laterality defects is complex, with both environmental and genetic factors potentially playing roles in the pathogenesis of laterality defects. It has been reported that viral infections, such as novel coronavirus (SARS‐CoV‐2), may be associated with the occurrence of laterality defects []. Genetic studies have shown that over 80 genes are involved in the development of normal asymmetric organs, and variants in a subset of these genes (e.g., Nodal, Pitx2, NKX2.5, CRELD1, LEFTY2 and ZIC3) have been identified in patients with laterality defects []. Currently, the majority of studies on laterality defects primarily focus on postnatal children or adults. Studies on the pathogenic genes associated with laterality defects have predominantly been conducted in patients with postnatal ciliary dyskinesia syndrome (PCD). Research on the prenatal ultrasound phenotypic characteristics and potential pathogenic genes of laterality defects in fetuses remains scarce. Our aim was to investigate the ultrasonographic characteristics and genetic etiology of lateral defect (including SIT and SA) in fetus in order to better evaluate the fetal prognosis and guide pregnancy management.

Methods
Methods Participants This was a retrospective study. Fetuses who were diagnosed with laterality defects (including situs inversus totalis and situs ambiguous) were recruited from Jan 2019 to Aug 2023 in the International Peace Maternity & Child Health Hospital (IPMCH). All fetuses underwent detailed fetal anomaly scan and fetal echocardiography performed by experienced ultrasound clinicians in the Department of Prenatal Diagnostic Center of IPMCH. An invasive procedure has been suggested to all pregnant women who have fetuses with laterality defects. If accepted, after signing informed consent, amniocentesis and the consequent genetic testing were conducted to detect the underlying pathogenicity. If parents chose to terminate the pregnancy, fetal autopsy was suggested. Data on prenatal ultrasound, genetic testing and fetal autopsy were obtained by reviewing the electronic medical records. For those who decided to continue the pregnancy, infants' information was obtained from telephone follow up from the parents. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of International Peace Maternity & Child Health Hospital with the number of (GKLW) 2019‐73. Prenatal Ultrasound Screening for fetal structural anomaly was conducted using color Doppler ultrasound instruments such as GE‐E10 and PHILIPS‐IPC7, with probe frequencies ranging from 2 to 9 MHz and 1–5 MHz, respectively. The operational procedure for fetal echocardiography was conducted according to the fetal cardiac screening guidelines published by the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) in 2023 []. The multi‐plane continuous scanning was performed, where initially determining the fetal orientation and confirming the position of fetal internal organs was crucial. In cases of abdominal visceral inversion, the inferior vena cava was located anterior to the left side of the spine, the abdominal aorta was anterior to the right side of the spine, the gastric bubble was on the right, the majority of the liver and gallbladder were on the left side of the abdominal cavity, and the spleen was on the right. In assessing the inversion of fetal thoracic organs, prenatal ultrasound was unable to distinguish the number of lung lobes. Therefore, the primary indicators of thoracic organ inversion were the position of the heart and its atria. Acquisition of the four‐chamber view of the heart revealed that in cases of complete visceral inversion (SIT), the heart was situated on the right side of the chest with the cardiac apex pointing rightwards. When ultrasound indicated partial visceral heterotaxy (SA), classification was based on the morphology of the auricles, distinguishing between a left isomerism group (where both atria were left‐sided) and a right isomerism group (where both atria were right‐sided). Fetal anomaly scan and fetal echocardiography were conducted by two senior sonographers at the Prenatal Diagnostic Center of International Peace Maternity & Child Health Hospital. Genetic Testing If parents accepted the invasive procedure, amniocentesis was performed, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and trio‐whole exome sequencing (trio‐WES) were both offered. Chromosomal microarray was performed according to the procedure guidelines: DNA was extracted from amniotic fluid cells using the established Qiagen DNA extraction Kit; then Affymetrix CytoScan 750K Microarray Chips (ThermoFisher Scientific, United States) were used for array CGH screening; chips were scanned with GeneChip Scanner; and finally, we transferred scanned images to data using Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS, Applied Biosystems, ThermoFisher Scientific, United States); All data were aligned to the Human Genome release 38 (hg38). Trio Exome Sequencing Ten milliliters of amniotic fluid was used for Trio Exome Sequencing. DNA samples obtained from the index family were sequenced using targeted next generation sequencing. The target region encompasses the exonic and adjacent flanking sequences (± 20bp) of over 20,000 genes. Library construction and paired‐end sequencing (2 × 100 bp) were performed at Beijing Genomics Institute (BGI) according to the manufacturer's protocols. Flited clean data were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh37/hg19 by BurrowsWheeler Aligner (BWA; v.0.7.12). GATK (version 3.5) and ANNOVAR9 were used for variant calling and annotation, respectively. All known OMIM morbid genes were analyzed, and only variants relevant to laterality defects or CHD were reported. The interpretation of variants was based on the ACMG/AMP guidelines10.

Results
Results Prenatal Ultrasound of Laterality Defects Among a total of 67 fetal cases of visceral inversus, 36 fetuses exhibited situs inversus totalis (SIT), while 31 fetuses presented with situs ambiguous (SA) (seen in Figures and ). Figure demonstrates the ultrasound findings of a fetus with SIT. Figure shows the fetal stomach bubble located on the right side, and Figure shows the heart positioned in the right thoracic cavity. Figure shows the ultrasound findings of a fetus with SA. Figure indicates a ventricular septal defect, and Figure reveals a double outlet right ventricle. Based on the position of the auricles, the cases of SA were further subclassified into left isomerism (LI: 12 cases) and right isomerism (RI: 19 cases). Ultrasound image of situs inversus totalis (SIT). (A) The gastric bubble was located on the right side of the abdominal cavity, and the heart was located on the right side of the thoracic cavity. ST: stomach. L: left. R: right. LST: Left Sacral Transverse. (B) Ultrasound imaging of mirror‐image dextrocardia. RA: right atrium. RV: right ventricle. LA: left atrium. LV: left ventricle. Ultrasound image of the echocardiography of situs ambiguous (SA). (A) Ventricle septal defect (VSD). RV: right ventricle, LV: left ventricle. (B) Double outlet right ventricle (DORV). AO: aorta, PA: pulmonary artery, RV: right ventricle. The majority of these SA fetuses (30/31) were accompanied by congenital cardiovascular malformations. These anomalies included, but were not limited to, interruption of the inferior vena cava (IVC), transposition of great vessels (TGA), anomalous pulmonary venous return (APVR), persistent truncus arteriosus (PTA), pulmonary atresia (PA), aortic atresia (AA) univentricular heart with single atrium (UVH), double outlet right ventricle (DORV), atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS), and right ventricular hypoplasia (HRH). To explore the distribution of different cardiac phenotypes across the LI and RI groups, we conducted a meticulous analysis based on the frequency of cardiac phenotypes within these groups. The results indicated that cases of UVH occurred in both LI and RI groups, but the incidence was significantly higher in the right RI group compared to the LI group (3/12, p = 0.029). Additionally, the incidence of DORV was significantly higher in the LI group than in the RI group (5/19, p = 0.022). For other types of cardiovascular malformations, no statistically significant differences in incidence were observed between the LI and RI groups (Table ). In the present study, our results revealed that only two of the 36 SIT fetuses exhibited cardiovascular structural malformations, whereas a striking number of 30 out of the 31 SA fetuses presented with cardiovascular malformations. The difference in CHD incidence between the two groups was statistically significant (p < 0.001, Table ). This finding unequivocally suggests that fetuses with SA have a significantly higher likelihood of concurrent heart malformations compared with those with complete visceral malposition (SIT) (Table ). Furthermore, the study identified six fetuses with extracardiac structural malformations. Among them, the SA group included one fetus with spina bifida, while the SIT group encompassed 5 fetuses with extracardiac structural abnormalities, specifically one case of cleft lip, one case of horseshoe kidney, one case of renal dysplasia, and two cases of intestinal obstruction. However, in terms of the incidence of extracardiac malformations, no statistically significant difference was observed between the SA and SIT groups (p = 0.203, Table ). Regarding fetal outcomes, among the 31 SA fetuses, 29 were terminated, with only two pregnancies continuing to term. Conversely, among the 36 SIT fetuses, 27 were successfully delivered at full term with good prognosis, while nine were selectively terminated. In terms of the termination rate, the SA group was significantly higher than the SIT group (p < 0.001, Table ). Genetic Testing of Cases With Laterality Defects In exploring the genetic etiology of 67 fetal cases with laterality defects, genetic testing was suggested for all patients. Twenty‐nine pregnant women accepted and underwent amniocentesis, including karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis of the fetuses. All fetal karyotyping and microarray results were negative. To further investigate the potential genetic causes of laterality defects, trio‐WES was suggested in all cases, and 18 cases underwent Trio‐WES, including 12 cases with SIT and 6 cases with SA. Genetic analysis revealed six fetuses with variants of uncertain clinical significance (VUS), four in SIT group and two in the SA group (Table ). The six cases carried two likely pathogenic (LP) variants and several variants of unknown significance, involving genes such as DNAH5, DNAH11, CFAP300, PKD1L1, CFAP52, CHD4, DNAH9, and KMT2D (details in Table ). These genes are predominantly associated with the ciliary structure, implying that these variants might be potential pathogenic causes of laterality defects. In Case 10, trio‐WES identified two compound heterozygous variants in DNAH5. As both variants were synonymous, they could only be classified as VUS according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines. For Case 12, trio‐WES only indicated the presence of a DNAH11 variation inherited from the unaffected mother (c.9974A>G). While the identification of a single heterozygous variant was not diagnostic for an autosomal recessive disorder like PCD, it could potentially have contributed to the phenotype as a modifying factor or in conjunction with other unidentified genes. For Case 20, ultrasound revealed situs inversus and mirror‐image dextrocardia. Trio‐WES showed that the fetus carried a maternal CFAP300 c.604delG variant (p.Val202*) and a paternal PKD1L1 c.2845T>C (p.Cys949Arg) variant. The CFAP300 variant caused premature termination at Val202, truncating the protein and deleting at least five β‐sheet domains. PyMOL modeling (https://github.com/schrodinger/pymol‐open‐source) demonstrated that mutant CFAP300 lacked five β‐sheet domains present in the wild‐type (Figure ). The normal three‐dimensional structures of CFAP300 protein was shown in Figure . Though the mother carried the CFAP300 variant asymptomatically, the fetus harbored both variants. Co‐inheritance of CFAP300 and PKD1L1 variants might underlie the digenic contribution to laterality defects. Protein structures of the wide‐type and mutated CFAP300. (A) Three‐dimensional structure of wide‐type protein of CFAP300. The five β‐sheet structures in the red frame were lost in the mutated protein. (B) Three‐dimensional structure of the mutated protein of CFAP300. In Case 21, trio‐WES identified compound heterozygous variants in trans within the CFAP52 gene. Based on the genotype‐phenotype correlation, these variants might represent the probable cause of the fetus' situs inversus with dextrocardia. In Case 27, trio‐WES found two variants of uncertain significance in CHD4 (paternal origin) and DNAH9 (maternal origin). The father carried the CHD4 variant but had no abnormal phenotypes, which might be due to the variable expressivity associated with CHD4 variant. For Case 40, ultrasound examination revealed situs ambiguous combined with single ventricle, transposition of the great vessels and pulmonary atresia. Trio‐WES indicated the fetus had a de novo c.16351T>C variant in KMT2D gene, which could be associated with Kabuki syndrome. Considering cardiac disease is the common phenotype for Kabuki syndrome, with the evidence of PM2_P+PP3+PM6, this variant could be graded as likely pathogenic. Among the six cases carrying VUS, four showed the presence of SIT detected by prenatal ultrasound. Three out of these four SIT cases chose to continue the pregnancies, and the fetuses had a good prognosis after being born at term. Two cases showed the presence of SA combined with severe cardiac defects. Both couples chose to terminate the pregnancy due to the presence of cardiac malformations.

Discussion
Discussion This study analyzed the prenatal ultrasounds of 67 fetuses with laterality defects, with the objective of elucidating the specific differences in cardiovascular and other structural malformations between situs inversus totalis (SIT) and situs ambiguous (SA). Our results indicate a significant correlation between the type of visceral inversion and the incidence of cardiovascular malformations. Specifically, compared to fetuses with situs inversus totalis (SIT), those with partial visceral inversion (SA) have a significantly higher likelihood of cardiovascular malformations. This finding aligns with conclusions reported in previous literature, further validating the impact of visceral inversion type on the risk of cardiovascular malformations [, , , ]. In the present study, the vast majority (30/31, 96.8%) of fetuses with SA had complex cardiovascular malformations, which encompassed various types including interruption of the inferior vena cava, transposition of the great vessels, and abnormal pulmonary venous return, etc. To investigate the phenotypic distribution of cardiovascular malformations in fetuses with SA, we further subdivided the SA cases into left isomerism (LI) and right isomerism (RI) groups. The most common cardiac malformations in the LI and RI groups were double outlet right ventricle (DORV) and univentricular heart with single atrium (UVH), respectively. The results revealed significant differences in the distribution of cardiac phenotypes between the two groups. Specifically, the incidence of UVH in the RI group was significantly higher than that in the LI group (63.16% vs. Twenty‐five percent, p = 0.029), suggesting that RI often leads to poor prognosis due to the co‐existence of severe cardiac malformations. According to literature reports, the probability of heart malformations in RI is almost 100%, and the cardiac malformations are typically more severe than those in LI []. Additionally, this study found a significantly increased incidence of DORV in the LI group, which was significantly higher than that in the RI group (41.67% vs. 5.26%, p = 0.022). These findings were slightly different from those reported in previous literature. According to the review of Buca et al. concerning to fetal heterotaxy, they reported atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) as the most common cardiac anomaly in both fetal LI and RI (59.28% and 72.86% respectively) []. We propose that the discrepancy might be due to differences in the study population and diagnostic criterion variations. The cases included in the present study were from a high‐risk referral center, which might have enriched complex malformations such as UVH and DORV. Our study confined AVSD diagnosis to complete endocardial cushion defects, whereas the literature might encompass partial forms, potentially causing statistical discrepancy. Visceral inversion is often accompanied by interruption of the inferior vena cava (IVC). In this study, a total of three cases of interrupted IVC were identified, all occurring in the LI group, further hinting at a potential relationship between left isomerism and IVC development (p = 0.048). This result is consistent with that of Wu Q et al.’s study. They found IVC interruption in 30 out of 33 cases of left isomerism (LI), but not a single case of interrupted IVC was found in 55 cases of right isomerism (RI) []. These results highly suggest that there is an intrinsic association between the occurrence of IVC and LI. Compared to fetuses with SA, those with SIT had a much lower incidence of cardiovascular structural malformations. In this study, only two fetuses with SIT had cardiovascular malformations (2/36, 5.56%), in stark contrast to the 30 fetuses with SA and cardiac disease (30/31, 96.8%). This significant difference indicates that the completeness of the laterality defect may be one of the key factors influencing the incidence of cardiovascular malformations. Therefore, in clinical practice, the type of visceral inversion should be carefully assessed in fetuses with visceral inversion to more accurately predict the risk of cardiovascular malformations. Genetic factors play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of laterality defects, with many genes having been confirmed to participate in their development []. The genetic etiologies of laterality defects exhibit significant differences between SIT and SA. SIT is primarily associated with variants in genes related to ciliary motility disorders (such as DNAH5, DNAH1, DNAH11, and CCDC39), which typically follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern [, ]. Variants in these genes lead to abnormal ciliary assembly or motility, thereby inducing left‐right axis developmental abnormalities. However, the genetic architecture of SA is more complex than that of SIT, which might be the reason for the higher incidence of congenital heart defects in SA fetuses. Many important genes such as ZIC3, LMBRD1 and NODAL have been reported to be possibly related to the occurrence of SA [, , ]. These genes are associated with various inheritance patterns, including autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X‐linked recessive inheritance. In the present study, a fetus (Case 27) with SIT and complex congenital heart disease (CHD) was identified to carry variants in CHD4 (c.3704–2A>G) and DNAH9 (c.4600G>A). CHD4 is the primary causative gene for Sifrim‐Hitz‐Weiss syndrome, which is characterized by neurodevelopmental disorders, heart defects, and other features with variable expressivity []. While CHD4 is an established CHD‐associated gene, this case provides the first clinical evidence linking it to a laterality defect. This finding suggests that CHD4 may play a broader role in embryonic left‐right patterning, possibly through its chromatin remodeling function. Our results highlight that “known” CHD genes may harbor unrecognized roles in the development of laterality defects, particularly those involved in ciliary or chromatin pathways. Notably, the genetic backgrounds of SIT and SA also exhibit overlap. During early embryonic development, cilia at the embryonic node generate leftward fluid flow (Nodal flow) through directional beating, initiating left‐specific signaling pathways (such as the Nodal‐Lefty‐Pitx2 pathway, with key genes including NODAL and LEFTY2) []. Structural abnormalities in cilia may disrupt the left‐specific Nodal signaling pathway, leading to SIT. Abnormality in the Nodal signaling pathway is also a critical mechanism in SA, variants in NODAL, LEFTY2, and other genes can also induce SA. Additionally, incomplete penetrance or variable expressivity of variants, along with the combined effects of digenic or polygenic interactions, are potential pathogenic causes of laterality defects [, ]. In this study, we identified a fetus with SIT (Case 20 in Table ) carrying two variants: CFAP300 c.604delG (p.Val202*), inherited from the non‐phenotypic mother, and PKD1L1 c.2845T>C (p.Cys949Arg), inherited from the father. Both genes are critical for embryonic left–right patterning. CFAP300, an evolutionarily highly conserved protein, plays a crucial role in the correct assembly of ciliary dynein arms [, ]. Mouse models demonstrated that Cfap300 loss‐of‐function leads to inner dynein arm defects and ciliary motility disorders []. Similarly, human cases with CFAP300 variants exhibited laterality defects []. PyMOL analysis showed that the c.604delG variant causes substantial structural changes, with the loss of at least five β‐sheets, likely impairing protein function. The PKD1L1 gene is widely recognized as a key causative gene influencing embryonic left–right patterning. Research indicates that during embryonic development, the PKD1L1 protein interacts with the NODAL signaling pathway to regulate intracellular Ca2+ signaling, thereby finely controlling embryonic left–right symmetry []. Notably, CFAP300 and PKD1L1 might play complementary roles: the former maintains ciliary structural integrity, while the latter regulates ciliary function. According to the proposal put forward by Alexander H. Li et al., multiple ‘hits’ are required to disturb the complex processes involved in early embryonic left–right patterning []. We propose that the combined effect of these two variants may underlie the fetus' potential laterality defect. However, to deeply uncover the specific mechanisms underlying this potential combined effect, further research is required for subsequent exploration and validation. Therefore, this study provides valuable insights into further elucidating the genetic basis and molecular mechanisms of situs inversus, while also pointing out the directions and priorities for future research. The strengths of the present study lie in the specialized investigation of the fetal population, coupled with the integration of ultrasonography and trio‐WES to conduct analyses from both phenotypic and genotypic perspectives. Additionally, the stratification of SIT and SA subtypes provided valuable epidemiological data. By examining potential protein structural changes induced by genetic variants, the study analyzed and evaluated the potential pathogenic roles of genetic variations in laterality defects. However, the study also has limitations. The small sample size compromised the statistical power and was prone to generating biases in genetic analysis. Large‐sample studies are still required to further validate the findings. Additionally, the variants identified in the present study still cannot be definitively characterized as pathogenic to date. In prenatal trio‐WES testing, VUSs with potential pathogenic risks are often encountered, but they cannot be upgraded to pathogenic because of insufficient evidence during pregnancy. For such variants, we propose that for VUSs located at typical splice sites, further RNA functional experiments could be considered to clarify whether the variants affect splicing and thus define their harmfulness. For missense variants, functional assays could be attempted, along with literature searches for relevant patient reports, to comprehensively assess pathogenicity. Reanalysis of the data after 6 months or 1 year is also recommended to reevaluate the nature of these VUSs.

Ethics Statement
Ethics Statement This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of International Peace Maternity & Child Health Hospital with the number of (GKLW)2019‐73.

Consent
Consent Patient consent were obtained from the pregnant women who participated in this study.

Conflicts of Interest
Conflicts of Interest The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

title: Prenatal diagnosis and genetic assessment of fetuses with single umbilical artery using chromosomal microarray analysis: a seven-year single-center retrospective study.
label_reason: SUA fetuses (ultrasound marker) tested by CMA.
abstract: The inherited causes behind fetuses with a single umbilical artery (SUA) are still poorly understood, largely because published studies are scarce. In the present research, efforts were made to uncover the genetic factors at play and to assess how SUA influences pregnancy outcome. A retrospective review was performed on 5,014 pregnant individuals who underwent prenatal diagnostic testing between September 2017 and April 2023. Of these, 123 fetuses were found to have SUA. Amniocentesis was carried out in all affected cases, with samples analyzed via conventional karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) to detect any chromosomal abnormalities. In the present study, four cases of chromosome aneuploid and two cases of chromosomal structural abnormalities were identified through karyotype analysis, with the chromosomal aberration detection rate being 4.88% (6/123). CMA confirmed every abnormality detected by conventional karyotyping and additionally identified 11 pathogenic copy number variants that had been missed. These novel findings included clinically significant conditions such as Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome, Xq28 duplication syndrome, 16p13.3 duplication syndrome, 16p11.2 deletion syndrome, and 22q11.21 deletion syndrome. Overall, CMA provided an incremental diagnostic yield of 8.94% (11/123) beyond what karyotyping alone achieved ( P  = 0.001). CMA markedly improved the identification of clinically relevant genetic alterations in fetuses presenting with a single umbilical artery, especially when the anomaly occurred in isolation. These findings highlight the value of CMA for uncovering the genetic contributors to SUA and advance the characterization of genotype–phenotype relationships in these cases. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12884-025-07886-5. Keywords: Single umbilical artery, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Copy number variants, Karyotype analysis, Prenatal diagnosis

Prenatal diagnosis and genetic assessment of fetuses with single umbilical artery using chromosomal microarray analysis: a seven-year single-center retrospective study

Introduction
Introduction Single umbilical artery (SUA) often results from either the failure of one artery to form or its later degeneration. Such structural or functional cord abnormalities can hinder fetal growth and are linked to a higher risk of intrauterine growth restriction and perinatal mortality [, ]. Estimates of SUA occurrence range from about 0.5–5%, depending on the study population and methods used [, ]. Notably, SUA is more frequently observed in multiple gestations [], and has been increasingly associated with chromosomal abnormalities [, ]. As such, comprehensive ultrasound evaluation and cytogenetic testing during the second and third trimesters are advisable. Conventional karyotyping continues to serve as the benchmark for detecting chromosomal abnormalities, though its sensitivity is limited to alterations larger than roughly 5–10 Mb. Previous investigations have shown that SUA is particularly associated with trisomy 13, trisomy 18, and sex chromosome anomalies, while its link to trisomy 21 is comparatively weaker []. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), by contrast, offers higher resolution and allows for genome-wide detection of both aneuploidies and submicroscopic copy number variants (CNVs) [, ]. In addition, CMA has been recommended as a first-line tool for prenatal diagnosis in all pregnant women who receive amniocentesis [, ]. Despite its advantages, there remains a paucity of data on the application of CMA for detecting chromosomal abnormalities and CNVs in fetuses with SUA. In the present study, among 5,014 pregnancies assessed at a tertiary center in Southeast China, 123 fetuses were found to exhibit SUA. This investigation aims to expand current knowledge regarding the genetic etiology of SUA and to provide clinically relevant data to inform genetic counseling and prenatal decision-making.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Subjects A total of 5,014 pregnancies presenting with various high-risk indications underwent prenatal diagnostic evaluation between September 2017 and April 2023 and were included in this study. Among these, 123 fetuses were identified with SUA anomalies. All affected cases underwent amniocentesis, followed by both conventional karyotyping and CMA. Study subjects were stratified into three groups based on the presence and type of concurrent ultrasound findings: 25 cases with isolated SUA, 21 cases with SUA accompanied by structural anomalies, and 77 cases with SUA in conjunction with soft ultrasound markers. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee of Quanzhou Women’s and Children’s Hospital (Approval No. 2023No.56). Karyotype analysis Approximately 20 mL of amniotic fluid was collected from each fetus and inoculated into amniotic fluid-specific culture medium. The samples were incubated at 37 °C for 7–10 days. Cultured amniotic fluid cells were harvested using the Sinochrome Chromprep II automatic chromosome harvesting system (Shanghai Lechen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.), following standard cytogenetic protocols []. For each case, thirty metaphase spreads were counted, and five karyotypes were fully analyzed. Chromosomal analysis and nomenclature were conducted in accordance with the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN 2020) guidelines []. Genomic DNA extraction Approximately 10 mL of amniotic fluid from each fetus and 2 mL of peripheral blood from the parents were collected for further CMA analysis. Genomic DNA was extracted from the enrolled subjects using the QIAamp DNA Blood Kit (QIAGEN, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines (www.qiagen.com). Chromosomal microarray analysis According to the procedures described in previous research by the present authors [, ], 250 ng of genomic DNA from each sample was enzymatically digested using the NspI restriction enzyme. The resulting DNA fragments were end-repaired and ligated, followed by amplification via polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The PCR products were subsequently purified, quantified, and subjected to fragmentation. Fragmented DNA was then labeled with biotin and hybridized to microarray probes on the chip. After hybridization, the arrays were washed, stained, and scanned to detect fluorescence signals. SNP genotyping and CNV analysis were performed using Genotyping Console and Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS) software. The databases of DGV (Database of Genomics Variations, http://dgv.tcag.ca/dgv), OMIM (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, https://omim.org/), DECIPHER (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/), and PubMed (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/), along with other databases were utilized for interpretation of the CNVs pathogenicity. Classification of CNV pathogenicity followed the joint guidelines established by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen) []. Statistical analysis Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 20.0 software. Statistical analysis was conducted between groups using the chi square test. If the chi square test results were not satisfactory, Fisher’s exact probability test was used for statistical analysis. A value of P < 0.05 was considered as statistically significant.

Results
Results Subjects information In the present study, 123 pregnancies with SUA anomalies were identified from a total of 5,014 cases undergoing prenatal diagnosis, resulting in an incidence rate of 2.45% (123/5014). All enrolled participants provided informed consent and successfully underwent amniocentesis. The cases were categorized into three subgroups: isolated SUA (n = 25), SUA with structural ultrasound anomalies (n = 21), and SUA with ultrasound soft marker anomalies (n = 77). Karyotype analysis results Karyotype analysis and CMA were successfully performed on the enrolled 123 cases with SUA anomalies. Karyotype analysis identified six cases with chromosomal abnormalities, yielding a detection rate of 4.88% (6/123). These included four cases of chromosomal aneuploidy—two cases of trisomy 18, one case of monosomy X (45,X), and one case of 47,XYY—as well as two cases with structural chromosomal abnormalities: 46,XN, del(18)(q21) and 46,XN, rec(4)dup(4p)inv(4)(p15.1q34.3)dpat (Figs. and ). Parental karyotyping revealed that the deletion on chromosome 18 was de novo, while the recombinant chromosome 4 resulted from a paternal pericentric inversion (Fig. ). Karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis results in a fetus with partial monosomy chromosome 18q. A The fetal karyotype showed 46,XN, del(18)(q21). B A 27.7 Mb deletion was confirmed in the fetus using chromosomal microarray analysis (arr[GRCh37]18q21.2q23(50,311,515_78,013,728)x1) Karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) results in a fetus with rec(4). A rec(4) was observed in the fetus using karyotype analysis (A), with parental analysis identifying a paternal inv(4)(p15.1q34.3) as the source (B). C CMA of the fetus uncovered a 9.4 Mb deletion at 4q34.3–q35.2 [arr(GRCh37) 4q34.3q35.2(181,472,405_190,957,460)x1] and a 31.1 Mb duplication at 4p16.3–p15.1 [arr(GRCh37) 4p16.3p15.1(68,346_31,236,026)x3]. D A 1.6 Mb Xp22.31 microduplication was also detected in the fetus using CMA Chromosomal microarray analysis results All chromosomal anomalies identified via karyotype analysis were confirmed by CMA (Figs. and ). Additionally, CMA detected 11 further cases of pathogenic copy number variants (pCNVs) that were not identified through karyotyping, as detailed in Table . These pCNVs included clinically significant syndromes such as Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, Xq28 duplication syndrome, 16p13.3 duplication syndrome, 16p11.2 deletion syndrome, a recurrent 16p13.11 CNV involving the MYH11 gene, and 22q11.21 deletion syndrome (Fig. ). This resulted in an additional diagnostic yield of 8.94% (11/123) for CMA over conventional karyotyping, a statistically significant improvement (P = 0.001). Pathogenic copy number variants detected in the fetuses using CMA. A A 1.5 Mb 16p13.11 microdeletion covering the 16p13.11 recurrent region (BP2-BP3) (includes MYH11) region was identified in a fetus using CMA. B A 7.7 Mb 16p13.3 microduplication covering the chromosome16p13.3 duplication syndrome was detected in a fetus using CMA. C A 873.7Kb Xq28 microduplication covering the Xq28 duplication syndrome was identified in a fetus using CMA. D A 295.4Kb microdeletion in Xq22.1 region was detected in a fetus using CMA Of the 11 cases with pCNVs, parental CMA verification was conducted in five cases (Fig. ; Table ). Among these, three pCNVs were identified as de novo, while two were inherited from phenotypically normal fathers. In Case 7, CMA identified a 5.5 Mb microdeletion in the 7q36.1q36.3 region [arr[GRCh37]7q36.1q36.3(149,828,704_155,396,147)x1] (Fig. ). This deletion was confirmed to be de novo based on parental testing. The fetus exhibited SUA along with additional ultrasound soft marker anomalies, and the pregnancy was electively terminated. Given the de novo origin, the recurrence risk for future pregnancies was considered low. In a subsequent pregnancy, the couple delivered a female infant with a normal prenatal CMA result and normal developmental milestones documented at 6-month follow-up. Pedigree analysis, ultrasound examination and chromosomal microarray analysis results in Case 7. A Pedigree analysis results in the family. B Ultrasound examination results indicated a single umbilical artery in the fetus. C, D A 5.5 Mb microdeletion in 7q36.1q36.3 region was detected in the fetus using CMA [arr[GRCh37]7q36.1q36.3(149,828,704_155,396,147)x1], which contained 43 OMIM genes In addition, five cases harbored VOUS were detected (Table ). Parental CMA analysis was performed in three of these cases. Two CNVs were maternally inherited and one was paternally inherited. Notably, in Case 14, a 249.5 Kb microdeletion in the 7q36.1 region was detected in the fetus [arr[GRCh37]7q36.1(151,797,859_152,047,392)x1], spanning exons 3 through 59 of the KMT2C gene (OMIM: 606833) (Fig. ). Parental testing confirmed the same deletion in the mother, who exhibited a congenital asymmetry in lower limb length. The infant was delivered at term with no overt anomalies and demonstrated normal development at a 5-year follow-up. Ultrasound examination and chromosomal microarray analysis results in Case 14. A, B Ultrasound examination results indicated increased nuchal translucency (4.6 mm) (A) and single umbilical artery (B) in the fetus. C, D A 249.5 Kb microdeletion in 7q36.1 region was identified in the fetus [arr[GRCh37]7q36.1(151,797,859_152,047,392)x1], covering partial fragments of the KMT2C gene Detection rates of chromosomal abnormalities among the groups A total chromosomal aberration detection rate of 13.82% (17/123) was observed in the present study. Subgroup analysis of detection rates among the three groups (isolated SUA, SUA with structural anomalies, and SUA with soft marker anomalies) is presented in Table . All cases of chromosomal aneuploidy occurred in the isolated SUA group, whereas all trisomy 18 cases were found in the SUA with soft marker anomalies group. The detection rates of pCNVs did not differ significantly among the groups (8.00% vs. 10.39% vs. 14.29%; P = 0.834), nor did the overall chromosomal abnormality detection rates (16.00% vs. 12.99% vs. 14.29%; P = 1.000). Pregnancy outcome Follow-Up Of the enrolled 123 cases, five cases were lost to follow-up. Among the four cases with chromosomal aneuploidy, three pregnancies were electively terminated, while one case with a 47,XYY karyotype continued to term, resulting in the birth of a male infant with normal physical features. Both cases involving structural chromosomal abnormalities also resulted in pregnancy termination. Among the 11 additional pCNVs identified by CMA, six families opted for termination of pregnancy. The remaining five continued their pregnancies: one resulted in a preterm birth, one infant was born with a ventricular septal defect, and the other three neonates were delivered with no apparent abnormalities (Table ). As elicited in Table , of the five cases with VOUS, one pregnancy was terminated, while the remaining four were carried to term. Of the 96 cases with normal CMA findings that were successfully followed up, two families chose termination. The remaining 94 pregnancies progressed to delivery. Among these, the majority (n = 85) resulted in the birth of infants with normal postnatal features. However, there were adverse outcomes in a few cases: two stillbirths, three preterm births, one case of congenital heart defect, one case of renal agenesis, one case of pulmonary artery stenosis, and one neonate who lacked spontaneous respiration and died shortly after birth.

Discussion
Discussion The incidence of SUA was identified to be approximately 2.45% in this study, which is similar to previous findings [, ]. SUA has been widely recognized as a prenatal marker associated with an elevated risk of both congenital anomalies and chromosomal abnormalities [, , ]. In addition, a previous study conducted by Murphy-Kaulbeck et al. [] indicated that fetuses and neonates with SUA had a 6.77 times greater risk of congenital anomalies and as high as 15.35 times greater risk of chromosomal abnormalities. Despite these associations, limited studies have explored the genetic underpinnings of SUA, and its precise etiology and pathogenesis remain poorly defined. In the present study, a total of 123 fetuses identified with SUA underwent detailed prenatal genetic evaluation, using both conventional karyotyping and CMA, to clarify genotype–phenotype associations and deepen understanding of the genetic underpinnings of SUA. Multiple studies have pinpointed trisomy 18 as the most common aneuploidy in fetuses with SUA [, ]. In the present cohort, karyotype analysis uncovered four aneuploidies: two trisomy 18 cases, one monosomy X (45,X), and one 47,XYY. Both trisomy 18 fetuses exhibited SUA alongside additional soft-marker anomalies, while the sex chromosome aneuploidies presented with isolated SUA, corresponding to an 8.00% aneuploidy rate within the isolated SUA subgroup. The lack of extensive population-based data, however, hampers precise quantification of the link between isolated SUA and chromosomal aneuploidies. Previous case reports have also suggested a potential link between structural chromosomal abnormalities and SUA. For instance, a study identified a fetus with a deletion at 18q21.3-qter and a terminal duplication of 1p36.32-p36.33, associated with multiple congenital anomalies including SUA []. Similarly, Cho et al. [] described a fetus with partial trisomy (18pter→q22) and partial monosomy (18q22→qter), also presenting with multiple anomalies including SUA. In the present study, one case with a de novo deletion was identified in the long arm of chromosome 18 [46,XN, del(18)(q21)], associated with SUA and other soft marker anomalies. This finding further supports a potential correlation between long arm abnormalities of chromosome 18 and the presence of SUA. In addition, a chromosomal structural abnormality was identified in a fetus with isolated SUA, characterized as 46,XN, rec(4)dup(4p)inv(4)(p15.1q34.3)dpat. Notably, a previous study reported a 17.8 Mb deletion in the 4q34.1–q35.2 region in a fetus presenting with SUA in combination with a ventricular septal defect and a small midline brain cyst. This suggests a possible association between microdeletions involving the distal region of chromosome 4q and the occurrence of SUA, warranting further investigation into the role of 4q structural variants in fetal vascular development. In the present study, an additional 11 cases of pCNVs were detected using CMA, which were not identified by conventional karyotyping. This corresponds to an incremental diagnostic yield of 8.94% for CMA over karyotype analysis. The clinical significance of pCNVs in fetuses with SUA, however, remains a subject of ongoing debate. A meta-analysis conducted by Kim et al. [], which included 124 fetuses with isolated SUA, reported no pathogenic CNVs, suggesting that isolated SUA may have one of the lowest rates of clinically significant CNVs among all ultrasonographic soft markers. Conversely, a more recent large-scale study involving 15,263 fetuses with various soft markers found that certain isolated markers, including SUA, thickened nuchal fold, mild ventriculomegaly, and absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, were associated with higher detection rates of pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNVs []. In the present cohort, an 8.0% pCNV detection rate was observed in the isolated SUA group, which aligns with findings from prior research []. Notably, the pCNVs identified in the present study did not exhibit a statistically significant enrichment pattern across specific genomic loci. Among the detected syndromes, Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome (WHS) is particularly relevant due to its association with relatively nonspecific prenatal ultrasound features. However, SUA has been reported in approximately 44.4% of fetuses with WHS, suggesting it may serve as an early indicator of this condition []. Additionally, a previous study conducted by Kohlschmidt et al. [] described cases involving partial monosomy 4 and partial trisomy 18 in a living male infant and a prenatally diagnosed male fetus, both of whom presented with a single umbilical artery, reinforcing the association between chromosomal imbalances involving chromosome 4 and SUA. Similarly, another report documented a fetus with partial monosomy 4p, who exhibited multiple prenatal anomalies including intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), SUA, cleft lip and palate, and other soft marker anomalies []. Notably, in Case 3 of the present study, a microdeletion in the 4p16.3p16.1 region accompanied by a microduplication in 18q23 was identified in a fetus presenting with SUA, increased nuchal fold, and intrauterine growth restriction. These findings mirror a previously documented case of partial monosomy 4p, which was followed by pregnancy termination at the family’s request []. This report further implicates microdeletions at 4p16.3, the critical region for Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome, in the development of SUA. A recent investigation [] has linked 16p11.2 deletions with SUA. In the present cohort, Case 8 presented with both SUA and a 1.7 Mb deletion at 16p11.2. However, developmental assessment at one year showed normal growth and no obvious deficits, implying that SUA in this instance may not reflect full phenotypic expression of the 16p11.2 microdeletion. In Case 10, a microdeletion at Xq22.1 was detected in an isolated SUA fetus, marking the first such report. Although this points to a novel genomic region of interest, additional studies are required to determine whether this represents a causal relationship or a coincidental finding. The detection of VOUS via CMA introduces substantial challenges in genetic counseling. Such ambiguous results can exacerbate parental anxiety and, in some cases, prompt termination of pregnancies that might otherwise yield healthy outcomes. Reliable interpretation of VOUS necessitates a multifaceted approach, including parental CMA testing, longitudinal detailed prenatal ultrasonography, and access to extensive population- and case-based databases to inform clinical decisions. In this cohort, five fetuses (4.07%) presented VOUS. Case 14 involved a 249.5 kb microdeletion at 7q36.1 inherited from the mother, who exhibited skeletal anomalies; however, no clinical issues were observed in the child over a five-year follow-up, suggesting that this deletion was unlikely to underlie the maternal phenotype. This example highlights the importance of prolonged surveillance and prudent interpretation of VOUS findings, while contributing valuable data to genetic counseling resources for similar future cases. In the present study, 96 fetuses had normal CMA findings, and 94 of these pregnancies reached term. Among them, there were two stillbirths, three preterm deliveries, and one neonatal death shortly after birth. Earlier studies have proposed that SUA might impair placental circulation and nutrient transport, which could lead to outcomes like small-for-gestational-age infants and stillbirth []. The link between SUA and preterm delivery, however, remains debated. A study conducted by Mailath-Pokorny et al. [] reported that isolated SUA is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth. In contrast, other findings suggest that isolated SUA does not elevate the risk of spontaneous preterm delivery []. In the present study, five pregnancies ended preterm, but without a matched control cohort, it was not possible to establish a causal relationship. Larger, controlled studies will be necessary to clarify whether SUA truly influences preterm birth rates. In conclusion, in the present study, 123 cases of fetuses with SUA were identified among 5,014 pregnant women undergoing prenatal diagnosis in Southeast China. Several pCNVs were found to be potentially associated with SUA, including microdeletions in regions 4q34.3–q35.2, 4p16.3 (associated with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome), and 16p11.2. Additionally, the findings further support a correlation between long arm abnormalities of chromosome 18 and the presence of SUA. These results highlight the significant role of CMA in the etiological evaluation of fetuses with SUA, including those with isolated findings. CMA provides a higher resolution than conventional karyotyping and contributes valuable insights for prenatal genetic diagnosis. The present study offers additional evidence to inform clinical decision-making and genetic counseling for families affected by SUA.

title: Tiny Lungs, Big Challenges: Navigating Fetal Pleural Effusion Outcomes, Long Term Follow-up and Implications for Future Pregnancies.
label_reason: Fetal pleural effusion with CMA on amniotic fluid.
abstract: Fetal pleural effusion is a rare condition involving fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity of the fetus. Invasive procedures are required to exclude chromosomal anomalies and infections, as treatment delays can lead to severe fetal complications. We discuss a case where a 30-year-old primigravida presented at 20 weeks gestation with fetal bilateral pleural effusion and mild ascites. At 23 weeks of gestation, thoracocentesis was performed which revealed chylothorax. The pleural effusion resolved spontaneously by 28 weeks. At 36 weeks, severe oligohydramnios prompted an emergency caesarean section. Postnatal genetic testing found two variants of uncertain significance. The baby improved and was discharged on day six, with no complications over 3.5 years of follow-up. The couple's subsequent pregnancy was uncomplicated. We propose a stepwise management protocol emphasising early diagnosis through ultrasound and cytological analysis, followed by thoracocentesis in severe cases. Regular follow-up is essential to monitor fluid dynamics and adjust management as needed. Keywords: Chylothorax, Lymphatic Malformation, Pleural Effusion, Pleuro-Amniotic Shunt, Thoracocentesis, Whole Exome Sequencing
text:
Tiny Lungs, Big Challenges: Navigating Fetal Pleural Effusion Outcomes, Long Term Follow-up and Implications for Future Pregnancies

Introduction
Introduction Fetal pleural effusion or hydrothorax is rare, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 15,000. [] However, the actual incidence is believed to be higher than this as many cases go undiagnosed due to missed ultrasound screenings, spontaneous resolution, or fetal abortion or death before any investigation can be conducted. [] Fetal hydrothorax can be unilateral or bilateral and arises from either primary(isolated) or secondary causes, such as structural anomalies, chromosomal abnormalities, or infections. Chylothorax is the leading cause of primary pleural effusion. [,] The presence of milky fluid indicates chylous effusion in infants and adults, as lymphatic fluid contains chylomicrons. However, in fetal chylo thoraces, pleural fluid is typically clear and straw-coloured due to the fetus's fasting state. A high lymphocyte count is often observed in cellular analysis of chylous effusion in fetuses. Studies also suggest that a pleural fluid with white blood cells (WBC) >1000/ml and over 80% lymphocytes indicate chylous effusion. However, other studies have shown that the WBC cell count in aspirated fluid may be inconsistent.[] Additionally, the pleural fluid triglycerides level >110 mg/dl, pleural fluid cholesterol >1.16 mmol/l or >45 mg/dl, and the ratio of pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to serum LDH >0.6 U/L suggests an exudate. Secondary causes of hydrops fetalis encompass a range of conditions, with cardiac and vascular diseases in 50% of cases. Chromosomal abnormalities, particularly trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome, contribute to 7-10% of cases. Other potential etiologies include fetal anaemia and haematological disorders, as well as infections like toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes (TORCH), and parvovirus B19. Additionally, causes may involve skeletal dysplasia and abnormalities affecting the placenta or umbilical cord [], all of which can disrupt normal fetal development and hemodynamics. Ultrasonography is the primary diagnostic tool for detecting pleural effusion. Prenatal invasive testing on amniotic fluid can yield critical information about the fetal karyotype and possible TORCH infections. Additional assessments include maternal blood group and typing, viral marker screening, and evaluation for antiphospholipid antibodies (APLA) and specific antibodies to rule out immune hydrops. [,] If hydrothorax develops during the first or second trimester of pregnancy, it can cause lung hypoplasia due to the compression effect that inhibits lung growth. This condition may also lead to complications such as mediastinal shift, hydrops, and polyhydramnios, which in turn may result in preterm delivery, neonatal asphyxia, and perinatal death. [] In this study, we closely followed the fetus throughout pregnancy, treating pleural effusion by fluid removal and ruling out primary and secondary causes of fetal pleural effusion. The child was monitored until 3.5 years of age, and the mother was followed during her subsequent pregnancy.

Case Presentation
Case Presentation This case was reported during the COVID-19 pandemic and followed up through 2024. A 30-year-old primigravida presented at 20 weeks gestation with the anomaly scan report that revealed bilateral mild pleural effusion (left >right) and mild ascites with no gross structural abnormality. There was no evidence of fetal skin oedema, tricuspid regurgitation, or pericardial effusion, and the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) was within normal limits. Maternal physical examination showed tachycardia and moderate pallor. Per abdominal examination indicated the fundal height of the uterus corresponding to 20 weeks gestation. Lab results revealed B+ blood type and moderate anaemia. Further investigations identified the mother as having sickle cell trait (SCT), while her spouse tested normal for SCT via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The rest of the routine investigations were within normal limits. The couple was counselled on fetal pleural effusion, including its causes both genetic and acquired, associated anomalies, and the possible risks and treatment options. A third-generation pedigree was drawn. The couple has a non-consanguineous marriage and is unaware of any inherited disorders in the family. Amniocentesis was performed to rule out genetic causes and TORCH infections for pleural effusion. Chromosomal microarray (CMA) and TORCH polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analyses of the amniotic fluid were normal. A follow-up ultrasound at 23 weeks revealed an increase in pleural effusion size, resulting in left lung collapse, mediastinal shift, and minimal ascites (Fig. 1a and b). Thoracocentesis was performed to treat the pleural effusion, and 20 ml of straw-colored fluid was aspirated (Fig. 1c and d). The cytologic analysis of the pleural fluid revealed lymphocytic effusion and elevated triglyceride levels, consistent with chylothorax. Details are given in . The couple was counselled for thoracocentesis. After undergoing thoracocentesis at 23 weeks, the fetus did not experience any complications. On ultrasonography at 25 weeks, there was persistent gross pleural effusion on the left side, along with significant ascites and skin oedema. The MCA-PSV was 0.84 multiples of the median (MoM), which is considered normal. The patient required urgent shunting and was referred to a higher medical facility. However, due to travel restrictions related to the coronavirus disease (COVID-19), she could not reach the referral centre in time. Surprisingly, during this delay, the pleural effusion resolved spontaneously by 28 weeks, and the shunting procedure was no longer required. During her next visit at 29+5 weeks, it was found that the fetus had only mild pleural effusion along with gross ascites with a volume of 132 cc (). The mother was advised for regular follow-up every two weeks, and at 32 weeks, moderate ascites was observed, measuring 40 cc, while no pleural effusion was present (Figure 1g and h). Ultrasonography findings at different gestational ages (a) Mild fetal ascites and (b) mild bilateral fetal pleural effusion (left>right) at 20 weeks of gestation. (c) Transverse section of the fetal thorax showing severe pleural effusion at 23 weeks and a right shift of the heart. Left lung compressed by the effusion. Antenatal thoracocentesis is performed to facilitate lung development. (d) Straw-coloured chylous pleural fluid after thoracocentesis. (e) Transverse section of the abdomen showing gross fetal ascites at 29+5 weeks. (f) The volume of Fetal ascites on 3D ultrasonography is ~132 ccs. (g) Transverse section of the abdomen showing mild ascites and no pleural effusion at 32 weeks gestation (h) Volume of Fetal ascites on 3D ultrasonography ~40 ccs. (i) Transverse section of the abdomen showing minimal residual ascites and no pleural effusion at 35.5 weeks gestation (j) Newborn at 36 weeks with no gross abnormality and APGAR 8/9 at 1 and 5 minutes. At 36 weeks, the fetus had minimal residual fetal ascites and no pleural effusion with MCA-PSV 1.09 MoM with severe oligohydramnios. () As a result, an emergency cesarean section was performed. A girl weighing 2576 grams was delivered, exhibiting mild breathing difficulties. () Postnatally, the whole exome sequencing was performed, encompassing a comprehensive panel of genes known to cause lymphatic disorders and rasopathy syndromes. No pathogenic variants were detected in either panel. However, two variants of uncertain significance (c.1178G>A and c.386T>C), suggestive of autosomal dominant lymphatic disorders, were noted (). Sanger sequencing confirmed that these variants were also present in the father in heterozygous form. To rule out the possibility of inborn errors of metabolism, tandem mass spectrometry and time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay were performed, yielding normal results. Fortunately, the baby's health improved, and she was discharged from the hospital on the sixth day after birth. The baby was monitored by a neonatologist for six days, during which her health improved. The baby is under follow-up, and medical records indicate no serious complications in the last 3.5 years. The couple planned their next pregnancy, which was delivered to our centre only, with no similar complications observed.

Discussion
Discussion Congenital hydrothorax is a condition that can be diagnosed prenatally through sonographic examination. This condition is characterized by a fluid-filled mass in the fetal chest that exerts pressure on the lungs. It may be associated with polyhydramnios. Fetal hydro thoraces, either unilateral or bilateral, may occur in isolation or with other intrathoracic structural abnormalities that hinder lymphatic drainage, primary lymphatic disorders or infections, and aneuploidies like Turner syndrome and Trisomy 21, or lung tumours. In the case presented, fetal infections, chromosomal disorders, and structural malformations were ruled out, indicating that the most likely cause could be a genetic mutation or a single gene disorder. This may include conditions such as Noonan Syndrome (Rasopathies), rarer syndromes like Gorham-Stout Syndrome, missense mutations in the integrin α9β1, yellow nail syndrome, etc. In the absence of any genetic pathology, the outcome depends on gestational age at presentation, the severity of effusion, progression or not, and the presence or absence of hydrops. Much literature suggests that pleural effusion at less than 32 weeks of gestation should be treated prenatally if feasible for optimal outcomes. The management strategy for fetal pleural effusion is based on symptom management.[] We followed the same protocol as described in . Prenatal therapy for pleural effusion can include a single thoracocentesis, serial thoracocentesis, or thoracic-amniotic shunt. Thoracocentesis is the initial procedure of choice because it can provide cytologic and biochemical diagnostic information and relieve intrathoracic compression. [] However, it may need to be repeated if the effusion increases. In cases where the effusion worsens, thoraco-amniotic shunting is the preferred treatment option. In such cases, the placement of thoraco-amniotic shunts can help restore normal intrathoracic anatomy, resulting in the resolution of associated hydrops and polyhydramnios. [] An alternative to shunting is pleurodesis, where a sclerosant substance is injected into the pleural cavity. []. Stage-based management of fetal pleural effusion Recent studies have reported survival rates of around 60% for patients treated with thoracoamniotic shunting, approximately 50% for those treated with thoracocentesis, and 35% to about 60% for those receiving conservative management. Hidaka et al. performed thoracocentesis in a fetus with bilateral isolated pleural effusion at 20 weeks POG, achieving complete resolution with a single procedure and uneventful outcomes. []. In our case, we performed thoracocentesis and cytological analysis of the fluid, confirming it to be chylothorax. Fortunately, the effusion resolved before proceeding for Pleuro- amniotic shunt. Post-natally. Tandem mass spectrometry and Time-Resolved Flouroimmunoassay screening for inborn errors of metabolism was negative. However, whole exome sequencing revealed the presence of variants of uncertain significance, as mentioned above. Post-test genetic counselling was conducted, and parents were offered Sanger sequencing for the same variants identified in the fetus. The baby is being followed in the paediatric department and is doing well in the second year of life. The survival rates for cases of fetal pleural effusion treated with thoracocentesis range from 50% to 60%. Better outcomes are reported when treatment occurs before the onset of hydrops. For instance, in this case, early thoracocentesis performed at 23 weeks of gestation prevented the progression to hydrops. This finding aligns with Wada et al., who reported a survival rate of 97.8% for cases managed prior to the development of hydrops, compared to 58% for hydrothorax cases with hydrops. [] Additionally, Aubard et al. reported a 75% survival rate in cases of primary hydrothorax without hydrops and only 24% when hydrops was present. [] Similarly, Rustico et al. observed survival rates of 73% in primary pleural effusion cases and 25% in those with hydrops. [] A study by Lee CJ et al. found that among 29 cases with a prenatal diagnosis at 34 weeks or earlier, infants who received prenatal therapy had a significantly higher survival rate than those who did not (76.9% vs. 11%, respectively; p = 0.008). [] A recent systematic review of cases with isolated fetal pleural effusion also concludes that these cases have a favourable outcome with a survival rate of 87.3% amongst the continuing pregnancies, and only a small number (1.1%) progress to hydrops. [] The fetus with a pleural effusion is at significant risk for developing hydramnios and preterm delivery. But in our case, she developed oligohydramnios, which is a contradictory finding. Jelin et al. performed exome sequencing on six cases affected by pleural effusions. A pathogenic variant was identified in one case (16.7%), while four cases had variants of uncertain significance (VOUS). [] In our case also, two VOUS were detected for Fraser syndrome 3 and lymphatic malformation 1. Fraser Syndrome is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It is caused by mutations in the GRIP1 (NM 021150.4) gene and is characterized by certain physical features such as syndactyly, cryptophthalmos, and abnormalities of the respiratory and urogenital tract. However, these features did not match the phenotype of the baby in our case. Lymphatic malformation 1 (OMIM# 153100) is a group of autosomal dominant disorders caused by mutations in the FLT4 (NM_182925.5) gene. This condition is associated with non-immune hydrops. Further analysis using Sanger sequencing revealed that the identified FLT4 and GRIP1 variants were inherited from the father in a heterozygous state. Functional assays suggested that these variants may impact lymphatic development, indicating a potential contributory role in the condition. This underscores the importance of parental segregation studies for determining the clinical significance of variants of uncertain significance (VOUS) in similar cases.

Conclusions
Conclusions Based on our findings, we propose a stepwise management protocol emphasising early diagnosis through ultrasound and cytological analysis, followed by thoracocentesis in severe cases. Regular follow-up is essential to monitor fluid dynamics and adjust management as needed. This approach aligns with guidelines from recent systematic reviews. Treating pleural effusion during pregnancy can save lives by alleviating symptoms, promoting lung development, and improving fetal outcomes. It is crucial to implement a stepwise treatment plan to ensure successful results. Additionally, genetic counselling is essential in these cases to help determine whether to pursue prenatal testing in future pregnancies. Exome sequencing can be helpful when the underlying cause is not diagnosed.
