Prenatal diagnosis of 1q21.1 microdeletions and microduplications: a retrospective case series

Introduction
Introduction Chromosomal copy number variations (CNVs) at the 1q21.1 locus are among the most well-characterized recurrent genomic rearrangements in humans, driven primarily by non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) between clustered low- copy repeats (LCRs) in the region []. This region (chr1:145.4-147.9 Mb, GRCh37/hg19) demonstrates particularly wide phenotypic variability, ranging from severe neurodevelopmental disorders to asymptomatic presentations [–]. Postnatally, affected individuals often present with neurodevelopmental disorders (global developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder), craniofacial anomalies (microcephaly/macrocephaly), congenital heart defects, and growth disturbances [, –]. Prenatally, these CNVs present unique diagnostic challenges, with only ~ 50–60%% of cases show detectable ultrasound anomalies [, , ]. The clinical significance of 1q21.1 CNVs stems from dosage-sensitive genes within the region, particularly GJA5 (cardiac conduction) and CHD1L (neural development) [, ]. Despite growing postnatal data, prenatal characterization of 1q21.1 CNVs remains limited, with fewer than 100 reported cases worldwide [, , , ]. This study analyzes 20 consecutive prenatal cases of 1q21.1 CNVs. The indication for prenatal testing, prenatal ultrasound features, inheritance of the CNVs, and the pregnancy outcome were studied. The aim of this study was to comprehensively review prenatal cases of 1q21.1 CNVs to improve understanding of this submicroscopic imbalance in prenatal diagnosis.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study design and population A retrospective analysis was conducted at the Prenatal Diagnosis Center of Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province (Wuhan, China). Twenty consecutive prenatal cases diagnosed with 1q21.1 CNVs between 2017 and 2024 were included. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the hospital’s Ethics Committee. Detailed information on these cases was extracted from the relevant medical records. Genetic testing Karyotyping Amniotic fluid (n = 19) or parental peripheral blood samples (n = 2) were obtained under sterile conditions. Giemsa staining was performed on metaphase chromosomes from cultured prenatal samples or peripheral blood using established methods, and the resolution of the haploid band was determined with an acceptable range of 320–400. Chromosome microarray analysis (CMA) Genomic DNA was extracted from uncultured amniocytes (n = 10) or parental peripheral blood (n = 8 couple) using the QIAamp DNA mini-kit (QIAGEN, Germany). DNA quality was assessed using the NanoDrop kit (Thermo Scientific; Waltham, MA, USA). The SNP array analysis was performed using the CytoScan®750 K Array (Affymetrix Inc, CA, USA). Genomic DNA labeling and hybridization were performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Data were interpreted via Chromosome Analysis Suite (v3.3) against GRCh37/hg19. Copy number variation sequencing (CNVseq) Copy number variation sequencing (CNVseq) was performed on uncultured amniocytes (n = 10) or parental peripheral blood (n = 8 couple) to detect chromosome anomalies at the low coverage whole-genome sequencing level. Genomic DNA (10 ng) was fragmented, and a DNA library was constructed as previously described [, ]. Multiple libraries were indexed, pooled in a single lane, and sequenced on the Nextseq CN500 instrument (Illumina, Inc.) to generate approximately 5 million 45-bp single end reads (including the 8-bp index sequence), resulting in an average sequencing coverage of ~ 0.2×. Genomic imbalances were reported using the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome.

Results
Results Over an 8-year period (2017–2024), 20 consecutive prenatal cases (from 19 families) with 1q21.1 CNVs were identified at our center, including 12 microdeletions (60%) and 8 microduplications (40%). Maternal age ranged from 23 to 42 years (mean 32 ± 5.1), with a median gestational age at diagnosis of 20 weeks (17–29 weeks). The main indications for invasive testing were: high-risk maternal serum screening or non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) (40%, 8/20), ultrasound anomalies (35%, 7/20) and advanced maternal age (AMA) ≥ 35 years (25%, 5/20). Microdeletions ranged from 0.516 to 2.6 Mb (median 1.9 Mb), and microduplications ranged from 1.28 to 2.5 Mb (median 2.0 Mb) (Table ). Ultrasound anomalies were detected in 55% (11/20) of cases (Table ). In the deletion group (8/12, 66.7%), the anomalies included two cases of fetal growth restriction (FGR), two cases of short femur, one case of ventricular septal defect (VSD), one case of persistent right umbilical vein accompanied by aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA), one case of ventriculomegaly, one case of increased nuchal translucency (NT), and one case of choroid plexus cyst. In the duplication group (3/8, 37.5%), anomalies consisted of two cases of hypoplastic nasal bone and one case of ventriculomegaly. Parental test results were available for 17 cases: the origin was de novo in 8 cases and inherited in 9 cases (from 8 families). Termination of pregnancy (TOP) was elected in 50% (10/20) of cases, predominantly for de novo CNVs (8/10). One case resulted in spontaneous abortion at 20 weeks’ gestation. The remaining 9 cases resulted in live births, with no overt abnormalities detected during postnatal follow-up (range: 3 months to 5 years). Detailed clinical and molecular characteristics of the 20 cases are summarized in Table .

Discussion
Discussion Our expanded cohort of 20 cases confirms and extends previous findings regarding the prenatal presentation of 1q21.1 CNVs. The 50% detection rate of ultrasound anomalies (10/20 cases) aligns with prior reports of variable expressivity in this region [, ]. This variability is not only a challenge for prenatal diagnosis but also indicates the complex nature of 1q21.1 CNVs, which involve multiple genes with diverse functions. Several studies have associated FGR or short stature with 1q21.1 CNVs [, , ], echoing the role of CHD1L in developmental processes. CHD1L encodes a multifunctional protein critical for chromatin remodeling, DNA replication, and cell differentiation, with its highest expression localized to the brain and placental tissues [, ]. Specifically, CHD1L haploinsufficiency disrupts normal neuronal differentiation and placental development through chromatin remodeling pathways [], ultimately leading to growth disturbances such as short stature, FGR, and organogenesis defects [, ]. This mechanistic link reinforces that FGR in 1q21 CNVs cases is likely a consequence of CHD1L dosage loss, rather than incidental comorbidity. As reported in the literature, the disruption of CHD1L’s function can lead to a cascade of events that affect placental function and fetal growth, highlighting the importance of this gene in normal development. Ventriculomegaly observed in 1q21 CNVs also linked to CHD1L. Given CHD1L’s highest expression in the brain, where it is pivotal for nervous system development, both CHD1L haploinsufficiency and overexpression can disrupt cortical development and cerebrospinal fluid flow, leading to ventricular dilation [, ]. This further emphasizes the role of CHD1L in Maintaining normal brain development and the consequences of its dysregulation in 1q21.1 CNV cases. GJA5 encodes connexin 40, a gap junction protein essential for cardiac conduction and septal morphogenesis; deletions of GJA5 disrupt intercellular communication in developing heart tissue, increasing risk of congenital heart defects (CHDs) like VSD. This aligns with previous finding that 1q21.1 rearrangements are overrepresented in CHD patients [, , , , ]. Recent research has shown that CNVs contribute to as Many as 10–15% of CHD cases, with 1q21.1 being one of the genomic hotspots recurrently enriched in CHD cohorts []. The specific role of GJA5 in cardiac development Makes it a key gene in understanding the association between 1q21.1 CNVs and CHDs, and our findings further support this established relationship. The absence of ultrasound anomalies in nearly half of our cases underscores the diagnostic challenge posed by this CNV’s variable expressivity, as many manifestations only emerge during postnatal neurodevelopment [, ]. This is consistent with the understanding that 1q21.1 CNVs often have reduced penetrance and pleiotropic effects on brain and heart development []. The complex genetic architecture of these CNVs, along with potential environmental and epigenetic factors, can lead to a wide range of phenotypes that may not be apparent prenatally. De novo CNVs were strongly associated with pregnancy termination, accounting for 80% of TOP decisions—markedly higher than the 11.1% TOP rate observed in inherited 1q21.1 CNV cases (1/9 inherited cases) in our cohort. This finding aligns with studies demonstrating that de novo CNVs are perceived as higher-risk variants due to their unpredictable neurodevelopmental outcomes [, ]. Parental anxiety regarding potential disabilities, coupled with limited prognostic data, likely contributed to the TOP rate. In addition, the incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of 1q21.1 CNVs, as seen in cases where the same CNV can lead to different outcomes within a family, add to the uncertainty. These observations emphasize the need for improved prenatal counseling protocols integrating genomic data, phenotypic severity, and psychosocial factors to support more informed decision making. Our findings underscore the complexities of inherited CNVs and their variable phenotypic expression, particularly highlighted by Cases 8 and 9. The siblings inherited the same 2.1 Mb deletion from a phenotypically normal father but exhibited different prenatal outcomes. Case 8 was referred for prenatal diagnosis at 28 weeks’ gestation due to FGR and short femur, leading to TOP after genetic counseling. Case 9—a subsequent pregnancy in the same family—demonstrated normal ultrasound findings and resulted in a healthy term birth. This prenatal phenotypic discordance within a single family exemplifies the incomplete penetrance characteristic of 1q21.1 CNVs, consistent with recent studies reporting 60–70% incomplete penetrance for neurodevelopmental phenotypes [, , ]. Notably, parents who carried the same 1q21.1 CNV (n = 9 cases) underwent genetic testing to confirm inheritance but did not receive formal cognitive assessments or neurodevelopmental evaluations. Thus, we cannot rule out subtle cognitive impairment in these parents—a limitation that should be addressed in future studies to further clarify the phenotypic spectrum of inherited 1q21.1 CNVs. Our study is limited by its retrospective methodology and modest sample size. Although we did not identify any specific prenatal signs of 1q21.1 CNVs, our findings are consistent with prior reports and comprehensive molecular characterization. Future studies should incorporate long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up and functional analyses of candidate genes (e.g., GJA5, CHD1L) to refine genotype-phenotype correlations. Emerging evidence implicates calcium signaling dysregulation in 1q21.1-associated neuropsychiatric disorders [], offering a potential mechanistic framework for future research. Additionally, larger cohort studies are needed to better understand the full spectrum of phenotypes associated with 1q21.1 CNVs, as well as the factors that contribute to their variable expressivity, such as genetic modifiers, epigenetic changes, and environmental exposures. This will not only improve our understanding of the underlying biology but also enhance prenatal diagnostic accuracy and counseling for families affected by these CNVs.

title: Diagnostic performance of chromosomal microarray and whole exome sequencing in fetal structural anomalies: a single-center retrospective study.
label_reason: CMA/WES in fetuses with sonographic anomalies.
abstract: Fetal structural anomalies detected by prenatal ultrasound were reported in 3–5% of pregnancies, and they range from a single, minor anomaly to multiple systemic anomalies. Tests designed to identify the genetic factors (chromosomal or monogenic) responsible for the vast majority of fetal structural anomalies play a crucial role in prenatal diagnosis. A retrospective analysis was performed to assess the diagnostic yield and clinical efficiency of prenatal chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and whole-exome sequencing (WES) in diagnosis of fetuses with structural anomalies, and to explore genotype–phenotype correlations. We retrospectively analyzed 391 fetuses referred for genetic testing due to sonographically detected structural anomalies. CMA was performed in 310 cases, and WES was conducted in 81 cases with prior negative CMA results. Detected copy number variants (CNVs) and sequence variants were classified according to ACMG guidelines. Cases were stratified into nine phenotypic categories based on ultrasonographic findings. CMA identified pathogenic CNVs in 13/310 cases (4.2%) and variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 13/310 (4.2%). WES revealed pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 18/81 cases (22.2%) and VUS in 9/81 cases (11.1%). The highest diagnostic yield for CMA was observed in fetuses with cardiovascular anomalies (12%), and for WES in those with central nervous system anomalies (46.1%) and skeletal system anomalies (38.8%). Notably, eight novel likely pathogenic variants were identified. Incidental findings were detected in 2 WES cases. CMA and WES provide complementary value in the genetic evaluation of fetal structural anomalies. While CMA remains a robust first-tier test, WES significantly enhances diagnostic yield, especially in cases with negative CMA and specific phenotypic features. Accurate ultrasonographic phenotyping and appropriate test selection are crucial for maximizing diagnostic outcomes in prenatal settings. Keywords: Fetal diagnosis, Genotype-phenotype correlation, Whole-exome sequencing, Fetal anomalies, Chromosome abnormalities
text:
Diagnostic performance of chromosomal microarray and whole exome sequencing in fetal structural anomalies: a single-center retrospective study

Introduction
Introduction Fetal malformations detected by ultrasonographic examination have been reported in approximately 3% of fetuses [–]. Heart defects, skeletal dysplasia, congenital anomalies, genitourinary system anomalies, craniofacial anomalies, and nervous system anomalies are the most common fetal structural anomalies []. Major fetal structural malformations occur in 2–3% of pregnancies and are responsible for approximately 25% of perinatal deaths [, –]. Aneuploidies, chromosomal structural rearrangements, and monogenic diseases are genetic causes that are associated with fetal structural anomalies. Conventional cytogenetic analysis is used as the first step in routine prenatal diagnosis, and the diagnostic value has been reported to be approximately 30% in prenatal samples with fetal ultrasonographic anomalies. The diagnostic value of conventional cytogenetic analysis used to detect chromosomal anomalies in cases with fetal structural abnormalities has been reported to be approximately 30% [, , ]. In the remaining cases, CMA and/or WES tests are used in the next step to detect the etiology of fetal anomalies. Chromosomal microarray, which detects submicroscopic changes not detected by standard karyotyping, contributes 10% to the diagnostic value in structurally malformed fetuses. The diagnostic value of prenatal WES varies between 8.5 and 39.4% in different studies [, ]. The genetic etiology of fetal structural anomalies remains unknown in the majority of cases (more than 60%) []. The data obtained through comprehensive genetic evaluations using tests such as chromosome microarray and whole-exome sequencing will contribute to the establishment of the phenotype-genotype relationship. They will be beneficial for elucidating the pathogenesis and genetic causes of fetal structural anomalies. The diagnostic yield of prenatal WES is primarily determined by accurate indications [–]. With the use of comprehensive studies such as WES and CMA, the number of variants of unknown significance (VUS) is increasing, and it is important to interpret these variants correctly. The pathogenic effects of these variants can be clarified by collecting data from new patients, which will benefit the establishment of phenotype-genotype correlation. It was aimed to evaluate the diagnostic contribution of CMA and WES in a cohort of fetuses with structural anomalies and to assess the genotype–phenotype correlations across major phenotypic categories. We also present novel variants and discuss their relevance to prenatal genetic counseling and decision-making.

Material & method
Material & method Study design and cohort This study was designed as a retrospective study aiming to analyze the genetic data (CMA or WES) of 391 fetuses with structural anomalies detected by prenatal ultrasonography. All cases were referred to a single tertiary center for genetic evaluation between April 2020 and April 2024. CMA was performed in 310 cases, and WES was applied to 81 cases with negative CMA results. Fetuses referred solely due to abnormal serum screening, high-risk non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), maternal anxiety, or familial known variants were excluded. Cases were categorized into nine major phenotypic groups based on ultrasonographic findings: Multisystem anomalies, Cardiovascular anomalies, Skeletal system anomalies, Central nervous system/cranial anomalies, Hydrops fetalis, Increased nuchal translucency (NT), Cystic hygroma, Urogenital anomalies/oligohydramnios, Digestive system anomalies/polyhydramnios (Table ). Sample collection and DNA extraction Genomic DNA was isolated from chorionic villus sampling (CVS), amniotic fluid, fetal tissue, or cord blood using the QIAamp DNA Blood or Tissue Kits (QIAGEN, Germany). Chromosomal microarray analysis Microarray analysis of fetal genomic DNA samples from 310 fetuses was performed using the Affymetrix Cytoscan Optima kit by the Affymetrix CytoScan test (Life Technologies, USA) and the Illumina HumanCytoSNP-12 kit (Life Technologies, USA) by the Illumina Iscan platform. Analysis of the array data was performed using Chromosome Analysis Suite software and BlueFuse software. Analysis of the obtained data and evaluation of pathogenicity were performed using DECIPHER, Database of Genomic Variants (DGV), ClinVar, and Franklin Genoox programs. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) Whole-exome sequencing was conducted using both the MGI DNBSEQ-G400 (MGI Tech, China) and Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, USA) platforms. Library preparation was performed using the Twist Exome 2.0 kit. The generated libraries were sequenced aiming to achieve a minimum of 20x read depth for more than 98% of the targeted bases. Sequencing data were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38 using Franklin Genoox software (https://franklin.genoox.com/clinical-db/home). Bioinformatic analysis of Whole-exome sequencing data was performed using the Franklin by Genoox Analysis program. Variant annotation and filtering were performed using a comprehensive set of public databases (ClinVar, the Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD), dbSNP), as well as population frequency datasets (Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC),1000 Genomes Project). Functional predictions were assessed using in silico tools, including PolyPhen-2, SIFT, MutationAssessor, and SpliceAI. Variant classification Variant classification was performed based on ACMG recommendations using a combination of standardized evidence criteria established to assess the pathogenic impact of the variant. These criteria include PVS1 (variants in genes where the disease mechanism is loss-of-function), PM2 (extremely rare variants not found in population databases or with low population frequency), and PP3 (variants suggested by many prediction tools to have a deleterious effect). Considering the data from functional studies, variant location and segregation analysis results, additional criteria such as PS1, PM1, and PP1 were also applied. Each variant’s classification as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, or variant of uncertain significance (VUS) was determined by integrating these evidence codes following ACMG recommendations []. The detected variants were classified as ‘Pathogenic,’ ‘Likely pathogenic,’ ‘Variant of unknown clinical significance (VUS),’ ‘Likely Benign,’ or ‘Benign’ according to specific ACMG/AMP guidelines []. Only pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and clinically relevant VUS variants were reported. Variants unrelated to the referral phenotype (e.g., neurodevelopmental disorders not detectable prenatally) were categorized as incidental findings. Pretest counselling was conducted to ensure that the fetal incidental findings, which are defined in the ACMG guideline, will be reported. The reporting criteria for fetal incidental findings were done according to ACMG guidelines []. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using Fisher’s exact test. The significance of differences in the diagnostic yield of chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and whole exome sequencing (WES) tests among phenotypic groups was assessed statistically. Statistical comparisons were made both at the overall level and within each of the nine defined phenotypic categories. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results Study cohort A total of 391 fetuses with sonographically identified structural anomalies were included. CMA was performed in 310 cases, and WES was applied in 81 fetuses with previously negative CMA results. The most common referral indications for CMA were multisystem anomalies (23.5%), cardiovascular anomalies (16%), and increased nuchal translucency (11.2%), respectively. The most common referral indications for WES were multisystem anomalies (25.9%), skeletal system anomalies (22.2%), and hydrops fetalis (16%), respectively. Diagnostic yield of chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) Of the 310 fetuses who underwent CMA, CNVs were detected in 26 cases (8.3%). Pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNVs were found in 13 cases (4.2%), and variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in another 13 cases (4.2%) (Table ). The highest diagnostic yield was observed in cardiovascular anomalies (12%), multisystem anomalies (9.5%), skeletal anomalies (8.8%), and increased NT (8.5%). The lowest yield was found in fetuses with digestive system anomalies (4.1%, 1/24) and cystic hygroma (6.6%, 1/15). The diagnostic rates of the detected variants according to phenotypic categories were represented in Table . Three cases were diagnosed with established CNV syndromes, including 9q34.3 deletion (Kleefstra syndrome), 15q13.3 microdeletion syndrome, and 22q11.21 microduplication syndrome (Table ). Deletions/duplications were detected in 26 of 310 patients: 13 deletions (6 pathogenic/likely pathogenic, 7 VUS) and 13 duplications (7 pathogenic/likely pathogenic, 6 VUS). In one case, the patient had two different copy number variants. The smallest chromosomal abnormality was a 195 kb heterozygous deletion of the 16q24.1 region, and the largest abnormality was a 34.5 MB heterozygous duplication of the 12p13.33p11.1 region. The maximum size of pathogenic/likely pathogenic deletions was 14.1 MB. The smallest size of pathogenic/likely pathogenic deletions was 618 kb. The maximum size of pathogenic/likely pathogenic duplications was 34.5 MB, and the smallest size of pathogenic/likely pathogenic duplications was found to be 514 kb. Diagnostic yield of whole exome sequencing (WES) Among the 81 WES cases, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were detected in 18 fetuses (22.2%). An additional nine fetuses (11.1%) carried VUS. The overall yield of reportable variants (pathogenic + VUS) was 33.3%. The highest diagnostic yield was observed in central nervous system anomalies (46.1%), skeletal anomalies (38.8%), hydrops fetalis (33.3%), and multisystem anomalies (28.5%). No pathogenic variants were detected in fetuses with isolated increased NT or cystic hygroma. The diagnostic rates of the detected variants according to phenotypic categories were represented in Table . A total of 34 different variants in 30 genes were detected in 27 of 81 cases: three frameshift, four stop gain, five splicing variants, twenty-one missense variants, and 1 Non-frameshift insertion/deletion variant. A compound heterozygous variant was detected in 1 case. Autosomal dominant (AD) conditions were detected in 11 of 20 cases, autosomal recessive (AR) conditions in 18 cases, X-linked recessive (XLR) conditions in 1 case, and X-linked dominant (XLD) conditions in 1 case (Table ). Details of individual gene variants, associated phenotypes, and ACMG classifications are presented in Table . Incidental pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants unrelated to the fetal phenotype were identified in 2 WES cases (2.4%). These included variants in PKD1 and CFTR, not associated with any prenatal ultrasound findings in the respective fetuses. Statistical comparison of diagnostic yields Statistical analysis revealed that there were significant differences in diagnostic yields between CMA and WES in all phenotypic groups (p < 0.05 for each comparison). The overall diagnostic yield for pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants was significantly higher in the WES cohort (22.2%) compared to the CMA cohort (4.2%) (p < 0.001). WES demonstrated markedly higher yields in fetuses with central nervous system anomalies (46.1% vs. 5.5%, p < 0.001), skeletal anomalies (38.8% vs. 8.8%, p < 0.001), and hydrops fetalis (33.3% vs. 8.0%, p < 0.001). In contrast, for fetuses with isolated increased nuchal translucency or cystic hygroma, WES identified no pathogenic variants, at the same time CMA contributed limited findings (8.5% and 6.6%, respectively), with both differences remaining statistically significant (p = 0.004 and p = 0.019).

Discussion
Discussion This study retrospectively analyzed the clinical and genotypic findings of 391 prenatal cases with fetal structural anomalies. CMA yielded pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.2% of cases, and this result aligns with prior studies, which have reported CMA diagnostic yields between 4% and 10% in fetuses with sonographic anomalies [, ]. The highest yield was observed in fetuses with cardiovascular anomalies (12%), consistent with prior reports supporting CMA as a first-tier test for congenital heart defects [, , ]. Interestingly, the overall VUS rate in our CMA cohort (4.2%) was slightly higher than the 1.6–3.4% reported in earlier studies, potentially reflecting higher resolution platforms and broader database integration [, –]. Lowest diagnostic rates of CNVs were observed for gastrointestinal system anomalies (4.1%, 1/24). Notably, 11.5% of CNV-positive cases were consistent with known CNV syndromes, including Kleefstra syndrome, 15q13.3 microdeletion, and 22q11.2 duplication syndrome, emphasizing the clinical relevance of submicroscopic chromosomal imbalances. 15q13.3 Microdeletion syndrome was detected in a case with the right aortic arch anomaly. 15q13.3 Microdeletion syndrome is characterized by a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders with no or mild dysmorphological features. We detected a 9q34 microdeletion in a case with pes equinovarus. 9q34 microdeletion causes Kleefstra syndrome, which is characterized by intellectual disability, hypotonia, speech delay, autism spectrum disorder, dysmorphic facial features, and varying additional clinical features. 22q11.2 duplication syndrome was detected in cases with micrognathia and nasal hypoplasia. 22q11.2 duplication syndrome is characterized by a highly variable phenotype, and one of the phenotypic features is micrognathia, which was presented in our case. Pathogenic/possibly pathogenic incidental copy number variants were detected in 8 cases. Among the cases with incidental findings—variants not related to the fetal ultrasound anomalies—two patients were diagnosed with CNV syndromes. WES achieved a diagnostic yield of 22.2% for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, with the highest rates seen in central nervous system anomalies (46.1%) and skeletal anomalies (38.8%). Negative WES results were observed in cases with increased NT and cystic hygroma because the majority of fetuses presenting with increased nuchal translucency (NT) or cystic hygroma are typically diagnosed through CMA or conventional karyotyping. Consequently, the likelihood of identifying additional monogenic causes via WES in these cases is reduced. The low diagnostic yield observed in the WES group with increased NT or cystic hygroma in our study may primarily be due to the prior exclusion of cases already diagnosed by CMA. This reflects the typical clinical workflow where WES is generally considered as a secondary test following negative CMA results. Similarly, Daum et al. (2019) reported a 25% diagnostic yield in fetuses with structural anomalies referred for exome sequencing, with the highest yields observed in those with multiple malformations and brain anomalies []. No pathogenic variants were detected in fetuses with isolated increased nuchal translucency, consistent with our findings. These results support the selective use of WES based on specific phenotypic features to maximize diagnostic efficiency. The current study’s pathogenic diagnostic rate for prenatal WES analysis was consistent with previous studies’ diagnostic rates (ranging from 10 to 30%) [–, ]. These results are aligned with meta-analyses and cohort studies that highlight the superior yield of WES in fetuses with single-system or syndromic malformations, especially when conventional tests are non-diagnostic [–, ]. Several studies give different diagnostic rates, which were affected by several factors such as cohort size variant interpretation, and prenatal indications (Table ) [, –] Consistent with recent literature higher diagnostic rates of WES were observed in cases with musculoskeletal anomalies (38,8%,7/18) and central nervous system anomalies (46,1%, 6/13) [, –]. The results reaffirm the role of WES in the evaluation of monogenic disorders in these systems. VUS and incidental findings in prenatal exome sequencing can create challenges in genetic counseling due to uncertainty in their clinical meaning []. This uncertainty may affect parental decision-making and cause anxiety. To address this, segregation analysis was recommended for all patients with VUS, and the parents were informed about VUS variant reporting by pretest counselling. Additionally, in line with guidelines, only VUS variants related to fetal ultrasound findings or family history were reported []. This approach helps to minimize unnecessary concern and supports clearer counseling. Overall, careful communication and follow-up studies are essential to manage the complexities of VUS in prenatal diagnosis. The VUS rate in our WES cohort was 11.1%, within the expected range of 10–20% reported in recent studies [, , ]. While interpretation challenges remain, especially in prenatal settings with limited phenotype information, integrating databases and cross-referencing with parental data may reduce uncertainty. In our prenatal exome sequencing cohort, incidental findings unrelated to fetal ultrasonographic anomalies were identified in two cases. These variants were not associated with the observed fetal phenotype but were detected as part of the comprehensive exome analysis. Incidental sequence variants predicted to be unrelated to referral reasons were detected in 2 cases with PKD1 and CFTR gene variants. The case with a likely pathogenic heterozygous PKD1 gene variant had central nervous system anomalies but no polycystic kidneys. The other incidental variant was found in the CFTR gene. Still, the fetus had no prenatal findings of cystic fibrosis, such as echogenic bowel, the absence of the gallbladder, and dilated bowel. Fetal ultrasonographic findings of this case with incidental CFTR gene variants were arthrogryposis, camptodactyly, and hydrops fetalis. No variant relevant to fetal ultrasonographic findings was detected in this case, but homozygous Class 3 CFTR gene variants were detected. 12 likely pathogenic variants in PKP2, ROR2, FKRP, GALNS, RYR1, INPPL1, CSF1R, SLC26A3, B9D2, NOTCH1, PKD1, MED12 genes were detected in our study. Among the 12 likely pathogenic variants identified, eight variants are novel, as they have not been previously reported in the scientific literature or recorded in any public variant databases. The remaining four variants have been documented solely in public databases but lack representation in published studies. The discovery of novel variants associated with fetal structural anomalies shows that WES analysis is a powerful tool for establishing the phenotype-genotype relationship in prenatal diagnosis. For example, the NOTCH1 novel variant was found in fetuses with increased NT and choroid plexus cysts at early gestation. NOTCH1 causes autosomal dominant Adams-Oliver syndrome (OMIM:616028) and Aortic valve disease (OMIM: 109730). The cardiac anomaly (aortic stenosis) was manifested in the following weeks of late pregnancy. The mother has a ventricular septal defect, and the mother’s sister has a bicuspid aortic valve. No genetic study had been done before for these patients, and we also found that they have the same variant. The baby was born with severe cardiac anomalies (severe aortic anomalies), and the phenotype was more severe than that of the mother and maternal aunt. Identifying novel variants and their entry into the databases will help predict how these variants will give ultrasonographic findings in the prenatal period. The identification of incidental variants in genes such as PKD1 and CFTR highlights one of the major dilemmas of prenatal exome sequencing—how to manage findings unrelated to the referral phenotype. Although such variants may not immediately affect prenatal decision-making, they have potential implications for postnatal follow-up and genetic counseling. Current professional guidelines suggest that such results should be discussed during pretest counseling, and our findings support that recommendation []. Although the significant contribution of WES and CMA analysis to prenatal diagnosis cannot be ignored, VUS variants and incidental variants can cause difficulties in counseling and prenatal decision-making. The significant differences in diagnostic yields between CMA and WES across all phenotypic subgroups underscore the complementary roles of these technologies in prenatal diagnosis. WES offered substantially higher diagnostic returns in cases involving the central nervous system, skeletal system, and hydrops fetalis. These findings statistically validate the phenotypic prioritization of WES as a second-tier test following negative CMA results. Interestingly, the absence of the diagnostic findings in WES for fetuses with isolated increased NT and cystic hygroma supports previous literature suggesting limited monogenic etiology in these isolated findings. The statistical significance of these observations reinforces the clinical utility of phenotype-driven testing strategies. A significant strength of this study is the relatively large, well-characterized cohort and the standardized classification of ultrasound phenotypes. Furthermore, the combined use of CMA and WES enables a layered diagnostic approach that reflects real-world clinical practice. However, there are several limitations. The study is single-center and retrospective, which may limit generalizability. First, due to its retrospective design, not all patients underwent both chromosomal microarray (CMA) and whole-exome sequencing (WES). WES was performed only in a subset of cases based on DNA availability, clinical prioritization, and parental consent. Consequently, a significant portion of CMA-negative cases were not further evaluated by WES, which may have limited the assessment of the actual added value of exome sequencing. Fu et al. (2018) conducted a study with a design similar to ours, where not all CMA-negative cases underwent WES []. Among 3949 fetuses, 18.2% had abnormal karyotypes. In those with normal karyotypes, CMA identified pathogenic CNVs in 8.2% (138/1680). WES was performed in a selected subgroup of 196 fetuses with normal karyotype and CMA results, revealing likely diagnostic variants in 24% of cases. These results support the added value of WES following normal CMA, even when applied to a selected group. Second, although the combined use of CMA and WES is emphasized as a layered diagnostic approach, in this study, the two methods were applied to different patient subgroups. This may have introduced a degree of non-uniformity in phenotype distribution across diagnostic categories, potentially affecting the generalizability of some conclusions. Our study categorized cases into phenotypic groups comprising both isolated and non-isolated structural anomalies. Previous literature has shown that diagnostic yields differ significantly between isolated and non-isolated anomalies, with isolated cases typically having lower yields. The predominance of non-isolated cases in our cohort may have therefore influenced the overall diagnostic yield reported for each group. Future studies with larger and more balanced cohorts are needed to perform stratified analyses better to understand the impact of anomaly complexity on diagnostic outcomes. Additionally, the accuracy of genotype-phenotype correlations is dependent on the quality and timing of prenatal imaging. Some cases had limited sonographic data, particularly in early gestation, which may affect variant interpretation. Despite these limitations, our findings support the routine integration of CMA and WES into the prenatal diagnostic workflow for fetuses with structural anomalies. The identification of both known and novel pathogenic variants enhances our understanding of fetal phenotypes, facilitates informed reproductive decision-making, and contributes to the expansion of prenatal variant databases.

Conclusion
Conclusion This study demonstrates that the combined application of chromosomal microarray analysis and whole-exome sequencing provides substantial diagnostic value in pregnancies complicated by fetal structural anomalies. CMA remains a valuable first-tier test, particularly in cases with cardiovascular and multisystem anomalies. WES significantly enhances the diagnostic yield, especially in fetuses with central nervous system and skeletal malformations, and contributes to novel gene discovery and genotype–phenotype correlation. Our findings support the integration of WES into routine prenatal diagnostic protocols, especially when CMA is uninformative and detailed phenotyping is available. As genomic technologies and variant interpretation frameworks evolve, their clinical implementation will further refine prenatal counseling, risk assessment, and pregnancy management. CMA and WES are powerful and complementary tools for prenatal genetic diagnosis. In our cohort, WES significantly increased diagnostic yield in cases with negative CMA results, particularly in central nervous system and skeletal anomalies. The integration of both tests enhances genotype-phenotype correlations and offers critical insights for clinical management. Future studies with prospective designs and larger cohorts are needed to define further optimal diagnostic strategies and the clinical utility of prenatal exome sequencing.

title: Exome Sequencing Analysis and Clinical Features of a Chinese Patient with 3M Syndrome and A Review of Literature.
label_reason: Prenatal increased NT noted but WES done postnatally on child.
abstract: 3M syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by significant intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction. There is limited research on its genetic basis within the Chinese population. We performed trio-based whole-exome sequencing to identify the pathogenic gene in the affected child and collected and organized clinical and imaging data. Relevant information was reviewed through a literature search. In this study, we present a case involving prenatal diagnostic abnormalities and postnatal confirmation of 3M syndrome, including detailed documentation of clinical features and associated genetic variants. Notably, during prenatal ultrasound examination, the fetus exhibited increased nuchal translucency (NT) and delayed limb development. Postnatally, whole-exome sequencing revealed the compound heterozygous mutations in the CUL7 gene: c.3646–2A>G and c.3355+5G>A. The splicing mutation c.3646–2A>G is a novel pathogenic mutation, while the c.3355+5G>A mutation has been previously reported. In-silico analysis predicted strong pathogenicity for both splicing mutations. Through follow-up, we observed that the patient’s height and weight are below the first percentile, with abnormal skeletal development and distinctive facial features. Based on literature review of reported cases, these mutations disrupt the normal function of CUL7-OBSL1-CCDC8 complex in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, leading to impaired growth regulation. This study identified a novel splicing mutation in the CUL7 gene in a patient with 3M syndrome, expanding the genetic spectrum of this disorder and contributing novel insights for clinical diagnosis and management.
