Prenatal diagnosis of fetuses with ultrasound soft markers

Introduction
Introduction The soft markers of the fetus are nonspecific, slight, and often temporary variations in fetal structure, including increased nuchal translucency (NT), absent nasal bone, choroid plexus cyst, short femur, mild ventriculomegaly, tricuspid regurgitation, aberrant right subclavian artery, echogenic bowel []. The incidence of isolated soft markers in normal fetuses is about 10% []. These markers often appear during a particular stage of fetal growth and development, and commonly resolve in the third trimester of pregnancy, but they may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities [, ]. Amniocentesis stands as the principal modality for prenatal genetic diagnosis, with a decades-long trajectory of clinical implementation. Although existing studies have demonstrated that this invasive procedure does not significantly increase the risk of pregnancy loss before 24 weeks of gestation, its clinical adoption remains constrained by procedural invasiveness []. Previous studies have investigated the prenatal diagnosis of cases with abnormal ultrasound soft markers, the clinical decision regarding whether pregnant women presenting ultrasound soft markers should undergo invasive diagnostic genetic testing remains complex [–]. Multiple modalities are currently available for chromosomal abnormality detection. As the gold standard for prenatal diagnosis, karyotype analysis enables reliable detection of aneuploidies. Meanwhile, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) based on comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) arrays and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays demonstrate superior performance in detecting copy number variations (CNVs) and uniparental disomy (UPD) [, ]. However, the optimal diagnostic strategy for pregnant women presenting with abnormal ultrasound soft markers remains to be determined. To provide further reference information, we have reviewed prenatal diagnosis cases from January 2019 to December 2021, focusing specifically on those with ultrasound soft markers for comprehensive analysis. Our primary objective is to investigate associations between ultrasound soft markers and fetal chromosomal abnormalities, and to compare the diagnostic performance of karyotype analysis versus CMA. The findings of this study will offer invaluable references for prenatal genetic counseling, guiding decisions on the necessity of prenatal diagnosis and the selection of appropriate methods in relevant cases.

Methods
Methods Participants The study retrospectively analyzed cases at the Dalian Women and Children’s Medical Center (Group) from January 2019 to December 2021, specifically focusing on pregnant women who underwent amniocentesis for genetic testing after fetal ultrasound examinations revealed the presence of soft markers. Notably, pregnant women with confirmed fetal structural abnormalities were excluded from this study. Ultrasound examination In our center, the ultrasound soft markers were identified during the first-trimester (11 ~ 13 weeks + 6 days) and second-trimester (20 ~ 24 weeks) scans (GE Voluson E8; GE Voluson E10). All ultrasound examinations were performed in strict accordance with the standardized protocols established by the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) and the Ultrasound Branch of the Chinese Medical Association [, ]. The ultrasound soft markers analyzed included: increased NT (11w ~ 13w + 6, ≥ 3.0 mm), absent nasal bone (including unilateral and bilateral absence), choroid plexus cyst (> 2 mm), short femur length (≤ 10 percentile), mild ventriculomegaly (≥ 10 mm and < 13 mm), tricuspid regurgitation, aberrant right subclavian artery, echogenic bowel (echo intensity equal to or exceeding that of adjacent bone), single umbilical artery, echogenic intracardiac focus, reversed A-wave in the ductus venosus, umbilical cord cyst, persistent right umbilical vein and pyelic separation (≥ 4 mm). The ultrasound soft markers evaluated in the first trimester include increased NT, absent nasal bone, reversed A-wave in the ductus venosus, and single umbilical artery. The remaining markers were assessed during the second trimester. Genetic counseling For cases with ultrasound soft marker anomalies detected in the first trimester, non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) or amniocentesis were recommended []. For soft marker anomalies identified in the second trimester, amniocentesis was primarily recommended. Amniocentesis was optimally performed between 18 and 24 weeks of gestation. Procedures outside this window required rigorous risk-benefit evaluation and multidisciplinary review, with emphasis on maternal-fetal safety and procedural feasibility. All participants must be duly informed about the potential for false-positive and false-negative outcomes in NIPT []. Additionally, participants were informed that amniocentesis carries potential complications including fetal loss, premature rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, fetal injury, and severe maternal complications, though the incidence rates of these adverse events are extremely low [, ]. For pregnant women with contraindications to invasive prenatal diagnosis, including threatened abortion, bleeding diathesis, active chronic pathogen infection, or Rh-negative blood type, amniocentesis is contraindicated. Instead, NIPT is suggested as an alternative []. All participants voluntarily chose whether to undergo amniocentesis after providing informed consent. Chromosome karyotype analysis The procedure involves collecting 20mL of the amniotic fluid from each patient under the ultrasound guidance (GE Voluson E10). For each sample, a minimum of 20 karyotypes were selected for counting, and an additional 5 karyotypes were selected for further detailed analysis, in accordance with the guidelines outlined in the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN 2016). The abnormalities diagnosed using chromosome karyotype analysis included aneuploidy, deletions, duplications, mosaicism, balanced and unbalanced translocations, inversions, small supernumerary marker chromosomes. However, chromosomal polymorphism was excluded from the diagnosis (relevant cases presented in Supplement Table 3). CMA For each case, 10mL of amniotic fluid was selected. The procedure was carried out in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines, as detailed in our previously published work []. Annotation was performed using the Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 37 (GRCh37), and the database utilized for data analysis has been detailed in our previous research []. The interpretation of CNVs was based on the consensus guidelines provided by the American College of Medical Genetics and Clinical Genome Resource (ACMG-ClinGen). CNVs were divided into five categories: pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign and benign. The study primarily focuses on the discussion of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CNVs as well as uniparental disomies (UPDs). Pregnancy outcomes and postnatal follow-up All cases underwent follow-up on pregnancy outcomes via telephone interviews and medical record reviews. For cases with abnormal prenatal diagnostic results who were born, a secondary follow-up was conducted at 3–5 years of age through telephone and in-person interviews to evaluate postnatal health examination outcomes, including systematic physical examinations, organ-specific functional assessments, metabolic/hematological testing, and neurobehavioral development evaluations. Statistical processing Statistical analysis was conducted using statistical software SPSS19.0. The forest plot was generated using R software (version 3.6.0). The count data were statistically described as the number of cases (percentage) [n (%)]. For the statistical analysis, cases of aneuploidy combined CNVs and aneuploidy combined translocation were classified into the aneuploid group. The chi-square (χ²) test or Fisher’s exact test was used to compare the prevalence of abnormal ultrasound markers across different prenatal diagnosis outcomes. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis were selected for multifactorial binary logistic regression and presented through a forest plot, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

Results
Results Case profiles The total number of cases was 622, including 545 cases in the isolated soft marker group and 77 cases in the multiple soft markers group. The average maternal age was 31.6 years, with a range of 19 to 43 years, while the average gestational age for prenatal diagnosis was 20w + 6, ranging from 17w to 28w + 3. Among our cohort, the majority of cases belonged to the increased NT group (294/622, 47.27%), followed by the absent nasal bone group (70/622, 11.25%) and the choroid plexus cyst group (48/622, 7.72%) (shown in Fig. ; Table ). Phenotypic characteristics of 622 prenatal cases Prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities In our cohort, the overall prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities was 11.41% (71/622). The chi-square (χ²) test or Fisher’s exact test revealed that increased NT, echogenic intracardiac focus, and multiple soft markers might be associated with chromosomal abnormalities (shown in Table ). Further multifactorial binary logistic regression analysis and the forest plot validated that echogenic intracardiac focus, particularly multiple soft markers, demonstrated a highly significant correlation with chromosomal abnormalities (shown in Table ; Fig. ). In the echogenic intracardiac focus group, trisomy 21 was identified in 1 case, while complex chromosomal mosaicism accounted for the remaining 2 cases. In the multiple soft markers group, 19 cases of trisomy 21, 5 cases of trisomy 18, 1 case of balanced translocation were identified, with no CNVs detected (shown in Table ). Statistical analysis using the χ² test revealed a significant difference in the proportions of aneuploidies between isolated and multiple soft marker groups (χ² = 38.519, P < 0.001). In contrast, no significant difference was observed in the rate of CNVs between these groups. Forest plot of abnormal ultrasound soft markers vs. prenatal diagnosis outcomes Results of chromosome karyotype analysis A total of 63 cases of the abnormality were diagnosed by the chromosome karyotype analysis with the prevalence of 10.13% (63/622). The largest number of these abnormalities was 47,XN,+21, followed by 47,XN,+18. Apart from aneuploidies, some special chromosomal abnormalities were diagnosed. There were two cases of complex chromosomal mosaicism, namely mos45,X[4]/47,XYY[38]/46,XY[5] and mos45,X[2]/47,XXX[2]/46,XX[57]. Five cases were diagnosed as balanced translocation. Two additional cases were aneuploidy combined translocation, both of which were 46,XX, rob(13;21)(q10;q10),+21. Meanwhile, one small supernumerary marker chromosome was detected, and further testing was required to identify its origin (shown in Table ). Results of CMA CMA was performed on 622 prenatal cases with ultrasound soft markers, resulting in the prevalence of 10.45% (65/622). There were 55 cases of aneuploidies, 1 case of the aneuploidy combined pathogenic CNVs, 6 cases of pathogenic CNVs, and 3 cases of likely pathogenic CNVs. The CNVs were associated with duplications of 17q12, 12p13.33p11.23, 16p13.11; deletions of 16p13.12p13.11, 3q29, 16p11.2, 15q11.2 and Xp22.31. The cases diagnosed with pathogenic or likely pathogenic CNVs had ultrasonic phenotypes that included tricuspid regurgitation, increased NT, absent nasal bone, and choroid plexus cyst (shown in Table ). Resulting comparison of the chromosome karyotype analysis and CMA In this study, all cases underwent chromosome karyotype analysis and CMA. In most cases, the results of the two tests were consistent, but there were still some cases with different results (shown in Table ). For instance, five balanced translocations (cases 1 ~ 5) and one pseudodiploid (case 6) were missed by CMA. In addition, two cases with CMA results of “arr(21)×3” were supplemented by karyotyping (cases 7 and 8). However, compared to karyotype analysis, CMA diagnosed 9 cases of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CNVs (cases 9 to 17) and supplemented a case initially diagnosed as aneuploidy by karyotype analysis, revealing the presence of both aneuploidy and pathogenic CNV in this case (case 18). It was noteworthy that case 15 was initially diagnosed as a small supernumerary marker chromosome by karyotype analysis and was identified as arr[GRCh37]12p13.33p11.23(173786-27350550) x4 by CMA. Results of pregnancy outcomes and postnatal follow-up A follow-up was conducted on the pregnancy outcomes of all 622 cases, confirming the outcomes of 604 cases (excluding 18 lost to follow-up in the prenatal diagnostic negative group). In the group with abnormal prenatal diagnostic results, one case resulted in stillbirth (prenatal ultrasound indicated absent nasal bone), 59 cases underwent termination of pregnancy, and 11 cases resulted in live birth (shown in Fig. ; Table ). Secondary follow-up at 3–5 years of age was conducted for the 11 live-born cases, revealing no significant phenotypic abnormalities. Follow-up of pregnancy outcomes

Discussion
Discussion This study focuses on the prenatal diagnosis of fetuses with soft markers using the chromosome karyotype analysis and CMA. The overall prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities was found to be 11.41% (71/622), which was consistent with the previous study performed by Cai et al. (10.17%) []. Furthermore, our data demonstrate that the prevalence of chromosomal aneuploidy is significantly higher in the multiple soft marker group compared to the isolated soft marker group. Additionally, through statistical analysis, it was found that the echogenic intracardiac focus may exhibit a correlation with chromosomal abnormalities. However, the number of related cases in this study is limited. Therefore, while this result has heightened our attention to the echogenic intracardiac focus, the current cases are insufficient to support the conclusion regarding its correlation with chromosomal abnormalities, and further validation with a larger cohort remains necessary. For increased NT, existing literature has reported a significant association with chromosomal abnormalities []. While a certain correlation was observed in this study, it did not reach statistical significance, indicating the need for further investigation with a larger sample size. Based on the finding of this study and existing literature, special attention should be paid to cases with multiple soft markers, echogenic intracardiac focus, the absent nasal bone and the increased NT [, , , ]. For these cases, the invasive diagnostic genetic testing should not be ignored. 5 cases of balanced translocations were diagnosed by chromosome karyotype analysis, and all of them had normal CMA results. This finding offers valuable reference for future reproductive health strategies of these individuals as they mature. Furthermore, the potential risks associated with balanced translocation should be addressed during prenatal genetic counseling. For example, the Philadelphia chromosome, characterized by ABL1-BCR fusion at translocation breakpoints, plays a critical role in leukemogenesis [, ]. In addition, a 46,XX, t(4;7)(q27;p22) case with PCDH10 and TNRC18 mutations at the translocation breakpoint presented neurodevelopmental delay, facial dysmorphism and high myopia []. Therefore, it is essential to assess the inheritance pattern and the family history, and gene sequencing of breakpoints should be considered for fetuses with de novo mutations. In this study, three of the five cases of the balanced translocation underwent parental genetic verification, and all of them were de novo mutations. Among the five cases, only one underwent pregnancy termination, while the remaining four demonstrated normal physical development during the 3–5year follow-up period. Certainly, their physical condition will be monitored continuously. In the current study, a limited number of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CNVs were identified, notably including two cases of 16p11.2 deletion syndrome and two cases of 16p13.11 duplication. The 16p11.2 deletion syndrome is mainly manifested as intellectual disability, developmental delay, epilepsy, overweight and spinal deformity, while skeletal deformity, cardiovascular deformity and central nervous system deformity are the predominant phenotypes in fetal period [, ]. In this study, both cases of 16p11.2 deletion were associated with increased NT, so as to supplement the fetal phenotype of 16p11.2 deletion cases. The 16p13.11 duplication is a neuro susceptible locus, and the clinical phenotype of patients mainly involves neurological diseases, such as schizophrenia []. Although few cases of 16p13.11 duplication fetuses have described phenotypes such as echogenic bowel and corpus callosum agenesis, no established consensus on clinical features exists [, ]. Notably, both 16p13.11 duplication cases in this study exhibited choroid plexus cysts, suggesting this finding as a potentially significant fetal phenotype. Both cases were delivered without complications, and a 3-year follow-up revealed no abnormal phenotypic features. However, given the 3-year follow-up limitation, delayed-onset manifestations cannot be entirely ruled out; thus, extended follow-up remains essential. Additionally, CMA analysis revealed 40 chromosomal variations classified as VUS, including 36 CNVs and 4 UPDs (shown in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Given that these variations are classified as VUS and the case presented in this article only involves abnormal ultrasound soft markers, we exercise caution in prenatal interpretations and do not definitively categorize them as chromosomal abnormalities. However, for reference, we present the ultrasound phenotype and CMA results, believing that they will contribute to the accumulation of information regarding the pathogenicity of these variants. It is noteworthy that this study detected 4 UPDs. CMA, which combines array-CGH and SNP-array, is not only capable of diagnosing CNVs but also UPDs, and performs well in prenatal diagnosis. In recent years, prenatal diagnosis has seen advancements with the introduction of the whole exome sequencing (WES) [, ]. Nevertheless, prenatal WES, as a phenotype-dependent testing, is not a routine detection method for detecting fetuses with abnormal ultrasound soft markers. According to the expert consensus, cases with abnormal soft markers are considered for WES testing only when increased NT, especially NT > 4 mm or multiple soft markers are present []. Therefore, CMA and karyotype analysis remain the main methods for prenatal diagnosis of fetuses with ultrasound soft markers []. Karyotype analysis has the advantages of intuitionistic analysis, especially in the diagnosis of aneuploidy, mosaicism, and chromosomal translocation. CMA can effectively compensate for the problem of low resolution of karyotype analysis, and can detect additional microdeletion, microduplication and UPDs. The combined use of these two tests can help reduce the risk of missing pathogenic variants.

Conclusions
Conclusions In conclusion, the study underscores the importance for pregnant women who exhibit ultrasound soft markers, particularly those with multiple soft markers, to proactively seek prenatal genetic diagnosis. The synergistic combination of CMA and chromosomal karyotype analysis has proven to be a potent tool in elucidating the underlying genetic factors associated with these soft markers, thereby enabling more informed medical decision-making and tailored care.

label_reason: Fetal CHD cohort with WGS and exome.
abstract:
Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a leading cause of infant morbidity and mortality in China, creating a significant healthcare burden. While prenatal diagnosis via fetal echocardiography is routine, it is prone to missed diagnoses, highlighting the need to explore genetic mechanisms for improved diagnostics and management. This retrospective study analyzed 412 fetuses diagnosed with CHD through echocardiography between December 2021 and March 2024. All parents received prenatal genetic counseling and provided informed consent for ultrasound-guided procedures. Genetic testing included Medium-Coverage Whole Genome Sequencing (CMA-seq) and Clinical Exome Sequencing (CES). CHD cases were stratified into simple or complex forms according to established pediatric cardiology criteria. Pathogenic variants were detected with CMA-seq and CES. Genetic abnormalities were found in 36.4% (150/412) of fetuses (P/LP + VUS), while the P/LP-only diagnostic yield was 19.4% (80/412). Detection was higher in non-isolated CHD cases (47.3%) compared to isolated cases (31.3%). Aneuploidies such as Trisomy 21 and 18 were commonly detected. Pathogenic copy-number variants (CNVs) were most frequent in right- and left-ventricular outflow tract obstructions. CES enhanced the detection of single nucleotide variants, particularly in complex CHD. Integrating CMA-seq and CES enhances prenatal CHD diagnosis by uncovering genetic etiologies, improving accuracy, and supporting personalized management strategies.

Medium-coverage whole genome sequencing (CMA-seq) combined with clinical exome sequencing (CES) achieved an overall genetic detection rate of 36.4% (P/LP + VUS) and a P/LP-only diagnostic yield of 19.4% (80/412) in 412 fetuses with congenital heart disease, with notably higher rates in complex and non-isolated CHD cases. CMA-seq detected pathogenic CNVs as small as 100 kb, covering over half of the clinically significant variants, while CES identified 60 pathogenic SNVs/indels involving key genes such as DNAH family genes, GATA, and MTHFR. Non-isolated CHD showed significantly higher rates of genetic abnormalities than isolated CHD (47.3% vs 31.3%, χ² p = 0.0017), with the highest yields observed in heterotaxy and anomalous pulmonary venous connection, suggesting stronger genetic contributions.
text:
Prenatal diagnostic value of medium-coverage WGS and clinical Exome sequencing in fetal congenital heart disease

Introduction
Introduction Congenital heart disease (CHD) refers to structural or functional abnormalities of the heart or great vessels due to underdevelopment during early embryonic development. Approximately 1.35 million children with CHD are born worldwide each year []. CHD has become a widely occurring congenital birth defect and is one of the major causes of noninfectious death in newborns []. The incidence of CHD varies in different countries or regions, with a prevalence rate of about 8.2‰ among live births in Europe, while in China the prevalence rate is slightly higher, at around 8.98‰ [] and is increasing annually. The total economic cost of newly diagnosed CHD over a lifetime amounts to 12.6 billion yuan each year, posing a substantial economic burden on the healthcare system and families []. Fetal CHD is classified based on the complexity of the structural abnormalities into simple and complex types. Clinically, simple CHD is more common, while complex CHD, although accounting for less than 1/5 of cases, is a significant risk factor for stillbirth, neonatal disability, or death []. The primary method for diagnosing fetal CHD is fetal echocardiography. However, due to factors such as fetal position in utero and other maternal factors during pregnancy, there is still a 43%-96% possibility of missed diagnoses [,]. Understanding the etiological mechanisms of CHD is crucial for developing targeted diagnostic and therapeutic strategies and improving prognosis. Known factors include maternal age or disease, genetic factors, and environmental exposures, with genetic factors playing a significant role in the pathogenesis of fetal CHD []. Genetic factors include chromosomal aneuploidy, copy number variants (CNVs), and single-gene mutations. Genetic testing methods for fetal CHD primarily include chromosomal karyotype analysis and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). With the increasing use of Clinical Exome Sequencing (CES) technology in prenatal diagnosis, exome sequencing (ES) is sequentially used to detect single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and insertions/deletions (indels) in fetuses with abnormal prenatal ultrasound findings and normal results from traditional methods, expanding the scope of genetic variation research []. However, this stepwise procedure has a relatively long turnaround time (4–8 weeks), impacting the timely provision of genetic counseling and diagnostic results []. With the promotion of new technologies in the clinical field, our hospital has recently adopted medium-coverage whole-genome sequencing (CMA-seq) for CNV detection in prenatal diagnosis, replacing CMA/single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays []. This technology offers high throughput, high resolution, and relatively low cost. Additionally, based on family-based CES, we identify SNVs/indels, focusing on essential genes associated with known diseases in clinical practice. Many genes have been reported, such as cardiac transcription factor GATA regulating myocardial cell proliferation and differentiation [], enzyme gene MTHFR related to folate/homocysteine (Hcy) metabolism [], and the transcription factor Nrf2 altering cardiovascular hemodynamics []. To better understand the genetic landscape of fetal CHD and improve diagnostic strategies, we conducted a retrospective study of 412 fetuses with echocardiographically identified CHD using this combined genomic approach. We hypothesize that CMA-seq with CES will enhance diagnostic yield in prenatal CHD evaluation and provide a more comprehensive understanding of its genetic basis.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study design and participant recruitment This retrospective study included 412 fetuses diagnosed with congenital heart disease (CHD) by fetal echocardiography between December 2021 and March 2024 at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University. The study was approved by the hospital’s Ethics Committee (Approval No. 2021-046-01), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Inclusion criteria: (1) Diagnoses were made by two qualified physicians, meeting the International Pediatric and Congenital Cardiac Code (IPCCC) standards, and confirmed with CHD through color Doppler echocardiography and surgical diagnosis; (2) Fetal parents agreed to invasive prenatal diagnosis through prenatal genetic counseling and signed relevant informed consent forms. Exclusion criteria: (1) Pregnant women with contraindications to invasive sampling or who refused diagnostic investigations; (2) Fetal cardiac phenotypes involving only arrhythmias or pericardial effusion. Exclusion of pregnant women with coagulation dysfunction, infection at the puncture site, or history of exposure to teratogens; (3) Pregnant women with psychiatric disorders unable to complete the investigation. All participants received prenatal genetic counseling and underwent ultrasound-guided transabdominal amniocentesis between 20 and 25 weeks of gestation. About 20 mL of amniotic fluid was collected using a 22 G needle. No procedure-related complications were observed. All samples were tested with CMA-seq. In selected cases, CES was additionally performed based on ultrasound findings or clinical indication. Echocardiographic data and classifications Pregnant women were examined using GE Voluson E8/E10 ultrasound systems. Following American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) and International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) ­guidelines, All fetal echocardiograms were independently interpreted by two senior fetal cardiologists (each with >8 years of dedicated fetal‑cardiac scanning experience) who were blinded to the genetic results. Diagnoses were coded according to the IPCCC and ICD‑10. Whenever the two primary readers disagreed, the images were re‑evaluated jointly until a consensus decision was reached. CHD was categorized as isolated (simple or complex) or non-isolated (with extracardiac malformations), based on the Ministry of Health of China’s guidelines, as follows: (1) Isolated CHD: include simple CHD and Complex CHD, simple CHD refers to a single intracardiac lesion that generally does not cause hemodynamic changes. Cases involving one or more types of complex CHD were classified as complex CHD. Multiple simple CHD cases were not considered complex CHD; (2) Non-isolated CHD: CHD with extracardiac malformations: Includes malformations in systems other than the circulatory system. Whole Genome sequencing Medium-coverage whole genome sequencing (5–8x coverage, also known as CMA-seq) was used to detect CNVs. Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) and sequenced on the AmCareSeq-2000 platform (AmCare Genomics Lab, Guangzhou, China) with >100 million raw reads per sample. Sequencing reads were cleaned by removing read when a base quality less than QC20. The sequencing reads were aligned to the reference human genome version hg19 using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner(BWA). CNVs were identified using an in-house bioinformatics pipeline (AmCare Genomics Lab, Guangzhou, China) based on read counts and Z-scores, with a bin size of 10 kb. The interpretation of CNVs was based on multiple sources: the Database of Genomic Variants (DGV, http://dgv.tcag.ca/dgv/app/home), DECIPHER (Database of Chromosomal Imbalance and Phenotype in Humans Using Ensembl Resources; https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/), Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM;https://www.omim.org/), peer-reviewed literatures and an internal database comprising data from 100,000 Han Chinese individuals maintained by AmCare Genomics Laboratorys. Variants detected by CMA-seq and CES were classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) and variants of uncertain significance (VOUS). Clinical Exome sequencing Genomic DNA was extracted in the same manner as in CMA-seq, followed by solution hybridization using custom-designed Amcare probes (AmCare Genomics Lab, Ltd., Guangzhou, China) to enrich target sequences. This included approximately 5000 clinically relevant pathogenic genes’ exonic regions []. The genes were selected based on their documentation in OMIM, the Human Gene Mutation Database(HGMD), and peer-reviewed literature. Known pathogenic variants in deep intronic and other non-coding regions of the targeted genes were also included. The enriched DNA samples were indexed and sequenced using the AmCareSeq-2000 sequencer (AmCare Genomics Lab, Ltd., Guangzhou, China). The average coverage depth was 200x, with over 98% of the target regions being covered by at least 20 reads. Sequence variants were identified using an in-house bioinformatics pipeline (AmCare Genomics Lab, Guangzhou, China), which includes AmCare’s proprietary algorithms for extracting Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) variant sites and the use of the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) HaplotypeCaller for insertions and deletions (InDels), followed by filtering with Variant Quality Score Recalibration (VQSR). Sequence variants were annotated using population and literature databases, including the Genome Aggregation Database (GnomAD; https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), OMIM, etc. Variants with a minor allele frequency (MAF) greater than 1% in gnomAD East Asian were excluded. Variant pathogenicity was assessed according to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG). The conservation and pathogenicity of the variants were predicted using software like SIFT, Polyphen2, MutationTaster, FATHMM, among others. Sanger sequencing was applied to validate suspicious variant sites, and this was also done for the fetus and its parents. Pregnancy counseling approach Our hospital offers a comprehensive counseling strategy for parents facing the difficult decision of terminating a pregnancy due to fetal CHD. Our multifaceted approach includes educating parents about the specific CHD, its severity, and potential impacts on the child’s future health and development. A team of fetal cardiologists, geneticists, and ethicists provide a balanced view on medical interventions and the child’s long-term prognosis, considering quality of life. Recognizing the importance of family and societal values in China, we include considerations of the social and familial impacts of the decision. Parents are encouraged to think about the diagnosis’s effects on family life, caregiving, and psychological and financial implications. Genetic counseling is vital, particularly for suspected hereditary CHD, to understand recurrence risks and genetic testing options. Our non-directive counseling respects parents’ autonomy, supporting them without pressure, ensuring decisions align with their values and beliefs. Statistical analysis Proportions were compared using Pearson χ2 or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables are presented as median (inter‑quartile range) and were compared with the Mann‑Whitney U‑test. A two‑sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed in SPSS v26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

Results
Results General cohort information This study included 412 fetuses with CHD. The most common defect was septal defects (24.03%, 99/412), predominantly ventricular septal defects (VSD) (19.17%, 79/412). Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) was the second most common (21.12%, 87/412), with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) (10.19%, 42/412) and coarctation of the aorta-interrupted aortic arch (CoA/IAA) (8.01%, 33/412) being notable subtypes. Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO) included 70 cases (16.99%), mainly hypoplastic right heart syndrome (HRHS) (11.41%, 47/412). Conotruncal defects (CTD) had 49 cases (11.89%), including tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) (4.13%, 17/412). Anomalous pulmonary venous connection (APVC) and heterotaxy (Hex) were recorded in 38 (9.22%) and 22 cases (5.34%), respectively. Isolated CHD was present in 281 cases (68.20%), while 131 cases (31.80%) had extracardiac abnormalities, as shown in . Frequency of genetic variants in different congenital heart disease categories Genetic abnormalities were detected in 36.4% (150/412) of fetuses. Septal defects had a 26.3% (26/99) positivity rate, with VSD at 25.3% (20/79). LVOTO showed a 31.0% (27/87) positivity rate, including HLHS at 23.8% (10/42) and CoA/IAA at 36.4% (12/33). RVOTO exhibited a 44.3% (31/70) rate, with HRHS at 42.6% (20/47). CTD had a 40.8% (20/49) positivity rate, with TOF at 41.2% (7/17) and PMVSD + CoA at 50% (7/14). APVC showed 39.5% (15/38), and Hex had the highest at 59.1% (13/22). Isolated CHD had a 31.3% (88/281) positivity rate, while non-isolated CHD had a significantly higher rate of 47.3% (62/131) (p < 0.05). Non-isolated RVOTO and APVC showed significantly higher rates of 60% (15/25) and 72.2% (13/18), respectively, compared to isolated cases (35.6% and 10%). Non-isolated CoA/IAA also had a higher rate (66.7%, 4/6) compared to isolated cases (29.6%, 8/27), as shown in . Chromosomal abnormalities in fetuses with cardiac and extra-cardiac findings CMA-seq identified aneuploidies in fetuses with cardiac and extra-cardiac abnormalities. Trisomy 21 was found in 11 cases, associated with septal defects (3), conotruncal defects (2), RVOTO (2), APVC (1), LVOTO (1), and other defects (2). Five of these cases also had extra-cardiac abnormalities, including renal, neurological, and lymphatic issues. Trisomy 18 was detected in 4 cases, each with cardiac and extra-cardiac abnormalities, such as renal and nervous system malformations and cystic hygroma. One case of Trisomy 14 was identified with septal defects. Sex chromosome aneuploidies included one case of chrY duplication with RVOTO and potential right renal agenesis, and one case of chrX duplication with septal defects, as shown in . Distribution of pathogenic and likely pathogenic CNVs in different CHD categories P/LP CNVs were identified across various CHD subcategories. Septal defects had 2 P/LP CNVs in VSD. LVOTO had 5 CNVs, including 3 in aortic stenosis (AS) and 1 in CoA/IAA. RVOTO showed the highest number of CNVs, with 8 identified, mainly in HRHS and PA/PS-IVS. CTD included 2 P/LP CNVs. APVC exhibited 6 CNVs, with 1 P/LP and 5 VOUS. No CNVs were detected in Hex. Isolated CHD had 8 P/LP and 3 VOUS CNVs, while non-isolated CHD had 10 P/LP and 6 VOUS CNVs. Isolated cases included CNVs in LVOTO, RVOTO, and CTD. Non-isolated cases had CNVs in septal defects, LVOTO, and APVC, as shown in . Distribution of pathogenic and likely pathogenic SNVs in different CHD categories The RVOTO category had the highest number of SNVs, with 65 variants (15 P/LP and 50 VOUS), closely followed by LVOTO with 64 variants (16 P/LP and 48 VOUS); CoA/IAA and HLHS were particularly burdened within the LVOTO group. Septal defects included 53 SNVs, primarily in VSD. APVC and Hex showed notable SNVs as well. Isolated CHD had 38 P/LP and 170 VOUS SNVs/indels, with most variants in PMVSD + CoA, Hex, and CoA/IAA. Non-isolated CHD had 22 P/LP and 98 VOUS SNVs/indels, with most variants in APVC, VSD, and HRHS, as shown in . Impact of Exome sequencing on detection rates of genetic variants in CHD categories CES notably improved variant detection across CHD subcategories. In terms of variant count, LVOTO had 16 additional SNVs identified through CES, particularly in CoA/IAA (8 variants) and HLHS (5 variants). RVOTO, especially HRHS, showed 11 additional SNVs, and septal defects had 6 new variants. When considering the number of newly diagnosed cases, CES identified 6 additional positive cases in septal defects, 10 in LVOTO, and 9 in RVOTO. Overall, CMA-seq alone yielded a detection rate of 8.50% (35/412), while CES alone increased the detection to 10.92% (45/412), as detailed in and .

Discussion
Discussion This study represents the first large-scale retrospective research in Zhengzhou, a key city in China’s Central Plains, focusing on fetuses prenatally diagnosed with congenital heart disease (CHD). The Central Plains region, a historical and cultural hub with deep-rooted family values, emphasizes maternal–child health, reproductive planning, and genetic risk reduction. Its tradition of early fetal screening, strong public health infrastructure, and increasing uptake of advanced molecular diagnostics reflect a long-standing commitment to reducing birth defects and congenital conditions [,]. Economic development and advanced medical resources in Zhengzhou further bolster these practices []. This study utilizes advanced CMA-seq combined with CES for prenatal CHD diagnosis, crucial for genetic syndrome identification, prenatal counseling, and prognosis evaluation. The clinical relevance of CNVs is related to the functional impact of microdeletions and/or microduplications, with a higher likelihood of phenotypic effects when mutation regions occur in key genes and important regulatory areas []. Consequently, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) remains the most widely used first-line test for prenatal CNV detection. Wu et al. applied CMA to 158 fetuses with aortic-arch anomalies and reported a 12.7% yield for pathogenic microdeletions/duplications []. In our unselected cohort the corresponding yield was 8.5% (35/412)—slightly lower, likely because 68.2% of our fetuses had isolated CHD and 50.2% had simple lesions, diluting the proportion of syndromic cases. A meta-analysis of 1 131 pregnancies by Jansen et al. showed a 7% overall CMA yield, with clear stratification between isolated (3.4%) and non-isolated CHD (9.3%), mirroring our figures []. Similar gradients have been confirmed in North-American and European registries, where detection climbs to 12–15% when extracardiac malformations or increased nuchal translucency coexist []. Moreover, guidelines now recommend reflex low-pass whole-genome sequencing when ultrasound demonstrates complex cardiac anatomy because it can uncover sub-100 kb CNVs that arrays may miss, boosting diagnostic yields by a further 3–5% []. Together, these data underscore the importance of phenotype-directed choice of CNV methodology in prenatal CHD evaluation. Among the aneuploidies, trisomy 21 was the most common, representing 61.1% (11/18). In our cohort, the predominant cardiac phenotype in trisomy 21 fetuses was septal defects (3/11, 27.3%), followed by conotruncal and right-ventricular-outflow-tract (RVOT) lesions. This distribution is consistent with patterns reported in previous large-scale prenatal and postnatal studies of congenital heart disease in trisomy 21 populations []. We also observed a disproportionately high CNV burden in RVOTO relative to other CHD subgroups. Previous outcome studies indicate that when CHD co-occurs with extracardiac malformations, gene-dosage imbalances—rather than single-gene point mutations—drive pathogenesis [,]. Our data support this view: non-isolated cases harbored significantly more CNVs than isolated cases. Leveraging CMA-seq as a first-line test is therefore justified; its ∼10-kb resolution exceeds the 5-Mb limit of karyotyping and outperforms many array platforms. Indeed, Shaffer et al. detected pathogenic CNVs < 10 Mb in 10.6% of neonates with prenatal cardiac anomalies [], while we identified 15/27 clinically significant CNVs < 5 Mb and 6 < 100 kb, underscoring the added value of sequencing-based CNV detection (Supplementary Table 1). Finally, the well-known association between conotruncal defects (CTD) and 22q11.2-deletion syndrome was replicated: three fetuses carried 22q11.2 deletions, two classified as CTD, reinforcing the dosage-sensitive role of TBX1 in outflow-tract morphogenesis [,,]. Exome sequencing has also been recommended in recent years as a diagnostic method for prenatal ultrasound anomalies. In this study, CES, as previously described [], is a custom-designed panel including OMIM, HGMD, and newly peer-reviewed literature identified human pathogenic genes, covering all exonic regions and 30 bp of exon-intron boundaries, as well as known pathogenic deep intronic variants [,], with an average sequencing depth of 200×, capable of detecting some CNVs (results consistent with CMA-seq omitted). CES produced its highest diagnostic yields in RVOTO, LVOTO, CTD and septal‑defect groups, consistent with prospective European and US data reporting an 8–15 % incremental yield over array techniques for outflow‑tract or multiple‑lesion CHD []. From a developmental standpoint, the outflow tract is shaped by second heart field progenitors and neural crest cells regulated by Notch and TGF-β signaling. Mutations in pathway genes such as NOTCH1, SMAD6, JAG1, and DLL4 can disrupt valve morphogenesis and ventricular alignment. These mutations, often missense or truncating, affect protein function without altering copy number, which may explain the predominance of SNVs over CNVs in these lesions [,]. In heterotaxy (Hex), no pathogenic CNVs were identified, but multiple likely pathogenic variants were detected in axonemal dynein genes, including DNAH1, DNAH5, and DNAH10. These results strengthen existing evidence that ciliary dysfunction contributes to laterality defects []. Pathogenic SNVs were more common in non-isolated CHD (16.8%) than isolated cases (13.5%), highlighting the increased genetic complexity when extracardiac anomalies are present. Our findings are comparable to the study by Li et al. [], which showed a 10% diagnostic yield from WES in fetuses with negative CMA, though they did not find a significant difference between isolated and non-isolated cases. These discrepancies may reflect differences in case selection or variant interpretation frameworks. In conclusion, integrating CMA and CES in prenatal CHD diagnosis is crucial for identifying genetic variations. This approach enhances genetic counseling and informed decision-making for prospective parents, aligning with the cultural emphasis on family health in the Zhengzhou Central Plains region. Limitation This study has several limitations. Its retrospective nature may introduce selection bias, and despite a relatively large sample size, it may not capture the full spectrum of genetic variations associated with CHD. High-resolution methods like CMA-seq and CES might miss certain mutation types, such as deep intronic variants and epigenetic modifications. Interpreting variants of unknown significance is challenging and requires further research. Additionally, understanding the functional roles of novel variants in heart development and managing fetuses with positive ultrasound but negative genetic findings pose significant challenges. Future research should focus on larger cohorts and diverse genetic testing methods to validate and extend these findings.

Conclusion
Conclusion Our study confirms that chromosomal aneuploidies, pathogenic copy‑number variants and single‑nucleotide variants all contribute substantially to the genetic architecture of fetal congenital heart disease. Integrating CMA-seq and CES significantly enhanced the detection of genetic abnormalities, particularly in complex CHD cases. This comprehensive approach to prenatal diagnosis aligns with the cultural emphasis on family health in the Zhengzhou Central Plains region. Our data indicate that a combined CNV and CES is a valuable, evidence‑based option for prenatally identified CHD cases in which the likelihood of an underlying genetic defect is elevated by sonographic or clinical features.

abstract: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in HNRNPK cause Au-Kline syndrome (AUKS), a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by congenital anomalies and developmental delay. Prenatal diagnosis of AUKS remains challenging due to nonspecific ultrasound findings, such as increased nuchal translucency (NT) and nuchal fold (NF), which overlap with other genetic conditions. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed on a fetus exhibiting increased NT and NF thickening, alongside parental samples. Identified variants were validated by Sanger sequencing, with structural and functional impacts predicted using bioinformatic tools. WES revealed a de novo heterozygous frameshift variant in HNRNPK ( NM_031263.4 : c.504_507del) in exon nine of 17, which has been deposited in the ClinVar database with accession number VCV003899365 and classified as pathogenic (P). This variant results in a truncated protein (p.Lys168AsnfsTer35): bioinformatic predictions indicate the resulting mRNA is likely subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), and any escaping mRNA would produce a severely truncated protein lacking critical functional domains, rendering it nonfunctional. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant was absent in both parental genomes. Ultrasound findings aligned with AUKS-associated nonspecific prenatal anomalies, and post-induction gross examination confirmed subtle AUKS-related craniofacial features, expanding the known prenatal phenotype of AUKS and providing phenotypic severity context. Structural and functional analyses provide mechanistic insights into the variant’s pathogenicity, highlighting HNRNPK ’s role in fetal development. These findings advocate for integrating genomic and phenotypic data to improve prenatal diagnosis of rare genetic syndromes.
