abstract:
Patient: Female, newborn
 
Final Diagnosis: Aplasia cutis • tetralogy of fallot (ToF)
 
Symptoms: Aplasia cutis • tetralogy of fallot
 
Clinical Procedure: —
 
Specialty: Genetics • Obstetrics and Gynecology • Pediatrics and Neonatology
 
Objective: Rare disease
 Aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) is a rare congenital defect involving localized absence of skin, occasionally associated with deeper tissue anomalies and congenital malformations. We report the case of a full-term newborn presenting with extensive ACC involving 40% of the scalp, alongside multiple congenital heart defects, ultimately consistent with tetralogy of Fallot (ToF). Initial management included conservative wound care, cardiologic and neurologic evaluations, and genetic testing. Despite clinical stability at discharge, the infant was readmitted 3 weeks later with hemorrhagic shock secondary to sagittal sinus bleeding, requiring surgical intervention and intensive care. Subsequent follow-up revealed tonic seizures and radiological findings suggestive of prior mild hypoxic injury. While the Rapid Aneuploidy Detection test confirmed a normal female karyotype (46,XX), whole-exome sequencing was pending; however, Adams-Oliver syndrome was strongly suspected. This case illustrates the diagnostic and management challenges posed by extensive ACC with syndromic associations. It also highlights the limitations of antenatal screening, as no abnormalities were detected during pregnancy despite fetal growth restriction. The case underscores the need for a multidisciplinary approach, parental education, and long-term follow-up. Early recognition and coordinated care are essential for managing potential complications and guiding prognosis in complex cases of ACC with associated congenital anomalies.
text:
Aplasia Cutis Congenita and Congenital Heart Disease: A Case Report, Highlighting the Limitation of Antenatal Screening

Introduction
Introduction Aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) is an uncommon birth defect characterized by the absence of skin in a localized area, with variable size and location. The most common presentation is a solitary, round, crusted, or ulcerated lesion observed shortly after birth near the neonate’s hair whorl [–]. Nevertheless, extensive, multiple or bullous lesions occur in rare cases, causing severe hemorrhage and other life-threatening complications [–]. The incidence of ACC is estimated at 1 in 3000 to 1 in 10 000 live births, with a highly variable prevalence globally [,,]. A population-based study in Europe conducted from 1998 to 2017, and involving 28 registries from 16 countries, showed a steady overall prevalence around 5.1 per 100 000 births, with significant variations across countries []. Regarding management, the therapeutic approach can involve conservative treatment or reconstructive surgery, the technique and extent of which depends on the size of the lesion and presence or not of bone aplasia [,,]. However, ACC can be associated with cranial dysraphism or other congenital malformations, which can greatly influence both management and outcome. These manifestations are highly polymorphic and can affect multiple systems and organs. Genetic or chromosomal abnormalities are also frequently observed in ACC [,,]. In a multinational European study, an associated congenital anomaly was observed in one-third of the cases, with CHD being found in 15.4% of the cases. Chromosomal anomalies were found in 5.2% of the cases, and familial cases accounted for 2% of cases []. Therefore, the presence of ACC should lead to exploring potential underlying syndromes and genetic abnormalities that can affect the management strategy and long-term outcomes []. We present the case of a newborn with ACC in whom multiple congenital heart defects were diagnosed, raising suspicion of a genetic abnormality and necessitating a multidisciplinary approach for further evaluation and management. We also discuss the feasibility and potential benefits of antenatal screening and management of these abnormalities.

Case Report
Case Report A full-term neonate (40+3 weeks gestational age) weighing 3.640 kg was delivered via emergency cesarean section due to an abnormal non-stress test (NST). The baby was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for evaluation of cyanosis, low Apgar scores, and respiratory distress, raising suspicion of an underlying genetic syndrome. Maternal and Birth History The mother, a Saudi woman, had a booked pregnancy and was gravida 3, para 2+1. Her medical history included gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) controlled with diet and a previous cesarean section for breech presentation. During the current pregnancy, mixed non-specific bacterial growth was detected in her urine culture and vaginal swab at 28 weeks of gestation. Serological tests, including TORCH (toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex, and HIV) and hepatitis B screening, were negative. There was no history of consanguinity, and her blood type was B+. The pregnancy was complicated by intrauterine growth restriction, necessitating multiple fetal medicine ultrasounds. A scan at 38 weeks showed fetal growth at the 8.4th percentile, with normal umbilical artery Doppler imaging. At 40 weeks 6 days, the mother was admitted for induction of labor, which ultimately ended in a cesarean section due to abnormal fetal heart tracing. At birth, the neonate had Apgar scores of 9 at 1 minute and 10 at 10 minutes. The birthweight was 3.640 kg and head circumference was 32 cm. Cord blood gases showed a pH of 7.21, pCO2 of 49.8 mmHg, HCO3 of 16.7 mmoL/L, lactate of 2.6 mmoL/L, and base excess of −7.5. Initial Examination and NICU Course Upon admission to NICU, the baby exhibited features of prematurity and respiratory distress but was otherwise active, moving all limbs, with good tone and reflexes. Examination revealed extensive aplasia cutis involving approximately 40% of the scalp area, with an open anterior fontanelle measuring 4 finger widths, absence of underlying bone, and no active oozing (). Head circumference was measured twice at 30 cm (decreased from birth measurement of 32 cm). Imaging and multidisciplinary evaluations The neonate initially exhibited respiratory distress but stabilized on room air, maintaining oxygen saturation >95%. No abnormal breath sounds were noted, and respiratory function remained stable throughout the hospital stay. The cardiologist’s examination revealed a cardiac murmur on auscultation. Echocardiography on day 3 of life (January 30, 2025), revealed a 3×4 mm perimembranous ventricular septal defect (PM VSD), a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with a small shunt, a tiny closing patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with left-to-right shunting, mild pulmonary valve stenosis (PSPG 27 mmHg), and normal ventricular function. The baby remained hemodynamically stable and did not require cardiac medication or immediate intervention. A follow-up was scheduled for 3 weeks after discharge. The abdomen was soft and non-distended. The baby was fed expressed breast milk (EBM) and had adequate urine output (6.3 mL/kg/h), with normal stooling. The neonate demonstrated weight gain, but at discharge its weight was 2.796 kg, reflecting a slight decrease from birth weight. Neurosurgery was consulted, but no immediate intervention was deemed necessary. An MRI brain scan performed on day 4 of life (January 31, 2025) revealed foci of diffusion restriction, suggestive of a mild hypoxic insult. The superior sagittal sinus and straight sinus appeared equivocal due to calvarial and skin defects, necessitating further evaluation with a CT venogram (CTV) if clinically indicated to rule out venous occlusion. Management The baby remained clinically stable throughout the hospital stay, with no seizures, abnormal movements, or significant feeding difficulties. Plastic surgery was consulted for the management of the scalp defect. Daily dressing with fusidic acid ointment and Surfatulle was applied to prevent desiccation, and pressure on the affected area was avoided. The baby received a 6-day ampicillin and gentamicin course for suspected sepsis, with no bacteriological confirmation (negative culture after antibiotic therapy start). Inflammatory markers remained low (CRP <3.31). CBC revealed hemoglobin 20 g/dL, WBC 16.47×109/L, and platelets 319×109/L. The multidisciplinary assessment identified an association between aplasia cutis and multiple congenital cardiac defects, raising the suspicion of an underlying genetic syndrome. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was recommended, targeting genes associated with ACC, including ARHGAP31, DLL4, RBPJ, NOTCH1, EOGT, DOCK6, BMS1, and TWIST2. The differential diagnosis included genetic syndromes such as Adams-Oliver syndrome, Bart syndrome, and Setleis syndrome, which are known to be associated with ACC and CHD. The family received comprehensive counseling from all the multidisciplinary teams involved in their infant’s care. Initially, the parents were concerned about the condition and its potential clinical implications. After a thorough discussion of diagnosis, anticipated progression, and management plan, the parents showed a clear understanding and commitment to the plan. They diligently followed the wound-care instructions and remained actively involved throughout their infant’s hospital stay and subsequent follow-up visits. Overall, the parents adjusted well once they had more precise knowledge and support from the medical team. First Discharge and Follow-Up Upon discharge on February 9, 2025 (12 days of life), the baby was thriving on oral feeding and had stable vital signs. Discharge medication included vitamin D3 drops (400 IU PO OD), iron drops (3 mg PO BID), and fucidic acid ointment for local wound care. Follow-up appointments included neonatology after 10 days, plastic surgery after 2 weeks, cardiology after 3 weeks, and genetics after 7 weeks. Readmission Three weeks after discharge (March 4, 2025), the infant was urgently readmitted to the PICU in a state of hemorrhagic shock secondary to sagittal sinus bleeding. On examination upon admission, the baby was hypotensive and tachycardic with a blood pressure of 52/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 180 bpm. In the emergency department, the infant received 3 normal saline boluses, each at 20 mL/kg, along with tranexamic acid at a dose of 15 mg/kg. Due to the severity of the condition, the baby was intubated for airway protection and stabilization. On the suspicion of sepsis, antibiotic therapy was initiated with intravenous cefepime 175 mg twice daily. The scalp lesion was assessed by the neurosurgery team in the operating room, where a dark, thick, yellowish slough was found over the previous dressing site. Surgical debridement was performed, and a hemostatic patch was applied. The wound was re-dressed using a layered technique: Surfatulle, followed by Silvercel, gauze, cotton roll, and a crepe bandage. A brain MRI conducted at that time showed interval resolution of the previously noted tiny foci of restricted diffusion in the left medial thalamus and right cerebral peduncle, with no new areas of diffusion restriction and no evidence of intra- or extra-axial hemorrhage. MRA and MRV were unremarkable, ruling out any major vascular complications. A repeat echocardiogram, performed on March 5, 2025, revealed findings consistent with stable tetralogy of Fallot (ToF). The infant remained clinically stable and was not on cardiac medication at the time. Following stabilization in the PICU, multidisciplinary team decision concluded to transferring the infant to the general ward under the care of the neurosurgery team. A dermatology referral was requested for further evaluation of the scalp defect. As per infectious disease recommendations, intravenous cefepime was to be continued for a total of 2 weeks. The family was updated, and a formal report was given to the parents to support extended care coordination. On March 21, 2025, at 01: 18 PM, the infant – at 1 month 24 days of life – was clinically stable, with no significant overnight events. The infant was feeding well, and vital signs were within acceptable limits. The dressing over the scalp wound remained clean, dry, and intact. The full 14-day course of cefepime was completed and the wound swab analysis revealed no microbial growth. During admission, the infant developed abnormal tonic movements, clinically suspected to be tonic seizures. The neurology team was consulted promptly. A repeat MRI was unremarkable. Management included initiating levetiracetam at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses. In case of further seizures, the status epilepticus management protocol was to be followed. Events were to be video recorded for diagnostic clarity, and a follow-up with the neurologist was scheduled for the post-discharge period. At the latest follow-up, the final results of the whole-exome sequencing (WES) remain pending. Genetic counseling showed no structural abnormalities, and the Rapid Aneuploidy Detection test confirmed a normal female karyotype (46,XX). However, given the association of aplasia cutis congenita, congenital heart defects, and recent neurological manifestations, Adams-Oliver syndrome is currently highly suspected as a potential underlying diagnosis. Parental education and further genetic investigations have been prescribed.

Discussion
Discussion This case was a rare combination of ACC and CHD – namely, ToF – raising concerns about an underlying genetic syndrome and the feasibility of antenatal screening and diagnosis. Follow-up was marked with hemorrhagic shock secondary to sagittal sinus bleeding and suspected sepsis, with no neurological or further complications. The case underscores the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach in managing congenital anomalies, ensuring optimal long-term outcomes through careful surveillance and coordinated care. One notable clinical feature in this case was the reported ‘features of prematurity,’ although it was a full-term baby, as reported by the obstetric and pediatric teams and confirmed by the NICU team. While such features have not been reported in the literature, non-isolated ACC is often associated with higher prematurity rates []. The first challenge in this case was the initial diagnosis and management, which required coordinated multidisciplinary interventions to evaluate the extent of lesions and associated anomalies, and to determine and implement an appropriate care plan. The early cardiologic investigations showed features consistent with a complex CHD, suggestive of an incomplete or evolving form of ToF due to normal ventricular function and absence of overt cyanosis. Subsequent assessments confirmed ToF diagnosis. ToF is one of the most common CHDs observed in non-isolated ACC, along with atrio-ventricular septal defects and hypoplastic left heart []. Exploration of the other systems, notably neurological, gastrointestinal, and ophthalmological, showed no further associated abnormalities in our case. Actually, ACC is classified into 9 categories, based on lesion localization, associated malformations, and inheritance patterns. The classification was originally proposed by Frieden and revised by Sathishkumar et al []. Type 1 represents isolated, non-syndromic scalp ACC, usually sporadic or autosomal dominant. Type 2 is syndromic, associated with limb and cardiovascular anomalies, typical of Adams-Oliver syndrome, with both autosomal dominant and recessive forms. Other types of ACC are linked to other structural malformations, genetic syndromes, teratogenic exposures, or skin fragility disorders, reflecting the broad clinical and etiological heterogeneity of the condition []. The present case was classified as type 2, pending the genetic testing results. In a case series by Baroudi et al, 3 female neonates with ACC had suspected Adams-Oliver syndrome, all presenting with large skin lesions and additional congenital anomalies. CHD was confirmed in 1 case and suspected in another. Adams-Oliver syndrome was clinically suspected in the first case due to the combination of a large scalp defect and terminal limb anomalies, although the diagnosis could not be confirmed before the infant’s death. The second case involved an extensive scalp lesion associated with intestinal obstruction; however, no cardiac anomaly or Adams-Oliver syndrome was diagnosed before the patient’s death. The third case, featuring a smaller fibrotic scalp lesion, presented with multiple cardiac abnormalities, including PFO, VSD, tricuspid insufficiency, and severe pulmonary stenosis, suggestive of syndromic association, although Adams-Oliver syndrome was not explicitly diagnosed. The outcomes were poor in the first 2 cases, both resulting in early neonatal death, while the third infant survived with ongoing cardiac evaluation []. The second challenge in this case was the readmission for severe bleeding leading to hemorrhagic shock. Given the severity of the presentation and the associated risk of sepsis, the patient was treated with antibiotic therapy along with management for hypovolemic shock. Sagittal sinus bleeding and infection are dreaded complications associated with poor prognosis and high mortality [,]. This risk is more pronounced in large defects where major vascular structures such as the sagittal sinus are exposed without protective tissue [,]. This was the case for the present patient, who had approximately 40% of the scalp area involved. However, the delayed occurrence of this complication, 3 weeks after discharge, raises concerns about eventual external factors such as trauma or inappropriate handling. Ulterior minor trauma or mishandling of lesions in babies with ACC can precipitate bleeding by disrupting the delicate tissue that covers underlying, often exposed, vascular structures []. Thus, recognizing the high sensitivity of ACC lesions to external trauma highlights the need to educate parents and healthcare providers on gentle handling, meticulous dressing, and careful consideration of surgical interventions to prevent hemorrhagic complications. A well-established long-term management plan may be necessary to prevent major events and guide preventive interventions. Beyond the diagnostic and management challenges, this case raised questions about the relevance and eventual benefits of antenatal diagnosis and management. In our patient, prenatal assessments, including multiple fetal ultrasounds conducted due to intrauterine growth restriction, did not reveal any scalp or cranial abnormalities. Despite careful fetal surveillance, the extensive aplasia cutis involving approximately 40% of the scalp area was only detected postnatally. Furthermore, antenatal ultrasounds failed to detect the CHD. This reflects the inherent limitations of antenatal diagnosis of ACC, especially when the lesion develops later in gestation or when sonographic signs remain subtle. Moreover, although intrauterine growth restriction was noted, which could potentially raise suspicion of underlying syndromic conditions, no specific fetal abnormalities were reported on antenatal imaging. In practice, antenatal diagnosis of ACC remains challenging due to the subtlety and non-specificity of sonographic signs, particularly in isolated cases without major malformations. Therefore, antenatal diagnosis is more feasible in cases associated with genetic abnormalities []. Furthermore, the timing of lesion development (usually in middle to late gestation) can make early detection even more challenging. As such, most cases are identified only postnatally during clinical examination. The reason why antenatal screening for ACC is non-specific is that the condition often does not present with identifiable symptoms or markers during pregnancy. Nonetheless, associations have been noted with multifetal pregnancies, particularly with cases of fetus papyraceus, where 1 twin dies in utero, leading to lesions in the surviving twin due to pressure [,]. Prenatal ultrasound plays a crucial role in assessing any associated anatomical anomalies, as certain genetic conditions linked to ACC can be identified through imaging techniques [,]. In these instances, detecting abnormal configurations can provide indirect evidence of a potential ACC diagnosis in utero []. Other rare instances of extensive ACC may be detected prenatally. Liu et al (2012) reported a twin pregnancy complicated by early intrauterine demise of 1 fetus, with subsequent ultrasound at 32 weeks revealing intrauterine growth restriction and absent abdominal skin in the surviving twin. Ultrasound showed loss of normal echogenicity over the abdominal wall, suggesting exposed liver tissue without intervening skin. No other anomalies were noted, and differential diagnoses such as gastroschisis and omphalocele were excluded. This case demonstrates that, although uncommon, extensive ACC can occasionally be suspected in utero through detailed sonographic assessment []. In the present case, prenatal data revealed no findings suggestive of fetal abnormalities that would warrant further investigation. The only noteworthy event was a non-specific bacterial growth detected in a urine culture and vaginal swab at 28 weeks of gestation. All serological test results were negative, and no additional investigations were conducted. It is also worth noting that the mother had a history of GDM and cesarean delivery in previous pregnancies. Genetic counseling and investigation may be helpful in prompting antenatal diagnosis, particularly in cases with a familial history of ACC or related syndromes, such as Adams-Oliver syndrome, which consists of ACC and limb defects []. Awareness of potential teratogenic links to certain medications, such as antithyroid drugs used during pregnancy, may aid in guiding antenatal diagnosis and preventive strategies, underscoring the importance of preconception counseling to mitigate associated risks [,]. In the present case, despite a normal female karyotype (46,XX) and no structural anomalies on genetic screening, the combination of ACC, congenital heart defects, and neurological signs raised the suspicion of Adams-Oliver syndrome. WES is pending, and continued genetic follow-up is essential for confirmation and family counseling. Antenatal diagnosis, when achievable, allows for tailored perinatal management and informed decision-making. Management of ACC typically necessitates a multidisciplinary approach involving pediatric dermatology and plastic surgery. Immediate postnatal care focuses on evaluating the extent of lesions and preventing infection, with more extensive surgical interventions depending on the lesion’s size, location, and associated anomalies. Skin grafts may be considered for larger lesions, while smaller lesions can heal spontaneously with conservative management [,]. The prognosis varies significantly based on the characteristics of the lesion and the presence of associated malformations. Comprehensive follow-ups are recommended to monitor for complications such as contractures or developmental delays [].

Conclusions
Conclusions This case presents a rare combination of ACC and ToF, suggestive of syndromic ACC under genetic exploration. The skin lesion was treated conservatively and follow-up revealed a hemorrhagic complication and tonic seizures. The case underscores the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach in managing congenital anomalies, ensuring optimal long-term outcomes through careful surveillance and coordinated care. In discussing antenatal diagnosis, the condition remains difficult to diagnose prenatally. Enhancing clinician awareness and integrating fetal imaging with genetic evaluation in selected cases may improve early recognition and inform perinatal planning.

title: Gene List Selection Matters: Missed Diagnoses in Prenatal Exome Sequencing-PanelApp R21 and HPO-Driven Versus OMIM-Based Gene Lists.
label_reason: Fetal anomaly cohort re-analysed by exome gene lists.
abstract:
To evaluate whether the causative variants found upon clinical exome sequencing in fetuses affected with selected structural anomalies would also be detected if PanelApp‐R21 or Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)‐driven gene selection terms were applied instead. During 9 years (2016–2024), the whole exome was sequenced in 206 pregnancies with selected fetal structural anomalies, with prospective interpretation of about 5000 morbid OMIM genes. Retrospectively, 79 causative and 19 incidental findings were reviewed and assessed for their detectability under two alternative strategies: PanelApp‐R21 or HPO‐driven gene lists. Among the 79 causative genes identified by interpreting morbid OMIM genes in 78 structurally abnormal fetuses, PanelApp‐R21 was able to detect 76 (96%) genes, while HPO‐driven terms identified only 56 (71%). For 19 incidental findings, the PanelApp‐R21 pathway could identify eight (42%), while HPO terms captured only one (5.3%). In prenatal ES, reliance on HPO‐driven gene selection significantly lowers diagnostic yield compared with clinical ES, with nearly one‐third of primary findings and most incidental findings missed. PanelApp represents a pragmatic alternative, preserving a high primary diagnostic yield while limiting incidental findings. Keywords: genetic counseling, genetic services, genetic testing, human genetics, inborn genetic diseases, prenatal diagnosis

What is already known about this topic? Prenatal exome sequencing (ES) is a widely accepted approach for identifying monogenic disorders that may underlie specific fetal structural anomalies. However, there are various strategies for selecting the gene set to analyze: one may sequence the entire exome or apply a targeted multigene panel. These panels can be based on different criteria, such as all known disease‐causing genes (morbid genes), genes linked to early‐onset severe diseases, or those associated with specific phenotypic features. What does this study add? The PanelApp‐R21 gene panel, focused on early‐onset severe diseases, captured 96% of the primary findings and 42% of incidental findings detected using a broader panel of morbid OMIM genes, consistent with its goal of minimizing incidental findings. In contrast, panels generated based on Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms captured only 71% of primary findings and 5.3% of incidental findings. This highlights key limitations of phenotype‐driven gene selection approaches in the prenatal setting.

Gene List Selection Matters: Missed Diagnoses in Prenatal Exome Sequencing—PanelApp R21 and HPO‐Driven Versus OMIM‐Based Gene Lists

Introduction
Introduction Prenatal exome sequencing (ES) has become a widely accepted method to identify monogenic disorders underlying fetal structural anomalies, particularly when conventional tests such as quantitative fluorescent PCR (QF‐PCR) and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) yield non‐informative results for aneuploidies and copy number variations. ES evaluates the entire coding genome, but data analysis is typically restricted to a subset of genes—most commonly, known disease‐causing genes—to optimize diagnostic yield and reduce the number of incidental findings. The selection of genes to be interpreted can be based on specific candidate gene analysis through panels, where filtering involves genes associated with the clinical phenotype to provide a more targeted approach []. In addition to the primary gene list or virtual panels established by each laboratory concerning specific diseases or phenotypes, there are 3 common approaches used in prenatal exome interpretation although the diagnostic yield of these different strategies is unknown: (a) the morbid Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) (https://www.omim.org/) genes (n ≈ 5000), called the “clinical exome”; (b) the R21‐pathway of PanelApp Genomics England (https://panelapp.genomicsengland.co.uk/panels/478/) (from now on PanelApp‐R21), which includes curated genes for severe early‐onset diseases (n ≈ 1514); or (c) a personalized panel including hundreds of genes driven by the fetal phenotype, specifically the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) (https://hpo.jax.org/) terms (HPO‐driven exome). More in detail about the strategies, OMIM serves as a comprehensive and authoritative compendium of human genes and genetic phenotypes, containing information on all known Mendelian disorders and over 26,000 genes, with a focus on the relationship between phenotype and genotype [, ]. PanelApp Genomics England is the compendium of genomic panels curated by England's Genomic Medicine Service and evaluated by the NHS Genomic Medicine Service []. Specifically, the fetal anomalies panel, called R21 (latest signed version v6.0), employs a targeted panel of 2332 genes associated with severe early‐onset human monogenic diseases []. The genes are divided into three lists: green, amber, and red. The green list is constituted by 1514 genes, and is the only one used to interpret variants, while the genes constituting the amber and red lists differ on the level of evidence supporting the association with fetal structural anomalies []. Finally, the HPO project provides a structured ontology of over 18,000 medically relevant phenotypes, disease‐phenotype annotations, and the algorithms that operate on these. The HPO approach follows a phenotype‐first strategy, prioritizing the detailed description of specific fetal anomalies to guide the selection of genes to interpret after ES [].

Methods
Methods Study Design and Participants This study aimed to retrospectively compare the yield of three strategies of variant filtering in clinical exome sequences at our center during 2016–2024. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether gene variants identified through clinical ES (whole ES and morbid OMIM gene interpretation) would also be identified using two alternative strategies: PanelApp‐R21 analysis and HPO‐driven gene selection. All patients with selected structurally abnormal fetuses in which a primary finding was demonstrated at clinical ES during 2016–2024 were included in the study. Initially, at our center, the use of clinical ES (morbid OMIM gene interpretation) was restricted to multisystem and recurrent fetal structural anomalies, relying on specific virtual multigene panels for other anomalies with a likely monogenic origin. However, due to the limitations of multigene panels curated according to postnatal phenotypes, the use of clinical ES was extended to almost all anomalies with a high risk of a monogenic disease. For this reason, during the initial years, there were four types of fetal structural anomalies considered eligible for ES as they presented the highest risk of a monogenic disorder: skeletal dysplasia, recurrent anomaly, multisystem anomalies, and complex anomaly of the central nervous system. More recently, three types of fetal anomalies: fetal hydrops, fetal akinesia, and large hyperechogenic or multicystic kidneys, were added to the above. Sequencing and Bioinformatics Analysis Until 2021, ES libraries were prepared using the Illumina Nextera Flex for Enrichment assay (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), and subsequent paired‐end sequencing (2 × 150 bp) of the whole ES was performed using the NextSeq 550 platform (Illumina). As of 2022, ES libraries were prepared using the DNA Prep with Enrichment (Illumina) and the SureSelect Human All Exon v8 kits (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Paired‐end sequencing (2 × 150 bp) of the exome was performed using the Illumina NextSeq 2000 sequencer (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). ES reached a targeted mean coverage of 100× for each proband, and a minimum of 90% of bases sequenced at least 20×. Bioinformatic analysis consisted of alignment to the reference human genome (hg38) using BWA MEM (v0.7.17) and Bowtie2 (v2.4.1) short‐read aligners, genotyping using Haplotype Caller from Genome Analysis Toolkit (v.4.2) and VarDict (v1.7.0) variant callers, and annotation using Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (v104). Variant interpretation and classification were performed according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) recommendations []. Among the 206 clinical exomes sequenced, 156 (76%) were sequenced as singletons, 44 (21%) as trios, and 6 (3%) as duos. The prioritization of solo sequencing was due to its lower cost. Strategies Assessed and Assessment Strategy Using the morbid OMIM genes as the reference standard, we retrospectively assessed whether the same primary and incidental diagnostic genes would be identified using PanelApp‐R21 [] and genes driven by HPO terms []. We defined as primary findings those pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants that can explain the observed phenotype, while incidental findings were those that are not associated with the fetal phenotype. Incidental findings were reported when the couple decided so during the pre‐test counseling session. No specific search was performed for secondary findings []. Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were not reported to the couple, except in genes overlapping the fetal phenotype as agreed by the multidisciplinary review board. Regarding the PanelApp‐R21 strategy, the genes identified in our sample were searched in the PanelApp‐R21green list. For HPO evaluation, the fetal anomalies found at ultrasound in ongoing cases and at post‐mortem studies of stillbirths and terminations of pregnancy were converted into HPO terms. Next, we searched whether the gene identified by clinical ES was included in the list of genes associated with any of the HPO terms. Subsequently, the same assessment strategy applied to primary findings was used for incidental findings. Ethics Approval Ethical approval from the IRB of Hospital Clinic Barcelona was obtained on the 31st July 2025 (HCB/2025/0819).

Results
Results Among the 206 clinical ES sequenced at our center during the study period (2016–2024), 79 primary findings were identified in 78 fetuses (38%), indicating that a causative gene related to the fetal phenotype harbored a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant. In addition, 19 (9.2%) incidental findings were identified, including 4 cases that also had a positive primary finding. Secondary findings were not actively sought. The genes included in PanelApp‐R21 were reviewed in March 2025, and 76/79 (96%; 95% CI: 89%–99%) were found in the green list of PanelApp‐R21 (Table ). Two genes were found in the amber list, suggesting a lower level of evidence: COL27A1 (Steel syndrome) and NSD2 (Rauch‐Steindl syndrome). No matches were found for the following gene and related disease: IREB2 (Neurodegeneration, early‐onset, with choreoathetoid movements and microcytic anemia). Initially, CPLANE1 (Orofaciodigital syndrome VI) and ARSL (Chondrodysplasia punctata, X‐linked recessive) were not found in the list. PanelApp‐R21's lack of updating gene name results in their previous names being found in the list (C5orf42 and ARSE, respectively). Among the 19 incidental findings, eight (42%; 95% CI: 20%–64%) genes would have been potentially identified by the green list. Furthermore, three genes (16%) can be found in the amber list: MYBPC3 (Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy 4) and SMPD1 (Acid Sphingomyelinase Deficiency) and PTEN (Cowden syndrome). Additionally, four (21%) genes are on the red list: COL4A4 (Alport syndrome), KCNQ1 (Long QT syndrome 1), COL5A2 (Ehlers‐Danlos syndrome) and AIRE (Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I, with or without reversible metaphyseal dysplasia). Finally, no matches were found for the following four genes and diseases: ETV6 (Thrombocytopenia 5), APPL1 (Diabetes type MODY 14), ATP7B (Wilson disease), and F12 (Angioedema). The phenotypic findings at prenatal ultrasound in ongoing pregnancies, together with those at postmortem studies in terminations of pregnancy or stillbirth, were searched in the HPO browser in March 2025. Seven phenotypic findings lacked an HPO match: abnormal subclavian artery morphology, abnormal brain stem, small vermis and corpus callosum, delayed sulcation, abnormal olfactory sulci, anomalous costal vertebrae and body stalk. Among the 79 causative genes, only 56 (71%; 95% CI: 61%–81%) causative genes were identified using specific HPO terms along with only one (5.3%; 95% CI 0%–15%) of the 19 incidental findings. The identification rate varied according to the type of fetal anomaly: 85% for complex central nervous system anomalies, 78% for skeletal dysplasias, 67% for multisystem anomalies, and 60% for recurrent anomalies (Table ). The single incidental finding detected by HPO terms was a MED13L case (Impaired intellectual development and distinctive facial features with or without cardiac defects).

Discussion
Discussion The retrospective use of PanelApp‐R21 in structurally abnormal fetuses at high risk of monogenic disorders, according to the anomaly type, and prospectively studied with clinical ES demonstrated high coverage, missing 4% (3/79) of the primary findings and 58% (11/19) of the incidental findings were undetected. In contrast, the alternative use of HPO‐driven strategies missed 29% (23/79) of the primary findings and 95% (18/19) of the incidental findings. These results highlight the limitations of phenotype‐driven approaches in prenatal ES, and particularly by HPO terms, producing a substantial decrease in diagnostic yield, both in primary and incidental findings. Our findings support the use of an agnostic approach in prenatal ES analysis, such as genes listed in the morbid OMIM or PanelApp‐R21, given that prenatal phenotypes are frequently incomplete, transient, or inadequately represented by current HPO terminology and current bioinformatics pipelines for gene prioritization in prenatal ES [, ]. The recommendation that fetal phenotype should be an integral component in the interpretation of sequencing data remains crucial when a likely pathogenic variant or a VUS may overlap with the fetal phenotype. This was exemplified in a case of lethal congenital contracture syndrome 11, where two GLDN variants were identified []. One fulfilled ACMG/AMP criteria for likely pathogenicity, while the second, though below threshold, was reclassified as disease‐causing based on the strong prenatal and postmortem phenotype–genotype concordance, prior reports of biallelic GLDN variants, and confirmation of two alleles in trans consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. This study is among the few to apply a stepwise framework for the reanalysis and interpretation of prenatal ES data, evaluating the diagnostic yield and clinical impact of phenotype‐driven approaches. Such efforts are essential, as clinical phenotypes play a critical role in the automated detection of rare disease diagnoses. However, the prenatal context poses a challenge for phenotype‐based approaches as many manifestations remain poorly characterized during fetal development or may emerge in the postnatal period. Nowadays, HPO is making efforts to adapt to the prenatal setting; it currently contains 15 terms explicitly labeled as “prenatal” and 151 terms related to fetal anomalies within the subhierarchy starting from “abnormality of prenatal development or birth” [HP:0001197], covering associations with approximately 554 diseases and 580 genes. The main advantage of phenotype‐driven methods for gene selection is minimizing the incidental findings, which is a classic aim of Clinical Geneticists. However, this view is not endorsed by most pregnant women when asked. In a previous study in our center, 84% of pregnant women and couples opted to be informed about incidental findings []. If we look back to when karyotyping was the standard genetic study performed in prenatal samples with a high risk of trisomy 21, all abnormal non‐trisomy 21 results were, in fact, incidental findings. At the time, this was considered more an advantage than a limitation. On reviewing the composition of the PanelApp‐R21 fetal anomalies panel, we found that three of the genes analyzed in our study were not present in the version of the green list used for comparison. Two of these genes were classified in the amber list. One, COL27A1, is associated with Steel syndrome [], for which we have recently reported new evidence, whereas the other, IREB2, was not included in any classification list. Reported cases of IREB2‐related disease typically present postnatally with features such as severe neurodevelopmental delay and microcytic anemia, rather than structural anomalies detectable in utero (OMIM #618451). The exclusion of IREB2 from PanelApp‐R21 is therefore consistent with the panel's intended purpose of omitting genes without a recognized prenatal phenotype. To date, IREB2 has been described in four children with neurodegenerative disorders, none of whom abnormalities had suspected on prenatal ultrasound. Postnatal MRI revealed cerebral volume loss and white matter atrophy in three cases, two of which also showed abnormalities of the corpus callosum; the remaining MRI was normal [, , , ]. In contrast, our prenatal case demonstrated cerebral ventriculomegaly and agenesis of the corpus callosum, anomalies that are detectable on the mid‐trimester anomaly scan. However, other corpus callosum anomalies that may be missed on routine mid‐trimester scans are typically detected using advanced imaging methods such as detailed neurosonography and fetal MRI. As routine prenatal ultrasound continues to improve, detection of corpus callosum abnormalities is likely to increase, potentially justifying the inclusion of IREB2 in future revisions of fetal anomaly panels. To our knowledge, a scarce number of studies have compared the various gene selection strategies applied in prenatal ES. Sukenik et al. (2021), in a postnatal series, reported that a significant proportion of genes (12%–23%) related to neurocognitive phenotypes were not included in some of the panels used for prenatal ES data interpretation. Interestingly, these were not only genes related to recently discovered disorders but also ones with well‐established gene‐phenotype associations []. In a prenatal setting, Norton et al. (2022) compared the diagnostic yield of ES with the simulated application of commercial targeted gene panels in a large cohort of fetuses with nonimmune hydrops fetalis. The commercial panels only covered 11%–62% of the primary findings identified by ES; thus, they concluded that the broader coverage of ES for genetically heterogeneous disorders makes it a superior alternative to targeted gene panel testing []. Current guidelines for the use of sequencing in prenatal diagnosis do not provide specific recommendations regarding the selection approach for gene analysis in next‐generation sequencing (NGS) diagnostic testing. Nevertheless, prioritization of variants in genes potentially related to the primary clinical indication is generally a consideration []. A restricted analysis based on such prioritization is commonly employed to simplify variant interpretation and reduce inconclusive findings. In this context, a collection of systematic reviews and meta‐analyses regarding prenatal ES [, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ], with a detailed revision of the gene selection methods of each study included, reveals substantial variability in the bioinformatic strategies. However, the most frequently adopted approaches include phenotype‐driven gene selection using the OMIM and HPO databases as well as curated gene panels, particularly for recurrent phenotypes, such as fetal hydrops, skeletal dysplasias, and congenital anomalies of the urinary tract. In the near future, genome sequencing (GS) has the potential to outperform current genetic tests like chromosomal microarray (CMA) and ES by detecting a broader range of variants, including copy number variants, complex structural rearrangements, intronic variants such as the those that cause RNU4atac‐opathy, short tandem repeat expansions and hard‐to‐sequence regions. However, a recent meta‐analysis showed only a modest incremental yield (1%) of GS over ES in fetuses with congenital anomalies, along with higher rates of VUS. Given the current balance of cost, turnaround time, and interpretive burden, ES remains a clinically efficient and relevant approach, although GS may ultimately become increasingly feasible as sequencing costs decline and bioinformatics advance [, ]. This study benefits from a well‐characterized cohort and consistent clinical and molecular practices over a 9‐year period. A major strength is the direct comparison of real‐world gene selection strategies in a prenatal diagnostic setting. The prospective use of the three strategies would provide an optimal assessment method. However, several limitations should be considered. One is the retrospective review of the results obtained by clinical ES using morbid OMIM genes as the selection criteria to interpret genes, as we focused on gene‐level retrieval, assuming prior interpretations were accurate. Furthermore, although incidental to the fetal phenotype, several genes (such as KCNQ1, MYBPC3, PTEN) carry actionable postnatal or parental implications, omitting them may forfeit opportunities for anticipatory guidance and cascade testing [, , ]. This study demonstrates that PanelApp‐R21 exhibits good gene coverage in prenatal ES. The phenotype‐driven strategy based on HPO terms may be used as a first step in ES; however, it should not be applied as a final approach until a better correspondence can be achieved between HPO terms and causative genes in the prenatal setting. Future integration of refined prenatal ontologies with agnostic approaches will be essential to optimize diagnostic yield, minimize missed diagnoses, and align genomic interpretation with both clinical practice and patient preferences.

Consent
Consent Patients undergoing clinical ES signed an informed consent accepting anonymous use of their data for scientific purposes; thus, a specific consent was not necessary for the present study.

Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are available on request from the corresponding author. The data are not publicly available due to privacy or ethical restrictions.

title: Prenatally Diagnosed 7q11.23 Copy Number Variations: A Retrospective Case Series.
label_reason: Prenatal CNV cases with US anomalies and SNP array/CNV-seq.
abstract: Williams‐Beuren syndrome (WBS; OMIM #194050), caused by 7q11.23 deletions, is well‐characterized postnatally, but prenatal manifestations remain poorly defined. This study aims to delineate the prenatal phenotypes, inheritance patterns, and outcomes of 7q11.23 copy number variations (CNVs). A retrospective study of 20 prenatal cases with 7q11.23 CNVs diagnosed by SNP array or CNV sequencing (CNV‐seq) was conducted. Clinical data, including ultrasound findings, genetic results, and pregnancy outcomes, were analyzed. Classic 7q11.23 deletions (1.42 Mb median size) were associated with ultrasound anomalies in 100% of cases (11/11), predominantly cardiovascular defects (36.4%, 4/11) and growth restriction (18.2%, 2/11). While 7q11.23 duplications (1.42–3.03 Mb) were associated with anomalies in 50% of cases (3/6), including cleft palate and ventriculomegaly. Inheritance pattern analysis revealed 50% of deletions (6/12) and 42.9% of duplications (3/7) were inherited, either from phenotypically normal or abnormal parents. Termination of pregnancy (TOP) occurred in 76.5% (13/17) of ongoing pregnancies, primarily for de novo CNVs. Four live births involved inherited CNVs. 7q11.23 CNVs exhibit significant prenatal phenotypic variability and inheritance heterogeneity. Advanced genomic testing and inheritance pattern analysis are critical for accurate diagnosis and counseling. Keywords: 7q11.23 microdeletion, genetic inheritance, prenatal counseling, prenatal ultrasound, SNP array, Williams‐Beuren syndrome

Prenatally Diagnosed 7q11.23 Copy Number Variations: A Retrospective Case Series

Introduction
Introduction Williams‐Beuren syndrome (WBS; OMIM #194050) is a multisystem disorder caused by a recurrent 1.5–1.8 Mb heterozygous deletion at chromosome 7q11.23. The syndrome is characterized by distinctive clinical features, including cardiovascular anomalies, intellectual disability, and a recognizable facial phenotype (Pober ). While the postnatal manifestations of WBS have been extensively documented, the prenatal presentation of 7q11.23 copy number variations (CNVs)—encompassing both deletions and rare duplications—remains poorly characterized, creating significant challenges for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling (Berg et al. ; Strømme et al. ; Morris and Mervis ). Current literature on prenatal WBS primarily consists of isolated case reports or small case series, with fetal growth restriction (FGR) and congenital cardiovascular defects emerging as the most frequently reported findings (Borrell et al. ; Yuan et al. ; Lv et al. ). However, emerging evidence suggests a broader spectrum of phenotypic variability, including less common associations such as aortic coarctation and persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) (Yuan et al. ; Lv et al. ; Wang et al. ). Furthermore, the clinical implications of atypical deletions or duplications outside the classic WBS critical region (WBSCR), as well as their correlation with fetal structural abnormalities, remain insufficiently explored (Alesi et al. ). In this study, we present a cohort of 20 consecutive prenatal cases diagnosed with 7q11.23 CNVs. We comprehensively analyzed the indications for genetic testing, prenatal ultrasound findings, inheritance patterns of the CNVs, and pregnancy outcomes. Our objective was to provide a detailed review of prenatal cases involving 7q11.23 CNVs, with the aim of improving the understanding of this genomic disorder in the context of prenatal diagnosis and facilitating more informed clinical decision‐making.

Materials and Methods
Materials and Methods Study Design and Participants This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Prenatal Diagnosis Center of the Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province (Wuhan, China). From April 2017 to December 2024, 18,459 prenatal samples were analyzed via SNP array/copy number variation sequencing (CNV‐seq), with 3261 (17.7%) diagnosed as chromosomal abnormalities. The study cohort included fetuses with confirmed 7q11.23 deletions or duplications identified through CNV‐seq or SNP array analysis, irrespective of ultrasound findings. Maternal demographics, gestational age at diagnosis, primary indications for genetic testing, ultrasound findings, comprehensive genetic results, inheritance patterns, and pregnancy outcomes were extracted from medical records. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province (Approval No. 230741011). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Genetic Testing Methods SNP Array Genomic DNA was extracted from uncultured prenatal samples (amniocytes, chorionic villi) and parental peripheral blood using the QIAamp DNA mini kit (QIAGEN, Germany). SNP array analysis was performed using the CytoScan 750 K Array following manufacturer protocols. Data were analyzed using Affymetrix Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS) v3.3, with genomic coordinates mapped to GRCh37/hg19 (Affymetrix Inc ). Copy Number Variation Sequencing (CNVseq) Genomic DNA (10 ng) was fragmented, ligated with adapters, and amplified to construct sequencing libraries as previously described. Libraries were sequenced on the NextSeq CN500 platform (Illumina, USA), yielding approximately 5 million 45‐bp single‐end reads. Reads were aligned to GRCh37/hg19, and CNVs were identified using in‐house bioinformatics pipelines (Wang et al. ; Dong et al. ).

Results
Results Demographics and Genetic Findings This study included 20 prenatal cases with 7q11.23 CNVs, comprising 13 deletions and 7 duplications, diagnosed between 2017 and 2024. The incidence of 7q11.23 CNVs was 0.11% (20/18,459) overall and 0.61% (20/3261) among chromosomal abnormalities. The mean maternal age was 28.3 years (range: 17–42 years), with a median gestational age at diagnosis of 21 weeks (range: 8–31 weeks). Genetic testing revealed deletions ranging from 0.98 to 4.1 Mb (median: 1.42 Mb) and duplications spanning 1.42–3.03 Mb (median: 1.58 Mb) (Table ). Seventeen cases (85%) involved the classic WBSCR (chr7:72,700,000–74,100,000). Among the remaining cases, two exhibited larger deletions or duplications extending towards the centromere (Case 5, 4.4 Mb deletion; Case 18: 3.03 Mb duplication), while one case carried a smaller 0.98 Mb deletion (Case 3). Three cases (Cases 12–14) were diagnosed in the first trimester (8–11 weeks) following ultrasound‐detected fetal demise. The remaining 17 cases underwent invasive prenatal testing due to ultrasound anomalies (n = 9), family history (n = 4), or high‐risk noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) results (n = 2). Phenotypic Spectrum Ultrasound anomalies were observed in 100% (11/11) of cases with available prenatal imaging (Cases 1–11, Table ). Cardiovascular defects were the most common anomalies, present in 36.4% (4/11) of cases, including PLSVC (Cases 2), aortic stenosis (Case 8), ventricular septal defect (VSD, Case 9), and interruption of the inferior vena cava (Case 11). Other recurrent phenotypes included fetal growth restriction (FGR 18.2%; 2/11; Cases 2, 4) and increased nuchal translucency (NT) (18.2%; 2/11; Cases 5, 7). Unique structural anomalies such as duodenal obstruction (Case 1), unilateral ventriculomegaly (Case 3), and rocker‐bottom feet (Case 10) were each observed in one case. Among duplication cases (Cases 15–20), ultrasound anomalies were observed in 50% (3/6), including cleft palate (Case 15), pulmonary artery crossover (Case 18), and unilateral ventriculomegaly (Case 19). Inheritance Patterns Inheritance pattern analysis was available for 19 cases. Deletions arose de novo in 50% (6/12) and were inherited in 50% (6/12) (Cases 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 11). Among the six maternal transmissions, three mothers (Cases 4, 5, 8) presented with mild ID. Two mothers (Cases 2, 4) had adverse pregnancy histories: Case 2's mother had a prior termination of pregnancy (TOP) due to FGR, and Case 4's mother had a child with developmental delay and ocular problem. Case 11 presented with micrognathia, while Case 3's mother was phenotypically normal. Duplications arose de novo in 57.1% (4/7) and were inherited in 42.9% (3/7) (Cases 16, 17, 20). Case 16's mother harbored 7q11.23 duplication and a 2p23.3‐p23.2 duplication, presenting with short stature (147 cm), poor speech communication, and strabismus. Case 20's mother had prior TOP due to the absence of cerebellar vermis. Case 17's father was phenotypically normal. Pregnancy Outcomes TOP was elected in 76.5% (13/17) of ongoing pregnancies, primarily for de novo CNVs or significant ultrasound anomalies (e.g., aortic stenosis, FGR). Families opted to continue the pregnancy in 23.5% (4/17) of cases, resulting in live‐born newborns, all involving inherited CNVs (Cases 3, 11, 17, 20).

Discussion
Discussion This study presents the largest single‐center prenatal cohort to date characterizing the phenotypic spectrum, inheritance patterns, and outcomes of 7q11.23 CNVs. Our findings expand current understanding of the intrauterine manifestations associated with these genomic alterations and have important implications for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling. The universal presence of ultrasound anomalies (100%) in classic WBSCR deletions confirms the high penetrance of prenatal phenotypes in WBS (Kozel et al. ). The predominance of cardiovascular defects (36.4%) in our cohort, including aortic stenosis and PLSVC, reinforces the crucial role of ELN (OMIM #130160) haploinsufficiency in vascular development. These observations align with the well‐established mechanism whereby ELN deficiency disrupts elastin fiber deposition, leading to arterial wall stiffening and subsequent stenosis (Urbán et al. ; Hoareau et al. ). The novel identification of prenatal markers, such as interrupted inferior vena cava (Case 11), may reflect broader developmental consequences of elastin pathway dysregulation (Collins II ). The chromatin‐remodeling gene BAZ1B (OMIM #605681) emerges as another critical contributor to the prenatal phenotype. Our observation of duodenal obstruction (Case 1) and craniofacial dysmorphism (Case 11) provides clinical evidence supporting BAZ1B's role in neural crest cell migration and differentiation (Lalli et al. ; Zanella et al. ). These findings suggest that BAZ1B haploinsufficiency may disrupt transcriptional networks governing both enteric nervous system development and craniofacial morphogenesis, offering a potential explanation for these structural anomalies. Our cohort included cases with atypical deletions extending beyond the classic WBSCR. Case 5, for instance, carried a 4.4 Mb deletion extending into the 7q21.11 region and exhibited increased NT (4.8 mm) and nuchal fold thickness (8.1 mm), indicative of severe fetal anomalies. Larger deletions often encompass additional genes, contributing to more severe and variable phenotypes, including pronounced neurodevelopmental and structural abnormalities (Weiss et al. ). Conversely, Case 3 carried a 0.98 Mb deletion and presented with moderate ventriculomegaly and an enlarged posterior fossa, despite the mother being phenotypically normal. This observation aligns with previous studies suggesting that smaller deletions may retain functional copies of some genes, resulting in attenuated clinical manifestations (Berg et al. ). The phenotypic variability observed in atypical WBS underscores the importance of precise molecular characterization of CNVs to improve clinical outcome prediction and facilitate informed genetic counseling (Manning and Hudgins ). While postnatal studies reported WBS as predominantly de novo, our cohort included maternal carriers with mild intellectual disability (Cases 4, 5, 8) who transmitted deletions of variable severity, as well as a phenotypically normal mother (Case 3) who passed a 0.98 Mb deletion. These findings highlight the necessity of parental testing, even in the absence of overt parental phenotypes (Bayés et al. ). The high TOP rate for de novo CNVs (76.5%) reflects parental concerns regarding neurodevelopmental risks, despite the limited prenatal predictability of WBS‐associated ID (Morris and Mervis ). Conversely, live births in cases with inherited CNVs (Cases 3, 11, 17, 20) suggest that familial variants may confer milder prognoses, emphasizing the need for nuanced risk communication during genetic counseling. This study is limited by its retrospective design and small sample size. Future studies should expand cohorts to refine phenotype–genotype correlations, particularly for duplications and atypical deletions. Evidence‐based guidelines should be developed for managing pregnancies with inherited CNVs, integrating molecular diagnostics and multidisciplinary counseling approaches.

Conclusion
Conclusion This study advances the prenatal understanding of 7q11.23 CNVs by delineating their heterogeneous phenotypes, inheritance patterns, and counseling challenges. The integration of molecular diagnostics into prenatal workflows is critical for accurate diagnosis and risk stratification. These insights underscore the importance of parental testing and personalized counseling to improve family outcomes. Future studies should prioritize long‐term follow‐up and functional validation to further elucidate the developmental consequences of these genomic alterations and optimize clinical management strategies.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: A Rare 7q Deletion Masquerading as a Common Aneuploidy on Prenatal Ultrasound.

abstract: Prenatal diagnosis of rare chromosomal microdeletions is challenging when fetal abnormalities mimic common aneuploidies. Traditional karyotyping may miss submicroscopic aberrations detectable by chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). We report a case of 7q31.1-q32.3 microdeletion syndrome identified through CMA, highlighting its diagnostic value. A 28-year-old primigravida at 29 weeks presented with polyhydramnios, fetal growth restriction, short nasal bone, and cardiac abnormalities suggestive of trisomy. CMA revealed a 21.58-megabase deletion at 7q31.1-q32.3. She delivered at 37 weeks by cesarean section. The neonate developed respiratory distress requiring intensive care and was found to have an atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery stenosis, ventriculomegaly, and feeding difficulties. This case demonstrates that prenatal ultrasound features suggestive of common aneuploidies may instead arise from other, less common genetic abnormalities. CMA offers superior diagnostic precision and should be considered in atypical prenatal presentations resembling aneuploidy. Keywords: 7q deletion, chromosomal microarray analysis, fetal growth restriction, prenatal diagnosis, ultrasound
text:
Hidden in Plain Sight: A Rare 7q Deletion Masquerading as a Common Aneuploidy on Prenatal Ultrasound

Introduction
Introduction Prenatal diagnosis has evolved significantly with the introduction of advanced cytogenetic techniques. Traditional karyotyping, while effective for detecting major chromosomal abnormalities and common aneuploidies such as trisomy 21, 18, and 13, has limitations in identifying submicroscopic chromosomal aberrations []. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) has improved prenatal diagnostics by identifying clinically relevant microdeletions and microduplications at 50-100 kb resolution, far surpassing conventional karyotyping []. The clinical challenge arises when fetal ultrasound abnormalities suggest common aneuploidies, but standard screening tests yield normal results. In such cases, the underlying pathology may involve rare microdeletion or microduplication syndromes that present with overlapping phenotypic features. The 7q deletion syndrome, particularly involving the 7q31-q32 region, represents one such rare chromosomal disorder that can present with features resembling more common genetic conditions []. We present a case of prenatal diagnosis of 7q31.1-q32.3 microdeletion syndrome identified through CMA, highlighting the diagnostic superiority of this technique over conventional karyotyping and emphasizing its importance in contemporary prenatal care when common fetal structural abnormalities are detected.

Case presentation
Case presentation A 28-year-old primigravida was referred at 29 weeks of gestation after routine ultrasonography revealed multiple fetal anomalies. Her medical, antenatal, and family histories were unremarkable for genetic conditions. Ultrasound demonstrated polyhydramnios, fetal growth restriction (biometry <1st percentile for gestational age based on Hadlock nomograms []), a short nasal bone, and a suspected atrioventricular septal defect with left ventricular dilatation (Figure ). Other structures were grossly normal (Figure ). Fetal cardiac ultrasound image showing suspected congenital abnormality. Image taken by the author. 3D ultrasound depicting grossly normal craniofacial structure despite a 2D finding of a short nasal bone. Image taken by the author. Amniocentesis was performed and sent for CMA. The results revealed a significant finding: a 21.58 megabase (Mb) deletion spanning the 7q31.1-q32.3 region of chromosome 7 (Figure ). This large interstitial deletion encompassed multiple genes known to be associated with developmental abnormalities and congenital anomalies. Chromosome ideogram demonstrating 7q31.1-q32.3 deletion. Figure reproduced with permission from the external laboratory. Fetal echocardiography at 30 weeks of gestation revealed a large atrial septal defect (ASD) with right and left ventricular discrepancy, and suspicion of coarctation of the aorta. She underwent an elective lower segment cesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation due to early onset fetal growth restriction (FGR) with breech presentation and polyhydramnios, and delivered a female neonate, with a birthweight of 2.11 kg (<2nd percentile). Initial newborn assessment revealed no obvious dysmorphic features on clinical examination. However, the neonate developed respiratory distress requiring non-invasive ventilatory support via continuous positive airway pressure. Postnatal echocardiography noted the presence of a large secundum ASD, small patent ductus arteriosus, right pulmonary artery stenosis, with pulmonary hypertension, and estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 25 mmHg. Repeated cranial ultrasonography was performed, which demonstrated ventriculomegaly, and is planned for brain MRI evaluation. Currently at 1.5 months of age, the infant remains hospitalized and requires ongoing non-invasive ventilatory support due to decompensated heart failure with pulmonary hypertension secondary to a large ASD while awaiting transfer for definitive ASD closure. Growth parameters have shown improvement, with weight increasing from 2.11 kg at birth to 2.85 kg at current assessment; however, long-term direct feeding is an issue due to poor sucking. The parents are currently awaiting consultation with a clinical geneticist for comprehensive genetic counseling regarding the 7q31.1-q32.3 deletion syndrome, including discussion of long-term prognosis, developmental expectations, and recurrence risk for future pregnancies.

Discussion
Discussion This case exemplifies the diagnostic challenges encountered in prenatal medicine when fetal abnormalities suggest common chromosomal disorders, but underlying rare microdeletion syndromes are the actual cause. 7q terminal deletion syndrome is a rare condition presenting with multiple congenital malformations, including abnormal brain and facial structures, developmental delay, intellectual disability, abnormal limbs, and sacral anomalies, but most literature focuses on postnatal diagnosis rather than prenatal detection []. CMA is cost-effective as a first-line test in fetuses with structural anomalies. Compared with traditional karyotyping, using CMA as a first-line approach increases diagnostic yield, detects clinically significant variants missed by karyotyping, and lowers the cost per genetic diagnosis despite higher per-test costs []. Table shows a comprehensive review, adapted from a paper published in 2024 by Aneja et al. [], which compiled ultrasound features associated with 7q deletions, including microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, and craniofacial abnormalities [-]. However, our case presented with a more limited phenotypic spectrum, primarily manifesting as fetal growth restriction and cardiac abnormalities, without the classical dysmorphic features typically associated with 7q deletion syndrome. The pattern of ultrasound findings in our patient, including polyhydramnios, short nasal bone, cardiac abnormalities, and a fetus with growth restriction, is classically associated with common aneuploidies such as trisomy 21, 18, or 13 []. The 21.58Mb deletion spanning 7q31.1-q32.3 in our case represents a particularly large interstitial deletion encompassing numerous genes critical for neurodevelopment. 7q terminal deletion syndrome commonly includes developmental delay, growth restrictions, intellectual disability, and microcephaly, and is associated with holoprosencephaly but often presents as microforms []. The early-onset fetal growth restriction observed in our case may be attributed to the loss of genes within the deleted region that are essential for normal fetal growth and development []. The genes within the 7q31-q32 region are known to play crucial roles in neurological development and function []. While direct literature linking 7q deletions to swallowing dysfunction is limited, the neurological abnormalities associated with this syndrome, including developmental delays and brain malformations, can potentially affect fetal swallowing mechanisms, hence the persistent polyhydramnios and poor sucking reflex []. Similar to other chromosomal deletion syndromes, such as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, where patients typically have trouble coordinating the suck/swallow/breath pattern, resulting in slow nipple feedings interrupted by gagging or regurgitation, the 7q deletion may have comparable effects on swallowing coordination and esophageal motility []. The neurological impact of 7q deletions on swallowing function represents an underexplored area that warrants further investigation, particularly given the potential implications for prenatal counseling and postnatal management planning. Continued research into rare genetic syndromes and their prenatal presentations will further enhance our ability to provide comprehensive genetic counseling and optimize perinatal care.

Conclusions
Conclusions This case demonstrates the diagnostic advantage of CMA over conventional karyotyping in detecting 7q31.1-q32.3 microdeletion syndrome, even when prenatal imaging suggests more common aneuploidies. CMA improves genotype-phenotype correlation and refines fetus-centered care planning, including optimized delivery, targeted post-delivery management, and family counseling.
