title: Moderate Diagnostic Yield of Exome Sequencing in Fetal Growth Restriction: Retrospective Insights.
label_reason: Cohort of FGR fetuses (ultrasound anomaly) with CMA and exome sequencing yields.
abstract:
To determine whether invasive genetic testing should be systematically proposed in cases of FGR. Descriptive retrospective study of 159 FGR cases (defined by an estimated fetal growth < 3rd percentile, regardless of Doppler findings) managed at the Toulouse Fetal Medicine Center (TFMC) during 2022–2023. Mean gestational age at diagnosis was 23.7 weeks. Head circumference < 3rd percentile was observed in 35% of cases, hemodynamic signs in 57%, and oligohydramnios in 11%. Invasive testing was performed in 56% ( n  = 89) of cases, with a diagnostic yield in cases with hemodynamic signs of 19% for genetic syndromes (whether chromosomal or monogenic), which dropped to 11% ( n  = 8) in isolated FGR. Postnatally, 50% ( n  = 67) of cases were attributed to placental causes, 31% ( n  = 41) to genetic disorders (of which 41% had a negative prenatal genetic workup), while 13% remained unexplained. Placental causes were most often due to chronic maternal vascular malperfusion (72%). Findings support the systematic offer of exome sequencing in second‐trimester FGR, regardless of whether it is isolated, associated with head circumference < 3rd percentile, or with abnormal hemodynamic profiles. Keywords: exome sequencing, fetal growth restriction, genetics, placental insufficiency, placental pathology, prenatal diagnosis, ultrasound

What is already known about this topic? FGR has been linked to perinatal and long‐term health issues. Although genetic testing can enhance diagnosis, its role in cases of isolated FGR with hemodynamic features is debated. Exome sequencing has a high diagnostic yield in the prenatal context when faced with multiple congenital malformations, but it is underused in cases of isolated FGR. What does this study add? It shows a 31% diagnostic yield for genetic syndromes in all FGR cases. It highlights an 11% diagnostic yield in cases of isolated FGR and with hemodynamic signs. It supports the use of exome sequencing in cases of early and severe FGR.
text:
Moderate Diagnostic Yield of Exome Sequencing in Fetal Growth Restriction: Retrospective Insights

Introduction
Introduction Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, as well as long‐term neurodevelopmental impairment []. However, its prenatal diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous definitions among international societies. The Society for Maternal‐Fetal Medicine (SMFM) defines FGR as an estimated fetal weight (EFW) or abdominal circumference (AC) below the 10th percentile, while the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) uses a stricter cut‐off of < 3rd percentile as a stand‐alone criterion [, ]. In France, the CNGOF distinguishes between small for gestational age (SGA) and FGR, considering severe SGA (< 3rd percentile), growth deceleration over time, Doppler abnormalities, or fetal compromise as indicators of pathological growth [, , , , ]. Although placental insufficiency is the leading cause of FGR, particularly in late‐onset cases with hemodynamic Doppler findings, early or severe FGR can also result from monogenic, chromosomal, or infectious etiologies [, , , , , ]. Prenatal genetic testing is widely recommended for FGR associated with structural anomalies or when detected before 32 weeks However, the role of genetic testing in isolated FGR, especially with hemodynamic features, remains controversial [, , ]. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is increasingly used and improves diagnostic yield by 5%–10% over conventional karyotyping []. However, monogenic conditions cannot be detected by CMA. Exome sequencing (ES), which may interpret the coding regions of more than 20,000 genes, has demonstrated diagnostic yields of 10%–30% in FGR fetuses with structural anomalies [, , , ]. However, its role in isolated FGR is poorly defined, and most guidelines do not differentiate FGR with or without Doppler abnormalities when considering the need for genetic testing. Furthermore, the absence of harmonized classification systems (e.g., growth charts, Doppler indices, timing) limits the ability to standardize genetic work‐up in FGR. As a result, ES remains underutilized despite its diagnostic potential. This study presents a retrospective analysis of all FGR cases referred to a tertiary prenatal diagnosis center over a 2‐year period. We aimed to describe the clinical characteristics, ultrasound features, and outcomes of all FGR cases (both isolated and non‐isolated) with a specific focus on the contribution of CMA and ES to etiological diagnosis in isolated (non‐malformative) and hemodynamic FGR.

Methods
Methods This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Toulouse University Hospital and confirmed that all ethical requirements were fully adhered to. This study is registered in the Toulouse University Hospital data study registry (number's register: RnIPH 2025–148) and complies with CNIL MR‐004 (CNIL number: 2206723 v 0). Study Population We conducted a descriptive, retrospective study of all records presented at the Toulouse Fetal Medicine Center (TFMC) for FGR cases during 2022 and 2023, a period when the prescription of prenatal ES was well established. In France, all pregnant women have been offered a first, second and third trimester ultrasound scan since the introduction of the national screening program in 2005. If a structural anomaly is suspected after one of these ultrasounds, patients are referred to a fetal medicine unit for advanced ultrasound examination, counseling by a multidisciplinary team and the cases are discussed during a TFMC meeting. The maternity unit at the University Hospital of Toulouse is a high‐capacity facility with approximately 5000 births annually. As a tertiary center specializing in fetal medicine, pediatric surgery, and rare diseases, it serves as the primary referral center for neonates with suspected fetal anomalies in the whole west Occitanie region. We included all cases with FGR in the TFMC database on the local software named “Viewpoint” during the years 2022 and 2023, regardless of gestational age at diagnosis. We extracted 330 records and analyzed their prenatal and postnatal clinical data. We removed duplicates (records presented multiple times), FGR cases with weight ≥ 3rd percentile, and multiple pregnancies. Thus, an FGR was considered only if the EFW was < 3rd percentile. Variables Analyzed We indicated if there was consanguinity between the two parents. We noted any history of SGA, FGR, intrauterine fetal death (FD), miscarriage (MIS) (a history of MIS was only considered if the patient had experienced at least three miscarriages), or other notable history during previous pregnancies. Family history (termination of pregnancy for medical reasons (TOP), genetic or chromosomal disease in previous children or the child's siblings), addictive substances (alcohol, tobacco), and chronic maternal pathologies (diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular or renal diseases) were also noted. Gestational age (GA) was systematically verified, determined either by the crown‐rump length measurements between 11 and 14 weeks or by the date of in vitro fertilization. In cases where the first‐trimester ultrasound was not performed, GA was based on the measurement of the head circumference after 14 weeks. We reported the percentiles of the different parameters used to calculate fetal weight according to Hadlock's formula (abdominal circumference, head circumference, femur length) [], and the EFW from the ultrasound diagnosis of FGR, as well as gestational age dating in weeks. We used the WHO growth charts, as recommended by the CNGOF and the French Society of Neonatology (SFN) []. We noted any ultrasound signs associated with the FGR, classifying them as: (i) major signs (corresponding to associated structural anomalies), such as cardiac defects or central nervous system malformation [, ]; (ii) and minor signs (corresponding to “soft markers”), such as intestinal hyperechogenicity or choroid plexus cysts, which are less severe and may or may not be associated with underlying fetal pathology. They are excluded from the European Surveillance of Congenital Anomalies registry given that their medical, functional and esthetic consequences would be minor []. FGR cases were stratified into two distinct groups: (i) “Isolated FGR”, defined as cases with no associated major structural anomalies on ultrasound examination indicating a non‐malformative phenotype. Fetuses exhibiting only minor signs were included in this “isolated” FGR group. (ii) FGR with associated anomalies, characterized by the presence of one or more major ultrasound signs. We considered Head Circumference (HC) < 3rd percentile (using WHO chart) [] as a separate variable, to easily distinguish between FGR with preserved HC from those with symmetric FGR. We also reported any abnormalities in the amount of amniotic fluid. Oligohydramnios was defined as an amniotic fluid index ≤ 5 cm, anhydramnios ≤ 2 cm, and polyhydramnios > 25 cm on ultrasound. We noted the presence of abnormal hemodynamic signs, both right and left uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) > 95th percentile. Invasive sampling during the pregnancy (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis) was also reported and the genetic tests prescribed was specified (CMA, exome, karyotype). Invasive procedures were recommended for women with FGR below the third percentile for gestational age that arose before 32 weeks. All patients who underwent amniocentesis (n = 81) were tested by PCR for CMV and parvovirus B19, while toxoplasmosis testing was performed only if the mother was non‐immune. We noted the results of these tests and classified them as followed: Placental‐confined chromosomal anomalies, Fetal chromosomal anomalies and copy number variations (CNVs) excluding Triploidy, Triploidy, Fetal monogenic disorders, and congenital infectious disorders. These categories were grouped for practical clinical decision‐making, emphasizing the clinical utility of consolidating etiologies detectable via amniocentesis, such as CNVs, monogenic disorders, and infectious diseases (PCR‐detectable pathogens) without implying pathophysiological overlap. We recorded gestational age at delivery and birth weight, as well as the pregnancy outcome (spontaneous delivery, labor induction, emergency cesarean sections, FD, TOP). We retrieved the pathology result of the placenta and classified placental anomalies into the following subgroups: velamentous cord insertion (V), chronic maternal vascular malperfusion (MVM), massive subchorionic thrombosis (MST), fetal vascular malperfusion (FVM), isolated placental hypotrophy without histological lesions, villitis and intervillitis according to the Amsterdam Placental Workshop Group Consensus Statement []. We reviewed the postnatal outcomes of the surviving newborns and classified the “final” etiological diagnoses as follows: placental, genetic (whether chromosomal or monogenic), isolated velamentous cord insertion (only if this sign was isolated), infectious, fetal alcohol syndrome, and unexplained. Statistics We subsequently used Easymedstat software (version 3.40) for statistical analysis. Descriptive statistics used were mean (± standard deviation and range [min‐max]) for continuous variables and number and percentage for categorical variables.

Results
Results A total of 159 patients with a fetus affected by FGR were included (flowchart on Figure ). Flowchart of the study. Maternal Characteristics The average maternal age was 33 years (33.05+/−5.65). 125 (78.6%) of the patients had no maternal pathology or personal history, 15% had a cardiovascular history, 5% had multiple miscarriages (≥ 3) (Distribution of detailed maternal condition is reported in Supporting Information : Table 1 and maternal history in Supporting Information : Table 2). Fetal Outcomes Among the 159 cases analyzed, the average gestational age at FGR detection was 23.7 weeks 35.8% of the FGR cases were associated with major ultrasound findings, while 57% exhibited abnormal hemodynamic ultrasound signs (Table ). There were no amniotic fluid volume abnormalities in 85% of cases, around 11% were associated with oligohydramnios, almost 2% with anhydramnios, and around 1% with polyhydramnios. HC < 3rd percentile was associated with FGR in 54 cases (35.3%). 58% of the fetuses had an EFW below the first percentile. 49% of the fetuses had a heart defect associated with FGR, all diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound. Pregnancy Outcomes 12% had induction of labor, 18.5% had spontaneous deliveries, 36% underwent emergency cesarean sections, 20% experienced TOP and 14% had a FD (Table ). The average gestational age at birth was 31 weeks with an average birth weight of 1.44 kg. Table reports the comparison of pregnancy outcomes between isolated FGR and FGR associated with major signs. Cesarean sections are more frequent in “isolated FGR” (43%) compared to “FGR with major signs” (23%). TOP are significantly more common in the “FGR with major signs” group (36%) compared to the “isolated FGR” group (10%). FD rates are higher in “FGR with major signs” (20%) compared to “isolated FGR” (10%). Invasive Procedure Tests Results More than half (n = 89/158, 56% (47.9–63.8)) of the FGR cases underwent CVS or amniocentesis. 51% had CMA performed, 21% underwent exome sequencing, and 9.5% had karyotyping, with a total of 25.8% having positive results (Supporting Information : Table 3). Among these “positive” cases, 27% were due to fetal monogenic disorders (identified by ES), 27% to fetal chromosomal anomalies (trisomies and CNVs detected by CMA and/or ES), 14% to triploidies (identified on karyotype), 23% to placental‐confined chromosomal anomalies (detected via CVS/amniocentesis discordance), and 9% to congenital infectious disorders (diagnosed by PCR‐detectable pathogens in amniotic fluid) (Supporting Information : Table 4). Among the 33 fetuses that underwent prenatal ES, 18% received a genetic diagnosis, primarily involving monogenic disorders (Supporting Information : Table 4). The diagnostic yield was identical between “isolated FGR” and “FGR with major signs”, with each group accounting for 9% of cases. Table reports the comparison of invasive procedure results between isolated FGR and FGR associated with major signs. Chromosomal anomalies were common in both groups (respectively 25% and 20%). Triploidy was more common in the “FGR with major signs” group (33%) compared to the “isolated FGR” group (2%). Confined chromosomal anomalies were more frequent in the “isolated FGR” group (20%) compared to the “FGR with major signs” group (8%). Infectious agents were identified as the cause of FGR in one case per group (isolated or associated), representing respectively 8% and 10% of positive diagnoses. Placental Pathology 76% (n = 116) of the placentas underwent post‐partum examination (Supporting Information : Table 5). Of these, 70% were diagnosed with chronic maternal vascular malperfusion, 6,8% (n = 5) with massive subchorionic thrombosis, 6,8% (n = 5) with isolated hypotrophy, 1,4% (n = 1) with isolated chorioangioma (event though 3 other placentas were also concerned with chorangioma but in association with other placental lesion), and 5,5% (n = 4) with isolated velamentous cord insertion. Postnatal Evaluation After postnatal evaluation, we had no information for 24 patients (15%). For the others, 50% (n = 67) of the FGR cases had a placental cause, 31% (n = 41) had a genetic cause (Table ) (of which 41% had a negative prenatal genetic workup and 15% had no prenatal sampling), 3% of the FGR fetuses had an isolated velamentous cord insertion, 2% had an infectious cause, and 13.4% of the FGR cases remain unexplained. Information on genetic diagnosis is shown in Supporting Information : Table 6. Among the 31% of FGR cases with a genetic cause (whether chromosomal or monogenic), more than 60% had associated major ultrasound findings (excluding HC < 3rd percentile), and 40% exhibited abnormal hemodynamic ultrasound signs. Specifically analyzing HC < 3rd percentile, about 30% of FGR cases with a genetic cause presented with HC < 3rd percentile, compared to 35% of FGR cases with a placental cause (Figure ). Decoding FGR Cases With Hemodynamic Signs Among FGR cases with abnormal hemodynamic ultrasound signs (n = 89), 19% (n = 17/89) had a genetic cause (Table ). Of these, 33% had not undergone prenatal sampling (either because it was not recommended by the TFMC or recommended but declined by the couple), and the diagnosis was made postnatally. For the other cases with hemodynamic ultrasound signs, 57% had a placental cause, only one case had an infectious cause, and 12% (n = 11/89) had unexplained prenatal FGR. For all FGR cases concerned by a genetic or chromosomal anomaly origin, the FGR diagnosis was always made before 28 weeks Table also reports etiological diagnosis when ultrasound hemodynamic signs exist in isolated FGR cases. If the majority of cases had a placental cause (65%, n = 42), 11% had a genetic cause (n = 8) even though abnormal hemodynamic signs existed.

Discussion
Discussion Given that 30% of FGR cases have a genetic cause, 50% are attributed to placental causes, and 13% remain unexplained, our findings highlight the potential value of systematically incorporating genetic analysis in the management of second‐trimester FGR, even in isolated and/or hemodynamically compromised presentations. Also, infectious etiologies, detectable via amniocentesis PCR, represent ∼10% of FGR cases identified through invasive procedures, regardless of whether the condition presents in isolation or with associated clinical signs. This highlights the need for routine infectious screening in all FGR evaluations. Invasive Sampling: What Kind of Tests Should Be Offered? Among 159 patients with fetuses affected by FGR, 56% of cases (n = 89), benefit from prenatal invasive sampling for genetic analysis, yielding conclusive results in 25.8% (n = 23) that included chromosomal or monogenic diagnoses (Supporting Information Table 4). All genetic or chromosomal (whether placental‐confined chromosomal anomalies, Fetal chromosomal anomalies and CNVs excluding Triploidy, Triploidy, Fetal monogenic disorders) anomaly‐related FGR cases were diagnosed before 28 weeks, suggesting that the definition of “early” FGR could potentially be adjusted to less than 28 weeks instead of the current 32 weeks threshold [, ]. Chromosomal Microarray Analysis In 2013, the French “Achropuce” network recommended CMA for prenatal signs like FGR < 3rd percentile []. The ACOG and ISUOG recommend an invasive test when FGR is associated with morphological anomalies or in isolation if detected before 32 weeks [, ]. CMA enhances diagnostic yield by 6% over FISH/karyotype []. In isolated FGR, FISH/karyotype find a diagnosis in 6% of cases, with no additional yield from CMA. In associated FGR cases, FISH/karyotype achieved 12.5% diagnostic yield, while CMA increased it to 15.4%. In our study, we found a 10% diagnostic yield for CMA in FGR cases, with 70% associated with major ultrasound findings, consistent with existing literature. Notably, three patients were not sampled due to abnormal hemodynamic ultrasound signs, while they had chromosomal abnormalities detected postnatally through CMA. Exome Sequencing Pauta et al., evaluated the diagnostic yield of ES in isolated FGR. Among 146 fetuses with isolated FGR, a pathogenic variant causative of the fetal phenotype was found in 17 cases, resulting in a 12% (95% CI: 7%–18%) diagnostic yield of ES []. Tran Mau‐Them et al., evaluated ES in fetuses with ultrasound anomalies []. In their cohort of 150 fetuses, 34% were found to have a causal genetic diagnosis. However, their cohort primarily included cases with multiple congenital anomalies, and only 21 fetuses were affected by FGR, of which 5 had a genetic diagnosis made by ES. However, none of these cases had isolated FGR. In a recent study, Shi et al. investigated the clinical utility of ES in the evaluation of isolated FGR in a cohort of 135 fetuses with normal CMA results []. Their findings revealed that ES identified causal variants in 16 fetuses (11.9%), though the study did not stratify or correlate these genetic findings with fetal hemodynamic parameters [].In our study, the diagnostic yield of exome sequencing was comparable to that of CMA, although prenatal CMA was performed more frequently than CMA combined with exome sequencing during the study period. Nevertheless, it is likely that exome‐based CNV detection will eventually replace CMA for identifying pathogenic CNVs, given its ability to detect both monogenic disorders and CNVs []. Additionally, ES is capable of identifying uniparental disomy, a rare condition associated with imprinting effects, as well as low‐level mosaic aneuploidies and homozygosity for pathogenic variants, all of which can contribute to FGR []. Fetal Pathological Examination A detailed analysis of fetuses in cases of TOP and FD showed that 68% exhibited major ultrasound signs, and 34% received prenatal genetic diagnosis, while 48% received genetic diagnosis through fetal pathological examination combined with postnatal genome sequencing. Fetal pathological examination in TOP and FD is essential for definitive diagnosis, enabling trio genome sequencing to enhance diagnostic yield. While prenatal ES has limitations in identifying all genetic syndromes, it should be reserved for prognostic stratification when pregnancy continuation is considered []. In cases of poor prognosis, combined fetal autopsy and genome sequencing are recommended to guide management. Genetic Diagnosis Yield Considering Hemodynamic Signs A meta‐analysis from 2023 compared exome sequencing's diagnostic yield in FGR cases, showing a 4% diagnostic yield for isolated FGR with Doppler anomalies and 30% for associated FGR without specifying the presence or absence of Doppler anomalies []. Another 2023 meta‐analysis showed that ES in isolated FGR, after normal CMA, had a 12% genetic diagnostic yield without indicating whether hemodynamic findings were excluded []. In these published series, the definition of isolated FGR is unclear. Literature studies do not clearly distinguish between FGR with or without abnormal hemodynamic signs. In our series, most patients sampled (n = 66) had no hemodynamic signs, consistent with CNGOF recommendations []. However, after postnatal reevaluation, 19% diagnostic yield was found for genetic abnormalities in FGR cases with hemodynamic ultrasound signs. Among these, 18% (n = 3) had not undergone prenatal testing due to the presence of hemodynamic ultrasound signs. When comparing the etiological diagnosis of FGR based on the presence of ultrasound hemodynamic signs, 47% of syndromic FGR cases have a genetic cause, while 11% of isolated FGR cases still exhibit a genetic etiology (Table ).A meta‐analysis of 452 cases with FGR or short long bones and normal CMA, conducted by Mone et al. in 2022, found an exome diagnostic yield of 50% (with 75% being de novo variants) []. Among these, the authors identified 61% isolated FGR versus 39% associated FGR in 116 FGR cases. Within them, 4% (95% CI, 5.0 to 12; I 2 = 0%) were isolated FGR with abnormal hemodynamic signs (based on screening tools such as uterine artery and fetal Doppler studies and maternal biomarkers) aligning with the findings of our study. Interestingly, all FGR cases with placental‐confined chromosomal anomalies, exhibited abnormal hemodynamic ultrasound signs in our study. Genetic Diagnosis of FGR Invasive genetic testing (Table ) revealed distinct genetic profiles between isolated FGR and FGR with major signs. While monogenic disorders predominated in isolated FGR, triploidies were more frequently observed in FGR with major signs, though these findings are based on a limited cohort size and warrant validation in larger studies. Chromosomal anomalies were common abnormalities in both groups (20%–25%), reinforcing the essential role of CMA in FGR evaluation, even in cases where it presents as an isolated finding. In terms of fetal chromosomal diagnoses, our findings include known FGR‐related syndromes, such as trisomy 18 and deletion syndromes such as 4p‐ or 22q11.2 (Supporting Information Table 4 and 6). For genetic syndromes found by exome or postnatal gene sequencing, no recurrent or predominant genetic syndromes were identified []. We detected a wide variety of syndromes with diverse transmission modes where FGR is not always a typical prenatal presentation. Unexpectedly, bone diseases commonly associated with FGR, such as achondroplasia or thanatophoric dwarfism, were absent, potentially due to immediate skeletal anomaly recognition by ultrasonographers that do not classify these cases in the FGR group but in “genetic skeletal disorders”, explaining why it does not appear in the study flowchart. They are more likely to present with isolated short long bones, or short long bones associated with other skeletal anomalies []. 34% of our genetic‐origin FGR cases showed no major ultrasound signs, and were considered isolated. Either isolated or associated FGR may signal a genetic syndrome with a broader phenotypic impact. Triploidy was overrepresented in the FGR with major signs group (33% vs. 20% in isolated FGR). But this difference is note significant, and usually the phenotype is evocative on ultrasound. Given its association with severe placental dysfunction and potential false‐negative CMA results, targeted testing (FISH/Karyotype) is critical when triploidy is suspected clinically. Conversely, confined placental mosaicism was more frequent in isolated FGR (20% vs. 8%). This supports placental‐specific testing (e.g., CVS) when amniocentesis is negative but hemodynamic signs persist. A Deep Dive Into Genetic versus Placental Causes Sankaran et al., identified 25% genetic causes, 39% maternal causes, and 6% placental causes for FGR []. In our series, 50% of FGR had a placental cause, 31% had a genetic cause, 3% had isolated velamentous cord insertion, 2.3% had an infectious cause, and 13.4% had unexplained causes (Table ). Our placental‐origin FGR rate is high compared to the literature, possibly due to the absence of placental pathological examination in published series. Interestingly, the presence/absence of associated HC < 3rd percentile in FGR does not indicate genetic or placental origin. Typically, preserved head circumference with hemodynamic ultrasound signs suggests a placental cause, but this was not observed in our series (HC < 3rd percentile in FGR was as frequent in genetic as in placental cases) (Figure ). Pregnancy and Fetal Outcome The risk of FD and neonatal death is well‐known in early and severe FGR. Our study found that 14% (n = 20) of FGR cases were associated with FD, comparable to the 12% of FD in the review made by Pels et al. []. We observed 4% neonatal death in comparison to the 8% of this study, possibly due to our high 20% rate of TOP in severe FGR cases. All FD fetuses had a birth weight far below the fifth percentile. When comparing pregnancy outcomes between isolated FGR and FGR associated with major signs, several key differences emerge. TOP are significantly more common in the FGR with major signs group (36% vs. 10%), and fetal demise (FD) rates are also higher in this group (20% vs. 10%). However, the higher rate of cesarean sections in the isolated FGR group (43% vs. 23%) is less intuitive and warrants further explanation. One plausible explanation for this discrepancy is that FGR with major signs is more likely to result in TOP or FD, thereby reducing the number of live births eligible for cesarean delivery. In contrast, isolated FGR may prompt increased fetal surveillance and intervention due to concerns about fetal well‐being. Clinicians may opt for proactive cesarean delivery in isolated FGR cases to mitigate risks associated with placental insufficiency, fetal hypoxia, or intrapartum complications. This proactive approach may not be as prevalent in the FGR with major signs group, where alternative outcomes (such as TOP or FD) are more common. Strengths and Limitations of the Study While our study offers valuable insights, and specifically analyze hemodynamic signs, it has limitations. Our analysis of fetuses with FGR is not exhaustive, and the genetic analyses vary widely (Supporting Information Table 3), but illustrates clearly the necessity of harmonizing our practices concerning the indications and types of genetic tests conducted during an amniocentesis when faced with FGR. For practical clinical decision‐making, we grouped all causes of FGR etiology diagnosable using invasive procedure, including infectious origin. However, this approach risks oversimplifying cases with multiple coexisting etiologies. Despite this, we optimized the study with available resources to contribute meaningfully to the field. The study's strengths include its large sample size from a 2‐year period at a tertiary referral center, providing extensive case analysis of FGR. Further research with standardized methods and a larger sample is needed to confirm and expand our findings.

Conclusions
Conclusions Our retrospective 2‐year study at Toulouse University Hospital revealed a significant diagnostic yield (19%) for monogenetic or chromosomal syndromes in FGR cases (with or without associated major signs) that presented with hemodynamic indicators. Furthermore, the high diagnostic yield for monogenetic or chromosomal syndromes in isolated FGR cases with hemodynamic indicators (11%) underscores the importance of offering genetic testing for all FGR cases, whether isolated or associated with ultrasound hemodynamic signs. Additionally, placental and fetal pathological examination in cases of TOP and FD is essential as well, as many genetic causes may not be detectable prenatally. Obtaining a clear etiological diagnosis enables more precise genetic counseling and the development of tailored management strategies for future pregnancies.

title: Prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of fetal cardiac rhabdomyoma and analysis of clinical outcomes.
abstract: Fetal cardiac tumors are relatively rare among congenital heart diseases (CHDs). The presence of cardiac rhabdomyoma (CR) during fetal development may serve as the earliest clinical sign of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), with multiple CRs being a strong predictor of TSC. This study aimed to summarize the ultrasound image characteristics of fetal CR and follow up the comprehensive information of prenatal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination, genetics, and postnatal changes in clinical outcomes to improve the detection rate and optimize the outcome of the diagnosis and treatment. A retrospective analysis was performed on prenatal ultrasound diagnostic data from 36 fetal CRs, including lesion characteristics (number, location, size, and associated complications), as well as follow-up information during pregnancy and within 1 year of birth. Among the 36 cases of CR, 11 patients (31%) underwent MRI examinations. Of these, five cases presented with subependymal nodules on cranial MRI, suggestive of TSC; one case showed asymmetric bilateral lateral ventricles and dilation of the vein of Galen; and one case revealed multiple hemorrhages in the cerebral parenchyma and subependymal regions, along with left lateral ventricular enlargement. The remaining four MRI results were negative. Genetic testing identified abnormalities in 6 cases (17%), including five with TSC-related gene mutations and one with a whole exome sequencing (WES) anomaly. Pregnancy was terminated in 12 cases (33%). Postnatal follow-up demonstrated no significant change in CR size in one case, a reduction in CR size in one case, and complete regression of CR in three cases. Echocardiography plays a critical role in diagnosing CR. For fetuses prenatally diagnosed with CR, routine cranial MRI and whole exome genetic testing should be performed to confirm the presence of TSC or other pathogenic variants, which is essential for early clinical intervention and decision-making. Keywords: Cardiac rhabdomyoma (CR), tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), prenatal echocardiography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), genetic testing

Prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of fetal cardiac rhabdomyoma and analysis of clinical outcomes

Introduction
Introduction Fetal cardiac tumors are rare among congenital heart diseases (CHDs), with an incidence ranging from 0.0017% to 0.4000%. The majority of fetal cardiac tumors are benign, with cardiac rhabdomyoma (CR) being the most common type during the fetal period (). According to the literature, CR typically presents as single or multiple round masses with higher echogenicity than the ventricular wall. These tumors vary in location and exhibit limited mobility during cardiac activity, with most growing inward; larger lesions may occasionally protrude outward, potentially causing compressive symptoms (). Fetal CR is often an early manifestation of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Although ultrasound alone cannot reliably distinguish isolated CR from TSC-associated CR, their prognoses differ significantly: Isolated CR (after excluding TSC) typically requires no intervention and often regresses spontaneously postnatally. TSC-associated CR carries a poor prognosis; early prenatal counseling and clinical intervention are strongly recommended (). This study aimed to summarize the ultrasound image characteristics of fetal CR and to explore the clinical value of CR detection by combining comprehensive information from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination, genetics, and postpartum clinical outcomes. Some cases were followed up to observe changes in CR from the prenatal period to 1 year postpartum, as well as the occurrence of TSC in affected children. Previous studies have primarily focused on the diagnosis of CR detected by prenatal ultrasound or the management of pediatric cardiac space-occupying lesions postnatally. To some extent, this study fills a gap in the integrated prenatal and postnatal management of CR, which may effectively improve overall fetal outcomes and the long-term quality of life for affected children. We present this article in accordance with the STROBE reporting checklist (available at https://qims.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/qims-2025-1208/rc).

Methods
Methods A total of 36 fetuses diagnosed with CR by prenatal ultrasound at Gansu Provincial Maternity and Child-Care Hospital between May 2021 and December 2023 were included in this study. The gestational age at diagnosis was 22–37 weeks (mean: 29±4 weeks); maternal age was 21–40 years (mean: 28.05±4.78 years); and all cases were singleton pregnancies. This study excluded pregnant women with other maternal diseases, fetuses with other complex malformations, and multiple pregnancies. All examinations are conducted by three physicians with specialist qualifications (at the level of deputy director or above) who had undergone standardized training in image interpretation consistency and passed the assessment. Images are retained for analysis, and in cases of disagreement regarding image analysis, the three physicians entered discussion to reach a consensus. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Gansu Provincial Maternity and Child-Care Hospital (approval No. 2021-30KYSL), and written informed consent was provided by all participating mothers and their families. Ultrasound examination protocol The fetal heart was diagnosed using the Voluson E10 color Doppler ultrasound diagnostic instrument (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) and an abdominal volume probe with a frequency of 2.0–5.0 MHz. All fetal cardiac ultrasound examinations were performed in strict accordance with the 2023 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) Guidelines for fetal cardiac screening, with systematic acquisition of the following standard views (): fetal heart position, four-chamber view, outflow tract, three vessels, and three-vessel tracheal view. The pediatric heart was diagnosed using the Philips EPIQ7C color Doppler ultrasound diagnostic instrument (Philips, Amsterdam, Netherlands), and the pediatric heart probe was placed at the apex of the heart and continuously tracked and scanned from longitudinal, transverse, and oblique directions, with a focus on observing whether there are space-occupying lesions in the heart chamber and myocardium. Measurements were taken using the maximum diameter, recording the location, number, size, and presence of associated secondary lesions of the CR. The evaluation also included determining whether there were concurrent malformations in other systems, with follow-up records of pregnancy outcomes maintained. MRI examination and methodology A Philips Achieva 1.5-T MRI scanner was used to perform standard axial, coronal, and sagittal scans of the fetal brain. The scans focused on detecting abnormal signals and their locations. The total acquisition time for all sequences did not exceed 15 minutes. TSC genetic testing and diagnostic approach Amniotic fluid obtained through amniocentesis or umbilical cord blood was subjected to karyotype analysis, single-nucleotide polymorphism-based comparative genomic hybridization, or whole exome sequencing (WES). According to the updated International Diagnostic Criteria and Management Recommendations for TSC (), in addition to the identification of pathogenic TSC gene mutations, the clinical diagnostic criteria encompass 11 major features and 7 minor features. The 11 major features include: Hypopigmented macules (≥3 lesions, each ≥5 mm in diameter), cephalic fibrous plaques or facial angiofibromas (≥3 lesions), ungual fibromas (≥2 lesions), multiple retinal hamartomas, shagreen patches, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, angiomyolipomas (≥2 lesions), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2 lesions), and CR. The seven minor features include: “confetti” skin lesions, intraoral fibromas (≥2 lesions), dental enamel pits (≥3 lesions), retinal achromic patches, multiple renal tumors, non-renal hamartomas, and sclerotic bone lesions. A definitive diagnosis of TSC requires either two major features or one major feature plus two minor features. A probable diagnosis requires one major feature plus one minor feature. The first seven major features and all minor features are typically non-assessable during fetal development. Therefore, the primary diagnostic indicators for fetal TSC are CR, abnormal signal nodules under the ependymal membrane, and abnormal signals in the cerebral cortex. If two criteria are met, TSC can be diagnosed.

Results
Results Fetal echocardiography examination results All 36 cases of CRs demonstrated the following sonographic features on echocardiography: circular or elliptical nodules with slightly high echogenicity, with relatively uniform internal echoes, clear contours, no posterior acoustic shadowing, no obvious blood flow signals inside, and the growth location could be distributed on the left and right ventricular surfaces of each atrium, ventricle, and interventricular septum, with the ventricle as the main focus. Among the 36 cases, there were 25 cases of multiple lesions (69.4%) and 11 cases of solitary lesions (30.6%), including 1 case in the left atrium, 6 cases in the right atrium, 24 cases in the left ventricle, 21 cases in the right ventricle, and 8 cases in the interventricular septum. The maximum diameter observed was 32 mm, and the minimum diameter was 4 mm (details are provided in ). Fetal MRI brain examination results A total of 11 routine fetal MRI examinations were performed, of which five cases showed subependymal nodules with abnormal signal intensity, suggestive of TSC. There was one case exhibiting multiple hemorrhagic foci in the bilateral brain parenchyma and subependymal regions; one case presented with asymmetrical bilateral lateral ventricles and dilatation of the vein of Galen; and four cases revealed no abnormalities on MRI. TSC1 and TSC2 gene family testing results Genetic testing was performed in six cases: three cases had TSC2 gene mutations, including one case where the pregnant woman herself carried a heterozygous TSC2 mutation, suggesting familial inheritance; two cases had TSC1 gene mutations; one case showed no significant abnormalities in chromosomal banding analysis, but WES detected a pathogenic variant in a gene associated with the clinical phenotype. Clinical outcomes In one case, isolated multiple CRs were detected on ultrasound without other abnormalities; the pregnancy was terminated. There was one case that presented with multiple CRs and compression-induced obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), leading to increased forward flow velocity; the pregnancy was terminated (). In another case, multiple CRs were detected on ultrasound and multiple subependymal and parenchymal hyperechoic nodules on MRI, suggestive of TSC; subsequent genetic testing confirmed a TSC2 mutation, and the pregnancy was terminated. Further, two cases with multiple CRs on ultrasound underwent genetic testing, both revealing TSC1 mutations, leading to termination. In one case, multiple CRs were detected on ultrasound, and genetic testing identified a fetal TSC2 mutation; the pregnant woman herself was a heterozygous TSC2 mutation carrier, and the pregnancy was terminated. There was one case diagnosed with multiple CRs at 31 weeks, followed by polyhydramnios at 33 weeks. Some five cases were diagnosed as CR during the fetal period. After birth, cardiac ultrasound showed that one case had no significant change in size, one case showed a slight decrease in size, and three cases showed the disappearance of CR 1 year after birth (). In one case, multiple CRs were detected by ultrasound (), and there were no obvious abnormalities in chromosomal banding analysis, but WES detected a pathogenic variant in a gene associated with the clinical phenotype. Partial clinical results of prenatal and postpartum follow-up of CRs. (A) CR compresses the LVOT, causing a decrease in its inner diameter. (B) CR compresses the LVOT, causing an increase in forward blood flow velocity. (C) Multiple CRs during fetal development. (D) At 1 year after the birth of the fetus shown in (C), cardiac ultrasound showed that CR disappeared. (E) Ultrasound image showed multiple CRs in the fetus, and the pregnant woman chose to terminate the pregnancy. Red arrows: fetal CR. CR, cardiac rhabdomyoma; LVOT, left ventricular outflow tract.

Discussion
Discussion CR is the most common cardiac tumor during the fetal and neonatal periods. It is not a true neoplastic lesion but rather a hamartoma formed by the abnormal proliferation of normal cardiomyocytes. These lesions exhibit the following distinctive characteristics: (I) predilection for females (male-to-female ratio approximately 1:1.3); (II) frequent multifocal growth (69.4% of cases in this study); and (III) unique growth patterns: may enlarge under the maternal hormonal influence during fetal development but often regress spontaneously after birth (). Clinical studies demonstrate that clinical manifestations of CR are closely related to lesion size: smaller lesions are typically asymptomatic and rarely cause hemodynamic changes, whereas larger lesions may interfere with the cardiac conduction system or compress outflow tracts. When causing significant arrhythmias, hemodynamic instability, or even syncope, surgical resection usually yields favorable outcomes (with a 5-year postoperative survival rate of 95%). The overall prognosis primarily depends on four key factors: number of tumors, maximum diameter, specific anatomical location, and presence of associated systemic abnormalities (). In recent years, the application of spatio-temporal image correlation technology has further clarified the impact of space-occupying lesions on the heart, improving diagnostic and therapeutic outcomes. Its volumetric analysis function enables three-dimensional spatial localization of tumors in the heart and allows for quantitative assessment of tumor volume changes over gestational weeks (). This technology has a high dependency on equipment and operator skill, and the success rate of data collection is low when gestational age is less than 20 weeks. In future studies, this technology should be actively integrated to conduct related research and enhance diagnostic accuracy. The detection of CR during fetal development may serve as the earliest clinical indicator of TSC, with multiple CRs representing a robust predictive marker for TSC (). TSC is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder caused by pathogenic variants in either the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Epidemiological studies report a TSC incidence of approximately 1/20,000 to 1/8,500 live births, with about 35% of cases showing familial inheritance patterns and 65% resulting from de novo mutations occurring during conception or early embryonic development. This multisystem disorder typically manifests with the involvement of multiple organ systems, including the brain, heart, kidneys, and skin. Postnatally, most affected individuals develop the classic clinical triad: facial angiofibroma, epilepsy, and intellectual disability. Notably, patients with TSC2 mutations generally exhibit more severe disease manifestations compared to those with TSC1 mutations, including more extensive cutaneous and renal involvement, as well as higher frequencies of epileptic seizures (). Current therapeutic approaches remain limited to symptomatic management, as no curative treatment exists for TSC. The condition carries a guarded prognosis with significant quality of life implications (). Consequently, the accurate prenatal diagnosis of CR assumes critical importance for timely pregnancy termination decisions in severe cases. Normal myocardial cells are arranged in regular bundles, whereas in patients with TSC-associated CR, the myocardial cells exhibit disorganized alignment with irregular intercellular connections and orientation. Additionally, hypertrophy of some cardiomyocytes may occur (). Peritumoral fibrosis often develops around the rhabdomyomas, forming fibrotic zones that restrict normal myocardial motion, impair electrical conduction, and compromise blood supply, thereby exacerbating myocardial injury (). Mechanical compression by the lesions on myocardial microstructure may also lead to reduced local contractile reserve. These pathological changes collectively decrease cardiac compliance, ultimately resulting in refractory arrhythmias and heart failure. Based on previous studies, ventricular ejection fraction (EF), myocardial strain rate, filling time fraction, and ejection time fraction serve as reliable indicators for assessing cardiac function. These parameters can effectively evaluate the impact of CRs on fetal cardiac function, with strain parameters being particularly sensitive for early detection of functional decline even when EF remains normal. Future research should focus on investigating the relationship between these functional parameters and postnatal regression patterns or complications. This study analyzed 36 cases of fetal CRs, with a particular focus on their sonographic characteristics, imaging findings, genetic associations, and pregnancy outcomes. Notably, multiple CRs demonstrated a stronger correlation with TSC compared to solitary lesions. Several studies have reported that fetal CRs may spontaneously regress within 2 years after birth. Partial resection of symptomatic tumors with residual masses has also been shown to undergo subsequent regression (). In our study cohort of four prenatally diagnosed CR cases, one case demonstrated complete resolution at 1-year postnatal follow-up; one case showed a slight reduction in tumor size on postnatal day 1; one case maintained stable dimensions at 1-year evaluation; one case developed LVOT obstruction due to compression by a CR, ultimately leading to pregnancy termination after parental counseling. These findings are consistent with existing literature regarding the natural history of fetal CRs. TSC exhibits diverse clinical phenotypes, often leading to missed diagnoses. According to literature reports, about 80–90% of TSC patients seek medical attention for the first time due to epileptic seizures (). In addition, about 63–78% of TSC infants will experience focal seizures and epileptic spasms (). Notably, most affected infants manifest their first seizure before 1 year of age, underscoring the need for early electroencephalogram (EEG) evaluation, as abnormal EEG patterns often precede clinical seizure onset (,). Timely intervention is necessary to mitigate neurological sequelae. Additionally, reports indicate that comparing brain tissue from fetuses with CHD undergoing termination of pregnancy with brain tissue from normal fetuses reveals overall vascular dysregulation in CHD fetuses, accompanied by central blood redistribution (low brain-placenta ratio), which may lead to impaired cerebral perfusion and subsequent neurodevelopmental disorders (). Future research should focus on the association between CR and embryonic neurodevelopmental abnormalities to further elucidate the causes of craniofacial-related growth abnormalities in CR. In this study, one case of fetal diagnosis was CR, and an additional MRI showed multiple hypoechoic nodules under the ependymal membrane. Therefore, the clinical prenatal diagnosis was TSC. In the first 2 months after birth, frequent tonic-clonic seizures were observed as the first manifestation, and treatment with oxcarbazepine was given. Occasionally, intermittent seizures occur after treatment. This suggests that a fetal head MRI examination should be performed when cardiac CR is detected before delivery to improve the diagnostic accuracy of TSC. In this study, one case was diagnosed with CR by prenatal ultrasound, and no abnormal signal nodules were found in the fetal head MRI examination. The genetic testing result confirmed the TSC1 mutation. Therefore, when a prenatal ultrasound combined with MRI cannot make a clear diagnosis, genetic testing should be performed. In addition, 10–15% of TSC patients who meet clinical diagnostic criteria cannot identify pathogenic variants of TSC1 or TSC2 through routine genetic testing (,). Therefore, when ultrasound detects no abnormalities in fetal CR combined with genetic testing, an MRI examination should also be performed to improve the detection rate of TSC. It can be seen that when CR occurs, in addition to TSC gene-related testing, WES can be performed to exclude other pathogenic gene variations. In addition, in this study, one fetus had multiple CRs, and genetic testing showed a TSC2 gene mutation in the fetus. The pregnant woman herself also had a heterozygous mutation in the TSC2 gene, indicating a familial predisposition, consistent with previous studies (). Precise genotyping forms the fundamental basis for genetic risk assessment in TSC. Current epidemiological data demonstrate that TSC2 mutations account for 70–80% of sporadic cases, whereas TSC1 mutations represent only 10–20% (). In families with TSC2 mutations, there remains an approximate 1–2% recurrence risk even when parental testing yields negative results (). When a parent is affected, offspring have a 50% inheritance probability (independent of the specific gene involved), though descendants inheriting TSC2 mutations typically manifest more severe phenotypic expressions. Patients with TSC1 mutations typically exhibit milder or delayed-onset symptoms, with some individuals presenting solely with cutaneous manifestations (e.g., facial angiofibromas) or mild epilepsy. In contrast, TSC2 mutations are associated with more severe clinical manifestations, including: higher incidence of cortical dysplasia (e.g., cortical tubers), significantly increased risk of cognitive impairment (including intellectual disability), greater prevalence of epilepsy (particularly infantile spasms), often with earlier onset, larger renal angiomyolipomas, and more frequent neurological lesions (e.g., SEGAs) (). Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for optimal outcomes, as evidenced by the fact that most infants with TSC experience their first epileptic seizure before 12 months of age. In addition to monitoring CR changes, long-term surveillance of subependymal nodules (which may potentially progress to SEGA) () is essential. Therefore, all TSC patients should undergo brain MRI scans every 1–3 years until they are 25 years old, when SEGAs are most prevalent. Recent studies indicate that known SEGAs may continue to grow during adulthood, and in rare cases, may newly develop in adult patients. Consequently, lifelong monitoring for potential SEGA growth is warranted. We recommend routine screening for TSC-associated brain lesions to improve early detection rates. Early intervention can significantly reduce the risk of seizure development and improve neurological outcomes. Notably, cardiac symptoms (such as arrhythmias) may serve as the initial manifestation of TSC, warranting prompt electrocardiogram (ECG) evaluation. For children with CR, asymptomatic patients should receive follow-up echocardiographic examinations every 1–3 years until documented regression of the CRs occurs. Inversetti et al. () found that in patients with CHD, placental perfusion was normal in early pregnancy, but levels of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A and placental growth factor were abnormally low, and urinary tract angiography hemodynamic parameters gradually increased. These findings may directly or indirectly indicate placental dysfunction. Fetal CHD may cause hemodynamic changes, which further affect placental structure and function. Additionally, placental abnormalities may lead to uteroplacental insufficiency, affecting fetal development, particularly cardiac development, creating a vicious cycle. The author believes that CR at different locations can cause different hemodynamic changes in fetal cardiac blood flow. Pregnant women with severe fetal cardiac malformations have a significantly higher risk of preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, and small-for-gestational-age infants. Future research should focus on exploring the common pathways between cardiovascular development and placental function, and investigating the relationship between the two. In this study, the average gestational age of fetal CR was found to be 29 weeks, which is in the late stage of pregnancy. Due to the dynamic process of fetal development, CR was not detected by echocardiography during mid-pregnancy fetal screening. Therefore, it is important to be alert to the occurrence of CR in the late stage of pregnancy (), highlighting the importance of scheduled prenatal checkups. There are certain limitations to this study: (I) the sample size is relatively small, and some cases have incomplete follow-up results for late pregnancy and postnatal information of CR. In this study, 12 cases (33.3%) lacked postpartum follow-up data for the following reasons: loss to follow-up across provinces (n=5), family refusal of follow-up examinations (n=4), and newborn transfer to another hospital for treatment (n=3). (II) A pregnant woman was diagnosed with multiple CRs at 31 weeks, and at 33 weeks, she was diagnosed with polyhydramnios, which is a known risk factor for premature birth or even fetal death in the uterus (). In future studies, attention should be paid to the relationship between the two. (III) Most of the cerebral nodules and cardiac hyperechoic nodules do not have clear pathological results and are only clinical diagnostic results. (IV) In this case, only one pregnant woman had a TSC gene mutation. The family history of TSC in other cases was not recorded, and there is limited research on familial inheritance.

Conclusions
Conclusions In summary, this study holds significant clinical value for the prognostic assessment of fetal CRs and early diagnosis of TSC. Prenatal echocardiography remains the primary diagnostic tool for fetal CRs. However, its efficacy may be compromised by maternal factors (e.g., thick abdominal wall, oligohydramnios) and fetal factors (e.g., suboptimal positioning, small cerebral structures). In recent years, fetal MRI has been increasingly utilized as an adjunct diagnostic modality when ultrasound detects abnormal fetal structures (). However, compared to ultrasonography, MRI examinations are more time-consuming and costly, thus serving as a secondary complementary diagnostic approach. When CR is detected on ultrasound but MRI is negative, TSC-related genetic testing is still necessary. If CR is detected on ultrasound but no TSC-related gene abnormalities are found, an additional MRI should still be performed, as it can improve the detection rate of clinical diagnosis. Since TSC is a hereditary condition, genetic testing should also include the parents. Combined imaging and genomics diagnosis can significantly improve clinical outcomes after fetal CR diagnosis and provide genetic information for those who wish to have children in the future, thereby achieving the goal of eugenics.

title: Pregnancy and early neurodevelopment after prenatal ventriculomegaly: a 2011-2024 single-center retrospective cohort of 983 cases.
label_reason: Fetal ventriculomegaly cohort with amniocentesis karyotype/CMA results.
abstract: To evaluate pregnancy and early neurodevelopmental outcomes in fetuses with prenatally diagnosed ventriculomegaly (VM) in a large single-center retrospective cohort (2011–2024), and to determine the independent predictive value of VM severity, isolation status, laterality, and intrauterine evolution for adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes among term survivors. This retrospective cohort study included fetuses diagnosed with VM at West China Second University Hospital from 2011 to 2024. VM was defined as a lateral ventricular width ≥ 10 mm measured on standardized axial trans-thalamo-ventricular planes and categorized as mild (10–12 mm), moderate (12.1–15 mm), or severe (> 15 mm) per SMFM/ISUOG guidelines. Pregnancy and neonatal outcomes were extracted from medical records. Neurodevelopmental outcomes in term liveborn infants were assessed through structured telephone interviews and clinical documentation; for children born between 2019 and 2024, systematic follow-up at 2–3 years of age was implemented, with Gesell Developmental Schedule assessments performed when developmental concerns were identified. For those born between 2011 and 2018, outcomes were based on parental reports and available medical records. Logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted associations. VM was identified in 983 of 154,436 deliveries (0.64%). Live birth rates were 94.8% for mild, 85.9% for moderate, and 24.6% for severe VM. Among 654 term survivors, 39 (5.96%) exhibited abnormal neurodevelopment. In univariable analyses, greater VM severity, bilateral VM, variation of ventricular width, and abnormal postnatal cranial ultrasound findings were significantly associated with adverse neurodevelopment. After adjustment, only ventricular severity remained independently predictive, with adjusted odds ratios of 2.77 (95% CI, 1.31–5.85) for moderate and 7.57 (95% CI, 1.34–42.61) for severe VM compared with mild VM. Non-isolated VM showed a nonsignificant trend toward increased risk (OR 1.64; 95% CI, 0.65–4.14). Ventricular severity was the only prenatal factor that remained independently associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in this cohort, whereas associations with laterality, isolation status, and postnatal imaging findings attenuated after adjustment. Through a unified diagnostic pathway incorporating systematic neurosonography, selective fetal magnetic resonance imaging, and chromosomal microarray testing, this large Asian cohort adds real-world data supporting severity-based risk stratification and illustrating the potential value of multimodal prenatal evaluation for perinatal counseling and management. Given the retrospective design and non-standardized follow-up, however, these associations should be interpreted with caution. Not applicable.
