Discussion
Discussion With the advanced use of CMA in prenatal diagnosis, more and more uncertain variants have been identified. In the current clinical practice, WES technology has been gradually used to investigate additional sequence variants in patients with normal CMA result or unexplained CNVs [–]. In the present study, a 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication was identified in the fetus with multiple ultrasound anomalies. The subsequent WES result demonstrated two compound heterozygous variants NM_001178010.2: c.[1512 C > T]; [326_329dup] in the CDC45 gene in the fetus, which may be responsible for the ultrasound anomalies observed in the fetus. Partial trisomy 13q is a rare chromosomal abnormality with variable clinical phenotypes. In our present study, a 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication was identified in the fetus, with no report of similar duplication was available in the literature, to our knowledge. A previous study identified a small 13q31.3 duplication encompassing the miR17-92 cluster and the first 5 exons of GPC5 in a patient, who exhibited familial dominant post-axial polydactyly type A, overgrowth, significant facial dysmorphisms and autistic traits []. In addition, another study identified a de novo 13q31.3 microduplication encompassing MIR17HG but without GPC5 in a female with developmental delay, skeletal and digital abnormalities, and other features []. The 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication in our present study only contains SLITRK5, and did not cover the above mentioned genes. SLITRK5 is widely expressed in the central nervous system, regulating and participating in many essential steps of central nervous system development []. However, there is no clear relationship between SLITRK5 and a certain disease, and the triplosensitivity effect of SLITRK5 is still unclear. In addition, the detected 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication was inherited from the father who had normal clinical features, thus, we consider that the fetal ultrasound anomalies may not be ascribed to the 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication. Meier-Gorlin syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder commonly characterized with microtia, patellar applasia/hypoplasia, and a proportionate short stature []. Previous studies indicated that microtia is present in 94% of patients with MGORS, and 97% of patients with MGORS would manifest intra uterine growth retardation in the fetal period [, ]. In addition, microcephaly (head circumference <−3SD) was present in 43% of the patients and rarely exhibit congenital cardiac anomalies, while, most of them had normal intellect [, ]. Few reports are available on revealing CDC45 variants, and the prenatal events are more rare. Biallelic variants in the CDC45 gene have been found to cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome, and manifest clinical phenotypes ranging from a classic MGORS presentation to syndromic craniosynostosis with short stature, but without other MGORS features [, , ]. In our study, two compound heterozygous variants NM_001178010.2: c.[1512 C > T]; [326_329dup] in the CDC45 gene were identified in the fetus. The ultrasound anomalies in the fetus included craniosynostosis, irregular skull, brachydactyly of the left thumb, microtia, FGR, genitalia abnormality, congenital heart defects and widened eye distance, which were consistent with the phenotype of MGORS7. The c.326_329dup(p.N111Ifs*11) variant of CDC45 identified in the present study was characterized as a pathogenic variant, whereas the clinical significance of the c.1512 C > T(p.H504=) variant in CDC45 remains elusive. Notably, published literature has described the detection of variants of uncertain significance in trans with the c.326_329dup(p.N111Ifs*11) variant in two patients diagnosed with MGORS7 [, ]. In addition, a previous study conducted by Knapp et al. [] reported a synonymous variant c.630G > A(p.Arg210=) in compound heterozygosity with a frameshift variant in two affected sibs that resulted in Meier-Gorlin syndrome with craniosynostosis. The synonymous variant of c.1512 C > T(p.H504=) has been previously identified in a patient causing MGORS7, but lacks of functional research []. In the present study, the synonymous p.H504 = variant was identified in a patient with MGORS7 again, and the mRNA splicing analysis using fetal aborted tissue indicated that the exon 4 and exon 15 may be spliced out in mRNA in the patient, which could explain the remarkable phenotypes in the patient. Notably, in our present study, a more severe irregular skull was observed. This study is also subject to certain limitations. In the fourth pregnancy of the enrolled family, the fetus also elicited multiple ultrasound anomalies, which may be due to disruption of the CDC45 gene, while, no specimen was available for further genetic study. Analysis of mRNA splicing in fetal muscle tissues yielded results inconsistent with those from minigene splicing assays, a finding that underscores the value of in vivo mRNA splicing analysis even in organs with low gene expression. Therefore, we contend that when patient-derived tissue samples are available, in vivo experimental approaches should be prioritized, as they more faithfully recapitulate physiological splicing dynamics. Regrettably, we are unable to provide Sanger sequencing data for fetal muscle tissue samples, owing to technical artifacts including double peaks or signal absence in sequencing reads, which have resulted in poor alignment quality. This observation is likely linked to the low expression level of CDC45 in skeletal muscle tissue and thus merits further in-depth investigation. In conclusion, this present study first described a more severe irregular skull of acrocephaly in a fetus with CDC45 variants leading to MGORS7. In addition, our study indicated that the familial 13q31.1q31.3 microduplication may be a benign CNVs. Moreover, our findings manifested that the c.1512 C > T(p.H504=) variant in CDC45 may influence mRNA splicing but the evidence remains incomplete. This findings further enhanced the application of value of WES in etiology diagnosis of fetuses with unexplained CNVs and provided more insight into genotype and phenotype correlation and molecular mechanism.

title: Prenatal diagnosis of distal Xq28 duplication syndrome: case reports and literature review.
label_reason: Three fetuses with ultrasound anomalies (nasal bone hypoplasia etc.) tested by karyotyping and CMA.
abstract: Xq28 duplications are a significant cause of X-linked intellectual disability (XLID). While the postnatal features of distal Xq28 duplication syndrome are well characterized, the prenatal phenotypes remain poorly defined due to limited data, posing challenges for genetic counseling. We identified three fetuses carrying 454–558 kb distal Xq28 microduplications through chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) from 13,084 prenatal cases at our center. The primary indications for diagnosis were abnormal ultrasound findings. Case 1 (male) and case 3 (female) exhibited nasal bone hypoplasia. Case 2 (male) showed increased nuchal translucency (NT) and a persistent right umbilical vein. After genetic counseling, two couples chose to terminate their pregnancies, while one couple continued the pregnancy and delivered a healthy child. Distal Xq28 duplications would present diverse prenatal phenotypes, ranging from normal to abnormal. Skeletal anomalies are the most common prenatal features in symptomatic fetuses with this duplication. Prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling are essential for providing clinical guidance to the affected families. The correlation between prenatal ultrasound findings and the distal Xq28 duplications requires further investigation in larger cohorts. Keywords: Xq28 duplications, Prenatal diagnosis, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Prenatal phenotypes, Genetic counseling

Prenatal diagnosis of distal Xq28 duplication syndrome: case reports and literature review

Introduction
Introduction X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder, accounting for approximately 5–10% of intellectual disability in males []. A major genetic cause is X-chromosome copy number variants (CNVs), particularly duplications in the Xq28 band. Due to the high gene density in this region, such duplications can lead to XLID accompanied by multisystem involvement []. Various duplications involving the Xq28 region lead to distinct XLID syndromes. One of the most frequently reported copy-number gains in this region involves the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 gene (MECP2), which typically causes neurodevelopmental disorders in males, often presenting mild to moderate intellectual disability (ID). More distally, the int22h1/int22h2-mediated Xq28 duplication has been recognized as a distinct XLID subtype. This microduplication spans a 0.5 Mb subregion of Xq28, flanked by low copy repeats (LCRs) within intron 22 homologous regions 1 and 2 []. Clinical features include varying degrees of ID, distinctive facial features and recurrent infections. The higher prevalence in males is due to ascertainment bias, as hemizygosity causes a more severe phenotype []. At present, the postnatal phenotypes associated with distal Xq28 duplications have been well characterized, while the prenatal phenotypes are scarcely delineated due to limited reports. This lack of prenatal data complicates the genetic counseling in clinical practice. In this study, we describe the prenatal phenotypes and molecular data of three fetuses (two males and one female) with distal Xq28 duplications and present a systematic review of prenatal features for this chromosome disorder.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Clinical data In the present study, three fetuses with distal Xq28 microduplications were identified through CMA from a cohort of 13,084 pregnancies referred for invasive diagnostic testing via amniocentesis at the First Hospital of Jilin University during October 2018 to September 2024. The primary indications for prenatal diagnosis were high-risk of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) results, high risk of maternal serum screening, ultrasound anomalies and advanced maternal age and so on. Karyotyping and CMA were performed for all pregnancies. Written informed consent was obtained from all the couples. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Hospital of Jilin University (No. 2021 − 706).

Cytogenetic analysis
Cytogenetic analysis With written informed consent, pregnant women underwent amniocentesis for karyotyping analysis. A total of 30 mL of amniotic fluid cells were collected. Routine cytogenetic analysis was performed on G-band metaphases at 400–500 banding resolution, prepared from 20 mL of cultured amniotic fluid cells according to standard laboratory protocols. In accordance with the International System for Human Cytogenetic Nomenclature 2016 (ISCN 2016), twenty metaphases were analyzed for each sample.

Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA)
Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) The genomic DNA was extracted from the amniotic fluid cells and parental peripheral blood with QIAamp® DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Inc., Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. After written informed consent was obtained, 10 mL uncultured amniotic fluid cells were collected through amniocentesis. Then the procedures are conducted using CytoScan 750 K array (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA, USA), in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol and our previous study []. The procedure included genomic DNA extraction, digestion and ligation, PCR amplification, PCR product purification, quantification and fragmentation, labeling, array hybridization, washing and scanning. Thresholds for genome-wide screening were set at ≥ 100 kb for gains and losses. The detected CNVs were comprehensively estimated by comparing them with published literature and the public databases: (1) Database of Genomic Variants (DGV) (DGV, http://dgv.tcag.ca/dgv/app/home), (2) Database of Chromosomal Imbalance and Phenotype in Humans using Ensemble Resources (DECIPHER, https://www.deciphergenomics.org/), (3) Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen, http://www.clinicalgenome.org/), (4) ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), (5) PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and (6) Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/omim). And all CNVs were classified as pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), variants of unknown significance (VOUS), likely benign (LB) and benign (B). Genomic positions refer to the Human Genome assembly Dec.2013 (GRCh38/hg38).

Case presentation
Case presentation Case 1 A 25-year-old, gravida 2, para 0, pregnant woman was referred to our center for prenatal diagnosis because of abnormal ultrasound findings. Prenatal ultrasound findings at 25 weeks of gestation showed that the fetus exhibited nasal bone hypoplasia. The couple was nonconsanguineous and healthy. The karyotype of the fetus was 46,XY. CMA detected a 458 kb duplication at Xq28: arr[GRCh38]Xq28(154892358–155334741)x2 (Fig. A). The couple refused to accept CMA verification, so the inheritance is not available. After genetic counseling, the pregnant woman chose to terminate the pregnancy. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) identifying distal Xq28 duplications in our case series. (A) Case 1: arr[GRCh38] Xq28(154892358–155334741)x2. (B) Case 2: arr[GRCh38] Xq28(154909475–155467409)x2. (C) Case 3: arr[GRCh38] Xq28(154881139–155334741)x3 Case 2 A 28-year-old, gravida 1, para 0, pregnant woman was referred to our center for prenatal diagnosis because of abnormal ultrasound findings and NIPT inferring high risk of sex chromosome aneuploidy. Prenatal sonography at 19 weeks of gestation showed that the fetus exhibited increased nuchal translucency (NT) and a persistent right umbilical vein. The couple was nonconsanguineous and healthy. The karyotype of the fetus was 46,XY. CMA detected a 558 kb duplication at Xq28: arr[GRCh38]Xq28(154909475–155467409)x2 (Fig. B), which was proved to be maternally inherited. After genetic counseling, the pregnant woman chose to terminate the pregnancy. Case 3 A 35-year-old, gravida 1, para 0, pregnant woman was referred to our center for prenatal diagnosis because of abnormal ultrasound findings. Prenatal sonography at 18 weeks of gestation showed that the fetus exhibited nasal bone hypoplasia. The couple was nonconsanguineous and phenotypically normal. The karyotype of the fetus was 46,XX. CMA detected a 454 kb duplication at Xq28: arr[GRCh38]Xq28(154881139–155334741)x3 (Fig. C). The couple declined CMA verification, so the inheritance is not available. After genetic counseling, the pregnant woman chose to continue the pregnancy and delivered a healthy child.

Discussion
Discussion In our study, we presented three prenatal cases with distal Xq28 duplications accompanied by abnormal ultrasound findings. Case 1 and case 3 exhibited nasal bone hypoplasia, carrying 458 kb and 454 kb Xq28 duplications, respectively. Case 2 showed increased NT and a persistent right umbilical vein, with a 558 kb Xq28 duplication. After genetic counseling, two cases chose to terminate the pregnancy, and one case chose to continue the pregnancy and delivered a healthy child. Since the first case was reported in 2011, more than 70 clinical cases of distal Xq28 duplications have been reported to date []. The prevalence of this chromosome disorder varied in different populations. It was reported that the incidence rate in postnatal probands was approximately 0.11% (9/8447) []. The int22h1/int22h2-mediated Xq28 duplication syndrome, mediated by specific repeated elements (int22h1 and int22h2), the frequency has been estimated as ~ 1 per 1,000 among males with intellectual disability []. The incident rate was limited in prenatal setting. According to our study, the detection rate of prenatally detected distal Xq28 duplications was 0.022% (3/13,084), which was higher than previous reporting 0.0017% (16/93,646) []. Therefore, larger-scale studies should be accumulated to further explore the frequencies of distal Xq28 duplications in the prenatal setting. As a rare X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (XLIDS), int22h1/int22h2-mediated Xq28 duplication is caused by recurrent ~ 0.5 Mb duplications in the Xq28 region (GRCh37/hg19: 154.1–154.6.1.6 Mb), typically resulting from non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) between the LCRs int22h1 and int22h2 [, ]. Males with Xq28 duplication syndrome commonly present intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe, facial dysmorphism, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), impulsivity, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) [, ]. The duplications in male carriers are usually maternally inherited [, , ]. Previous review showed that 100% of assessable males with Xq28 duplications presented ID []. However, the findings from Billes et al. showed that ID was observed in 11/17 (65%) live-born male carriers, which indicated the existence of incomplete penetrance of this CNV in male hemizygous carriers. It was assumed that a two-hit model might be responsible for this []. Heterozygous female carriers display a broad phenotypic spectrum, ranging from asymptomatic to mild cognitive impairment, subtle dysmorphic features, or behavioral issues. This variability is partly influenced by the degree of skewed X-chromosome inactivation (XCI), which modulates the expression of the duplicated allele []. As an X-linked condition, carrier females have a 50% chance of transmitting the duplication to their offspring []. However, no clear correlation between affected females and skewed X-inactivation has been yet established. The first prenatally identified Xq28 duplication was reported in 2020, and the accumulation of prenatal data on this finding remains limited. To provide a better understanding of Xq28 duplications in prenatal period, we conducted a literature review on fetuses carrying the distal Xq28 duplications according to the literature review [, , , –]. A total of 32 prenatal cases with distal Xq28 duplications were collected. The gestational ages ranged from 12 to 27 weeks, and the duplicated size varied from 0.080 Mb to 0.873 Mb. Among these cases, 17/32 were male and 15/32 were female. Regarding inheritance, 18/32 were parentally inherited, 2/32 cases were de novo, and 12/17 cases were not available. The indications for prenatal diagnosis included abnormal ultrasound findings (13/32), adverse pregnancy history (2/32), maternal carrier status of F8 intron 22 inversion (1/32), advanced maternal age (1/32), high risk of sex chromosome aneuploidy (1/32) and elevated maternal hCG (1/32). Notably, 19/32 were discovered incidentally without abnormal prenatal symptoms and 13/32 presented abnormal ultrasound findings. This suggested that asymptomatic fetuses with distal Xq28 duplications may be more common than symptomatic ones in the prenatal setting. Overall, these findings indicated that distal Xq28 duplications were associated with a wide spectrum of prenatal phenotypes, ranging from normal to abnormal. In addition, a higher rate of ultrasonographic anomalies in males (47.1%, 8/17) than in females (33.3%, 5/15) was discovered, although no statistically significant differences were observed (P > 0.05). Whether the incidence of ultrasonographic anomalies differs by fetal sex requires further investigation in larger cohorts. Among these prenatally detected Xq28 duplications, 13 of which presented abnormal ultrasound findings (Table ; Fig. ). 10/13 were directly mediated by int22h1 and int22h2 segmental duplications, and 3/13 seems to be also mediated by the more telomeric int22h3. Recurrent ultrasound anomalies in symptomatic fetuses included skeletal abnormalities (4/13), increased nuchal translucency, nasal bone hypoplasia, genitourinary, and cardiovascular anomalies (each 2/13). Based on the findings above, the distal Xq28 duplications exhibit phenotypic diversity in the prenatal setting. Skeletal anomalies are the most common prenatal features in symptomatic fetuses associated with this duplication. However, the fetus 8 presenting ventriculomegaly in Levy et al. carried trisomy 21 except for Xq28 duplication. Since ventriculomegaly is one of the possible signs of trisomy 21 in the prenatal period [], the correlation between ventriculomegaly and distal Xq28 duplications remains to be explored. It was worth noting that these ultrasound anomalies observed in distal Xq28 duplications are nonspecific and frequently encountered in prenatal medicine practice, which would usually lead to prenatal genetic testing. So the abnormal findings in our study could be incidental, and further studies with larger cohort are needed to explore the prenatal phenotypes for this chromosome disorder. Scale representation of the duplicated region in distal Xq28 duplication (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/): (A) Genes located within the distal Xq28 region; (B) Previously reported prenatal distal Xq28 duplications and the duplicated fragments in our cases. Genomic parameters are from GRCh38/hg38 According to the DECIPHER database, the duplicated Xq28 region in our cases contains two disease-relevant genes. F8 (OMIM: 300841), which encodes coagulation factor VIII-deficiencies in this factor cause hemophilia A (OMIM: 306700) []. RAB39B (OMIM: 300774) is a dosage-sensitive gene associated with X-linked intellectual developmental disorder-72 (XLID72), characterized by macrocephaly, epilepsy, and ASD []. Mutations in RAB39B also cause Waisman syndrome (OMIM: 311510), an X-linked neurological disorder featuring delayed psychomotor development, impaired intellectual development, and early-onset Parkinson disease []. RAB39B plays a crucial role in brain development by regulating synapse formation and maintenance in hippocampal neurons [, ]. The duplicated segment also includes CLIC2 (OMIM: 300138), a gene linked to cognitive impairment, seizures and cardiac anomalies []. Increased expression of RAB39B and CLIC2 has been correlated with neurocognitive impairment []. However, the precise pathogenic mechanisms and functional impacts of these genes within the Xq28 duplications require further investigation. Compared with karyotype analysis, CMA can detect subchromosomal imbalances smaller than 5 Mb at the molecular level, delineating precise duplicated or deleted regions and the relevant genes involved. Despite normal karyotypic results in our cases, CMA successfully identified distal Xq28 duplications, providing a more accurate basis for genetic counseling. The clinical impact of Xq28 microduplications is highly complex and is influenced by phenotypic variability, incomplete penetrance, and inheritance patterns. In our study, two couples (case1 and case 2) chose to terminate their pregnancies. In case 1, parental CMA testing was not performed, so it remained unclear whether the duplication was de novo or inherited. In case 2, preimplantation genetic testing would be an appropriate option for future pregnancies, and prenatal diagnosis may be considered if the couple intend to conceive again. Due to the unpredictable patterns of XCI, affected females may present a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations. As for case 3, the child is still very young, long-term follow up involving growth and development details is essential.

Conclusion
Conclusion In conclusion, we described three prenatal cases with Xq28 microduplications presenting diverse abnormal ultrasound findings. Distal Xq28 duplications would present diverse prenatal phenotypes, ranging from normal to abnormal. Skeletal anomalies were the most frequently observed prenatal features in symptomatic fetuses with this duplication, but further investigation is still necessary to explore the prenatal genotype-phenotype correlation. For prenatally detected Xq28 duplications, genetic counselling should be offered by combining phenotypic variability, incomplete penetrance, and inheritance patterns. In addition, long-term follow-up involving postnatal development is recommended into adulthood.

title: Chromosomal microarray analysis for the prenatal diagnosis in fetuses with fetal echogenic bowel: a retrospective cohort study.
label_reason: Echogenic bowel cohort with CMA.
abstract: Fetal echogenic bowel (FEB) is often accompanied by the presence of chromosomal abnormalities. Here, we intend to evaluate the efficiency of chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) for identifying fetal risks associated with FEB, with a focus on chromosomal abnormalities and adverse pregnancy outcomes linked to FEB. This retrospective study included a total of 446 pregnant women who underwent CMA and had intrauterine fetuses with FEB. This cohort was classified into multiple subgroups for analysis, so as to obtain the relationships among FEB in different groups, chromosome microarray results, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. For fetuses with non-isolated FEB, the pathogenicity rate and microarray abnormality rate were higher than those with isolated FEB. Surprisingly, this study found that the detection rate of pathogenic copy number variations (CNVs) in FEB during the second trimester was higher than that in the third trimester. Conversely, the detection rate of FEB with variants of uncertain significance (VOUS) in the third trimester was higher than that in the second trimester. The pathogenic CNVs in cases with combined ultrasound soft markers was higher than those without, and the more soft markers were combined, the higher the abnormal rate and pathogenic rate. The detection rate of FEB with VOUS in pregnant women with a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes was higher than those without such a history. The correlations between soft markers and FEB or gestational age (GA) at diagnosis and FEB were risk factors for abnormal CMA results in FEB cases. The correlation between GA at diagnosis and FEB was a risk factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes in FEB cases. Both the GA at diagnosis and soft markers are important factors for predicting CMA abnormalities. The correlation between the GA at diagnosis and FEB is also a risk factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes of FEB. Keywords: Fetal echogenic bowel, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Prenatal diagnosis, Ultrasound abnormalities, Adverse pregnancy outcomes

Chromosomal microarray analysis for the prenatal diagnosis in fetuses with fetal echogenic bowel: a retrospective cohort study

Introduction
Introduction Fetal echogenic bowel (FEB) refers to fetal intestinal echogenic enhancement, which is often defined as intestinal echo that resembles or is stronger than bone and is a prenatal ultrasound finding. Echogenic bowel may be focal, diffuse, and multifocal []. It’s reported that the incidence of high echogenic fetal bowel in mid-pregnancy fetuses ranges from 2% to 18% [, ]. What’s more, hyperechoic fetal bowel also increased the risk of cystic fibrosis, fetal growth retardation, congenital infections, thalassemia, intraamniotic bleeding, and perinatal death, and therefore require thorough antenatal management and postnatal follow-up [, ]. Multiple studies have demonstrated that echogenic bowel increases the probability of chromosomal abnormalities, especially trisomy 21 []. Currently, CMA offers additional diagnostic benefits by revealing submicroscopic imbalances or copy number changes when diagnosing chromosomal abnormalities compared to traditional karyotyping, demonstrating unique advantages [, ]. It’s reported that CMA can provide an additional 3.0% diagnostic value for isolated systemic ultrasound abnormalities or non-specific abnormalities with normal karyotypes []. CMA has become a standard tool for investigating patients with unexplained developmental disorders and/or birth defects in genetic diagnosis []. Up to date, limited studies have explored how CMA findings correlate with different subtypes of FEB and their clinical implications, therefore, we aim to clarify the relationship between FEB classifications and CMA results, as well as adverse pregnancy outcomes, to provide better guidance for prenatal management of fetuses with FEB.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Participants This retrospective study involved the data of 446 pregnant women from the Affiliated Hospital of Jining Medical University who had increased intestinal echogenicity in the intrauterine fetus by ultrasound from March 2019 to July 2024. Amniocentesis and/or umbilical cord blood sampling was performed on these pregnant women to obtain fetal CMA results. Informed consent was obtained from all participants and their families, and all experiments were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Chromosomal microarray analysis The Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K SNP Array chip, which includes 200,000 SNP markers and 550,000 CNV markers, is utilized for detection purposes. This chip conducts screening for chromosomal copy number variations at a specific resolution, examining the entire genome’s chromosomes. However, it does not encompass all loci across the entire chromosomal set; rather, it focuses on known clinically significant abnormalities related to chromosomal microdeletions, microduplications, and subtelomeric deletion syndromes. The data were analyzed according to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). This guideline classifies all selected copy number variations (CNVs) into pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), variants of uncertain significance (VOUS), likely benign, or benign. Pathogenic CNVs (pCNVs), likely pathogenic CNVs (lpCNVs), and VOUS were recorded, while likely benign or benign CNVs were not taken into consideration []. Follow-up outcomes The follow-up for all cases was conducted via telephone to obtain patients’ information related to the development, pregnancy outcomes, and postnatal growth of fetuses with intestinal echogenicity enhancement; subsequently, the pregnancy outcomes were verified using medical records, birth certificates, and other written documentation. Regarding follow-up completeness, no cases were lost to follow-up throughout the study period. Almost all pregnancy outcomes were systematically retrieved and verified from the electronic medical record system, ensuring the accuracy and completeness of the clinical data included in the final analysis. For the remaining few cases, follow-up confirmation was completed via telephone communication. Statistical analysis Data entry was conducted using EXCEL, while data analysis was performed with SPSS 25.0. Categorical data were expressed as n%, and statistical differences in detection rates were assessed using chi-square tests and Fisher’s exact tests. Logistic regression analysis was employed to identify risk factors associated with abnormal CMA results or adverse pregnancy outcomes in fetuses with FEB. Stratified analysis was used to control the confounding effects of age on the results. P < 0.05 is considered statistically significant.

Results
Results This study involved a total of 446 fetuses exhibiting hyperechogenic bowel, of which 183 (41.0%) are isolated and the other 263 (59.0%) are non-isolated EB. The age of the included pregnant women ranged from 18 to 47 years, and the gestational age was between 17+ 5 and 33 weeks. And We defined the second trimester as 14 to 27+ 6 weeks of gestation and the third trimester as ≥ 28 weeks until delivery, with 28 weeks of gestation as the demarcation point. In the present study, adverse pregnancy outcomes included induction of labor (indicated for chromosomal abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, polyhydramnios, intrauterine fetal demise, and other etiologies) and premature rupture of membranes. The non-isolated FEB were categorized into three groups: isolated with ultrasound soft marker abnormalities (247 cases, 93.9%)、 isolated with structural abnormalities (9 cases, 3.4%), a combination of both (7 cases, 2.7%) (shown in Fig. ). In the study of fetuses with isolated hyperechogenic bowel, 10 cases (5.5%) exhibited chromosomal microarray abnormalities, with 6 cases (3.3%) presenting pathogenic anomalies. In contrast, among those with non-isolated findings, 38 cases (14.4%) showed CMA abnormalities, and 25 cases (9.5%) had pathogenic anomalies. The statistical analysis indicates that both the abnormality rate and the pathogenicity rate were significantly higher in the non-isolated group compared to the isolated group, with statistical significance (5.5% vs. 14.4%, P = 0.003; 3.3% vs. 9.5%, P = 0.011). The distribution of various types of fetal echogenic bowel in this study. FEB, Fetal echogenic bowel; P, Pathogenic CNVs; LP, Likely Pathogenic CNVs; VOUS, variants of uncertain significance All cases were classified according to the gestational age (GA) at the discovery of FEB, the presence or absence of combined soft marker abnormalities, the age of the parturient, and the presence or absence of a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistical analysis showed that for fetuses diagnosed with FEB in the second trimester, the detection rate of pathogenic variants was higher than those diagnosed in the third trimester, while the detection rate of VOUS in FEB in the third trimester was higher than that in the second trimester (P = 0.002, P = 0.006). The detection rate of pathogenic CNVs in FEB with soft marker abnormalities was higher than that in cases without, and the detection rate of normal results in FEB cases without soft marker abnormalities was higher than that in cases with soft marker abnormalities, and both differences were statistically significant (P = 0.004, P = 0.001). Interestingly, a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes did not affect the detection rate of pathogenic CNVs in FEB, but the detection rate of variants of uncertain significance was higher than that in cases without a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes (P = 0.041) (shown in Table ). The results of the logistic regression analysis showed that the correlations between GA at diagnosis and FEB, soft markers and FEB were the main risk factors for predicting chromosomal aberrations in FEB fetuses. At the time of diagnosis, GA was negatively correlated with the probability of chromosomal aberrations (OR = 0.925, p = 0.041), and soft markers were positively correlated with the probability of chromosomal aberrations (OR = 2.990, p = 0.003) . In addition, there was a significant association between GA at diagnosis and adverse pregnancy outcomes, also showing a negative correlation (OR = 0.788, p = 0.000) (shown in Fig. ). Logistic regression analysis of risk factors for CMA abnormalities and adverse outcomes in FEB. A depicts the results for CMA abnormalities, while B illustrates the outcomes associated with adverse pregnancy events The CMA abnormality was used as the dependent variable, and age, soft markers, GA (weeks) at the diagnosis of FEB, and history of adverse pregnancy outcomes were included as independent variables in the regression model. A hierarchical regression method was adopted. In the first layer, sociodemographic factors were controlled. In the second layer, three dimensions including soft markers, gestational weeks at the diagnosis of FEB, and history of adverse pregnancy outcomes were incorporated. The proportion of CMA abnormality that could be explained by a certain type of factors was represented by ΔR2 (the change in R2). The contributions of these two types of factors in explaining CMA abnormality were 0.3% and 3.4% respectively (shown in Table ). Furthermore, Table presents the number of cases with pathogenic copy - number variations (CNVs) and their respective proportions among cases with different numbers of combined soft markers. The results indicate that the more soft markers are combined, the higher the rates of pathogenic and abnormal CMA results and adverse pregnancy outcomes. In the specified order, the respective CMA abnormality rates were 10.8%, 20.3%, 36.8%; the corresponding pathogenicity rates were 4.5%, 18.6%, 31.6%; the corresponding rates of adverse pregnancy outcomes were 5.7%, 15.3%, 36.8%. After multiple comparisons, all P values were less than 0.05, indicating statistical significance. Table presents the clinical characteristics of all cases with pathogenic and likely pathogenic CNVs. The average GA at diagnosis is 19 + 3 weeks. There are 6 isolated cases. The commonly combined soft markers are echogenic intracardiac focus, nuchal translucency thickening, and nasal bone dysplasia. Additionally, two cases are respectively combined with abnormal right subclavian artery (ARSA) and ventricular septal perforation, and one case is combined with fetal growth restriction (FGR). The majority of pathogenic CMA results were primarily trisomy 21, microdeletions and microduplications of gene segments. The parents of the vast majority of fetuses with pathogenic CNVs chose to terminate the pregnancy. However, 6 cases had successful deliveries, and follow - up examinations showed no abnormalities in the newborns.

Discussion
Discussion At present, the pathophysiology of FEB is not fully understood. Its occurrence may be related to physiological meconium accumulation in late pregnancy, and most cases are isolated. Therefore, for fetuses with FEB, a detailed medical history and systematic ultrasound examination are necessary before deciding on interventional procedures such as CMA []. However, it is important to take it seriously when FEB correlated with structural malformations or abnormal soft indicators. A previous study showed that approximately 55.6% of patients had solitary echogenic bowel and that the rate of chromosomal abnormalities in the isolated group was lower than in the group with other structural malformations or soft marker abnormalities []. In this study, a total of 41.0% of patients had isolated FEB, of which 3.3% had pathogenic or likely pathogenic conditions, 5.5% had chromosomal abnormalities, while the non-isolated group had a higher pathogenicity rate (9.5%) and a microarray abnormality rate (14.4%) than the isolated group, and the statistical analysis was significant. In addition, our results showed that the greater the variety of combined soft indicators, the greater the risk of anomalies and adverse pregnancy outcome. However, the role of CMA in evaluating fetuses with FEB remains controversial. The Society for Maternal - Fetal Medicine (SMFM) suggests that for pregnant women with negative serum or cfDNA screening results and isolated fetal echogenic bowel, further aneuploidy assessment is not recommended []. Some studies have found that FEB combined with abnormal ultrasonic soft markers does not increase the incidence of chromosomal abnormalities []. However, our study has found that the incidence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic CMA in FEB cases combined with ultrasound soft markers is higher than that in cases without such combination. Moreover, the correlation between ultrasound soft markers and FEB is a risk factor for CMA abnormalities in FEB. The results of the hierarchical regression analysis further verified that soft markers and gestational weeks at diagnosis are important factors for predicting CMA abnormalities. Moreover, there is a positive correlation between soft markers and CMA abnormalities, indicating that the presence of soft markers will increase the risk of CMA abnormalities. In contrast, there is a negative correlation between gestational weeks and CMA abnormalities, suggesting that the larger the gestational weeks, the lower the risk of CMA abnormalities. In our study, the greater the number of combined soft markers, the higher the ratio of CMA abnormalities, the pathogenicity rate and the rate of adverse pregnancy outcomes. In addition, we also investigated the impact of the gestational age at the diagnosis of FEB and the history of adverse pregnancy outcomes on the detection rate of CMA abnormalities. For the first time, we discovered that the incidence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic CMA in the second trimester is higher than that in the third trimester. Interestingly, however, the incidence of CMA with uncertain clinical significance in the third trimester is higher than that in the second trimester. The incidence of aneuploidy abnormalities with uncertain clinical significance detected by CMA in the fetuses of pregnant women with a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes is higher than that in those without such a history. All of the above results are statistically significant. A key finding of this study is the trimester-specific variability in CMA performance when evaluating fetuses with FEB, a discrepancy that necessitates further clarification of CMA’s clinical utility and practical implications in the diagnosis of third-trimester FEB cases. In contrast to the second trimester—where an adequate timeframe permits comprehensive prenatal counseling and pregnancy management planning—the third trimester offers only a narrow window for clinical interventions following an FEB diagnosis. Additionally, intestinal hyperechogenicity detected during this late-gestation period may arise from benign physiological processes such as meconium accumulation, further complicating the interpretation of CMA results. Thus, CMA implementation for third-trimester FEB requires rigorous risk-benefit stratification: it is critical to avoid the identification of variants of uncertain significance (VOUS) with no clear clinical relevance, as these findings do not alter perinatal care pathways but may impose considerable psychological distress on affected families. Synthesizing our findings, the evaluation of fetuses with third-trimester FEB faces three core challenges: low detection rates of pathogenic CNVs via CMA, a high burden of VOUS, and a narrow window for clinical intervention. We therefore advocate for a personalized risk-stratified approach for such pregnancies: CMA should be selectively recommended for high-risk third-trimester FEB cases (e.g., non-isolated FEB), whereas testing may be deferred for isolated FEB cases. This targeted strategy not only strengthens the clinical applicability of our findings but also provides actionable guidance for addressing the distinct challenges associated with late-pregnancy FEB diagnosis. In recent years, research has indicated that the detection of FEB by prenatal ultrasound may increase the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, with the incidence of adverse pregnancy outcomes being approximately 20%. Some studies have found that the later the first diagnosis of FEB during pregnancy, the higher the likelihood of a favorable neonatal prognosis. This result may be related to the physiological increase in meconium content in the intestines and colon in the later stages of pregnancy []. In our study, there were a total of 37 adverse pregnancy outcomes, with an incidence of 8.3%. The results of logistic regression analysis showed that the gestational age at the diagnosis of FEB was negatively correlated with adverse pregnancy outcomes (OR = 0.788, P = 0.000). That is, the greater the gestational week at detection, the lower the incidence of adverse pregnancy outcomes, which is consistent with previous findings. Previous studies have demonstrated the incidence of aneuploidy in FEBs ranging from 3 to 27%, and multiple studies have demonstrated a strong association between FEB and Down syndrome [–]. In our study, a total of 48 FEBs had microarray abnormalities (10.8%, 48/446) and 31 had pathogenic/likely pathogenic abnormalities (7.0%, 31/446). Among the pathogenic abnormalities, 16 cases has trisomy 21, 1 case was trisomy 21 chimerism, and the rest were Xp21.1, Xp22.31, Yp11.2q11.221 and Yq11.221q11.23, Xq26.3q27.3, 17p12, 7q11.23, 16p13.11, 15q11.2 microdeletion, 22q11.21, 16p13.11, Xq28 microduplication, and 1 case was combined with 9p22.2p13.1 microduplication and 9p24.3p22.1 microdeletion, 1 case was combined with 3q24q29 microduplication and 4q34.3q35.2 microdeletion. According to the Pubmed database, the clinical phenotype of Yp11.2q11.221 may manifest as fetal gonadal dysgenesis, ambiguous external genitalia, and in males, it is often accompanied by spermatogenic disorders such as azoospermia [–]. Multiple studies have found that 16p13.11 microdeletion and 22q11.21 microduplication may lead to clinical symptoms such as mental retardation, epilepsy, and hypotonia, with penetrance insufficiency or variable expression, with penetrance rates of about 13.1% and 21.9% [, ]. The Xq26.3q27.3, Xp22.31 microdeletions, and Xq28 microduplications all exhibited sex-related characteristics. Men are often more affected, while women have milder clinical presentations [–]. Hela Ben Khelifa et al. reported that Xp22.3 microdeletion was also associated with ichthyosis []. It is worth noting that studies have reported that 15q11.2, 7q11.23 microdeletion not only bring mental and intellectual abnormalities, but also increase a series of problems such as congenital heart disease, endocrine abnormalities, craniofacial malformations, and connective tissue abnormalities [, ]. Some research reports have shown that 17p2 microdeletion can cause hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP), and the clinical manifestations are motor and sensory peripheral neuropathy [, ]. Nowadays, there is no clear literature on Xp21.1 microdeletion and 9p22.2p13.1, 3q24q29microduplication. Due to the continuous improvement of variant classification standards, the definition of VOUS is also changing []. The lack of evidence, especially the existence of the particularly rare form of VOUS, makes it difficult for VOUS to be used in clinical practice and can only be overcome by continuously collecting evidence []. The incidence of VOUS in the population ranges from 0.9% to 12%6. In our study, a total of 3.8% of patients (17/446) had VOUS, which is consistent with previous studies. Most of the VOUS pregnancy outcomes were not abnormal, with only two pregnant women choosing induction of labour to terminate the pregnancy, and there was no abnormality in the appearance of the induced infants. In our study, the higher VOUS detection rate in third-trimester FEB and patients with adverse pregnancy histories informs clinical practice. Pre-test counseling should highlight VOUS potential and limited clinical utility to manage expectations and prevent overdiagnosis or unnecessary interventions. Postnatal follow-up of VOUS cases—most with favorable outcomes in our study—aids real-world data accumulation for variant reclassification, especially valuable in regions hindered by CMA costs. Our findings support risk stratification for fetuses with FEB: CMA should be prioritized for high-risk cases (e.g., second-trimester diagnosis or combined soft markers, which are associated with higher pathogenic CNV rates), adopt stepwise screening (e.g., cfDNA) for low-risk subgroups in resource-limited/non-insured regions to balance accuracy and cost. VOUS-related pre-test counseling and postnatal follow-up aid variant classification. Large prospective studies are needed to validate this model, assess cost-effectiveness, and refine guidelines globally. The limitations of this study mainly stem from its retrospective nature. We were unable to evaluate all potential confounding factors, such as medication use. Additionally, the genetic assessment in our study relied solely on microarray analysis. Consequently, single - gene mutations cannot be excluded, and further whole - genome sequencing will be necessary for investigation.

Conclusion
Conclusion This is the first study to demonstrate that for fetuses with FEB, the detection rate of pathogenic CNVs via CMA is significantly higher when FEB is diagnosed in the second trimester (14 ~ 27 + 6 weeks) than in the third trimester (≥ 28weeks), whereas FEB diagnosed in the third trimester is more likely to be associated with VOUS. Pregnant individuals with adverse pregnancy history also have higher VOUS-FEB detection rates.

title: Genetic architecture and prognostic significance of suspected fetal microcephaly: evidence from prenatal exome sequencing in a large prospective cohort.
label_reason: Microcephaly fetuses with exome.
abstract:
Fetal microcephaly (FMIC) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with heterogeneous etiologies and uncertain prenatal prognosis. Discrepancies between prenatal and postnatal head circumference (HC) measurements may confound ultrasound-based diagnosis, underscoring the need for genetic stratification to improve risk assessment. This prospective cohort study analyzed data from 301 fetuses with suspected FMIC collected between 2014 and 2022. Trio-prenatal exome sequencing (pES) was performed in 301 fetuses with suspected FMIC and normal results on karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis. Diagnostic yield, molecular spectrum, and pathway enrichment were analyzed. Clinical follow-up was conducted to correlate genetic findings with postnatal neurodevelopmental outcomes. Molecular diagnoses were achieved in 41 cases (13.6%). Diagnostic yield was significantly higher in complex FMIC compared with isolated FMIC (15.9% vs. 10.1%, p  < 0.01), and peaked in cases with family history (26.7%). Our findings expand the prenatal phenotypic spectrum for six genes (TUBB2A, DUOX2, EBP, FAM111A, FGFR3, PEX1), indicating that microcephaly can be a primary presenting feature in the fetus for conditions where it was previously considered a secondary or postnatal finding. Pathogenic variants were enriched in neurogenesis and extracellular matrix–related pathways, implicating dysregulated cell cycle progression and synaptogenesis. Importantly, HC standard deviation (HC-SD) correlated with diagnostic yield and, as demonstrated by multivariable analysis, served as an independent predictor of postnatal prognosis (aOR: 2.1 per 1-SD decrease; 95% CI: 1.5-3.0), whereas fetal growth restriction appeared nonspecific. This prospective cohort study provides the largest prenatal genomic and prognostic analysis of FMIC to date, revealing potential genotype–phenotype associations, pathogenic pathways, and prognostic markers. These findings enhance understanding of FMIC mechanisms and provide essential evidence for prenatal genetic counseling and individualized risk assessment.
