text:
Genetic architecture and prognostic significance of suspected fetal microcephaly: evidence from prenatal exome sequencing in a large prospective cohort

Introduction
Introduction Fetal microcephaly (FMIC) is a significant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a head circumference (HC) more than three standard deviations (SD) below the mean for gestational age, according to the reference criteria proposed by Jeanty and colleagues [, ]. The global incidence of FMIC varies considerably, ranging from 8.7 per 10,000 live births in the United States to 33 per 10,000 in Guangzhou, South China, and is influenced by factors such as ethnicity, genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, and differences in diagnostic criteria across populations [–]. FMIC is commonly associated with an interplay of genetic and environmental factors and can lead to intellectual disability, motor dysfunction, and other neurological complications. Based on the classification of cortical developmental malformations [], microcephaly is broadly divided into two types according to the timing of disruption relative to glial and neuronal migration stages: primary microcephaly (PM) and secondary microcephaly (SM). The etiology of FMIC is highly heterogeneous, with genetic factors playing a prominent role []. An extensive postnatal study reported that genetic causes account for 47.5% of known microcephaly cases, while the etiology remains unknown in approximately 40% of cases []. Previous research has shown that chromosomal abnormalities are present in approximately 23.3% of FMIC cases [], and exome sequencing (ES) can yield an additional diagnostic yield of up to 37% []. Traditional prenatal biometric methods are associated with a high false-positive diagnostic yield, often leading to recommendations for pregnancy termination in countries where it is legally permitted. False-negative diagnoses are less common but may result in the birth of infants with symptomatic microcephaly []. Although conventional genetic screening offers some potential for early detection, these methods lack molecular-level precision in predicting and diagnosing FMIC. The rapid advancement of genomic technologies—particularly the application of ES []—has significantly transformed the study of genetic disorders. A landmark prenatal exome sequencing (pES) cohort study published in The Lancet in 2019 evaluated fetuses with structural anomalies (SA) detected by ultrasound as part of the PAGE (Prenatal Assessment of Genomes and Exomes) project. After excluding aneuploidies and large copy number variations (CNVs), the study assessed the presence of pathogenic variants in developmental disorder-associated genes in affected fetuses and their parents []. pES enables the detection of mutations across all coding regions of the genome [], facilitating the identification of potentially pathogenic variants underlying neurodevelopmental disorders []. Compared to traditional genetic screening methods, pES offers superior sensitivity and accuracy, particularly in detecting de novo mutations, which are critical for diagnosing rare and complex genetic conditions [, ]. As pES technology matures, it has become a powerful tool for detecting gene mutations associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, especially those linked to rare or orphan diseases []. In prenatal diagnosis, pES enables earlier identification of potential FMIC cases, increases diagnostic yield, and provides a valuable molecular foundation for clinical decision-making and early intervention strategies []. Despite these advances, most research on the prenatal diagnosis of FMIC has been limited to case reports or small-scale studies. There is a notable lack of large-cohort investigations that systematically link pES findings with pregnancy management decisions and long-term clinical outcomes. Our previous work began to address this by analyzing 224 FMIC cases with chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and pES, expanding the known mutational spectrum [], and reporting specific gene-phenotype associations []. However, a significant gap remains in understanding how genetic results correlate with postnatal neurodevelopment and how to build an integrated “genotype-phenotype-outcome” framework for clinical practice. This study aims to fill that gap by leveraging a large prospective cohort to analyze the relationship between genetic findings, HC severity, and long-term prognosis. We seek to establish a more robust evidence base for prenatal risk stratification, improve diagnostic accuracy, and refine genetic counseling for families affected by FMIC.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Sample collection and processing This study was conducted as a prospective cohort study. Eligible fetuses were identified and enrolled contemporaneously at the time of diagnosis between January 2014 and December 2022 at Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center (GWCMC), Guangzhou Medical University, and Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Trio-pES was performed during the pregnancy, and the results were a key factor in parental decisions regarding pregnancy continuation or termination. All subsequent outcome data, including postnatal follow-up, were collected prospectively from the time of enrollment. Fetal samples were obtained from amniotic fluid cells or umbilical cord blood, while parental samples were collected from peripheral blood. Genomic DNA was extracted using the Qiagen DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany), following the manufacturer’s standard protocol. Inclusion criteria were fetuses with an HC measured by prenatal ultrasound to be less than − 2 SD for gestational age and microcephaly confirmed by fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although FMIC is typically defined as HC < -3 SD, cases between − 2 SD and − 3 SD were also included due to the high variability in prenatal HC measurements. This broader threshold may introduce variability when comparing diagnostic yields with studies adhering to the < -3 SD definition. As the participating centers are tertiary referral units, the cohort is enriched for cases diagnosed at later gestational ages and those exhibiting more complex or severe phenotypes, reflecting the typical case mix of such settings. Cases were enrolled regardless of additional SA, family history, or pregnancy history. Exclusion criteria included evidence of Zika virus or other intrauterine infections (e.g., TORCH) confirmed by maternal serology or amniotic fluid PCR. Family and pregnancy histories were not considered in the inclusion/exclusion process to focus the analysis on the independent effect of molecular biomarkers. The inclusion/exclusion workflow is illustrated in Fig. . Flowchart of subject recruitment and experimental procedures This study was reviewed and approved by the ethics committees of GWCMC, Guangzhou Medical University, and Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine (Ethics Approval No. 356B01). All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant national ethical guidelines and regulations. Before any invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures, detailed information regarding the study’s objectives, methodology, potential risks, and benefits was provided to participating couples. Informed written consent was obtained from all participants, indicating their complete understanding and voluntary participation in the study. The research team placed a high priority on maintaining participant privacy and data security. All personal information was kept strictly confidential and used exclusively for scientific analysis within the scope of this study. These measures ensured full ethical compliance and safeguarded the rights and well-being of all participants. pES and data analysis Target enrichment was performed using the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon kit (Agilent Technologies, USA), followed by 150-base pair paired-end sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (Illumina, USA). Quality control metrics included a mean sequencing depth of ≥ 100×, ≥ 98% coverage of target regions, and a Q30 base call accuracy of ≥ 85%. Sequence data analysis involved a three-step pipeline—quality control, sequence alignment, variant calling, and annotation—based on our previously published protocol [], ensuring data accuracy and consistency. Variant classification followed the 2015 guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) []. All variants were independently reviewed and double-blinded by two clinical geneticists and three molecular diagnostics specialists, with final pathogenicity assignments determined through multidisciplinary consensus discussion. Variant validation and gene functional analysis Clinically significant variants identified through pES were validated using Sanger sequencing. Sequence alignment and mutation confirmation were performed with BioEdit software (version 7.2.5). Functional enrichment analysis of the implicated genes was conducted using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG, https://www.kegg.jp) and Gene Ontology (GO, http://geneontology.org) databases. The R package clusterProfiler was employed to identify key biological processes and signaling pathways associated with microcephaly. Mutation spectrum analysis All genes harboring pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified through pES were manually extracted for analysis. Based on clinical phenotype data, all confirmed FMIC cases were categorized into two subgroups: isolated FMIC and complex FMIC. The number of mutation events for each gene was calculated separately within each subgroup. Standardized mutation frequencies (%) were then determined using the total number of cases in each group as the denominator (isolated: n = 119; complex: n = 182). Data processing was conducted using Python (version 3.10), and heatmaps were generated with the Seaborn and Matplotlib packages to visualize mutation frequencies, with color gradients indicating frequency intensity (white representing 0% and blue indicating high-frequency mutations). Fisher’s exact test was applied for genes with high mutation frequencies to assess enrichment differences between phenotype groups. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Clinical follow-up Clinical follow-up was conducted through December 2023. Postnatal health and developmental outcomes were collected via telephone interviews and electronic medical record review. Data included assessments of physical growth, motor development, sensory function, and other relevant clinical parameters. GO and KEGG enrichment analysis GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were performed using R software (version 4.2.1). The input gene list was first annotated using the org.Hs.eg.db package to convert gene symbols to standardized human gene IDs (Homo sapiens). Subsequently, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were conducted using the clusterProfiler package (version 4.4.4). The results were visualized with the ggplot2 package (version 3.3.6) to illustrate significantly enriched biological processes and signaling pathways. Data analysis and results interpretation Data processing and statistical analysis were performed using SPSS (IBM SPSS Statistics version 29) and R software (version 4.3.1). The workflow included data cleaning, handling of missing values, and final statistical evaluation. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to assess differences in clinical phenotype means across groups with different genetic variants, followed by post hoc multiple comparisons to verify the accuracy of intergroup differences. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using Fisher’s exact test, which is particularly suited for small sample sizes or imbalanced categories. Chi-square tests were also applied to examine the independence between categorical variables. For continuous variables, Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess linear relationships, such as between gene expression levels and clinical phenotypic traits. Spearman’s rank correlation was applied for robustness when data deviated from a normal distribution. To address the tiny sample size in the subgroup with HC ≤ -4SD (n = 5), we conducted robustness analyses. Initially, we applied a Bayesian two-proportion model with a Beta (0.5,0.5) before comparing the HC ≤ -4SD group with other groups, deriving posterior distributions and 95% credible intervals for outcome rates, risk difference (RD), risk ratio (RR), and log odds ratio (logOR), and reporting the probability Pr(RD > 0). Subsequently, a Bayesian logistic regression with weakly informative priors (regression coefficients ~ Normal(0,1)) was employed, adjusting for covariates such as gestational age, structural malformations, and fetal growth restriction (FGR), to obtain posterior odds ratios (OR) and 95% credible intervals. Finally, we performed 10,000 stratified bootstrap iterations using percentile/BCa methods to estimate the confidence intervals for RD/OR and assess robustness. All analyses were conducted in R (using the brms/rstanarm and boot packages), with convergence diagnostics checked (R-hat ≈ 1.00, ESS > 1000). For candidate genes with insufficient evidence but plausible biological rationale, only “suggestive” interpretations were provided, separate from “confirmed diagnoses (P/LP)” (Table S5). Variant interpretation followed ACMG/AMP guidelines. Candidate genes harboring variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were defined as those meeting a structured evaluation framework comprising: (i) in silico functional prediction scores (CADD, SIFT, PolyPhen-2); (ii) phenotypic concordance between the fetal presentation and established gene functions; and (iii) published evidence linking the gene to neurodevelopment or related biological pathways. A gene was assigned candidate status only when the multidisciplinary team reached consensus that the aggregated evidence provided a reasonable biological basis, while still falling short of P/LP classification. All statistical analyses accounted for data distribution and potential confounding factors. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify independent predictors of a positive molecular diagnosis and postnatal outcomes.Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to evaluate the consistency of the results under different model assumptions, thereby enhancing the reliability of the findings.

Results
Results Classification overview of FMIC pES was successfully performed on 301 singleton fetuses with suspected microcephaly, using samples from amniotic fluid cells (n = 231) or umbilical cord blood (n = 70). At the time of testing, the median maternal age was 31 years (range: 21–42 years), the median paternal age was 32.3 years (range: 20–50 years), and the median gestational age was 29.4 weeks (range: 21-36.1 weeks). Detailed clinical characteristics are summarized in Table . Based on the presence or absence of additional anomalies, cases were classified into two major groups: isolated and non-isolated FMIC. The isolated group included 119 cases and was further stratified by the standard deviation of head circumference (HC-SD) into three subgroups: -2 SD to -3 SD (84 cases), -3 SD to -4 SD (30 cases), and ≤ -4 SD (5 cases). The non-isolated group comprised 182 cases, which were further divided into seven subgroups according to HC-SD and associated findings: -2 SD to -3 SD with FGR (63 cases); -2 SD to -3 SD with soft ultrasound markers (12 cases); -2 SD to -3 SD with SA (65 cases); -3 SD to -4 SD with FGR (15 cases); -3 SD to -4 SD with soft markers (0 cases); -3 SD to -4 SD with SA (10 cases) and ≤ -4 SD (16 cases) (Table ). Overall molecular diagnostic rate and genetic characterization of pES In a cohort of 301 fetuses with suspected microcephaly, we identified 55 distinct variants across 33 unique genes as potential molecular diagnostic candidates. A total of 33 fetuses, accounting for 11% of the sample (33/301), were diagnosed with microcephaly and carried pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic variants. Additionally, 8 cases (2.7%, 8/301) were classified as “possibly diagnostic,” as they carried one variant of uncertain significance (VUS) and one P/LP variant, consistent with an autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance pattern. Therefore, the overall molecular diagnostic rate in this study was 13.6% (41/301) (Table ). Among the 55 diagnostic variants, 19 (34.5%) were newly identified. Of the 41 confirmed cases, 21 (51.2%) followed an autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance pattern, 15 (36.6%) adhered to an AR inheritance pattern, 4 (9.8%) were X-linked dominant (XLD), and 1 (2.4%) was X-linked recessive (XLR). In the subgroup of 30 fetuses with a family history or adverse pregnancy outcomes, the molecular diagnostic rate was 26.7%, significantly higher than the 12.2% observed in sporadic cases (p < 0.01). Notably, the recurrent pathogenic genes identified in this study included NIPBL, FGFR3, UBE3A, WDR62, and ARCN1, which play crucial roles in the pathogenic mechanisms of microcephaly and its associated syndromes. Population-based comparison of pES detection results across different case cohorts Among the 119 cases classified as isolated FMIC, 12 were confirmed by molecular diagnosis, resulting in a diagnostic yield of 10.1% (12/119). Stratification by HC Z-scores revealed a trend of increasing diagnostic yield with greater severity of HC reduction, as summarized in Table and Table S2. Specifically, the diagnostic yield was 7.1% in the − 2 SD to -3 SD group (84 cases), 13.3% in the − 3 SD to -4 SD group (30 cases), and 40.0% in the ≤ -4 SD group (5 cases). Given the very small sample size, this point estimate is unstable and should be interpreted with caution. We present this as a preliminary observation that requires confirmation in larger cohorts. For the subgroup with HC ≤ -4 SD (n = 21, including both isolated and non-isolated cases), we further performed robustness analyses using a Bayesian model with a Jeffreys prior and bootstrap resampling. Both methods produced estimates and uncertainty intervals consistent with the primary analysis (Table S3; Figure ), supporting the reliability of the findings despite the limited sample size. This trend suggests that the likelihood of a positive molecular diagnosis increases with the degree of microcephaly. In the complex FMIC group (n = 182), 29 cases were molecularly diagnosed, yielding a diagnostic yield of 15.9%, which was significantly higher than that of the isolated FMIC group (p < 0.01). The diagnostic yield in the complex group was 5.8% points higher than in the isolated group (15.9% vs. 10.1%; OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.25–2.31). The diagnostic yield in the complex group was 57.4% higher than in the isolated group (15.9% vs. 10.1%; OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.25–2.31). The complex FMIC group was further stratified into seven subgroups based on HC Z-scores and SA. Diagnostic yields in these subgroups ranged from 3.2% to 40.0%; however, the differences among subgroups were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Despite this, the overall diagnostic yield in complex FMIC was consistently higher than that in isolated cases. Impact of family history and adverse pregnancy history on diagnostic yield Among the 301 FMIC cases, those with a positive family history or adverse pregnancy history showed a significantly higher diagnostic yield of 26.7%, compared to 12.2% in sporadic cases (p < 0.01), as detailed in Table . This finding underscores the substantial influence of familial and obstetric history on the likelihood of identifying a genetic etiology in FMIC. Frequently detected pathogenic genes in these cases included NIPBL, FGFR3, ASPM, UBE3A, WDR62, and ARCN1, several of which appeared recurrently. These genes are central to the molecular pathogenesis of FMIC, highlighting the distinct genetic characteristics of familial microcephaly. Diagnostic findings of FMIC associated with FGR As previously described, among the 301 cases suspected of FMIC, 123 cases (40.9%) were accompanied by FGR. Among these 123 FMIC cases associated with FGR, 7 received a positive genetic diagnosis, resulting in a diagnostic yield of 5.7% (7/123). Based on the presence or absence of other abnormalities, FGR-related cases were further divided into three subgroups: suspected FMIC without other anomalies (85 cases), FMIC + FGR + USM (ultrasound soft markers; 18 cases), and FMIC + FGR + SA (20 cases). The diagnostic yields for the three subgroups were 5.9% (5/85), 5.6% (1/18), and 5.0% (1/20), respectively (Table S4). To formally test whether FGR was an independent predictor of a molecular diagnosis, we performed a multivariable logistic regression analysis, adjusting for key clinical confounders. After accounting for the severity of microcephaly (HC-SD), the presence of other SA, and gestational age at diagnosis, FGR was not significantly associated with the likelihood of a positive genetic diagnosis (Adjusted Odds Ratio [aOR]: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.35–2.05; p = 0.72). In contrast, both a more severe HC-SD and the presence of other SA were strong independent predictors of a molecular diagnosis in the same model (Table S5). This analysis confirms that the presence of FGR, in itself, does not significantly increase the likelihood of identifying a monogenic cause for FMIC when the severity of microcephaly and other anomalies are considered. Gene classification and biological pathway analysis The affected genes were classified into four categories based on the correlation between molecularly diagnosed genes and microcephaly. Category I includes specific microcephaly primary hereditary (MCPH) genes: ASPM, KNL1, STIL, and WDR62. Category II comprises known disease-causing genes broadly associated with microcephaly and other clinical phenotypes, such as ANKRD11, ARCN1, ARPC4, CDC45, COL4A1, CASK, DOCK6, FANCI, HDAC8, KMT2D, LARP7, MYO18B, NBEA, NIPBL, OSGEP, PDHA1, PHGDH, PQBP1, RAC3, UBE3A, and ZEB2. Category III includes genes previously reported in isolated cases of microcephaly, such as COL1A1 and COL4A5. Category IV comprises genes for which the prenatal phenotypic spectrum may plausibly extend to primary microcephaly, including TUBB2A, DUOX2, EBP, FAM111A, FGFR3, and PEX1. These putative phenotypic extensions are distinct from the confirmed pathogenic findings in Categories I–III. Evidence supporting the classification of each variant is summarized in Table S6, with additional details provided in Table . GO and KEGG enrichment analyses in this study (Table ) indicated that genes associated with microcephaly are primarily concentrated in several key biological processes and molecular mechanisms. Biological process analysis revealed significant enrichment of these genes in head and facial morphogenesis pathways, suggesting that abnormalities in genes involved in these developmental processes may lead to defects in the nervous system and craniofacial structures (Fig. A). In particular, variants in genes such as ANKRD11, NIPBL, and COL1A1 may directly affect the morphological formation of the brain and skull. Molecular function (MF) analysis identified several genes playing central roles in protein binding and interaction networks—for example, HDAC8, DUOX2, and RAC3. Dysfunction in these genes may disrupt signal transduction and transcriptional regulation in cells, thereby impacting multiple pathways involved in brain development (Fig. B). Cellular component (CC) analysis emphasized the role of the extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly the collagen gene family (COL4A1, COL1A1, COL4A5), which may be essential for maintaining tissue structure, regulating cellular behavior, and mediating signal transduction. Abnormal ECM components may contribute to developmental disorders by altering cell-matrix interactions (Fig. B). KEGG pathway analysis further revealed that ECM-receptor interaction and cell cycle regulation are significantly enriched pathways. The former may influence neural crest cell development by regulating cellular adhesion, migration, and differentiation, while the latter is closely associated with neuronal proliferation, differentiation, and cell fate determination (Fig. C-D). Gene profiling showed that pathogenic genes are mainly enriched in neurogenesis-related pathways (such as the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway) and ECM signaling pathways.Notably, our findings suggest that six genes (TUBB2A, DUOX2, EBP, FAM111A, FGFR3, PEX1) may be associated with a primary fetal microcephaly presentation, thereby potentially expanding the genetic spectrum of the disease (Fig. E). These analytical results provide important insights into the complex pathophysiology of microcephaly, involving multi-level abnormalities ranging from molecular signaling to tissue architecture, with particularly significant impacts on developmental pathways and ECM-related signaling. Classification of genes associated with microcephaly and enrichment analysis of biological signaling pathways. A BP’s GO enrichment analysis shows significant enrichment of microcephaly-related genes in multiple developmental and morphogenetic processes. Significance is indicated by GeneRatio and adjusted p-values (padj), with dot size representing the number of enriched genes. B GO enrichment for MF and CC, revealing protein binding and ECM-related signaling pathways. Color represents p-values; dot size indicates gene count. C KEGG pathway analysis identifies significantly enriched pathways, including ECM-receptor interaction and PI3K-Akt signaling. GeneRatio and padj reflect enrichment significance; dot size indicates gene count within each pathway. D Distribution of different genes across enriched KEGG pathways. Blue squares indicate gene participation in the respective pathway. E A newly identified mutation spectra heatmap shows that ASPM and WDR62 are frequently mutated in isolated FMIC (mutation frequency > 15%), while NIPBL and FGFR3 exhibit cross-phenotypic distribution in complex FMIC. The color gradient indicates normalized mutation frequency (dark blue: high frequency; white: no mutation) To further analyze the distribution characteristics of pathogenic genes across different phenotypic subgroups, we constructed mutation spectrum heatmaps for isolated and complex FMIC based on standardized mutation frequencies (Fig. E). The results showed that neurogenesis-related genes such as ASPM and WDR62 exhibited higher mutation frequencies (> 15%) in isolated FMIC, whereas genes such as NIPBL and FGFR3 were more frequently observed in complex FMIC, displaying cross-system phenotypic distributions. In addition, mutations in collagen-related genes such as COL1A1 and COL4A1 were predominantly found in complex FMIC cases, suggesting that ECM pathway abnormalities may be involved in the disease mechanism. These findings enrich the molecular profiling of FMIC subtypes and contribute to future mechanistic research and precision classification. Clinical follow-up and neurodevelopmental assessment Of the 301 cases in the study, 287 (95.3%) completed postnatal follow-up, with durations ranging from 1 to 10 years. Follow-up data revealed a strong correlation between prenatal HC measurements and clinical outcomes, particularly in cases of isolated FMIC, as detailed in Table . Among fetuses with HC between − 2 SD and − 3 SD, 80% had favorable outcomes, whereas only 16.7% of those with HC between − 3 SD and − 4 SD experienced favorable neurodevelopment, suggesting that the HC Z-score is a critical predictor of prognosis. In the complex FMIC group, 58.1% of cases had favorable outcomes, while 41.9% exhibited poor prognosis—a statistically significant difference from the isolated group (p < 0.05). Additionally, among FMIC cases associated with FGR, 64.9% of liveborn infants had favorable outcomes, indicating that the severity of HC reduction and the presence of FGR are key prognostic factors. Cognitive and growth outcomes in cases with poor prognosis All 62 patients with poor neurodevelopmental outcomes underwent formal cognitive assessments, revealing a median intelligence quotient (IQ) of 34 and a median language score of 35. Among these patients, 58.0% (36/62) exhibited mild intellectual disability, while 12.9% (8/62) had moderate to severe intellectual impairment. Additionally, 25.8% (16/62) experienced epileptic seizures, and 17.7% (11/62) presented with visual impairments. Notably, 82.3% (51/62) demonstrated short stature, indicating that overall growth restriction is strongly associated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities. These findings highlight the broad spectrum of adverse outcomes in severe FMIC cases, particularly in cognitive function, language development, and physical growth domains. HC-SD as an independent prognostic predictor To validate the prognostic value of HC-SD, a multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of poor postnatal outcome. After adjusting for potential confounders, including gestational age at diagnosis, FGR, and the presence of other SA, a more severe HC-SD remained a strong and independent predictor of poor prognosis. For each 1-SD decrease in HC, the adjusted odds of a poor outcome increased significantly (Adjusted Odds Ratio [aOR]: 2.1; 95% CI: 1.5-3.0; p < 0.001). This confirms that HC-SD provides prognostic information beyond the presence of co-occurring anomalies and gestational timing of diagnosis .

Discussion
Discussion This large prospective cohort of 301 fetuses with suspected FMIC demonstrates the clinical utility of pES, yielding a 13.6% diagnostic rate among cases with normal karyotype and CMA results. Two principal findings emerge from this study. First, the diagnostic yield shows a strong phenotype dependence, being higher in complex FMIC than in isolated FMIC (15.9% vs. 10.1%) and increasing with greater reductions in HC. Second, prenatal HC-SD is a robust and independent predictor of postnatal neurodevelopmental outcome, providing clinically actionable risk stratification, particularly when pES does not identify a causative variant. Collectively, these results offer quantitative support for an integrated genotype-phenotype-outcome framework to inform prenatal counseling and management. Functional insights and phenotypic expansion of candidate genes In this study, we identified variants in six genes (TUBB2A, DUOX2, EBP, FAM111A, FGFR3, and PEX1) that may indicate an expansion of their established prenatal phenotypic spectrum to include a primary fetal microcephaly presentation. These findings should be interpreted with caution, as the strength of evidence linking each gene to a primary FMIC phenotype differs. As summarized in Table S6, the variants in EBP, FAM111A, and FGFR3 (Fig. ), the de novo variant in TUBB2A, and the compound heterozygous variants in DUOX2 were classified as Pathogenic or Likely Pathogenic. The PEX1 case was considered a “possible diagnosis” based on one Likely Pathogenic and one VUS variant. Schematic of cellular and molecular pathways driven by six novel pathogenic genes in FMIC For several of these genes, such as FGFR3 (skeletal dysplasia) [, ], EBP (chondrodysplasia punctata) [], and FAM111A (Kenny–Caffey syndrome) [, ]. microcephaly has historically been regarded as a secondary or minor feature of the associated postnatal syndromes. Our data suggest that, in a prenatal context, microcephaly can represent a prominent presenting feature. The de novo Likely Pathogenic variant in TUBB2A, a gene implicated in cortical malformations [, ], supports its involvement in severe prenatal-onset neurodevelopmental disorders. The Pathogenic and Likely Pathogenic variants in DUOX2, primarily associated with congenital hypothyroidism [, ], raise the possibility that FMIC may represent a rare or severe manifestation, although a secondary effect of prenatal thyroid hormone deficiency cannot be excluded. Similarly, the PEX1 case (Likely Pathogenic + VUS), a gene known to cause Zellweger spectrum disorders [, ], represents one of the earliest associations with a primary prenatal microcephaly phenotype. Collectively, these findings highlight that genes traditionally linked to systemic syndromes may manifest prenatally with a primary neurodevelopmental presentation. As these observations reflect potential expansions of the recognized clinical spectrum, the associations should be regarded as suggestive rather than definitive pending additional reports and functional validation. HC-SD as a quantifiable prenatal risk stratification indicator A central finding of this study is the strong prognostic value of HC-SD, which is particularly critical for the nearly 90% of cases in which pES is non-diagnostic. Our data provide quantifiable estimates that can directly inform prenatal counseling. Among isolated FMIC with an HC between − 2 SD and − 3 SD, 80% had a favorable outcome. However, when HC decreased to between − 3 SD and − 4 SD, this rate dropped sharply to 16.7%. In severe isolated FMIC (HC ≤ -4 SD), no fetuses survived, consistent with previous reports []. These findings demonstrate that HC-SD functions not only as a diagnostic parameter but also as a powerful marker for risk stratification. In pES-negative cases, where genetic counseling is most challenging, HC-SD becomes the primary objective measure for prognostication. Our finding that the risk of an adverse outcome in the − 2 to -3 SD group is 20%, higher than the previously reported 10.5% [], provides updated evidence for counseling. Although comparisons must be interpreted cautiously due to differences in cohort characteristics and outcome definitions, the 83.3% rate of poor prognosis in the − 3 to -4 SD group is also substantially higher than the 57.1% reported in earlier literature [], underscoring the value of our large, contemporary cohort. This stratification framework enables clinicians to move beyond a binary diagnosis of “microcephaly” and provide nuanced, data-driven risk assessment. Our multivariable regression analysis further supports the central role of HC-SD. After adjusting for FG), other SA, and gestational age at diagnosis, each 1-SD decrease in HC remained associated with approximately a twofold increase in the risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcome (aOR = 2.1). This establishes HC-SD as a cornerstone metric for FMIC prognosis and highlights its value as the most objective, quantitative indicator for risk stratification and genetic counseling, particularly in the many cases where pES does not yield a diagnosis. Genetic heterogeneity and distinct profiles of isolated vs. complex FMIC This study demonstrates that isolated and complex FMIC exhibit distinct genetic architectures. In isolated FMIC, the diagnostic yield increased proportionally with the severity of microcephaly, rising from 7.1% to 40.0% as HC-SD worsened. This pattern suggests that isolated FMIC is frequently driven by monogenic defects in key neurodevelopmental genes, with phenotypic severity reflecting the functional impact of the underlying mutation. Consistent with this, canonical primary microcephaly genes such as ASPM and WDR62 [, ] were more commonly identified in the isolated group. In contrast, complex FMIC exhibited a higher overall diagnostic yield (15.9%) that was less dependent on HC-SD. The genetic spectrum was enriched for pleiotropic syndromic genes, including NIPBL (Cornelia de Lange syndrome) and FGFR3 (skeletal dysplasias). These findings suggest that, in complex FMIC, microcephaly represents one component of a broader developmental disturbance, frequently involving pathways related to the extracellular matrix (e.g., COL4A1) or systemic signaling. This distinction, monogenic neurodevelopmental drivers in severe isolated FMIC versus pleiotropic syndromic genes in complex FMIC, provides a conceptual framework for interpreting genetic results and guiding further diagnostic evaluation. International cohort comparisons and distinctive features of this study Our cohort displays several characteristics that differentiate it from previously published large-scale studies. The proportion of severe cases (HC ≤ − 4 SD) was 7.0% (21/301), higher than the 2%–4% reported in European cohorts [], suggesting a potential referral bias toward more severe phenotypes in our centers. The median gestational age at diagnosis (29.4 weeks) was also later than that reported in many Western cohorts, which typically diagnose FMIC at 20–24 weeks [, ]. This later ascertainment likely contributes to an overrepresentation of phenotypes that develop or become detectable in the third trimester, limiting the generalizability of our findings to earlier, population-based screening settings. The termination-of-pregnancy rate for severe microcephaly (HC ≤ − 4 SD) in our cohort was 100%, reflecting a strong association between perceived severity and clinical decision-making, consistent with prior longitudinal observations []. Additionally, our study design excluded cases with confirmed intrauterine infections, resulting in an enrichment of genetic etiologies compared with population-based cohorts, in which infections account for a meaningful proportion of cases []. Taken together, these differences in case composition, timing of diagnosis, and etiological focus underscore the distinct value of our dataset. Specifically, our findings provide important complementary insights into the genetic architecture and prognosis of severe, late-onset, and predominantly genetically mediated FMIC—phenotypes that are underrepresented in earlier cohorts. Clinical value and diagnostic implications The 13.6% incremental diagnostic yield of pES over standard genetic testing underscores its essential role in the FMIC diagnostic workflow. The diagnostic yield was markedly enriched in cases with a family history or adverse pregnancy history, reaching 8/30 (26.7%), more than double that of sporadic cases. Establishing a molecular diagnosis provides families with a definitive etiological explanation, accurate recurrence-risk counseling, and prognostic information—elements that are critical for informed reproductive decision-making. The greater clinical challenge arises in isolated FMIC when genetic testing is negative. In these cases, prognostic uncertainty is substantial, increasing the risk of both unnecessary termination and missed severe outcomes. A key contribution of this study is the development of a refined HC-SD–based risk-stratification framework specifically for this group. The finding that isolated cases with HC between − 2 SD and − 3 SD have an 80% likelihood of a favorable outcome provides reassurance and supports continuation of pregnancy with appropriate surveillance. Conversely, the markedly poor prognosis associated with HC < -3 SD offers a strong evidence base for intensified counseling and management. This stratified, data-driven approach has the potential to optimize clinical decision-making, reduce unwarranted pregnancy terminations, and improve maternal–fetal outcomes. Limitations and future directions This study has several limitations. First, maternal comorbidities and placental insufficiency were not applied as strict exclusion criteria. Although this approach better reflects real-world clinical decision-making, it may have allowed the inclusion of secondary, non-genetic forms of microcephaly, such as those arising from impaired placental perfusion or adverse intrauterine environments. As a result, the cohort may include fetuses with environmentally or physiologically mediated microcephaly, potentially leading to an underestimation of the true diagnostic yield of pES in pure primary FMIC. Second, recruitment from tertiary referral centers likely introduced selection bias toward late-gestation diagnoses and more severe phenotypes, limiting generalizability to earlier, population-based screening cohorts. Second, the number of cases with variants in specific genes was small, which may underestimate their contribution. The pES approach used here focused on coding regions, reducing sensitivity for non-coding variants, structural rearrangements, repeat expansions, and low-level mosaicism. Although pathogenic CNVs account for 3%–14% of developmental delay cases [] and only 0.34% of high-confidence pathogenic variants are located in non-coding regions [], the overall diagnostic yield reported here may remain an underestimate. Moreover, functional validation was not performed, leaving several candidate gene associations suggestive rather than confirmed. The long study period (2014–2022) introduces additional heterogeneity, as analytical pipelines and gene–disease knowledge evolved over time and were not uniformly re-applied to early cases. Differences in population characteristics and methodological approaches compared with prior studies may also contribute to inter-cohort variability. Certain subgroups, such as isolated FMIC with HC ≤ -4 SD (n = 5) and the total severe group (n = 21), were small, leading to unstable point estimates despite Bayesian and bootstrap analyses. These findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously and regarded as preliminary until validated in larger prospective cohorts. Finally, prognostic analyses were based on aggregated outcome data, limiting full adjustment for confounders and necessitating cautious interpretation of risk estimates. Given the rapid evolution of prenatal genomics, ongoing literature updates beyond our analysis cutoff will be essential. Future research recommendation Future research should prioritize functional validation of the candidate genes identified in this study by using cellular and animal models to confirm their pathogenic relevance. Expanding beyond pES to whole-genome sequencing may improve detection of non-coding variants that were not captured by the current approach. A direct extension of this work would be the experimental validation of the most compelling candidate variants, for example through CRISPR Cas9 genome editing in cellular systems to investigate their effects on neurodevelopmental pathways. From a clinical perspective, the integration of genomic data with quantitative fetal MRI parameters such as brain volume and cortical folding, as demonstrated in recent studies [–], may substantially enhance diagnostic precision. Looking ahead, a multidimensional diagnostic framework that combines pES with long-read sequencing, incorporates fetal MRI radiomic features, and includes maternal plasma cfDNA methylation biomarkers could provide a more comprehensive assessment of FMIC. Establishing a nationwide FMIC case registration network would enable standardized data collection and longitudinal evaluation of intervention outcomes, ultimately supporting the development of precision medicine strategies for affected children.

Conclusion
Conclusion This prospective analysis of 301 fetuses with suspected FMIC represents one of the largest clinical investigations to date, integrating pES-based molecular diagnosis with long-term outcome assessment. The diagnostic yield of pES was 13.6%, underscoring its value in the evaluation of FMIC. Lower HC-SD scores, a positive family history, and adverse reproductive history were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of obtaining a molecular diagnosis. Prognostic analyses across isolated, non-isolated, and FGR-associated FMIC revealed marked differences. Outcomes in isolated FMIC were strongly correlated with HC-SD, providing a critical framework for risk stratification, particularly when pES is nondiagnostic. In contrast, non-isolated cases demonstrated poorer prognoses, indicating that phenotypic complexity has substantial influence on clinical outcome. Collectively, these findings provide an evidence base for genetic counseling and support the clinical utility of pES in the prenatal evaluation of FMIC. By linking genotype, phenotype, and long-term outcomes, this study facilitates more individualized prenatal and postnatal management strategies and establishes a foundation for future research aimed at improving outcomes for affected children.

title: Application of chromosomal microarray analysis and trio whole-exome sequencing in first-trimester prenatal diagnosis for high-risk pregnancies.
label_reason: CVS CMA and WES in fetuses with ultrasound abnormalities.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate and compare the clinical utility of chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and trio whole-exome sequencing (trio-WES) in a consecutive cohort of high-risk pregnant women who underwent chorionic villus sampling (CVS), as well as to develop a stratified diagnostic strategy based on first-trimester pregnancy indications. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 338 singleton pregnancies that underwent CVS during the first trimester (11 + 0 -13 + 6 weeks of gestation) between December 2023 and April 2025. High-risk pregnancies were defined by the presence of at least one of the following criteria: (1) advanced maternal age (AMA); (2) ultrasound detection of one or more soft markers or structural fetal anomalies; (3) abnormal first-trimester serum screening results; or (4) a history of adverse obstetric outcomes. Each chorionic villus sample underwent CMA using the Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K chip following DNA extraction, and 25 cases presenting with ultrasound abnormalities were subsequently analyzed using trio-WES on the MGISEQ-2000/DNBSEQ-T7 platform. Pregnancy outcomes and management decisions were prospectively monitored. Among the 338 patients, CMA identified chromosomal abnormalities in 56 cases (16.6%), including 23 cases of aneuploidy and 33 cases of copy number variation (CNV). The detection rate was significantly higher in the ultrasound abnormality group compared to the high-risk group identified through first-trimester serum screening (25.3% vs. 7.1%, p < 0.001). Within the ultrasound abnormality group, chromosomal abnormalities were most frequently observed in fetuses exhibiting both soft markers and structural anomalies (9/20, 45%). Moreover, the incidence of chromosomal abnormalities was higher among fetuses with nuchal translucency (NT) ≥ 4.5 mm and choroid plexus cystic hygroma (CH) (42.9% and 35.7%, respectively), though these differences were not statistically significant. Among CMA-negative cases with abnormal ultrasound findings, trio-WES identified an additional 5 of 22 (22.7%) genetic abnormalities, with a single-gene disease detection rate of 37.5% (3/8) in cases of multisystem malformations. The likelihood of single-gene disorders was significantly increased in pregnancies with NT ≥ 4.5 mm or multisystem malformations. Genetic findings had a substantial impact on clinical decision-making: termination rates were 95.7% (22/23) for aneuploidy, 50.0% (6/12) for pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs, and 100% (5/5) for P/LP monogenic variants identified by WES. Conversely, pregnancies with normal results had an 80.4% live birth rate, representing 94.4% of followed-up cases with normal findings. CMA remains essential for first-trimester prenatal diagnosis, while trio-WES provides a significant advantage in detecting single-gene disorders, particularly in fetuses with severe ultrasound anomalies. The strong association between genetic results and clinical decision-making highlights the clinical value of the proposed stratified diagnostic approach, offering evidence-based recommendations for optimizing first-trimester prenatal diagnostic strategies. Keywords: First trimester, Chorionic villus sampling, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Trio whole-exome sequencing, Copy number variations, Ultrasound phenotype stratification
