Application of chromosomal microarray analysis and trio whole-exome sequencing in first-trimester prenatal diagnosis for high-risk pregnancies

Introduction
Introduction According to data from the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 300,000 newborns worldwide die within the first 28 days of life due to congenital diseases. Genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities and single-gene defects, are among the leading causes of these birth defects [], which place a substantial burden on both families and society. Prenatal diagnosis allows for the early identification of congenital anomalies or genetic disorders in the fetus before birth, serving as an essential measure to prevent severe birth defects and improve perinatal outcomes []. In China, the widespread adoption of first-trimester combined screening has facilitated the early detection of high-risk indicators such as abnormal serum screening results, increased nuchal translucency (NT), and ultrasound-detected anomalies that may lead to neonatal birth defects. Consequently, a growing number of high-risk pregnant women are choosing to undergo prenatal diagnostic procedures during the first trimester. This earlier diagnostic window provides families with more time for genetic counseling and informed decision-making while significantly reducing maternal risks associated with later pregnancy termination. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) serves as the primary method for obtaining fetal genetic material during the first trimester, and its integration with high-resolution detection technologies has become a crucial component in optimizing prenatal diagnostic strategies. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) employs high-density DNA probes immobilized on a substrate to hybridize with complementary chromosomal sequences, thereby enabling the detection of copy number variations (CNVs) and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to determine genomic abnormalities. This technique is now widely applied for identifying fetal chromosomal aneuploidies and microdeletion/microduplication syndromes (MMS) []. CMA can detect chromosomal deletions and duplications as small as 50–100 kb, offering a resolution nearly 100 times higher than that of traditional karyotyping, along with advantages in speed, accuracy, and sensitivity. In recent years, whole-exome sequencing (WES) has emerged as another powerful tool in prenatal diagnosis, providing single-nucleotide resolution for the precise identification of subtle genetic variations within exonic (protein-coding) regions. Despite its high precision, the clinical application of WES during the first trimester remains limited by factors such as high testing costs and insufficient first-trimester-specific clinical data. Previous research on prenatal diagnosis has primarily focused on amniotic fluid samples obtained during mid-to-late pregnancy; however, the biological characteristics of chorionic villi in the first trimester differ fundamentally, and the diagnostic scope of first-trimester combined screening remains limited. Therefore, directly applying conclusions derived from studies on mid-to-late pregnancy amniotic fluid samples to guide first-trimester diagnosis may result in inaccuracies. At present, research specifically targeting prenatal diagnosis in the first trimester is relatively scarce. Critical questions remain unanswered, such as: What is the diagnostic value of CMA during the first trimester? Which high-risk factors necessitate further testing using the more expensive WES approach? And do distinct types of fetal malformations correspond to specific genetic mutation patterns? To address these questions, large-scale studies focused on early pregnancy are urgently needed to provide robust evidence. In this study, CMA data from 338 CVS cases were analyzed, and 25 cases with ultrasound abnormalities were further validated using trio-WES. We systematically evaluated the diagnostic performance of CMA and WES in the first trimester, examined genetic etiological variations across different indication groups, and explored the relationship between phenotypic complexity and genetic variations based on diverse ultrasound abnormality phenotypes. These findings offer valuable guidance for clinicians in assessing the applicability of CMA and WES technologies in prenatal diagnosis and the prevention of birth defects. Furthermore, we examined the influence of these genetic results on pregnancy outcomes to develop an evidence-based, stratified diagnostic strategy for clinical implementation.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study design This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single center and consecutively enrolled 338 singleton pregnant women who underwent CVS between December 2023 and April 2025 at the Anhui Provincial Women and Children’s Medical Centre. The inclusion criteria were as follows: advanced maternal age (AMA); fetal ultrasound abnormalities identified in accordance with the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG) first-trimester ultrasound guidelines; high-risk results from first-trimester serum screening tests; or a history of complicated obstetric outcomes, including two or more previous miscarriages, fetal malformations, or a family history of genetic diseases. Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis was performed for all fetal samples to exclude maternal cell contamination (MCC). Cases were excluded if the collected villus tissue weighed less than 5 mg, if DNA quality was suboptimal (OD260/280 < 1.8), or if fetal abnormalities were determined to be caused by non-genetic factors. All ultrasound examinations were conducted by physicians certified by the Anhui Province Prenatal Ultrasound Diagnosis Qualification Board. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) and sample processing The collected samples were washed with physiological saline to isolate the villi. Uncultured chorionic villi containing trophoblasts and mesenchymal cells were subsequently subjected to CMA. Portions of the samples weighing ≥ 10 mg were flash-frozen within 30 min of collection and stored at -80 °C, while the remaining portions were preserved for potential cell culture backup. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) DNA analysis was performed using the Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K array (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA, USA), which contains approximately 750,000 probes. To ensure consistency in clinical reporting, conservative size thresholds were applied, 500 kb for deletions (losses) and 1 Mb for duplications (gains), as primary filtering criteria. However, it is important to note that the platform’s practical detection resolution is approximately 50 kb. All CNV calls, including those below the established thresholds that were technically validated and considered potentially relevant, were manually reviewed and incorporated into the dataset to achieve a comprehensive analysis encompassing smaller variants of uncertain significance (VUS). The resulting data were cross-referenced with multiple clinical databases, including the Database of Genomic Variants (DGV), Decipher, and OMIM. Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines into five categories []: pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), benign (B), likely B (LB), and VUS. For fetuses with identified CNVs, parental validation was conducted to determine inheritance patterns. Whole-Exome sequencing (WES) Trio-WES samples from core family members were collected from peripheral blood. Genomic DNA from 25 fetuses with ultrasound-detected abnormalities was extracted from chorionic villus tissue and used as the test material. The DNA was fragmented, and sequencing libraries were constructed. Target gene exons and adjacent splice sites were captured and enriched using the Roche KAPA HyperExome chip. Sequencing was performed on the MGISEQ-2000 or DNBSEQ-T7 platform, achieving an average target region depth of ≥ 200×. Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19/GRCh37), and duplicate reads were removed. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) was used for base quality recalibration, single-nucleotide variant (SNV) and insertion/deletion (INDEL) calling, and genotyping. ExomeDepth was employed for exon-level CNV detection. Gene nomenclature followed the human gene nomenclature committee (HGNC) guidelines, and variant nomenclature adhered to Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) standards. Variant classification was conducted according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines, referencing ClinVar, gnomAD, and OMIM databases []. Variants were categorized as P, LP, VUS, LB, or B. Only P/LP variants associated with fetal phenotypes were classified as positive findings. All reported P/LP variants were identified based on high-confidence genotype calls from deep sequencing (mean depth ≥ 200×) and were bioinformatically validated through trio-based inheritance analysis, which provides an effective internal control to exclude sequencing artifacts. Although Sanger sequencing was not utilized as an independent validation method, the trio-based analytical approach is widely recognized as a robust strategy for confirming variant authenticity and inheritance patterns in prenatal genomic research []. Data collection and statistical analysis Data analysis primarily focused on evaluating the detection rates of genetic abnormalities identified through CMA and trio-WES as the main outcome measure. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 27.0. Categorical variables were expressed as percentages, and between-group comparisons were conducted using the χ² test or Fisher’s exact test when expected cell counts were fewer than five. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Pregnancy outcomes were tracked for all participants, and available follow-up data were descriptively summarized to assess the relationships between genetic findings, clinical management decisions (such as pregnancy termination), and postnatal phenotypes. The overall follow-up rate was 84.9%, and cases lost to follow-up were included in the denominator when calculating outcome rates.

Results
Results Baseline characteristics of the study cohort All 338 samples included in this analysis successfully passed quality control, and no exclusions were identified. As shown in Table , the maternal ages of participants ranged from 18 to 45 years, with 287 (84.9%) classified as non-advanced-age pregnant women (< 35 years) and 51 (15.1%) as advanced-age pregnant women (≥ 35 years). The mean maternal age was 30.7 years, and the gestational age ranged from 11+ 0 to 13+ 6 weeks. The indications for CMA were categorized into five groups: AMA (n = 9), ultrasound abnormality (n = 158), high-risk serum screening (n = 127), combined high-risk serum screening and ultrasound abnormality (n = 11), and adverse obstetric history (n = 33). The ultrasound abnormality group was further subdivided based on phenotypic complexity as follows: isolated soft marker abnormalities (ISFMs), including isolated NT thickening (≥ 2.5 mm), absence of the nasal bone, and similar findings (n = 94); multiple soft marker abnormalities (MSMMs), defined as the presence of two or more soft marker abnormalities (n = 13); isolated structural malformations (ISMs), such as cystic hygroma (CH) and cardiovascular malformations (n = 25); multiple structural malformations (MSMs), defined as structural anomalies affecting two or more systems (n = 6); and structural malformations combined with soft marker abnormalities (S+SFMs) (n = 20). Patients who underwent WES were divided into four groups according to indication: ISFM (n = 6), MSFM (n = 3), ISM (n = 8), and S + SFM (n = 8). Overall detection results of the CMA In this study, DNA was successfully extracted from all 338 chorionic villus samples analyzed by CMA, achieving a 100% diagnostic yield. A total of 56 chromosomal abnormalities (16.6%, 56/338) were identified, including 23 cases of aneuploidy (6.8%, 23/338). Among these, 15 cases (4.4%, 15/338) were trisomy 21, one case (0.3%, 1/338) was trisomy 9, one case (0.3%, 1/338) was trisomy 18, and six cases (1.8%, 6/338) were Turner syndrome (45,XO). Additionally, CMA detected 33 cases of CNVs (9.8%, 33/338). Of these CNVs, nine were classified as P (P-CNVs) (2.6%, 9/338), three as LP (LP-CNVs) (1.0%, 3/338), and twenty-one as VUS (6.2%, 21/338). The detailed results of individual CMA analyses are presented in Table . Differences in diagnostic performance among clinical indication groups Among patients with ultrasound abnormalities, the primary indication for prenatal testing in this cohort, 40 cases (25.3%, 40/158) of chromosomal abnormalities were detected. Of these, 20 (12.7%, 20/158) were chromosomal aneuploidies, 7 (4.4%, 7/158) were P/LP-CNVs, and 13 (8.2%, 13/158) were VUS. In the high-risk serum screening group, nine chromosomal abnormalities (7.1%, 9/127) were identified, including one case of trisomy 9 (0.8%, 1/127), one case of X monosomy (0.8%, 1/127), and seven cases of CNVs (5.5%, 7/127). Among cases presenting with both ultrasound abnormalities and high-risk serum screening results, one case of trisomy 21 (9.1%, 1/11) and two cases of VUS (18.2%, 2/11) were detected. In the adverse obstetric history group, four chromosomal abnormalities (12.2%, 4/33) were identified, comprising two P CNVs (6.1%, 2/33) and two VUS (6.1%, 2/33), one of which was maternally inherited. In pregnancies where AMA was the sole indication, no abnormalities were detected by CMA. Compared with other indications, the association between chromosomal abnormalities and high-risk serum screening was weaker. A statistically significant difference was observed between the ultrasound abnormality group and the non-ultrasound abnormality group (P < 0.05). Furthermore, the frequency of chromosomal aneuploidy among pregnant women aged ≥ 35 years was 13.7% (7/51), compared to 5.6% (16/287) among those aged < 35 years. The higher aneuploidy rate in older pregnant women was statistically significant (P < 0.05), consistent with the findings of Elmerdahl et al. [], reaffirming the well-established association between AMA and increased risk of chromosomal aneuploidy. Heterogeneity of abnormal etiologies in ultrasound abnormality subgroups Table presents the subgroup-specific statistical outcomes of ultrasound abnormalities. Among the five ultrasound abnormality groups, the S + SFM subgroup exhibited the highest incidence of chromosomal abnormalities (45.0%, 9/20), followed by ISM (28.0%, 7/25), MSFM (23.1%, 3/13), and ISFM (21.3%, 20/94), whereas the MSM subgroup showed the lowest rate (16.7%, 1/6). Within the 25 ISM fetuses, 35.7% (5/14) of cases in the CH group (n = 14) exhibited chromosomal abnormalities, including two cases of trisomy 21, one case of trisomy 18, one case of 15q13.3 microdeletion, and one case of 9q33.1 microduplication. In the urinary system abnormalities group (n = 3) and the cardiovascular system abnormalities group (n = 6), one case of chromosomal aneuploidy was detected in each, while no abnormalities were identified in the fetal edema and body wall malformations group (n = 2). Among the 94 ISFM fetuses, the NT thickening subgroup (n = 85) represented 90.4% (85/94), within which 19 cases of chromosomal abnormalities (22.4%, 19/85) were identified. CNVs accounted for 73.7% (14/19) of these cases, including four P variants (Case 20: 1p32 deletion; Case 104: Xq28 duplication; Case 274: Xp22.31 deletion; Case 338: Xp22.33p21.1 deletion) and ten VUS, five of which were confirmed through parental verification to have originated from a healthy mother or father. Notably, the chromosomal abnormality rate in the MSM subgroup (16.7%, 1/6) was lower than that in the ISFM subgroup (21.3%, 20/94). The small sample size of the MSM subgroup (n = 6) and the likelihood of non-chromosomal or monogenic etiologies within this group are key factors to consider when interpreting this observation, which is further elaborated in section (). Detailed characteristics of CNVs and their associations with phenotypes Table provides a summary of 33 cases with identified CNVs (P/LP/VUS), comprising 16 cases of copy-number gains and 18 cases of copy-number losses. Among the nine pCNV fetuses, four exhibited chromosomal microdeletion or microduplication syndromes, including one case of Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1 A, two cases of ichthyosis, and one case of Xq28 duplication syndrome. The remaining five cases involved deletions or duplications of large chromosomal segments encompassing multiple genes. Patient 104 was confirmed through parental testing to have a paternal-origin mutation. Among the three lpCNV fetuses, one (Patient 1) shared the recurrent region of 15q13.3 (D-CHRNA7 to BP5), while another (Patient 57) exhibited both a microdeletion and a large-scale duplication associated with Holoprosencephaly 4/Bosma arhinia microphthalmia syndrome and overgrowth, respectively. These mutations were identified as de novo. Additionally, one patient (Patient 205) was diagnosed with 1q21.1 duplication syndrome. Regarding the VUS fetuses, CMA detected 21 cases, representing 71.4% of all CNVs (21/33). Of these, 10 cases underwent parental verification, which revealed that seven fetuses inherited the CNV from a phenotypically normal parent, suggesting these CNVs were B. Five cases were found to have de novo mutations of uncertain clinical significance, and, along with the 11 fetuses whose parents declined verification, were categorized as VUS. Positive diagnostic results detected by WES Twenty-five pregnant women underwent Trio-WES testing either concurrently with or subsequent to CMA testing, yielding a cumulative detection rate of 40.0% (10/25). Among these, chromosomal abnormalities were identified by CMA in three patients, two with trisomy 21 (MSFM group) and one with a high-level X chromosome mosaic deletion (ISFM group). The WES results were fully consistent with the CMA findings (Kappa value = 1.0), confirming the high reproducibility of the technique. In the remaining 22 CMA-negative samples, five clinically significant variants and two VUS were detected (see Table for the Trio-WES report and individual clinical details), providing an additional diagnostic yield of 22.7% (5/22). The highest positive detection rate was observed in the S + SFM group (37.5%, 3/8), followed by the ISFM group (16.7%, 1/6) and the ISM group (12.5%, 1/8). The five monogenic hereditary disorders identified through Trio-WES comprised four autosomal dominant conditions caused by mutations in the CHD7, RIT1, COL1A2, and CREBBP genes, and one autosomal recessive condition resulting from a compound heterozygous mutation in the CANT1 gene. Trio-WES also revealed VUS in two additional cases. In one hydropic fetus (Patient 130), a secondary finding was noted: a maternally inherited heterozygous P variant in the ABCC6 gene. Although this variant is linked to an autosomal recessive disorder, the severe fetal hydrops phenotype suggested the potential involvement of a second undetected P allele, leaving the causal relationship inconclusive. In another sample (Patient 114), two VUS in the PI4KA gene were identified, both inherited from the parents and lacking sufficient evidence for pathogenicity; thus, this case was not classified as a positive diagnostic finding. Pregnancy outcomes To assess the influence of CMA and Trio-WES findings on clinical decision-making, pregnancy outcomes were analyzed across the entire cohort, achieving a follow-up rate of 84.9% (287/338). The stratified results are presented in Table . Genetic findings demonstrated a substantial impact on pregnancy management and outcomes. Among the 275 cases with normal genetic results, the majority (80.4%, 221/275) resulted in the birth of phenotypically normal infants, while 4.7% (13/275) of pregnancies were electively terminated, primarily due to severe ultrasound anomalies detected at a later stage, or resulted in fetal demise. In marked contrast, P findings were strongly correlated with the decision to terminate pregnancy (TOP). This trend was evident in cases of fetal aneuploidy, which exhibited an extremely high TOP rate of 95.7% (22/23), as well as in cases with P/LP variants detected by Trio-WES, all of which led to termination (100.0%, 5/5), as shown in Table . Similarly, P/LP CNVs were associated with a high TOP rate of 50.0% (6/12), with detailed outcomes provided in Table . In comparison, outcomes for cases involving VUS were more variable: among those with VUS identified via CMA, 52.4% (11/21) of pregnancies resulted in normal live births, while 14.3% (3/21) were terminated. Of the two pregnancies with VUS detected by Trio-WES, one (50.0%) was terminated following subsequent ultrasound findings of severe abnormalities.

Discussion
Discussion Since Kazy introduced CVS under ultrasound guidance in 1982, the procedure has undergone significant advancements in both success and safety rates, making it a routine prenatal diagnostic technique in clinical practice. Studies have demonstrated that chorionic villi originate from fertilized ova and consist of trophoblasts and extraembryonic mesodermal tissue, sharing a common developmental origin with the fetus. Therefore, the genetic status of the chorionic villi can accurately reflect the true fetal condition. Unlike conventional amniocentesis or umbilical vein puncture, CVS offers distinct advantages, including the ability to be performed during the early stages of pregnancy []. This study integrates CMA and WES technologies for first-trimester prenatal diagnosis in high-risk pregnant women, aiming to evaluate their diagnostic performance, characterize the distribution of genetic variations in chorionic villus samples during the first trimester, and explore their dynamic correlations with ultrasound phenotypes to provide evidence for optimizing early prenatal diagnostic strategies. The central role of CMA Compared with traditional G-banding karyotyping, CMA offers a substantially higher diagnostic yield for detecting chromosomal abnormalities. Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of CMA in identifying microdeletions and microduplications in at-risk pregnancies []. Clinically, CMA has been shown to markedly enhance the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in fetuses presenting with ultrasound anomalies [, ]. On a global scale, CMA is now recommended as the first-line prenatal diagnostic tool for identifying chromosomal abnormalities following ultrasound-detected structural anomalies []. In this study, the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in the first trimester using CMA (16.6%) was significantly higher than that reported for traditional karyotyping in the literature (approximately 5.1–7.8%) [, ]. This improvement is primarily attributed to CMA’s broader detection capability, which allows for the identification of submicroscopic abnormalities that conventional karyotyping cannot detect. A notable example is Case 338, in which the ultrasound suggested CH, and CMA identified a 15q13.3 microduplication (0.422 Mb) involving the CHRNA7 gene (OMIM: 118511), classified as LP. The 15q13.3 microduplication syndrome is associated with neurodevelopmental defects and fetal lymphatic system malformations. In this case, CMA detected a CNV highly consistent with the observed phenotype during the first trimester, providing crucial genetic counseling evidence for the family. CMA precisely identifies P variants, thereby uncovering potential genetic mechanisms underlying CH that may be overlooked by traditional karyotyping when dealing with microstructural chromosomal abnormalities. The diagnostic yield of clinically relevant (P/LP) CNVs in this study was 3.6%, consistent with previous literature [, , ], with 2.4% (8/338) of samples exhibiting submicroscopic (< 10 Mb) yet clinically significant copy-number alterations. Although the sample size was limited and may introduce selection bias, the frequency of chromosomal abnormalities in the ultrasound abnormality group was markedly higher than in the high-risk serum screening group (25.3% vs. 7.1%, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the abnormality rate in the high-risk serum screening group with concurrent ultrasound abnormalities reached 27.3%, comparable to the ultrasound abnormality group. These findings emphasize that first-trimester ultrasound anomalies are key indicators of genetic abnormalities and that combining high-risk serum screening with ultrasound phenotyping can significantly enhance diagnostic efficacy. Interestingly, in the present study, the detection rate of CMA was higher than that reported in previous studies utilizing amniotic fluid samples collected during mid-pregnancy, where the positive rate typically remains below 10% []. This discrepancy may be explained by the process of natural embryonic selection: fetuses carrying severe genetic mutations are more likely to result in miscarriage during the first trimester, with fewer genetically defective fetuses surviving into mid-pregnancy. Consequently, first-trimester embryonic phenotyping may more accurately reflect the genetic defects underlying early embryonic development, whereas mid-pregnancy abnormalities often involve a broader interplay of environmental and multifactorial influences. Additionally, the capability of CMA to identify CNVs linked to single-gene disorders is noteworthy. In a case of charcot-marie-tooth disease type 1 A (CMT1A) in this study (Case 96), CMA directly detected a 17p12 microduplication encompassing the PMP22 gene, thereby confirming the diagnosis of CMT1A. This approach enabled diagnosis more than two weeks earlier than WES and at a lower cost, underscoring the practical screening value of CMA for single-gene disorders associated with CNVs. Incremental value and indication optimization of Trio-WES CMA is constrained by its resolution and is unable to detect SNVs or compound heterozygous mutations associated with recessive genetic disorders. The emergence of WES has provided a promising solution to this limitation. WES systematically screens exonic regions to identify variations responsible for single-gene disorders []. Previous studies have demonstrated that WES offers an incremental diagnostic yield ranging from 10% to 40% in patients who test negative through CMA [, , ] [], particularly in cases involving complex phenotypes such as multisystem malformations and skeletal developmental anomalies. Trio-WES, which involves sequencing the exomes of the fetus and both parents simultaneously, enables precise differentiation between de novo and inherited variants, substantially enhancing the detection rate of P mutations and the elucidation of recessive disease etiologies (e.g., compound heterozygous mutations) []. Katia et al. highlighted its potential to become a routine diagnostic tool in prenatal testing, especially when ultrasound abnormalities are present []. The present study similarly found that Trio-WES is a valuable complement to CMA. Among CMA-negative cases, Trio-WES achieved an additional diagnostic yield of 27.3% (6/22), aligning with the findings reported by Katia et al. A notable case (Case 36) revealed that a compound heterozygous mutation in the CANT1 gene resulted in Desbuquois dysplasia (OMIM 251450), characterized by markedly increased NT thickness (9.1 mm) and lymphocystic hydrocephalus, underscoring the diagnostic advantage of Trio-WES in detecting recessive genetic conditions. While CMA cannot identify compound heterozygous point mutations, Trio-WES facilitates the interpretation of P variants through family co-segregation analysis. Interestingly, 80.0% (4/5) of WES-positive variants were identified as de novo mutations. Although the sample size was limited, this observation supports the “early embryonic somatic mutation burden hypothesis” proposed in Nature Genetics [], which suggests that the earliest stages of embryogenesis (e.g., zygote and cleavage stages) are critical periods for de novo mutation events. The elevated rate of de novo mutations detected in first-trimester chorionic villus samples in this study further substantiates this hypothesis. Additionally, research indicates that the diagnostic yield of WES is influenced by the nature of fetal abnormalities. A meta-analysis conducted by Mellis et al. [] found that the detection rate of single-gene disorders was significantly higher in fetuses with multisystem structural malformations compared to those with isolated defects. Consistent with these findings, the present study reported the highest detection rate in S + SFM fetuses (37.5%, 3/8), followed by the ISFM (20%, 1/5) and ISM (16.7%, 1/8) groups. Although the difference was not statistically significant due to the small sample size (p = 0.6), the trend suggests that larger cohorts would likely confirm this pattern. Notably, all positive cases (5/5) displayed markedly increased NT measurements (≥ 4.5 mm) and/or multiple ultrasonographic abnormalities, with four cases exhibiting both. In line with Mellis’ conclusions, this study reinforces that fetuses presenting with NT ≥ 4.5 mm or combined structural and soft-marker anomalies have a higher probability of harboring monogenic diseases. Such phenotypic patterns may serve as important clinical indicators for prioritizing WES in prenatal diagnostics. Clinical translation of ultrasound phenotyping stratification: from mechanism to Decision-Making Several studies have shown that fetuses exhibiting multiple structural abnormalities have a significantly higher prevalence of chromosomal abnormalities than those with a single ultrasound-detected anomaly [, ]. In the CMA results of the present study, the S + SFM group demonstrated the highest frequency of chromosomal abnormalities, mainly involving aneuploidy and large-scale CNVs. These findings further indicate that the complexity of ultrasound phenotypes tends to increase in parallel with the severity of genetic deviations. This observation aligns closely with a recent large-scale cohort study by Zeng et al., which reported that multisystem anomalies represented one of the phenotypic categories with the highest molecular diagnostic yield (36.1%) among fetuses presenting ultrasound abnormalities []. Mechanistically, substantial genetic alterations, such as aneuploidy or large CNVs, can give rise to multisystem structural abnormalities because they directly impair the function of key regulatory genes during early embryonic development. Given that genes are highly sensitive to changes in copy number, such imbalances disrupt the intricate coordination of developmental processes across various organ systems, resulting in widespread structural anomalies. Furthermore, these profound genetic variations are often associated with high embryonic mortality during the early stages of development, meaning that fetuses surviving long enough to be detected are likely to exhibit extensive and severe structural defects. Therefore, the interplay between two mechanisms, the disruption of multisystem developmental coordination caused by gene dosage sensitivity and the natural selection pressures acting during embryogenesis, explains why multisystem structural abnormalities serve as a strong indicator of severe chromosomal abnormalities. Interestingly, our cohort revealed a somewhat unexpected pattern, a lower CMA abnormality rate in the MSM subgroup compared with the ISFM subgroup. Although this finding appears counterintuitive, it may largely reflect the small MSM sample size (n = 6), which makes the results more vulnerable to statistical variation. More importantly, this observation underscores a crucial etiological distinction: complex structural anomalies identified during the first trimester are not solely associated with chromosomal abnormalities but are often influenced by a substantial monogenic component. Supporting this, our WES data demonstrated a relatively high diagnostic yield (37.5%) within the S + SFM group, which shares significant phenotypic overlap with MSM. This evidence suggests that the “missing” diagnoses in CMA-negative MSM cases could potentially be detected through WES, emphasizing the importance of adopting a sequential or concurrent WES testing approach for fetuses presenting with multiple anomalies. Second, within the solitary anomaly group, chromosomal abnormalities were observed more frequently in the CH subgroup (35.7%) than in the cardiovascular anomaly subgroup (16.7%), which contrasts with findings from previous studies []. This discrepancy may be explained by the partial manifestation of fetal phenotypes during the first trimester, suggesting that structural malformations in various systems at this stage may share specific genetic mechanisms. Consequently, there is a need for targeted selection of appropriate detection techniques. Earlier studies have identified increased NT, the most common marker in prenatal diagnosis, as an independent predictor of fetal chromosomal aneuploidy []. However, in the present study, CNVs in fetuses with isolated NT thickening accounted for 72.2% (13/18) of chromosomal abnormalities, a rate significantly higher than that reported in comparable mid-pregnancy studies (p < 0.01) [, ]. These CNVs represented P variants that predisposed fetuses to cardiomyopathy, such as the 1p32 deletion involving the TNNI3K gene, rather than merely serving as indicators of aneuploidy. This finding challenges the traditional notion that “NT thickening equals aneuploidy” and reinforces the recommendation to use CMA as the first-line diagnostic test in cases of isolated NT thickening. Therefore, integrating the above genotype-phenotype correlations with cost-benefit considerations, we propose a tiered diagnostic strategy for clinical application. Fetuses presenting with multisystem anomalies or an isolated NT measurement of ≥ 4.5 mm should undergo concurrent CMA and trio-WES testing to efficiently detect both chromosomal and monogenic etiologies. For cases involving isolated NT thickening (2.5–4.5 mm), other single isolated ultrasound findings, high-risk serum screening results, or a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes, CMA should be prioritized as the first-line diagnostic tool to ensure a high detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in a cost-effective manner. This stratified approach aims to maximize clinical utility while accounting for the economic constraints inherent in healthcare systems. Correlation of genetic findings with pregnancy outcomes and clinical Decision-Making The pregnancy outcome data serve as a crucial indicator of the real-world clinical effectiveness of our proposed genetic diagnostic strategy. A strong association was observed between genetic findings and subsequent pregnancy management decisions. Notably, when both CMA and trio-WES results were normal, the majority of pregnancies (80.4%) culminated in the delivery of phenotypically normal infants. This high negative predictive value holds considerable clinical significance, as it offers substantial reassurance to both families and healthcare providers when managing high-risk pregnancies. On the other hand, managing pregnancies with abnormal genetic findings required a nuanced approach, involving a thorough evaluation that combined molecular diagnostic results with serial ultrasound assessments and familial genetic history. While TOP was nearly universal for non-mosaic aneuploidies, as demonstrated by a record linkage study encompassing more than 26,000 pregnancies [], the management of fetuses carrying P/LP variants was far more individualized. Reported cases that resulted in TOP generally involved de novo variants or ultrasound features strongly indicative of a severe genetic syndrome. In contrast, pregnancy continuation was often considered when the P/LP variant was inherited from an unaffected parent, implying variable expressivity or incomplete penetrance, or when the associated disorder was consistent with a reasonable quality of life and serial ultrasounds revealed no worsening of fetal anomalies. These carefully tailored decisions highlight a fundamental principle of prenatal genomics: the management of abnormal genetic results must rely on an integrated evaluation that combines molecular findings with serial ultrasound observations and familial genetic context. For instance, interpreting X-linked variants necessitates sex-specific counseling approaches because of biological mechanisms such as X-chromosome inactivation []. Likewise, decisions involving VUS or incompletely penetrant CNVs are highly individualized, with strong consideration given to inheritance patterns and the longitudinal stability of the ultrasound phenotype. Ultimately, this multifaceted decision-making process reinforces the notion that a genetic finding does not equate to a predetermined outcome; rather, it must be understood within the broader framework of the patient’s overall clinical picture. Given this complexity, the observed 100% termination rate following a P/LP diagnosis through trio-WES in our cohort underscores the profound influence of a positive genetic result and highlights the necessity of a rigorous, phenotype-driven analytical framework. To enhance clinical relevance and reduce interpretive ambiguity, we adopted a policy of tightly correlating WES results with the observed fetal phenotype, thereby avoiding the challenges associated with incidental findings or VUS. Moreover, our experience with complex cases, such as the heterozygous ABCC6 variant (Case 130) and the PI4KA VUS (Case 114), illustrates the critical importance of interpreting genetic results within the context of the fetal presentation. Thorough evaluation and, when appropriate, conservative reporting of variants with uncertain phenotypic alignment are vital in prenatal diagnostics to ensure clear and responsible clinical guidance. This prudent approach guarantees that the diagnostic potential of WES is utilized optimally within our proposed stratified diagnostic model. Limitations of the study Several limitations should be acknowledged in this study. Its single-center, retrospective design introduces the possibility of selection bias. Moreover, the limited sample sizes within certain ultrasound phenotypic subgroups may have reduced the statistical power of the stratified analyses. From a technical standpoint, although high-depth sequencing and trio-based analysis provide strong internal validation, a key limitation is that not all WES-detected variants were confirmed through Sanger sequencing. Additionally, complete postnatal follow-up data were unavailable for some cases, particularly those involving VUS or inherited findings, thereby constraining our ability to fully delineate the corresponding phenotypic spectra. Beyond these methodological and technical constraints, it is essential to address the generalizability of our findings. This research was carried out in a specialized tertiary care facility equipped with advanced genomic technologies. Consequently, the widespread adoption of trio-WES, as proposed in our tiered diagnostic framework, may vary depending on the availability of expertise, infrastructure, and financial resources across different healthcare systems. Therefore, evaluating the cost-effectiveness of the proposed model in broader and more diverse clinical environments remains a crucial next step. Finally, it is important to address the inherent biological challenge associated with first-trimester diagnosis, confined placental mosaicism (CPM). Although CVS offers the significant advantage of enabling diagnosis approximately 8–10 weeks earlier than amniocentesis, placental mosaicism remains an intrinsic limitation of this technique. The overall incidence of CPM is relatively low, estimated at around 1–2% []; however, it can lead to both false-positive results, when an abnormality is present in the placenta but absent in the fetus, and false-negative results, resulting from reverse mosaicism. Moreover, certain CPM conditions, such as trisomy 16, can manifest as abnormal ultrasound findings or pregnancy complications due to impaired placental function []. A comprehensive evaluation of the specific clinical implications of CPM was beyond the scope of this study, primarily due to incomplete data on pregnancy outcomes, a significant limitation when interpreting the broader impact of first-trimester findings. Future prospective, multi-center studies incorporating systematic long-term follow-ups are essential to validate and refine the proposed diagnostic strategy, as well as to provide a clearer understanding of the overall impact of CPM.

Conclusions
Conclusions This study highlights CMA as a fundamental technology in early prenatal diagnosis, offering crucial insights through its ability to detect aneuploidies and CNVs, thereby supporting informed clinical decision-making. At the same time, trio-WES serves as a valuable complementary approach, substantially enhancing the detection rate of single-gene disorders and minor genetic variations. Nonetheless, to advance prenatal diagnostics toward greater precision, minimize birth defect risks, and optimize pregnancy outcomes, further comprehensive research and data accumulation remain essential.

abstract: ACTA1 -related congenital myopathies are rare neuromuscular disorders with significant genotypic heterogeneity, often causing severe neonatal multisystem involvement. This study presents a severe neonatal case with a pathogenic ACTA1 variant and reviews literature to highlight diagnostic and management challenges. A female infant was born via cesarean section at 39 +1 weeks to a non-consanguineous mother. Prenatal ultrasound showed polyhydramnios. She presented with severe birth asphyxia (Apgar 3 at 1 min, 5 at 5 min), requiring immediate resuscitation. Physical examination revealed profound hypotonia, absent spontaneous movements, respiratory insufficiency necessitating mechanical ventilation, expressionless facies, and bulbar dysfunction. Laboratory tests indicated metabolic acidosis and elevated lactate and creatine kinase. Electromyography (EMG) demonstrated reduced motor amplitudes and spontaneous fibrillations. Whole-exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous pathogenic variant in ACTA1 (c.227G>A, p. Gly76Asp), confirming ACTA1 -related congenital myopathy. Care was withdrawn on day 18 due to poor neurologic recovery. This case highlights three critical implications: (1) the significant clinical overlap between ACTA1 myopathy and perinatal asphyxia, underscoring the necessity of genetic testing in hypotonic neonates with atypical presentations; (2) the grave prognosis of early-onset ACTA1 mutations, which mandates early palliative care consultation; and (3) the essential role of a precise genetic diagnosis in defining phenotypes and informing future targeted therapies, such as gene therapy. ACTA1-related congenital myopathy in a neonate: a case report and literature review

Introduction
Introduction Congenital myopathies represent a heterogeneous group of inherited neuromuscular disorders characterized by structural abnormalities in skeletal muscle fibers. They typically present with hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory insufficiency beginning in infancy or early childhood (). Among the various genetic causes, mutations in the ACTA1 gene, which encodes skeletal muscle α-actin, account for approximately 15%–25% of cases. These mutations are associated with distinct histopathological subtypes, including nemaline myopathy, actin aggregate myopathy, and congenital fiber-type disproportion (CFTD) (, ). Neonatal-onset ACTA1-related myopathy is particularly severe, often manifesting as fetal akinesia, arthrogryposis, polyhydramnios, and immediate respiratory failure at birth (). Despite advances in genetic diagnostics, the condition is frequently misdiagnosed as hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) or spinal muscular atrophy due to overlapping clinical features (). This diagnostic delay impedes timely genetic counseling and complicates prognostication and family planning. The prognosis is generally poor, with over 40% of neonatal cases succumbing to respiratory complications within the first year of life (). Given the severity, phenotypic variability, and challenges in early recognition, there is a continued need to delineate the clinical and genetic spectrum of this disorder. In this article, we report a severe neonatal case caused by a pathogenic ACTA1 variant, and provide a comprehensive review of previously reported cases to improve awareness, facilitate early diagnosis, and highlight multidisciplinary management challenges.

Case presentation
Case presentation The proband was a female infant born at 39+1 weeks via cesarean section to a 29-year-old G3P2 mother with a history of uterine scarring. Prenatal ultrasound detected polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid volume: 2,500 ml), but no other structural anomalies were identified. There was no consanguinity between parents, and family history was negative for neuromuscular or metabolic disorders. The proband's 7-year-old sibling exhibited normal motor development. At delivery, the infant demonstrated severe birth asphyxia, with Apgar scores of 3 and 5 at 1 and 5 min, respectively, necessitating immediate resuscitation. Upon transfer to the neonatal intensive care unit, she exhibited lethargy, poor responsiveness, and an expressionless facies. Neuromuscular examination revealed profound generalized hypotonia and absence of spontaneous movements, with only minimal finger and toe motion observed. She developed respiratory insufficiency requiring mechanical ventilation. Bulbar dysfunction was prominent, manifesting as weak sucking and swallowing reflexes along with excessive oral secretions. Primitive reflexes including Moro and grasp were absent, although ocular movements remained intact (). Three-panel image of a newborn undergoing medical treatment. Panel a and c show the baby lying on their back with monitoring devices attached. Panel b shows the baby lying on their side with similar equipment. Initial laboratory studies revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.27, pCO₂ 46.2 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L, SBE −5.3 mmol/L) with elevated lactate (2.7 mmol/L). Cardiac evaluation demonstrated markedly elevated creatine kinase (peak 578 U/L, normalizing by Day 9), while electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia (177 bpm) with ventricular ectopy. Echocardiographic findings were notable for a hemodynamically insignificant patent ductus arteriosus (1.2 mm) with preserved left ventricular function (ejection fraction 53%). Neurophysiological assessment identified multifocal epileptiform discharges and subclinical seizures on Day 1 electroencephalography (EEG), with subsequent electromyography (EMG) on Day 10 showing reduced motor amplitudes (median nerve: right 0.64 mV, left 1.94 mV) and spontaneous fibrillations in limb muscles. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated periventricular T1/T2 hyperintensities with diffusion restriction, though no structural anomalies were observed (). Axial MRI of the brain. The image demonstrates punctate lesions with short T1 and short T2 signal intensity (arrows) adjacent to the bilateral lateral ventricles. These lesions show restricted diffusion on diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) mapping. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed to investigate the underlying genetic etiology of the patient's severe neonatal presentation. WES identified a heterozygous missense variant in the ACTA1 gene, specifically at position c.227G>A, resulting in the amino acid substitution p. Gly76Asp. This variant was not detected in either parent via Sanger sequencing, confirming its de novo origin. In accordance with the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG)/Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) guidelines, the variant was classified as pathogenic. The evidence supporting this classification included the following: PS2 (de novo occurrence in a patient with the disease and no family history); PM1 (located in a mutational hot spot and/or critical functional domain well-established in disease pathology); PM2 (absent or very low frequency in population databases such as gnomAD); and PP3 (multiple computational predictions support a deleterious effect on the gene or gene product). Seen in . The validation results by sanger sequencing for the ACTA1 variants. The infant demonstrated a complicated clinical course, requiring prolonged respiratory support—initially with 7 days of mechanical ventilation, followed by unsuccessful attempts at weaning to non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). Neuroprotective measures, including therapeutic hypothermia and vitamin B1/B12 supplementation, were implemented to mitigate neurological injury. Swallowing rehabilitation therapy was initiated but yielded minimal functional improvement. Although serial EEG monitoring showed gradual improvement by Day 7, the infant exhibited persistent, profound neuromuscular weakness inconsistent with typical hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy recovery. Given the poor prognosis and lack of meaningful neurological recovery, the family elected to withdraw life-sustaining care on Day 18, and the infant passed shortly thereafter. Discussion
Discussion This case illustrates a severe neonatal presentation of ACTA1-related myopathy, associated with a de novo heterozygous pathogenic variant (c.227G>A, p. Gly76Asp) in the ACTA1 gene. The infant exhibited classic features including profound hypotonia, respiratory failure, bulbar dysfunction, arthrogryposis, and an expressionless facies, consistent with previously reported cases of neonatal-onset actinopathy (–). Notably, the initial clinical picture complicated the diagnostic process due to significant overlap with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), particularly given the observed perinatal asphyxia and metabolic acidosis. However, the persistence of severe neuromuscular weakness beyond the typical recovery window for HIE, along with the absence of significant hypoxic injury on neuroimaging, raised suspicion of an underlying neuromuscular disorder. This diagnostic challenge underscores the necessity of including genetic myopathies in the differential diagnosis of floppy infants, even with suggestive perinatal complications. Genetic testing played a pivotal role in confirming the diagnosis. WES identified the missense variant p. Gly76Asp, affecting a highly conserved residue within the skeletal muscle α-actin protein. Previous functional studies of variants at this residue and adjacent amino acids have demonstrated detrimental effects on actin polymerization and filament stability, further corroborating its pathogenicity (). The genetic inheritance of ACTA1-related disorders is complex, predominantly autosomal dominant. In this pattern, a pathogenic variant in a single allele (heterozygosity) is sufficient to result in the disease phenotype. This genetic finding is consistent with the severe clinical phenotype observed in the proband. In accordance with ACMG guidelines, the variant was classified as pathogenic based on several criteria: its de novo occurrence (PS2), low population frequency (PM2), localization within a critical functional domain (PM1), and supportive computational evidence of deleterious impact (PP3) (, –). The absence of the variant in both parents—confirmed via Sanger sequencing—further supports its de novo origin, which is a common inheritance pattern in severe neonatal cases (, ). The predominance of missense mutations, distributed throughout the gene without a clear hotspot, is well-documented in ACTA1-related disease, and this case reinforces that observation (, –). The multisystemic manifestations observed here highlight the severe functional impact of ACTA1 mutations on striated muscle and related systems. Beyond generalized weakness and respiratory failure, the patient also showed elevated creatine kinase levels and cardiac ectopy, suggesting subclinical cardiac involvement—a finding occasionally noted in severe phenotypes (, ). Additionally, the combination of hypertonic contractures against a background of global hypotonia illustrates the complex and often paradoxical effects of actin dysfunction on muscle tone and contractility. Tragically, the clinical course in this case was fatal, consistent with the poor prognosis associated with neonatal-onset ACTA1 myopathies. As reported in the literature, such patients often experience rapid progression of respiratory insufficiency leading to early mortality, despite maximal respiratory and nutritional support (, , ). This outcome reinforces the devastating natural history of this condition and highlights the limited efficacy of current supportive interventions in altering disease progression in the most severe forms. The family's decision to withdraw life-sustaining care, though profoundly difficult, is not uncommon in such contexts and reflects the severe neurodevelopmental prognosis and lack of disease-modifying therapies (, , ). This study has several limitations that warrant discussion. First, as a single-center case report, our conclusions are based on the observation of a solitary patient. Given the significant phenotypic heterogeneity associated with ACTA1-related myopathy, the generalizability of these findings to the broader patient population should be interpreted with caution. Second, this study lacks independent verification via muscle biopsy, which remains the traditional diagnostic gold standard. However, in the contemporary era of advanced molecular diagnostics, genetic testing has become a central pillar for the definitive diagnosis and classification of congenital myopathies, providing a reliable diagnostic pathway for critically ill patients where invasive biopsy is not feasible. Despite these limitations, the detailed clinical course and genetic information documented in this case provide a crucial natural history dataset and phenotypic framework. Current management of ACTA1-related myopathy remains primarily supportive; however, a deeper understanding of its pathological mechanisms—specifically delineating between loss-of-function and toxic gain-of-function effects—is driving a paradigm shift toward etiology-targeted treatments (, ). For loss-of-function mutations, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene replacement therapy represents a highly promising strategy (). The data from this report are essential for designing future clinical trials of such advanced therapies, particularly for application in the most severe neonatal population, as they can inform patient stratification, biomarker selection, and endpoint determination.

Conclusion
Conclusion This case highlights the critical role of early genetic testing, such as rapid WES, in the diagnostic evaluation of neonates with unexplained hypotonia and respiratory failure. A definitive genetic diagnosis is essential to guide clinical management, facilitate accurate prognostic counseling, and inform family-centered decision-making. Future efforts should focus on elucidating genotype-phenotype correlations, developing targeted therapies, and establishing international registries to improve outcomes for patients with severe ACTA1-related congenital myopathies.

title: The Importance of a Multidisciplinary Team Approach in a Rare Case of Antenatally Diagnosed Tonne-Kalscheuer Syndrome.
label_reason: Antenatally diagnosed TOKAS case; ultrasound anomalies and fetal genetic test likely but not fully seen.
abstract: Tonne-Kalscheuer syndrome (TOKAS) is a rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder with very few reported cases. We describe the case of a male neonate born at 27 weeks’ gestation to a 41-year-old mother, with a diagnosis of TOKAS established antenatally through whole-exome sequencing after ultrasound revealed nuchal translucency, hydrops fetalis, structural cardiac abnormalities, and severe fetal growth restriction. The infant survived for nearly two hours after birth and was cared for and held by his parents and extended family. This case highlights the essential role of multidisciplinary collaboration, including maternal-fetal medicine, genetics, neonatology, pathology, and palliative care, in providing coordinated, compassionate, and family-centered care in the setting of a life-limiting fetal diagnosis. It also contributes to the limited literature on the prenatal presentation and perinatal course of TOKAS. Keywords: holistic care for patients, multidisciplinary care team, palliative management, tokas, tonne-kalscheuer syndrome
text:
The Importance of a Multidisciplinary Team Approach in a Rare Case of Antenatally Diagnosed Tonne-Kalscheuer Syndrome

Introduction
Introduction Tonne et al. first described a novel X-linked intellectual disability syndrome in 2015, identifying a missense mutation in the RLIM gene located at Xq13.2 as the underlying cause []. Subsequent reports by Frints et al. [] confirmed that additional pathogenic variants in RLIM were associated with X-linked neurodevelopmental disorders. As recognition of this entity expanded, a broader constellation of clinical features emerged, reflecting the phenotypic variability associated with RLIM mutations. This multiple congenital anomaly syndrome is now known as Tonne-Kalscheuer syndrome (TOKAS) (OMIM #300978) []. To date, only 18 antenatally diagnosed cases have been reported. In the original family described by Tonne et al. [], a Tyr356Cys missense mutation was identified in four affected individuals []. Since then, nine additional missense variants in RLIM have been documented across the literature with variable severity []. Among these, Arg611Cys is the most frequently reported and is considered one of the most deleterious variants. The clinical phenotype of TOKAS is diverse. Affected children may exhibit neurodevelopmental impairments, including motor and speech delays, autism spectrum features, and mild to profound intellectual disability [,]. Characteristic facial features, short stature, and multisystem congenital anomalies have been described, with some individuals developing seizures, structural brain malformations, or congenital cardiac defects [,-]. Most fetuses with severe presentations do not survive to delivery, often due to congenital diaphragmatic hernia and/or pulmonary hypoplasia, consistent with the high prenatal lethality reported in severe RLIM variants [,]. Because TOKAS is X-linked, the condition primarily affects males; however, female carriers may exhibit milder manifestations such as short stature, subtle skeletal findings, or hormonal abnormalities, including primary ovarian insufficiency []. Despite growing recognition, knowledge about TOKAS remains limited, and ongoing case reporting is essential to further define its genotypic and phenotypic spectrum. Given the complexity and severity of many presentations, optimal care for affected pregnancies requires a coordinated multidisciplinary team both antenatally and postnatally, including maternal fetal medicine, genetics, neonatology, cardiology, neurology, pathology, and palliative care, to ensure comprehensive counseling, informed decision-making, and high-quality supportive care for families.

Case presentation
Case presentation The patient’s mother was a 40-year-old G2P0010 who presented for obstetric care with a confirmed single, living intrauterine pregnancy (IUP) at 8 weeks’ gestation. Her medical history was significant for polycystic ovarian syndrome, class II obesity, depression and anxiety, insulin resistance, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic ethmoidal sinusitis, and migraines. She was an asymptomatic carrier for congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Her surgical history included a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by stomal stenosis and a suction dilation and curettage for a prior miscarriage. Conception followed five months of ovulation induction using letrozole, luteinizing hormone (Ovidrel®), and follicle-stimulating hormone (Gonal-F®). At the initial eight-week ultrasound, the IUP appeared normal aside from a small subchorionic hemorrhage. Concern for an underlying genetic abnormality arose during the first-trimester nuchal translucency ultrasound performed at 11 weeks 5 days’ gestation (Figure ). Findings included a markedly enlarged cystic hygroma >95th percentile (Figure ), reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus, persistent non-visualization of the stomach, a small bladder, and minimal fetal movement. A prenatal genetic counselor reviewed screening and diagnostic options. The mother elected to undergo cell-free fetal DNA screening for expanded aneuploidy and five common microdeletion/duplication syndromes; results were negative. She initially declined invasive testing. Nuchal translucency on prenatal ultrasound. Cystic hygroma on prenatal ultrasound. The parents were subsequently offered single-gene cfDNA (cell-free DNA) screening, diagnostic testing, or continued ultrasound surveillance. At 18 weeks 4 days’ gestation, the mother elected amniocentesis. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for chromosomes 13, 18, 21, and X/Y chromosomes, single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) microarray, and trio whole-exome sequencing (WES) were ordered. Both FISH and SNP microarray results were normal. While WES results were pending, an anatomy scan at 21 weeks 5 days’ gestation showed poor fetal growth, bilateral cleft lip and palate, suspected congenital heart disease, thickened nuchal fold, and a small cerebellum. A fetal echocardiogram at 24 weeks 1 day gestation demonstrated a mildly hypoplastic aortic valve, a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD), and a trivial effusion. Hydrops fetalis was diagnosed at 24 weeks 3 days’ gestation and was found to be progressively worsening on serial ultrasounds. A repeat fetal echocardiogram at 26 weeks 3 days’ gestation revealed worsening hydrops, moderate perimembranous VSD, a trivially hypoplastic mitral valve, possible aortic isthmus narrowing, bilateral superior vena cavae without a bridging vein, and a left superior vena cava draining to the coronary sinus. At 27 weeks 2 days’ gestation, severe fetal growth restriction was noted, with estimated fetal weight below the first percentile. The neonatology team was consulted at 26 weeks 3 days’ gestation for counseling regarding the anticipated complications related to the extensive congenital anomalies, including cleft lip and palate, significant cardiac defects, and evolving hydrops. At that time, WES remained pending, whereas all other genetic testing had been unremarkable. Counseling included discussion of expected perinatal instability, anticipated need for neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, potential respiratory support, invasive procedures, blood product administration, imaging, and prolonged hospitalization. The parents were reassured that a multidisciplinary team would follow them both antenatally and postnatally to support decision-making and ensure coordinated care for their medically fragile infant. WES results became available at 27 weeks 4 days’ gestation and revealed a pathogenic maternally inherited RLIM missense variant (Arg611Cys), confirming the diagnosis of TOKAS. Given the severe phenotype, progressive hydrops, and the universally poor prognosis reported in the literature, the NICU team revisited goals of care with the parents, together with a palliative care provider. Prior cases of TOKAS have largely resulted in intrauterine demise or neonatal death shortly after birth, with only a single severely affected survivor reported into early childhood. After discussion of the expected futility of aggressive resuscitation, the parents elected a do-not-resuscitate plan. Because the parents strongly desired a live birth, delivery via cesarean section was recommended to reduce the risk of intrapartum fetal demise. A two-dose course of betamethasone had been initiated at 27 weeks 3 days’ gestation, before confirmation of the genetic diagnosis, although no further steroid administration was planned after transitioning to comfort-focused goals. The perinatal palliative care team provided support, coordinated memory-making activities, and facilitated communication among obstetrics, neonatology, cardiology, genetics, and nursing. A scheduled cesarean section was performed under epidural anesthesia. At birth, the infant exhibited faint activity, cyanosis, and a heart rate <100 beats/minute. In accordance with the established comfort-care plan, he was dried, wrapped, and immediately placed in the arms of his parents. He lived for 1 hour and 48 minutes, passing peacefully in his mother’s arms. The organization Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep photographed the family shortly after birth. Additional memory-making activities, including handprints, footprints, and clay impressions, were completed in the hours following his passing, facilitated by the palliative care team and supported using CuddleCot. A complete autopsy was performed at the parents’ request. Anthropometric measurements were consistent with a 24-25-week gestational-age fetus. All major organ weights, including brain, liver, lungs, heart, thymus, spleen, kidneys, and adrenal glands, were below average for gestational age. Total body weight was 800 g (average = 1,096 g for 28 weeks; 95% range = 684-1,508 g), and crown-rump length was 18 cm (average = 25.7 cm; 95% range = 22.5-28.9 cm). Major autopsy findings included: (1) severe bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia, with lung weight of 1.11 g (reference = 10-44.8 g), although histologic maturation was appropriate for gestational age (Figure ). (2) Biventricular hypertrophy. (3) Perimembranous VSD with mitral valve hypoplasia. (4) Complete bilateral diaphragmatic agenesis, likely the primary contributor to neonatal demise. (5) Bilateral lobulated kidneys with islands of adipose tissue (Figure ). (6) Mild-to-moderate pleural and peritoneal effusions, ascites, and hepatic congestion. (7) Bilateral superior vena cavae. (8) Bilateral cleft lip and palate (Figure ). (9) Brain weight below average with cerebellar hypoplasia and mixed microgyria/pachygyria pattern (Figure ). (10) Hypoplastic fingernails and toenails (Figure ). (11) Multiple external anomalies documented in gross photographs. Bilateral hypoplastic lungs not visible in the chest cavity. The heart and liver are visible. Bilateral lobulated kidneys. Bilateral cleft lip. Brain with cerebellar hypoplasia and mixed microgyria-pachygyria pattern. Hypoplasia of the fingernails and anomaly of the fingers. The family continued to be involved in post-natal counselling. At her postpartum follow-up visit, the mother was coping appropriately and expressed interest in pursuing fostering/adoption.

Discussion
Discussion This case highlights not only the severe phenotype associated with the RLIM Arg611Cys mutation but also the importance of a coordinated multidisciplinary approach in supporting families facing a diagnosis of TOKAS. Given the rarity of this disorder, with fewer than 50 genetically confirmed cases described, the body of evidence guiding counseling and perinatal management remains limited [,,]. As demonstrated in this case, individualized care integrating maternal-fetal medicine, fetal cardiology, neonatology, genetics, pathology, and perinatal palliative care is essential to ensure comprehensive assessment, anticipatory guidance, and family-centered support. Shared decision-making was central to this process, allowing the family to align the birth plan with their priorities, while early involvement of palliative care facilitated clear communication, memory-making, and psychosocial support. Among known pathogenic RLIM variants, Arg611Cys is the most frequently reported and is consistently associated with a severe prenatal phenotype characterized by congenital anomalies, hydrops, and early lethality [,,,]. Cuinat et al. [] described the largest fetal cohort of TOKAS to date and noted recurring findings such as facial dysmorphism, palate abnormalities, hypoplastic nails, congenital heart disease, thoracic anomalies, hydrops, and profound fetal growth restriction. Many of these manifestations were present in our case. Certain findings in this infant, such as bilateral cleft lip and palate, lobulated kidneys, and bilateral superior vena cavae, have been reported infrequently or not at all in prior cohorts, further expanding the clinical spectrum of TOKAS. Notably, diaphragmatic agenesis and severe pulmonary hypoplasia were striking findings at autopsy and likely the leading contributors to early neonatal demise. Such anomalies are consistent with reports demonstrating the critical role of RLIM/RNF12 in embryonic diaphragm, lung, and cardiac development [,,]. Overall, the constellation of anomalies observed in this case aligns with the severe end of the phenotypic spectrum associated with loss-of-function or destabilizing RLIM variants, especially Arg611Cys. Of the 18 antenatally diagnosed cases previously published, 12 involved the Arg611Cys substitution; with the addition of this case, 13 of 19 reported antenatal cases are now attributed to this single variant. Consistent with prior reports, all cases have been inherited from an asymptomatic carrier mother []. TOKAS is caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked RLIM (RNF12) gene, which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in transcriptional regulation, stem cell differentiation, and X-chromosome inactivation. Functional studies demonstrate that RLIM is dosage-sensitive and plays a critical role during early embryogenesis, particularly in the development of the brain, diaphragm, heart, and musculoskeletal system [,,]. Variant Arg611Cys lies within a highly conserved region essential for ubiquitin ligase activity and protein stability. Experimental studies show that variants affecting this region, including Arg611Cys, result in impaired protein function, dysregulated developmental signaling, and widespread disruption of organogenesis [,,]. These molecular findings correlate with the multisystem anomalies and prenatal lethality frequently observed in affected male fetuses. Once a maternally inherited RLIM pathogenic variant is identified, recurrence risk counseling becomes essential. As an X-linked disorder, each future pregnancy has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutation, with male offspring having a 50% chance of being affected and female offspring having a 50% chance of being carriers [,,,]. Female carriers are generally asymptomatic but may have subtle or variable findings such as short stature, mild skeletal differences, or menstrual or ovarian dysfunction []. Given the recurrence risk and severity of outcomes in affected males, options such as preimplantation genetic testing, in vitro fertilization, early invasive prenatal diagnosis, or targeted cfDNA screening may be considered in future pregnancies. Because of the nature and severity of TOKAS, many affected pregnancies likely go undiagnosed. Severe cases may result in miscarriage, intrauterine fetal demise, stillbirth, or death shortly after birth, and a definitive diagnosis cannot be established without WES [,,]. Limited access to advanced prenatal imaging, specialized genetic testing, or postmortem evaluation, as well as personal preference to decline testing, further contributes to the under-recognition of this condition. As TOKAS is uniformly associated with poor perinatal survival when severe anomalies or hydrops are present, early involvement of a multidisciplinary team is crucial. In this case, maternal-fetal medicine guided antenatal imaging and diagnostic testing, genetics facilitated interpretation of the RLIM variant and recurrence counseling, neonatology provided anticipatory guidance regarding expected postnatal instability, and palliative care ensured that the family’s goals and values shaped the overall plan. Memory-making activities, psychosocial support, and bereavement resources were essential components of holistic care. This case underscores how coordinated, compassionate, and comprehensive care can honor family goals while navigating the clinical uncertainty and emotional complexity of a rare, life-limiting diagnosis.

Conclusions
Conclusions TOKAS is an underrecognized rare genetic disorder and is uniformly associated with poor perinatal survival. In this case, obtaining a diagnosis provided clarity regarding prognosis and allowed the care team to guide decision-making in alignment with the family’s goals. When combined with serial ultrasound findings, the genetic diagnosis supported individualized, compassionate, and realistic counseling. This approach required a coordinated multidisciplinary effort across maternal-fetal medicine, genetics, neonatology, pathology, and palliative care. Our experience underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and integrated team-based care when managing pregnancies complicated by rare, life-limiting genetic conditions.
