The Clinical Utility of Sequence‐Based Genetic Testing for Fetal Edema Following Non‐Diagnostic Microarray Results: A Population‐Based Cohort Study

Introduction
Introduction Fetal edema comprises conditions such as increased nuchal translucency (NT), cystic hygroma (CH), fetal hydrops, or isolated fetal edema, such as ascites, pleural or pericardial effusions, or skin edema. It is associated with a broad differential diagnosis and a range of outcomes, including normal variation, genetic disorders, congenital infections, structural abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, fetal demise and developmental delay. Genetic etiologies for prenatal ultrasound findings of fetal edema have been described using a variety of methodologies [, , , , , , , , ]. The diagnostic yield for rapid aneuploidy detection (RAD), karyotype, and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) following ultrasound findings of increased NT, CH, fetal hydrops, or isolated fetal edema is 30%–40% []. Sequence‐based testing can provide an incremental diagnostic yield of 30% [, , ]. The current study is a population‐based retrospective cohort evaluation of all fetuses that had genetic testing done for a prenatal ultrasound finding of non‐specific fetal edema, and was designed to evaluate the use and yield of sequence‐based testing following non‐diagnostic testing results for RAD and CMA. This study involved a review of clinical data already available in a population‐based genomics laboratory information system and health records, including consultant, laboratory, and imaging reports. Specifically, the objectives were to assess the use of targeted gene panels and exome analysis in cases of fetal edema, to determine the diagnostic yield of this testing based on selected clinical criteria, to examine the clinical value of review by multidisciplinary teams, and to clarify the specific fetal edema indications (increased NT, CH, non‐immune hydrops, or other types of edema restricted to one body cavity) that would benefit best from sequence‐based methods in a low resource clinical practice setting, to optimize counseling and management for patients.

Methods
Methods Data from the IWK Health Clinical Genomics Laboratory Information System (CGLIS) in Halifax, Nova Scotia, was combined with health records review from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2022 to conduct a retrospective, population‐based cohort study. The CGLIS performs or coordinates all publicly funded genetic testing in the Canadian Maritime Provinces (including Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island) for anomalies detected by fetal ultrasound, and securely stores cytogenetic and molecular genetic information related to testing indications, types of samples, and testing results. For the duration of the study, RAD (QF‐PCR for common aneuploidy), karyotype (during earlier years of the study), and CMA (for causative copy number variants, CNV) comprised first‐tier genetic testing at IWK Health, with sequence‐based testing (genes, gene panels, or exomes) offered for selected cases meeting the specific testing criteria developed collaboratively by IWK Health Maritime Medical Genetics and Clinical Genomics services. Testing criteria during the study period at IWK Health included a standard 17‐gene RASopathy panel for NT greater than 5 mm, single gene or gene panels based on assessed clinical phenotype, and exomes based on one or more of the following findings: two or more affected organ systems, progressive clinical course, and recurrence of phenotype in a subsequent pregnancy. Following review of ultrasound findings of fetal edema and structural anomalies, patients have the opportunity for consultation with the Medical Genetics service, who offer additional sequence‐based testing within the clinical presentation and the IWK laboratory criteria; for ongoing pregnancies during the study period, referral to the Medical Genetics service was required to access the opportunity for genetic testing beyond assessment for aneuploidy. All fetal samples with abnormal ultrasound findings of fetal edema (chorionic villus sampling (CVS), amniocentesis, fetal blood, and products of conception (POC)) were identified by CGLIS, as well as cord blood or newborn samples within 4 weeks of delivery, based on prenatal fetal ultrasound detection of fetal edema with or without structural anomalies. Genetic testing using RAD, karyotype and CMA was done in‐house. For gene sequencing, testing was done at either locally or through accredited commercial referral laboratories. A panel was restricted to one or more genes, while exome analysis involved phenotype‐driven testing. Single genes and small gene panels, such as RASopathy, were performed in‐house, whereas larger gene panels (> 200 genes) and exomes were performed by referral laboratories. Classification of variants for testing done locally followed the America College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) criteria [], and for other testing, classification was done according to the referral laboratory procedure. The clinicians involved in the care of the patient provided interpretation of the variants as clinically relevant pathogenic variants or variants of uncertain significance. Findings of fetal edema included cases with NT ≥ 3.5 mm, CH, hydrops, and other types of fetal edema restricted to one body cavity (such as ascites, effusions, or skin edema). Eligible samples were those identified by the CGLIS as having undergone RAD and CMA and had non‐diagnostic results; health records review was performed for information on patient demographics, such as maternal age and gestational age at initiation of fetal testing, multidisciplinary review (including consultation and counseling with Medical Genetics service, Maternal Fetal Medicine, and other relevant subspecialists as needed, such as cardiology, neurosurgery, orthopedics), associated ultrasound findings and findings from other imaging modalities, autopsy, newborn examination, and the results of genetic testing. A descriptive analysis of the study population was performed and evaluated the number of genetic tests and the diagnostic yield of causative microarray and single gene variants in a cohort of fetuses with edema, as well as the clinical collaboration with a multidisciplinary team. Chi‐square (or similar test for small numbers) and t‐test statistical analyses were performed (for categorical and continuous variables, respectively, significance set at p < 0.05) using Open Epi (Version 3.01, 2013). Aggregate cell sizes < 5 were suppressed to protect patient privacy in compliance with local data management principles. IWK Health Research Ethics Board approval was obtained (IWK REB Project #1024606).

Results
Results The CGLIS identified 593 prenatal and neonatal cases eligible for chromosomal microarray testing after non‐diagnostic RAD results, based on prenatal detection of structural abnormalities, 127 of which involved fetal edema as a primary feature (Figure ). Cases with anemia and congenital infections were previously excluded. The majority of samples tested were from CVS, amniocentesis, fetal blood, and POC (103/114, 90.4%). Of these 127 cases, 13 (10.2%) had a diagnostic CMA result and 105 (82.6%) participated in a multidisciplinary review either before or after CMA testing. Table summarizes the demographic characteristics of the study population, grouped by presentation type (increased NT, CH, hydrops, or other types of fetal edema). Sixteen (61.5%) other types of fetal edema had skin edema. A difference in mean maternal age was noted for cases presenting with increased NT (p = 0.04) and hydrops (p = 0.047), but not CH or other types of fetal edema (p > 0.05), compared to the overall mean maternal age. Cases with increased NT were less likely to be associated with nulliparity (p = 0.01), compared to overall nulliparity, with no differences noted for CH, hydrops, or other types of fetal edema (p > 0.05). There was no difference in mean body mass index (BMI) in any of the groups compared with overall BMI (p > 0.05). The mean gestational age at the time of initiating genetic testing was 19.0 weeks overall, with lower gestational ages for cases with increased NT and CH, and with higher gestational ages for cases presenting with hydrops and other types of fetal edema (p < 0.001 for all groups) compared to the overall gestational age. One or more structural anomalies were present in 55/127 (43.3%) cases of fetal edema, the majority of which were cardiac and/or renal anomalies, and were more commonly seen in cases with hydrops (51.6%) and other types of fetal edema (69.2%) compared to the total (p = 0.01 and p < 0.001, respectively). Flow diagram determination of study population, IWK health clinical genomics laboratory information system, 2014–2022. RAD = rapid aneuploidy detection, CMA = chromosomal microarray analysis, NT = nuchal translucency, *other types of fetal edema restricted to one body cavity (such as ascites, effusions, or skin edema). Table summarizes the yield of diagnostic microarray results, participation in multidisciplinary review, and additional sequence‐based testing among fetal edema cases according to presentation group. Overall, 10.2% of cases had a diagnostic CMA result; there was no difference in diagnostic yield in each of the groups of fetal edema compared to the total (p > 0.05), although cases presenting with other types of fetal edema had a clinically lower diagnostic yield (3.9%). Multidisciplinary review, including consultation with the Maritime Medical Genetics Service, occurred in 82.7% of the cases overall; those presenting with increased NT were more likely to undergo multidisciplinary review compared to the total (p < 0.01), while those cases with fetal hydrops were less likely to undergo multidisciplinary review compared to the total (p < 0.01); there was no difference for CH and other types of fetal edema (p > 0.05). A total of 95 cases that did not have a diagnostic CMA result underwent multidisciplinary review and assessment for additional sequence‐based testing. Overall, 51 of these cases (53.7%) had additional sequence‐based testing ranging from targeted single genes, targeted gene panels, and exomes. Additional testing was higher in cases presenting with CH (p < 0.001) and hydrops (p = 0.01), but not with increased NT or other types of fetal edema (p > 0.05); additional testing with increased NT was clinically lower than in the other groups. For those cases undergoing additional testing, aside from cases with increased NT where structural anomalies may have been more difficult to detect, 84% of testing was done in the context of fetal phenotype, including the presence of structural anomalies, consistent with established institutional testing criteria during the study period. Supporting Information : Table 1 summarizes the targeted sequence‐based testing used in the study. Table summarizes the types of additional sequence‐based genetic testing that were performed, categorized by fetal edema group, following a CMA result that was non‐diagnostic; in 12 cases (24% of tested samples), more than one additional sequence‐based test was performed. A RASopathy gene panel was the most frequently used sequence‐based test, performed for 27 cases, representing 53.0% of all cases having additional testing. RASopathy testing was used more often in the setting of increased NT (33.3%) and CH (42.9%), while other types of fetal edema (5.0%) less commonly had RASopathy testing. There was no difference in the types of additional sequence‐based testing in cases presenting with fetal hydrops (27.8% for all). Other targeted sequencing included single genes (9 cases) and defined gene panels (10 cases) based on the presenting phenotype, the most common of which was the fetal arthrogryposis/akinesia panel. Targeted testing other than the RASopathy panel was rarely used in cases presenting with increased NT (5.6%), and more consistently used in the setting of CH (23.8%), hydrops (27.8%), and other types of fetal edema (35.0%). Exome analysis was used in 18 cases (20%) overall, either as an initial sequencing test (10 cases) or after other sequencing (8 cases). Table also shows the diagnostic yields according to type of sequencing test (RASopathy panel, other targeted gene/panel sequencing, and exome analysis) and total diagnostic yields of additional sequence‐based testing. Supporting Information : Table 2 summarizes the gene variants that were considered diagnostic. In this study, exome analysis included 9 singleton exomes and 9 trio or quad exomes with parental samples (including, e.g., samples from a second affected fetus in the case of quad analyses); it was a clinical practice setting where both parents were not always available for trio analysis, or where the geneticist had made a clinical decision to proceed only with a singleton analysis. For those cases tested following review by the Maritime Medical Genetics Service because of a non‐diagnostic CMA result, higher diagnostic yields were observed more frequently for cases presenting with hydrops (50.0%) and other types of fetal edema (50%), and less frequently for increased NT (7.7%) and CH (31.3%). While RASopathy testing did not provide a diagnosis for cases with other types of edema, a diagnosis was provided by RASopathy panel testing in 7.7% of cases presenting with increased NT, 12.5% with CH, and 16.7% with hydrops (relative to the total number of RASopathy panel tests performed, n = 27). Targeted single genes or gene panels other than RASopathy infrequently provided a diagnosis for cases presenting with increased NT (0%), CH (6.3%), or hydrops (8.3%), and more frequently provided a diagnosis for cases presenting with other types of fetal edema (30%, p < 0.001 compared to both CH and hydrops). Testing by exome analysis provided a diagnosis in 12.5% of cases with CH, 25.0% of cases with hydrops, and 20% of cases with other types of edema.

Discussion
Discussion The current study evaluated the use of sequence‐based testing following a non‐diagnostic microarray result, for different presentations of fetal edema detected by prenatal ultrasound, in a low‐resource clinical practice setting. During the study time frame, CMA and sequence‐based testing were offered for cases based on clinical phenotype and/or family history meeting specific institutional testing criteria. Most cases of fetal edema accessed multidisciplinary review, including consultation with the IWK Health Maritime Medical Genetics Service, either before or after CMA, with additional sequence‐based testing providing diagnostic yields comparable to published literature. A RASopathy gene panel was the most frequently used sequence‐based test in the study cohort. Sequence‐based testing had the highest diagnostic yield in cases of fetal hydrops and other types of fetal edema restricted to one body cavity compared with increased NT or CH. The current study demonstrated diagnostic yields from additional sequence‐based testing, including RASopathy testing, other targeted sequencing, and exome analysis, for cases presenting with either increased NT ≥ 3.5 (7.7%) or CH (31.3%) that are similar to recent published literature. RASopathies are common genetic causes of fetal edema; prenatal findings are not specific but may include increased NT, CH, hydrops, pleural effusions, and polyhydramnios [, ] While additional structural anomalies may be present, 20% of fetuses found to have RASopathies have isolated fetal edema on ultrasound. In a systematic review and meta‐analysis, Makhamreh et al. [] demonstrated that the rate of RASopathy diagnoses among cases with non‐immune fetal hydrops with a genetic diagnosis was 23% following non‐diagnostic RAD and CMA results, while in a review of fetuses with NT ≥ 3.5 mm, a RASopathy panel provided a diagnosis in 1.44% []. Current literature shows that a limited gene panel for RASopathies with fetal edema has a diagnostic yield of 9%–30% following non‐diagnostic RAD and CMA results, although limited gene panels may not typically be part of a standardized assessment for fetal edema [, , ]. The current study demonstrated a similar diagnostic yield for RASopathies, including 16.7% for cases presenting with fetal hydrops and 7.7% and 12.5% for those presenting with increased NT and CH cases, respectively. The higher yield for increased NT and CH in the current study is likely due to the institutional testing criteria during the study period (i.e., RASopathy testing was primarily used in the setting of NT greater than 5 mm), resulting in a smaller subset of cases eligible for sequence‐based testing than has been examined in the literature. Beyond RASopathy testing, reports in the literature of other sequence‐based testing using targeted single genes or gene panels to investigate fetal edema were rare, and were more likely to evaluate associated findings (such as arthrogryposis/akinesia) []. Low diagnostic yield of targeted gene sequencing other than RASopathy testing was also demonstrated in the current study, and did not provide a diagnosis for cases presenting with increased NT (case numbers were also small). However, in the context of typical clinical practice, exomes performed for cases meeting specific criteria, which included the presence of fetal anomalies, provided high diagnostic yields comparable to those in published literature. A recent systematic review investigating increased NT in the early first trimester showed a high prevalence of chromosomal, genetic and structural abnormalities in fetuses with persistent and resolved increased NT, and in particular, they demonstrated that diagnostic yields with exome sequencing for single gene disorders with increased NT were 7.6% []. Studies have shown diagnostic yields for exome sequencing to be low in cases of isolated increased NT ≥ 3.5 mm (1.8%–4.8%) [, , ], but significantly higher for increased NT in the presence of additional structural anomalies (17%–37.5%) [, , ]. Another study [] demonstrated a diagnostic yield of 34.3% using exome analysis for NT thickening > 95th percentile and CH; however, this was in a selected subgroup of ongoing pregnancies, including the possibility of other structural abnormalities. In the current study, exome analysis was restricted to specific institutional testing criteria; thus, for increased NT, exome testing was rare, and no diagnostic variants were reported. Prospective and meta‐analysis information in the literature related to non‐immune fetal hydrops with or without concurrent anomalies demonstrated diagnostic yields from exome sequencing ranging from 17% to 50% [, , , , ]. Gulrajani et al. [] also demonstrated diagnostic yields for fetal hydrops (26%) and single compartment effusions (22%) in their prospective study with exome sequencing. With lower rates of multidisciplinary review for cases with fetal hydrops (and potentially less opportunities for sequence‐based testing), the current study demonstrated similar diagnostic yields from exome analysis in cases with fetal hydrops and other fetal edema (33% and 20% respectively), and higher diagnostic yields when including RASopathy testing and other targeted sequencing as well as exome sequencing (50% and 50%, respectively). Collaboration with and assessment by multidisciplinary teams with genetic testing is a recognized and valued resource [, , ]. While a high percentage of cases of increased NT, CH and other cases of fetal edema were reviewed by multidisciplinary teams in the current study, cases with fetal hydrops were less likely to have had this involvement (64%), despite the finding that this group had the highest diagnostic yields from additional sequence‐based testing. This is likely a consequence of later timing of diagnosis of hydrops and subsequent pregnancy loss (spontaneous or induced) that may have resulted in these cases undergoing genetic testing at autopsy; local protocol for fetal genetic testing in the setting of demise with hydrops includes CMA as a standard test, but additional sequence‐based testing requires consultation with the medical genetics service. Importantly, access to this service may facilitate postnatal phenotyping genetic reanalysis as variants are further defined, which can provide additional information about etiologies and recurrence risk. A key recommendation by the Canadian College of Medical Geneticists [] in the care of pregnant patients in Canada included comprehensive access to consultation with the medical genetics service, which was identified as an area of improvement in our population. The current study employed data from a population‐based data source to assess the diagnostic yield of sequence‐based testing following a non‐diagnostic CMA result. It demonstrated higher diagnostic yields than those reported in the literature in some groups of fetal edema (hydrops, and other types of fetal edema) based on clinical presentation; this may be attributed to the fact that testing was representative of a clinical practice setting with testing requested based on clinical phenotype within the limits of laboratory testing criteria during the study period. The medical genetics team that provides service to Nova Scotia and the other Maritime provinces is based at IWK Health. Limitations included a small amount of missing data from health record review, particularly for those cases not from Nova Scotia. In addition, the differences in mean maternal age and gestational age at genetic testing likely represented the challenges in universal access to dating ultrasounds, NT assessment, and the timing of the clinical presentation of fetal hydrops and other cases of fetal edema.

Conclusion
Conclusion In the context of fetal edema, the presence of additional clinical features can inform appropriate genetic testing strategies to optimize diagnostic results. This study showed that sequencing of a RASopathy gene panel and whole exomes has a high diagnostic yield in cases with non‐specific findings of increased NT, CH, or hydrops following a non‐diagnostic CMA result. This testing is therefore warranted for such cases, and targeted RASopathy gene panel testing should be offered in parallel with CMA if exome analysis cannot be offered due to limited health care resources, or until there is a clear indication for performing exome analyses. Correlation of new and developing prenatal and postnatal findings, along with multidisciplinary team review, may inform additional testing, counseling and pregnancy management options, and is particularly important to consider in cases presenting with non‐immune fetal hydrops.

title: A Novel Nonsense Variant in Ankyrin Repeat and Sterile Alpha Motif Domain-Containing 6 Promotes Polycystic Kidney Disease in Han:SPRD- Cy Rats and Its Homozygosity Is Prenatally Lethal.
label_reason: Rat model study.
abstract:
A novel nonsense variant ( mcy ) in ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain-containing 6 ( Anks6 ) promotes rapid disease progression in the Han:SPRD- Cy rat carrying a missense variant in Anks6 . mcy −/− rats exhibit prenatal lethality characterized by laterality and cardiovascular abnormalities. These findings indicate that ANKS6 nonfunction in rats leads to prenatal lethality, whereas misfunction leads to polycystic kidney disease development. 
 A novel nonsense variant ( mcy ) in ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain-containing 6 ( Anks6 ) promotes rapid disease progression in the Han:SPRD- Cy rat carrying a missense variant in Anks6 . mcy −/− rats exhibit prenatal lethality characterized by laterality and cardiovascular abnormalities. These findings indicate that ANKS6 nonfunction in rats leads to prenatal lethality, whereas misfunction leads to polycystic kidney disease development. Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) encompasses a group of genetic disorders characterized by the proliferation of fluid-filled renal cysts, leading to progressive renal failure and death. A key feature of PKD is its variable expressivity across patients, even when caused by the same variant, highlighting the importance of genetic background in PKD expression. We identified an ostensibly healthy Sprague Dawley rat line with a variant that modifies PKD expressivity in Han:SPRD- Cy rats (caused by a missense variant [p.Arg717Trp] in the ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain-containing 6 [ Anks6 ] gene), which we named mcy (modifier of Cy ). We used whole-genome sequencing and segregation analysis to identify the mcy variant, quantitative PCR and mRNA sequencing to evaluate its effects on gene expression, western blotting and immunohistochemistry to assess its protein consequences, and ultrasound and histology to examine its impact on rat embryonic development. We identified a nonsense variant in the Anks6 gene as the genetic basis of the mcy phenotype (c.1126G>T [p.Glu376X]). Although mcy 
 +/− rats are ostensibly healthy and do not develop PKD, mcy −/− rats exhibit laterality defects and die prenatally at E16.5 because of apparent perturbations in cardiovascular development. Notably, mcy 
 +/− 
 Cy +/− rats develop PKD much more rapidly than Cy 
 +/− rats, and in a timeframe consistent with Cy −/− 
 rats . Transcripts with the mcy variant allele seem to undergo nonsense-mediated decay, and no ANKS6 protein is detected. However, gene expression patterns in the kidneys did not differ significantly between age-matched mcy +/+ and mcy 
 +/− rats, indicating that ANKS6 insufficiency does not cause PKD. We identified a novel nonsense variant in Anks6 . The findings indicate that the absence of wild-type ANKS6 accelerates PKD development in the Han:SPRD- Cy rat and that complete ANKS6 deficiency prevents normal embryonic development in rats.

A Novel Nonsense Variant in Ankyrin Repeat and Sterile Alpha Motif Domain-Containing 6 Promotes Polycystic Kidney Disease in Han:SPRD-Cy Rats and Its Homozygosity Is Prenatally Lethal

Introduction
Introduction Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) encompasses a group of genetic disorders characterized by the proliferation of fluid-filled renal cysts, which causes progressive damage to the normal renal parenchyma, leading to renal failure and death., Most PKD cases are autosomal dominant PKD (ADPKD), which occurs in all ethnicities with an incidence of 1:400–1000 and afflicting approximately 12.5 million individuals worldwide. Approximately 85% of ADPKD cases are caused by pathogenic variants in the polycystin 1 (PKD1) gene,, and the remaining 15% are caused by pathogenic variants in the polycystin 2 gene., Less common but more severe forms of PKD primarily manifest in children and are autosomal recessive. These include autosomal recessive PKD, which affects 1:20,000 newborns and is caused by pathogenic variants in the polycystic kidney and hepatic disease 1 gene,– and nephronophthisis (NPHP), which affects 1:50,000–80,000 newborns and is caused by pathogenic variants in more than 25 identified genes that encode proteins necessary for correct ciliary and renal tubular development and function.– A key feature of the various forms of PKD is their variable phenotypic expression. Individuals with different pathogenic variants in PKD1 can develop enlarged cystic kidneys in utero or have normal renal function into old age. By contrast, NPHP can occur with isolated kidney involvement or in combination with various extrarenal manifestations, including cardiac, ophthalmic (Senior–Løken syndrome), neurologic (Joubert syndrome), hepatic (Meckel–Gruber syndrome), and skeletal (Jeune syndrome) anomalies.,, Studies of rodent PKD models support the importance of modifier genes and variants.– PKD progression differs among strains with the same PKD-causing pathogenic variant, suggesting that their genetic background influences PKD expressivity. However, only a few modifier genes have been identified, including catechol-O-methyltransferase (Comt), hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 homeobox B (HNF1B), and PKD1. Importantly, related human patients with PKD caused by the same pathogenic variant also exhibited marked variability in PKD expression.– Differences in PKD progression among ethnicities also support the importance of genetic background in human PKD pathophysiology. An investigation of the role of modifier genes and variants in patients with ADPKD found differences in PKD expression between patients with the same PKD-causing pathogenic variant and different genetic backgrounds to be as varied as between patients with different PKD-causing pathogenic variants and genetic backgrounds. Although 18%–59% of PKD phenotypic variability in humans was estimated to be due to differences in genetic background, the identities of other modifiers and how they influence PKD expressivity remain to be described. Several rodent PKD models harbor pathogenic variants that cause renal cysts in affected animals.– One of the commonly used models over the past 30 years has been the Han:SPRD-Cy rat,, which has a missense pathogenic variant (named Cy; c.2149C>T [p.Arg717Trp] according to Ensembl release 89 of build Rnor6 of the Rattus norvegicus [R. norvegicus] genome) in the ankyrin repeat and sterile alpha motif domain-containing 6 (Anks6) gene, an ortholog of the human ANKS6 (formerly NPHP16) gene whose disruption causes NPHP. Although + has traditionally been used to denote the variant allele in the literature on the Han-SPRD-Cy rat, we adopt the standard convention in genetics of + representing the wild-type (WT) allele and − representing the variant allele. The ANKS6 protein is present in the renal proximal tubules, forming heteromeric complexes with several other NPHP proteins important for correct renal development. Cy−/− rats exhibit rapid disease progression and die of renal failure by approximately 3 weeks, although Cy +/− rats do not progress to renal failure until at least approximately 7 months. In Cy−/− and Cy +/− rats, renal cysts form from proximal tubules because of increased epithelial cell proliferation, morphologic dedifferentiation, basement membrane thickening, and monocyte infiltration and aggregation.,– Importantly, ANKS6 interacts with bicaudal C family RNA binding protein 1 (BICC1), a Pkd2 transcriptional regulator whose disruption causes the PKD phenotype in the jcpk and bpk mouse models. Although the missense pathogenic variant responsible for PKD in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat disrupts the formation of ANKS6 homodimers, it does not disrupt the interaction between ANKS6 and BICC1. Therefore, although both ANKS6 and BICC1 seem to function in a common molecular pathway whose perturbation causes PKD, these observations would be compatible with each causing PKD through distinct mechanisms. In this study, we describe the chance discovery of a Sprague Dawley rat line harboring a variant of uncertain significance that modifies PKD expressivity in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat. Rats that are heterozygous for this variant, which we named mcy (modifier of Cy), are ostensibly healthy and their kidneys seem normal under histologic examination. However, rats that are compound heterozygous for the Cy and mcy variants develop PKD much faster (renal failure by approximately 3 weeks, rapid-PKD) than is typical for that of heterozygous Han:SPRD-Cy rats (renal failure after 7 months, slow-PKD). Moreover, homozygosity for the mcy variant seems to be prenatally lethal. We first use next-generation whole genome sequencing (WGS) to identify the mcy variant, then explore its effects on gene and protein expression in the kidney and its apparent prenatal lethality in homozygous form.

Methods
Methods Ethics and Animal Use This study was conducted according to protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Manitoba (approval numbers: AC10876 and AC11319) and followed the Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments guidelines. The University of Manitoba maintains the Canadian Council of Animal Care certificate for Good Animal Practice. All rats were housed in accordance with standard animal care and use guidelines, including enrichment, in the Biological Sciences Animal Housing Facility at the University of Manitoba. Rats were euthanized by exsanguination under isoflurane anesthesia, and their kidneys or embryos were harvested. No rats or embryos were excluded from analyses. See Supplemental Methods for further details on animal use. Phenotyping and Kidney Harvesting We created an inbred pedigree in which the mcy and Cy variants segregated, and overall background genetic variation was reduced, by mating mcy-carrier (mcy +/− Cy+/+) and slow-PKD (mcy+/+ Cy+/−) rats. We determined the Cy status of each pup using a previously reported RFLP assay. Because the mcy variant's identity was unknown, we determined each rat's mcy status by the presence of rapid-PKD pups (mcy +/− Cy+/−) among the viable offspring when it was crossed with a slow-PKD rat. We harvested kidneys from rapid-PKD rats at 2 weeks of age—beyond this age, the rats are too sick to be kept alive—and from slow-PKD, mcy-carrier, and WT (mcy+/+ Cy+/+) rats at 4 months of age and stored them at −80°C. At these times, PKD in both rapid-PKD and slow-PKD rats involves extensive cyst development; therefore, we expect their pathophysiology to be broadly commensurable. Genomic DNA, Total RNA, and Protein Preparation We extracted genomic DNA, total RNA, and total protein from approximately 30 mg of renal cortex tissue using the AllPrep DNA/RNA/Protein Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD) after homogenization on ice for 45 seconds with a CH-6010 homogenizer (Kinematica, Luzern, Switzerland). Genomic DNA was also prepared from tail tips using the method of Laird et al. WGS and Analysis All library preparations and WGS were performed by The Center for Applied Genomics (TCAG) at The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, ON, Canada). Genomic DNA was processed using the TruSeq Nano DNA library preparation kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA) according to the manufacturer's recommended protocol, except without PCR amplification. Approximately 180 Gb of 150-bp paired-end raw sequence data were generated for each sample (see Supplemental Methods for more details) using the Illumina HiSeq X platform, providing an average genome-wide read depth of 41.72×±4.40× (32.83×–46.97×) across samples. We processed reads and then discovered and genotyped genetic variants according to the SpeedSeq pipeline using Ensembl release 89 of build Rnor6 of the R. norvegicus genome (European Bioinformatics Institute, Hinxton, the United Kingdom). We predicted the effects of the genetic variants on transcription, translation, and protein function using SnpEff on the basis of the Ensembl database (release 89). Prenatal Lethality Determination Prenatal lethality because of homozygosity for the mcy variant was determined by ultrasound. All embryos were harvested approximately 2 days after the first appearance of nonviable embryos, and tail tips were collected for genomic DNA extraction. To explore the cause of death, we mated two further pairs of mcy-carrier rats, harvested their embryos or embryo hearts at stage E14.5, and fixed them in formalin. Further details are in Supplemental Methods. mRNA Sequencing and Analysis All library preparations and next-generation mRNA sequencing (mRNA-seq) were performed by TCAG. First, mRNA was isolated from total kidney RNA using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA). Next, libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra Directional RNA for Illumina Kit and adapters from the NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina Kit. Then, between 79,408,510 and 115,339,665 126-bp paired-end reads (96,919,401±10,222,661) were generated for all samples using the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform. We processed raw reads according to the HISAT2 pipeline using Ensembl release 89 of build Rnor6 of the R. norvegicus genome and transcriptome. Further details are in Supplemental Methods. Validation of the mcy Variant The candidate mcy variant creates a BfaI restriction enzyme site in exon 7 of Anks6. We PCR-amplified the genomic region encompassing the mcy variant using forward (5′-GTC​CAG​GAG​GTG​GAA​CCT​G-3′) and reverse (5′-GCT​TAT​CCC​TGG​GCT​CGT​C-3′) primers designed on the basis of the reference sequence (National Center for Biotechnology Information [NCBI] accession: NC_005104.4) and the Platinum Hot-Start Taq DNA Polymerase Master Mix (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Then, we digested PCR products (10 µl each) with BfaI or FspB1 (New England Biolabs) for 2 hours at 37°C and then analyzed them by 8% PAGE. In the presence of the mcy variant, the 329 bp PCR product was cleaved into 164 and 165 bp fragments. Allele-Specific Gene Expression We conducted quantitative PCR (qPCR) using a custom-designed TaqMan Gene Expression assay to quantify the relative abundances of Anks6 transcripts carrying the mutant (5′-TCT​GAC​TAG​CCT​GAG​C-3′) and WT (5′-TCT​GAC​GAG​CCT​GAG-3′) alleles using a predesigned assay (rn01437052_m1), as described in the Supplemental Methods. Kidney and Embryo Histology We fixed rat kidneys, embryos, or hearts in formalin overnight; washed them in PBS; and processed them for paraffin embedding. Then, we stained paraffin sections (5 µM) with hematoxylin and eosin or Goldner Trichrome Method (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA) and visualized them under a light microscope. Western Blotting and Immunohistochemistry The complete western blotting procedures are described in detail in the Supplemental Methods. In brief, immunohistochemistry was performed as described previously, except we used a rabbit anti-ANKS6 primary antibody (1:1000; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) followed by a horseradish peroxidase–conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:2000; Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA) and counterstained the slides with methylene blue.

Results
Results The mcy Variant Modifies PKD Expressivity We identified by chance an ostensibly WT Sprague Dawley rat line that seemed to carry a genetic aberration that modifies PKD expressivity in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat line. When a mcy rat was crossed with a Han:SPRD-Cy+/− rat, approximately 25% of the offspring rapidly developed cystic kidneys that are easily detectable by palpation at approximately 2 weeks of age (rapid-PKD). Visual inspection of 2-week-old rapid-PKD pups' kidneys during necropsy confirmed the presence of multiple cysts (Figure A). Their rapid PKD development more closely resembles that of Han:SPRD-Cy−/− rats (Figure B) but contrasts with that of Han:SPRD-Cy+/− rats, which develop cysts at a much slower rate and do not go into renal failure until they are much older (≥7 months, slow-PKD; Figure C); approximately 25% of the offspring of a mcy×Han:SPRD-Cy+/− cross developed PKD consistent with this timeframe. Importantly, when rapid-PKD pups were genotyped for the Cy variant, their genotype was the same as that of slow-PKD pups (Cy+/−). Kidney examinations during necropsy of four generations of rats carrying only the mcy variant (i.e., Cy+/+) showed no histologic evidence of renal disease up to 11 months of age (Figure D). The phenotypic ratio among pups from these crosses indicates that mcy-carrier rats are heterozygous for an autosomal variant that does not cause disease but enhances the expressivity of the Cy variant. Kidney histology for each phenotype. H&E-stained kidney sections from a (A) 2-week-old rapid-PKD (Cy +/− mcy+/−) pup from a Cy +/− mcy+/+×Cy+/+ mcy +/− mating, (B) 2-week-old rapid-PKD (Cy−/− mcy+/+) pup from a Cy +/− mcy+/+×Cy +/− mcy+/+ mating, (C) 4-month-old slow-PKD (Cy +/− mcy+/+) rat from a Cy +/− mcy+/+×Cy +/− mcy+/+ mating, and (D) 11-month-old mcy-carrier (Cy+/+ mcy+/−) rat from the mcy line. The amorphous white voids in the kidney sections in parts (A–C) are fluid-filled renal cysts. H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; PKD, polycystic kidney disease. Genetic Basis of the mcy PKD Modifier Phenotype We performed high-coverage WGS on genomic DNA extracted from four WT and four mcy-carrier rats randomly chosen from those in the ninth and tenth generations of an inbred pedigree within which the mcy and Cy variants segregate. We identified 2,368,462 genetic variants relative to build Rnor6 (Ensembl release 89) of the R. norvegicus reference genome: 1,823,718 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), 179,738 insertions, 197,598 deletions, 42,633 balanced multi-nucleotide polymorphisms, and 124,775 unbalanced multi-nucleotide polymorphisms. We filtered them conditionally on heterozygosity in all four mcy-carrier rats and on homozygosity for the reference allele in all four WT rats, creating a list of 24,291 candidate variants, which were then assessed for their putative functional effects using SNPeff. Filtering these candidates, conditionally on a high predicted likelihood of affecting gene or protein function, reduced the list to three. Two were unbalanced multi-nucleotide polymorphisms predicted to cause a frameshift in hypothetic genes present in the Ensembl gene database but absent from the NCBI and the University of California, Santa Cruz databases. The final variant was an SNV (c.1126G>T) that introduced a premature stop codon (p.Glu376X) in exon 7 of the Anks6 gene (Table ), a known NPHP-associated gene, whose dysfunction is the biologic basis of the PKD phenotype in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat (p.Arg717Trp; note that this position was reported as p.Arg823Trp by Brown et al. on the basis of an earlier protein sequence prediction). Read depth at this position was 29×–52× among WT rats (38.50±9.88) and 33×–51× among mcy-carrier rats (45.50±8.39), in whom reads were evenly balanced between alleles (mean 0/1 ratio=1.074±0.245). Considering 58 reference genomes containing a high-confidence ortholog of rat Anks6 reported in the Ensembl database (Supplemental Figure 1A), 55 genomes (94.8%) have glutamic acid (Glu, E), and three genomes (5.2%) have aspartic acid (Asp, D) at position 376, which is between the ANKS6's N-terminal ankyrin domain and the C-terminal sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain. Similarly, all reference genomes contained arginine (Arg, R) at position 717 (Supplemental Figure 1B), which is in the C-terminal SAM domain. The high conservation observed at these positions indicates their importance for correct ANKS6 structure and/or function. This candidate mcy variant in Anks6 created a BfaI restriction enzyme site, and we developed an RFLP assay to genotype it (see Methods). The genotyping of ten rats with each of the four phenotypes for the candidate mcy variant found all mcy-carrier and rapid-PKD rats to be heterozygous and all WT and slow-PKD rats to be homozygous for the reference allele (Supplemental Figure 2), consistent with it being the genetic basis of the observed mcy PKD modifier activity. Prenatal Lethality at Developmental Stage E16.5 During the characterization of the mcy rat line, it became apparent that litters of mcy-carrier×mcy-carrier matings were smaller than those of mcy-carrier×slow-PKD matings. The mating of seven distinct pairs of mcy-carrier rats resulted in an average litter size of 8.9±2.0. By contrast, the mating of ten of these 14 mcy-carrier rats with slow-PKD rats resulted in an average litter size of 14.9±3.6. This apparent approximately 40% reduction in litter size with mcy-carrier×mcy-carrier matings strongly suggested that homozygosity for the mcy variant allele was prenatally lethal. Indeed, none of the 47 pups in litters resulting from mcy-carrier×mcy-carrier matings that we genotyped were mcy−/−. Ultrasound monitoring of developing embryos in three mcy-carrier dams after mating with a mcy-carrier sire found that four of the 17 embryos (23.5%) died at around stage E16.5. Genotyping of all embryos showed that those that died were all mcy−/− (Supplemental Figure 3), although all remaining viable embryos were either mcy+/− (n=7, 41.2%) or mcy+/+ (n=6, 35.3%). These findings support the notion that homozygosity for the mcy variant allele is prenatally lethal. Histologic investigation of three pairs of E14.5 embryos (each pair included one mcy−/− and one mcy +/− or mcy+/+ littermate) revealed developmental abnormalities in the mcy−/− embryos reminiscent of those described in the Anks6−/− mouse. Two of the three mcy−/− embryos exhibited laterality defects with complete left–right reversal of the liver, stomach, and pancreas (Figure , A and B). Dissection of one pair of mcy +/− and mcy−/− embryos showed apparent situs inversus in the mcy−/− embryo, with the heart rotated to the right, and the position of the liver and stomach reversed compared with the mcy +/− embryo (Supplemental Figure 4, A and B). The lungs were severely underdeveloped, making it challenging to determine if they exhibited situs inversus (Supplemental Figure 4, C and D). Histologic analysis also showed abnormal rotation of the heart (Figure , C and D), and imaging of whole hearts from E14.5 embryos revealed a range of complex defects in those from mcy−/− embryos (Supplemental Figure 5). As expected, pathology was also evident in the livers of mcy−/− embryos, with decreased cellularity evident around the periphery (Figure ). Heart histology in E14.5 WT and homozygous mcy embryos. Modified Goldner Trichrome-stained coronal whole-body sections from littermate (A and C) mcy+/+ and (B and D) mcy−/− embryos. Note that inverted position of the liver, stomach, and pancreas in the mcy−/− embryos in (B) and (D). The rotation of the heart is also visible in (B) and (D) compared with (A) and (C), resulting in the abnormal positioning of the right (red asterisk) and left (green asterisk) atria. The arrows in (A) and (B) highlight the opposite directions of the invaginating walls of the heart in mcy+/+ and mcy−/− embryos. H, heart; L, liver; P, pancreas; S, stomach; WT, wild-type. Effects of the mcy Variant on ANKS6 Levels The mcy variant's recessive expressivity and prenatal lethality contrast with the Cy variant's dominant expressivity and developmental tolerance. Given the location (Supplemental Figure 1) and nature of the two variants, and the expectation that the mcy variant will result in nonsense-mediated decay, their contrasting effects likely reflect the difference between the absence of the SAM domain with the mcy variant and its perturbation with the Cy variant. Using qPCR, we quantified gene and allele-specific Anks6 expression in kidney-derived RNA from six rats (three males and three females) with each of the four phenotypes (Table ). Anks6 expression was significantly lower (i.e., higher ΔCt) in mcy +/− rats (mcy-carrier and rapid-PKD) than in mcy+/+ rats (WT and slow-PKD, P = 0.02). However, it did not differ significantly between mcy-carrier and rapid-PKD (P = 0.49) or WT and slow-PKD (P = 0.24) rats, suggesting that this difference is due to the mcy variant. In addition, transcripts with the mcy variant allele were present at a significantly lower level (i.e., higher ΔCt) than transcripts with the mcy reference allele in mcy-carrier and rapid-PKD rats (P = 9.8×10−4, Table ), with modest but significant ΔΔCt values (P = 0.02 and 0.03, respectively). Interestingly, ΔΔCt values were significantly higher in mcy-carrier than in rapid-PKD rats (P = 0.03), potentially reflecting perturbed mRNA regulation in diseased (rapid-PKD) compared with nondiseased (mcy-carrier) kidneys. Moreover, they were nonsignificantly higher in male (Supplemental Table 1) than in female (Supplemental Table 2) mcy-carrier (1.867±0.385 versus 0.714±0.022, P = 0.10) and rapid-PKD (0.607±0.380 versus 0.308±0.045, P = 0.40) rats, indicating more rapid degradation of transcripts with the mcy variant allele in males than in females. Similar analyses using genomic DNA indicated that the probe with the mcy variant allele had slightly better binding kinetics (i.e., lower ΔCt) than the probe with the mcy reference allele (mean ΔΔCt=−0.185±0.098, P = 0.03). Consequently, the RNA-based ΔΔCt values may underestimate the relative decrease in transcripts with the mcy variant allele. Therefore, these data suggest that the lower Anks6 expression observed in mcy +/− rats is because of fewer transcripts with the mcy variant allele, consistent with their degradation via nonsense-mediated decay, whose efficiency may differ by sex and PKD status. To further explore the effects of the mcy variant on gene expression patterns in the kidney, we performed mRNA-seq on kidney-derived RNA from the same four WT and four mcy-carrier female rats examined by WGS. Unlike the qPCR findings, Anks6 expression did not differ significantly between mcy-carrier and WT rats in our mRNA-seq data (P = 0.929), potentially reflecting the smaller sample sizes in the mRNA-seq (four per phenotype) than in the qPCR (six per phenotype) analyses. Nevertheless, in mcy-carrier rats, the fraction of reads with the mcy variant allele was notably <50% (26.1%±7.66%); the number of reads spanning the mcy variant was slightly but nonsignificantly lower in mcy-carrier (44.25±8.73) than in WT (56.25±14.01) rats (P = 0.20). Consistent with the modest ΔΔCt values in the qPCR analysis, these findings indicate a lower abundance of transcripts containing the mcy variant relative to the mcy reference allele, likely because of their degradation via nonsense-mediated decay. We performed western blots to determine whether a truncated ANKS6 protein is produced from transcripts containing the mcy variant allele and present in kidney cells. ANKS6 levels in WT, mcy-carrier, and rapid-PKD kidneys were very low compared with the high ANKS6 levels in slow-PKD kidneys (Figure ). Although the ANKS6 antibody detected several cross-reacting bands, no truncated form of ANKS6 was detected in mcy-carrier or rapid-PKD kidneys. The cross-reacting protein patterns differed between kidneys with and without cysts, suggesting that PKD alters the lysates' protein composition. ANKS6 detected in kidney lysates for each phenotype. Lysates (50 µg protein) from WT (Cy+/+ mcy+/+), mcy-carrier (Cy+/+ mcy+/−), slow-PKD (Cy +/− mcy+/+), and rapid-PKD (Cy +/− mcy+/−) rat kidneys were separated by 7.5% SDS-PAGE, transferred to nitrocellulose, and stained with anti-ANKS6 (top) or ponceau S (bottom). The arrow indicates the ANKS6 protein band present in slow-PKD kidneys but much lower in the other three phenotypes. The asterisk indicates a strong cross-reacting band present in all samples. Other cross-reacting bands are variable, reflecting the highly variable components present in the cystic and noncystic kidneys. To further confirm that transcripts with the mcy variant allele are not translated into a truncated ANKS6 protein, we performed immunohistochemistry to detect ANKS6 in mcy+/+ and mcy−/− E14.5 embryos. ANKS6 was readily detected in the fetal liver of mcy+/+ embryos but absent in the liver of mcy−/− embryos (Figure ). Altogether, these findings indicate that transcripts with the mcy variant allele are not translated into a stable truncated ANKS6 protein, consistent with their apparent degradation via the nonsense-mediated decay pathway, as suggested by the qPCR and mRNA-seq data. Immunohistochemical ANKS6 detection in coronal liver sections from mcy+/+ and mcy−/− E14.5 embryos. Anti-ANKS6 antibody staining is in brown, and methylene blue counterstaining is in blue. A strong ANKS6 signal (brown) was observed in the cytoplasm of liver cells from mcy+/+ embryos in the presence of anti-ANKS6 but not in controls treated only with secondary antibody or in liver cells from mcy−/− embryos.

Discussion
Discussion We have described the first example of a naturally occurring variant of uncertain significance in Anks6 that does not itself cause PKD but instead modifies the expressivity of a different pathogenic variant that does cause PKD, leading to much more rapid progression. Pathogenic variants in human ANKS6 that cause NPHP occur throughout the protein (Supplemental Figure 6) and behave in an autosomal recessive manner. Their expressivity contrasts with the autosomal dominant p.Arg717Trp pathogenic variant in ANKS6 in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat, potentially reflecting a unique property of this variant—which has not been described in humans to date—or evolutionary differences between humans and rats in the biologic pathways and processes within which ANKS6 functions. Naturally occurring benign SNVs leading to amino acid changes are also common throughout ANKS6 based on population-scale and targeted resequencing (Supplemental Table 3). However, they are present at low frequencies in human populations worldwide, compatible with substitutions at most positions in ANKS6 generally being well tolerated. Notably, no nonsense or frameshift variants were detected in the 2504 individuals in The 1000 Genomes Project. However, one NPHP-causing pathogenic variant (p.Gln441Arg) was detected with a frequency of 0.2% in South Asians, although no prevalence is available for NPHP in India, precluding speculation on the potential clinical significance of this observation. The existence of the nonsense mcy variant in a gene known to cause PKD (Anks6), but which does not itself cause disease, provides new insight into the mechanism by which ANKS6 disruption causes PKD. We have shown that the mcy variant decreases the abundance of the Anks6 transcript and does not result in any ANKS6 protein. Gene expression patterns and development were unaltered in the kidneys of mcy +/− rats, indicating that haploinsufficiency for fully functional ANKS6 is not the underlying cause of PKD in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat. Mutagenesis of the SAM domain has shown that changes, including the PKD-causing pathogenic variant in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat, destabilize its three-dimensional conformation in the folded protein and disrupt homodimerization, as well as ANKS6's interaction with ankyrin repeat and SAM domain containing 3., Together with our findings, these observations would suggest that PKD is caused by SAM domain dysfunction rather than nonfunction in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat; that is, perturbations caused by the presence of the mcy-containing SAM domain in homodimers or heterodimers, or the inappropriate binding of the mcy-containing SAM domain to an existing or novel partner, initiate biologic processes leading to PKD development and progression rather than disrupting the binding of the SAM domain to an existing partner and perturbing one or more processes required for normal kidney function. ANKS6 levels normally decrease substantially postnatally,, as we observed in western blots of kidney extracts from WT and mcy-carrier rats; however, we detected high ANKS6 levels in kidney tissue from adult slow-PKD rats. Elevated ANKS6 levels have previously been reported in adult Han:SPRD-Cy rats and in the cystic kidneys of mice with alterations in the Nphp3 and inversin (Inv) genes. Interestingly, ANKS6 was found to be in its nonphosphorylated form in these mouse models, indicating a failure in phosphorylation by never in mitosis, gene A-related kinase 8 (NEK8), despite a normal complex between ANKS6 and NEK8. Whatever the mechanism, the normal post-translational regulation of ANKS6 levels is disrupted in the cystic kidneys of slow-PKD rats but seems to be restored in rapid-PKD rats, which contain no WT ANKS6. The dominant-negative activity of ANKS6 with an abnormal SAM domain also seems to affect its post-translational modification. Further studies of the post-translational regulation of ANKS6 may yield additional insights into the mechanism of PKD. Our study showed that the coexistence of the PKD-causing Cy variant in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat and the mcy variant led to more rapid PKD progression, indicating that the WT ANKS6 that did function normally was important in delaying PKD development in the slow-PKD rat. ANKS6 is part of a multiprotein complex (INV, NPHP3, NEK8, and ANKS6), and its ankyrin repeat domain plays an important role in localizing the complex to the Inv compartment of the cilia. Notably, ANKS6 forms a highly stable interaction with the protein kinase NEK8, serving as both its activator and substrate. Without WT ANKS6 to target NEK8, ANKS6 will not be phosphorylated. ANKS6 deficiency in turn leads to NEK8 deficiency, and both NEK8 and ANKS6 deficiencies can cause PKD. Therefore, WT ANKS6 may be needed to stabilize Cy-mutant ANKS6 because no ANKS6 seems to be detected when WT ANKS6 is missing in the rapid-PKD rat. In addition to its modifying effect on the Cy variant, homozygosity for the mcy variant allele is prenatally lethal at stage E16.5, presumably because of perturbation of cardiac development. Both histologic and gross morphologic analyses demonstrated that the heart was abnormal in all mcy−/− embryos, and other internal organs (liver, stomach, and pancreas) were on the opposite side in three of the four examined mcy−/− embryos. Although a full characterization of the embryo hearts was beyond the scope of our study, several of the mcy−/− hearts seemed to have abnormalities of the great arteries, which were also present in Anks6−/− hearts. These observations are compatible with Anks6 knockout in the mouse, in which Anks6−/− embryos died at around stage E14.5 (equivalent to stage E16.5 in the rat), before the completion of atrial septation, and often exhibited heterotaxy. Moreover, they are consistent with observations that splice site and truncating pathogenic variants in ANKS6 cause cardiovascular defects in addition to PKD in humans and zebrafish., As described above, ANKS6 is one of several proteins in the Inv compartment that are involved in the normal function of the cilia. All members of the INV complex are required for determining left–right symmetry and for the normal development of the kidney, liver, and heart, with their mutation resulting in laterality defects and abnormalities in these organs. However, embryonic death before full development of these organs limited their analysis in mcy−/− rats. Nevertheless, our phenotypic findings of mcy−/− rats are consistent with a complete deficiency of ANKS6. In conclusion, we have identified a novel variant of uncertain significance in Anks6 that is not translated into a stable ANKS6 protein. Although the identified mcy variant results in no apparent abnormalities in heterozygous mcy-carrier rats, its combination with the Cy variant in the Han:SPRD-Cy rat results in a more rapid PKD progression. Thus, the rapid-PKD rat represents a novel direct demonstration of a PKD-causing pathogenic variant's expression being modified by its genetic background. Furthermore, when homozygous, the mcy variant was associated with prenatal lethality characterized by laterality defects and cardiovascular abnormalities.

title: Clinical outcomes after nondiagnostic prenatal exome sequencing: Need for balancing reassurance and residual risks in genetic counseling.
label_reason: Fetuses with structural anomalies had prenatal exome sequencing, nondiagnostic results followed up.
abstract: The clinical application of prenatal exome sequencing (pES) for fetal structural anomalies is relatively new. Although a prenatal genetic diagnosis has been shown to have high clinical and personal utility for families, nearly 70% of pregnancies undergoing pES will receive nondiagnostic results. Currently, there is little literature on postnatal outcomes following a nondiagnostic pES result in fetuses with structural anomalies, making it difficult to interpret the postnatal significance of the nondiagnostic result and tailor anticipatory guidance for expectant parents. This retrospective chart review identified trends in clinical outcomes following nondiagnostic pES results for 63 pregnancies and the resulting 61 liveborn children at a specialized maternal and newborn tertiary care hospital. Postnatal clinical outcome measures, including premature delivery (54%), NICU admissions (85%), hospitalizations (52%), surgical interventions (62%), and deaths (20%), highlight the complex care needs of the children in this cohort. However, the clinical outcomes were predominantly predictable, with 69% of the children having clinical care needs as expected based on what was counseled to parents prenatally. The results of this study affirm the assumptions that nondiagnostic pES does not equate to less medical complexity for children with prenatally identified structural anomalies, and that nondiagnostic pES results should not be interpreted as broadly reassuring. Comprehensive post‐test counseling is essential and should address the residual risk related to the severity of the identified anomaly or anomalies, the potential for unanticipated or complex clinical outcomes, and the limitations of antenatal ultrasound in capturing the full phenotypic spectrum. Keywords: clinical outcomes, posttest genetic counselling, prenatal exome sequencing, prenatal genetic counselling
