Clinical outcomes after nondiagnostic prenatal exome sequencing: Need for balancing reassurance and residual risks in genetic counseling

INTRODUCTION
INTRODUCTION Fetal structural anomalies are detected in approximately 2%–4% of pregnancies through ultrasonography (Lazier et al., ). Prenatal exome sequencing (pES) is a relatively new technology in prenatal diagnosis with an approximate 30% incremental diagnostic yield after normal chromosomal studies, depending on the type and number of fetal structural anomalies detected (Lazier et al., ; Mellis et al., ; Monaghan et al., ; Wapner et al., ; Zhang et al., ). When diagnostic, pES can have high clinical utility (a test result's ability to lead to better health outcomes) and personal utility (a test result's ability to inform a patient's decisions, actions, or understanding, including and beyond healthcare) (Lazier et al., ). Identifying the underlying genetic cause of fetal structural anomalies enables care providers to address the specific needs of expectant parents by enhancing prognostic understanding and informing perinatal management (Dempsey et al., ; Guadagnolo et al., ; Mone et al., ; Poljak et al., ). Perinatal care modifications can include implementing specific supportive measures, such as palliative care, or more targeted interventions, such as targeted treatments, surgical procedures, and specialist referrals (Dempsey et al., ; Guadagnolo et al., ; Mone et al., ; Poljak et al., ). Diagnostic pES can also promote personal utility with the potential to inform social, financial, and family planning, as well as allowing for increased accuracy in recurrence risk estimates (Lazier et al., ; Lugli et al., ; Talati et al., ). Although exome sequencing has significantly increased the number of genetic diagnoses made prenatally, the majority of pregnancies will receive nondiagnostic results (Mellis et al., ). To date, literature has focused on the diagnostic yield and utility of pES diagnoses in promoting care modifications, whereas literature on long‐term postnatal clinical outcomes following nondiagnostic pES is limited (Best et al., ; Dempsey et al., ; Guadagnolo et al., ; Lord et al., ; Mone et al., ; Poljak et al., ; Talati et al., ). Post‐test counseling is an essential component of prenatal genetics care, facilitating informed and supported decision‐making, but its effectiveness depends on the available evidence to guide discussion (Lugli et al., ). To date, post‐test genetic counseling recommendations have focused primarily on discussing the possibility of an unidentified underlying genetic diagnosis or interpretation of uncertain results; however, when pES is nondiagnostic, expectant parents frequently shift their focus from concern about a complicating genetic etiology to wanting to better anticipate clinical outcomes and prognosis for their future child to inform decision‐making (Talati et al., ). In the absence of longitudinal outcome data, genetic professionals have limited information to tailor post‐test counseling in an evidence‐based manner specifically relating to this residual risk. This residual uncertainty presents a unique challenge in counseling expectant parents: While some may experience heightened anxiety due to lack of clarity, others may derive a false sense of reassurance from the nondiagnostic result, assuming it equates to a low likelihood of serious postnatal outcomes. The aim of this study was to identify trends in postnatal clinical outcomes of children born after the identification of fetal structural anomalies and nondiagnostic pES results to inform the post‐test genetic counseling of expectant parents.

METHODS
METHODS We performed an exploratory retrospective chart review at the BC Children's and Women's Hospital, a tertiary care center in Vancouver, Canada. Approval to conduct this retrospective chart review was obtained from the Research Ethics Board of the University of British Columbia (REB #H23‐00861). This study's population includes patients offered pES prenatally at the Provincial Medical Genetic Program, which provides prenatal genetic services for residents of British Columbia, excluding Vancouver Island, between 2016 and 2022. Inclusion criteria for this study required patients to have been seen clinically in the context of an ongoing pregnancy with detection of one or more fetal structural anomalies meeting both the clinic's pES eligibility criteria (Reilly et al., ) and our additional inclusion criteria (Table ). Patients must have received nondiagnostic results from prenatal genetic investigations, including chromosomal studies and pES. Cases where chromosomal variants were identified were only included in this study if the finding was interpreted by a medical geneticist as unlikely to explain the fetal phenotype. Pregnancies with alternative etiologies, including infectious or teratogenic exposures, were excluded. Soft markers for aneuploidy were not considered as fetal structural anomalies in this study. For the purposes of this study, nondiagnostic pES results include those with (1) negative, meaning no identified disease‐causing gene variants to explain the prenatal phenotype, (2) uninformative variants of uncertain significance (VUS), or (3) incidental findings only, meaning pathogenic variants identified were not associated with the prenatal phenotype or related to carrier status. Genetic investigations were performed on DNA extracted from amniocytes, and pES was performed by various commercial laboratories, all of which used the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics 2015 guidelines for variant classification and reporting (Richards et al., ). Cases were excluded if a diagnosis was obtained based on clinical interpretation of a VUS by a medical geneticist as explanatory for the fetal phenotype. Pregnancies were excluded if termination of pregnancy was pursued; however, cases were included if pregnancies resulted in a stillbirth or intrauterine demise after results disclosure. Twin pregnancies were excluded. Data were collected from prenatal charts of 63 singleton pregnancies, including 2 cases of fetal demise, and the postnatal charts of the resulting 61 liveborn children. Data from the charts of the liveborn children included chart entries up to July 2023, or up to 5 years of age. The data were collated into descriptive categories. Prenatal phenotypes in this study were categorized as either an isolated anomaly, if a single system was affected, or multiple anomalies, which include multisystem structural anomalies or a single system structural anomaly in the context of a dynamic anomaly, such as abnormal fetal growth or amniotic fluid levels. For liveborn children, we collected the postnatal phenotype, including additional anomalies, dysmorphism, and functional features, such as developmental delay, seizures, and hearing loss. Descriptive statistics were used to describe prenatal presentations and postnatal outcomes of the study population, with proportions presented as percentages for categorical data and means with standard deviations for numeric data. Predictability of the liveborn children's clinical outcomes was classified into one of 4 categories: resolved, simplified, expected, or more complex. Predictability was determined by comparing the expected spectrum of possible clinical outcomes counseled to families that was documented in the prenatal records and the postnatal clinical outcomes of the liveborn children. Classification of predictability for each case was determined by consensus among study authors SA, AS, and JLZ. Descriptive statistics were used to describe predictability outcomes in the study population, and statistical measures of effects were used to compare predictability outcomes between the isolated and multiple anomalies cohorts. Significance of the difference between these groups was determined using risk difference and fisher exact probability test, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.

RESULTS
RESULTS Study population There were 132 pregnancies identified to have fetal structural anomalies for whom pES was ordered between 2016 and 2022. Of these, 102 pregnancies received nondiagnostic results (73%). Six pregnancies were excluded due to limited information available on the resulting child due to relocation of care to a different care center. A further 29 pregnancies were excluded due to termination of pregnancy (28%), as well as 4 twin pregnancies (3%). Data were collected for the remaining 63 pregnancies. Pregnancy details and distribution of the ages of the children at the time of data collection can be seen in Table . A trio exome sequencing approach was used for 91% of pregnancies. Nondiagnostic pES results included negative (52%), VUS (40%), and incidental (16%) findings. Multiple result types (VUS and incidental findings) were present in 8% of the cohort. Of all incidental findings reported, half were in disease‐associated genes unrelated to the fetal phenotype, whereas the other half were identification of carrier status in the fetus or a parent. Pregnancies with isolated fetal structural anomalies (49%) were categorized based on the system affected can be seen in Table . Pregnancies with multiple anomalies (51%), described in Table , included both multisystem anomalies (72%), as well as a single system anomaly plus an abnormality of growth or fluid in 22% and 6% of pregnancies, respectively. Our multiple anomalies cohort had between 2 and 5 systems affected prenatally, with the average being 2.3 ± 1.4. For both the isolated and multiple anomalies cohorts, cardiac anomalies were the most common type of fetal structural anomaly. Clinical outcomes In our cohort, 62% (n = 39) of cases had prenatal phenotypes that were unchanged throughout gestation after the ordering of pES. Prenatal phenotype modifications in the remaining 38% included clarification of the fetal structural anomalies by follow‐up imaging (echocardiogram or fetal MRI) (n = 9; 14%), identification of additional findings on subsequent imaging (n = 8; 13%), or resolution of previously identified anomalies (n = 8; 13%). In two cases, pregnancy resulted in fetal demise in the third trimester (3%), one intrauterine demise and one stillbirth, both with fetal hydrops as part of their phenotype. Of the 61 pregnancies resulting in liveborn children, there were 19 pregnancies (54%) where delivery was premature, defined as prior to 37 weeks gestation. The majority of the children were admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) immediately after birth (85%), with the same number of children admitted from both the isolated and multiple anomalies cohorts (n = 26 multiple; n = 26 isolated; Table ). Prenatal phenotypes were highly predictive for the type of care required in the NICU. Of the 14 life‐sustaining admissions to the NICU (27%), 6 (43%) were admitted in the context of prematurity prior to 34 weeks gestation. The remaining 8 children were born full term, and all but one case had intensive care needs predicted prenatally. Of these 14 children requiring life‐sustaining care in the NICU, 8 were living at the time of data collection and 6 were deceased. A total of 12 (20%) of the liveborn children died (Table ). There were 11 deaths in the first 6 months of life (18%), with most occurring within the first 28 days of life (n = 8; 13%). All children who died within the first 6 months were predicted to have extensive care needs or life‐limiting structural anomalies based on their prenatal presentation. There was 1 unexpected death reported after 6 months of age; a child who passed away at 32 months old following life‐long intensive life‐sustaining care for an isolated complex cardiac anomaly. Hospitalizations of children following initial discharge from the NICU, and surgical interventions were required in 52% and 62%, respectively (Table ). Postnatal functional features observed in liveborn children, including developmental delays, seizures, and hearing loss, are described in Table . Developmental delays were observed in 8 children, with 2 (25%) having CNS anomalies as a part of their prenatal presentation, and one who suffered a hypoxic brain injury at birth. Of the children presenting with seizures postnatally (4 cases), none had prenatal CNS findings. Predictability of outcomes of liveborn children Predictable postnatal clinical outcomes within the prenatally anticipated range were seen in 69% of the liveborn children (Table ). Predictability was 28% higher for children born from pregnancies with isolated anomalies (83%) compared to those with multiple anomalies (55%; p = 0.026). In 8% of liveborn children, postnatal clinical outcomes were more complex than predicted prenatally. Unexpectedly complicated outcomes were observed in similar rates from both the isolated and multiple anomalies cohorts (RD = 4%; p = 0.67). A more complex outcome was primarily due to additional structural anomalies only identified after birth. Structural anomalies identified after birth were variable but included postnatal identification of craniosynostosis (n = 2), urogenital anomalies (n = 2), and complex limb anomalies (n = 2), with some having multiple anomalies identified only post birth. There was an additional child whose isolated cardiac anomaly unexpectedly evolved postnatally into a transplant‐dependent cardiac defect. A larger proportion of our study population had phenotypes simplify (15%) or resolve (8%) on postnatal assessments. Children with multiple anomalies detected prenatally were more likely to have simplified or fully resolved (39%) clinical presentations than those with prenatal isolated anomalies (7%; RD = 32%; p = 0.005). Simplified clinical outcomes in the multiple anomalies cohort were most often related to the resolution of dynamic anomalies throughout gestation, including anomalies related to growth (n = 5), amniotic fluid volume (n = 3), or hydrops (n = 1). Non‐dynamic anomalies involved in simplified postnatal presentations often included kidney‐related phenotypes: In two cases, echogenic kidneys resolved, and another case of hypoplastic and dysplastic kidneys with postnatal ultrasound showing a normal right kidney and an ectopic, but typically formed, left kidney. Interestingly, 2 of the children from the multiple anomalies cohort whose care needs were fully resolved both had a prenatal phenotype of bilateral ventriculomegaly and polyhydramnios. Notably, a case of Dandy–Walker malformation was confirmed to be an isolated arachnoid cyst after birth, and a prenatally presumed syndromic multiple suture craniosynostosis was revealed to be isolated single sagittal suture craniosynostosis after birth. There were also 2 cardiac anomalies that were not confirmed on follow‐up imaging: a ventricular septal defect and a hypoplastic aortic arch. The prenatally observed phenotype was not confirmed postnatally in a total of 8% of liveborn children.

DISCUSSION
DISCUSSION Nondiagnostic pES is the most common type of result received by those who undergo prenatal diagnosis for fetal structural anomalies. This study provides important insight for tailoring post‐test counseling of expectant parents at the time of nondiagnostic pES results disclosure in the context of fetal structural anomalies. As could be predicted based on our inclusion criteria, the liveborn children from pregnancies undergoing pES experienced a high degree of postnatal care needs, especially within the neonatal period (0–28 days of age). In our study population, 54% were born premature, 85% required NICU admission, and 13% died in the neonatal period. The ongoing medical complexity experienced after initial discharge for many of the liveborn children is reflected in the proportion of children who required surgical interventions (62%) and hospitalizations (52%). The magnitude of care needs was predominantly predicted prenatally based on the anticipated severity of the underlying fetal structural anomaly or anomalies. Our results suggest that a nondiagnostic pES does not equate to a favorable prognosis overall and genetic professionals should take care not to minimize the degree of care needs that may be required in this population. In the absence of a genetic diagnosis, the expected spectrum of clinical outcomes becomes the critical factor in decision‐making for parents (Talati et al., ). Our study did show a high degree of predictability in postnatal clinical outcomes, with the vast majority of the liveborn children having postnatal care needs as expected or simplified based on the prenatally detected fetal structural anomaly (92% had expected, simplified, or resolved clinical outcomes). The overall predictability of the clinical outcomes for children with isolated prenatal anomalies was higher compared to those with multiple anomalies. However, the multiple anomalies cohort showed higher rates of phenotypes simplifying or resolving. This was most notable when anomalies were related to fetal growth parameters, renal anomalies, amniotic fluid measurements, and ventriculomegaly. Additionally, phenotype evolutions were noted prior to birth in 38% of cases, with follow‐up imaging providing further clarity, complexity, or resolution of findings following the ordering of pES, many of which involved non‐dynamic anomalies (Mastromoro et al., ). Our study demonstrated the residual risk of a postnatal clinical outcome more complex than predicted prenatally, even with ongoing pregnancy monitoring. Notably, it highlighted the residual risk of undetected structural anomalies in the prenatal period, which primarily included craniofacial, genitourinary, and limb defects, which is in keeping with previous reports on postnatal phenotype modifications (Aarabi et al., ; Monier et al., ; Swanson et al., ; Thauvin‐Robinet et al., ). Although unexpectedly complex postnatal clinical outcomes were relatively infrequent in this study population (8%), they were seen in nearly equal rates between cases of isolated and multiple anomalies. Even for pregnancies with seemingly simple presentations, the limitations of ultrasound in detecting all structural anomalies present remains (Dulgheroff et al., ). The relatively small, phenotypically heterogeneous, and high selectivity of the study population included in our study may limit the generalizability and predictive power of our findings. In addition, a large proportion of the cohort was born within the critical years of the COVID‐19 pandemic, and it is unclear how this may have impacted parents' decision making and the course of care delivery in the prenatal and neonatal period (Arnaez et al., ; Gholami et al., ). The short follow‐up period restricts our understanding of long‐term functional outcomes such as development, cognition, and evolving care needs. The relatively high rate of VUSs reported in our study population highlights the commercial labs' more lenient approach to VUS reporting than suggested by published guidelines that recommend exclusion of VUS that do not clearly align with the prenatal ultrasound findings or that are not clinically relevant for pregnancy management, as previously reported (Cornthwaite et al., ; de Koning et al., ). Additionally, assessing the postnatal residual risk for a genetic condition was outside the scope of this study, and as such, children in this study population may harbor undiagnosed genetic syndromes. Current care recommendations suggest reinterpretation of pES should be considered after 12 months or in the context of phenotypic modifications (Lazier et al., ; Monaghan et al., ). Further study on the children born from pregnancies with nondiagnostic pES results is needed in order to ensure that continuity of care by genetic providers is sufficiently capturing the needs of this population. Suggested points of emphasis for genetic counseling Based on our findings, we suggest the following counseling points be emphasized to parents during prenatal genetic counseling appointments. Our findings underscore the need to communicate the dual realities of reassurance and residual uncertainty following nondiagnostic pES for fetal structural anomalies. Prognosis is largely dependent on the prenatal phenotype. Address the natural history of the identified anomaly or anomalies. Emphasize that prognosis following nondiagnostic pES is dependent largely on the prenatal phenotype rather than the test result, and that the absence of a molecular diagnosis does not exclude the possibility of a severe or life‐limiting clinical outcome (Lazier et al., ; Mone et al., ). Phenotypes can evolve. Emphasize that prognostic information at the time of result disclosure is inherently limited by the evolving nature of fetal development. Highlight the need for ongoing monitoring throughout pregnancy (Dulgheroff et al., ; Lugli et al., ; Mastromoro et al., ; Mone et al., ). Discuss the possibility of reassessment by medical genetics postnatally, and that postnatal pES reanalysis may be considered in the context of phenotype modifications or after 12 months (Lazier et al., ; Monaghan et al., ). Phenotyping by prenatal ultrasound has limitations. Explicitly acknowledge the inherent limitations of prenatal phenotyping by ultrasound, such as limited visualization of structural differences, and the inability to assess for functional features, such as hearing loss, seizures, and developmental delays. Emphasize the possibility of both overestimation and underestimation of severity (Brabbing‐Goldstein et al., ; Lugli et al., ; Mone et al., ; Poljak et al., ). Even for pregnancies with seemingly simple presentations, structural anomalies may be missed prenatally. Parents should be counseled on this residual risk regardless of the number or complexity of anomalies identified prenatally. Predicting prognosis is challenging. Explain that the predictability of outcomes may decrease as the number of fetal anomalies increases. Emphasize the challenges in predicting the long‐term impact of anomalies that may be dynamic in nature, including findings identified primarily through abnormal measurements, which can be highly variable and may change over time.

CONCLUSION
CONCLUSION While a nondiagnostic result may alleviate parental concern regarding a definitive genetic diagnosis, most expectant parents predominantly seek guidance on clinical trajectory for informed decision making (Lugli et al., ; Talati et al., ). Our cohort affirmed that prognosis is driven more by phenotype than lack of a genetic diagnosis and demonstrated substantial medical complexity among liveborn children. Although ultrasound remains a powerful tool, all expectant parents should be counseled on its limitations and the persistent risk of unpredictable complications before and after birth. Post‐test counseling should prepare families for a range of outcomes, from resolution to unexpected complexity. Clear communication of these nuances can better support informed decision‐making and set realistic expectations during an inherently stressful and uncertain time.

title: Prenatal Molecular Diagnosis of COL2A1-Associated Stickler Syndrome: Genotype-Phenotype Correlation in a Resource-Limited Healthcare Setting.
label_reason: Fetus evaluated by anomaly scan, trio sequencing for COL2A1.
abstract: Stickler syndrome is a monogenic connective tissue disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in collagen-related genes, most commonly COL2A1 . Prenatal diagnosis remains challenging, particularly in healthcare systems with limited access to molecular genetic testing. We report a prenatal case of suspected craniofacial anomaly detected on second-trimester ultrasound. Fetal DNA obtained by amniocentesis underwent next-generation sequencing. Parental testing was performed to assess inheritance. It was confirmed that autosomal dominant Stickler syndrome type I (ORPHA:90653) was caused by a heterozygous pathogenic frameshift variant in COL2A1 (c.3137del) that was inherited from the mother and identified in the fetus. Micrognathia was identified during prenatal ultrasound, and postnatal evaluation revealed characteristics that were consistent with Pierre Robin sequence and connective tissue involvement. The molecular discoveries elucidated the observed phenotype and facilitated multidisciplinary perinatal management. This case underscores the indispensable function of molecular diagnostics in the prenatal identification of monogenic disorders, including Stickler syndrome, in cases where conventional karyotyping is inadequate. Targeted clinical surveillance and family counseling are facilitated by early genetic confirmation. The report also emphasizes the necessity of incorporating molecular diagnostics into routine prenatal care for rare genetic diseases and the systemic limitations in access to genomic testing. Although the identified variant has been previously reported, this case highlights the clinical and diagnostic value of prenatal molecular confirmation in a resource-limited healthcare setting. Keywords: Stickler syndrome, COL2A1 , frameshift variant, prenatal molecular diagnosis, monogenic connective tissue disorder, genotype–phenotype correlation
text:
Prenatal Molecular Diagnosis of COL2A1-Associated Stickler Syndrome: Genotype–Phenotype Correlation in a Resource-Limited Healthcare Setting

1. Introduction
1. Introduction DNA, RNA, chromosomes, proteins, or metabolites are analyzed to identify heritable disease-related genotypes, mutations, phenotypes, or karyotypes for clinical purposes. This process is known as genetic examination. This is essential for the diagnosis of monogenic disorders, carrier detection, disease risk prediction, and precision clinical management, and it encompasses a wide variety of techniques, such as targeted gene sequencing, whole-exome sequencing (ES), whole-genome sequencing (GS), and cytogenetic methods [,]. The diagnostic yield for rare inherited diseases has been significantly enhanced by the simultaneous interrogation of multiple disease-associated genes at single-base resolution, as demonstrated in large clinical studies reported in the literature [,], primarily due to advancements in next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, particularly ES and GS. Pathogenic variants are identified in approximately 25–52% of patients with suspected rare genetic disorders by NGS-based approaches, which significantly outperform conventional cytogenetic techniques in diagnostic sensitivity, particularly when trio sequencing is employed. Karyotyping is a specific type of genetic examination involving microscopic evaluation of chromosome number and structure in metaphase cells and remains the gold standard for detecting aneuploidies and large chromosomal rearrangements. It is commonly employed in the evaluation of congenital anomalies, recurrent pregnancy loss, and hematologic malignancies; however, it is fundamentally restricted to the detection of macroscopically visible abnormalities [,]. Genetic examination therefore represents a broad category of laboratory techniques, whereas karyotyping specifically targets large-scale chromosomal alterations and lacks the resolution necessary to identify pathogenic single-gene variants [,,]. In monogenic connective tissue disorders, the distinction between conventional cytogenetic approaches and molecular sequencing-based methods is particularly important, as the causative mutations are typically submicroscopic—such as single-nucleotide variants, small insertions/deletions, or splice-site mutations—and are therefore imperceptible to karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis [,]. Conversely, targeted gene panels, ES, and GS facilitate the direct interrogation of disease-associated genes that encode extracellular matrix components, such as collagen genes, thereby significantly increasing diagnostic sensitivity and facilitating precise molecular classification. Stickler syndrome is a hereditary connective tissue disorder that is distinguished by a variety of ocular abnormalities, including congenital high myopia and vitreoretinal degeneration, which are associated with a high risk of retinal detachment. Additionally, the disorder is characterized by sensorineural hearing loss; distinctive craniofacial features, such as midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, cleft palate, or bifid uvula; and early-onset joint hypermobility and osteoarthritis [,,,]. The most common mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant, as a result of pathogenic variants in COL2A1, COL11A1, and COL11A2. Conversely, the rarer autosomal recessive forms involve COL9A1, COL9A2, or COL9A3 [,,,]. The type II collagenopathy spectrum, which includes Stickler syndrome type I (OMIM #108300), spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, and Kniest dysplasia, is primarily caused by mutations in COL2A1 []. Stickler syndrome type I and ocular-predominant phenotypes are most frequently associated with haploinsufficiency resulting from nonsense or frameshift variants in COL2A1. Missense mutations that affect the collagen triple-helix domain frequently produce more severe skeletal and craniofacial manifestations, reflecting substantial genotype–phenotype heterogeneity [,]. Prenatal diagnosis of Stickler syndrome is feasible when a pathogenic variant has been identified in a parent. According to published clinical literature, targeted molecular testing may be performed on fetal DNA obtained via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, and preimplantation genetic testing is an additional option []. In the absence of a known familial variant, ultrasound may reveal suggestive but nonspecific findings, such as micrognathia or the Pierre Robin sequence, although normal imaging does not exclude the diagnosis [,,,]. Karyotyping is not diagnostic for Stickler syndrome because the pathogenic variants are submicroscopic and necessitate sequencing-based molecular methods for identification []. Notwithstanding the international recommendations from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) advocating for molecular testing of suspected type II collagen disorders, access to NGS-based diagnostics is markedly inconsistent across healthcare systems due to disparities in infrastructure, reimbursement, and specialist availability []. In Bulgaria, karyotyping is presently the sole genetic test routinely reimbursed by national health insurance, making prenatal molecular diagnosis of Stickler syndrome predominantly unattainable. Due to the inability of cytogenetic methods to identify pathogenic variants in collagen genes, prenatal assessment is limited to ultrasound results and familial history, lacking conclusive genetic verification [,]. This constraint hinders genetic counseling, recurrence risk evaluation, and informed reproductive choices [,,]. This diagnostic gap illustrates the overarching difficulty of incorporating genomic medicine into standard prenatal care for rare monogenic disorders, resulting in delayed diagnoses, diminished clinical readiness, and ongoing health disparities, as emphasized in recent studies on genomic medicine implementation [,]. Although the pathogenic variant identified in this case has been previously reported, the present study focuses on the clinical and diagnostic pathway leading to prenatal molecular confirmation, the integration of fetal imaging with parental phenotyping, and the implications of genomic diagnosis in a healthcare system with limited access to sequencing-based testing.

2. Materials and Methods
2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Ethical Considerations and Informed Consent The prenatal diagnostic procedure was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Clinical genetic counseling was provided to the parents prior to any intervention. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents for the performance of invasive prenatal diagnosis, molecular genetic testing, and the subsequent publication of this case report, including all clinical data and imaging. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical University–Pleven (approval number: P16/2025). 2.2. Prenatal Imaging and Clinical Evaluation High-resolution ultrasound was employed to evaluate the fetal anatomy. A comprehensive second-trimester anomaly scan was performed at 21 weeks and 2 days of gestation, following a standard first-trimester screening at 12 weeks and 0 days of gestation. To assess the sagittal fetal facial profile and identify craniofacial markers, a GE Voluson E8 ultrasound system was implemented. The Fetal Medicine Unit, University Hospital “Saint Marina,” Pleven, Bulgaria, conducted all assessments. 2.3. DNA Isolation and Sample Acquisition At 23 weeks of gestation, ultrasound-guided amniocentesis was employed to obtain fetal DNA. To facilitate a trio-based sequencing method and determine the inheritance pattern of any detected variants, peripheral venous blood samples were simultaneously collected from both parents. Genomic DNA was extracted from parental blood specimens and uncultured amniocytes. Prior to sequencing, Qubit fluorometric quantification was implemented to assess the quantity and quality of DNA. 2.4. Bioinformatics Processing and Genetic Analysis An average coverage of approximately 30× was achieved by HaploX (Hong Kong) with an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform for next-generation sequencing (NGS). The GRCh38/hg38 human reference genome was used to align the raw sequencing data. Standard clinical bioinformatics pipelines were employed to execute variant calling and annotation, which included the filtration of infrequent, protein-altering variants in genes associated with disease. 2.5. Interpretation and Variant Nomenclature The Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) nomenclature was used to characterize the identified variant in the COL2A1 gene (c.3137del). Variant pathogenicity was assessed in accordance with the standards established by the ACMG. The clinical classification was verified by ClinVar and curated variant databases, while population allele frequencies were assessed using gnomAD. A trio-based analysis was employed to assess segregation, thereby validating maternal inheritance. 2.6. Data Accessibility Sequencing data that verify the findings of this study can be obtained from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

3. Results
3. Results The aim of this case report is to present a neonate with molecularly confirmed Stickler syndrome type 1 (ORPHA:90653; OMIM:108300) and to emphasize the roles of prenatal ultrasound suspicion, sequencing-based genetic diagnosis, and multidisciplinary perinatal management and the clinical impact of limited access to molecular testing. A 27-year-old pregnant woman was managed at the Fetal Medicine Unit at University Hospital “Saint Marina,” Pleven, Bulgaria, for routine first-trimester screening. The maternal medical history was unremarkable, and no known hereditary disorders were reported. There was no reported consanguinity or family history of congenital anomalies. A non-invasive prenatal test performed at 10 + 1 gestational weeks indicated low risk for common chromosomal aneuploidies in a male fetus. First-trimester ultrasound at 12 + 0 weeks demonstrated normal fetal anatomy, and combined screening revealed low risk for major chromosomal abnormalities. During routine second-trimester evaluation at 21 + 2 weeks of gestation, fetal growth parameters were within normal limits; however, pronounced micrognathia was identified on sagittal facial profile ultrasound (). No additional structural anomalies were detected. Mild maternal micrognathia was also observed on clinical examination, raising suspicion of a possible inherited craniofacial phenotype. Following the genetic confirmation, a retrospective clinical evaluation of the mother revealed that she had previously experienced mild manifestations consistent with the syndrome, including unspecified myalgia/arthralgia and ophthalmalgia, which had not been formally investigated prior to the fetal diagnosis. Based on these findings, a monogenic connective tissue disorder was considered, and genetic counseling was arranged. Results of a prenatal ultrasound: Marked micrognathia is evident in the sagittal fetal facial profile at 21 + 2 weeks of gestation, which is indicative of craniofacial involvement associated with monogenic connective tissue disorders. The arrow indicates the region of mandibular hypoplasia consistent with micrognathia. An uncomplicated amniocentesis was conducted at 23 weeks of gestation after rigorous counseling. A genome-based approach was employed to conduct NGS on fetal DNA, which was subsequently followed by parental testing. Stickler syndrome type I (ORPHA:90653) was confirmed by the identification of a heterozygous pathogenic frameshift variant in the COL2A1 gene (c.3137del) in the fetus. The variant was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG-ClinGen criteria and is expected to lead to the haploinsufficiency-induced loss of function of type II collagen. The mother’s mild clinical phenotype was correlated with the detection of the same variant. No additional pathogenic variants that were clinically relevant were identified. The alignment of sequencing reads revealed a consistent heterozygous deletion at the affected locus in both fetal and maternal samples (). Molecular confirmation of COL2A1 frameshift variant. An identical variant was detected in the maternal sample, which is consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. The COL2A1 gene in fetal DNA has a heterozygous deletion, c.3137del, as demonstrated by a next-generation sequencing read alignment. Given the ultrasound diagnosis of solitary micrognathia, conventional cytogenetic testing was explored as part of the differential diagnostic work-up, specifically to rule out chromosomal aneuploidies or structural rearrangements linked to craniofacial deformities. However, in the absence of additional structural abnormalities and given the maternal craniofacial phenotype suggestive of a heritable connective tissue disorder, sequencing-based molecular analysis was prioritized to detect a potential monogenic etiology that would be undetectable by standard karyotyping. A personalized perinatal care plan was developed by a multidisciplinary team that included fetal medicine specialists, clinical geneticists, neonatologists, otorhinolaryngologists, orthopedic specialists, and surgical consultants as soon as the molecular diagnosis was confirmed. Genetic counseling addressed inheritance risk, anticipated clinical course, and long-term surveillance strategies. At 38 weeks of gestation, a spontaneous vaginal delivery occurred at the University Hospital “Saint Marina” in Pleven, Bulgaria. The neonate’s birth weight was 3100 g, and its length was 48 cm. Its head circumference was 34 cm. The Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 10 at five minutes. Distinct dysmorphic characteristics, including a cleft palate, a short lingual frenulum, a flat forehead, downslanting palpebral fissures, significant micrognathia, and microretrognathia, were identified during the postnatal examination, which indicates a Pierre Robin sequence. Additional observations indicated that the toes were wide, with underdeveloped nails, and there was a clinical suspicion of joint hypermobility. On the second day of life, the molecular diagnosis was verified through genetic consultation. Annual ophthalmologic surveillance, audiologic evaluation, and orthopedic evaluation were recommended as post-diagnostic measures. Due to feeding difficulties associated with craniofacial anomalies, the neonate required enteral nutrition via orogastric tube for 8 weeks during the initial hospitalization period. Transfontanelle ultrasound examination demonstrated normal brain anatomy, and microbiological studies were normal. The initial newborn hearing screening revealed bilateral abnormalities; however, the results were reconciled to normal during a subsequent examination at 12 weeks of age. Growth parameters at discharge were normal for the newborn charts. Postnatally, the infant has been followed by an ophthalmologist in an outpatient setting; however, detailed clinical findings from these examinations were not formally recorded in the available hospital medical records at the time of this report. During four months of follow-up, the infant demonstrated physiological neurodevelopmental progression and successful oral feeding without tube support. Corrective palatal surgery is planned at approximately 10 months of age.

4. Discussion
4. Discussion Stickler syndrome is a hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by variable combinations of ocular, craniofacial, auditory, and musculoskeletal abnormalities. The most common clinical features include high myopia, vitreous anomalies, and a markedly increased risk of retinal detachment; craniofacial findings such as midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, and cleft palate; sensorineural hearing loss; and early-onset joint hypermobility and osteoarthritis. Skeletal manifestations may include epiphyseal dysplasia and spinal abnormalities such as scoliosis or platyspondyly. The severity and combination of features that affect individuals vary significantly [,,,,]. This clinical heterogeneity is particularly relevant in prenatal settings, where manifestations may be incomplete or subtle, complicating phenotype-based recognition. In the present case, variability was evident in the discordance between the mild maternal phenotype and the more pronounced neonatal craniofacial involvement. This variability is indicative of both genetic heterogeneity and mutation-specific molecular mechanisms that affect collagen biosynthesis and extracellular matrix integrity, and type II collagenopathy summaries [,]. Such intrafamilial variability has important implications for prenatal risk assessment and counseling, as parental manifestations may be minimal despite transmission of a pathogenic variant. The most prevalent genetic causes are autosomal dominant mutations in collagen genes, specifically COL2A1 (type I Stickler syndrome), COL11A1, and COL11A2. Rare autosomal recessive forms are the result of biallelic mutations in COL9A1, COL9A2, or COL9A3, and they may be distinguished by more severe ocular findings and hearing loss [,,,,]. Hearing loss and joint disease are more frequently associated with COL11A1/2 and COL9A1/2/3 mutations, while ocular findings are most frequently associated with COL2A1 mutations. The specific gene involved can affect the phenotype []. Large cohort genotype–phenotype analyses, including the 100-patient series by Hoornaert et al. [], support this gene-dependent phenotypic pattern and further underscore marked intrafamilial variability. Importantly, the pathogenic COL2A1 variant identified in this case has been previously reported in clinical variant databases and published genotype–phenotype cohorts, including the series described by Hoornaert et al. []. Therefore, the contribution of the present report does not lie in the identification of a novel molecular finding, but in the clinical documentation of prenatal diagnostic reasoning, phenotype–genotype integration, and management implications in a real-world healthcare setting with restricted access to genomic testing. Diagnostic methods rely on clinical evaluation supported by molecular genetic testing. In the present case, clinical suspicion was triggered by prenatal ultrasound findings and strengthened by recognition of subtle maternal craniofacial characteristics, which together prompted targeted molecular investigation. This illustrates the diagnostic value of integrating fetal imaging with parental phenotyping when evaluating suspected inherited connective tissue disorders. This case therefore highlights how previously characterized pathogenic variants may still present substantial diagnostic and management challenges depending on the timing of detection, clinical presentation, and healthcare infrastructure in which prenatal evaluation is performed. The diagnosis is confirmed by using targeted gene panels or next-generation sequencing to identify pathogenic variants in the relevant collagen genes. Karyotyping is not diagnostic, as the causative mutations are submicroscopic. In families with a known mutation, molecular testing is essential for the definitive diagnosis, genetic counseling, and prenatal or preimplantation genetic diagnosis [,,,]. In addition to confirming diagnosis, molecular testing has the potential to reduce irreversible morbidity by enabling genotype-informed risk stratification, cascade testing in relatives, and earlier deployment of surveillance strategies. In this case, molecular confirmation directly influenced perinatal management, enabling anticipatory planning for airway support, feeding difficulties, and early specialist follow-up. This demonstrates that prenatal molecular diagnosis functions not only as a diagnostic tool but also as a management-directing intervention. The COL2A1 gene (Collagen Type II Alpha 1 Chain, OMIM:120140) encodes the alpha-1 chain, which is the primary component of type II collagen. Type II collagen is crucial for the normal development of the inner ear, eyes, and joints, as it provides structure and strength to connective tissues []. A broad range of autosomal dominant collagenopathies, which primarily affect the skeleton, joints, eyes, and occasionally the inner ear, are associated with pathogenic heterozygous variants in COL2A1. Although missense mutations in COL2A1 are linked to more severe forms of skeletal dysplasias, loss-of-function variants have been primarily described in patients with milder phenotypes, such as Stickler syndrome type I []. The clinical picture observed and the diagnosis of Stickler syndrome type I are elucidated by the heterozygous state of the examined fetus, which carries a known pathogenic COL2A1 variant (c.3137del) inherited from the mother. The probability of inheritance in the offspring of heterozygotes is 50%, irrespective of their gender. The observed phenotype is consistent with a loss-of-function mechanism, which aligns with the expected clinical spectrum associated with haploinsufficiency of type II collagen. On a mechanistic level, frameshift variants like COL2A1 c.3137del typically introduce premature termination codons, which lead to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and reduced production of functional type II collagen (haploinsufficiency) rather than the synthesis of an abnormal dominant-negative protein [,]. This haploinsufficiency mechanism is consistent with the Stickler syndrome type I spectrum and explains the predominance of ocular and craniofacial involvement with comparatively milder skeletal disease []. Conversely, missense variants, particularly glycine substitutions in the collagen triple-helix domain, are frequently linked to more severe skeletal dysplasias and result in dominant-negative effects, as delineated in mutation [,]. The limitations of karyotyping and the necessity for molecular genetic testing to detect causative mutations are the primary challenges associated with the prenatal diagnosis of Stickler syndrome. Because these are single-gene mutations (primarily in COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2, COL9A1, COL9A2, or COL9A3) that are submicroscopic and not visible at the chromosomal level, karyotyping is unable to detect the pathogenic variants responsible for Stickler syndrome. Therefore, karyotyping is not a diagnostic tool for Stickler syndrome and will miss cases unless there is a rare, large chromosomal rearrangement involving these genes, which is not the typical mechanism in Stickler syndrome [,]. Molecular genetic testing is required to identify causative mutations. The diagnosis can only be established by detecting a pathogenic variant in one of the Stickler syndrome-associated genes. In the present case, isolated fetal micrognathia prompted consideration of both chromosomal and monogenic etiologies. Although conventional cytogenetic testing was considered, sequencing-based analysis was prioritized due to clinical suspicion of a single-gene disorder and the limited sensitivity of karyotyping for such conditions. This reflects real-world diagnostic reasoning in prenatal medicine. For prenatal diagnosis, the procedure requires prior identification of the familial mutation in an affected parent. Once the familial mutation is known, targeted molecular testing can be performed on fetal DNA obtained by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis []. In the absence of a known familial mutation, prenatal diagnosis is not possible by molecular methods, and ultrasound findings (such as cleft palate or micrognathia) are nonspecific and insufficient for diagnosis. Furthermore, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that single-gene disorders like Stickler syndrome require targeted molecular testing for prenatal diagnosis, and karyotyping is only useful for detecting chromosomal abnormalities, not single-gene disorders []. The inability of karyotyping to detect single-gene mutations and the requirement for prior identification of a familial pathogenic variant for molecular testing are the principal challenges in prenatal diagnosis [,]. Beyond the specific context of Stickler syndrome, multiple prenatal genomics cohorts demonstrate that sequencing-based methods substantially increase diagnostic yield in fetuses with ultrasound-detected structural anomalies, supporting the approach used in this case where imaging prompted molecular investigation. Specifically, a substantial number of fetuses with structural findings contain pathogenic single-gene variants that are unidentifiable by cytogenetic testing, as evidenced by large studies and exome sequencing cohorts [,]. This supports the idea that ultrasound is most effective when utilized as a trigger for sequencing, rather than as a standalone diagnostic tool. The present case provides a practical example of this diagnostic model. Molecular genetic testing is not routinely available or covered by health insurance in Bulgaria, and karyotyping is covered but diagnostically inadequate. Karyotyping can only detect large chromosomal abnormalities and cannot identify the single-gene pathogenic variants in COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2, COL9A1, COL9A2, or COL9A3 that cause Stickler syndrome. The diagnosis requires molecular genetic testing, either gene-targeted panels or comprehensive genomic sequencing, to detect these variants []. Patients and families in Bulgaria are unable to access definitive diagnostic tools necessary for accurate diagnosis, genetic counseling, and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing since insurance coverage is restricted to karyotyping. This restriction obstructs cascade testing in at-risk relatives and prevents confirmation in suspected cases. Consequently, clinical management is contingent upon phenotype and family history, unless patients independently finance molecular testing [,]. This case therefore has translational relevance beyond a single family, illustrating how system-level constraints in genomic medicine implementation can directly impact diagnostic accuracy, timeliness of counseling, and clinical preparedness for monogenic disease, consistent with broader observations in genomic medicine for undiagnosed diseases [] and large-scale rare disease genome sequencing evaluations []. In this instance, access to sequencing enabled definitive prenatal diagnosis and structured perinatal planning that would otherwise not have been possible. Accordingly, the clinical relevance of this report lies in illustrating a practical diagnostic pathway for integrating ultrasound findings, parental phenotyping, and targeted sequencing in healthcare systems where molecular genetic testing is not routinely accessible. Early counseling is essential for families to comprehend the spectrum of clinical manifestations, recurrence risks, and inheritance patterns. This knowledge is essential for informed reproductive decision-making and preparation for potential neonatal complications, such as airway obstruction or feeding difficulties caused by craniofacial anomalies []. Psychological support is essential for families to navigate uncertainty, particularly when a definitive prenatal diagnosis is not feasible due to the absence of molecular testing. According to the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the most recent literature on counseling models, counseling should address the emotional impact of risk, facilitate value-based decision-making, and provide support for coping strategies [,]. By acknowledging the limitations of the available testing and the potential for undetected complications, realistic expectations and reduced decisional regret are ensured. In the present case, molecular confirmation allowed individualized counseling based on a confirmed genetic etiology rather than probabilistic risk estimation. To optimize outcomes for hearing, joint, and craniofacial issues, as well as to prevent irreversible complications, such as blindness from retinal detachment, postpartum follow-up planning is essential. This is because these complications can be prevented through the early identification and multidisciplinary management of affected neonates. The prophylactic vitreoretinal interventions and prevention-focused approaches have been linked to significant reductions in the risk of retinal detachment and blindness in Stickler syndrome [,,]. Proactive ophthalmologic surveillance is particularly beneficial in this context. As a result, early molecular confirmation can be regarded as a gateway intervention that enables the timely referral of specialists, the provision of risk education, and the investigation of prophylactic strategies before the occurrence of irreversible complications. Sequencing-based analysis was prioritized in this instance due to the clinical suspicion of a monogenic disorder and the known limited sensitivity of karyotyping for single-gene conditions, despite the fact that conventional cytogenetic testing was a consideration following the detection of fetal micrognathia. The intrafamilial variability observed in this case—mild maternal manifestations in contrast to more pronounced fetal/neonatal craniofacial involvement—emphasizes the limitations of phenotype-based prediction in at-risk relatives and emphasizes the significance of molecular confirmation when prenatal findings raise suspicion for a monogenic connective tissue disorder. In the final analysis, molecular confirmation should be prioritized. Overall, this case illustrates how prenatal molecular diagnosis can refine clinical decision-making, improve perinatal preparedness, and enhance risk assessment in healthcare settings with limited access to genomic testing. Although the molecular finding itself is not novel, the present case provides clinically relevant insight into the practical implementation of prenatal genomic diagnostics and demonstrates how early molecular confirmation can directly influence counseling, perinatal planning, and multidisciplinary management.

5. Conclusions
5. Conclusions Although the identified pathogenic variant has been previously reported, this case illustrates the critical role of sequencing-based molecular diagnostics in enabling prenatal etiologic clarification, guiding perinatal management, and improving clinical preparedness in healthcare systems with limited access to genomic testing. By integrating molecular confirmation with prenatal imaging, an accurate etiologic diagnosis was achieved, thereby enabling early multidisciplinary intervention and targeted perinatal planning. The findings are indicative of a more extensive systemic challenge in Bulgaria’s prenatal healthcare, as the country’s diagnostic precision, genetic counseling, and informed reproductive decision-making are all constrained by the limited availability of molecular genetic testing. Consequently, it is essential to expand insurance coverage for sequencing-based diagnostics to address this diagnostic gap and guarantee that clinical practice is in accordance with international genomic medicine standards. The provision of comprehensive genetic counseling and coordinated specialist care is equally important, as they together facilitate early surveillance, complication prevention, and long-term outcome optimization for children who have been affected. In general, this report underscores the importance of early molecular diagnosis in precision medicine for rare genetic disorders. It improves clinical preparedness, reduces irreversible morbidity, and resolves structural obstacles to equitable genomic healthcare. The diagnostic pathway described here may provide a clinically applicable framework for implementing prenatal molecular diagnosis of monogenic disorders in resource-constrained healthcare systems.

title: Residual risk of clinically significant copy number variations in fetuses with ultrasonographic soft markers following exclusion of non-invasive prenatal screening-detectable findings.
label_reason: Fetuses with soft markers tested by CMA.
abstract: To evaluate the residual risk of clinically significant copy number variations (CNVs) in fetuses with ultrasonographic soft markers by its various types after excluding theoretically non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS)-detectable abnormalities. This study included 2005 fetuses with soft markers undergoing chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) between 2015 and 2024. Theoretically NIPS-detectable findings were categorized into three subgroups: 3-chromosome NIPS, 5-chromosome NIPS, and genome-wide NIPS. The residual risk was calculated and compared with a low-risk control cohort. We further assessed their clinical outcomes. The overall diagnostic yield of clinically significant CMA findings in fetuses with soft markers was 6.38%. Overall, the residual risk was 4.67% for 3-chromosome NIPS, 4.19% for 5-chromosome NIPS, and 3.25% for genome-wide NIPS. Except for isolated single umbilical artery (genome-wide NIPS), echogenic intracardiac focus, and aberrant right subclavian artery (all NIPS models), the residual risk was significantly higher for most soft marker types when compared with the control cohort. Among fetuses with normal CMA results and successful follow-up, a significantly lower rate of normal infant was identified in fetuses with four types of soft markers (mild ventriculomegaly, echogenic bowel, short femur length, and mild pyelectasis) compared with the control cohort. The residual risk in fetuses with multiple soft markers and most isolated soft markers (absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, mild ventriculomegaly, thickened nuchal fold, echogenic bowel, short femur length, mild pyelectasis, and choroid plexus cysts) was higher than that in low-risk pregnancies. CNV analysis is recommended for such fetuses, regardless of whether NIPS has been performed previously. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00404-026-08373-8. Keywords: Ultrasonographic soft marker, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Non-invasive prenatal screening, Residual risk, Copy number variation
text:
Residual risk of clinically significant copy number variations in fetuses with ultrasonographic soft markers following exclusion of non-invasive prenatal screening-detectable findings

Introduction
Introduction Ultrasonographic soft markers, which are nonspecific and often minor transient ultrasound findings observed during pregnancy, can be associated with a potential increased risk of fetal aneuploidy [–]. They are present in at least 10% of normal fetuses []. Recent research has demonstrated the correlation between soft markers and pathogenic copy number variations (CNVs), with an incidence ranging from 2.60 to 4.53% in these fetuses [–]. Therefore, soft markers may assist in predicting fetal chromosomal abnormalities, and further genetic evaluation is crucial for prenatal counseling. In the last decade, non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) has become the most sensitive and specific screening test for fetal common aneuploidies [, ]. It is reported that the sensitivities and specificities of NIPS for the common trisomies (21, 18, and 13) varied from 97.47 to 100% and 99.93 to 100%, respectively [–]. Notably, when using genome-wide NIPS, the sensitivities and specificities remain over 99% even for sex chromosomal aneuploidies (SCAs) and CNVs ≥ 7 Mb [, ]. However, the accuracy of genome-wide NIPS for CNVs < 7 Mb is relatively low [, ]. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) has replaced karyotyping as the first-line test for fetuses with structural anomalies []. Previous studies manifested that CMA identified additional 1.11 to 3.27% of pathogenic CNVs compared with karyotyping [, ]. Currently, CMA has been frequently applied to fetuses with soft markers [, , , ]. As the use of NIPS has increased worldwide, several pregnant women underwent NIPS prior to the observation of soft markers during the second trimester. However, large-scale research focusing on the residual risk of clinically significant CNVs in fetuses with soft markers following normal NIPS has scarcely been reported. Meanwhile, no consensus has been reached concerning the optimal prenatal genetic testing for fetuses with certain soft markers, such as absent or hypoplastic nasal bone [, ]. Thus, comparing the yield of CMA to NIPS is essential for providing the optimal prenatal genetic testing. We aimed to investigate the residual risk of clinically significant CNVs in fetuses with soft markers by its various types after excluding theoretically NIPS-detectable abnormalities. In addition, we evaluated the association between specific soft markers and specific chromosomal abnormalities. Finally, we assessed their clinical outcomes.

Methods
Methods Study population and sample collection Between June 2015 and June 2024, all pregnancies undergoing CMA testing due to soft markers observed during the second trimester (from 14+0 to 27+6 weeks of gestation) ultrasound examination in Nanjing Women and Children’s Healthcare Hospital were recruited as case cohort in this study. All ultrasound examinations were performed by two qualified fetal sonographers in accordance with the guidelines of the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology []. All participants received comprehensive prenatal genetic counseling, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The samples consisted of amniotic fluid obtained via ultrasound-guided amniocentesis. We excluded pregnancies with multiple fetuses, increased nuchal translucency (≥ 3.0 mm), positive serum screening results, or structural anomalies observed by ultrasound examination prior to CMA testing. The following 11 types of soft markers were included [, ]: absent or hypoplastic nasal bone (absent or length < 2.5th percentile of Chinese population []), mild ventriculomegaly (≥ 10 mm and < 15 mm), thickened nuchal fold (≥ 6 mm between 18 and 24 weeks), echogenic bowel, single umbilical artery, short femur length (< 2.5th percentile), mild pyelectasis (≥ 4 mm and < 10 mm), choroid plexus cysts, echogenic intracardiac focus, aberrant right subclavian artery, and enlarged cisterna magna (≥ 10 mm). Of note, some cases of absent or hypoplastic nasal bone were described previously []. In addition, 993 pregnancies without any medical indication for invasive prenatal diagnosis, in which amniocentesis was performed solely due to maternal anxiety, were defined as a low-risk control cohort. In this cohort, only pregnancies with normal serum screening results, maternal age < 35 years, and normal ultrasound examination were included. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Nanjing Women and Children’s Healthcare Hospital (2025KY003-001). CMA A QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany) was used to extract fetal genomic DNA from amniotic fluid samples. Chromosomal abnormalities were identified utilizing two CMA platforms, namely HumanCyto12-SNP array (Illumina, USA) or CytoScan 750K array (Affymetrix, USA). CMA procedures were conducted as described previously []. Taking GRCh37/hg19 as reference genome, CNVs were called at a minimal resolution of 100 kb and 50 kb within well-established haploinsufficient or triplosensitive genes covered by higher probe density. According to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen) guideline [], we re-evaluated the clinical significance of CNVs. The following variations would be reported, including clinically significant CMA findings and variations of uncertain significance (VOUS) (deletions ≥ 500 kb and duplications ≥ 1 Mb). Of these, clinically significant CMA findings encompassed aneuploidies, partial aneuploidies (CNVs ≥ 10 Mb), and pathogenic microdeletions/microduplications (CNVs < 10 Mb). Based on clinical penetrance, pathogenic microdeletions/microduplications were further categorized into complete, high, variable, low, or unknown penetrance CNVs [–]. Complete penetrance CNVs were defined as recurrent CNVs with 100% penetrance (e.g., 6q27 microdeletion), containing CNVs with no cognitive phenotype—17p12 microdeletion including PMP22 gene, related to hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, and Xp22.31 microdeletion including STS gene, related to X-linked ichthyosis. High penetrance CNVs were defined as recurrent CNVs with ≥ 40% penetrance (e.g., 15q13.3 microdeletion). Variable penetrance CNVs referred to recurrent CNVs with 10 to 40% penetrance (e.g., 16p13.11 microdeletion). Low penetrance CNVs were defined as recurrent CNVs with ≤ 10% penetrance (e.g., 15q11.2 microdeletion). Unknown penetrance CNVs were defined as incomplete penetrance reported in previous studies but without clear penetrance (e.g., 10q11.2 microdeletion). Residual risk Given the relatively high sensitivity of NIPS for common trisomies, SCAs and CNVs ≥ 7 Mb [–], we assumed that NIPS has the sensitivity of 100% for these chromosomal abnormalities in this study. Hence, of the clinically significant CMA findings, theoretically detectable NIPS findings were classified into three subgroups: (1) 3-chromosome NIPS: trisomies 21, 18 and 13; (2) 5-chromosome NIPS: trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and SCAs; (3) genome-wide NIPS: all chromosomal abnormalities ≥ 7 Mb. The residual risk of clinically significant CNVs in fetuses with soft markers was calculated following the exclusion of theoretically NIPS-detectable abnormalities. Clinical follow-up assessments Clinical outcomes were conducted via telephone interview or electronic medical records ranging from half a year to eight years after birth. Outcomes were divided into four categories: normal phenotype after birth, termination of pregnancy (TOP), intrauterine fetal death (IUFD), and birth with defect. We further collected the detailed information regarding the reasons for TOP, postnatal conditions, fetal growth and development, and types of birth defect. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed with the use of SPSS (version 27.0) and R (version 4.4.2). Comparison between subgroups was conducted using χ2 test, χ2 trend test, or Fisher exact test. Relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) was used to calculate the effect estimates. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results A total of 2005 fetuses with soft markers who met the inclusion criteria were included in this study (Fig. ). The mean maternal age was 30.0 ± 4.4 years, and the average gestational week (at the time of CMA) was 24.8 ± 3.5 weeks. The flow diagram of the study. CMA chromosomal microarray analysis, NIPS non-invasive prenatal screening Overall diagnostic yield of CMA in fetuses with soft markers and the control cohort Overall, the detection rate of clinically significant CMA findings in fetuses with soft markers was 6.38% (128/2005) (Table ). Of note, fetuses with soft markers demonstrated a significantly higher detection rate of clinically significant CMA findings compared with the control cohort. Among these 128 cases with chromosomal abnormalities, 48 (2.39%) exhibited aneuploidies (Table ), and 80 (3.99%) presented pathogenic CNVs. Of the 80 cases with pathogenic CNVs, 15 (0.75%) showed partial aneuploidies (Table ) and 65 (3.24%) had pathogenic microdeletions/microduplications (Tables ). In addition, VOUS were identified in 78 cases (3.90%). The 48 fetuses with aneuploidies comprised 30 trisomy 21, six trisomy 18, two 45, X, four 47, XXY, three 47, XYY, one 47, XXX, and two mosaicisms (including one mosaic trisomy 7 and one mosaic trisomy 12). Of the 65 fetuses with submicroscopic pathogenic CNVs, 25 were characterized with complete penetrance (containing three with no cognitive phenotype) and the remaining 40 were featured with incomplete penetrance (including 13 with high penetrance, 14 with variable penetrance, 10 with low penetrance, and three with unknown penetrance) (Table ). In the control cohort of 993 low-risk pregnancies, clinically significant CMA findings were detected in eight cases (0.81%), including three with aneuploidies (one trisomy 21, one 47, XXY and one 47, XYY) and five with submicroscopic pathogenic CNVs. Of these, one (0.10%) was 3-NIPS-detectable findings, three (0.30%) were 5-NIPS-detectable findings, and three (0.30%) were genome-wide NIPS-detectable findings. The remaining five (0.50%) findings were considered as detectable only by CMA: 5q35.2q35.3 microdeletion (4.92 Mb, complete penetrance), 15q11.2 microdeletion (512 kb, low penetrance), 16p11.2 microdeletion (916 kb, high penetrance), 16p11.2 microduplication (585 kb, variable penetrance), and 17q12 microdeletion (1.60 Mb, high penetrance). Moreover, the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities significantly increased with increasing number of soft markers (χ2 trend = 12.86, P < 0.01). Compared with the control cohort, the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities was significantly higher for most soft markers. Fetuses with multiple soft markers had a higher residual risk than those with isolated soft markers. Compared with the control cohort, the residual risk was significantly higher for overall soft markers, for isolated and multiple soft markers, and for most soft marker types, except for isolated single umbilical artery for genome-wide NIPS, isolated echogenic intracardiac focus and aberrant right subclavian artery for all NIPS models. Clinical follow-up assessments Among 2005 fetuses with soft markers, 1849 (92.22%) were successfully followed up. Clinical outcomes were unavailable in the remaining 156 cases (7.78%), including three (0.15%) procedure-related pregnancy losses after amniocentesis and 153 (7.63%) lost to follow-up (Table ). In the 128 fetuses with clinically significant CMA findings, 19 exhibited a normal phenotype after birth, including five with aneuploidies (one with 45, X, three with 47, XYY and one with 47, XXX) and 14 with submicroscopic pathogenic CNVs (one with 1q21.1 microdeletion, five with 15q11.2 microdeletion, one with 16p11.2 microdeletion, one with 16p11.2 microduplication, four with 16p13.11 microdeletion, one with 17p12 microdeletion and one with 22q11.2 microduplication). Two cases were identified with clinical defects after birth: one with 1q21.1 microduplication was born with lower digestive tract atresia, and another with Xp22.33 or Yp11.32 microdeletion had a short stature below the fifth percentile at the age of two years. Of the fetuses with normal CMA results and successful follow-up, the rates of normal infant, TOP, IUFD, and birth with defect were 89.36% (1470/1645), 6.93% (114/1645), 0.67% (11/1645), and 3.04% (50/1645), respectively. Overall, fetuses with soft markers had a significantly lower rate of normal infant compared with the control cohort (89.36% vs 93.60%; RR, 0.95; 95% CI 0.93–0.98). Among fetuses with isolated soft markers, the rate of normal infant was significantly lower in fetuses with isolated mild ventriculomegaly (86.96% vs 93.60%; RR, 0.93; 95% CI 0.88–0.98), echogenic bowel (85.34% vs 93.60%; RR, 0.91; 95% CI 0.84–0.99), short femur length (74.26% vs 93.60%; RR, 0.79; 95% CI 0.71–0.89), and mild pyelectasis (76.19% vs 93.60%; RR, 0.81; 95% CI 0.72–0.92) compared with the control cohort. The primary reasons for TOP included hydrocephalus, worsening of femoral length, severe intrauterine growth restriction, and multiple structural anomalies observed during the third trimester ultrasound after CMA. For fetuses with clinical defects after birth, their clinical manifestations included intellectual disability, developmental delay, delayed speech and language development, epilepsy, hydrocephalus, congenital cardiac defect, lower digestive tract atresia, hydronephrosis, and short stature.

Discussion
Discussion This study focused on evaluating the residual risk of clinically significant CNVs in fetuses with soft markers following normal NIPS in a large cohort. Overall, fetuses with soft markers had a significantly higher residual risk compared with the control cohort. Subgroup analyses revealed that a higher residual risk was observed in fetuses with multiple soft markers than in those with isolated soft markers, suggesting that the existence of multiple soft markers would elevate the residual risk. Among fetuses with isolated soft markers, compared with the control cohort, the residual risk was significantly increased for most soft marker types, except for isolated single umbilical artery (genome-wide NIPS), echogenic intracardiac focus and aberrant right subclavian artery (all NIPS models), most probably because the risk of chromosomal abnormalities in such fetuses is a priori [, , , ]. After excluding CNVs with low penetrance or no cognitive phenotype, in addition to the three aforementioned soft markers, the residual risk of isolated mild pyelectasis (genome-wide NIPS) also displayed no significant difference compared with the control cohort. Accordingly, our data support that CMA should be performed in fetuses with absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, mild ventriculomegaly, thickened nuchal fold, echogenic bowel, short femur length, mild pyelectasis, choroid plexus cysts and multiple soft markers. Of note, if CNVs with low penetrance or no cognitive phenotype were disregarded, CMA was not necessary for fetuses with mild pyelectasis. In this study, the incidence of procedure-related pregnancy loss after amniocentesis was 0.15%, which falls within the range reported in previous studies (0.11%–0.30%) [, ]. This risk was not significantly different from that observed in pregnant women who did not undergo any invasive testing. Admittedly, invasive testing involves the potential of relatively high financial costs and over-utilization of medical resources. However, our study revealed that the residual risk in fetuses with multiple soft markers and most isolated soft markers varied from 2.37 to 7.38%, which was significantly higher than that in the control cohort. These findings highlight the clinical benefit of invasive prenatal diagnosis for such fetuses. Therefore, comprehensive prenatal genetic counseling, including the potential procedure-related risks (such as pregnancy loss) and associated invasive testing costs, should be provided for fetuses with soft markers before performing CMA. The association between specific soft markers and specific aneuploidies has been well-established [–]. However, reports on the association of specific soft markers with specific CNVs are currently limited. In this study, several CNVs occurred more frequently in certain soft markers. Specifically, mild ventriculomegaly was associated with 6q27 microdeletion, likely due to haploinsufficiency of TBP leading to hydrocephalus [–]. Short femur length was associated with Xp22.33 or Yp11.32 microdeletion, attributed to haploinsufficiency of SHOX causing skeletal dysplasia [, , ]. Mild pyelectasis was associated with 17q12 microdeletion, potentially resulting from haploinsufficiency of HNF1B leading to renal dysplasia [, ]. More importantly, we identified that short femur length was associated with 17q12 microdeletion, and aberrant right subclavian artery was associated with 1q21.1 microdeletion, which further broadened the clinical phenotypic spectrum of these CNVs. Bhargav et al. [] reported that 17q12 microdeletion was detected in a girl with growth faltering, dysmorphic facies and developmental delay, indicating the potential association between short femur length and 17q12 microdeletion. Similarly, 1q21.1 microdeletion has been reported in association with congenital heart disease [–], and aberrant right subclavian artery is known to increase the risk of congenital heart disease [, ]. Consequently, aberrant right subclavian artery may be linked to 1q21.1 microdeletion. In summary, 17q12 microdeletion and 1q21.1 microdeletion may be considered as candidate CNVs for fetuses with short femur length and aberrant right subclavian artery, respectively. In recent years, NIPS has been widely recognized as the optimal screening test for fetal common trisomies [, ]. However, it must be emphasized that NIPS was not equivalent to diagnostic testing. Even genome-wide NIPS could yield false-positive and false-negative results. Previous studies reported that the positive predictive value of genome-wide NIPS for the common trisomies, SCAs, rare autosomal aneuploidies, and CNVs varied from 80.95 to 97.93%, 30.77 to 90.17%, 13.33 to 47.83%, and 40.80 to 55.56%, respectively [, , ]. It is evident that NIPS may not be sufficiently effective for fetuses with soft markers. This knowledge should be conveyed to pregnant women to facilitate informed decisions regarding the choice between prenatal screening and diagnostic testing. This study is the first to evaluate the residual risk of clinically significant CNVs in fetuses with soft markers by its various types following normal NIPS in a large cohort. In addition, we assessed their clinical outcomes. These findings will provide comprehensive and precise information for prenatal genetic counseling in fetuses with soft markers. However, our study also has several limitations. The main one is the assumption that all NIPS-detectable abnormalities will indeed be identified, disregarding the possible false-negative, which could lead to an underestimation of the calculated residual risk. Additionally, although the sample size of this study was large, the distribution of different types of soft markers varied considerably. For instance, absent or hypoplastic nasal bone and mild ventriculomegaly were the most common soft markers, whereas the number of aberrant right subclavian artery and enlarged cisterna magna was relatively limited.

Conclusion
Conclusion Fetuses with multiple soft markers and most isolated soft markers (absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, mild ventriculomegaly, thickened nuchal fold, echogenic bowel, short femur length, mild pyelectasis and choroid plexus cysts) following normal NIPS had a higher residual risk of clinically significant CNVs compared with low-risk pregnancies, implying that CMA but NIPS is recommended for such cases. In addition, our study further defined the genotype–phenotype correlation for soft markers, providing more comprehensive and precise information for prenatal genetic counseling.
