Prenatal genetic diagnosis and pregnancy outcomes of the surviving co-twin after spontaneous single intrauterine fetal demise

Introduction
Introduction In the past decade, the incidence of twin pregnancies has increased significantly due to the widespread use of ovulation induction and assisted reproductive technologies. Spontaneous single intrauterine fetal demise (SSIUFD) is a well-recognized complication of twin pregnancies, with reported incidences of SSIUFD ranging from 3.5% to 8.1% of all twin pregnancies–. Twin pregnancies are categorized by chorionicity into dichorionic twins and monochorionic twins. SSIUFD is more frequently observed in monochorionic twins pregnancies compared to dichorionic twins pregnancies,. Genetic abnormalities are a well-established etiology of spontaneous fetal loss in singleton pregnancies. Genetic testing of products of conception is essential for elucidating the underlying etiology and guiding management in subsequent pregnancies. However, in twin pregnancies complicated by SSIUFD, clinical attention understandably shifts to the surviving co‑twin. Etiologies vary by chorionicity and include twin–twin transfusion syndrome, selective intrauterine growth restriction, placental insufficiency or abruption, cord accidents, etc. Following SSIUFD, current guidelines recommend a detailed anatomic scanning of the surviving twin, with serial ultrasound scans assessment to monitor for potential complications and structural malformations. Abnormal ultrasound findings not only signal potential chromosomal aberrations but also predict adverse perinatal outcomes of the surviving co-twin. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) has revolutionized genetic diagnosis in stillbirths, providing an additional 4–10% increase in diagnostic yield compared with conventional karyotyping–. The role of genetic abnormalities in SSIUFD is primarily relevant in MCDA pregnancies, where twins originate from a single zygote and are expected to share a common genetic background. In contrast, for DCDA pregnancies, the genetic status of the surviving twin is largely independent of the demised co-twin, and testing is therefore guided mainly by individual clinical indications such as abnormal ultrasound findings, advanced maternal age, rather than the occurrence of SSIUFD itself. Despite these biological distinctions, the contribution of genetic abnormalities to SSIUFD and their implications for the surviving co-twin, particularly in relation to chorionicity and pregnancy outcomes, remain incompletely understood. Therefore, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of twin pregnancies complicated by spontaneous SSIUFD between November 2015 and November 2024. Our primary aim was to: (1) characterize the genetic test results of surviving co-twins by karyotyping and CMA; (2) analyze serial ultrasound findings and other clinical indications; (3) analyze pregnancy outcomes of twin pregnancies following SSIUFD.

Patients and methods
Patients and methods Patients We performed a retrospective analysis of twin pregnancies complicated by spontaneous SSIUFD between November 2015 and November 2024. Cases with elective fetal reduction, or undetermined chorionicity, or ambiguous timing of demise were not included. A total of 88 pregnancies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 48 naturally conceived pregnancies (54.5%) and 40 pregnancies (45.5%) resulting from assisted reproductive techniques. Genetic analysis including karyotyping and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis was performed on amniotic fluid samples (n = 85) and umbilical cord blood (n = 3) obtained from the surviving co-twin via invasive prenatal testing. Method All methods were carried out in accordance with with the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. The experimental protocols were approved by the Fujian Maternity and Child Health Hospital. Diagnostic criteria for SSIUFD (1) First trimester (≤ 12 weeks): Initial ultrasound confirmation of two gestational sacs followed by subsequent disappearance of one sac with no residual embryonic structures. It is clinically termed as vanishing twin syndrome (VTS); (2) Second trimester (> 12 weeks): ultrasonographic examination of cardiac activity cessation and absence of fetal movement in one twin, with confirmed viability of the co-twin. All diagnoses required independent confirmation by two certified sonographers. Determination of gestational age at demise Gestational age is corrected using the most recent reliable ultrasound performed prior to fetal demise. The gestational age at demise was established by biometric parameters including crown-rump length (CRL) or from the last confirmed viable scan with post-demise measurements including head circumference (HC), biparietal diameter (BPD), femur length (FL), and abdominal circumference (AC). Cell culture and karyotyping Lymphocytes from umbilical cord blood were cultured in phytohemagglutinin-stimulated media for 68–72 h, entering mitosis. Amniotic fluid cells were cultured for 7 days before mitotic arrest with colchicine. Cells were then subjected to hypotonic treatment, fixation, slide preparation, trypsin digestion, and Giemsa staining to produce G-banded chromosome slides. Karyotyping was performed with a resolution of 320–500 bands, following local laboratory protocols. Karyotypes were described according to the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN, 2020). SNP array analysis Genomic DNA was extracted from uncultured amniotic fluid and fetal cord blood using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini kit (QIAGEN, Germany). SNP array analysis was performed using the Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K array, which includes over 200,000 SNP markers and 550,000 copy number variation (CNV) markers. The raw data were analyzed with the Chromosome Analysis Suite (CHAS 3.2), and CNV were compared to public databases: Database of Genomic Variants (DGV), the Database of Chromosome Imbalance and Phenotype in Humans Using Ensemble Resources (DECIPHER), the International Standards for Cytogenomic Arrays Consortium, and the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM). Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) guidelines: pathogenic, benign, likely pathogenic, likely benign, and variants of uncertain significance (VOUS). Pregnancy outcomes Information on pregnancy outcomes was collected from the hospital’s electronic clinical database or through direct telephone interviews. The assessed outcomes included term birth, preterm birth, miscarriage or stillbirth, and termination of pregnancy. Mode of delivery, including vaginal delivery and cesarean section, was also recorded. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software v26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Categorical comparisons were performed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. A two-tailed p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results Clinical baseline characteristics Details of the baseline characteristics are summarized in Table . The cohort included 54 dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) and 34 monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancies. The gestational age at fetal demise was determined by the first ultrasound confirmation of fetal death, ranging from 7 to 22 weeks. Based on the gestational age at which one twin demised, cases were categorized as first-trimester (≤ 12 weeks) and second-trimester SSIUFD (> 12 weeks and ≤ 28 weeks). First-trimester demise occurred in 47.1% (16/34) of MCDA pregnancies and 67.0% (36/54) of DCDA pregnancies, whereas second-trimester demise occurred in 52.9% (18/34) of MCDA pregnancies and 33.0% (18/54) of DCDA pregnancies. The difference between the two groups showed no statistical significance. Advanced maternal age (AMA) is defined as maternal age ≥ 35 years at the expected date of delivery. In this study, 60 involved non-AMA pregnancies, of which 24 underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis solely due to spontaneous SSIUFD, including 18 DCDA pregnancies and 6 MCDA pregnancies. The remaining 36 had additional clinical indications (Table ). The other 28 cases occurred in AMA pregnancies (maternal age ≥ 35 years at expected delivery), with clinical indications summarized in Table . Karyotyping results Among the cohort of 88 cases undergoing karyotyping, only one case (1.1%) exhibited a chromosomal abnormality of trisomy 21. This case involved a 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. Both she and her husband were healthy and had no family history of Down syndrome or other congenital anomalies, and her first child was healthy. The current pregnancy, was a naturally conceived MCDA twin gestation. At 12 weeks of gestation, both fetuses showed increased nuchal translucency (NT) of 4.4 mm and 3.2 mm, respectively. By 16 weeks, the fetus with NT of 4.4 mm demised, with a crown-rump length (CRL) consistent with 14 weeks and 2 days. At 18 weeks, the surviving fetus revealed fetal growth restriction (FGR) and multiple structural anomalies on ultrasound. 18 DCDA pregnancies and 6 MCDA pregnancies Among the 24 cases tested solely due to SSIUFD, no clinically significant chromosomal abnormalities were detected (0/24, 0%). With respect to maternal age, the chromosomal abnormality rate in the AMA (≥ 35 years) group was 3.6% (1/28), whereas no abnormalities were identified among the 60 younger women (< 35 years). Additionally, in the two cases with abnormal NIPT results, no corresponding chromosomal abnormalities were confirmed in the surviving fetuses. SNP array analysis results SNP-array testing was not available in our center until late 2016. Therefore, 20 cases in the earlier part of the study period did not undergo SNP-array analysis. A total of 68 cases underwent SNP array analysis concurrently, including the previously described trisomy 21 case. Among the remaining 67 fetuses with normal karyotypes, two (Cases 15 and 18) harbored copy‑number variants (CNVs) and one (Case 63) exhibited regions of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (Table ). Both CNVs were classified as likely benign, as parental SNP arrays confirmed maternal inheritance from a phenotypically normal mother. Case 3 showed multiple runs of homozygosity on chromosomes 5, 10, 14, and 17; following genetic counseling, the patient denied any further examination. All these three pregnancies resulted in the birth of healthy infants, and no abnormal phenotypes were observed over a three-year postnatal follow‑up period. Pregnancy outcomes Follow-up data were successfully obtained for 94.3% (83/88) of the cohort, with five cases lost to follow-up. Among the 83 cases, outcomes comprised 67 term deliveries, 8 preterm deliveries, and 7 pregnancy terminations. Notably, the termination rate in the MCDA group was significantly higher at 19.4% (6/31) compared to 1.9% (1/52) observed in the DCDA group (p < 0.05). The clinical indications for pregnancy termination included one case of trisomy 21, six cases of severe ultrasound anomalies and one case of stillbirth. Details were described in Supplementary Table . Preterm delivery (PTB) rates were 13.5% in the DCDA group and 6.5% in the MCDA group, while rates in pregnancies complicated by VTS and second-trimester SSIUFD were 6.0% and 15.2%, respectively. However, these differences did not reach statistical significance. Detailed outcomes are presented in Table .

Discussion
Discussion To the best of our knowledge, large-scale data on the genetic characteristics of surviving co-twins after SSIUFD are limited, particularly in cases without other clinical indications. Our results did not observe an increased detection rate of clinically significant chromosomal abnormalities, especially in DCDA pregnancies. However, in MCDA pregnancies where both fetuses present similar ultrasound anomalies or additional clinical risk factors, such as advanced maternal age, genetic evaluation of the surviving twin should be considered. In our cohort, chromosomal abnormalities were identified in 1.1% (1/88) of surviving co-twins after SSIUFD. In comparison, our previously published twin cohort from the same center reported clinically significant chromosomal abnormalities in 7.9% of twin pregnancies overall, including detection rates of 5.2% by karyotyping with an additional 1.6% clinically significant CNVs in DCDA fetuses and 4.4% in MCDA fetuses. Although direct comparison is limited by differences in study design and testing indications, our findings do not suggest an increased detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in surviving co-twins following SSIUFD. The only case of trisomy 21 was identified in an MCDA pregnancy and occurred in a woman with AMA, with multiple structural anomalies detected in both the first and second trimesters. Given the MCDA placentation and concordant first-trimester ultrasound anomalies in both twins, it is highly likely that the demised fetus also had trisomy 21, despite the lack of genetic confirmation in the demised twin. Furthermore, SNP array analysis revealed no pathogenic submicroscopic aberrations in the 67 fetuses with normal karyotypes, with detected CNVs and LOH regions classified as benign or of uncertain significance after parental testing. MCDA twins originate from a single zygote, and theoretically share identical genetic profiles, although discordant chromosomal anomalies have been reported in MCDA twins, with rates ranging from 1.1% to 8.8% in cases where both fetuses survived–. In our cohort of 34 MCDA pregnancies complicated by SSIUFD, we observed only one lethal chromosomal abnormality, contributing to a frequency far below the 50–60% rate reported for chromosomal anomalies in singleton pregnancy loss–. This finding may suggest that the etiology of SSIUFD in twin pregnancies likely involved factors beyond chromosomal aberrations, underscoring a more complex etiology than that seen in singletons. However, as genetic testing was not performed on the demised twins, the contribution of chromosomal abnormalities to SSIUFD cannot be completely excluded. DCDA pregnancies, originating from two distinct zygotes, are more prone to genetic discordance. In our previous study, we observed an 8.8% discordant rate among 353 live-born DCDA twin pairs, with anomalies predominantly trisomy 21, trisomy 18, and monosomy X. The findings suggest that chromosomal abnormalities may contribute more substantially to SSIUFD in DCDA pregnancies compared to MCDA pregnancies. However, confirming such hypotheses remains challenging, particularly in VTS cases. Kirsten J. et al. utilized SNP-based noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) to detect triploidy, unrecognized twins, and vanishing twin pregnancies, suggesting that it is reasonable to assume that the rate of aneuploidy among vanished twins is similar to that found in analysis of POC samples. Importantly, the biological rationale for genetic testing differs between MCDA and DCDA twin pregnancies. MCDA twins originate from a single zygote and are typically genetically identical; therefore, testing the surviving co-twin may provide indirect insight into the genetic status of the demised twin and help clarify the etiology of SSIUFD. In contrast, DCDA twins are usually dizygotic and genetically independent, and fetal demise in one twin does not imply shared genetic risk. Accordingly, in DCDA pregnancies, genetic testing should be guided by individual clinical indications rather than the occurrence of SSIUFD itself. Couples experiencing SSIUFD are often concerned about the health and development of the surviving co-twin. Close ultrasound surveillance is suggested and essential for them to monitor growth, anatomy, and potential complications. Prenatal genetic indications for the surviving twin are similar to those in singleton pregnancies, particularly in DCDA pregnancies. Advanced maternal age (AMA) is a well-recognized independent risk factor for fetal chromosomal abnormalities. In our study, the incidence of chromosomal abnormalities among AMA pregnancies was 3.5%, which is lower than the rates reported in singleton AMA pregnancies in previous studies,. Although NIPT has shown good performance in twin pregnancies–, SSIUFD is a recognized cause of false-positive NIPT results due to residual genetic material from the demised twin,–. A recent study by van Eekhout et al. reported that in 655 vanishing-twin pregnancies, NIPT achieved a sensitivity of 100%, specificity of 98.5%, and a PPV of 41.2% for trisomy 21, while no trisomy 18, trisomy 13, or additional abnormalities were confirmed in the surviving fetuses. These findings indicate that although NIPT can effectively identify trisomy 21 in twin or multiple pregnancies complicated by fetal demise, its interpretation should be made with caution due to the potential influence of residual fetal DNA from the demised co-twin. In addition, 18 DCDA pregnancies and 6 MCDA pregnancies underwent invasive testing solely because of SSIUFD, and no pathogenic chromosomal abnormalities were identified. In present study, only two cases underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis due to positive NIPT results, and no corresponding abnormalities were confirmed in the surviving fetuses. Given that NIPT results may be confounded by DNA originating from the demised twin, invasive testing of the surviving fetus provides a more accurate and reliable assessment of its genetic status. Overall, the present study did not identify sufficient evidence to recommend routine invasive prenatal diagnosis following SSIUFD, particularly in surviving co-twins without other indications. Further research with a larger sample size is required to evaluate the predictive value of SSIUFD for chromosomal abnormalities in the surviving co-twin. The impact of SSIUFD on the perinatal outcomes of the surviving co-twin maybe influenced by the gestational age at fetal demise and chorionicity; however, current evidence remains controversial. SSIUFD occurring during the first trimester are clinically termed as VTS, with a reported prevalence of 53–78% in twin pregnancies. While some cohort studies suggest VTS pregnancies were associated with increased risk for PTB and small-for-gestational-age neonates compared to singleton pregnancies–, others demonstrate comparable perinatal outcomes when managed with intensive fetal surveillance and singleton-based delivery protocols–. Notably, our study revealed no significant difference in PTB rates between VTS pregnancies and second-trimester SSIUFD cases. In a meta-analysis by Mackie et al., PTB occurred in about 58.5% and 53.7% in MCDA and DCDA pregnancies. In our study, the PTB rates in DCDA and MCDA pregnancies complicated with SSIUFD were 11.5% and 6.5%, respectively. The discrepancy can be largely explained by selection bias, as our selection bias, as only those underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis were exclusively included in our study, and the majority of SSIUFD events occurred during early pregnancy. Importantly, we observed a significantly higher rate of pregnancy termination in MCDA pregnancies (19.4%) compared with DCDA pregnancies (1.9%), primarily due to severe fetal growth restriction, abnormal umbilical artery Doppler findings, and stillbirth in the mid-to-late gestation. These findings suggest the adverse outcomes of MCDA following SSIUFD, emphasizing the need for vigilant monitoring in such cases. Currently, there is no standardized guideline for the management of the surviving co-twin after SSIUFD, and clinical decisions are often influenced by maternal health status and history of cesarean delivery. In our cohort, the cesarean section rate among liveborn infants was 50%, consistent with previous reports, and slightly higher than the 38.6% rate reported by Evron et al. Nonetheless, the overall cesarean section rate following SSIUFD remains elevated compared with singleton pregnancies. This study has several limitations. First, the inclusion criteria were restricted to twin pregnancies underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis following SSIUFD, resulting in a selection bias. Second, lack of genetic analysis on the demised fetuses precludes definitive evaluation of potential chromosomal contributions to SSIUFD etiology, particularly in differentiating potential concordance in MCDA twins versus genetic discordance in DCDA twins. Third, the follow-up period was limited to within three years, and the number of live-born infants was small. Although no neurodevelopmental abnormalities have been observed so far, longer follow-up and larger sample sizes are needed to better assess potential neurological outcomes in surviving co-twins after SSIUFD. Finally, higher-resolution genomic technologies such as whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing were not utilized. Restricting genetic evaluations to conventional karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis may have led to undetected pathogenic variants.

Conclusion
Conclusion Our findings do not provide evidence for an increased detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities in surviving co-twins after SSIUFD, particularly in the absence of other risk indicators in the surviving co-twin. During the study period, approximately 200 twin pregnancies complicated by this condition were managed at our center, of which 88 (44%) underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis; as testing was more often performed in pregnancies with additional clinical concerns or parental anxiety, a degree of selection bias is unavoidable. MCDA pregnancies were associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes, including termination and subsequent fetal demise, highlighting the importance of close monitoring in these cases. Overall, individualized risk assessment based on chorionicity, gestational age of SSIUFD, and the presence of additional ultrasound anomalies is crucial for guiding clinical decision-making.

Second Prenatal Diagnosis of Bosch–Boonstra–Schaaf Optic Atrophy Syndrome in a Fetus With a 5q14.3q15 Deletion: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

Introduction
Introduction Bosch–Boonstra–Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome (BBSOAS, OMIM# 615722) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a spectrum of clinical features of cerebral visual impairment, developmental delay, and intellectual disability []. In 2014, Bosch et al. [] described the first six individuals with heterozygous missense variants or deletions in the NR2F1 gene; all showed optic nerve abnormalities and intellectual impairment. Accumulated case series provided evidence for genotype–phenotype correlations by heterozygous loss‐of‐function variants in the NR2F1 gene and by haploinsufficiency due to a deletion encompassing the gene [, ]. The NR2F1 gene, also known as COUP‐TFI, is mapped at 5q15 and encodes a protein that acts as a nuclear receptor and transcriptional regulator []. The prevalence of BBSOAS is estimated to be about 1/100,000–1/250,000 people worldwide []. To date, approximately 100 newborn and pediatric patients have been reported, but only one fetus was diagnosed prenatally [, , ]. This substantial discrepancy highlights a significant gap in the current understanding of the disease during the prenatal stage, with its prenatal phenotypic spectrum, natural history, and optimal prenatal diagnostic strategies yet to be elucidated. In view of this, each newly confirmed prenatal case is particularly valuable, not only enriching our knowledge of the prenatal manifestations of BBSOAS but also providing critical information for optimizing genetic counseling and perinatal management. Here, we report one fetus with BBSOAS caused by a deletion of 5q14.3q15 encompassing the NR2F1 gene, representing the second prenatal case described in the literature. By detailing the prenatal ultrasound findings, cell‐free DNA (cfDNA) screening results, molecular diagnostic process, and family validation for this case, we aim to (1) further expand the prenatal phenotypic spectrum of BBSOAS; (2) highlight the clinical utility and challenges of cfDNA screening in detecting such microdeletion syndromes; and (3) provide practical references for clinicians and genetic counselors regarding diagnostic strategies, prognostic counseling, and perinatal management when encountering similar cases.

Case Presentation/Examination
Case Presentation/Examination A 32‐year‐old pregnant woman, gravida 2, para 1, was found to have a nuchal translucency (NT) measurement of 0.26 cm and a high‐risk serum screening result of 1/20 for trisomy 21 during first‐trimester screening. Subsequent cfDNA screening excluded high risk for chromosomal aneuploidies but unexpectedly revealed a 7.64‐Mb deletion at chromosome 5q14.3q15. This pregnancy was conceived naturally. The couple were nonconsanguineous, healthy without any histories of drugs, infections, or genetic diseases. The amniocentesis was performed at 17 weeks of gestation for the purpose of prenatal diagnosis to confirm the fetal karyotype and to verify the 5q14.3q15 deletion detected by cfDNA screening after fully written consent. Conventional G‐banded karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) using a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array platform by Affymetrix CytoScan 750 K arrays were performed as previously described []. CMA on the DNA extracted from uncultured amniocytes revealed the result of arr[GRCh37] 5q14.3q15(89009930_96465325)x1 with a 7.46‐Mb deletion encompassing 22 Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) genes. The minor discrepancy in size between the cfDNA and CMA results is due to differences in the sample source and testing principles as well as the depth of coverage of the two methods. Simultaneous karyotyping on the cultured amniocytes revealed the result of 46,XN,del(5)(q14.3q15) (Figure ). The absence of fetal sex information in the prenatal diagnosis report is due to legal prohibitions against sex determination for non‐medical reasons. The deletion fragment at 5q14.3q15 involved the whole NR2F1 gene, and haploinsufficiency of this gene was associated with BBSOAS. The karyotyping of the couple showed normal results and indicated a de novo deletion in the fetus. (A) Karyotype showed 46,XN,del(5)(q14.3q15). (B) Chromosome 5 and the deletion fragment of chromosome 5 (red arrow). (C) CMA result showed a 7.46‐Mb deletion on 5q14.3q15 (89009930_96465325) (GRCh37/hg19). The region of 5q14.3q15 is boxed in red.

Methods (Differential Diagnosis, Investigations and Treatment Related to the Current Case)
Methods (Differential Diagnosis, Investigations and Treatment Related to the Current Case) The primary differential diagnosis for the fetal 5q14.3q15 deletion identified by cfDNA screening and confirmatory testing was BBSOAS, caused by NR2F1 haploinsufficiency—the only well‐characterized monogenic disorder associated with deletions in this chromosomal region. Additional differential considerations for 5q14.3q15 deletions included other rare neurodevelopmental disorders caused by haploinsufficiency of other OMIM genes within the deletion fragment (22 total OMIM genes in this case). Key differential diagnoses were as follows. MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome (OMIM# 613443): Caused by deletion/mutation of MEF2C (not included in the 5q14.3q15 deletion in this case), characterized by intellectual disability, epilepsy, autism, and brain malformations excluded via CMA gene content analysis. Isolated 5q14.3q15 microdeletion syndrome: A rare non‐syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping features (developmental delay) but no optic atrophy; distinguished from BBSOAS by the inclusion of NR2F1 in the deletion (the defining feature of BBSOAS). Other syndromic microdeletion disorders: 5q chromosomal deletions outside the 5q14.3q21.3 region (e.g., 5q31 deletion syndrome) were excluded via precise CMA mapping of the deletion breakpoints. All investigative procedures were performed in accordance with clinical prenatal diagnosis guidelines of the Chinese Medical Association and the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). No in utero therapeutic interventions were indicated for this case, as BBSOAS is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder with no curative prenatal or postnatal treatment available.

Conclusion and Results (Outcome and Follow‐Up Related to the Current Case)
Conclusion and Results (Outcome and Follow‐Up Related to the Current Case) Even though prenatal ultrasound at 21 weeks of gestation did not detect any fetal structural abnormalities, the couple chose to terminate the pregnancy at 22 weeks of gestation after receiving thorough genetic counseling and being well informed of fetal possible severe adverse outcomes after labor. This process was approved by Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital Ethics Committee. In summary, this case was the second prenatal case with BBSOAS caused by a deletion of 5q14.3q15. The prenatal ultrasound findings of BBSOAS are non‐specific and may include bilateral mild ventriculomegaly, intracranial cysts, increased NT, polyhydramnios, and soft ultrasound markers. All the 17 reported cases of BBSOAS caused by deletions at 5q14.3q21.3 contained the NR2F1 gene, and approximately 82% of deletions are de novo and 18% are inherited. This study reported for the first time the detection of a BBSOAS fetus presenting with increased NT, expanding the prenatal phenotypic spectrum of the disease. It also represents the first reported case of a 5q14.3q15 deletion identified through cfDNA screening and confirmed by prenatal diagnosis and underscores the importance of cfDNA screening, particularly for fetuses without severe structural abnormalities on ultrasound. For cases with positive screening results, prenatal diagnosis should be performed for confirmation. Given the uncertainty in predicting prenatal phenotypes of BBSOAS, molecular diagnostic techniques are crucial for the prenatal diagnosis of affected fetuses. For clinicians and genetic counselors working on prenatal cases, information from cfDNA screening, ultrasound examination, invasive prenatal testing for cytogenetic and molecular genetics, family history, and parental testing should be provided and integrated to facilitate informed counseling and decision‐making for these families.

Discussion
Discussion We systematically searched all literature on NR2F1 gene deletions in the PubMed database using keywords including NR2F1 or BBSOAS. Cases that were confirmed by genetic testing and had clearly defined deletion breakpoints were included (Table , Figure ) [, , , , , , , ]. All 17 cases carried a deletion ranging from 198 Kb to 17 Mb at 5q14.3q21.3. With the exception for the two fetuses, the ages of these NR2F1 deletion patients ranged from 2 years old to 37 years old. Of the 11 cases with follow‐up parental analysis, nine (82%) had de novo deletions and two (18%) were inherited from a maternal or paternal carrier. All cases involved the NR2F1 gene, which has a haploinsufficiency score of three. In addition to this gene, case 2 [] also involved the haploinsufficiency gene MEF2C. The case was a 5‐year‐old girl whose clinical manifestations included severe developmental delay, absence of speech, epilepsy, and minor dysmorphic features. MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome (OMIM# 613443) is characterized by intellectual disability, epilepsy, autism, abnormal movements, brain abnormalities, and some dysmorphic features. These clinical features are similar to the clinical manifestations of BBSOAS, except for the visual impairment specific to BBSOAS, which includes optic nerve atrophy, optic nerve hypoplasia, and cortical visual impairment. Therefore, it cannot be determined whether the causative gene in this child is NR2F1, MEF2C, or a combination of both genes. Cytogenomic mapping and genotype–phenotype correlations for candidate genes of 5q14.3q21.3 [UCSC Genome Browser on Human (GRCh37/hg19)]. A cytogenomic map for sizes of deletions and candidate genes of 5q14.3q21.3. The upper panel shows chromosome 5 with the band location information. The region of 5q14.3q21.3 is boxed in red. The middle panel shows the size and location of the 17 deletions. The lower panel shows OMIM genes in 5q14.3q21.3. The green dashed line indicates the location of the NR2F1 gene. The first fetal case with BBSOAS was reported in 2022 []. The fetus presented with bilateral mild ventriculomegaly and intracranial cyst by imaging examinations in the late second and early third trimester. Copy number variation sequencing (CNV‐Seq) combined with karyotyping confirmed a novel 7.94 Mb deletion on 5q14.3q15 (89340000_97280000), involving the whole NR2F1 gene. The pregnancy was terminated in the end. The authors suggested that fetal intracranial phenotype abnormality may originate from the deletion of the NR2F1 gene. Postnatal neuroimaging of BBSOAS patients also revealed ventricular enlargement and asymmetry, and BBSOAS mouse models demonstrate ventricular enlargement due to neocortical malformations during neurogenesis []. Here, we reported the second prenatal case with BBSOAS caused by a deletion of 5q14.3q15. The size of the deletion is similar to that of the first fetal case, and both involved the whole NR2F1 gene. However, the fetal case we reported did not show structural abnormalities on ultrasound except for the increased NT. It was referred for prenatal diagnosis merely due to abnormal ultrasound soft markers, high‐risk results in serum screening, and abnormal cfDNA screening findings. Therefore, this clinico‐cytogenomic association of hydrocephalus with deletions of 5q14.3q15 still remains to be verified from more prenatal cases or related animal research results. It is known that increased NT is closely related to adverse pregnancy outcomes such as fetal chromosomal abnormalities, fetal malformations, and genetic syndromes and has become an important indicator for prenatal screening []. This study reported for the first time the detection of BBSOAS in a fetus with increased NT, expanding the prenatal phenotypic spectrum. In addition to efficient screening for trisomy 21, 18, and 13, cfDNA screening also has good detection efficiency for sex chromosome abnormalities and even CNV. The screening efficiency of cfDNA screening for pathogenic CNVs with fragments larger than 6 Mb can reach 83.0%–90.9% [, ]. This is the first reported case of a 5q14.3q15 deletion confirmed by prenatal diagnosis after being identified through cfDNA screening. In addition to the two fetal cases, another 9‐year‐old child with BBSOAS caused by a frameshift mutation in the NR2F1 gene had polyhydramnios during the fetal period []. To the best of our knowledge, these are the prenatal manifestations of BBSOAS cases reported so far. It can be seen from this that there are no specific prenatal ultrasonic manifestations of BBSOAS. Hence, molecular diagnostic techniques are critical for prenatal diagnosis on fetus with BBSOAS.

title: Case Report: Rare triple-line chromosome 9 mosaicism (47,XX,+del(9)(q13)/47,XX,+9/46,XX) associated with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and congenital anomalies.
abstract: Chromosome 9 abnormalities are rare. Full trisomy 9 is mostly incompatible with postnatal survival, whereas mosaic trisomy 9 permits survival with highly variable clinical manifestations. Triple-line mosaicism involving both full trisomy 9 and structural chromosome 9 abnormalities is exceptionally rare. A 1-year-old girl, conceived via IVF, had normal nuchal translucency and NIPT. Prenatal ultrasound showed a single umbilical artery, lower abdominal cyst, borderline ventriculomegaly at 28 weeks, and late polyhydramnios. She was born at 40 weeks, 3,430 g, 49 cm, head circumference 36 cm, Apgar 8/9/9, requiring mild oxygen supplementation. At age 1 year, she exhibited dysmorphic facial features (prominent forehead, hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, short philtrum, low-set mildly dysplastic ears, retrognathia), bilateral ovarian cysts, minimal clinodactyly of the right fifth finger, palmar and plantar crease abnormalities, hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), patent foramen ovale (PFO), previously closed muscular ventricular septal defect (VSD), severe hypotonia, global developmental delay, convergent strabismus, and feeding difficulties requiring gastrostomy. Cranial ultrasound revealed ventriculomegaly, grade II intraventricular hemorrhage, slightly thin corpus callosum, and altered posterior cranial fossa. Postnatal genetic evaluation, including array CGH (comparative genomic hybridization), conventional karyotyping, FISH (fluorescent in situ hybridization), and QF-PCR (Quantitative Fluorescence Polymerase Chain Reaction), identified a complex mosaicism comprising three cell lines: 47,XX,+del(9)(q13)[60%]/47,XX,+9[20%]/46,XX[20%]. This case expands the phenotypic spectrum of chromosome 9 mosaicism and highlights the diagnostic value of multimodal genomic analysis for accurate detection and counselling.

Case Report: Rare triple-line chromosome 9 mosaicism (47,XX,+del(9)(q13)/47,XX,+9/46,XX) associated with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and congenital anomalies

Introduction
Introduction Trisomy 9 is a rare chromosomal condition. Complete, non-mosaic trisomy 9 is usually incompatible with postnatal survival, whereas mosaic trisomy 9 permits survival but presents highly heterogeneous phenotypes, depending on the proportion and tissue distribution of abnormal cells (; ). Survivors may display craniofacial dysmorphism, skeletal anomalies, congenital heart defects, genitourinary malformations, growth retardation, and significant neurologic impairment (). Partial duplications of chromosome 9, especially 9p, represent a separate group of rare chromosomal imbalances. Individuals with 9p duplication syndrome show distinctive facial features, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and congenital anomalies affecting central nervous system (CNS) and cardiovascular systems (; ). Phenotypic overlap between mosaic trisomy 9 and 9p duplication complicates genotype–phenotype correlation. Mosaic cases combining both numerical (full trisomy) and structural (partial duplication/deletion) abnormalities of chromosome 9 are exceedingly rare (). Such cases likely arise via postzygotic mitotic errors and/or sequential chromosomal rearrangements, resulting in clonal diversification. Tissue-specific mosaic distribution strongly influences phenotype. Because of this variability, accurate genotype–phenotype correlation remains challenging, and longitudinal clinical data are scarce (; ). High-resolution genomic technologies have highlighted limitations of single-method diagnostics. Chromosomal microarray (CMA/aCGH) can detect copy-number imbalances but may underestimate mosaicism. FISH and QF-PCR are required to reveal minor or structural abnormal clones (; ). Multimodal cytogenetic evaluation is therefore essential when clinical features suggest mosaicism beyond array detection. Here, we report a 1-year-old girl with three coexisting chromosome 9 cell lines: 47,XX,+del(9)(q13)/47,XX,+9/46,XX, presenting with severe neurodevelopmental impairment, feeding difficulties, dysmorphism, ovarian cysts, and congenital cardiac anomalies. We provide comprehensive clinical, radiologic, and molecular characterization.

Case description
Case description The patient is a one-year-old girl, the first child of her family, conceived via in vitro fertilization (IVF) after 12 months of unexplained infertility, to a 38 years mother and a 40 years old father. Her prenatal course was generally unremarkable, with normal first-trimester screening and non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). Prenatal ultrasound revealed a single umbilical artery, a cyst in the lower abdomen, and borderline ventriculomegaly at 28 weeks. Polyhydramnios developed in the late third trimester, prompting closer monitoring. She was delivered at 40 weeks gestation, weighing 3,430 g (≈50th percentile), 49 cm in length (≈10th percentile), and with a head circumference of 36 cm (≈90th percentile). Apgar scores were 8, 9, and 9 at 1, 5, and 10 min, respectively, and mild oxygen supplementation was required. At 1 year of age, the patient displayed characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism, including a prominent forehead, hypertelorism, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, a short philtrum, retrognathia, and low-set, mildly dysplastic ears. Cardiac examination revealed a symmetrical chest with a regular rhythm; a previously hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus had been closed percutaneously, a muscular ventricular septal defect had spontaneously closed, and a patent foramen ovale persisted. Abdominal and genitourinary examination was unremarkable, though ultrasonography identified bilateral ovarian cysts. Hands exhibited a suggestive four-finger crease, and the feet showed slight alterations in plantar creases, with minimal clinodactyly of the right fifth finger. Neurologically, eye contact was brief, bilateral convergent strabismus was present, and generalized hypotonia was noted. Spontaneous motor activity was limited, and she was unable to sit independently. Persistent feeding difficulties necessitated a gastrostomy tube. Cranial ultrasonography revealed ventriculomegaly, grade II intraventricular hemorrhage, a slightly thin corpus callosum, and alterations of the posterior cranial fossa. The patient remains under ongoing multidisciplinary follow-up with pediatric cardiologists, neurologists, endocrinologists, gastroenterologists, and developmental specialists.

Genetic findings
Genetic findings During pregnancy, routine prenatal screening, including first-trimester nuchal translucency measurement and NIPT, did not reveal an increased risk for common aneuploidies. Ultrasound examinations identified a single umbilical artery, a cyst in the lower abdomen, borderline ventriculomegaly at 28 weeks, and polyhydramnios in late pregnancy. No invasive prenatal genetic testing was performed with normal result. Postnatally, genetic evaluation at 1 year of age included conventional karyotyping and FISH on cells isolated from peripheral blood, and isolated DNA for array CGH, and QF-PCR analysis. On 200 metaphases examined: 100 using GTG banding and 100 using FISH (CEP9(aqua)+9qter(red)): 160 metaphases reveled the karyotype 47,XX,+del(9)(q13), 2 metaphases: 47,XX,+9 and 38 metaphases were normal: 46,XX (, ). Additional 400 interphase were examined by FISH, 240 nuclei showed + del(9)(q13), 80 cells: +9 and 80 cells were normal (). Array CGH demonstrated a gain of the entire short arm of chromosome 9 in ∼80% of cells and a gain of the long arm in ∼20%: arr(9p)x3[0.8],(9q)x3[0.2] (). QF-PCR confirmed a third cell line representing full trisomy 9. The final mosaic karyotype according to ISCN 2024: Karyotype of the majority of the cells: 47,XX,+del(9)(q13). (A) Metaphase FISH using CEP9 (aqua) and 9qter (red) DNA probes (Vysis-Abbott) showing metaphase with additional 9p (left) and full trisomy 9 (right). (B) Interphase FISH using 9p21 (red) and 9q21 (green) DNA probes (Kreatech-Leica) showing all three cell lines: normal (left), +9p (middle), +9 (right). SurePrint G3 Custom CGH Array 4 × 180K, CytoGenomics 5.0.0.38 (Agilent Technologies): arr(9p)x3[0.8],(9q)x3[0.2]. mos 47,XX,+del(9)(q13)[160]/47,XX,+9[2]/46,XX[38].nuc ish(CDKN2Ax3,9q21x2)[240/400]/(CDKN2A,9q21)x3[80/400].arr (9p)x3[0.8],(9q)x3[0.2]. Both parents were evaluated for the presence of low-level mosaicism using FISH with CEP 9 DNA probes. Interphase FISH analysis and metaphase karyotyping were performed on cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes. A total of 200 interphase nuclei and 100 metaphase cells were examined for each individual. Normal results were obtained.

Follow-up and prognosis
Follow-up and prognosis Since birth, the patient has required close multidisciplinary monitoring. Neurodevelopmental impairment remains severe, with persistent hypotonia and limited motor activity. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed bilateral convergent strabismus. Cardiac anomalies have been managed, including closure of PDA and spontaneous resolution of VSD, with ongoing monitoring of PFO. Feeding difficulties persist and are managed via gastrostomy. Early intervention, physical and occupational therapy, and nutritional support are essential. Given the complex chromosomal mosaicism, long-term neurodevelopmental prognosis remains guarded. Prognosis in mosaic trisomy 9 spectrum disorders is highly variable and depends primarily on (1) the proportion of full trisomy 9 cells, (2) the presence of major organ malformations, and (3) the degree of central nervous system involvement. In contrast to complete trisomy 9—which is frequently associated with perinatal lethality—long-term survival has been documented in mosaic cases, particularly when a substantial euploid cell line is present. Based on previously reported mosaic trisomy 9 cases, survival into childhood and adolescence is possible, particularly in individuals without major organ system failure. The prognosis for our patient appears favorable for survival, guarded for neurodevelopmental outcome and dependent on early supportive interventions. Her phenotype suggests an intermediate severity within the mosaic trisomy 9 spectrum. The presence of a normal cell line likely mitigates the lethal potential while central nervous system involvement remains the principal determinant of long-term functional outcome ().

Discussion
Discussion Mosaic trisomy 9 exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity, ranging from mild dysmorphic features to severe multi-system involvement with profound developmental impairment (; ). Craniofacial dysmorphisms—prominent forehead, hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, short philtrum, retrognathia, and low-set or dysplastic ears—are consistent and were present in our patient (; ). Cardiovascular involvement is frequent, including PDA, VSD, ASD, and other structural anomalies (; ). Our patient presented with a PDA, muscular VSD (spontaneously closed), and PFO, consistent with previous reports (; ). CNS anomalies, such as ventriculomegaly, intraventricular hemorrhage, corpus callosum thinning, and posterior fossa alterations, correspond with severe global developmental delay and hypotonia (; ). The proportion of abnormal cells in the CNS may exceed that in peripheral blood, illustrating the limitations of blood-based cytogenetic assessments (; ). Genitourinary anomalies are sporadically reported in 9p duplication and trisomy 9 mosaicism (; ). Our patient had bilateral ovarian cysts, expanding the phenotypic spectrum. In our patient with several clinical features, including typical craniofacial dysmorphism, ventriculomegaly, hypotonia, developmental delay, mild limb anomalies, and congenital heart defects, specifically patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and ventricular septal defect (VSD), at the same time, several of the more severe anomalies commonly reported in mosaic trisomy 9 are not present. These include major limb malformations, severe renal anomalies, clefting, complex congenital heart defects, holoprosencephaly or other severe brain malformations, and seizures (). This relatively milder structural presentation is consistent with mosaicism, meaning the presence of a normal cell line. It may also indicate a lower proportion of cells with full trisomy 9 or a tissue-specific distribution of abnormal cell lines. Mosaic trisomy 9 is known to have one of the broadest phenotypic spectra among autosomal trisomies. Based on the current clinical findings, this patient appears to fall toward the moderate end of the severity spectrum rather than the severe or lethal end. In vitro fertilization (IVF) has been raised regarding a possible increase in congenital malformations and inborn errors among assisted reproductive technologies (ART) conceived offspring. The absolute risk increase is small, and the majority of ART-conceived children are healthy. Although ART is associated with a slightly elevated relative risk of congenital malformations and rare imprinting disorders, the overall prognosis for ART-conceived children remains favorable. The increased risk of congenital malformations discussed in ART is generally multifactorial and modest, whereas partial or complete trisomy 9 mosaicism represents a specific chromosomal abnormality with intrinsically high malformation risk, independent of ART itself (; ; ). The triple-line mosaicism likely resulted from early postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction followed by structural rearrangement. A normal cell line in mosaic trisomy 9 can arise through trisomic rescue, and this mechanism creates a theoretical and biologically plausible risk of uniparental disomy (UPD) 9. Parents refused additional molecular testing that would explain the origin of chromosomes 9 in the girl. Even minority abnormal cell populations may impact phenotype, especially in vital organs (; ; ). Diagnostic challenges necessitate a multimodal approach. CMA/aCGH detects copy-number variations but may underestimate low-level mosaicism; karyotyping identifies structural rearrangements; FISH and QF-PCR allow detection and quantification of minor abnormal clones (; ). Discrepancies between methods are common when mosaicism is tissue-limited or low-level (; ; ). Genotype-phenotype correlation remains challenging. This case underscores the importance of multidisciplinary follow-up for cardiac, neurologic, endocrine, gastroenterologic, and developmental support. Early interventions may improve quality of life, though neurodevelopmental outcomes remain guarded in severe mosaic cases (; ; ). Reporting such rare cases enhances genotype-phenotype correlations, informs prenatal counseling, and guides management strategies (; ; ).

title: Antenatal discovery of mosaic trisomy 14 in an early-onset malformative syndrome.
label_reason: Case report with US anomalies and FISH/CVS cytogenetics.
abstract: Trisomy 14 mosaicism is a rare chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of an extra chromosome 14 in a subset of cells. Its true prevalence is unclear due to frequent early pregnancy loss. Clinical manifestations vary widely and include fetal growth restriction, craniofacial dysmorphia, cardiac and genitourinary anomalies, with no consistent correlation between mosaicism level and severity. We report a case of prenatal trisomy 14 mosaicism diagnosed via chorionic villus sampling and confirmed in fetal tissue. Ultrasound at 15 weeks showed multiple congenital anomalies affecting the craniofacial region, heart, and limbs , along with growth restriction. Given the severity, termination of pregnancy was performed at 17 weeks. Postmortem examination confirmed the anomalies, including abnormal male external genitalia. FISH analysis on muscle tissue demonstrated trisomy 14 mosaicism in approximately 35% of nuclei. This case contributes to the limited prenatal literature on trisomy 14 mosaicism and emphasizes the value of early imaging and cytogenetic analysis in diagnosis and counselling. It highlights the importance of concurrent detailed early sonographic evaluation and targeted cytogenetic testing in suspected malformative syndromes, as well as the diagnostic value of postmortem tissue-specific FISH to better characterize the mosaic distribution. Because mosaicism levels may vary markedly between tissues and do not necessarily correlate with phenotypic severity, this case also illustrates the limitations of chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis, and supports multi-tissue sampling in fetopathological assessment to refine prognostic evaluation and genetic counselling. Keywords: Trisomy 14, Mosaicism, Antenatal diagnosis, Sonography, Multiple congenital anomalies, Fetopathology
text:
Antenatal discovery of mosaic trisomy 14 in an early-onset malformative syndrome

Background
Background Trisomy 14 mosaicism is a rare genetic disorder in which some cells of the body have an extra 14th chromosome. Its exact prevalence is unknown due to its rarity and the fact that it frequently leads to early spontaneous miscarriages. It has a 3:1 female-to-male ratio []. One of the predisposing factors that can lead to trisomy 14, apart from advanced maternal age, is the presence of a balanced Robertsonian translocation in one of the parents. A partial or full correction of the trisomy can occur early on, leading respectively to a mosaic trisomy 14 or a uniparental disomy (UPD), resulting in Kagami-Ogata or Temple syndrome. Anomalies frequently associated with this pathology include growth restriction, craniofacial anomalies (microcephaly, hypertelorism with abnormal palpebral fissures, broad nose, auricular anomalies including low-set ears, cleft palate, micro-retrognathia), congenital heart defects and genitourinary anomalies [–]. There is a diversity and variability of clinical signs, and the severity of these manifestations is not correlated with the rate of mosaicism []. The definitive diagnosis of trisomy 14 mosaicism cannot be established by ultrasound alone, but may be suspected when suggestive imaging findings are present []. Therefore, further case reports are needed to better characterize this condition. Here, we describe a case of trisomy 14 mosaicism initially suspected following abnormal first-trimester screening, with atypical maternal serum markers indicating high risk for aneuploidy, confirmed by chorionic villus sampling and fetal muscle biopsy.

Case presentation
Case presentation This was the second pregnancy of a woman in her 30 s; her first child was a healthy 3-year-old boy. There was no consanguinity or family history. The mother had Graves’ disease treated with Propylthiouracil. For this pregnancy, the first-trimester ultrasound (using a Voluson™ system) revealed an increased nuchal translucency of 2.6 mm for a crown-rump length of 51.4 mm, which was between the 95th and 99th percentiles. The first-trimester serum markers were 0.18 MoM for PAPP-A and 0.15 MoM for free β-HCG (atypically low levels), leading to an estimated combined risk of aneuploidy of 1/16 (high risk), indicating the need for chorionic villus sampling at 15 weeks of gestation. Array-CGH performed on DNA extracted from native chorionic villi identified a complete and homogenous trisomy 14, with a log-ratio of 0.541. Based on the log-ratio, we could extrapolate a mosaicism of 91% (Fig. ). However, considering the mechanism underlying trisomy 14 and the limitations of array-CGH in detecting whole chromosome imbalances, the final formula according to the International System for human Cytogenetic Nomenclature (ISCN 2024) was arr (14)x3. No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic Copy Number Variation (CNV) was detected. Cell culture was unsuccessful and did not produce usable mitoses. Array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (array-CGH; hg19) performed on DNA extracted from native chorionic villus sampling showed a complete and homogeneous trisomy 14, with a log-ratio of 0.541 (corresponding to a mosaicism level of 91%). The final result, according to ISCN 2024, was arr (14)x3 A referral ultrasound performed at 15 weeks + 1 day of gestation (using a Voluson™ system with color, pulsed and continuous Doppler modes) revealed multiple malformations including a unilateral cleft lip and an anomaly of the caudal spine, a positional abnormality of the left foot and widening of the first interdigital toe space (Fig. ). A cardiac malformation that was difficult to characterize was also identified, including a small pulmonary artery, a ventricular septal defect, and a right aortic arch (Fig. ). Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), at the 3rd percentile, was also noted, affecting abdominal and femoral growth. A termination of pregnancy was performed at 17 weeks + 4 days of gestation. Obstetric ultrasound performed via the abdominal approach at 15 weeks + 1 day. A: widening of the first right intertoe space (axial section of the right foot); B: positional abnormality of the left foot with a varus appearance (sagittal section); C-D: unilateral cleft lip (axial (C) and coronal (D) section of the face, respectively); E–F–G: axial sections of the heart showing, respectively, pulmonary artery hypoplasia (E: slender pulmonary trunk; F: slender left pulmonary artery branch, thin arrow), a right aortic arch (F: thick arrow), and a ventricular septal defect (G) The parents consented to an external examination, radiography and a muscle biopsy, but declined a complete autopsy. This external examination revealed a male fetus with growth restriction : fetal weight of 109.3 g (−1.71 Standard Deviation (SD) according to Guihard-Costal et al. references []), crown-heel length of 180 mm (−1.61 SD), crown-rump length of 120 mm (−1.71 SD), head circumference of 135 mm (−0.62 SD) and foot length of 21 mm (−1.25 SD). The fetus had hypertelorism and malar hypoplasia. The external eye examination was unremarkable. The ears were low-set and posteriorly rotated, with normal auditory canals and patent choanae. A right-sided cleft lip and alveolus was observed, along with a high-arched closed anterior palate and a posterior cleft palate. There was a slight micro-retrognathia. In the limbs, there was a clinodactyly of the fifth fingers and a bilateral clubfoot, reducible and less pronounced on the right. The patellae were present, and all four limbs were thin. The nipples were closely spaced along the midline. A sacrococcygeal dimple was present. The external genitalia were male but appeared abnormal, with a bifid scrotum, a short and arched genital tubercle, and hypospadias. The anus was anteriorly displaced (Fig. ). Fetal photographs. A: Whole-body, right profile view; B-C: Cephalic pole respectively from the front and from the right profile, notably showing facial dysmorphism and the right labioalveolar cleft; D: external genitalia and perineum, frontal view: bifid scrotum, short and curved genital tubercle, hypospadias, anteriorly displaced anus; E: left equinovarus foot Radiologically (Fig. ), there was a notable segmented platyspondyly associated with structural abnormalities of the vertebral bodies, particularly visible at the thoracolumbar junction, with abnormally concave vertebral endplates, creating a characteristic fish-vertebra appearance. The nasal bones were present, with a depressed nasal bridge. The femoral length was measured at 18 mm, which is below the 3rd percentile for a gestational age of 17 weeks, without any abnormalities in bone mineralization or maturation. Post-mortem fetal radiographs from the front and side The placental examination revealed a normally configured placenta with a weight at approximately the 10th percentile for gestational age and no notable macroscopic or histological abnormalities. Interphase Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH, Fig. ) performed on a fetal quadriceps muscle biopsy using a subtelomeric 14qter probe in red (14q32.33) and RP11-642H22 in green (non-commercial Bacterial Artificial Chromosome probe) confirmed the presence of mosaic trisomy 14 in approximately 35% of examined nuclei (after a double-blind analysis). A) Interphase Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) performed on fetal muscle biopsy showing three red (14qter = 14q32.33) and three green (RP11-642H22) signals in trisomic nuclei. B) Schematic representation of probe localization on chromosome 14 and expected signal patterns in disomic and trisomic cells The full formula according to ISCN 2024 was nuc ish (RP11-642H22,dJ820M16)x3[87/248]. The karyotypes of both parents were normal.

Discussion
Discussion In a 2013 literature review studying mosaic trisomy 14 diagnosed antenatally, Chen et al. [] found that at least 50% of cases exhibited significant phenotypic abnormalities, including a wide range of antenatal ultrasound findings such as microcephaly, facial dysmorphism, brain and cardiac abnormalities, genital anomalies, limb deformities and polyhydramnios. In our case, early ultrasound indeed revealed fetal growth restriction, a cleft, cardiac anomalies, and lower limb deformities. These observations are consistent with those reported in the study by Shinawi et al. []. Common characteristics included growth restriction (present in all cases), developmental delay of varying severity, congenital anomalies (including cardiac defects, skeletal abnormalities, neurological anomalies, clefts and micrognathia), pigmented skin lesions, and dysmorphic features. These findings are also in line with other reports in the literature [, ]. A literature search was conducted using PubMed and Google Scholar with the keywords “trisomy 14,” “mosaic,” and “prenatal diagnosis,” identifying 14 reported cases [–, , –]. We describe here a fifteenth case. (Table ) However, this review is not exhaustive, as it was not performed as a formal systematic review and publication bias is likely to happen given the rarity of this condition. On top of the anomalies previously described, four cases of congenital heart defects were reported antenatally. It is important to note that some of these cases are relatively old and reflect past clinical practices. Since then, obstetric ultrasound techniques have improved significantly and become more standardized, despite continuous improvements in ultrasound techniques, some cardiac malformations can remain hard to detect and characterize, as seen with our case. However, several studies suggest that there is no clear correlation between phenotypic abnormalities and the level of mosaicism detected in accessible tissues such as amniotic fluid [, ]. For example, in the case reported by Cheung et al. [], the mosaicism rate at amniocentesis was only 9% (initially absent on the first reading), yet the fetus exhibited severe phenotypic anomalies after birth, including marked facial dysmorphism, cleft palate, micrognathia with glossoptosis, anteriorly placed anus, clubfoot (equinovarus), left kidney agenesis and congenital heart disease (ventricular septal defect and interatrial communications) with postnatal pulmonary hypertension. After multiple hospitalizations for apnea with cyanosis and vomiting with growth restriction, and placement of a tracheostomy at 4 months because of feeding-related hypoxia, the child ultimately died following cardiorespiratory arrest. Interestingly, the mosaicism rate was 37% in postnatal blood and 0% in the skin, suggesting a discordance between the ectodermal and the mesodermal layers. In this case, severity appeared to be mainly related to the numerous malformations, particularly the heart defect and possibly the Pierre Robin sequence. Conversely, the case reported by Lambert et al. []. illustrates the opposite situation. Amniocentesis performed at 17 weeks and repeated at 21 weeks due to advanced parental age, revealed high levels of trisomy 14 mosaicism (71.4% and 60%) despite the absence of ultrasound anomalies. At autopsy following termination of pregnancy, the female fetus exhibited only mild growth restriction, moderate micrognathia and pulmonary hyperlobulation, without other abnormalities. The mosaicism rate varied between tissues (32% in ovarian tissue, 12.9% in skin and 4% in kidney), although these organs were otherwise normal. These contrasting observations suggest that there is no specific mosaicism threshold above which a severe phenotype is certain, nor below which a severe phenotype can be excluded. In living individuals, the degree of intellectual disability may depend on the level of mosaicism in brain tissue; however, most reported cases exhibited moderate to severe intellectual disability, and again, severity is not correlated with the mosaicism rate in circulating blood []. An interesting perspective would be to the possibility to correlate the degree of intellectual disability to the rate of mosaicism from DNA extracted from keratinocytes. Indeed, DNA is usually extracted from cultured fibroblasts, reflecting the mesodermal layer, whereas DNA extracted directly from keratinocytes reflects the ectodermal layer, which gives rise to the neuroectoderm and, consequently, to most brain cells. Overall, phenotypic variability is more likely explained by an unequal distribution of trisomic cells across tissues rather than solely by the detected blood mosaicism rate. Consequently, the timing of the chromosomal anomaly during embryonic development may also play an important role in determining clinical variability and severity. The origin of mosaicism may influence phenotype. Mosaic trisomy 14 mainly results from partial correction of a full trisomy (“trisomy rescue”), or very rarely from a post-zygotic mitotic error. In either case, since chromosome 14 contains imprinted genes, abnormal expression of these genes may worsen the clinical presentation, as illustrated in the case reported by Zhang et al. []. Moreover, the consequences could be even worse in the case of an isodisomy, that could reveal an autosomal recessive disease for which one of the parents is a carrier. While the clinical features observed in cases of UPD without trisomy are very similar (both – Kagami-Ogata and Temple syndromes – mainly present with IUGR), a majority of these features are also observed in trisomy 14, which explains the strong phenotypic overlap between these three conditions. In addition, the distribution of trisomic cells among tissues could still remain a major determinant of phenotypic severity. If a high proportion of trisomic cells is present in critical organs such as the brain or heart, severe manifestations may still occur. The main difficulty lies in the fact that genetic analyses are usually performed on a limited number of tissues, which only indirectly reflect the distribution of trisomic cells across embryological layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm). In our case, complete trisomy 14 was first identified by array-CGH on chorionic villi, while FISH analysis on fetal muscle biopsy estimated that 35% of nuclei carried the extra chromosome, suggesting a pre-mitotic origin. However, as discussed above, the clinical severity ultimately depends on the distribution of abnormal cells across tissues. Finally, certain chromosomal structures, such as isochromosomes, can generate more complex phenotypes depending on the chromosomal regions affected. For example, isochromosomes involving the long arm of chromosome 14 (14q) can undergo additional rearrangements, sometimes leading to the formation of chromosome 14 rings, which may further complicate the phenotype [, ]. Given the instability of these structures, the supernumerary chromosome could also be lost across the consecutive mitotic divisions, and could ultimately lead to either a complete rescue or a UPD. Recently, in the systematic literature review conducted by Kovaleva et al. (2022) [] analyzed 194 cases of complete trisomy 14 and two cases of mosaic among 21,082 tested spontaneous abortions, as well as 76 individuals carrying trisomy 14 mosaicism diagnosed prenatally or postnatally. The authors observed a marked female predominance and an association with advanced maternal age, strongly suggesting an exclusive prenatal origin of the trisomy 14. Moreover, 25% of families had a history of reproductive disorders, suggesting a possible genetic predisposition to chromosomal nondisjunction. An unusually high proportion of isochromosomes was also noted. Regarding prenatal diagnosis, cases were diagnosed between 11 and 26 weeks of gestation, once again confirming that diagnosis may be achieved as early as the first trimester through chorionic villus sampling, although subsequent confirmation by amniocentesis may sometimes be required to rule out confined placental mosaicism, particularly in the absence of clear ultrasound anomalies. However, as seen previously, amniocentesis can still be insufficient for trisomy restricted to the mesodermal layer. Finally, this study confirmed that complete trisomy 14 is almost always lethal and that only mosaic cases, though very rare, can survive. Overall, factors influencing survival to live birth versus early pregnancy loss in mosaic trisomy 14 remain poorly defined. As stated previously, no clear correlation has been established between the level of mosaicism and phenotypic severity [, ]. While complete non-mosaic trisomy 14 is typically associated with first-trimester miscarriage, partial trisomy 14q is a rare condition with poorly defined genotype-phenotype correlations []. Current evidence suggests that outcomes are more likely driven by the distribution of the trisomic cell line between fetal and placental tissues, as well as the presence and severity of structural anomalies, with true fetal involvement more often associated with adverse outcomes, including pregnancy loss []. The resulting phenotype is likely influenced by the extent of the duplicated 14q segment, associated chromosomal abnormalities, parental origin of the rearrangement and gene dosage effects within the imprinted 14q32 region []. The role of UPD 14 and imprinting effects may further contribute to clinical variability [, ]. In addition, epidemiological observations (female predominance, advanced maternal age and prior adverse obstetric history) support the implication of meiotic error and trisomy rescue mechanisms, which may partly explain the heterogeneity of outcomes []. Among prenatal imaging findings, micrognathia likely represents one of the most significant prognostic features, given its association with tracheoesophageal obstruction and death []. To date, no studies have specifically investigated the link between trophoblastic mosaicism in trisomy 14 and macroscopic or histological placental lesions. We conducted a retrospective, single-center investigation using the Defgen software to identify cases of trisomy 14 diagnosed over the past ten years. Only three cases were recorded in the context of prenatal diagnosis. Among these, two underwent complete pathological examination of the placenta, and no major abnormalities were identified. These two cases included the present one and another case of trisomy 14 with a 10% mosaicism rate in the amniotic fluid. The trophoblast was not tested in this second case, which involved multiple congenital anomalies identified in the third trimester. This case also showed maternal heterodisomy of chromosome 14. In the third case, chorionic villus sampling was performed due to high-risk maternal serum markers, and a fetoplacental discrepancy was found: direct analysis showed a 47,XY,+14 karyotype, while the cultured mesenchymal core yielded a normal 46,XY result. The amniotic fluid karyotype was also 46,XY, confirming confined placental mosaicism to the cytotrophoblast (chorionic ectoderm), while absent from the mesoblast and embryonic ectoderm. No uniparental disomy was detected. Placental data were limited to a macroscopic examination, which revealed no abnormalities. Although data remain limited, no association was identified between trophoblastic mosaicism and placental pathology.

Conclusion
Conclusion This case illustrates an early antenatal ultrasound presentation of trisomy 14 mosaicism associated with severe and multiple congenital anomalies, consistent with those described in the literature. It also highlights the marked phenotypic variability of trisomy 14 mosaicism and the absence of a clear correlation between the level of mosaicism detected in each tissue and the severity of clinical manifestations, which may depend on the initial distribution of trisomic cells across different embryonic layers. Early recognition of suggestive ultrasound findings is therefore important to prompt appropriate genetic investigations and improve diagnostic accuracy. The combined use of detailed imaging and cytogenetic analyses is essential to refine prognostic evaluation and provide appropriate pregnancy, neonatal, and genetic counselling to affected families.
