title: Prenatal diagnosis and molecular cytogenetic analysis of Xp22.31 microdeletions and microduplications in Chinese populations.
label_reason: Fetuses with Xp22.31 CNVs; ultrasound abnormalities reported per fetus alongside CMA and WES.
abstract: Chromosome rearrangements are frequently observed in the Xp22.31 region. Xp22.31 microdeletion is linked to X-linked ichthyosis, whereas the pathogenicity of Xp22.31 microduplication remains a subject of controversy. In the present study, 52 additional foetuses with Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications were presented, with the aim of providing further insights into the prenatal diagnosis and genetic counselling of Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications. A retrospective analysis was conducted involving a total of 4,251 pregnant women who received amniocentesis of prenatal diagnosis in our hospital from January 2017 to August 2022. All of the subjects were subjected to karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) for evaluation of chromosomal abnormalities. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was subsequently employed to explore additional variants in individuals presenting unexplained clinical features. Among the enrolled subjects, a total of 52 cases with Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications were detected using CMA, with a detection rate of 1.22% (52/4251). A total of 35 foetuses carried Xp22.31 microduplications and most of them exhibited normal developmental milestone after birth, except one case with motor and speech developmental delay. Additionally, 17 foetuses harbored Xp22.31 microdeletions, 10 male foetuses exhibited ichthyosis after birth, 6 female foetuses manifested normal clinical features, and the remaining were terminated based on parental request. In the present study, WES was further conducted on a foetus with renal abnormalities; however, no likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants in genes related to the observed phenotype were identified. The present authors propose that Xp22.31 microduplication may be a benign copy number variant. In addition, the findings reveal, for the first time, a previously unknown association between renal agenesis and Xp22.31 microdeletion, thus expanding the range of clinical manifestations associated with Xp22.31 microdeletions. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12884-026-09113-1. Keywords: Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications, Chromosomal microarray analysis, Karyotype analysis, Prenatal diagnosis, Whole exome sequencing
text:
Prenatal diagnosis and molecular cytogenetic analysis of Xp22.31 microdeletions and microduplications in Chinese populations

Introduction
Introduction The Xp22.31 segment of the human X chromosome short arm is characterised by a high level of genomic instability and is frequently subject to rearrangements. This instability is attributed to the presence of low copy repeats (LCRs) dispersed around the S232 region []. Previous studies have indicated that unequal recombination events involving the flanking regions of the two S232 elements can result in the loss of genetic material in the steroid sulfatase (STS) region. This frequently leads to the formation of a recurrent Xp22.31 microdeletion spanning approximately 1.6 Mb in size []. Xp22.31 microdeletions covering the STS gene account for approximately 90% of cases of X-linked ichthyosis (OMIM 308100, XLI), which is an X-linked recessive inheritance disease, with an incidence rate of 1/1300 ~ 1/1500 [–]. The remaining 10% of XLI cases may be attributed to mutations or other structural variants occurring within the STS gene itself. XLI is typically characterised by the presence of widespread shedding of large, firmly attached, dark brown scales, and may also be associated with corneal opacity and cryptorchidism []. Although Xp22.31 microdeletion is well defined, the pathogenicity of Xp22.31 microduplication remains unclear and there is a scarcity of available reports. Xp22.31 microduplications have been observed in the healthy general population, but also in patients with abnormal clinical features []. At present, there is ongoing controversy regarding the role of Xp22.31 microduplications in contributing to a distinct clinical phenotype. Several studies have reported that Xp22.31 duplication may be a benign variant [–], while others have proposed its potential pathogenicity [, ]. Moreover, there are studies suggesting that these duplications could be classified as variants of unknown significance (VOUS) [, ]. In the present study, a retrospective study with prenatal ultrasound features was conducted. Molecular characterisation and postnatal clinical findings were collected in 52 cases with Xp22.31 microdeletions and microduplications. In addition, whole exome sequencing was further performed to detect sequence variants in foetuses with unexplained clinical features. The aim of the study was to provide further insights into the relationship between genotype and phenotype in the context of Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications and offer additional data for genetic counselling.

Material and methods
Material and methods Subjects Between January 2017 and August 2022, a total of 4,251 pregnant women, each presenting various high-risk factors such as ultrasound anomalies, advanced maternal age, an elevated risk of Down syndrome, a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes, and a heightened risk associated with Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing, were advised to undergo amniocentesis for prenatal diagnosis at Quanzhou Women's and Children's Hospital. All the enrolled subjects were subject to karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis following the provision of written informed consent. Ethics Committee approval was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee of Quanzhou Women’s and Children’s Hospital to the commencement of the study (2020No.31). Karyotype analysis Approximately 20 ml amniotic fluid was collected from the foetuses for karyotype analysis. As described in a previous report by the present authors [], the amniotic fluid cells were harvested using a SinochromeChromprepII automatic chromosome harvesting system according to the standard protocol (Shanghai Lechen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.). Giemsa staining was employed, and a total of thirty karyotypes were observed and documented. Subsequently, five of these karyotypes were subjected to detailed analysis. The nomenclature and diagnosis of these karyotypes were determined in accordance with the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN 2020). Genomics DNA extraction About 10 ml of amniotic fluid was collected from the foetuses, while 2 ml of peripheral blood was drawn from the parents. As described in a previous report by the present authors [], genomics DNA were extracted from enrolled subjects for Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and Whole exome sequencing (WES) detection using the QIAamp DNA Blood Kit (QIAGEN, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol (www.qiagen.com). Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) CMA was performed using a single-nucleotide polymorphism based Affymetrix Cytoscan 750 K chip (Life Technologies, American) []. The detected copy number variants (CNVs) were further assessed using the Database of Genomic Variants (DGV), Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM), DECIPHER and PubMed databases, as well as other databases []. For the interpretation of CNVs, a collaborative consensus approach was employed, aligning with the standards and guidelines established jointly by the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) and the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen) []. Whole exome sequencing (WES) Genomic DNA extracted from the patient was subsequently subjected to WES analysis. The quantification of DNA was performed using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The genomic DNA was fragmented to achieve an approximate mean fragment length of 150–200 base pairs using the Covaris LE220 (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA). Subsequently, the sheared DNA fragments were utilised for library preparation, targeting specific genomic regions, through the employment of the SureSelect whole-exome capture kit (Agilent). The Illumina DNA Standards and Primer Premix Kit (Kapa Biosystems, Boston, MA, USA) were used for the quantification of sequencing libraries. The libraries were sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) []. Data analysis The specific process of data analysis was conducted according to a previous report by the present authors [, ]. In brief, the data analysis encompassed several steps, including variant calling, annotation, and variant screening. The dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, Exome Aggregation Consortium and Exome Variant Server databases were used for searching the minor allele frequencies (MAF < 0.1%) of all known variants. The OMIM, ClinVar, Human Gene Mutation Database and SwissVar databases were used to determine the harmfulness and pathogenicity of the detected variants []. According to the ACMG guidelines, variants were classified as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variants of unknown significance (VOUS), likely benign and benign [].

Results
Results Subjects’ information In the present study, a total of 52 cases with Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications were detected using CMA, with a detection rate of 1.22% (52/4,251). Among them, 35 foetuses carrying Xp22.31 microduplications and 17 foetuses carrying Xp22.31 microdeletions were detected. The majority of cases yielded normal karyotype results, with the exception of one case that also exhibited a balanced translocation between chromosome 3 and 12, characterised as (46,XY,t(3;12)(q21;q24)). As demonstrated in Table , the size of the Xp22.31 microdeletions ranged from 1.5 Mb to 1.6 Mb. As listed in Table , the size of the Xp22.31 microduplication fragments ranged from 117.1 Kb to 1.6 Mb. Following the standards and guidelines established by ACMG and ClinGen, Xp22.31 microdeletions were interpreted as pathogenic variants. However, Xp22.31 microduplications were classified as VOUS. Parental CMA verification was conducted in seven cases of the Xp22.31 microdeletions. Among these cases, two were identified as de novo occurrences, while the remaining five were inherited from the mother (Table ). Further, parental verification was conducted for 19 cases of Xp22.31 microduplications. Among these cases, 13 were inherited from the mother, while 6 were inherited from the father (Table ). Prenatal ultrasound examination results Out of the 17 foetuses with Xp22.31 microdeletions, prenatal ultrasound examination results were available for 11 cases. Among these, nine exhibited soft marker anomalies, one had structural anomalies, and one showed normal ultrasound examination results. As demonstrated in Table , cardiac hyperechogenicity, pyelic separation, and polyhydramnios were the most common ultrasound anomalies. Moreover, Case 16 presented with a structural anomaly characterised by left renal agenesis (Table ). Additionally, 31 out of 35 foetuses with Xp22.31 microduplications had available prenatal ultrasound detection results. The ultrasound findings indicated that among the foetuses studied, one displayed a structural anomaly in the form of a small ventricular septal defect, 17 foetuses exhibited soft marker anomalies, and the remaining 13 cases showed normal results upon ultrasound examination. As delineated in Table , the most common ultrasound anomalies were cardiac hyperechogenicity, bowel hyperechogenicity, and polyhydramnios. Pregnancy outcome follow up The follow-up results of pregnancy outcomes in the 17 cases with Xp22.31 microdeletions revealed that one male foetus with left renal agenesis was delivered through induced labour, while the remaining 16 cases continued their pregnancies. Subsequent one-year postnatal follow-up results showed that 6 females exhibited normal clinical features, whereas all 10 males presented with ichthyosis as the sole clinical manifestation, without any additional clinical features (Table ). As shown in Table , 34 cases were successfully followed up, and one case was lost to follow-up. Among these cases, 4 opted for pregnancy termination, while the rest continued their pregnancies. Of those who continued, 29 cases showed normal features upon follow-up. However, one girl with a 1.6 Mb Xp22.31 microduplication exhibited speech and motor developmental delay at the age of 3 (Table ). Additional variants investigation using WES An additional pedigree investigation was conducted for a subject with Xp22.31 microdeletion (Case 16 of Table ) (Fig. ). Familial CMA verification results elicited that the Xp22.31 microdeletion was inherited from the mother who had normal clinical features. In addition, the variant was also transmitted to the elder brother in this family who had abnormal clinical phenotypes including ichthyosis, cryptorchidism, micropenis, and left renal agenesis. The pedigree information and genetic analysis results of the enrolled family. The pedigree information of the enrolled family. The ultrasound examination results delineated a left renal agenesis in the fetus. Chromosomal microarray analysis indicated a 1.6 Mb Xp22.31 microdeletion in the fetus. Trio whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a NM_001142966.2: c.4060G > C (p.E1354Q) in the GREB1L gene in the fetus. Sanger sequencing results confirmed the variant in the GREB1L gene detected by WES, and indicated that the variant was inherited from the father In order to explore the aetiology of the extremely rare renal anomalies in the family with Xp22.31 microdeletion, trio-WES was performed. None of the pathogenic or likely pathogenic gene variants associated with the observed phenotype was detected by trio-WES. However, an uncertain significance missense variant of NM_001142966.2: c.4060G > C (p.E1354Q) in the GREB1L gene was identified in the foetus, which was inherited from the father who had a normal phenotype. Notably, the same missense variant was absent in the proband's older brother, who also exhibited renal agenesis.

Discussion
Discussion The Xp22.31 region is known for its high instability and frequent rearrangements, primarily due to LCRs. In prenatal diagnosis, Xp22.31 deletions and duplications are commonly encountered. Xp22.31 microdeletions have been consistently interpreted as pathogenic variants and are typically associated with ichthyosis in males. In contrast, the pathogenicity of Xp22.31 microduplications remains a subject of debate. In the present study, the aim was to present an additional 52 cases of CNVs occurring in the Xp22.31 region. The hope is that this data will contribute valuable information to enhance prenatal consultations concerning both deletions and duplications in the Xp22.31 region. The prevalence of Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications in prenatal diagnosis was estimated to be 0.64–1.09% [–]. In the present study, the Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications detection rate was 1.22%, which is similar to previous studies. The typical Xp22.31 deletion is approximately 1.6 Mb in size and usually covers OMIM genes such as STS (OMIM:300747), PUDP (OMIM:306480), PNPLA4 (OMIM:300102) and VCX (OMIM:300229). This deletion is commonly associated with XLI in males. In addition, cryptorchidism, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and developmental delay have also been observed in male patients [, ]. The STS gene encodes the enzyme steroid sulfatase. A deficiency of this enzyme is associated with XLI []. VCX belongs to a family of genes that can vary in copy number on the X and Y chromosomes. Notably, RT-PCR experiments have detected VCX transcripts primarily in testis tissues, suggesting that this gene is predominantly active in the testicular context []. Moreover, a previous study also indicated that the absence of VCX genes could contribute to a mental retardation phenotype []. PNPLA4 encodes a protein with both triacylglycerol lipase and transacetylase activities. It is expressed in a wide range of human tissues []. Moreover, a previous study conducted by Labonne et al. [] suggested that PUDP and PNPLA4 were associated with X-linked intellectual disability, because of the high transcript levels in the human brain. In the present study, it was observed that all 17 individuals with Xp22.31 microdeletions had the characteristic 1.6 Mb deletion encompassing the four OMIM genes. All male patients born with this deletion exhibited XLI as a clinical manifestation, although no apparent mental developmental disorders were observed at the time of assessment. The possibility of such developmental disorders emerging in the future cannot be completely ruled out. In the present study, a case with Xp22.31 microdeletion elicited left renal agenesis, which has never been reported in patients with Xp22.31 microdeletions. To investigate this further, trio-WES was conducted within the family. However, no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with renal abnormalities were detected, suggesting that the underlying mechanism of renal agenesis in this case remains elusive. Following a thorough analysis of pedigree genetics, it was determined that the inherited uncertain significant variant NM_001142966.2: c.4060G > C (p.E1354Q) in the GREB1L gene may not be the underlying cause of renal abnormality within the family. In contrast, as delineated in the DECIHPHER database, of the total 280 cases of Xp22.31 microdeletions, two of them had renal abnormalities (DECHIPHER ID: 295004, 380514). To the best of our current knowledge, only one study by Schierz et al. [] has documented renal abnormalities in a patient with Xp22.31 microdeletion. These abnormalities included left renal hypoplasia, right renal dysplasia, and moderate hydronephrosis—observations that confirm STS deletion, as the core underlying pathomechanism, is not restricted to oculocutaneous phenotypes but may also precipitate the co-occurrence of renal abnormalities. In Case 16 of our study (arr[hg19]Xp22.31(6897849_8521023) × 0), which harbors an Xp22.31 microdeletion, the STS gene was also included within the deleted region, and the patient manifested renal agenesis. Consequently, we postulate a robust association between renal agenesis and Xp22.31 microdeletion. At present, the pathogenicity of Xp22.31 microduplications remains controversial. In the public database of ClinGen, no triplosensitivity evidence was observed in the typically enrolled genes. Further, previous studies have also indicated that the prevalence of the recurrent Xp22.31 microduplication was not significantly different between patients and controls [, ]. A prior study by Qiao et al. [] described an Xp22.31 duplication case with hypotonia, malformations, and developmental delay; subsequent WES identified a pathogenic PURA variant, which may explain variable expressivity in Xp22.31 duplication carriers. Another study [] performed WES on an Xp22.31 microduplication patient with refractory epilepsy and skill regression, detecting a de novo pathogenic MECP2 variant (c.338C > G, p.Pro113Arg) that could underlie variable expressivity in such cases. However, the pathogenicity of the Xp22.31 microduplications is still uncertain. In the present study, the after bith follow-up results elicited that 29 cases with Xp22.31 microduplications were born with normal features. Notably, in contrast to Xp22.31 microdeletions, the breakpoints of Xp22.31 microduplications are highly variable. However, the duplication in nearly all cases of the present study includes or encompasses the STS gene—with the exception of Case 33 (arr[hg19]Xp22.31(8135644_8641612) × 3), whose duplication involves VCX2, VCX3B, and ANOS1, and who exhibited normal development during postnatal follow-up. Overall, in the present study, most individuals with Xp22.31 microduplications show essentially normal postnatal developmental outcomes; only one female case presented with speech and motor developmental delay, indicating the necessity of further genetic diagnostic testing (e.g., WES). Regrettably, the family declined to undergo additional genetic analyses at the time of this study. In conclusion, 52 additional foetuses with Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications were reported, which may provide further insights into the relationship between genotype and phenotype in the context of Xp22.31 microdeletions/microduplications and offer additional data for genetic counselling. Based on the findings from previous studies and the results presented in the present report, the believe of the present authors is that Xp22.31 microduplications may be considered benign CNVs. Additionally, the present study contributes to uncovering the previously unrecognised association between renal agenesis and Xp22.31 microdeletions, thus expanding the spectrum of clinical manifestations associated with Xp22.31 microdeletions.

title: <i>SRSF1</i> haploinsufficiency drives the neurodevelopmental phenotype of the 17q22 deletion syndrome.
label_reason: Single fetus, abnormal ultrasound, CMA and WES.
abstract: The 17q22 deletion syndrome is associated with a range of clinical phenotypes, primarily due to differences in the size and position of the deleted genomic segment. In all previously reported cases, diagnoses were made postnatally, with clinical manifestations such as intellectual disability, visual impairment, and other neurological abnormalities. Karyotype analysis, chromosomal microarray analysis, and whole-exome sequencing were performed to identify the genetic etiology of a fetus with nuchal pellucida thickening. Summarize the previously reported cases of similar 17q22 deletions and conduct a systematic review. Chromosomal microarray analysis revealed an arr[GRCh37] 17q22(55,501,204_56,476,808) × 1, which was confirmed as a de novo variant by whole-exome sequencing. Comprehensive prenatal sonography revealed multiple structural abnormalities in the fetus, including neurodevelopmental abnormalities and distinct craniofacial features. A comprehensive search uncovered 24 postnatal cases with 17q22 deletions overlapping our findings. All these cases showed consistent neurological abnormalities, further supporting the genotype–phenotype association. Integrating the genetic findings in this fetus, the abnormal ultrasound structural phenotype, and the clinical characteristics of existing cases, we conclude that SRSF1 haplotype deficiency is the fundamental genetic cause underlying the observed fetal ultrasound abnormalities. This report of the 17q22 deletion (include SRSF1 ) provides an essential reference for prenatal genetic counseling and phenotypic interpretation. Keywords: 17q22 deletion, craniofacial anomalies, neurological abnormalities, prenatal diagnosis, SRSF1
text:
SRSF1 haploinsufficiency drives the neurodevelopmental phenotype of the 17q22 deletion syndrome

Introduction
Introduction The 17q22 deletion is a rare chromosomal aberration characterized by genomic imbalances in this region that are associated with a spectrum of complex clinical manifestations, including neurodevelopmental delays, psychiatric disorders, facial malformations, and skeletal or urogenital abnormalities (). Microdeletion at 17q22 (include NOG) has been reported. The NOG gene encodes a bone morphogenetic protein antagonist that is essential for the development of bones, joints, and neural tubes (, ). NOG loss-of-function mutations cause skeletal disorders, including proximal interphalangeal joint fusion and multiple synostoses syndrome (). However, it is worth noting that many cases of 17q22 deletion are also associated with neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including intellectual disability, developmental delay, attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder, which cannot be explained by NOG haploinsufficiency alone, suggesting that other genes critical for neurodevelopment are present in this region. In 2023, a study systematically characterized syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders arising from SRSF1 haploinsufficiency (). This finding implicates SRSF1 as a core driver gene for the neurodevelopmental phenotype in 17q22 deletion. Notably, SRSF1 and NOG are physically separated by >1 Mb, allowing SRSF1 deletions to occur independently of NOG loss. Consequently, the phenotypic spectrum associated with SRSF1 haploinsufficiency is distinctly different from the “classic 17q22 deletion” phenotype. We report a fetus with chromosome 17q22 deletion syndrome (include SRSF1) presenting with abnormal ultrasound findings. We reviewed and statistically analyzed cases of overlapping 17q22 deletions to delineate the SRSF1-associated phenotypic spectrum. Current literature focuses on postnatal phenotypes, leaving a gap in evidence on prenatal detection and raising questions about the effectiveness of genetic counseling. Ultrasound-detected structural abnormalities often correlate with genetic anomalies (). Therefore, this study presents a novel prenatal case of 17q22 deletion syndrome identified via ultrasound and genetic diagnosis, and conducts a systematic literature review to summarize the phenotypic spectrum and explore genotype–phenotype correlations, providing a reference for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling.

Methods
Methods Clinical report A 31-year-old pregnant woman, G2P1, reported no family history of genetic disease, consanguinity, drug use during pregnancy, or exposure to radioactive or toxic substances. The fetal ultrasound examination at 16 weeks revealed a thickened nuchal translucency (NT) measuring 4.3 mm, which warranted close monitoring and further diagnostic evaluation at a more advanced gestational age. G-banding karyotype analysis Amniotic fluid cells were cultured using the in-situ cell culture method, and chromosomes were prepared for karyotyping. Chromosomal karyotype analysis was performed at a 400-band level, strictly following the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN 2024) (). Chromosomal microarray analysis A total of 15 mL of amniotic fluid and 2 mL of maternal peripheral blood were collected. Following exclusion of maternal cell contamination by quantitative fluorescent PCR (QF-PCR), CMA was performed using the CytoScan 750 K Arrays (Biosan, China). Copy number variations (CNVs) results were cross-validated by integrating single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) probes and CNV-specific probes. Pathogenicity interpretation of CNVs was conducted in accordance with the Clinical Guidelines (). Whole-exome sequencing analysis Amniotic fluid and peripheral blood from the pregnant woman and her spouse were collected. DNA was extracted using the Tiangen Biotech DNA Extraction Kit, followed by library preparation, quality control, and high-throughput sequencing. The raw sequencing data underwent quality control, alignment, variant calling, filtering, and annotation, and genetic pathogenicity analysis was conducted based on the processed data. Similar cases review In September 2025, we searched PubMed, DECIPHER (), and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) for cases with 17q22 deletions using the keyword “17q22.” Inclusion criteria were: full-text availability, human clinical and genetic data, and deletions overlapping or closely aligning with our case. All eligible publications were reviewed and data systematically extracted.

Results
Results Ultrasound examination To track fetal growth and development and structure of various systems, fetal ultrasound examination at 23 weeks showed fetal biological parameters, including growth parameters lower than China gestational age reference standard, mild bilateral ventricular enlargement, no visible parieto-occipital sulcus, micrognathia, mild frontal lobe flat with frontal lobe soft tissue thickening, trace tricuspid regurgitation, and enlarged foramen ovale (). Fetal ultrasonography findings. (A) Bilateral parieto-occipital sulci are not visualized on the transcranial axial view. (B) Transthalamic axial plane: BPD (5.44 cm) and HC (20.00 cm) both < expected for gestational age. (C) Thickening soft tissue. (D) Frontal soft tissue thickening with a mandibular-facial angle <49° and micrognathia. (E) Right lateral ventricle posterior horn 10.9 mm (far-field standard plane). (F) Left lateral ventricle 10.8 mm (non-standard near-field imaging plane). Genetic analysis Fetal amniotic fluid G-banding karyotype was 46, U. with no detected abnormalities. The CMA result indicated arr[GRCh37] 17q22(55,501,204_56,476,808) × 1dn (, ). The results showed that there was a deletion of 976Kb in the 17q22 segment in this sample, involving 15 protein-coding genes such as SRSF1, MKS1, VEZF1, DYNLL2, MPO, spanning the exon 7–14 region of the MSI2 gene (NM_138962) and the exon 3–10 region of the RNF43 gene (NM_017763). WES results confirmed the fetal CMA finding, and the variant was not detected in either parent’s peripheral blood. Deletion localization and identification by CMA. (A) Fragment copy deletion in region 17q22. (B) CMA identified the 17q22 deletion variant. Cases search results Cases were screened to find those describing deletions overlapping or adjacent to the chromosomal segment relevant to our case. A total of 24 previously reported cases met these criteria: 9 from PubMed, 14 from the Decipher database, and 1 from CNKI ( and ). UCSC track summaries 17q22 deletion cases.

Discussion
Discussion Current reports of 17q22 deletion are mainly in pediatric and adult populations, with prenatal cases exceedingly rare. As ultrasonography is the primary tool for detecting fetal structural anomalies, characterizing the prenatal sonographic phenotypes associated with 17q22 deletion—alongside underlying genetic mechanisms—will provide essential diagnostic references and inform future research into the developmental pathogenesis of this disorder. In this case, NT thickening was detected by fetal ultrasound screening during early pregnancy. Genetic diagnostic investigations identified a de novo CNV. The segment contains 15 protein-coding genes, including SRSF1, MKS1, VEZF1, and MPO. VEZF1 and SRSF1 demonstrate elevated haploinsufficiency scores and were predicted to exhibit haploinsufficiency at the gnomAD database (Accessed September 20, 2025) (). SRSF1 encodes a serine/arginine-rich splicing factor that interacts with other components of the spliceosomal complex to prevent exon skipping, thereby ensuring splicing fidelity and regulating alternative splicing (). Haploinsufficiency of SRSF1 shows a strong association with syndromic neurodevelopmental abnormalities characterized by intellectual disability (), the primary manifestations include speech delay, behavioral abnormalities, and non-specific craniofacial anomalies. Analysis of the gnomAD database revealed marked intolerance to loss-of-function (LoF:pLI = 1, o/e = 0.04 (0.01–0.17) < 0.35). The Clingen database (Accessed September 20, 2025) () recognized SRSF1 as a dose-sensitive gene, with haploinsufficiency linked to neurodevelopmental abnormalities, including dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities. Current evidence indicates a direct link between SRSF1 haploinsufficiency and fetal neurological and craniofacial anomalies. A summary of cases from our case, databases and the existing literature reveals that among 15 cases with confirmed deletions encompassing SRSF1, the incidence of intellectual disability (ID) or global developmental delay (GDD) was 86.67% (13/15), indicating near-complete penetrance. The remaining two cases lacked assessment due to infant death or other reasons. A detailed breakdown shows that among the 12 cases explicitly documented with ID, 40.0% (6/15) also presented with GDD. Speech/language delay, another key indicator, was observed in 46.67% (7/15) of cases and frequently co-occurred with ID. Among the 10 cases without SRSF1 deletion, only 20.0% (2/10) presented with ID or GDD, both involving deletions of other neurodevelopmental candidate genes. The remaining cases with other neurodevelopmental phenotypes—such as cognitive impairment or nonspecific developmental delay—also all harbored deletions involving such candidate genes. These observations suggest that the neurodevelopmental manifestations in these cases are likely attributable to dosage alterations of genes other than SRSF1 within the deleted intervals, rather than to SRSF1 haploinsufficiency itself. Craniofacial anomalies represent the second most characteristic feature after neurodevelopmental disorders, with an incidence of 80.0% (12/15), presenting a recognizable pattern. Although the specific manifestations are diverse, common elements include micrognathia (33.33%, 5/15), hypertelorism or epicanthal folds, thin upper lip vermilion, low-set ears, and a broad nasal root or bulbous nose. SRSF1 haploinsufficiency appears to constitute a “necessary foundation” for both neurodevelopmental and craniofacial abnormalities. Microcephaly, a key quantifiable sign, was present in 40.0% (6/15) of cases. In-depth analysis revealed that these 6 microcephaly cases, the deletion interval encompassed both SRSF1 and NOG in 100% ( and ). The crucial role of NOG in skeletal development might exacerbate the impact of SRSF1 deletion on craniofacial morphology. When the deletion extends to include NOG, the phenotypic spectrum demonstrates an “additive effect”: on the foundation of core neurodevelopmental disorders, the incidence and distinctiveness of craniofacial anomalies—particularly microcephaly—and skeletal malformations become significantly more pronounced, culminating in a more complete and classic syndromic facies. VEZF1 is a key transcription factor essential for vascular system development, playing pivotal roles in vascular network formation, endothelial cell function, and the regulation of collagen deposition. Zou et al. () reported that Vezf1 haploinsufficiency causes partial vascular disruption, suggesting 50% expression may support basic cardiovascular development. This is supported by Das et al., who showed that residual VEZF1 synergizes with ETV2 to activate Flt1, likely maintaining sufficient target gene expression for minimal requirements (). In summary, haploinsufficiency of VEZF1 may occur without manifesting overt structural cardiovascular phenotypes. In our case series, we found that all CNVs encompassing SRSF1 invariably included VEZF1. Among these 15 co-deletion cases, cardiovascular anomalies were identified in 5 (33.33%), cases 17 and 25 exhibited patent ductus arteriosus, case 19 had aortic hypoplasia, and both cases 23 and our case presented with tricuspid regurgitation. The role of VEZF1 in embryonic vascular development is well established, primarily through haploinsufficiency and regulation of protein interactions. The vascular network abnormalities observed in cases 17, 19, and 25 are strongly supported by evidence. Tricuspid regurgitation in cases 1 and 23 may result from VEZF1’s role in regulating early cardiovascular precursor cells in the embryonic mesoderm. The physical proximity of VEZF1 and SRSF1 predisposes them to codeletion in 17q22 CNVs. SRSF1 deletion drives intellectual disability and developmental delay, while VEZF1 haploinsufficiency—a dosage-sensitive vascular transcription factor—likely causes cerebrovascular abnormalities, compromising neural blood supply and exacerbating neurological deficits. Their synergistic haploinsufficiency disrupts overlapping yet complementary pathways, contributing to the complex multisystem phenotype of 17q22 deletion syndrome. Prenatal diagnosis is challenging and often involves rare cases, as ultrasound examinations frequently miss specific subtle structural abnormalities. Therefore, minor ultrasound anomalies play a significant role in indicating potential fetal abnormalities. In the present case, routine prenatal screening at 16 weeks of gestation revealed an NT thickening, raising suspicion of underlying chromosomal or structural defects. Although NT thickening is a non-specific soft marker with heterogeneous etiologies and cannot guide clinical decisions independently, the abnormal phenotypic findings provided a clear indication for invasive prenatal testing and comprehensive genetic analysis. Subsequent investigations identified a constellation of sonographic features—including fetal biometric parameters below Chinese reference standards for gestational age, mild ventriculomegaly, indistinct parieto-occipital sulcus, flattened frontal lobe, increased nuchal soft tissue, micrognathia, reduced frontal horn dimension, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and an enlarged foramen ovale—that were associated with a fetal copy number variant: a heterozygous deletion at 17q22 encompassing the SRSF1 and VEZF1 genes. To our knowledge, this is the first prenatal report of a 17q22 deletion syndrome (include SRSF1), providing novel insights into the genetic basis of a distinct prenatal ultrasound phenotype characterized by neurodevelopmental and craniofacial anomalies.

title: Prenatal SNP-array chromosomal microarray analysis in 3,549 pregnancies: indication-specific yields and clinical implications.

abstract: SNP-based chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is widely used in invasive prenatal diagnosis, yet real-world performance across contemporary referral pathways, especially in the NIPT era, remains incompletely characterized. We retrospectively analyzed 3,549 prenatal invasive samples tested by SNP array, and evaluated diagnostic yield overall and by referral indication and ultrasound phenotype. In total, we identified 398 pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants across 386 fetuses, resulting in an overall diagnostic yield of 10.9% (386/3,549). These findings comprised 223 aneuploidies and 175 pathogenic CNVs. In contrast, variants of uncertain significance (VOUS) were detected in 12.0% (426/3,549) of cases. Diagnostic yields were heavily stratified by indication: yields peaked in NIPT high-risk referrals (38.9%) and were intermediate in ultrasound-based cases (~ 11%), but dropped significantly in the advanced maternal age (AMA; 4.2%) and serum screening (~ 5–6%) groups. Conversely, VOUS rates remained remarkably stable across all referral categories. Sub-analysis of ultrasound abnormalities revealed that multisystem anomalies conferred the highest risk (27.3%), driven predominantly by aneuploidies; among soft markers, increased nuchal translucency (NT) emerged as the strongest predictor of chromosomal pathology. In our cohort, SNP-array identified clinically actionable findings in 10.9% of cases. NIPT enriched diagnostic yields, particularly for aneuploidies, and NT thickness was strongly associated with pathogenic findings. These results support an indication-based approach to genomic testing, with NIPT as a triage tool for aneuploidy and CMA for high-risk populations, while improving VOUS counseling. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-026-09187-x . text:
Prenatal SNP-array chromosomal microarray analysis in 3,549 pregnancies: indication-specific yields and clinical implications

Introduction
Introduction While G-banded karyotyping has historically anchored prenatal diagnosis, its 5–10 Mb resolution limits the detection of submicroscopic copy-number variants (CNVs). SNP-based chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) overcomes this by offering genome-wide, high-resolution CNV detection alongside identification of uniparental disomy (UPD) and mosaicism [–]. Pivotal trials have established that CMA delivers an incremental diagnostic yield of ~ 1.7–6% over karyotyping, depending on indications []. Subsequent large-scale cohorts in both Western and Asian populations have confirmed overall abnormality detection rates of ~ 10–13%, though yields vary significantly between high-risk ultrasound findings and referrals solely for advanced maternal age (AMA) [–]. However, the widespread adoption of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) has fundamentally restructured the referral landscape for invasive diagnosis, limiting the direct applicability of historical diagnostic baselines and necessitating re-evaluation of diagnostic yields in the post-NIPT era. In contrast to historical datasets in which invasive testing often served as a primary screen, contemporary invasive cohorts exhibit a distinct “enrichment effect”: cfDNA screening triages many low-risk pregnancies away from invasive procedures, thereby increasing the pre-test probability and concentrating clinically complex referrals within the invasive-testing population. Consequently, new data are required to guide contemporary counseling. Current literature often aggregates heterogeneous “high-risk” pregnancies or focuses narrowly on ultrasound anomalies, failing to provide granular, indication-specific yields for aneuploidies versus pathogenic/likely pathogenic CNVs (pCNVs) [, ]. Furthermore, the specific “risk gradients” of ultrasound markers (e.g., structural vs. soft markers, increasing nuchal translucency) remain under-quantified [, ]. In parallel, although NIPT now dominates primary screening, current data remain limited on how NIPT-positive referrals enrich CMA cohorts and on indication-specific VOUS rates, which constrains the translation of recurrent CNV patterns into precise prenatal counseling [, ]. Finally, while AMA is the primary driver for aneuploidy screening [, ], recent evidence suggests pCNV risk is independent of maternal age [, , ]—a paradigm shift requiring validation in large, unselected cohorts to refine counseling for younger women. In this retrospective study, we analyzed the diagnostic outcomes of SNP-based CMA in 3,549 pregnancies managed under a structured hierarchical referral framework at a tertiary center in Central China. Moving beyond aggregate diagnostic yields, this study aimed to: (i) characterize the specific “enrichment effect” of NIPT on the spectrum of invasive diagnostic outcomes; (ii) establish high-resolution benchmarks by dissecting ultrasound anomalies into distinct organ-specific defects versus isolated soft markers; (iii) delineate the risk trajectory of nuchal translucency (NT) thickness, specifically contrasting the likelihood of pathogenic findings against the burden of VOUS; and (iv) assess the uncoupling of pathogenic CNV risk from maternal age. These data serve to provide indication-specific evidence that supports precise test selection and refines pre-test counseling in the post-NIPT era.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods Study design and population This was a single-center, retrospective cohort study conducted at Changzhi Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital in central China. All consecutive pregnancies that underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis with SNP-array between November 2016 and December 2024 were eligible for inclusion. NIPT was implemented at our institution in 2013. Annual NIPT volume increased from 142 tests in 2013 to 3,308 tests in 2016 and remained high thereafter (2017–2024: 13,098 ± 2,239 tests per year). Within the study period, 3,549 fetuses underwent CMA and constituted the diagnostic cohort. Invasive samples consisted of amniotic fluid, chorionic villus and umbilical cord blood samples, which were obtained according to gestational age and clinical indication. Pregnancies were referred from the hospital’s obstetric clinics and from primary and secondary care institutions across the surrounding region. All pregnant women received pre-test counseling from obstetricians and clinical geneticists before undergoing invasive testing. Written informed consent for the invasive procedure, CMA testing, and the use of anonymized data for research purposes was obtained from all participants. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and all procedures complied with the Declaration of Helsinki, the Measures for the Administration of Prenatal Diagnosis Technology (Ministry of Health Order No. 33, revised 2019), and the Measures for the Ethical Review of Biomedical Research Involving Humans (NHFPC Order No. 11, 2016). Indications for invasive testing and subgroup definitions Indications for invasive prenatal diagnosis were recorded at referral and categorized as: (i) apparent structural anomalies (AUS), defined as major ultrasound-detected malformations and further grouped by the primarily affected system (cardiovascular, nervous, skeletal, urinary, multisystem, or other); (ii) soft ultrasound markers, including increased nuchal translucency (NT), mild ventriculomegaly, fetal growth restriction (FGR), echogenic bowel (EB), isolated intracardiac echogenic focus (EICF), single umbilical artery (SUA), polyhydramnios, pyelectasis, absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, and other commonly recognized soft markers (iii) STSS high-risk, defined by second-trimester serum screening results exceeding national/local high-risk thresholds (trisomy 21: > 1:270; trisomy 18: >1:350); (iv) STSS intermediate risk, defined as a second-trimester serum screening risk between 1:270 and 1:1,000 for trisomy 21, and 1:350–1:1,000 for trisomy 18; (v) NIPT high-risk, defined as high-risk NIPT calls for common trisomies (21/18/13), sex-chromosome aneuploidies, rare autosomal trisomies, or segmental imbalances; (vi) advanced maternal age (AMA), defined as maternal age ≥ 35 years at the expected date of delivery without other high-risk indications; (vii) adverse pregnancy history (APH), including recurrent miscarriage, a prior fetus/child with chromosomal abnormalities or congenital anomalies, unexplained stillbirth, or other major adverse outcomes; and (viii) elective testing, defined as CMA performed at parental request after genetic counseling in the absence of guideline-based indications. Referral indications were not mutually exclusive and were assigned using a predefined hierarchical scheme. When multiple indications coexisted, each pregnancy was categorized into a single primary indication group according to the following priority order: ultrasound abnormalities (AUS/soft markers) > NIPT high-risk or APH > STSS (high-risk or intermediate risk) > AMA > elective testing. In our center, routine examinations were adjudicated by senior attending physicians (Associate Chief Physician or higher). Subsequently, all patients scheduled for invasive prenatal diagnosis underwent a definitive pre-procedural confirmatory scan by a designated Chief Physician. This final assessment served to validate fetal status and corroborate the phenotypic anomalies documented in the initial referral. All invasive prenatal sampling procedures and subsequent genetic counseling were performed by physicians with Associate Chief Physician rank or above. Sample collection and laboratory procedures Chorionic villus sampling (CVS), amniocentesis, and umbilical cord blood sampling were performed under ultrasound guidance. CVS was generally performed at 11–13 weeks of gestation, amniocentesis at 17–24 weeks, and cord blood sampling at 25–36 weeks. Fetal genomic DNA was extracted from uncultured amniotic fluid cells, chorionic villi, or fetal cord blood using the Microsample Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (DP316, Tiangen Biotech Co., Ltd., Beijing, China), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA concentration and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific), and samples were stored at − 20 °C until further processing. SNP Array Analysis Genome-wide CMA was performed using the Affymetrix CytoScan® 750 K array kit (Affymetrix, Inc., Santa Clara, CA, USA) following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Briefly, ~ 250 ng of high-quality genomic DNA was digested, ligated to adaptors, PCR-amplified, purified, fragmented, labeled, and hybridized to the array. After hybridization and washing, arrays were scanned, and raw data were processed using Affymetrix Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS) software (version 3.3) or later. CNVs and regions of homozygosity/UPD were called using the software’s default algorithms, with laboratory-validated settings for probe quality, signal-to-noise ratio, and minimum segment size. For clinical interpretation, we focused on rare CNVs above a minimum size threshold consistent with current prenatal practice (typically ≥ 100 kb for deletions and duplications), while known benign and common polymorphic CNVs were filtered out based on internal and public population databases, including gnomAD and the Database of Genomic Variants (DGV) [, ]. Pathogenicity assessment The pathogenicity of CNVs was evaluated using published literature and several public databases, including DGV (http://dgv.tcag.ca/dgv/app/home), ClinGen (https://www.clinicalgenome.org/), DECIPHER (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/), gnomAD (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/) and OMIM (https://www.omim.org/). This analysis followed the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen), using the 2020 classification standards []. While initial clinical reporting followed the guidelines active at the time of diagnosis—transitioning from empirical laboratory thresholds (≥ 100 kb and ≥ 50 markers) to the point-based framework in 2020—all variants in this cohort were retrospectively re-curated according to the ACMG/ClinGen standards to ensure longitudinal uniformity. Each CNV was classified into one of the following categories: pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), variant of uncertain significance (VOUS), likely benign, or benign. For the purposes of this study, fetal-level CMA outcomes were grouped as follows: (i) P/LP: fetuses carrying at least one pathogenic or likely pathogenic abnormality; (ii) VOUS: fetuses with only VOUS and no concurrent P/LP abnormality; (iii) Normal: fetuses with no reportable CNV or only benign/likely benign variants. Aneuploidies (numerical chromosome abnormalities) were recorded separately from pCNVs to allow stratified analyses of their respective contributions. Recurrent CNVs were defined as pCNVs mapping to well-established microdeletion/microduplication syndromes or known genomic hotspots (e.g., Xp22.31, 22q11.2, 15q11.2) [, ]. Clinical follow-up and outcome assessment Pregnancy and postnatal outcomes were ascertained whenever possible through structured telephone interviews and/or outpatient visits. For each pregnancy, we recorded pregnancy outcome as livebirth, termination of pregnancy (TOP), miscarriage, stillbirth, or neonatal/postnatal death; for liveborn children: sex, major congenital anomalies, growth, neurodevelopment, and other clinically relevant features at last contact; reasons for TOP when applicable (e.g., confirmed chromosomal abnormality, severe structural malformation, or parental decision). Cases were categorized as “lost to follow-up” if families could not be contacted after at least three attempts or explicitly declined participation. Outcome data were summarized overall and stratified by CMA result category (normal, aneuploidy, pCNV, VOUS). Statistical Analysis All statistical computations and data visualizations were executed in Python (version 3.12.1) using standard analytical libraries (e.g., matplotlib, seaborn). Categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Continuous variables were analyzed using one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal–Wallis H test as appropriate, with post hoc pairwise comparisons using Student’s t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Associations between clinical indicators and diagnostic outcomes (normal, VOUS, P/LP) were evaluated using univariable multinomial logistic regression, reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), based on complete-case data. Discriminative performance of NT was assessed using ROC curves, with AUC and 95% CIs estimated by bootstrap resampling. Given the retrospective design and limited uniformly collected covariates, interaction terms and multicollinearity diagnostics were not evaluated. Diagnostic yields were stratified by referral indication and ultrasound findings, and recurrent pCNV patterns were visualized using forest plots and heatmaps. A two-sided p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results
Results Population characteristics and indications for prenatal CMA During the study period, 3,549 fetuses underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis by CMA. The mean maternal age at sampling was 31.3 ± 5.0 years (range: 18–49 years). The median gestational age at sampling was 19.3 weeks (range: 11.0–34.9 weeks). Most procedures were performed on amniotic fluid (3441/3549, 97.0%), followed by chorionic villi (93/3549, 2.6%) and fetal cord blood (15/3549, 0.4%). Clinical indications for invasive testing were diverse. The most frequent indications were STSS high-risk (1229/3549, 34.6%), soft ultrasound markers (670/3549, 18.9%), and AMA (503/3549, 14.2%). Additional indications included high-risk NIPT results (398/3549, 11.2%), AUS (329/3549, 9.3%), APH (304/3549, 8.6%), STSS intermediate-risk (74/3549, 2.1%), and parental voluntary testing without standard indications (42/3549, 1.2%). At the fetal level, CMA identified P/LP abnormalities in 386 fetuses (Supplemental Table ), yielding a detection rate of 10.9% (386/3,549). A total of 426 fetuses (12.0%, 426/3,549) carried VOUS, encompassing 446 VOUS events, and the remaining 2,737 fetuses (77.1%, 2,737/3,549) had normal CMA results. In total, 398 P/LP abnormalities were identified in these 386 fetuses, comprising 223 aneuploidies (56.0%, 223/398) and 175 pCNVs (44.0%, 175/398). Twelve fetuses harbored two P/LP abnormalities each. The diagnostic yield of CMA varied substantially across referral indications (Fig. ). The diagnostic yield of P/LP findings varied markedly across referral indications (χ² = 391.3, df = 7, p < 0.001): it was highest in the NIPT high-risk group (155/398, 38.9%), intermediate in ultrasound-based indications (11.6% for AUS and 11.2% for soft markers), and lowest in AMA (4.2%) and STSS-based indications (5.9% for STSS high-risk and 5.4% for STSS intermediate risk). In contrast, VOUS rates were broadly similar across indication categories (range 9.5–14.8%; χ² = 7.5, df = 7, p = 0.38). Comprehensive analysis of CMA results in prenatal diagnosis. Diagnostic yield and distribution of CMA results across different clinical indications. Total P indicates the aggregate rate of definitive pathogenic findings (aneuploidies + pCNVs) Chromosomal abnormalities in fetuses with ultrasound abnormalities Of the 3,549 fetuses in the CMA cohort, 999 (28.2%) had ultrasound abnormalities at referral, including 670 with soft ultrasound markers and 329 with AUS. In this ultrasound-abnormal subgroup, the overall fetal-level rate of clinically significant chromosomal abnormalities was 11.3% (113/999), comprising 67 aneuploidies (6.7%, 67/999) and 46 pCNVs (4.6%, 46/999). VOUS were identified in 13.3% (133/999), and CMA results were normal in 75.4% (753/999). In fetuses with AUS (n = 329), the overall P/LP yield was 11.6% (38/329), with 6.1% (20/329) aneuploidies and 5.5% (18/329) pCNVs. VOUS were detected in 10.9% (36/329), and CMA results were normal in 77.5% (255/329). Across AUS subgroups defined by affected organ system, the diagnostic yield of CMA varied substantially (Fig. A). In the heatmap, this variation followed a stepwise risk gradient, with the “multiple systems” group showing the highest overall P/LP rate (27.3%, 15/55). In this group, aneuploidies predominated (20.0%, 11/55), occurring significantly more often than in any single-system anomaly group (P < 0.001). Among isolated structural defects, nervous system (11.4%, 4/35) and urinary system anomalies (11.3%, 7/62) had intermediate pathogenic yields, largely driven by pCNVs, whereas skeletal anomalies showed the lowest P/LP yield (3.7%, 1/27). Skeletal anomalies also had a relatively high proportion of VOUS (7/27, 25.9%), while cardiovascular anomalies exhibited a moderate P/LP rate (7.5%, 5/67) with VOUS detected in 10.4% (7/67). A Heatmap showing the distribution of CMA results across different ultrasound anomaly systems. B Pathogenic detection rates across ultrasound soft-marker subtypes. Points indicate the P/LP detection rate (P/LP cases divided by total cases in each marker subtype), and error bars denote 95% confidence intervals calculated using the Wilson score method. Marker size is proportional to the subgroup sample size (n) When ultrasound soft markers were analyzed as a group (n = 670), the overall P/LP detection rate was 11.2% (75/670), including 7.0% (47/670) aneuploidies and 4.2% (28/670) pCNVs; VOUS were observed in 14.5% (97/670). A forest plot analysis showed that increased NT had the highest diagnostic utility among isolated markers (Fig. B), with a P/LP detection rate of 21.0% (38/181). Isolated markers such as EB, absent or hypoplastic nasal bone, and EICF yielded no pathogenic findings. We assessed the combined risk of multiple markers by comparing diagnostic outcomes in fetuses with multiple versus single soft markers. In an initial analysis, the P/LP rate for multiple markers (13.6%, 16/118) did not differ significantly from that for all single markers combined (10.7%, 59/552; OR = 1.31, 95% CI 0.68–2.42; p = 0.430, Fisher’s exact test). After excluding NT, a high-risk marker, from the single-marker group, the P/LP rate for multiple markers (13.6%, 16/118) was significantly higher than for single markers without NT (5.7%, 21/371), with an odds ratio of 2.61 (95% CI 1.22–5.47; p = 0.008, Fisher’s exact test). Numeric NT measurements were available for 173 of 181 fetuses with increased NT, and these cases were included in the continuous NT analysis. NT values differed by result category: the P/LP group showed significantly higher NT measurements than the normal group (P = 0.003), whereas NT measurements in the VOUS group were not significantly different from normal (P = 0.92; Fig. A). In a multinomial logistic regression model with the normal group as the reference, each 1-mm increase in NT was associated with a significantly increased odds of a P/LP result (OR = 1.62, 95% CI 1.25–2.08; p < 0.001), but showed no significant association with VOUS (OR = 1.09, 95% CI 0.77–1.53; p = 0.64; Fig. B). The NT measurement demonstrated limited standalone discriminative performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.667 (95% CI 0.550–0.777) (Fig. C). Association between NT thickness and SNP-array findings. A Distribution of NT thickness across SNP-array outcome groups (normal, VOUS, and P/LP). B Model-predicted probabilities of normal, VOUS, and P/LP outcomes as a function of NT thickness, based on a multinomial regression model with NT entered as a continuous predictor. Curves represent probabilities estimated from a multinomial logistic regression model with the normal group as the reference and NT entered as a continuous predictor (n = 173). C Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of NT for discriminating P/LP CNVs from non-P/LP results (normal + VOUS); the AUC (0.667) and its 95% confidence interval (0.551–0.775) are shown, and performance at selected NT thresholds is indicated CMA findings in non-ultrasound-based indications A large proportion of fetuses in this cohort underwent CMA for non-ultrasound-based indications, including STSS high-risk or intermediate-risk results, high-risk NIPT results, AMA, APH, and parental voluntary testing. Among the 1,229 fetuses referred for STSS high-risk, the fetal-level P/LP yield was 5.9% (72/1,229), comprising 27 aneuploidies (2.2%) and 45 pCNVs (3.7%); VOUS were detected in 12.1% (149/1,229). In the STSS intermediate-risk subgroup (n = 74), the P/LP yield was 5.4% (4/74), with no aneuploidies identified; VOUS occurred in 10.9% (8/74), and 83.8% (62/74) of fetuses had normal CMA findings. Over the study period, the contribution of NIPT to the overall prenatal screening pathway increased progressively, with both the number and proportion of invasive procedures triggered by high-risk NIPT results rising year by year (Fig. A; Supplemental Table ). In this group (n = 398), CMA identified P/LP abnormalities in 155 fetuses (38.9%, 155/398; Fig. B), and VOUS were detected in 11.6% (46/398). When stratified by the type of NIPT call, P/LP yields were highest for high-risk trisomy 21 (T21) results, with P/LP abnormalities detected in 50 of 58 fetuses (86.2%), followed by trisomy 18 (T18; 46.7%, 14/30) and trisomy 13 (T13; 28.6%, 6/21). High-risk sex-chromosome calls and “other” high-risk calls (including rare autosomal trisomies and segmental imbalances) showed lower but still clinically relevant P/LP rates of 33.3% (45/135) and 24.7% (38/154), respectively. The corresponding positive predictive values (PPVs) of NIPT for the targeted abnormalities were 86.2% (50/58) for T21, 46.7% (14/30) for T18, 23.8% (5/21) for T13, 31.9% (43/135) for sex-chromosome abnormalities, and 22.7% (35/154) for other indications. VOUS were relatively infrequent in T21 and sex-chromosome high-risk cases (3.4% and 7.4%, respectively), but more common in T18 (23.3%), T13 (9.5%), and “other” calls (16.2%). Integrated analysis of NIPT performance and maternal age characteristics in the diagnostic cohort. A Annual evolution of NIPT referrals and diagnostic yield. B Positive predictive value (PPV) and outcome concordance of NIPT stratified by indication Among fetuses referred solely for AMA (n = 503), the P/LP yield was 4.2% (21/503), driven mainly by 2.2% (11/503) aneuploidies and 2.0% (10/503) pCNVs. VOUS were observed in 9.5% (48/503). A Kruskal-Wallis test revealed significant differences in maternal age across the four outcome groups (Fig. , H = 11.90, P = 0.0077). Women in the Aneuploidy group (n = 223) were the oldest (mean 32.0 ± 5.5 years), whereas those in the pCNV group (n = 163) were the youngest (mean 30.2 ± 4.7 years). Maternal age in the pCNV group was significantly lower than in both the Normal (P = 0.0043) and Aneuploidy (P = 0.0017) groups. The VOUS group (n = 426) showed no significant age difference from the Normal group (P = 0.3768). Maternal age distribution across different CMA result categories. Parental voluntary testing (n = 42) yielded no P/LP abnormalities, VOUS in 14.3% (6/42), and normal CMA in 85.7% (36/42). Spectrum and recurrence of pathogenic CNVs Across the entire cohort, CMA identified 175 pCNVs from 163 fetuses. Deletions constituted roughly two-thirds of events (113/175, 65.1%), whereas duplications accounted for the remaining one-third (61/175, 34.9%). One additional case involved pathogenic UPD of chromosome 15. We identified a total of 115 recurrent pCNVs associated with well-defined microdeletion or microduplication syndromes (Fig. A). The most frequently detected abnormality was the Xp22.31 recurrent region (including the STS gene), which accounted for 28.9% (33/115) of all recurrent findings. This was followed by the 22q11.2 recurrent region (n = 16, 14.0%) and the 17p12 recurrent (HNPP/CMT1A) region (n = 10, 9.6%). Other clinically significant findings included the 15q11.2 (BP1-BP2) region (n = 8), the 16p11.2 proximal BP4-BP5 region (n = 7), and 4p16.3 (Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome, n = 6). Spectrum and clinical associations of recurrent pathogenic CNVs in the prenatal cohort. A Frequency spectrum of recurrent pCNVs detected by CMA. B Distribution of clinical referral indications associated with recurrent pathogenic CNVs. C Heatmap showing the association between the top seven recurrent CNVs and clinical referral indications We further examined the referral indications for fetuses carrying recurrent pathogenic CNVs (Fig. B). High-risk NIPT was the most common indication, accounting for 32 recurrent cases (28.1% of all recurrent CNV-positive fetuses), followed by STSS high-risk (n = 30). Ultrasound-based indications also contributed substantially, with 16 recurrent CNVs detected in fetuses referred for soft markers and 13 in those with structural anomalies (AUS). The distribution of the seven most frequent recurrent pathogenic CNVs across referral categories is shown in Fig. C. Xp22.31 deletions consistent with STS deficiency were predominantly observed in fetuses referred for STSS high-risk or intermediate-risk screening (20/33, 60.6%), with an additional 9 cases (27.3%) detected in pregnancies with a high-risk NIPT result and only a few cases arising from other referral indications. In contrast, 22q11.2 deletions/duplications were distributed across a broader spectrum of indications, including high-risk NIPT, STSS high-risk, AUS, AMA and other categories. The remaining recurrent loci represented in the top-seven panel, such as 15q11.2 (BP1-BP2), 17p12 (HNPP/CMT1A), 16p11.2 and other less frequent regions, were likewise scattered across multiple referral indications (including STSS high-risk, soft markers, AMA, APH and AUS) without a clear enrichment in any single category. Clinical follow‑up assessments All 3,549 pregnancies were approached for telephone or outpatient follow-up. Outcome information was successfully obtained for 3,276 cases (92.3%, 3,276/3,549), whereas 273 cases (7.7%) were lost to follow-up or declined participation. Among pregnancies with known outcomes, 517 (14.6%) underwent termination of pregnancy (TOP), 15 (0.4%) ended in miscarriage or stillbirth, and 2,744 (77.3%) resulted in livebirth. Among liveborn infants, 8 (0.2%) experienced neonatal/postnatal death. When stratified by CMA result, fetuses with normal CMA (n = 2,737) showed the most favorable outcomes: 2,334 pregnancies (85.3%) resulted in livebirths, 165 (6.0%) were electively terminated, 7 ended in miscarriage or stillbirth, and 231 (8.4%) were lost to follow-up or declined participation. In the aneuploidy subgroup (n = 223), most pregnancies were electively terminated (207/223, 92.8%), and two ended in early embryonic demise. Thirteen pregnancies (5.8%) resulted in live births. Among these, two trisomy 21 pregnancies were continued after genetic counseling: one child (aged 5 years) had intellectual disability and absent speech, whereas the other family declined follow-up at 4 months of age. One infant with trisomy 18 died shortly after birth. The remaining nine liveborn infants comprised eight with sex-chromosome abnormalities and one with low-level mosaic trisomy 16; all were reported to have age-appropriate development at the time of assessment. In the pCNV subgroup (n = 163), 106 pregnancies (64.8%) underwent termination of pregnancy (TOP), 49 (30.1%) resulted in live births, and 8 (4.9%) were lost to follow-up or declined participation. Among the 49 live births, two infants died in infancy, and three were lost to follow-up without postnatal details. Postnatal phenotypic information was available for the remaining 44 children: 29/44 (65.9%) were reported to have age-appropriate growth and neurodevelopment at last contact, whereas 15/44 (34.1%) had abnormal clinical findings. Reported abnormalities most commonly included xerosis/ichthyosis consistent with Xp22.31 deletions, short stature, mild speech delay and hydronephrosis. For fetuses with VOUS (n = 426), clinical outcomes were generally favorable. A total of 348 pregnancies (81.7%) resulted in livebirths, 39 (8.9%) underwent TOP, 6 (1.4%) ended in miscarriage, and 33 (7.7%) were lost to follow-up or declined participation. Among the 348 liveborn fetuses with VOUS, 335 (96.3%) were reported to have normal growth and neurodevelopment during follow-up, and only 10 children (2.9%) had recorded clinical abnormalities. Discussion and conclusion The enrichment effect: NIPT as a high-efficiency triage tool The integration of NIPT into prenatal screening has reshaped invasive-testing referrals and enriched clinically significant findings among NIPT-positive cases. In our cohort, the NIPT high-risk pathway was the most enriched subgroup, with the highest yield of confirmed chromosomal abnormalities, supporting NIPT as a high-efficiency triage tool in contemporary practice [, , ]. Regarding diagnostic accuracy, 6 of 155 confirmed positives (~ 4%) showed discordant or off-target findings. Such discrepancies are biologically plausible and may reflect confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal mosaicism, or other maternal cfDNA contributions [–]; additionally, some confirmed P/LP CNVs may be incidental and unrelated to the original indication for invasive testing. Consistent with known technical limitations, “other” NIPT calls showed lower confirmatory yields than common trisomy calls [, ]; this is in line with the recognized limitations of conventional low-coverage sequencing for microdeletion detection. Against this backdrop, and without increasing per-test costs or departing from current regional policy constraints in China, algorithmic refinements within a standard-depth NIPT workflow allowed additional rare CNVs and other atypical chromosomal findings to be flagged, resulting in a modest but clinically meaningful improvement in the overall diagnostic yield of prenatal chromosomal assessment. Stratified diagnostic utility across organ systems Consistent with the high burden of chromosomal macro-aberrations in complex phenotypes, fetuses with multisystem anomalies exhibited the highest diagnostic yield, underscoring the urgency of prompt invasive assessment [, ]. For isolated cardiovascular anomalies, the presence of clinically relevant pCNVs is consistent with known recurrent microdeletion associations (e.g., 22q11.2), reinforcing CMA as an appropriate first-tier test when conventional karyotyping may miss submicroscopic etiologies. In contrast, skeletal anomalies showed limited yield by CMA, in line with the predominance of monogenic causes in fetal skeletal dysplasia []. Therefore, an indication-based sequential strategy should be considered, with trio-based sequencing (e.g., WES) particularly when CMA is negative and a monogenic disorder is suspected. Delineating the dose-response of nuchal translucency NT thickness increases the likelihood of P/LP findings, while VOUS rates remain stable, suggesting NT enriches for actionable genetic findings rather than diagnostic ambiguity. Although NT showed limited standalone discriminative performance (AUC 0.667, 95% CI 0.550–0.777), it should be integrated into broader clinical risk assessment rather than used as a sole triage tool. While an ROC-optimized cutoff (e.g., 5.7 mm) maximizes specificity, applying this strict threshold in practice would be clinically detrimental, as it would fail to capture ~ 60% of affected fetuses presenting with intermediate thickening (3.5–5.5 mm). Therefore, to prioritize diagnostic sensitivity over statistical specificity, clinical protocols must retain lower thresholds (e.g., 3.0–3.5 mm) for invasive testing referrals. The age paradox: rethinking risk in younger pregnancies Our cohort reveals an age paradox in prenatal diagnosis. While the risk of aneuploidy rises with increasing maternal age, the likelihood of pCNVs does not follow the same age gradient. In our dataset, pCNVs were more frequently observed among younger mothers (median age 29.0 years). This pattern is biologically plausible, as recurrent microdeletion/microduplication syndromes typically arise through NAHR or replication-based mechanisms rather than age-related nondisjunction. Consequently, screening strategies that heavily rely on AMA may under-serve younger women who still face clinically significant CNV risks. Therefore, while AMA remains a key risk factor for common trisomies, it should not overshadow the consideration of pCNVs in younger pregnancies when ultrasound anomalies, marker combinations, or abnormal screening results are present. Recurrent CNVs and counseling translation The marked enrichment of Xp22.31 deletions in our cohort (33/3,549; 1 in 108), which substantially exceeds published male prevalence estimates (~ 1/1,500–1/6,000) [, ], likely reflects ascertainment effects related to prenatal screening–driven referral patterns and/or regional clustering. This observation provides a concrete example of how phenotype-informed counseling can influence clinical decision-making. Historically (pre-2021), parental decisions were often shaped by anxiety about ichthyosis and potential neurodevelopmental sequelae [, ], and were associated with higher termination rates. After we updated counseling to emphasize that the cutaneous phenotype is typically manageable and that developmental expectations are generally favorable in apparently isolated STS presentations, decisions shifted toward pregnancy continuation (14/16). Preliminary follow-up of live births after 2021 is consistent with this approach: infants showed the expected ichthyotic skin changes, and none exhibited early neurodevelopmental red flags. Nevertheless, longer-term follow-up remains necessary. Similar challenges emerge when counseling for low-penetrance susceptibility loci (e.g., 17p12, 15q11.2, 16p11.2), which often lack specific prenatal phenotypic correlates. Historically, a dichotomous “health-versus-disease” counseling frame was associated with higher termination rates, most notably for 17p12 deletions (100% [7/7] before 2023). After parental segregation testing was introduced, decisions shifted substantially, with the termination rate decreasing to 25% (1/4) for 17p12. This pattern suggests an important counseling implication: families tend to respond more strongly to concrete segregation results (e.g., inheritance from an unaffected parent) than to probabilistic risk estimates alone. In contrast, termination rates remained high for 16p11.2 and 15q11.2, where parental testing was frequently declined or incomplete. Together, these discordant outcomes indicate a clear need to integrate parental segregation analysis more systematically, supported by workflows that increase testing uptake and standardize risk communication to help reduce potentially avoidable terminations. The VOUS challenge and defensive reporting The VOUS rate in our cohort is substantially higher than the ~ 1.4–5.2% range generally reported in prenatal CMA series of fetuses [, , ]. Notably, a similar proportion of 12% has been reported in a Brazilian postnatal neurodevelopmental-disorder cohort []. Many prenatal centers adopt a conservative reporting policy to limit VOUS disclosure (e.g. size thresholds ≥1 Mb) [, ]. However, reporting practices vary across laboratories. In our setting, the institution follows a broader disclosure strategy driven by medico-legal considerations, especially when ultrasound abnormalities are present. CNVs meeting ACMG/ClinGen technical criteria for VOUS were reported, even when clinical context suggested benign interpretation (e.g., duplications involving autosomal-recessive genes or loci primarily constrained by haploinsufficiency). This practice led to follow-up data showing a small proportion (1.9%, 8/426) of terminations due to anxiety over uncertain findings, despite explicit counseling favoring continuation. At the same time, these data caution against treating VOUS as uniformly benign. Beyond the infant deaths and clinically significant abnormalities, one illustrative case involved a fetus with an apparent heterozygous STRC deletion reported prenatally as a carrier state but later confirmed postnatally as biallelic pathogenic, resulting in deafness. This highlights a known limitation of array-based CNV calling in complex genomic regions []. Accordingly, reducing VOUS rates will require more than stricter filtering; it also calls for nationally harmonized reporting standards and clearer validation pathways that balance the risk of false reassurance against the harms of iatrogenic anxiety. Limitations Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this retrospective single-center study may be subject to selection bias, although the large sample size partially mitigates this concern. Second, 7.7% of cases were lost to follow-up, and postnatal follow-up was heterogeneous and relatively short for neurodevelopmental outcomes; thus, outcomes—particularly for VOUS and low-penetrance CNVs—should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, the absence of systematic WES in fetuses with structural anomalies and normal CMA limited evaluation of monogenic etiologies. Future work will focus on prospective standardized prenatal phenotyping with structured postnatal follow-up and an indication-based sequential strategy that offers trio-based sequencing (e.g., WES) after negative CMA in structurally anomalous fetuses.

Conclusion
Conclusion This large-scale study confirms the pivotal role of SNP-array in the post-NIPT era, delivering clinically actionable findings while presenting a concurrent counseling challenge. Our data validate the NIPT-driven ‘enrichment effect,’ concentrating complex pathologies within the invasive testing cohort, and highlight the utility of NT as a risk marker for pathogenic findings. These results support a stratified diagnostic model, using NIPT as a broad-spectrum aneuploidy screen and CMA for structural anomalies and high-risk indications. The independence of pathogenic CNVs from maternal age emphasizes the value of invasive diagnosis beyond aneuploidy detection, reinforcing the need for precision counseling to address VOUS and incidental findings.

title: Prenatal diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia with mosaicism of chromosomes 17q and 18q in Iran: a case report.
label_reason: Fetal CDH on ultrasound with chromosomal mosaicism detected.
abstract: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a prevalent birth defect characterized by high mortality and morbidity rates. It is defined as the protrusion of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity through an abnormal aperture in the diaphragm of the fetus or neonate. This anomaly is multifactorial in etiology, encompassing both genetic and environmental components, and may be associated with various syndromes. Among the chromosomal abnormalities associated with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, trisomies 21, 18, and 13 are the most frequently observed. Additionally, complex chromosomal aberrations such as mosaicism have been documented. The presentation of this case underscores the novelty of identifying mosaicism involving chromosomes 17q and 18q, emphasizing the significance of genetic evaluation in elucidating congenital diaphragmatic hernia. This rare genetic finding is not extensively reported in literature. A 34-year-old Iranian woman in her second pregnancy was referred for an ultrasound examination at the 16th week of gestation owing to the diagnosis of a fetus with a left diaphragmatic hernia containing the stomach and without the umbilical cord, accompanied by a defect in the abdominal wall. The first trimester screening tests were within normal parameters. Amniocentesis and karyotype analysis revealed mosaicism of chromosomes 17q and 18q, and the presence of a left diaphragmatic hernia was confirmed in the fetus. This rare genetic finding provides insight into potential contributing factors in the development of congenital diaphragmatic hernia. In light of the presence of mosaicism of chromosomes in this instance, it is suggested that a potential genetic factor may play a role in the emergence of congenital diaphragmatic hernia, necessitating additional research. This case underscores the significance of genetic testing in the prenatal diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and emphasizes the necessity for comprehensive counseling for affected families.
