abstract: 临床上16p11.2微缺失胎儿出生后的表型主要包括孤独症、精神分裂症和智力障碍，并伴有肥胖和先天性畸形等表现，但有关16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前表型研究有限，本研究旨在通过分析16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声与遗传学特征的相关性，为临床遗传咨询提供参考。 收集2016年10月至2024年12月多中心产前诊断为16p11.2微缺失的60例胎儿临床资料，包括孕妇年龄、羊水穿刺的指征及孕周、胎儿超声检查及全基因组拷贝数变异测序(copy number variation sequencing，CNV-seq)检测结果，对胎儿父母同时进行CNV-seq检测，以明确变异来源，并对所有病例进行妊娠结局随访。结合产前超声表现、遗传学检测结果及妊娠结局，对16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声表型及基因组变异特征进行系统分析。 在43 721例行CNV-seq检测的胎儿中共发现60例16p11.2微缺失(60/43 721，0.14%)，其中49例为近端缺失(BP4-BP5)、9例为远端缺失(BP2-BP3)、2例为大片段缺失(BP2-BP5)。49例16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)胎儿中18例存在结构异常(6例为半椎体并脊柱侧弯、4例为肾发育异常、2例为主动脉缩窄、6例为其他)、26例为超声软指标[11例为NT增厚(其中1例合并单脐动脉)、6例为轻度脑室扩张(其中1例合并羊水过多)、9例为其他]和5例为超声检查无异常。9例16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)胎儿中2例存在宫内生长受限、4例为超声软指标(2例为鼻骨缺如、1例为单脐动脉、1例为NT增厚)及3例为超声检查无异常。2例16p11.2大片段缺失(BP2-BP5)胎儿中1例表现为膈疝，1例为NT增厚。72%的病例为新发变异(36/50)，28%遗传自父母(14/50)，67%的病例选择终止妊娠(35/52)。 16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声表型具有高度异质性，其中16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)产前主要表现为半椎体并脊柱侧弯、肾发育异常及NT增厚。而16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)则可能与宫内生长受限和超声软指标相关。
text:
60例16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声及遗传学特征分析

对象与方法
对象与方法 伦理声明 本研究已获得中南大学湘雅医院伦理委员会批准[审批号：伦审科快第(科202211714)]。研究对象均签署了侵入性产前诊断的书面知情同意书。 对象 收集2016年10月至2024年12月来自多中心的43 721例产前样本，每例孕妇均接受超声检查和全基因组拷贝数变异测序(copy number variation sequencing，CNV-seq)检测，共纳入13 312例超声异常、17 679例超声软指标和12 730例超声正常且孕妇高龄样本。孕妇在行CNV-seq检测前均接受详细的遗传咨询，包括遗传检测的适用性、局限性和风险。 方法 样本采集、检测方法和结果分析 从羊水、脐带血中提取DNA进行全基因组CNV-seq检测。采用DNeasy血液和组织试剂盒(德国Qiagen公司产品)提取基因组DNA。采用Qubit 2.0荧光计测定基因组DNA的浓度和纯度。采用HiSeq2000平台(美国illumina公司)进行CNV-Seq检测，36 bp单端测序，测序深度为0.1x，共获得500万条原始测序读长，其检测拷贝数变异(copy number variation，CNV)的分辨率约为100 kb。 根据2019年美国医学遗传学与基因组学学会(American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics，ACMG)发布的标准化判读指南[]对CNV的临床意义进行评估，依照证据总得分将CNV的致病性分成5类，包括致病(pathogenic，P)、可能致病(likely pathogenic，LP)、临床意义不明(variants of uncertain significance，VUS)、可能良性(likely benign，LB)和良性(benign，B)。 随访 通过医院信息系统查询病历资料并结合电话随访，对产前诊断为16p11.2微缺失的病例进行妊娠及出生后结局追踪。收集内容包括家系验证结果、产前超声检测发现及妊娠结局。对于继续妊娠的病例，记录孕期超声动态变化、产检情况及分娩结局，对活产儿进行定期随访并记录其生长发育情况。

结 果
结 果 基本特征 在43 721例行CNV-seq检测的胎儿样本中共检测到16p11.2微缺失60例，检出率为0.14%(60/43 721)。60例16p11.2微缺失的范围为0.22~1.72 Mb，根据断裂点位置分为3类：其中49例为近端缺失(BP4-BP5)，9例为远端缺失(BP2-BP3)，2例为大片段缺失(BP2-BP5)。此外，6例合并其他染色体片段缺失/重复变异，具体包括胎儿Y2008140002合并4q35.2重复1.36 Mb、胎儿Y2003120077合并Xp21.1重复0.42 Mb、胎儿Y2009220222合并18p11.31-p11.23重复0.52 Mb、胎儿Y2009250094合并4q22.3重复1.56 Mb、胎儿FDLV01E1合并Xp22.31重复1.66 Mb、胎儿Y1801090070合并Xp22.31缺失1.66 Mb，上述合并的拷贝数变异除了Xp22.31缺失1.66 Mb为致病性变异，其余均为临床意义未明变异。在50例经父母验证后的病例中，36例为新发变异，14例为遗传自父母(其中母源性遗传10例，父源性遗传4例)。经遗传咨询后，有35例(包括新发变异24例、遗传变异6例、来源不明5例)选择终止妊娠，17例活产，8例失访。 超声征象 与16p11.2微缺失相关的产前超声特征详见。49例16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)胎儿中，18例为结构异常[包括半椎体并脊柱侧弯6例，肾发育异常4例(其中肾实质回声增强2例、右肾缺如1例、左肾发育不良1例)，主动脉缩窄2例，肠管扩张、腹水、肺囊腺瘤、脑积水、心包积液及胼胝体缺如合并透明隔腔缺如各1例]；26例为超声软指标[包括NT增厚(其中1例合并单脐动脉)11例、轻度脑室扩张6例(其中1例合并羊水过多)、单脐动脉2例、右锁骨下动脉迷走2例、永存左上腔静脉2例、心室强光点2例、轻度肾盂分离合并羊水过多1例]；5例为高龄且超声检查无异常。 在9例16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)的胎儿中，4例为超声软指标[包括鼻骨缺如2例、NT增厚和单脐动脉各1例]；2例为宫内生长受限[为16p11.2大片段缺失(BP2-BP5)的胎儿，膈疝和NT增厚各1例]；3例为高龄且超声检查无异常。 超声表型与相关基因 49例16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)胎儿中6例出现半椎体并脊柱侧弯，缺失范围为0.49~0.59 Mb，其中胎儿Y1904120016缺失的范围最小，为0.49 Mb，在孕27周超声发现胎儿第8和9胸椎半椎体并脊柱侧弯()，最小共同区间覆盖的在线人类孟德尔遗传数据库(Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man，OMIM)基因有KIF22、PRRT2、TLCD3B、ALDOA、TBX6和CORO1A，其中TBX6基因变异会导致脊椎肋骨发育不全(OMIM：122600；)。此外，有4例16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)胎儿出现肾发育异常，包括右肾缺如1例、左肾发育不良1例、肾实质回声增强2例；缺失范围为0.48~0.60 Mb，缺失范围最小的2例表型有差异，右肾缺如1例，肾实质回声增强合并NT增厚及脉络丛囊肿1例。最小共同区间覆盖的OMIM基因有KIF22、PRRT2、TLCD3B、ALDOA、TBX6和CORO1A()。 胎儿Y1904120016的产前超声表现(半椎体及脊柱侧弯) Figure 1 Ultrasonography (hemivertebra and scoliosis) of fetus Y1904120016 胎儿Y1904120016的CNV结果 Figure 2 CNV findings of fetus Y1904120016 A: CNV-seq genome-wide copy number variation analysis revealed a copy number abnormality involving chromosome 16. B: A high-resolution view of chromosome 16 demonstrates a 0.49 Mb deletion in the 16p11.2 region. CNV: Copy number variation. 4例有肾发育异常表型的16p11.2微缺失位点示意图 Figure 3 Schematic diagram of the 16p11.2 microdeletion in 4 cases of renal abnormality Red bars indicate the deletion regions associated with 4 cases of renal developmental abnormalities. 9例16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)的胎儿中2例表现为宫内生长受限，缺失范围为0.22~0.84 Mb，最小共同区间覆盖的OMIM基因有ATP2A1、CD19、LAT、SH2B1和TUFM。本研究中16p11.2微缺失片段最大的2个病例(缺失大小分别为1.70 Mb和1.72 Mb)，产前超声表型差异显著，1例提示为膈疝，另1例仅表现为NT增厚，缺失区域共同包含的致病基因有10个，分别是ALDOA、ATP2A1、CD19、CLN3、KIF22、LAT、PRRT2、SH2B1、TBX6和TLCD3B。

讨 论
讨 论 本研究回顾性分析60例16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声特征及遗传学特点，是目前已知的最大样本阐述16p11.2微缺失产前表型的研究之一。本研究发现16p11.2微缺失的总体产前检出率为0.14%。这与之前的研究[]结果一致。16p11.2微缺失的产前表型谱跨度较大，可从无明显异常到严重结构畸形，16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)的主要产前表型为半椎体并脊柱侧弯、肾发育异常及轻度脑室扩张，而16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)则主要表现为宫内生长受限和超声软指标异常。 进一步细化表型后发现，半椎体并脊柱侧弯是16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)产前最常见的超声特征。一项纳入12例16p11.2近端缺失胎儿表型的研究[]显示，5例胎儿存在骨骼系统异常，其中3例为半椎体，1例为蝴蝶椎，1例为椎体小。本研究中49例16p11.2近端缺失胎儿有6例出现半椎体并脊柱侧弯，为16p11.2微缺失和椎体发育异常的相关性提供支撑和依据。16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)包含的TBX6基因变异可通过影响蛋白转录活性从而导致脊椎肋骨发育不全(OMIM：122600)，特别是同时携带亚效等位基因时，其先天性脊柱侧弯的发病率可达11%[]。Lin等[]研究发现半椎体/蝴蝶椎是TBX6基因相关先天性脊柱侧弯最显著的特征，因此TBX6可能是导致16p11.2微缺失胎儿半椎体并脊柱侧弯表型的关键基因[]。近年研究[-]发现TBX6还是参与先天性肾与泌尿道畸形的新基因，其单倍剂量不足可能是16p11.2微缺失肾发育缺陷的潜在驱动因素。在TBX6基因突变小鼠模型中，TBX6杂合缺失可导致13%的单侧肾发生[]。本研究中4例16p11.2近端缺失胎儿表现出多样的肾发育异常表型，涵盖肾缺如、肾发育不良和肾实质回声增强。综上，TBX6基因单倍剂量不足可能是16p11.2微缺失骨骼与泌尿系统相关表型的共同核心驱动因素[]。 除了结构畸形外，本研究还发现16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)与超声软指标密切相关，其中NT增厚是最常见的超声软指标(11/49)，其次是轻度脑室扩张(5/49)，这2项超声软指标在16p11.2微缺失胎儿中既往已有报道[, -]。值得关注的是，在本研究病例中观察到的永存左上腔静脉和右锁骨下动脉迷走在以往报道[, ]的16p11.2微缺失胎儿中仅有极少数的散发病例记录。16p11.2微缺失是导致精神发育障碍的复发性致病性拷贝数变异，部分病例产前可能并没有典型的结构异常，而仅仅表现为超声软指标或正常超声。 与16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)表型特征不同，16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)产前则主要表现为宫内生长受限，重叠区域共包含5个致病基因，其中CD19和LAT基因与免疫缺陷相关。TUFM基因的纯合或复合杂合突变会导致联合氧化磷酸化缺陷4型，表现为严重早发性乳酸酸中毒和进行性致死性婴儿脑病。而ATP2A1基因突变则主要导致肌肉发育异常。SH2B1基因是瘦素和胰岛素信号的中介因子，该基因的缺失可以导致肥胖和糖尿病[]，也有研究[]认为包含SH2B1基因的16p11.2微缺失是引发胎儿宫内生长受限的危险因素，然而目前ClinGen数据库中关于SH2B1基因单倍剂量不足的证据较少。16p11.2远端缺失与宫内生长受限这一表型相关的基因还有待进一步研究。16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)产前还可以表现为单脐动脉、鼻骨缺如或超声无异常。总体上，16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)产前更常见的是宫内生长受限和超声软指标，而非结构畸形。 膈疝是16p11.2微缺失病例中比较罕见的表型特征，研究[]发现TBX6的剂量失衡(重复或缺失)与先天性膈疝的发生相关，并推测16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)可能与膈疝相关。但另有研究[]报告了1例合并膈疝的16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)胎儿，并提出ATP2A1可能是16p11.2微缺失胎儿膈疝发生的候选基因，同时推测该表型的发生可能还需要与其他参与膈肌发育的基因发生等位变异后的联合作用。Pan等[]的研究亦证实ATP2A1基因的靶向破坏会影响新生小鼠的膈肌发育。本研究同样发现1例合并膈疝的16p11.2微缺失胎儿，其缺失范围更大，覆盖BP2-BP5区域，ATP2A1基因和TBX6基因均包含在内。因此，与16p11.2微缺失膈疝表型相关的基因还有待进一步探究。 本研究通过分析60例16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前超声和遗传学特征，明确了不同断裂点类型的16p11.2微缺失胎儿的主要产前特征。16p11.2微缺失胎儿的产前表型具有高度异质性，可涵盖从超声无异常到多种结构畸形的广泛表现，其中16p11.2近端缺失(BP4-BP5)最主要的结构异常为半椎体并脊柱侧弯及肾发育异常，而最常见的超声软指标为NT增厚及轻度脑室扩张。而16p11.2远端缺失(BP2-BP3)则可能与宫内生长受限和超声软指标相关。

title: 22q11.2 duplication syndrome and LZTR1-related Noonan syndrome type 10 overlapping phenotypes in a dual diagnosis - fetal hydrops: a case report.
label_reason: Hydrops fetus with karyotype, CMA, WES.
abstract: Nonimmune factors are the most common cause of fetal hydrops, which are characterized by the accumulation of pathological fluid due to various causes. The etiology of this disease is complex, with a relatively high mortality rate, and the prognosis largely depends on the underlying cause. Notably, fetal hydrops attributable to genetic causes, such as chromosomal abnormalities or gene mutations, are typically associated with a poor prognosis. A fetus diagnosed with severe nonimmune fetal hydrops at 27 weeks of gestation presented with multiple abnormalities on prenatal ultrasound, including progressively thickened nuchal translucency (NT) and nuchal fold (NF), cystic hygroma, pleural effusion, and renal pelvis duplication. Amniotic fluid cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal karyotype. Integrated chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and trio-based whole-exome sequencing (Trio-WES) revealed a pathogenic 2.82 Mb duplication at chromosome 22q11.21, designated as arr[GRCh37] 22q11.21(18984188–21804597)x3, associated with 22q11.2 duplication syndrome, which was inherited from the father. Additionally, a heterozygous missense variant in the LZTR1 gene NM_006767.3 : c.848G > A (p.Arg283Gln) was detected and classified as pathogenic, associated with Noonan syndrome type 10, maternally inherited. After comprehensive counseling and careful consideration, the parents elected to terminate the pregnancy. This study revealed that fetuses carrying both a pathogenic copy number variant of duplication in the 22q11.2 region and a heterozygous pathogenic missense variant of the LZTR1 gene (c.848G > A) simultaneously constitute the main genetic basis for its multisystem abnormalities and severe hydrops. This study highlights the role of multiple genetic superimposition effects in the formation of complex fetal phenotypes and emphasizes that in genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis, a combined strategy of CMA and Trio-WES should be adopted to improve the detection rate of complex genetic diseases and the accuracy of recurrence risk assessment.
text:
22q11.2 duplication syndrome and LZTR1-related Noonan syndrome type 10 overlapping phenotypes in a dual diagnosis - fetal hydrops: a case report

Background
Background Fetal hydrops is a severe pregnancy complication defined by pathological fluid accumulation in fetal soft tissues and body cavities. The ultrasound diagnostic criteria require at least two abnormal fluid collections in body cavities, including pleural effusion, ascites, pericardial effusion (thickness > 3 mm), or skin edema (thickness > 5 mm), and are frequently associated with polyhydramnios or placental thickening (≥ 4 cm during the second trimester) []. The estimated incidence ranges from approximately 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 1,700 pregnancies. It is broadly classified into immune and nonimmune forms, with nonimmune fetal hydrops (NIHF) accounting for 85–95% of all cases []. NIHF has a complex etiology, being associated with a generally poor prognosis and a high mortality rate. The clinical outcome often depends on the underlying cause. Common etiologies include cardiovascular malformations, hematologic abnormalities secondary to fetal anemia, thoracic structural defects, intrauterine infections, placental or umbilical cord abnormalities, and genetic factors []. Among the genetic causes, chromosomal abnormalities account for approximately 28.8% of NIHF cases, and monogenic diseases account for about 17.8% []. Notably, genetically mediated fetal hydrops is typically associated with poor prognosis. Thus, comprehensive etiological evaluation is crucial for guiding clinical management and providing accurate genetic counseling. Current genetic testing strategies for NIHF primarily include karyotype analysis, CMA, and next-generation sequencing (NGS) approaches. Karyotype analysis can identify chromosomal aneuploidy abnormalities, whereas CMA is used to detect genomic abnormalities such as microdeletions and microduplications. With the development of sequencing technology, NGS techniques (such as exome sequencing) have been gradually applied to cases of NIHF with unknown causes, providing an effective means to identify pathogenic gene variations []. This study reports a fetus that presented with multiple prenatal ultrasound abnormalities, including thickened NT and NF, pleural effusion, and renal pelvis duplication, which subsequently progressed to severe hydrops fetalis. Through combined CMA and Trio-WES testing, the fetus was diagnosed with a dual diagnosis of 22q11.2 duplication syndrome and Noonan syndrome type 10 associated with an LZTR1 pathogenic variant. This is the first reported case of disease manifestation due to the co-occurrence of these two conditions, providing novel clinical and genetic evidence for understanding the polygenic superimposition mechanism underlying NIHF.

Case presentation
Case presentation The pregnant woman was 32 years old, gravida 1, para 0, and had conceived naturally. At 13+ 3 weeks of gestation, ultrasound screening revealed a singleton viable intrauterine pregnancy with increased NT measuring 4.0 mm. At 23+ 1 weeks of the second trimester, an ultrasound examination revealed a thickened NF (6.9 mm) in the fetus, right pleural effusion (maximum depth of approximately 2.3 mm), and suspected right renal pelvis duplication. Both parents reported no significant medical history, denied consanguinity, and had no family history of genetic disorders. To further clarify the diagnosis, ultrasound-guided amniocentesis was performed, and 30 mL of amniotic fluid was collected for cytogenetic and molecular genetic prenatal diagnosis. Additionally, 3 mL peripheral blood samples were collected from each parent for family genetic variation analysis. The results were as follows: Chromosome karyotype analysis: G-banding results revealed that the fetal karyotype was 46,XX, with no numerical or structural abnormalities. CMA: Using SNP array technology (Cytoscan 750K chip), a 2.82 Mb duplication in the 22q11.2 region was detected, with the genomic coordinates arr[GRCh37] 22q11.21(18984188-21804597)×3. This variant was rated as pathogenic and was associated with 22q11.2 duplication syndrome (Fig. A). Trio-WES: Sequencing was performed using the high-throughput sequencing platform MGISEQ-2000. A heterozygous missense variant NM_006767.3: c.848G>A (p.Arg283Gln) was detected in the LZTR1 gene of the fetus. This variant is recorded in ClinVar (ClinVar ID: 561716). According to the updated ACMG/AMP guidelines for variant interpretation issued by the ClinGen RASopathy Variant Curation Expert Panel (VCEP) [], the variant is classified as pathogenic(PM2_supporting + PP3 + PS4 + PM6_strong), associated with autosomal dominant Noonan syndrome type 10. Pedigree analysis revealed that the missense variant was inherited from the mother, whereas the 22q11.2 duplication was inherited from the father. Sanger sequencing verification: Primers were designed for the above LZTR1 variant site for amplification and sequencing. The results confirmed that both the fetus and the mother carried the heterozygous c.848G>A (p.Arg283Gln) missense variant (Fig. B). A CMA revealed that the fetus carries arr[GRCh37] 22q11.21(18984188–21804597)×3. B Sanger sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic missense variant, NM_006767.3:c.848G > A (p.Arg283Gln), in the LZTR1 gene in both the fetus and the mother, while the father was found to carry the wild-type genotype At 27 weeks of gestation, a follow-up ultrasound revealed that the NF had further thickened to 9.56 mm with associated lymphatic cyst formation, bilateral pleural effusion (maximum depths of approximately 12 mm on the left and 27 mm on the right), bilateral renal pelvis duplication, and polyhydramnios, consistent with progression to nonimmune fetal hydrops. (Fig. ). Ultrasonic image of the fetus at 27 weeks of gestation. A Increased nuchal fold thickness (9.56 mm). B Formation of a lymphatic cyst in the posterior cervical region. C Right pleural effusion. D Left pleural effusion. E Right renal pelvis duplication. F Left renal pelvis duplication After genetic counseling and informed consent from the family, the pregnant woman decided to terminate the pregnancy and underwent induction at 27+ 2 weeks. The induced fetus was female, and the manifestations of “short neck and thickened neck skin”, and “full chest contour” were consistent with the prenatal ultrasound findings. Additionally, low-set ears, micrognathia and abdominal protrusions were observed; no abnormalities were found in the spine, limbs, or external genitalia (Fig. ). Owing to the family’s refusal of autopsy, no further pathological examination was conducted. Images of the fetus after termination of pregnancy

Discussion
Discussion This study reports a fetus with severe fetal hydrops. Comprehensive genetic testing confirmed the co-occurrence of a 22q11.2 duplication and a heterozygous LZTR1 gene variant c.848G > A, corresponding to 22q11.2 duplication syndrome and Noonan syndrome type 10, respectively. By integrating clinical phenotypic findings with molecular genetic data, this study systematically analyzes the phenotypic features of the two syndromes, explores potential mechanisms underlying their copathogenic effects, and summarizes the implications for genetic counseling. The 22q11.2 region is highly susceptible to nonallelic homologous recombination due to its enrichment in low-copy repeats (LCRs), which frequently leads to recurrent deletions or duplications, constituting the primary genetic mechanism underlying 22q11.2 deletion/duplication syndrome []. In this case, the fetal 2.82 Mb duplication is located between LCR-A and LCR-D and shows high overlap (96.71%) with the typical 22q11.2 duplication syndrome region—22q11.2 recurrent (DGS/VCFS) region (proximal, A-D) (including TBX1) [ISCA-37446], encompassing multiple critical genes including TBX1, LZTR1, PI4KA, and CRKL. The region has a triplosensitivity score of 3, indicating established pathogenicity. The penetrance of 22q11.2 duplication is approximately 21.9% [], with clinical manifestations exhibiting substantial heterogeneity, ranging from asymptomatic or mildly affected individuals to those with severe malformations, developmental delay, and intellectual disability. Additional clinical features include cleft palate, hypotonia, thymic aplasia, congenital heart disease, and urogenital malformations. Approximately, 70% of 22q11.2 duplications (LCR A-D) are inherited from parents who exhibit normal or only mild phenotypic abnormalities []. Nevertheless, even individuals inheriting duplication from clinically unaffected or minimally affected parents may develop significant clinical manifestations, posing a major challenge for prenatal genetic counseling in cases of fetal 22q11.2 duplication. Mary et al.‘s [] cohort study demonstrated that NT thickening and cardiovascular malformations are key prenatal ultrasound features associated with 22q11.2 duplication. Among 43 fetuses carrying the 22q11.2 duplication (LCR A-D), 15 (34.9%) exhibited NT thickening and 16 (37.2%) had cardiovascular malformations, including atrioventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, and valvular abnormalities. Notably, two fetuses in this cohort presented with renal pelvis duplication and fetal hydrops, both of whom died during the neonatal period, suggesting that this phenotypic combination may be indicative of a poor prognosis. Although no cardiac structural abnormalities were detected in the present case, the presence of NT thickening, renal pelvis duplication, and subsequent development of hydrops is consistent with the more severe end of the phenotypic spectrum observed in 22q11.2 duplication syndrome. The application of Trio-WES enabled the identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant c.848G > A (p.Arg283Gln) in the LZTR1 gene in this fetus. The LZTR1 protein plays a critical role in regulating the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway, and its dysfunction is associated with impaired lymphatic drainage and cardiovascular abnormalities []. Prenatal features of Noonan syndrome due to LZTR1 variants include NF thickening, increased NT, lymphatic cysts, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, polyhydramnios, fetal hydrops, cardiac malformations, and renal anomalies [–]. The LZTR1 c.848G > A (p.Arg283Gln) variant identified in this case has been repeatedly reported in association with Noonan syndrome type 10, a condition predominantly characterized by lymphatic dysplasia, including NT/NF thickening, ascites, chylothorax, peripheral edema, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with variable phenotypic heterogeneity among individuals [–]. The observed findings in this fetus, NF thickening with lymphatic cyst formation, progressive pleural effusion, and severe hydrops—are highly consistent with the core phenotypic manifestations of Noonan syndrome. Notably, the LZTR1 gene is located within the 22q11.2 region and has been implicated as a candidate gene for the bladder exstrophy-epispadias complex (BEEC) phenotype in individuals with a 22q11.2 duplication []. This dual association suggests that LZTR1 may contribute to disease pathogenesis through distinct genetic mechanisms: it can cause Noonan syndrome via a monogenic inheritance pattern, while also playing a role in urinary tract malformations in the context of 22q11.2 duplication. The bilateral renal pelvis duplication observed in this fetus may reflect the shared impact of LZTR1 dysregulation on urinary system development across both genetic contexts. In this case, the parents were asymptomatic carriers of a 22q11.2 duplication and an LZTR1 pathogenic variant, respectively. The fetus exhibited severe hydrops fetalis, supporting the “second-hit” pathogenic model []. The 22q11.2 duplication provides a genetic susceptibility background, with increased gene dosage in the region potentially disrupting the development of multiple organ systems. The LZTR1 variant is primarily associated with impaired lymphatic drainage. The existence of a direct functional interaction between the two remains undetermined. However, it is plausible that the combined effects of 22q11.2 duplication mediated genetic dosage alteration and the LZTR1 variant driven dysregulation of the RAS/MAPK pathway may impair lymphatic and cardiovascular development, and might be related to to the severity of fetal hydrops. This mechanistic hypothesis requires validation through targeted functional studies. In terms of genetic counseling, this case indicates that even if both parents are asymptomatic carriers, the fetus may still present with severe clinical manifestations due to the genetic additive effect. In subsequent pregnancies, offspring inheriting both variants (with a 25% recurrence risk) are at high risk of severe fetal hydrops, whereas those inheriting only one variant (with a 50% recurrence risk) may exhibit milder or atypical phenotypes. To reduce the risk of recurrence, preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) is recommended to select embryos that are either unaffected or heterozygous for a single variant. Additionally, for fetuses with prenatal findings such as increased NT thickness and pleural effusion suggesting lymphatic dysplasia, even if CMA has identified pathogenic copy number variants (CNVs), if there is a low penetrance situation, the necessity of performing Trio-WES should still be considered to comprehensively assess coexisting monogenic variations, providing a more complete basis for genetic counseling and perinatal management. This study has the following limitations: First, the family refused an autopsy, thus no pathological evidence of the fetal internal organs and lymphatic system could be obtained, and all phenotypes relied on prenatal ultrasound. Second, although the parents reported being asymptomatic, they did not undergo systematic clinical physical examinations (such as special facial feature assessment, echocardiography, developmental tests, etc.), so it cannot be completely ruled out that the parents have mild phenotypes. Third, as the family decided to terminate the pregnancy after genetic counseling, no intrauterine intervention (such as thoracentesis or pleuroamniotic shunt) was performed, precluding assessment of treatment responsiveness in this specific form of fetal hydrops. Fourth, as previously mentioned, the functional interplay between the two variants remains undetermined, and the proposed combined effect requires experimental validation through targeted functional assays.

Conclusion
Conclusion This case indicates that the co-occurrence of a 22q11.2 microduplication and a heterozygous LZTR1 c.848G > A (p.Arg283His) missense variant in the fetus is strongly associated with severe non-immune hydrops fetalis and multisystem congenital anomalies. In prenatal cases of complex non-immune fetal hydrops, even when both parents are asymptomatic carriers, clinicians should consider both incomplete penetrance and the potential superposition effect of multiple concurrent genetic variants. Accordingly, a comprehensive genetic evaluation integrating CMA and Trio-WES is recommended to enable accurate genotype–phenotype correlation, thereby supporting evidence-based genetic counseling and reliable recurrence risk estimation.

title: Prenatal Diagnosis and Functional Analysis of Two Compound Heterozygous Variants in the KLHL40 Gene Causing Nemaline Myopathy 8.
label_reason: Fetus with ultrasound anomalies, ES found KLHL40 variants.
abstract: Nemaline myopathy (NEM) is a rare congenital muscular disorder characterized by slow progression or static neuromuscular symptoms, which is mainly caused by variants in genes encoding the myofilament protein of skeletal muscle sarcomere. This study aimed to conduct prenatal diagnosis and functional analysis of variants in the KLHL40 gene causing NEM 8. A Chinese family who experienced multiple pregnancies with recurrent prenatal ultrasound anomalies (such as clubfoot and polyhydramnios) and subsequent neonatal death was enrolled in this study. Etiology diagnosis was conducted using karyotype, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and exome sequencing (ES). Quantitative real‐time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and western blotting were performed to investigate the transcription and expression levels of the defective gene. Hematoxylin–eosin (HE) stain and modified Gomori staining were used for further pathological examination. No chromosomal abnormalities were detected by karyotype and CMA in the proband of this family. However, the ES results revealed two compound heterozygous variants in KLHL40 gene NM_152393.4 :c.[1516A> C p.(T506P)]; [1327G> A p.(G443S)] in the fetus. The c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variant was interpreted as pathogenic, whereas the p.G443S variant was rarely reported and classified as a variant of uncertain significance. Interestingly, the subsequent western blotting analysis elicited a significantly decreased expression level of KLHL40 protein in fetal skeletal muscle tissues compared with the controls. In addition, the HE and modified Gomori stains demonstrated nemaline bodies in the fetus using skeletal muscle tissue. Combining prenatal ultrasound and ES testing increases diagnostic yield among NEM‐affected fetuses. Our results extend the mutational spectrum of the pathogenic KLHL40 variant c.1327G> A p.(G443S) linked to NEM8 and aid genotype–phenotype correlation analysis.
text:
Prenatal Diagnosis and Functional Analysis of Two Compound Heterozygous Variants in the KLHL40 Gene Causing Nemaline Myopathy 8

Introduction
Introduction Nemaline myopathies (NEM) are congenital muscular disorders that affect people worldwide and are characterized by muscle weakness and hypotonia. The condition is considered rare, with an incidence rate of approximately 1:50,000 (North et al. ). NEM has clinical heterogeneity with a broad phenotypic spectrum, ranging from severe neonatal presentations to milder childhood‐onset disease. Currently, the condition can be divided into six types: (i) severe nemaline myopathy, (ii) intermediate nemaline myopathy, (iii) typical (mainstream, classical) congenital nemaline myopathy, (iv) mild (childhood or juvenile) onset form, (v) adult‐onset forms, and (vi) other (unusual) forms (Sewry et al. ). To date, it is commonly known that NEM may be caused by pathogenic variants in over 12 genes (Sewry et al. ), including ACTA1, CFL2, KBTBD13, KLHL40, KLHL41, LMOD3, MYPN, NEB, TNNT1, TNNT3, TPM2, and TPM3. Nemaline myopathy‐8 (NEM8) is a severe autosomal recessive muscle disorder caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants in the KLHL40 gene, which is typically characterized by fetal akinesia or hypokinesia, symptoms apparent at birth, such as contractures, fractures, respiratory failure, and swallowing difficulties (Ravenscroft et al. ). Deficiency KLHL40 expression results in significant reduction of leiomodin 3 and nebulin proteins, structural sarcomere irregularities, and a lethal loss of muscle function (Garg et al. ). The majority of diagnosed patients die in infancy, and most of the skeletal muscle biopsies conducted show a large number of nemaline bodies in muscle fibers (Ravenscroft et al. ). However, only a small number of patients have obvious abnormal myofibril (Ravenscroft et al. ). In recent years, exome sequencing (ES) has been widely used in prenatal diagnosis due to its advantages in detecting pathogenic variants at the single gene level for fetal etiology diagnosis (Jelin and Vora ; Petrovski et al. ; Quinlan‐Jones et al. ; Tang et al. ; Yadava and Ashkinadze ). A study conducted by Lord et al. (Lord et al. ) enrolled a total of 610 fetuses with ultrasound structural abnormalities for ES detection, and after excluding karyotype abnormalities and copy number variants, the ES technology could effectively diagnose 52 subjects, increasing the standard diagnostic rate by 8.5%. Therefore, the potential of ES technology to explore the pathogenesis of fetal ultrasound structural abnormalities is of great value to the scholarly community and a phenomenon worthy of attention. In the present study, ES was performed for prenatal genetic diagnosis of a fetus with structural ultrasonographic anomalies. Two compound heterozygous variants in the KLHL40 gene were identified, which were deemed the pathogenic drivers underlying NEM8 as well as the fetal ultrasound abnormalities. We further adopted multiple molecular characterization assays to elucidate the genotype–phenotype correlation in this affected fetus.

Material and Methods
Material and Methods Subjects We herein report a Chinese family featuring three successive pregnancies affected by repeated prenatal ultrasound structural abnormalities, all resulting in neonatal demise (Figure ). The parents stated there was no consanguinity between them, and no hereditary diseases were noted in either side of the family. Clinical examination revealed unremarkable phenotypes in both parents. During her first pregnancy, polyhydramnios was diagnosed at 34 weeks of gestation. The woman delivered a preterm female infant with hand malformation, who died shortly after birth. Her second pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios detected at 32 weeks gestation; a preterm male infant with foot malformation was delivered and also succumbed soon after delivery. The third pregnancy resulted in an unremarkable full‐term male newborn without any evident congenital anomalies. In the fourth pregnancy, fetal polyhydramnios and clubfeet were identified prenatally, and the infant died shortly postnatally. No definitive genetic etiology was established to explain these three cases of neonatal demise. Prenatal ultrasound anomalies of the fetus and the clinical features after induced labour. (A): Pedigree genetic map of the enrolled family. The arrow indicates the proband. (B): Prenatal ultrasound examination results revealed a left clubfoot in the fetus. (C): A right clubfoot was also observed. (D): At the gestational age of 27+6 weeks, polyhydramnios was also detected by ultrasound. (E, F): Both clubfeet were also confirmed after induced labour at the third trimester pregnancy. In the fifth pregnancy, structural fetal anomalies were visualized on prenatal ultrasound. The couple therefore consulted our Prenatal Diagnosis Center for genetic counseling. After a thorough review of the complete obstetric history and acquisition of written informed consent from the family, three prenatal genetic testing modalities were performed: karyotype analysis, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and ES. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institutional Ethics Committee of Quanzhou Women's and Children's Hospital (2022No.69). Karyotype Analysis and Chromosomal Microarray Analysis Approximately, 10 mL of amniotic fluid (fetus) and 2 mL of peripheral blood (family members) were collected for karyotype analysis. Chromosome karyotype analysis was prepared using the automatic chromosome harvesting system Sinochrome Chromprep II (Lechen Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China) (Zhuang et al. ). About 10 mL of amniotic fluid (fetus) and 3–5 mL of peripheral blood (family members) were collected for CMA, ES and the subsequent Sanger sequencing. Genomic DNA was extracted using a QIAamp DNA Blood Kit (QIAGEN, Germany) according to the manufacturer's protocol (www.qiagen.com). CMA was performed using a single‐nucleotide polymorphism‐based Affymetrix Cytoscan 750 K chip (Life Technologies, American) as previously reported (Zhuang et al. ). Exome Sequencing Genomic DNA was subjected to ES using the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), after DNA quantification, DNA shearing, library preparation of targeted regions, and sequencing libraries quantification (Zhuang et al. ). Data analysis, including variant calling, annotation, and variant screening, was performed referring to the description of our previous study (Zhuang et al. ). After variant calling, annotation, and variant screening, the dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, Exome Aggregation Consortium, and Exome Variant Server databases were used for searching the minor allele frequencies (MAF < 0.1%) of all known variants. Following the ACMG guidelines (Richards et al. ), variants were classified as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variants of unknown significance (VOUS), and likely benign or benign. Sanger sequencing was used to verify the variants detected by ES. Quantitative Real‐Time PCR (qPCR) Analysis Total RNA was extracted from the fetal skeletal muscle tissue and three age‐matched controls using the Trizol method. Subsequently, an ultraviolet spectrophotometer and agarose electrophoresis were used for RNA purity and quality detection. A SuperScriptIII First‐Strand Synthesis SuperMix test kit was used for cDNA synthesis and a Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix kit was used for real‐time PCR (Bio‐Rad, USA). The target gene and internal control primer sequences are as follows: KLHL40‐F 5′‐GACTCGGTCATGTGCTACGA‐3′, KLHL40‐R 5′‐GTGTTGGCCATACACGTAA‐3′; GAPDH‐F 5′‐CCATGACACTTTGGTATCGTGGAA‐3′, GAPDH‐R 5′‐GGCCATCACGCCACAGTTTC‐3′. Then, the relative mRNA expression level of the KLHL40 gene was calculated using the 2−△△CT method. Western Blotting Analysis Total protein was extracted from the fetal skeletal muscle tissue and three age‐matched controls using the RIPA Buffer (89,900, Thermo Pierce) and qualified by BCA assay (P0010, Beyotime). After this procedure, 60 μg of total protein was loaded per lane on 8 ~ 12% SDS‐PAGE gels electrophoresis for about 2 h and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (PVDF, Bio‐Rad). After the completion of the membranes transfer, we placed the PVDF in T‐TBS (containing 5% BSA) and sealed it at room temperature for 1 h. A primary antibody of KLHL40 (Thermo Fisher, PA5‐113673) was used to detect the KLHL40 protein with a 1:1000 diluted concentration. GAPDH was used as an internal control (Abcam, ab181602). Developing and fixing was performed according to operation procedure. Finally, Image J 1.8.0 image processing software was used to analyze the optical density of the detected bands. Hematoxylin–Eosin (HE) Stain The skeletal muscle tissue of the fetus with KLHL40 variants and the controls was fixed with 4% of paraformaldehyde and then embedded in paraffin. Conventional histological sections were prepared. After dewaxing and graded ethanol dehydration, HE staining was performed according to the manufacturer's protocol. After dehydration, clearing, and mounting with neutral balsam, the morphology was observed under a light microscope. Modified Gomori Stain The prepared sections were stained with prepared Weigert hematoxylin for 5–10 min, and rinsed with running water for 5–10 min. Over‐stained sections were differentiated in acid alcohol. The subsequent steps were presented as follows: (i) washing with distilled water 2–4 times; (ii) dyeing with Gomori stain solution for 20–40 min; (iii) washing with Gomori differentiation working solution for 30s‐90s. After dehydration, clearing, and mounting, the sections were examined under optical microscopy.

Results
Results Clinical Information The most recent pregnancy of this family demonstrated a normal NT and serological screening results in the first and second trimesters. However, at the gestational age of 25 weeks, clubfeet were observed in the fetus using ultrasound examination (Figure ). In addition, polyhydramnios was identified at the gestational age of 27+6 weeks, which was similar to the clinical phenotypes of the previous pregnancies. After obtaining the written informed consent, the pregnant woman was recommended to undergo amniocentesis for prenatal diagnosis. Genetic Analysis Results After conducting karyotype and chromosomal microarray analyses, no chromosomal abnormalities were detected in the fetus nor the parents. Subsequently, ES technology was performed to investigate the sequence variants in the fetus. The ES detection result identified two compound heterozygous variants in the KLHL40 gene NM_152393.4:c.[1516A> C p.(T506P)];[1327G> A p.(G443S)] in the fetus and the results were further verified by Sanger sequencing (Figure ). Trio‐ES detection outcomes revealed that the variants were inherited from parents, respectively. However, the proband's brother who had normal clinical conditions did not carry either of the variants (Figure ) (PP1). The c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variant had a low frequency in normal populations (PM2_Supporting) and was reported as a hotspot variant among the Chinese population (PM3_Very Strong). The computer‐aided analysis predicted that the variant may affect the structure or function of the protein (PP3), which was interpreted as pathogenic according to the ACMG guidelines (PM3_Very Strong, PM2_Supporting, PP1, PP3). The c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant also had a low frequency in normal populations (PM2_Supporting) and forming a compound heterozygous variants with c.1516A> C p.(T506P) (PM3). Following the ACMG guidelines, the c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant was classified as VOUS (PM3, PM2_Supporting, PP1). Finally, the family chose to terminate the pregnancy (Figure ). In addition, no compound heterozygous or homozygous variants in other relevant genes were detected. Exome sequencing (ES) and Sanger sequencing results in the enrolled family. Sanger sequencing results indicated a c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variant compounded with c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant in the proband, which were transmitted from the parents respectively. None of the variants of the KLHL40 gene were detected in the proband's brother. Conservation Analysis and 3D Protein Structure Simulation We further conducted a conservation analysis of the two variants detected in the KLHL40 gene and the results showed that both of the variants were highly conserved in different species (Figure ). In addition, we simulated the protein structure of two variants of KLHL40. As shown in Figure , the number of hydrogen bonds changed from 2 to 3 after c.1327G> A p.(G443S). In contrast, the number of hydrogen bonds decreased from 3 to 2 after c.1516A> C p.(T506P) (Figure ). Conservation analysis and 3D structure prediction of the detected KLHL40 variants. (A, B): Conservation analysis of p.(G443S) and p.(T506P) showed a highly conserved state in different species. (C): Before the p.(G443S) variant, Gly443 and Cys434 had two hydrogen bond connections. (D): An additional hydrogen bond connection was observed between Gly443 and Trp442 after the p.(G443S) variant. (E): Before the p.(T506P) variant, Thr506 and Ile513/Val507 had three hydrogen bonds. (F): The hydrogen bond length 3.06 between Thr506 and Val507 disappeared. Expression and Translation Levels of the KLHL40 Gene In order to further analyze the impact of KLHL40 variants on gene expression and translation, the skeletal muscle tissues from the proband and three age‐matched controls were collected for qPCR and western blotting analysis. The results of qPCR showed a slight decrease in the level of KLHL40 mRNA in the mutant fetus compared with the controls, but with no statistically significant difference (Figure ). However, the outcomes of the western blotting analysis revealed a significant decrease in the levels of KLHL40 protein in the skeletal muscle tissue of the mutant fetus compared with the controls (Figure and Figure ). Expression and translation detection using qPCR and western blotting analysis. (A): The total mRNA was extracted from the mutant fetus and three age‐matched controls' muscle tissue for qPCR analysis, and the qPCR detection showed a slightly lower level of KLHL40 mRNA in the patient compared with the controls, while with no significant difference. (B): The total protein was extracted from the mutant fetus and three age‐matched controls' muscle tissue for western blotting analysis, a~69KDa band was detected using KLHL40 antibody, and the GAPDH protein was used as a control. (C): A significant decrease in KLHL40 protein was observed in the mutant fetus compared with the controls. Pathological Examination Results Pathological and genetic diagnosis is the gold standard for diagnosing NEM. In order to investigate whether there was a considerable number of muscle fiber changes and nemaline bodies in the proband, samples of fetal skeletal muscle tissue of the proband and the controls were collected for HE staining and modified Gomori staining. The HE staining results demonstrated that the shape and size of the muscle fibers in the control group were regular, but the features were significantly altered in the proband (Figure ). In addition, a small number of nemaline bodies were also observed, which were stained dark red. Subsequently, the modified Gomori stain results also confirmed the nemaline bodies in the muscle tissue of the proband (Figure ). Unfortunately, electron microscopy for further nemaline body verification was not available in this study. Pathological examination using HE staining and modified Gomori staining. Mutant fetal skeletal muscle tissue and the age‐matched controls were collected for HE staining (A, B) and modified Gomori staining (C, D). The arrows indicate the nemaline bodies. A, C: Control. B, D: Patient.

Discussion
Discussion Nemaline myopathy is a group of congenital myopathies first described by Shy et al. (Shy et al. ) in 1963. At least 12 genes have been reported to be associated with nemaline myopathy. NEM8 is typically a severe autosomal recessive disorder, commonly caused by the KLHL40 gene variants (Dofash et al. ; Ravenscroft et al. ). Most patients die during infancy, with an average age of 5 months. The KLHL40 gene is crucial for muscle production and the maintenance of skeletal muscle functions, so defects in this gene lead to sarcomere defects, followed by muscle dysfunction and early neonatal death (Garg et al. ). In this study, ES technology was performed for prenatal genetic diagnosis of a fetus with ultrasound structure abnormalities (e.g., clubfeet). Two compound heterozygous variants NM_152393.4:c.[1516A> C p.(T506P)]; [1327G> A p.(G443S)] in the KLHL40 gene were detected, which may be the cause of NEM8 and responsible for the fetal anomalies. At present, few scholars have researched KLHL40‐related nemaline myopathy. Most of the patients reported in the available literature are from South China, and there is an estimated disease incidence of 2.47/100,000 in the region (Yi et al. ). Missense variants in KLHL40 are the most common variants that lead to NEM8, followed by frameshift and nonsense variants. Yeung et al. (Yeung et al. ) conducted a study with six patients with NEM8 from five unrelated Chinese families; all of them were carrying homozygous or compound heterozygous c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variants. The fetuses exhibited prenatal ultrasound anomalies including decreased fetal movement, excessive amniotic fluid, clubfeet, increased head circumference, and other anomalies. Similar studies conducted by the same research group have suggested that the c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variant is a hot spot pathogenic variant of KLHL40 in Southern China (Lee et al. ; Yeung et al. ). Complementarily, a recent study conducted by Yuan et al. (Yuan et al. ) enrolled five individuals from four unrelated Chinese families with NEM8, and their ES results revealed the presence of recurrent missense variants c.1516A> C p.(T506P) in the patients. In our study, a c.1516A> C p.(T506P) variant in the KLHL40 gene was also identified, which was classified as a pathogenic variant according to the ACMG guidelines and the reports in the literature. In addition, an extremely rare c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant of the KLHL40 gene was also identified in our study and further was classified as a VOUS. We have carefully examined the relevant literature and found only one report referring to the c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant (Lee et al. ). It is noteworthy that its pathogenicity is still unclear. In order to further clarify these relevant details and amplify the knowledge of genotype and phenotype correlations, we performed qPCR and western blotting analysis to investigate the expression and translation levels of KLHL40. The experimental results demonstrated that the KLHL40 protein levels in the fetus were downregulated. However, no statistical difference was observed in the KLHL40 mRNA between positive and controls, which may be due to the limited number of test samples. The diagnosis of nemaline myopathies was based on pathological and genetic detection. The characteristic pathological change is the deposition of a large number of nemaline bodies in muscle fibers (Liu et al. ; Ravenscroft et al. ). Our study further used HE staining and modified Gomori staining to clarify the morphology of muscle fibers in the proband and identify the nemaline bodies in muscle fibers. Interestingly, there are not a large number of nemaline bodies identified in the fetal muscle fibers of the present fetus, with only a small amount of nemaline bodies identified. Notably, in a previous study (Lee et al. ) that reported the same variant of c.1327G> A p.(G443S) in KLHL40, no definite nemaline bodies were identified. Although only a small amount of nemaline bodies was present in the patient's muscle fibers, our study further adds to the pathogenic evidence of the rare c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant in the KLHL40 gene. Therefore, according to the results presented here, we believe that the rare c.1327G> A p.(G443S) variant could be interpreted as a likely pathogenic variant that would explain fetal ultrasound abnormalities and recurrent neonatal death in the present family. However, more work needs to be done to confirm the existence of nemaline bodies in the patient, such as the application of electron microscopy. Notably, this study lacks functional validation via cellular and animal models, and follow‐up investigations will be required to fully elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. In our study, NEM8 was diagnosed in a fetus based on pathological and genetic detection. Combining the use of prenatal ultrasound and ES detection can effectively diagnose fetuses with NEM and reduce the occurrence of birth defects. Our findings may broaden the pathogenic variant of c.1327G> A p.(G443S) in the KLHL40 gene causing NEM8 and clarify the genotype and phenotype correlation. In addition, our study further strengthened the application value of ES in etiological diagnosis of fetuses with congenital myopathy diseases and facilitated genetic counselling for patients with NEM8.

title: Clinical characteristics and genetic analysis of different Dandy-Walker malformation.
label_reason: Fetal Dandy-Walker cohort with genetic testing per subgroup.
abstract: Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM) is a rare congenital malformation of the central nervous system (CNS). It is characterized by variable hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle, with or without an enlarged cisterna magna. Given that large-sample genetic analysis of DWM has not been conducted to date, this study aims to provide more comprehensive genetic counseling for prenatal diagnosis by summarizing the clinical features and genetic findings of DWM. Between January 2010 and May 2025, among 22,048 pregnant women, there were 487 cases of fetal DWM that underwent prenatal diagnosis. Karyotyping, copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), single-nucleotide polymorphism array (SNP-array) or whole-exome sequencing (WES) were employed for prenatal genetic diagnosis. The results of ultrasonography, genetic analyses, and prognoses were tabulated. Among the 487 cases, 35 (7.19%) were diagnosed with classic Dandy-Walker malformation (cDWM), 59 (12.11%) with vermian hypoplasia (VH), and 393 (80.70%) with mega cisterna magna (MCM) according to ultrasonography. A total of 245 cases (50.31%) presented with additional ultrasound abnormalities; central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities were the most prevalent (21.36%), among which ventriculomegaly constituted the primary finding. Prenatal genetic abnormalities were detected in 50 cases (10.27%). Karyotyping identified chromosomal abnormalities in 42 cases (8.62%), including numerical abnormalities, structural abnormalities, and chromosomal mosaicism, with trisomy-18 (2.26%) being the most commonly detected. There were 8 cases with normal karyotypes, but among them, 6 cases were detected with chromosomal abnormalities by CNV-seq/SNP-array, and 2 cases were detected with gene mutations by WES. Advanced maternal age was associated with an increased risk of chromosomal abnormalities, a proportion of which may present with DWM. Among the 453 cases that underwent follow-up, the cDWM and VH groups exhibited a significantly higher incidence of pregnancy terminations compared to the MCM group. Subsequent follow-up of cases with continued pregnancies revealed 1 case of neonatal death in the VH group and 5 cases in the MCM group. Additionally, there was 1 case of abnormal postnatal development in the cDWM group and 3 cases in the MCM group. Pregnant women carrying DWM fetuses should undergo prenatal diagnosis including karyotyping, CNV-seq/SNP-array and WES if necessary, especially for fetuses with cDWM or VH, as the fetuses with cDWM or VH showed higher rates of genetic abnormalities. The pregnancy outcomes of most fetuses with MCM are favorable, while fetuses with cDWM or VH are prone to adverse gestational outcomes. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-026-09656-3 . Keywords: Dandy-Walker malformation, karyotype analysis, CNV-seq, SNP-array, WES
text:
Clinical characteristics and genetic analysis of different Dandy-Walker malformation

Background
Background Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM) is a rare congenital malformation of the CNS, characterized by varying degrees of cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle, with or without an enlarged cisterna magna. It belongs to the category of congenital posterior fossa malformations, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 25,000 to 35,000. DWM can be associated with CNS malformations or non-CNS malformations, and CNS malformations are more prevalent, followed by cardiovascular, urinary system, and digestive system malformations, etc [–]. Although DWM has been recognized for an extended period, its precise etiology and pathogenic mechanism remain unclear. Alcohol consumption, maternal diabetes, rubella and cytomegalovirus infections may contribute to the occurrence of DWM. A significant proportion of DWM patients exhibit genetic abnormalities, including chromosomal aneuploidies (e.g., trisomy 13, 18, and 21), chromosomal microdeletions (e.g., in regions 1q25.3-q32.1 and 3q22-q24), chromosome 9p duplication, and mutations in genes ZIC1, ZIC4, FOXC1, etc [, , ]. The diagnosis of fetal DWM relies primarily on ultrasound examination and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Advances in prenatal examination technology and increased awareness of prenatal screening have improved the detection rate of these abnormalities. Based on the degree of cerebellar vermis development, DWM is classified into classic Dandy-Walker malformation (cDWM), vermian hypoplasia (VH, also referred to as Dandy-Walker variant), and mega cisterna magna (MCM) []. In our previous study [], we focused on cDWM and VH fetuses, detailing their clinical and genetic characteristics, but did not include MCM cases. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, this study incorporates MCM fetuses into the cohort to systematically describe the clinical features and genetic profiles of these three subtypes. To further elucidate the pathogenesis and prenatal diagnosis of DWM, the clinical data and genetic test results of 487 fetuses with DWM were summarized in this study.

Methods
Methods From January 2010 to May 2025, a total of 22,048 pregnant women underwent prenatal diagnosis, and 487 pregnant women whose fetuses presented with DWM underwent amniocentesis or cordocentesis under ultrasound guidance for genetic testing. Based on the degree of cerebellar vermis development, DWM is classified into cDWM, VH, and MCM. cDWM is a relatively rare condition characterized by the complete or partial absence of the cerebellar vermis, an enlarged cisterna magna that communicates with the dilated fourth ventricle; VH or Dandy-Walker variant is characterized by cerebellar vermian hypoplasia, cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle, with a normal posterior fossa. MCM presents as a simple enlarged cisterna magna, without underdevelopment or dysplasia of cerebellar vermis, and with normal fourth ventricle and supratentorial structures of the cerebellum [, ]. MRI images showed DWM in the following Fig. . DWM, dysplasia of the cerebellar vermis, and enlarged cisterna magna communicates with the fourth ventricle The results of intracranial and extracranial ultrasound abnormalities, as well as genetic analysis results of the fetuses were tabulated. Fetal ultrasonography was conducted by experienced sonographers using a 5 MHz transducer (IU22, Philips; VOLUSON E8, GE). Karyotyping was performed for all 487 cases as the first-line prenatal diagnostic test following invasive sampling. CNV‑seq or SNP-array was performed in selected cases including fetuses with structural anomalies (one or multiple), sonographic soft markers highly associated with pathogenic copy number variations, or inconclusive karyotyping results, etc []. WES is indicated for fetuses with abnormal prenatal imaging findings (e.g., multiple congenital anomalies, skeletal abnormalities, cardiovascular malformations, central nervous system malformations) after conventional karyotyping and CNV testing have revealed no abnormalities, or for cases with suspected rare genetic syndromes, etc []. The choice of genetic testing was determined by the severity and complexity of sonographic findings, clinical indications, and parental preferences. All samples were subjected to rapid prenatal karyotyping, whereas only 104 and 5 cases underwent CNV-seq/SNP-array or WES, respectively. Statistical analyses were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences Version 27.0 (SPSS, IBM, Chicago, IL, USA). The chi-square test was employed for comparisons between groups (P = 0.05). To adjust for multiple comparisons, the Bonferroni method was applied, and the corrected significance threshold was set at 0.0167 (0.05/[3(3 − 1)/2]). Two-sided tests were performed, and P < 0.0167 were considered statistically significant. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to adjust for gestational age and sampling method, with a two-sided P < 0.05 considered significant.

Results
Results Among 22,048 pregnant women, 487 cases with fetal DWM underwent invasive sampling procedures, including 65 amniocenteses and 422 cordocenteses. The median maternal ages were 28.00 (25.00,32.00) years, 28.00 (24.00,31.00) years, and 29.00 (25.50,32.00) years respectively. The maternal age data of the three groups did not follow a normal distribution (P < 0.05), and the differences were not statistically significant as evaluated by the Kruskal-Wallis H test (P > 0.05). The median gestational ages were 27.00 (20.00,31.00) weeks, 24.00 (20.00,29.00) weeks, and 31.70 (29.40,33.30) weeks respectively. The gestational age data of the three groups did not follow a normal distribution (P < 0.05), and the differences were statistically significant as evaluated by the Kruskal-Wallis H test (P < 0.05). The gestational weeks of the MCM group were significantly higher than those of the other two groups. (Table ). Among the 487 cases, 35 (7.19%) were diagnosed with cDWM, 59 (12.11%) with VH, and 393 (80.70%) with MCM. A total of 245 cases (50.31%) of DWM were accompanied by other ultrasound abnormalities. Among the other ultrasound-associated abnormalities of DWM, CNS malformations were the most frequently observed, accounting for 21.36%. The most common CNS malformation was ventriculomegaly, accounting for 14.37%. Cardiovascular system malformations accounted for 9.45%, and the most prevalent cardiovascular system abnormality was ventricular septal defect (3.70%). Other ultrasound-detected abnormalities included polyhydramnios (9.65%), urinary system abnormalities (9.03%), digestive system abnormalities (6.16%), single umbilical artery (2.87%), extremity abnormalities (2.26%), etc. (Table ). Among the 487 cases, 50 (10.27%) presented prenatal genetic abnormalities, including 13 (37.14%) in the cDWM group, 17 (28.81%) in the VH group, and 20 (5.09%) in the MCM group (Table ). To account for the significant differences in gestational age across subgroups (Table ), logistic regression was performed with adjustment for gestational age and sampling method. After adjustment, both the cDWM group (OR = 7.39, 95% CI:2.98–18.35, P < 0.001) and the VH group (OR = 4.48, 95% CI:1.81–11.06, P = 0.001) showed significantly higher genetic abnormality rates compared with the MCM group. No significant difference was observed between the cDWM and VH groups (OR = 1.65, 95% CI: 0.27–10.14, P = 0.287). Gestational age (P = 0.102) and sampling method (P = 0.855) were not statistically significant in the model, indicating that neither variable independently influenced the genetic abnormality rate after adjustment. To account for potential confounding by gestational age, a subgroup analysis restricted to cases diagnosed between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation after gestational age matching was performed; the results are provided in the supplementary materials (Table S1). Among the 487 fetuses who underwent karyotype examination, 42 (8.62%) exhibited an abnormal karyotype. These included 5 cases (1.03%) of chromosomal mosaicism, 14 cases (2.87%) of chromosomal structural abnormalities, and 23 cases (4.72%) of chromosomal numerical abnormalities. The numerical abnormalities consisted of 11 cases of trisomy 18, 8 cases of trisomy 21, 3 cases of trisomy 13, and 1 case of triploidy (69, XXX), with trisomy 18 being the most commonly occurring. Structural abnormalities included chromosomal translocations, inversions, deletions, derivative chromosomes, marker chromosomes, etc. A more detailed list of abnormal karyotypes with chromosomal structures can be found in supplementary materials (Table S2). Among the 42 cases with chromosomal abnormalities, 12 originated from the cDWM group (n = 35, 34.29%), 16 were from the VH group (n = 59, 27.12%), and 14 were from the MCM group (n = 393, 3.56%), as shown in Table . Logistic regression was also performed with adjustment for gestational age and sampling method. After adjustment, both the cDWM group (OR = 9.22, 95% CI: 3.50–24.30, P < 0.001) and the VH group (OR = 5.98, 95% CI: 2.28–15.69, P < 0.001) showed significantly higher karyotype abnormality rates compared with the MCM group. No significant difference was observed between the cDWM and VH groups (OR = 0.648, 95% CI: 0.253–1.660, P = 0.366). Gestational age was independently associated with karyotype abnormalities (OR = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.80–0.99, P = 0.039), while sampling method was not significantly associated with karyotype abnormalities (P = 0.462). CNV-seq/SNP-array was performed in 104 cases, and WES was performed in 5 cases, and the results demonstrated variable concordance with the karyotyping. Prenatal genetic abnormalities were also identified in 8 cases with normal karyotyping but abnormal CNV-seq/SNP-array or WES results. The copy number variants (CNVs) identified by SNP-array or CNV-seq included pathogenic CNVs, likey pathogenic CNVs and variants of uncertain significance(VUS). CNV-seq/SNP-array identified 6 chromosomal aberrations, including 2 microdeletions, 3 microduplications, and 1 case of chromosome 12 mosaicism with a 20% mosaicism level. WES identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic gene mutations in 2 cases, involving RAF1, KDM6A, and GAA gene. Among the 487 pregnant women, 64 (13.14%) were of advanced maternal age and 16 (25%) of these women had fetal chromosomal abnormalities; 423 (86.86%) were of non-advanced maternal age and 32 (7.57%) of these women had fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Meanwhile, we further stratified the analysis by maternal age within each of the three subgroups. The rate of fetal chromosomal abnormalities was consistently higher in the advanced maternal age group compared to the younger maternal age group (all P < 0.05).(Table ). As presented in Table , a follow-up was conducted on 453 cases of fetal DWM. A total of 99 (21.85%) pregnancies opted for pregnancy termination, among which 24 (70.59%) cases were in the cDWM group, 42 (76.36%) in the VH group, and 33 (9.07%) in the MCM group. The incidence of pregnancy terminations in the cDWM or VH group was significantly higher than that in the MCM group (P < 0.001 for both comparisons after Bonferroni correction). A total of 354 (78.15%) cases continued the pregnancy. Nevertheless, 1 case of neonatal death was noted in the VH group, whereas 5 cases were documented in the MCM group. One of these cases was associated with cytomegalovirus infection, which could be the cause of death in this case. Additionally, prenatal genetic examinations conducted on these six fetuses revealed no genetic abnormalities. Among the live-birth cases, there was one newborn with developmental abnormalities in the cDWM group and three newborns in the MCM group. These cases manifested as severe sensorineural deafness, somnolence, lethargy, feeding difficulties, swallowing difficulties, epilepsy, or hypertonia. In these four cases, pathogenic chromosomal microdeletions or gene mutations were detected in two cases via CNV-seq or WES. Detailed information on cases of neonatal death and abnormal postnatal development can be found in Table .

Discussion
Discussion Fetal ultrasound and MRI are efficacious approaches for detecting DWM. During prenatal screening, DWM is frequently associated with other CNS malformations or non-CNS malformations, including ventriculomegaly, corpus callosum dysplasia, meningocele, congenital cardiovascular malformations, renal system malformations, limb abnormalities, etc. The other ultrasound anomalies were predominantly observed among CNS malformations, with ventriculomegaly being the most prevalent. Subsequently, cardiovascular system malformations and renal system abnormalities were also commonly detected [, ]. This study also yielded consistent results, and polyhydramnios was also frequently observed among the accompanying abnormalities. Further in-depth investigation into the relationship between these systems’ abnormalities and DWM can provide more references for early screening and intervention. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation of these systems during prenatal examinations is essential to improve the early detection of DWM, especially in cases involving the CNS, cardiovascular system, or polyhydramnios. Genetic factors play an important role in the etiology of DWM. In the present study, the abnormality rate of prenatal genetic analysis was 10.27%, with the rates in the three groups being 37.14% (n = 13), 28.81% (n = 17), and 5.09% (n = 20), respectively. The abnormality rates in both the cDWM group and the VH group were significantly higher than that in the MCM group. This finding implies that the incidence of genetic abnormalities in cases featuring a simple enlarged cisterna magna without cerebellar vermis dysplasia is notably lower. When fetal cerebellar vermis dysplasia is present, the risk of genetic abnormalities increases, particularly chromosomal aneuploidy, which is consistent with the results of other studies [–]. Although the abnormal rate in the cDWM group was higher than that in the VH group, statistical significance was not observed. Given that not all cases in this study underwent karyotype analysis, CNV-seq/SNP-array and WES, the actual rate of genetic abnormalities is likely higher than the rate reported herein. Furthermore, advanced maternal age is associated with an increased risk of chromosomal abnormalities, a proportion of which may present with DWM. The genetic abnormalities identified in this study included aneuploidy, chromosomal structural abnormalities, pathogenic/likely pathogenic CNVs, chromosomal mosaicism, and gene mutations, which were consistent with previous research [, , ]. Trisomy 18 was the most prevalent chromosomal abnormality in this study. Karyotype analysis did not always exhibit consistency with CNV-seq/SNP-array and WES, particularly in the detection of chromosomal structural abnormalities and gene mutations, where discrepancies were observed. Karyotype analysis is only capable of detecting chromosomal fragments larger than 5 Mb and is ineffective against submicroscopic chromosomal aberrations. CNV-seq/SNP-array can compensate for this deficiency and detect pathogenic/likely pathogenic CNVs [–]. Previous research has indicated that DWM fetuses may be linked to mutations in genes such as ZIC2, ZIC4, FOXC1, SIL1, and EXOC3L2 [, ]. In the present study, WES identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in 2 cases, involving the KDM6A, GAA, RAF1 gene and no chromosomal aberrations were found. WES has emerged as a potent tool for prenatal diagnosis in cases with abnormal ultrasound findings or congenital malformations, playing a significant role in identifying pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations associated with clinical phenotypes. WES has improved the genetic diagnostic rates of fetuses with ultrasound abnormalities, particularly in cases involving kidney abnormalities, amniotic fluid abnormalities, and nervous system anomalies, etc [, ]. Therefore, karyotyping, CNV-seq/SNP-array, and WES are recommended for fetuses with DWM. Maternal primary cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection exerts a significant impact on the development and prognosis of the fetus, with manifestations including ventriculomegaly, fetal growth restriction, and enlarged cisterna magna, etc. Congenital infection may result in sensorineural hearing loss and central nervous system involvement [–]. Therefore, it is crucial to conduct comprehensive CMV testing during early pregnancy. The clinical manifestations of DWM include mental and motor developmental delay, hydrocephalus, increased intracranial pressure, spastic paralysis, and hearing impairment [, ]. The prognosis of DWM is associated with multiple factors, such as the presence of chromosomal abnormalities or genetic mutations, other ultrasound abnormalities, the degree of cerebellar vermis absence, and the severity of hydrocephalus []. It is extremely challenging to accurately assess the prognosis solely based on ultrasound findings. Even if no abnormalities are detected in the fetal genetic testing, some families may still choose to terminate the pregnancy due to concerns about potential adverse outcomes [, , ], especially in the cDWM group and the VH group. Although most fetuses with isolated MCM have favorable outcomes, adverse postnatal events (including neonatal death and neurodevelopmental abnormalities) can still occur in a small proportion of cases, sometimes due to non-genetic causes such as congenital cytomegalovirus infection. Therefore, postnatal follow-up remains necessary even when prenatal genetic testing is negative. This study further analyzed the genetic and clinical characteristics of DWM to enhance the comprehension of this condition. When an enlarged cisterna magna is detected via ultrasound, it is imperative to conduct a further examination of the integrity of the cerebellar vermis. Fetal MRI can serve as a complementary tool to the ultrasound examination for achieving a definitive diagnosis. Transvaginal neurosonography represents a targeted high-resolution ultrasound technique that substantially improves the assessment of the fetal posterior fossa, particularly the cerebellar vermis, enabling detailed qualitative and quantitative evaluation of this structure. When used in addition to standard ultrasound and fetal MRI, transvaginal neurosonography serves as a valuable complementary tool, offering high-resolution anatomical detail that optimizes prenatal evaluation of posterior fossa anomalies [, ]. Upon the identification of DWM, genetic analysis should be carried out on the affected fetuses. Karyotype analysis in combination with CNV-seq/SNP-array can screen out the majority of chromosomal aberrations, and WES can detect potential pathogenic gene mutations. In this study, several gene mutations potentially associated with DWM were detected, which broadens the genetic spectrum of this disorder. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. This is a retrospective study, the definition of ‘genetic abnormality’ in this study was a composite outcome encompassing karyotypic abnormalities, CNVs, and gene mutations. However, the coverage of testing methods varies across subgroups, all 487 cases underwent karyotyping, but only 104 cases were tested by CNV-seq/SNP-array, and only 5 by WES. Consequently, the reported rates of genetic abnormalities in the DWM fetuses may underestimate the true prevalence, particularly for submicroscopic CNV abnormalities and gene mutations that are not detectable by karyotyping alone. Future multicenter studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to systematically collect cases that undergo karyotyping, CNV testing, and WES, in order to more accurately estimate the true genetic abnormality rates in DWM fetuses. Additionally, subtype classification relies solely on prenatal ultrasound, lacking MRI validation or diagnostic consistency assessment. While ultrasound is the primary screening modality for fetal posterior fossa anomalies, it has inherent limitations in assessing cerebellar vermis development and fourth ventricular morphology, particularly when distinguishing mild vermis hypoplasia from MCM. Fetal MRI can serve as an essential auxiliary tool to ultrasound for achieving a more definitive diagnosis and refining subtype classification. The absence of MRI may have introduced classification bias in this study. Future studies should incorporate systematic MRI evaluation and ultrasound-MRI concordance analysis to improve diagnostic accuracy.

Conclusion
Conclusion Genetic factors contribute to a subset of fetal DWM cases, particularly cDWM and VH. Fetal DWM are frequently accompanied by other ultrasound abnormalities, with the CNS abnormalities are the most prevalent. Fetal isolated MCM carries a low risk of chromosomal abnormalities and is generally associated with favorable outcomes; however, adverse postnatal events can still occur in a small proportion of cases, sometimes due to non-genetic causes. Therefore, postnatal follow-up remains necessary even when prenatal genetic testing is negative. However, for the cDWM or VH, the incidence of chromosomal aberrations increases significantly and tending towards a poor prognosis. Consequently, prenatal detection of DWM need detailed evaluation of fetal systemic structural abnormalities, with particular emphasis on the central nervous and cardiovascular systems. It is necessary to carry out further prenatal genetic testing including karyotype analysis, copy number variation sequencing and WES.
