title: Incremental yield of genome sequencing after exome sequencing for nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum.
label_reason: Nonimmune hydrops fetuses with karyotype/CMA/ES then genome sequencing.
abstract:
Exome sequencing (ES) detects a monogenic disorder in approximately 30% of pregnancies with unexplained nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum (NIHFS), defined as the presence of one or more pathologic fetal fluid collection. Since genome sequencing (GS) can identify additional genetic variants not detectable by ES, we sought to determine the proportion of cases with new reportable findings on GS following non-diagnostic standard of care testing, including ES, for NIHFS. Cohort study of pregnancies with NIHFS that had nondiagnostic results of karyotype and/or chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and ES. Eligible fetal fluid collections included at least one of: ascites, pleural or pericardial effusions, skin edema, cystic hygroma, and/or nuchal translucency ≥3.5 mm. Pregnancies with NIHFS that did not receive a clear diagnosis with prior testing underwent additional testing with GS. ES and GS were performed in a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments–approved laboratory, and genetic variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines. Primary outcome was the proportion of new reportable pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants identified on GS and resulting in a new diagnosis. Secondary outcome was the incremental yield of GS for detecting new secondary findings and variants of uncertain significance (VUSs). Overall, 118 fetal samples underwent GS following negative ( n =102) or inconclusive ( n =16) ES. GS identified four P/LP copy number variants previously not detected by karyotype, CMA, or ES that led to a new genetic diagnosis in three pregnancies, providing a new positive finding yield of 2.5% (3/118). Additionally, one secondary finding and four VUSs were identified by GS in four different pregnancies. In contrast to the primary outcome, these additional findings were largely the result of updated analytical tools and literature rather than GS-specific technology. GS has a small but clinically relevant increased diagnostic yield over chromosome studies and ES for NIHFS, particularly for identifying copy number variants. As interpretation of noncoding regions and complex genomic variations improves, the incremental positive finding yield of GS is expected to further increase. Keywords: copy number variants, exome sequencing, fetal fluid collection, genetic testing, genome sequencing, nonimmune hydrops fetalis, prenatal diagnosis, single-gene disorders

Genome sequencing offers an incremental positive finding yield of 2.5% over chromosomal analysis and exome sequencing for nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum.
text:
Incremental yield of genome sequencing after exome sequencing for nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum

Introduction
Introduction The landscape of prenatal genetic testing has evolved rapidly in recent decades, increasing our ability to identify fetal genetic diseases, optimize multidisciplinary management, and pave the way for emerging fetal therapies. Karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) have traditionally been the first-line prenatal genetic tests and can detect large chromosomal abnormalities and smaller subchromosomal copy number variants (CNV), respectively., Over the past few years, exome sequencing (ES) has become increasingly clinically available and utilized to identify fetal single-gene disorders not detected by first-line testing in anomalous pregnancies.– ES interrogates the 1% to 2% of the genome that codes for proteins, and can detect single nucleotide changes and intragenic insertions and deletions (indels) less than 50 to 100 base pairs (bp).– Since the implementation of ES for prenatal diagnosis, the analytical pipelines, variant calling algorithms, and knowledge of gene-disease relationships have improved substantially. More recently, genome sequencing (GS) has emerged as a diagnostic tool with a faster turnaround time than ES and the ability to assess nearly the entire genome. GS has improved coverage of some protein-coding regions,, examines nonprotein-coding regions, and can detect aberrations difficult to ascertain on ES such as moderately sized CNVs ≥50 bp., Developments in genetic testing technology have been particularly impactful for the diagnosis and management of pregnancies with nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum (NIHFS), for which single-gene disorders are a frequent cause. Many of the same underlying single-gene disorders are known to underlie pregnancies with single versus multiple fluid collections; the term NIHFS represents this diagnostic overlap and highlights the importance of a complete evaluation for pregnancies with one abnormal fluid collection. The term NIHFS was recently recognized in a consult from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.,,– Several studies utilizing ES have identified single-gene disorders in approximately 30% of pregnancies with NIHFS after nondiagnostic first-line testing.– The types of single-gene disorders leading to NIHFS are broad and associated with variable long-term prognoses, including those affecting the lymphatic, cardiac, hematologic, metabolic, and other pathways. Little has been published to date on the diagnostic yield of GS for prenatal diagnosis in the context of fetal anomalies, with findings of small incremental positive finding yields over ES and only one study that focused on NIHFS specifically., GS offers the potential to uncover novel genetic variants for pregnancies with NIHFS that are not explained by karyotype, CMA, and ES, and has important implications for diagnosis and management of these complex pregnancies. This study addresses a critical gap in the literature by evaluating the incremental positive finding yield of GS in pregnancies with unexplained NIHFS. Specifically, we aim to quantify the incremental positive finding yield of GS for identifying disease-causing variants in pregnancies with NIHFS that underwent deep phenotyping and received nondiagnostic ES results after an uninformative karyotype and/or CMA. We hypothesized that GS would provide an increase in positive finding yield over ES, primarily through identification of structural and nonprotein-coding variants undetectable by other genetic tests.

Materials and methods
Materials and methods This is a cohort study of pregnancies with NIHFS that remained unexplained after standard of care genetic testing, including ES. Pregnancies were enrolled from across the United States between 2018 and 2022 and underwent ES after nondiagnostic CMA and/or karyotype and other standard evaluations for NIHFS., ES results and methodology for this cohort have been previously described., We enrolled pregnancies with NIHFS, including at least one of the following: fetal ascites, unilateral or bilateral pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and/or skin edema. We also enrolled pregnancies with cystic hygroma (CH) or increased nuchal translucency (NT≥3.5 mm). Pregnancies were eligible for inclusion if the abnormal fetal fluid collections were documented at any time during pregnancy, including prior to stillbirth, termination of pregnancy, or delivery of a liveborn. Pregnancies with concurrent structural anomalies were also included. Pregnancies with an identified etiology for NIHFS such as alloimmunization, congenital infection, placental chorioangioma, or twin–twin transfusion syndrome were excluded. Pregnancies were additionally excluded if insufficient high-quality DNA remained from the original fetal samples. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Institutional Review Board (IRB 17-21662 and 22-36344). Participants who did not receive a clear diagnosis following consent to the initial ES study and who consented to future research were eligible for inclusion in the current study and underwent GS. Those with clear pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants identified on ES that established an explanation for the NIHFS were excluded, as were those with insufficient or poor quality fetal or infant DNA samples available for GS. Prior to initiation of GS, charts were systematically reviewed, and additional records were obtained to extract any new phenotypic information identified during and/or after pregnancy to inform variant filtering and interpretation., This included collection of postnatal phenotype where available and for as long as possible among survivors. Using the updated phenotype, ES reanalysis was requested for all cases within one year prior to initiating GS. Pregnancies for which ES reanalysis clearly identified one or more diagnostic variant did not undergo GS. We allowed inclusion of pregnancies with variants of uncertain significance (VUSs) on ES given the clinical uncertainty of those variants. Extracted DNA remaining from the original ES was used to perform GS. Medical records were reviewed to extract obstetric and family history; laboratory results, including infectious and genetic studies; imaging reports from throughout the pregnancy (antenatal ultrasound, fetal echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging); pre and postnatal pathology results; pregnancy complications; delivery outcomes; and postnatal clinical data including laboratory studies, imaging reports, dysmorphic features, and comorbidities. Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms were used to describe pre and postnatal phenotypes to inform variant interpretation for ES reanalyses and GS.– Pregnancies were categorized according to the type(s) of abnormal fetal fluid collections observed across the entirety of each pregnancy: (1) increased NT or CH without other abnormal fluid collections; (2) single abnormal fetal fluid collection including any one of: pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, ascites, or skin edema; or (3) two or more abnormal fetal fluid collections, consisting of pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, ascites, and/or skin edema. The presence or absence of additional structural anomalies was also documented, including those affecting the abdominal wall, central nervous system, face, gastrointestinal tract, genitalia, heart, lungs, renal system, or musculoskeletal system. GS was performed between 2022 and 2024 at the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments program (CLIA)-certified UCSF Genomic Medicine Laboratory. For each sample, paired-end sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq 6000) was done after DNA was prepared using the Roche KAPA EvoPlus PCR-free prep kit. The data were aligned to the human reference genome build GRCh38 (hg38) utilizing Illumina’s DRAGEN (Dynamic Read Analysis for GENomics) algorithm. This streamlined method takes raw sequencing data (FASTQ files) and converts it into fully genotyped variant call formats (VCF/gVCF) with high precision and sensitivity. DRAGEN employs a suite of integrated algorithms to accurately identify the entire spectrum of genetic variations. It simultaneously calls single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), insertions/deletions (Indels), structural variants (SVs), and CNVs from a single dataset. The average read depth of samples was 40×. The VCF files (SNV, SVS, and CNV) were uploaded to Moon (Diploid) or Emedgene (Illumina) for analysis. Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Association for Medical Pathology recommendations. Laboratory clinical bioinformatic experts performed an initial manual variant curation, and variant classification was finalized during a weekly multidisciplinary meeting with experts in clinical informatics, bioinformatics, statistical/population genetics, clinical genetics, pathology, perinatology, pediatrics, and other relevant clinical specialties at UCSF. Variants were reviewed in the context of the clinical history and phenotype to provide an overall case classification. See for additional details on ES and GS protocols, variant calling, and analysis. Primary findings were biallelic or single variants classified as LP or P that resulted in a new diagnosis and were thought to explain the abnormal fluid collection(s). VUSs were reported if gene- or variant-level evidence was suggestive of potential clinical significance but insufficient for a classification of LP. Incidental findings were defined as variants with health implications that did not clearly explain the abnormal fluid collection(s), and these were reported due to inherent limitations of prenatal phenotyping and the potential for phenotypic expansion. Secondary findings were variants in genes associated with actionable health conditions as defined by the ACMG Secondary Findings List v3.2 and were only reported if participants originally consented to receiving these findings. All reportable variants were confirmed with orthogonal testing in the form of in-house Sanger sequencing or multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification at an independent CLIA-certified lab (University of Pittsburgh Medical Center). GS was run as proband-only, and inheritance of newly identified variants was clarified with follow-up targeted testing of parental samples at the time of orthogonal confirmation of the variant in the proband. In some cases, results of this parental testing did affect variant classification. The primary outcome was the incremental positive finding yield of GS for detecting P/LP variants not identified by prior ES and associated with a new diagnosis. In addition to primary variants that explained the NIHFS, incidental GS findings were also considered part of the primary outcome either because they resulted in a new diagnosis or they offered the potential for phenotype expansion. Secondary outcome was the incremental diagnostic yield for new secondary findings and VUSs. Proportions with exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% confidence intervals calculated using the binomial distribution were reported for primary and secondary outcomes. Demographic and phenotypic variables were summarized as proportions or median values with interquartile ranges as appropriate. Data were analyzed using R version 4.5.1 and RStudio software.

Results
Results In total, 141 pregnancies with NIHFS and nondiagnostic results of karyotype and/or CMA as well as ES were potentially eligible. Of these, three were positive on ES reanalysis, and 20 had insufficient high-quality DNA for GS. GS was therefore completed in 118 cases (). Among the cases that underwent GS, 16 had previously inconclusive ES results with at least one VUS that was not clearly the cause of the NIHFS, whereas 102 had negative ES results. Flow diagram of case selection and outcomes related to the primary indication for testing following genome sequencing. ES, exome sequencing; GS, genome sequencing. Source: Boutin. Incremental yield of genome sequencing after exome sequencing. Am J Obstet Gynecol MFM 2026. The median duration between the initial ES and GS was 153 weeks (35 months). A minimum of two antenatal ultrasounds were available for phenotypic data for each pregnancy. Additional cohort characteristics and pregnancy outcomes are described in . Most participants were from the Western United States and approximately half self-identified as non-White. The median gestational age at diagnosis of the initial abnormal fetal fluid collection(s) was 19.7 weeks (IQR, 13.1–22.3). With regards to pregnancy outcomes, miscarriage or stillbirth occurred in 27.1%, pregnancy termination or selective reduction in 27.9%, and neonatal or childhood death in 14.4% of pregnancies. Approximately one third of pregnancies resulted in a live birth, with a median gestational age at delivery for all live births of 33.5 weeks (IQR, 29.1–37.0). Among pregnancies that underwent GS, the indication for testing was an increased NT (≥3.5 mm) or CH with or without concurrent structural anomaly in 19.5%, a single non-NT/CH abnormal fluid collection in 19.5%, and two or more abnormal fluid collections in 61.0% (). Within the single and multiple fluid collection subgroups, the majority of pregnancies also had a concurrent structural anomaly, whereas the opposite was true among pregnancies with increased NT/CH. Types of structural anomalies identified in the cohort are described in . Overall, GS detected four new disease-causing variants not previously identified with ES in three pregnancies (), providing an incremental positive finding yield of 2.5% (3/118; 95% CI, 0.5%–7.3%) over previously performed standard of care genetic testing, including ES. All new diagnostic variants detected by GS were CNVs ranging in size from 135 to 387,976 bp, and all were located in protein-coding regions of the genome. In all three cases, previous CMA and ES had not detected these variants due to the size of CNVs being below and above the resolution of these tests, respectively. Three of the new variants detected by GS were inherited. In terms of types of fluid collections, the first fetus with a new finding on GS had two abnormal fluid collections, the second had a CH, and the third had a single abnormal fluid collection (pleural effusion), respectively. All three fetuses with a new diagnosis on GS had additional structural anomalies beyond abnormal fetal fluid collections. The first fetus with a new diagnosis identified by GS had a paternally inherited primary finding; this was a contiguous deletion encompassing HBA1 and HBA2 that was not previously seen with ES. In combination with a maternally inherited missense HBA2 variant (hemoglobin Adana) in trans that was previously seen with ES (and again detected with GS), this led to a diagnosis of hemoglobin H-Adana-related alpha thalassemia. The second fetus had two new disease-causing primary variants that were identified by GS; this fetus was found to have biparentally inherited compound heterozygous deletions encompassing the LARGE1 gene associated with autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy (MDD). The third fetus had a de novo duplication of SMC1A and HUWE1 on the X chromosome, estimated on orthogonal testing to be mosaic at a level of 1.5 to 1.6X. This duplication is associated with X-linked nonsyndromic intellectual disability based on overlap of the involved region with the Xp11.22 microduplication syndrome (MIM 300705) and emerging evidence of triplosensitivity for HUWE1., Given the lack of known phenotypic overlap between this duplication and abnormal fetal fluid collections, this new molecular diagnosis was categorized as a likely incidental finding. Pregnancy and family history for two of the three cases were unremarkable; in the hemoglobinopathy case, there was a family history of intrauterine fetal demise at 24 weeks’ gestation in the maternal grandmother, and the patient had a history of two previous spontaneous abortions. Additional details of the variants and genetic conditions detected on GS are outlined in . In contrast to the new molecular diagnoses corresponding to primary and incidental findings, all five variants in four pregnancies that were newly identified with GS and categorized as secondary findings and VUSs were SNVs that could be seen with ES. They became reportable with GS due to updated literature and/or new ClinVar entries in the intervening time between the ES reanalysis and later GS ( and ). New VUSs were reported in 3/118 (2.5%; 95% CI, 0.5%–7.3%) pregnancies. These included one fetus with two VUSs in RYR1 associated with an autosomal recessive primary finding, and two cases each with a single VUS (PRPF8 and FBXO11) associated with autosomal dominant disease that were categorized as likely incidental findings due to the lack of clear phenotypic overlap (). Among the 118 cases that underwent GS, 104 consented to disclosure of secondary findings. Only one LP variant associated with an autosomal dominant secondary finding of vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome was reportable following GS (1/104, 1.0%; 95% CI, 0.0%–4.6%). Finally, all VUSs that were originally seen with ES in 16 cases were again seen with GS.

Comment
Comment Principal findings In this large, national cohort of 118 pregnancies with NIHFS that remained unexplained following standard of care genetic testing, including ES, GS had a small but clinically important incremental positive finding yield of 2.5%. Specifically, GS detected deletions and duplications too small to be detected on CMA but too large to be detected on ES in three pregnancies, all in protein-coding regions of the genome. These variants are associated with a broad range of disease categories, including alpha thalassemia, MDD, and X-linked intellectual disability. In addition, the incremental yield for secondary findings and VUSs was 2.5% and 1.0%, respectively, although these were largely due to updated analytical tools and literature rather than GS-specific technology. The majority (5/9; 56%) of reportable variants following GS with known inheritance were inherited, highlighting the reproductive implications for biological parents of fetuses with NIHFS. Results in the context of what is known Two of the new genetic diagnoses made by GS in our study, alpha thalassemia due to hemoglobin H-Adana and MDD, have been previously reported in association with NIHFS.– However, prior reports of MDD in association with NIHFS document genes other than LARGE1,, and our case expands the MDD genes known to be associated with NIHFS. Additionally, microduplication of SMC1A and HUWE1 associated with nonsyndromic intellectual disability has not been previously reported in association with NIHFS. Based on current evidence, this molecular diagnosis most likely represents an incidental finding given the lack of clear phenotypic overlap and uncertain postnatal outcomes. However, microduplications involving HUWE1 have been identified in patients with seizures, abnormal neuroimaging findings, fetal growth restriction, and hypotonia., Additionally, there is increasing literature suggesting a potential association between neurodevelopmental disorders and NIHFS,– making it possible that NIHFS represents a phenotypic expansion of HUWE1-associated duplication disorders. Notably, all three new genetic diagnoses made with GS were the result of GS technology and its ability to identify deletions and duplications not detectable by CMA and ES. In contrast, the additional secondary findings and VUSs that became reportable following GS were largely the result of updated analytical tools and literature rather than GS-specific technology. It is well known that sequencing technology has continued to advance rapidly,, but the value of increasing knowledge about gene- and variant-disease relationships over time is also critical to highlight. Consistent with previous studies, the primary value of GS in our study was its ability to identify disease-causing SVs that were not detected by CMA and ES.– The CNVs we detected exclusively with GS were below the reporting threshold for CMA and larger than typically detected with ES. ES typically detects smaller insertions and deletions (<20–50 bp), but alignment and variant resolution are hindered by incomplete genomic coverage and short captured fragments (~150–300 bp) that limit the ability of this technology to detect larger SVs and precisely define breakpoints that lie outside targeted exons. No new complex structural rearrangements, intronic single-nucleotide changes, or exonic single-nucleotide changes were detected by GS in our cohort. Likewise, while we did not detect any repeat expansion disorders, conditions such as congenital myotonic dystrophy type I have been associated with NIHFS– and can be detected with GS. Few studies to date have investigated the diagnostic utility of GS following uninformative karyotype, CMA, and ES in the context of fetal anomalies. Based on limited data, the incremental positive finding yield of GS is approximately 1% to 3% for unselected cohorts with single or multiple fetal anomalies.,– It is clear from the literature that the diagnostic yield of ES for NIHFS is relatively high compared to anomalous pregnancies without NIHFS.– GS appears to have a similar incremental positive finding yield for NIHFS relative to what has been reported with other fetal anomalies, and the genetic variants uncovered with GS that we identified were all in protein-coding regions of the genome. It is likely that over time, the yield of GS for NIHFS and other fetal abnormalities will increase as more becomes understood about the relationship between nonprotein-coding regions of the genome and fetal disease.– Clinical implications These data contribute valuable information about the modest incremental positive finding yield of GS over standard of care genetic testing, including ES, expanding our knowledge of the genetic variants leading to fetal disease and the types of abnormal fluid collections indicative of specific underlying diseases. ES has already been transformative for prenatal diagnosis in the setting of fetal anomalies, with particularly high diagnostic yields for NIHFS that approximate 30%.– GS has the potential to detect variants that would be seen with both ES and CMA and contributes a small but meaningful incremental yield over these tests with implications for clinical management. Balancing risks and benefits, it is reasonable to offer GS as a follow-up test for information-seeking patients whose pregnancies are complicated by NIHFS when prior testing with karyotype and/or CMA is nondiagnostic. While further studies are needed to generate additional evidence for prenatal testing utilizing GS as a first-line genetic test along with its cost-effectiveness, it may soon serve as an effective test to more efficiently arrive at a diagnosis for these complex pregnancies. Overall, given the diagnostic utility of both ES and GS, it is increasingly important to offer these tests for prenatal diagnosis and to increase equitable access to these technologies for patients with NIHFS. Research implications Despite the high burden of single-gene etiologies underlying NIHFS, the incremental positive finding yield of GS following nondiagnostic ES is comparable to that observed for other fetal structural anomalies.,, As our understanding of gene-disease relationships and nonprotein-coding regions of the human genome expands, the incremental positive finding yield of GS is likely to increase. Indeed, the number of known disease-associated genes has nearly quadrupled since the first diagnosis of human disease using ES over 15 years ago, and there is increasing evidence of the role for the “dark genome” (ie, nonprotein-coding DNA) in human disease.– Even within our cohort, we observed a similar incremental positive finding yield for ES reanalysis and GS, emphasizing the rapid evolution of knowledge in gene-disease relationships. Furthermore, emerging technologies such as long-read GS deserve further study for uncovering complex structural rearrangements, abnormal methylation, and other aberrations associated with NIHFS but not detected by other genetic testing, including the short-read GS as performed in our study., Moving forward, research focused on the implementation of GS clinically for pregnancies with NIHFS and other anomalies will be important. Performing a karyotype and/or CMA before ES as currently practiced as standard of care can add delay to a timely diagnosis when a single-gene disorder is present. GS can detect genetic variants that would be identified through karyotype and/or CMA as well as ES, in addition to other genomic abnormalities such as the disease-causing CNVs that we report.,,,– GS uses smaller amounts of DNA and can return results faster than ES and is likely that in the future, GS will replace the sequential first-line tests currently performed. Furthermore, our data suggest that with careful variant interpretation, GS does not lead to an unmanageable increase in secondary findings or VUSs. However, additional studies are needed to confirm the validity and cost-effectiveness of GS as a first-line test before it can be routinely implemented for pregnancies with NIHFS and other anomalies. Strengths and limitations Our study adds valuable data on the incremental positive finding yield of GS for NIHFS following nondiagnostic karyotype and/or CMA as well as ES, including a systematic approach to ES reanalysis prior to GS. We report not only primary findings, but also secondary findings, incidental findings, and VUSs. These data are beneficial for counseling given the lack of data published on the utility of GS for NIHFS and provide direction for future study. Our use of detailed phenotype with standardized HPO terms over the course of pregnancy and after delivery in bioinformatic analyses optimized the likelihood of identifying disease-causing variants. Additionally, we used a robust multidisciplinary and iterative process to review candidate variants for reporting in order to determine their classification and clinical significance. Limitations include the small number of new findings with GS despite the relatively large sample size for a rare condition, and further study will allow for a deeper view of the types of variants and conditions that GS has the capacity to uncover in the context of NIHFS. Prenatal phenotyping is inherently limited as it is unable to identify features such as neurodevelopmental disorders or vision impairment. In addition, the unique fetal phenotypes of some genetic diseases are incompletely understood, and not all genotypes capable of causing fetal disease are known. As a result, certain variants may have been overlooked on ES or GS due to an apparent mismatch with the genotype and phenotype. Furthermore, in cases of pregnancy termination, intrauterine fetal demise, or stillbirth, it was not possible to evaluate phenotypic evolution, and this may have limited our ability to identify relevant disease-causing variants. The proband-first GS design and the unavailability of all parental samples to determine the inheritance of genetic variants could have affected the identification or classification of some variants. Finally, although we requested ES reanalysis within a year of completing GS, a study design comparing CMA plus ES against concurrent GS using the most up to date high-resolution CMA technology and ES variant calling algorithms that include CNV calling would have allowed for a more direct comparison of the diagnostic yield of these tests. Future research will be required to systematically compare the turnaround time and costs of GS versus ES.

Conclusions
Conclusions In this large, national study of pregnancies with NIHFS, we identified an incremental positive finding yield of 2.5% for GS following previous nondiagnostic standard of care genetic testing, including ES. GS detected clinically relevant SVs associated with autosomal recessive and X-linked conditions, which were not identified by prior genetic tests. Despite the ability of GS to detect variants in nonprotein-coding regions of the genome, all new diagnoses were the result of SVs in protein-coding regions, which highlights the need for further research to explore the role of intronic and intergenic genomic regions in fetal disease. In contrast, the new secondary and uncertain variants we identified were largely the result of updated analytical tools and literature, rather than GS-specific technology. Additional studies are needed to further characterize the utility of GS for detecting disease-causing variants underlying NIHFS, determine the validity and cost-effectiveness of GS as a potential first-line prenatal diagnostic tool, and inform guideline development for the use of GS in pregnancies with NIHFS.

AJOG MFM at a Glance Why was this study conducted? Single-gene disorders represent an important cause of nonimmune hydrops fetalis and single abnormal fetal fluid collections (ie, nonimmune hydrops fetalis spectrum; NIHFS). Genome sequencing has the potential to identify novel genetic variants not detected by karyotype and/or chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and exome sequencing. The diagnostic potential of genome sequencing for NIHFS and other fetal anomalies has not been well studied. What are the key findings? Genome sequencing has an incremental positive finding yield of 2.5% for NIHFS following nondiagnostic karyotype and/or CMA plus exome sequencing, identifying clinically relevant copy number variants (DNA insertions or deletions ≥50 base pairs). What does this study add to what is already known? Genome sequencing offers the ability to detect additional structural variants underlying NIHFS, allowing for improved clinical diagnosis and management.

title: Fetal Kabuki syndrome caused by a novel gene variation in KMT2D with primary carnitine deficiency: a case report.
label_reason: Fetus with multisystem ultrasound anomalies; family exome sequencing found KMT2D variant.
abstract: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is an autosomal dominant syndrome involving multiple organs and systems and can be caused by mutation in KMT2D and KDM6A genes. Here, we report the case of a pregnant woman who underwent prenatal family full-exon sequencing due to fetal multi-system abnormalities on ultrasound. Analysis revealed that the fetus had two rare congenital diseases: KS type 1 caused by mutation in the KMT2D and primary carnitine deficiency caused by mutation in the SLC22A5 gene, thus enriching our understanding of the prenatal ultrasound phenotype and gene mutation spectrum of KS. This case of fetal KS was caused by a novel frameshift mutation at the KMT2D gene locus c.14132_14133del which is not included in the ClinVar or Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD) professional databases. Prenatal ultrasound findings of KS are not unique, and the pathogenic genes associated with KS cannot be detected by conventional karyotype/microarray analyses. Consequently, the prenatal diagnosis of KS remains very difficult. However, whole-exome sequencing is recommended when multiple system abnormalities are present, routine testing is negative, and there is a high suspicion of a monogenic disorder. This strategy will identify fetal gene deletion or mutation early, allow informed genetic counselling, and help reduce the incidence of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Fetal Kabuki syndrome caused by a novel gene variation in KMT2D with primary carnitine deficiency: a case report

Introduction
Introduction Kabuki syndrome (KS) is a rare congenital disease that occurs in children and was first reported by Japanese researchers []. KS is predominantly caused by a loss of functionality in two different genes, KMT2D and KDM6A, leading to type 1 and type 2 KS, respectively. Type 1 KS, arising from the mutation of the KMT2D gene is more common than the type 2 form [, ]. With a global prevalence of 3.2 million, the main clinical manifestations of KS are facial deformity, growth retardation, and mental and motor abnormalities []. The incidence of KS is known to vary geographically; for example, the incidence of KS in Japan is approximately 1/32000; this compares to an incidence of 1/86000 in Australia and New Zealand. No specific data is available for other countries []. KS generates serious psychological pressure and economic burden to both families and society. Here, we report the case of a pregnant woman in which multi- system fetal abnormalities were detected by ultrasound prior to delivery. Ultimately, prenatal family full exon sequencing was performed. Analysis confirmed that the fetus possessed two rare congenital diseases: KS type 1 caused by mutation of the KMT2D gene and primary carnitine deficiency caused by mutation in the SLC22A5 gene. In addition, KS in this case was caused by a frameshift mutation at the KMT2D gene locus c.14132_14133del, which was not included indoles not feature in the ClinVar database and HGMD professional databases, thus confirming that this is a novel mutation. Collectively, our findings enrich the spectrum of gene variation in KS and provides a new basis for the diagnosis and genetic counseling of this disease.

Case report
Case report A 29-year-old pregnant woman (G1P0) at 12 + 4 weeks-of-gestation underwent nuchal translucency (NT) color Doppler ultrasound in our hospital, revealing thickening of the fetal nuchal translucent layer (thickness: 0.62 cm) (Fig. a-b) and reversal of the alpha wave for the venous catheter spectrum (Fig. c). Further targeted fetal ultrasound examination revealed cystic lesions in the back of the fetal neck (2.1 × 0.7 × 1.8 cm in size) containing a clear fluid, suggesting a diagnosis of fetal lymph hygroma. Given the number of gestational weeks, fetal heart morphology, structure and blood flow were not significantly abnormal, although the alpha wave of the fetal venous catheter spectrum was inverted. The patient reported a regular menstrual cycle, a natural and stable pregnancy, no particular discomfort, no history of smoking or drinking alcohol, no family history of fetal abnormalities, and no history of drug use, poisons or radiation exposure. Fetal ultrasound findings at 12 + 4 weeks-of-gestation: a Thickening of nuchal translucency (sagittal plane). b Thickening of nuchal translucency (transverse plane of the cervico-occipital region).c Reversal of the alpha wave for the venous catheter spectrum Amniocentesis chromosome microarray analysis at 21 + 4 weeks-of-gestation failed to identify any abnormalities. The fetal head circumference and femur measured by grade III ultrasound at 22 + 6 weeks-of-gestation were below the usual biological means, the echo from the fetal abdominal cavity and intestinal canal was enhanced, and a small amount of fluid had collected in the intestinal space (maximum depth:3.3 mm) (Fig. a, b). Fetal cardiac ultrasound revealed that a small amount of fluid had collected in the pericardial cavity, and that the functionality of the fetal cardiovascular system was within the normal range (maximum diameter: 2.7 mm) (Fig. c). Fetal ultrasound findings at 22 + 6 weeks-of-gestation: a A small amount of fluid in the intestinal space. b The echo of abdominal cavity and intestinal canal was enhanced. c A small amount of fluid in the pericardial cavity

Gene detection
Gene detection At 26 + 4 week-of-gestation, the patient underwent prenatal family full-exon sequencing including second-generation sequencing. On June 11, 2025 (at 26 + 4 week-of-gestation), the results showed that c.14132_14133del is a pathogenic variant of the KMT2D gene and associated with abnormal phenotype of the tested fetus. This mutation was not detected in the parents and there was no previous family history, thus suggesting that the mutation was new. The gnomAD Popmax allele frequency was zero and this mutation was not present in the ClinVar and HGMD databases. According to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics(ACMG) standards and guidelines for genetic variation analysis, we concluded that the novel mutation was the cause of our patient's clinical phenotype. PVS1 PS2_Supporting PM2_ Supporting. 2. The c.1400c > G variation in the SLC22A5 gene (maternal origin) is a pathogenic variation associated with the abnormal phenotype of the tested fetus, and c.415 g > A mutation in the SLC22A5 gene (paternal origin) may be associated with the abnormal phenotype of the tested fetus, although the clinical significance is not clear.

Diagnosis
Diagnosis According to the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database: (1) autosomal dominant (AD), abnormal branchial arch, retro-nasal atresia, nipple absence, hearing loss and hypothyroidism syndrome; AD: Kabuki syndrome type 1; (2) autosomal recessive (AR), systemic primary carnitine deficiency.

Treatment
Treatment After careful consideration, the pregnant woman and her family decided to terminate the pregnancy; labor was induced on June 17, 2025 (at 27 + 3 week-of-gestation), and a stillborn baby girl was delivered.

Discussion
Discussion KS is a rare genetic disease that causes birth defects and was first reported by Niikawa et al. and Kuroki et al. in 1981 [, ]. In 2010, Ng et al. were the first to show that pathogenic functional variants in a gene encoding lysine methyltransferase (KMT2D) caused KS []. In 2012, Lederer et al. identified an X-linked form of KS that was caused by the loss of function in lysine specific demethylase 6A as a result of a pathogenic variant in the KDM6A gene []. However, the pathogenic genes responsible for KS remain unknown in approximately 30% of patients. In addition, a variety of structural chromosomal abnormalities have been reported to cause the same phenotype as KS []. KMT2D is a member of the family of histidine methyltransferases and contains a SET domain that is responsible for the trimethylation of histidine H3 at lysine 4; this represents an epigenetic marker associated with transcriptionally active genes. The KDM6A gene encodes histone H3 lysine-27 demethylase, which releases the silencing of developmental genes. The KMT2D and KDM6A genes work together on the same set of core developmental regulatory networks to ensure that these genes are correctly expressed at a specific time and location []. Studies involving animal models have shown that the knockout of KMT2D and KDM6A genes in zebrafish led to defects in the tissues usually involved in KS patients, including visceral structures in the skull, heart and brain []. Thus far, more than 600 mutations have been reported in the KMT2D gene in patients with KS; approximately 84% of these mutations will cause truncation of the KMT2D protein, leading to a loss of protein functionality; these mutations include nonsense mutations, small fragment insertion/deletion/duplication, shear site mutations, and frameshift mutations [, ]. The case reported herein was diagnosed by full exon sequencing as KS type 1 following the identification of multiple system abnormalities by color Doppler ultrasound. The fetus possessed a frameshift mutation (c.14132_14133del) in the KMT2D gene, with a protein change to p.P4711fs; the gnomAD Popmax allele frequency was zero and this variation was not identified in the ClinVar and HGMD databases, and due to data limitations, frequency data from local databases were not analyzed. This mutation is located within the SET domain of KMT2D, leading to the movement of open reading frames and premature termination of translation, ultimately resulting in the synthesis of truncated proteins. The truncation mutation of this core functional region will completely destroy the protein structure and eliminate physiological functions. Based on the targeted capture of the second-generation sequencing results by parents, this mutation was not detected and was identified as a new variant (PS2-Supporting). This study did not conduct experiments such as microsatellite typing or Sanger sequencing to exclude non biological relationships or sample confusion. However, based on the typical clinical phenotype of the patient, the location of the mutation in the core SET functional domain, and multiple pathogenic evidence, we still determine that this mutation is a true new variant. This mutation further enriches our knowledge of the gene variation spectrum associated with KS and provides a new basis for the diagnosis of KS and the genetic counseling of patients affected by this condition. Since its discovery in 1981 [, ], the diagnosis of KS has been solely dependent on typical postpartum clinical manifestations (specific facial features, growth retardation, mental retardation, and skeletal abnormalities) and auxiliary examinations. At this stage, prenatal diagnosis is almost impossible due to the fact that little is known of the pathogenic genes responsible. Only a few cases are suspected of having a genetic syndrome due to the accidental discovery of a variety of structural abnormalities (such as congenital heart defects, diaphragmatic hernia and kidney abnormalities) by prenatal ultrasound, but cannot be specifically diagnosed as KS. Diagnosis can be completed by clinical evaluation after birth. In 2010 and 2012, Ng et al. and Lederer et al. identified two pathogenic genes responsible for KS: KMT2D and KDM6A, respectively [, ]. These key findings led to molecular diagnosis becoming the gold standard for KS. Once a pathogenic gene has been determined in families possessing a familial pathogenic mutation, it is possible to acquire fetal DNA by amniocentesis during pregnancy. Sanger sequencing or targeted gene analysis can then be performed to detect whether the fetus carries the same pathogenic mutation []. With the continuous development of ultrasound technology, researchers continue to summarize the ultrasound soft index and structural abnormalities related to KS as clues to initiate prenatal gene detection. However, because KS is caused by a small variation in a single gene, conventional karyotype/microarray analysis (CMA) cannot detect the pathogenic genes responsible for K. However, family full-exon sequencing can effectively detect new variations in the KMT2D or KDM6A genes, especially for fetuses with multi-system abnormalities detected by ultrasound but normal results arising from CMA, thus achieving a prenatal diagnosis for KS []. In 2019, a group of international experts jointly developed specific diagnostic criteria for KS, a disease that can occur in male or female patients of any age with a history of infantile hypotonia, growth retardation and/or intellectual disability and meeting one or both of the following main criteria: (1) pathogenic or potentially pathogenic variants of KMT2D or KDM6A, and (2) typical malformation characteristics at a certain point in life []. These clinical manifestations are increasingly obvious during the development of children but are not obvious during the fetal period. The clinical manifestations of patients with KS are complex, and the outcomes are often very poor, generating serious psychological pressure and economic burden to the patient’s family and society. Therefore, it is essential to establish the early clinical suspicion of KS by prenatal ultrasound and apply genetic testing to reach a specific diagnosis. Ultrasound is a common method and can readily detect fetal malformations in routine prenatal examinations. A previous literature review found that ultrasound scans of patients with KS showed a series of abnormalities, including increased nuchal transparency, pleural effusion, cardiac abnormalities, kidney abnormalities, intrauterine growth restriction, polyhydramnios, oligohydramnios, non-immune edema, and a single umbilical artery [, ]. Studies have also shown that heart defects are one of the most common postpartum manifestations of fetuses with KS; these defects exist in 25–93% of postpartum patients []. In addition, cardiac defects are the most common prenatal finding in KS []. A meta-analysis of 1793 cases involving prenatal genetic diagnosis revealed that the most common syndrome in fetuses diagnosed with congenital heart disease by prenatal ultrasound was KS []. However, these ultrasound findings are not unique, and can also be seen in other types of genetic disease, thus making it very difficult to achieve an accurate prenatal diagnosis of KS. The fetus described in this case report showed abnormalities on ultrasound, including thickening of the zona pellucida, fetal lymphohydrocystoma, fetal venous catheter spectrum alpha wave inversion, and pericardial effusion. These findings enhance our understanding of the prenatal phenotype of patients with KS patients, and provide a useful foundation for investigating the prenatal diagnosis of KS. The fetus described herein also possessed a compound heterozygous mutation (missense mutation, c.1400c > G (maternal); c.415 g > A (paternal)), which causes systemic primary carnitine deficiency (PCD); c.415 g > A (paternal) represents a novel mutation. PCD is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of the SLC22A5 gene. And in the Chinese population, the most common mutations types are c.51c > g, c.760c > t and c.1400c > g []. PCD arises due to functional defects in the carnitine transporter OCTN2; this prevents long-chain fatty acids from entering the mitochondria efficiently to complete β oxidation, thus resulting in damage to tissues and organs with high energy demand, such as the heart, liver and skeletal muscle. Due to the high energy consumption and energy dependence of the heart, the damage incurred by the heart is more prominent; therefore, cardiomyopathy is the most common phenotype of PCD [, ]. Carnitine supplementation can effectively improve the symptoms of PCD, except for those with irreversible consequences, such as central nervous system involvement due to hypoglycemia []. Studies have confirmed that levocarnitine can achieve good therapeutic effects, but would need to be provided over the entire lifetime; following withdrawal, hypoglycemia will occur repeatedly, and there is even a risk of sudden death []. However, without timely treatment patients with PCD are prone to severe arrhythmia and sudden death due to abnormally low levels of carnitine in the cells and whole body [, ]. Therefore, if PCD is diagnosed early and treated in time, the prognosis is good. Therefore, in China, PCD has been included in the free screening programs in some regions[]. To the best of our knowledge, there are no reports of KS complicated by PCD in existing literature. This fetus was affected by two concurrent rare hereditary disorders: Kabuki syndrome and primary carnitine deficiency. To date, there have been no published reports describing prenatal ultrasound manifestations of PCD. In children with symptomatic PCD, cardiomyopathy and metabolic decompensation generally develop after the neonatal period [, ]. Wattanasirichaigoon D et al. reported a complex case of primary systemic carnitine deficiency (PSCD) complicated with pericardial effusion []. The underlying mechanism is that PCD impairs myocardial fatty acid oxidation and induces energy depletion, which further leads to myocardial edema, cardiac dysfunction and increased serous exudation, ultimately resulting in pericardial effusion. We speculate that a similar pathophysiological process may also occur in fetuses with severe PCD. Prenatal ultrasonography also revealed increased bowel echogenicity and mild intestinal fluid accumulation in this fetus. Children with severe PCD may experience gastrointestinal dysfunction secondary to systemic metabolic disorders after birth []. We presume that the intestinal abnormalities observed herein are partially associated with in utero metabolic disorders caused by PCD, while intestinal developmental defects due to KS also serve as potential contributing factors. Maternal carnitine status and placental carnitine transport are essential for maintaining fetal carnitine homeostasis []. In this case, the mother was a heterozygous carrier of the SLC22A5 c.1400C > G variant with normal clinical phenotypes. Combined with the fetal genetic findings, the PCD-related manifestations in the fetus were mainly attributed to its own pathogenic variants, rather than maternal carnitine insufficiency or defective placental transport function. Collectively, these two disorders involve overlapping organ systems, predominantly the cardiovascular and gastrointestinal systems, and their pathological impacts may exert additive effects on fetal development. Accordingly, it is inappropriate to attribute all prenatal phenotypic abnormalities solely to KS.

Conclusion
Conclusion Prenatal ultrasound findings of KS are not unique and can also be seen in other types of genetic disease. Furthermore, since KS is caused by a small variation in a single gene, the pathogenic genes responsible for KS cannot be detected by CMA, thus making it very difficult to diagnose KS in an accurate manner. However, whole-exome sequencing is recommended when multiple system abnormalities are present, routine testing is negative, and there is a high suspicion of a monogenic disorder to detect fetal gene deletions or mutations early, thus reducing the incidence of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Due to the lack of sufficient literature on fetal PCD phenotypes, the correlation between intestinal ultrasound manifestations and fetal PCD remains to be further verified in more clinical cases.

title: Prenatal Etiology Diagnosis of Rare Compound Heterozygous PROC Gene Variants in a Fetus With Ocular Ultrasonic Anomaly Using Whole Exome Sequencing.
label_reason: Fetus with ocular ultrasound anomaly; trio WES and Sanger found PROC variants.
abstract: This study aims to present novel compound heterozygous PROC gene variants in a fetus. These variants cause protein C deficiency‐associated thrombophilia and are accompanied by prenatal ocular anomalies in the affected fetus. A fetus presenting with prenatal ocular ultrasound anomalies was enrolled for genetic prenatal diagnosis. Trio whole‐exome sequencing (WES) was performed on the fetus and parental samples to explore the genetic etiology. Sanger sequencing was subsequently applied to verify the identified genetic variants. WES result revealed two likely pathogenic compound heterozygous variants NM_000312.4 : c.[378G>A(p.W126*)]; [658C>T(p.R220W)] in PROC gene in the fetus, which were inherited from the parents, respectively. Notably, a likely pathogenic homozygous variant of NM_176824.3 :c.728G>A(p.C243Y) in BBS7 gene, and a heterozygous variant of NM_012193.4 :c.112G>A(p.G38R) in FZD4 gene, as well as a pathogenic heterozygous variant of NM_000435.3 :c.1630C>T(p.R544C) in NOTCH3 gene were observed in the mother, which may explain her clinical abnormalities. The maternal BBS7 variant was transmitted to the fetus, whereas the FZD4 and NOTCH3 variants were not detected in the proband. The father exhibited a clinical phenotype of cleft lip and palate, but no corresponding pathogenic genetic variants were identified. This study first reports two rare compound heterozygous PROC variants in a Chinese fetus, which expands the mutational spectrum of protein C deficiency‐related thrombophilia in the Chinese population. Furthermore, our findings highlight the robust clinical application value of trio‐WES in the etiological diagnosis of complex prenatal genetic disorders.
text:
Prenatal Etiology Diagnosis of Rare Compound Heterozygous PROC Gene Variants in a Fetus With Ocular Ultrasonic Anomaly Using Whole Exome Sequencing

Introduction
Introduction The PROC gene is located at chromosome 2q14.3, contains nine exons and spans approximately 11 kb (Plutzky et al. ). Pathogenic variants in the PROC gene are associated with autosomal dominant thrombophilia due to protein C deficiency (THPH3; 176860) and autosomal recessive thrombophilia due to protein C deficiency (THPH4; 612304). THPH4 is extremely rare, with an incidence of 1 in 500,000–750,000 individuals (Kottke‐Marchant and Comp ). Protein C deficiency constitutes a critical risk factor for adult pulmonary embolism (PE) and represents an important cause of cardiovascular mortality. It promotes hypercoagulability by impairing the inactivation of blood coagulation factors Va and VIIIa (Martinez Licha et al. ; Cooper et al. ). Protein C deficiency has been reported to manifest as neonatal purpura fulminans, intracranial hemorrhage or infarction, ophthalmologic complications, renal infarction, and rarely, colonic perforation (Mizumoto et al. ; Song et al. ; Goldenberg and Manco‐Johnson ). Heterozygous PROC carriers can develop recurrent venous thrombosis or remain asymptomatic in adulthood. In contrast, homozygous or compound heterozygous PROC mutations can result in severe neonatal disorders or milder late‐onset thrombophilia (Millar et al. ). Currently, reports describing the prenatal clinical phenotypes of protein C deficiency remain scarce. In this study, whole‐exome sequencing was performed to diagnose a fetus harboring compound heterozygous PROC variants. Prenatal ultrasound examination of the fetus revealed only ocular abnormalities, which provide supplementary data for clinical genetic counseling and research on the genotype–phenotype correlation of this disease.

Methods
Methods Subjects A Chinese family from the Quanzhou region, China was recruited in this study. In this core family, the parents are both in their early twenties and this is their first pregnancy. The couple denied having a consanguineous marriage and any family history of genetic diseases. The father had a cleft lip and palate, for which he has undergone surgery, with no other abnormal clinical manifestations. The pregnant woman, however, presents with multiple clinical phenotypes, including intellectual disability, polydactyly (for which she has undergone surgery) (Figure ), brachydactyly of both hands, retinal atrophy, and obesity. After signing the written informed consent, trio‐WES was performed to investigate the possible phenotype associated variants in this family. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Quanzhou Women's and Children's Hospital (2025No.83). Pedigree analysis and clinical findings of the enrolled family. (A) Pedigree analysis of the enrolled family. (B–D) Polydactyly (for which she has undergone surgery) was observed in the pregnant woman in the family. (E) Bilateral strong ocular echoes were observed in the fetus by ultrasound screening at third trimester pregnancy. Genomic DNA Extraction Genomic DNA was extracted from the fetal aborted tissue and parental peripheral blood samples. DNA extraction was conducted using the QIAamp DNA Blood Kit (QIAGEN, Germany) in accordance with the manufacturer's standard protocols (www.qiagen.com). Whole Exome Sequencing Genomic DNA samples collected from the family members were subjected to WES analysis. DNA concentration and quality were quantified using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Genomic DNA was then fragmented to a mean fragment length of 150–200 bp using the Covaris LE220 ultrasonicator (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA). Exome library preparation was performed with the Human Whole Exome Detection Kit (Berry Genomics, Beijing, China), and library amplification was carried out using HiFi HotStart ReadyMix (KAPA). Qualified libraries were subjected to paired‐end 150 bp sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Data Analysis Raw data analysis was performed according to a previously published study (Zhuang et al. ), which included variant calling, annotation and variants screening. We manually transferred the ultrasound findings into Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms. Hence, a published phenotypic scoring algorithm Phrank based on HPO terms was employed to assist in prioritizing alterations. Annotated variants and CNVs were then prioritized and filtered according to phenotype relativity, inheritance mode, allele frequency, read depth, literature, and in silico prediction. All candidate variants and CNVs were cross‐referenced with the latest public databases, including ClinVar, ClinGen, DECIPHER, DGV, the Human Gene Mutation Database, and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM). Combined with the clinical phenotypic information of the proband and family members, all candidate variants were classified into five categories (pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance, likely benign, and benign) in strict accordance with the ACMG variant classification guidelines (Richards et al. ). Sanger Sequencing After conducting quality inspection on the sample genomic DNA which was extracted previously, specific primers were designed targeting the detected variants by WES. The target fragments were amplified via PCR and then purified. Using the purified product as a template, bidirectional Sanger sequencing was performed; after the product was purified again, it was loaded onto the sequencer for Sanger sequencing. The Chromas and SeqMan software were used to align the sequences with the peak plots, so as to determine whether the variant loci were consistent with the WES results.

Results
Results Subjects' Information The pregnant woman is gravida 1, para 0. During this pregnancy, the NT screening result was normal (1.4 mm). However, serological screening in the second trimester indicated an intermediate risk of trisomy 21 (1/601). In the third trimester, prenatal ultrasound detected bilateral strong ocular echoes in the fetus, suggestive of possible persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (Figure ). The family chose to terminate the pregnancy. The aborted fetal tissue and parental peripheral blood samples were subsequently collected for genetic analysis. Whole Exome Sequencing Results Trio‐WES result revealed two rare compound heterozygous variants NM_000312.4:c.[378G>A(p.W126*)]; [658C>T(p.R220W)] in the PROC gene in the fetus, which was inherited from the parents respectively and verified by Sanger sequencing (Figure ). Both of the variants in the PROC gene were interpreted as likely pathogenic variants according to the ACMG guidelines (PVS1 + PM2_Supporting; PM1 + PM3 + PP3 + PS3_Supporting + PM2_Supporting). Interestingly, trio‐WES results also revealed a likely pathogenic (PM3_Strong + PP3_Moderate + PP1 + PM2_Supporting) homozygous variant of NM_176824.3:c.728G>A(p.C243Y) in the BBS7 gene in the mother (Figure ), which may explain the clinical anomalies in the mother. In addition, a NM_012193.4:c.112G>A(p.G38R) in the FZD4 gene was observed in the mother (Figure ), which was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (PM2_Supporting), which was not present in the fetus and may contribute to the retinal atrophy observed in the mother. Moreover, a pathogenic variant (PS4 + PP1_Strong + PP2 + PM2_Supporting) of NM_000435.3:c.1630C>T(p.R544C) in the NOTCH3 gene was also detected in the mother (Figure ), which was not transmitted to the fetus, and may partially contribute to intellectual disability in the mother. However, no relevant genetic variations have been detected to be associated with cleft lip and palate manifested in the father. Sanger sequencing results in the family. (A) The variant of NM_000312.4:c.378G>A(p.W126*) in PROC gene detected in the fetus was verified by Sanger sequencing. (B) The c.658C>T(p.R220W) in PROC gene detected in the fetus was verified by Sanger sequencing. (C) A homozygous variant of NM_176824.3:c.728G>A(p.C243Y) in BBS7 gene in the mother. (D) A NM_012193.4:c.112G>A(p.G38R) in FZD4 gene was identified in the mother. (E) A NM_000435.3:c.1630C>T(p.R544C) in NOTCH3 gene was verified by Sanger sequencing in the mother. Bioinformatics Analysis Results The rare variant of c.378G>A(p.W126*) in PROC gene was not present in gnomAD, ExAC and other normal population databases, whereas it has been presented in the ClinVar database and classified as likely pathogenic (Variation ID: 3380948). The subsequent bioinformatics analysis via computer software indicates that the PROC:c.378G>A mutation is located in the EGF_CA domain. Structural prediction indicated the secondary and tertiary structures of the mutation is prematurely truncated at the 126th amino acid residue (Figure ). The other variant of c.658C>T(p.R220W) in PROC gene have been described in the CinVar database (Variation ID: 668) and classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic in the database. Bioinformatics analysis results of the rare PROC gene variant. (A) The subcellular localization of the PROC gene indicates that its localization is restricted to vesicles. (B) The PROC:c.378G>A mutation is located in the EGF_CA domain. (C) Prediction of the secondary structure of the protein encoded by the PROC gene before the c.378G>A mutation. (D) Prediction of the secondary structure of the protein encoded by the PROC gene after the c.378G>A mutation. (E) Panoramic view of the three‐dimensional (3D) protein structure of the PROC gene. (F) Before the c.378G>A mutation in the PROC gene, there is a hydrogen bond interaction between Trp and Arg, with an interaction strength of 3.01. (G) Panoramic view of the three‐dimensional (3D) protein structure after the c.378G>A mutation in the PROC gene.

Discussion
Discussion Whole exome sequencing (WES) confers distinct advantages for identifying single‐gene variants and has also been reported to reliably detect small copy number variants (CNVs) (Zeng et al. ). In current clinical practice, WES is increasingly implemented in prenatal genetic testing to clarify the genetic etiology of fetuses presenting with abnormal ultrasonic structural findings (Petrovski et al. ; Lord et al. ). In this study, we performed trio‐WES on a family affected by multiple clinical malformations; several single‐gene variants were identified among family members, which likely account for the observed clinical phenotypes in affected individuals. Autosomal recessive protein C deficiency is a rare and severe inherited coagulation disorder caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous PROC mutations. This disease is defined by markedly reduced protein C activity, with neonatal purpura fulminans serving as its predominant clinical manifestation. It progresses rapidly in clinical settings, featuring high mortality and substantial difficulties in diagnosis and treatment (Song et al. ). Even so, timely detection and early intervention can effectively improve the overall prognosis of affected patients. In the present study, WES results revealed two likely pathogenic compound heterozygous variants NM_000312.4:c.[378G>A(p.W126*)]; [658C>T(p.R220W)] in the PROC gene in the fetus. Meanwhile, prenatal ultrasound examination only revealed limited abnormal manifestations, presenting as persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous. Existing studies have confirmed that the c.658C>T variant combined with other PROC variants to form compound heterozygous mutations can result in severe congenital protein C deficiency (Martos et al. ; Wu et al. ). The rare c.378G>A in the PROC gene was described only in the study conducted by Martos et al. (Martos et al. ) and has been classified as a likely pathogenic variant. Currently, prenatal cases of this disease are rarely reported. Sufficient clinical data are still required to supplement the ultrasonic phenotypic spectrum of prenatal protein C deficiency and provide more evidence for clinical genetic consultation. Severe protein C deficiency can lead to a variety of neurological problems. There have been reports of some prenatal cases describing that fetuses carrying compound heterozygous variants or homozygous variants of the PROC gene present abnormal intrauterine ultrasound phenotypes such as lateral ventricular widening and hydrocephalus (Kirkinen et al. ; Yan et al. ). In addition, ocular lesions are commonly observed in patients with protein C deficiency. Relevant studies have demonstrated that intraocular thrombotic events occurring during fetal development can interfere with ocular vascular development, ultimately leading to persistence of fetal intraocular vasculature (Douglas et al. ). Bilateral absence of the pupils and other ocular dysplasia phenotypes have also been documented in protein C deficiency patients in previous clinical studies (Almarzouki et al. ; Ghassemi et al. ). Consistent with the findings of the present study, multiple investigations have verified abnormal ocular developmental phenotypes in fetuses with protein C deficiency during the prenatal period (Douglas et al. ; Almarzouki et al. ), corroborating a causal link between fetal ocular malformations and pathogenic PROC variants. Notably, some fetuses with genetically confirmed severe protein C deficiency show completely normal prenatal ultrasonic performance (Song et al. ), which greatly increases the difficulty of early prenatal screening and identification of this disease. Biallelic mutations in the BBS7 gene cause autosomal recessive Bardet–Biedl syndrome type 7 (BBS7), which is characterized by intellectual disability, postaxial polydactyly, obesity, retinitis pigmentosa, renal anomalies, and hypogenitalism, among other manifestations (Harville et al. ). In this study, trio‐WES identified a likely pathogenic homozygous variant in the BBS7 gene of the mother: NM_176824.3:c.728G>A (p.C243Y). This variant has been previously reported in patients with BBS7 (Shin et al. ; Hirano et al. ). Retinitis pigmentosa is known to eventually progress to retinal atrophy (Bruninx and Lepièce ). Thus, we propose that the homozygous BBS7 variant may be the primary cause of the clinical abnormalities observed in the mother, including intellectual disability, obesity, retinal atrophy, and polydactyly. In the present study, trio‐WES results revealed a novel variant in the FZD4 gene of the mother. FZD4 is associated with familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, and individuals with FZD4 mutations have also been reported to present with retinal atrophy (Schatz and Khan ). Therefore, we cannot rule out the potential contribution of the FZD4 variant to the mother's retinal atrophy. Furthermore, an unexpected pathogenic variant NM_000435.3:c.1630C>T (p.R544C) in the NOTCH3 gene was identified in the mother. This variant is associated with middle‐aged onset cerebral infarction. Clinical consultation should be provided, and full attention should be paid to this variant in future prenatal diagnosis or preimplantation genetic testing. This study also has several limitations. First, the fetus harbored two likely pathogenic compound heterozygous variants of the PROC gene; however, further verification was not performed to determine whether protein C activity levels were significantly reduced. Additionally, additional work is needed to conduct functional studies on the identified variant of unknown significance in the FZD4 gene. In conclusion, our study is the first to describe the compound heterozygous variants in the PROC gene in a Chinese individual, which may broaden the mutation spectrum of protein C deficiency in the Chinese population. Notably, prenatal ultrasound of the fetus only revealed ocular abnormalities, providing additional data support for clinical consultation and research on genotype–phenotype correlations. In addition, our findings demonstrate that trio‐WES is a powerful tool to simultaneously clarify multiple unrelated monogenic diseases in the proband and parents, which provides reliable information for subsequent genetic counseling and targeted prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies of this family.

title: Case Report: Prenatal clues and postnatal evolution: a case of williams syndrome diagnosed following progressive cardiovascular phenotypes.
label_reason: Williams syndrome case with fetal CoA/FGR plus review of nine fetuses with ultrasound findings and CMA-confirmed deletion.
abstract: Williams syndrome (WS) is a rare genetic disorder often missed prenatally due to nonspecific presentations. We describe an infant with Williams syndrome diagnosed after progressive cardiovascular changes during infancy. Prenatal ultrasonography showed fetal growth restriction, persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC), left-right cardiac chamber disproportion (LRCCD), and suspected coarctation of the aorta (CoA). Early postnatal echocardiography revealed mild aortic isthmus hypoplasia without definite supravalvular aortic or pulmonary arterial stenosis. Serial follow-up subsequently demonstrated supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS) and right pulmonary artery stenosis by 7 months of age, and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) confirmed a 1.42 Mb deletion at 7q11.23. At 5 years and 3 months of age, the child remained clinically stable, with stable SVAS and near resolution of pulmonary arterial stenosis. A retrospective review of nine fetuses with prenatally confirmed 7q11.23 microdeletion showed that prenatal cardiovascular abnormalities were present in 6 cases, mainly involving the aortic and pulmonary arterial systems, often with extracardiac findings such as renal anomalies and fetal growth restriction (FGR). WS may show dynamic cardiovascular evolution from nonspecific prenatal or neonatal findings to characteristic vascular lesions during infancy. Fetal cardiovascular abnormalities combined with FGR or other extracardiac anomalies should raise suspicion for WS and prompt consideration of CMA. Serial postnatal echocardiography may help clarify prenatal clues and facilitate earlier diagnosis and management.
