Beyond the Negative: Insights From Postnatal Medical Genetics Follow‐Up After Nondiagnostic Prenatal Exome Sequencing

Introduction
Introduction Fetal structural anomalies are detected in approximately 2%–4% of pregnancies through ultrasonography []. In recent years, prenatal exome sequencing (pES) has been used as a second‐tier genetic investigation following normal chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). In pregnancies with structural anomalies, this technology has proven to have significant clinical utility, with an incremental diagnostic yield of ∼30%, depending on the type and number of structural anomalies identified [, ]. Early genetic diagnosis may modify obstetrical care and establish condition‐specific care plans for postnatal life. Prenatal diagnosis allows for informed decision‐making during an uncertain, time‐sensitive and emotionally complex time. Although exome sequencing has significantly increased the number of genetic diagnoses made prenatally, the majority of pregnancies undergoing pES for fetal structural anomalies will receive nondiagnostic results [, ]. The molecular interpretation of exome sequencing data is challenging in the prenatal setting for several reasons: the fetal presentation of many genetic conditions remains unknown [, , ], fetal phenotypes often evolve throughout pregnancy, and non‐structural functional differences such as sensory or cognitive deficits cannot be assessed []. Moreover, clarification of variants of uncertain significance may rely on evidence from investigations currently unavailable in the prenatal period []. Evidence on the clinical utility of postnatal pES reinterpretation is beginning to emerge. Postnatal phenotyping and pES reinterpretation have been associated with an incremental diagnostic yield of 2%–20% [, , ]. While universal pES reinterpretation with postnatal phenotyping or postmortem evaluation has demonstrated a low diagnostic yield of 2%, targeted pES reinterpretation for cases with postnatal phenotype evolution has reported yields up to 7% []. Collectively, these findings suggest that unselected reinterpretation provides limited incremental yield and may not be sustainable in resource‐limited healthcare systems, whereas more selective approaches have greater potential for clinical utility. Current evidence suggests that interval reinterpretation of exome data in pediatric and adult populations could increase diagnostic yield by 10%–12%, depending on the time elapsed, presence of phenotype modification, and original indication for testing [, , , ]. Even in the absence of phenotypic evolution, the CCMG and ACMG suggest considering reinterpretation of pES data after 12 months to account for discovery of new disease‐causing genes, genotype‐phenotype correlations, as well as evolution of data analysis tools and bioinformatic pipelines [, ]; however, guidance and standardized frameworks have not been established. Key questions remain regarding patient selection criteria and the optimal timing for implementing reinterpretation. This study describes the clinical context of postnatal reassessment by medical genetics providers and the incremental diagnostic yield of postnatal pES reinterpretation for liveborn children with fetal structural anomalies who received nondiagnostic prenatal CMA and pES results at a tertiary care center in Canada. By characterizing these trends, we aim to better understand the clinical value of postnatal reassessment and reinterpretation of pES data in a prenatally undiagnosed population.

Methods
Methods We performed an exploratory retrospective chart review at the BC Children's and Women's Hospital, a tertiary care center in Vancouver, Canada. Approval to conduct this retrospective chart review was obtained from the Research Ethics Board of the University of British Columbia (REB #H23‐00861). The data detailed in this paper are drawn from a subpopulation from a larger cohort previously described by Albert et al. []. In contrast to the larger cohort (N = 63) described by Albert et al., which investigated trends in postnatal clinical outcomes, this study's population only included data collected from liveborn children (N = 61) and focuses on the context surrounding the postnatal reinvolvement of medical genetics providers and the incremental diagnostic yield from postnatal pES reinterpretation. This study's population included liveborn children from singleton pregnancies who received nondiagnostic CMA and pES results after being seen prenatally by the Provincial Medical Genetics Program of British Columbia between 2016 and 2022 in the context of ultrasound detection of one or more fetal structural anomalies meeting previously reported inclusion criteria []. Cases were excluded if termination of pregnancy was pursued, or if pregnancies resulted in a stillbirth or intrauterine demise. The term nondiagnostic pES results is used in this study to describe those with (1) negative, meaning no identified disease‐causing gene variant(s) to explain the prenatal phenotype; (2) uninformative variants of uncertain significance (VUS) lacking sufficient supporting evidence to explain the prenatal phenotype; (3) incidental findings only, meaning pathogenic variants identified were not associated with the prenatal phenotype or were related to carrier status. Prenatal exome sequencing of DNA extracted from amniocytes was performed at various established high‐volume commercial clinical laboratories routinely used for prenatal exome sequencing at this tertiary care center. While detailed laboratory‐specific reporting practices were not available for review, all laboratories used ACMG/AMP‐based variant classification frameworks and phenotype‐driven interpretation approaches in the context of fetal structural anomalies []. Variants considered for prenatal reporting required sufficient genotype‐phenotype correlation with the HPO terms provided. Variants with limited phenotype correlation, insufficient clinical evidence, or low suspicion for contributing to the fetal phenotype may not have been prioritized for prenatal reporting. Reporting practices for the return of variants of uncertain significance may also have varied between laboratories and throughout the study period. Variants in candidate genes were not routinely reported. Cases were excluded if a diagnosis was based on a medical geneticist's clinical interpretation of the prenatally identified VUS as explanatory for the fetal phenotype. Cases where chromosomal variants were identified were only included in this study if the copy number variants were unlikely to explain the fetal phenotype. Data were collected from both the 61 charts of the pregnant persons, and the charts of the 61 liveborn children. Postnatal chart review included chart entries up to July 2023, or up to 5 years of age (Table ). The data were collated into descriptive categories. Prenatal phenotypes in this study were categorized as either an isolated anomaly, if a single system was affected, or multiple anomalies, including multisystem structural anomalies or a single system structural anomaly in the context of a dynamic anomaly, such as abnormal fetal growth or amniotic fluid levels. Soft markers for aneuploidy were not considered as fetal structural anomalies in this study. We collected postnatal phenotypes for the liveborn children, including additional anomalies, dysmorphism, and functional features such as developmental delay, seizures, and deafness, available from medical genetics appointment notes or assessments by providers at the tertiary care center. Postnatal reassessment refers to the re‐evaluation of the patient's phenotype by medical genetic care providers after birth. This may prompt pES reinterpretation, which can include clinical variant reinterpretation (reassessing the clinical fit of previously identified pES variants) or reanalysis (formal pES data review to prompt variant re‐prioritization or reclassification). An explanatory diagnosis refers to a postnatal genetic diagnosis that is considered sufficient to account for the fetal phenotype that prompted prenatal testing. In this study, three drivers for medical genetics reassessment were identified: (1) VUS identified in the prenatal period by pES, (2) prenatal phenotype of fetal multisystem structural anomalies or unexplained hydrops (FMH), and (3) postnatal phenotype modifications (PPM), defined as the identification of new major clinical features after birth, represented by new HPO terms that were not appreciable on prenatal imaging. Only clinically significant findings, including newly recognized structural anomalies, dysmorphic features, neurologic manifestations (including seizures and hypotonia), and developmental delay identified through postnatal clinical assessment, specialist evaluations, or investigations/imaging, were included; minor or transient features were not included. Descriptive statistics were used to depict the clinical presentations, and postnatal medical genetics follow‐up, with proportions presented as percentages for categorical data and means with standard deviations for numeric data. Diagnostic outcomes were evaluated across three different denominators: (1) all liveborn children (N = 61), (2) children reassessed postnatally by medical genetics (n = 25), and (3) children who underwent postnatal pES reinterpretation (n = 11).

Results
Results Study Population As previously reported by Albert et al., 132 pregnancies with fetal structural anomalies underwent pES between 2016 and 2022 at this tertiary care center, of which 102 pregnancies received nondiagnostic results, indicating an overall diagnostic yield of 23%. A total of 41 cases were excluded from this study for the following reasons: termination of pregnancy (n = 29), limited information available due to relocation of care (n = 6), twin pregnancy (n = 4) and fetal demise (n = 2). The final cohort included 61 liveborn children, as described in Table , and the pathways by which they obtained postnatal medical genetics care are shown in Figure . Observed Postnatal Medical Genetics Follow‐up and Diagnostic Pathways. Acronyms: pES, prenatal exome sequencing; VUS, variant of uncertain significance; P/LP, pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant. The study population was classified based on the number of anomalies identified prenatally, either isolated (n = 30) or multiple (n = 31) (Table ). The multiple anomalies cohort included both pregnancies with multisystem anomalies (n = 22; 71%), as well as pregnancies with single system anomalies plus an abnormality of growth (n = 7; 23%) or fluid (n = 2; 6%). Medical Genetics Reassessment Of the 61 liveborn children with nondiagnostic prenatal genetic investigations, 41% (25/61) underwent reassessment by medical genetics within the data collection period (Figure , ). Most initial medical genetics reassessments occurred during NICU admissions (68%, 17/25). The remaining reassessments occurred on an outpatient basis for children between the ages of 5 weeks–27 months, with the majority (75%, 6/8) occurring before 6 months of age. Observed Clinical Contexts and Timing of Medical Genetics Reassessments. Observed drivers for follow‐up include VUS: prenatal identification of variant of uncertain significance by pES, FMH: prenatal presentations including fetal multisystem structural anomalies and/or unexplained hydrops, and PPM: postnatal phenotype modification. (A) Comparison of clinical contexts between children who did or did not receive postnatal medical genetics reassessments. Total number of liveborn children = 61. Children represented by percentages within subgroups made up of children who did receive medical genetics reassessment (Reassessed; n = 25) and those who did not (Not reassessed; n = 36). Colors within the bars indicate prenatal presentations of the children; Isolated (single system fetal structural anomaly; n = 8 reassessed, 22 not reassessed) or Multiple (Multiple fetal anomalies, including multisystem structural anomalies or single system structural anomaly in the context of abnormal fetal growth or amniotic fluid; n = 17 reassessed, 14 not reassessed). Subgroupings by drivers observed do not equate to 100% as children were counted in multiple categories when multiple clinical contexts were observed. (B) Clinical contexts and timing of reassessment by Medical Genetics. Total number of children who received medical genetics reassessments = 25. Timing represented by the ages of children at the time of initial medical genetics reassessment. Children represented by percentages within subgroups made up of cases with the same number of drivers: 3 drivers (n = 5), 2 drivers (n = 6), 1 driver (n = 12) and 0 drivers (n = 2). Driver groups subcategorized into specific clinical contexts (see legend): 0 drivers if none were observed, 1 driver included VUS, FMH, or PPM only; 2 drivers included combinations VUS + FMH or VUS + PPM with no child having FMH + PPM as the only two driver combination; 3‐drivers included children presenting with all 3 drivers (VUS + FMH + PPM). No children in this study presented with a combination of complex prenatal phenotype and postnatal phenotype modification. [Correction added on 28 September 2026, after first online publication: Figures 2 and 3 were swapped to show the correct images.] Medical genetic reassessment primarily occurred under three observed clinical contexts, referred to as drivers: (1) VUS identified by pES, (2) prenatal phenotype of fetal multisystem structural anomalies or unexplained hydrops (FMH), and (3) postnatal phenotype modifications (PPM). At least one of these drivers was observed in 92% (23/25) of children who received medical genetic reassessments (Figure ). Two children were reassessed by medical genetics in the context of zero drivers. Of children with VUS identified by pES, 63% (15/24) had postnatal reassessment by medical genetics. Reassessment occurred in 76% (13/17) of children born following identification of fetal multisystem structural anomalies or unexplained hydrops (FMH), and in all 11 children with postnatal phenotype modifications (PPM). Most children who received reassessments presented with multiple drivers (44%, 11/25), with 24% (6/25) presenting with two drivers and 20% (5/25) with three drivers. Those with more drivers were often seen by medical genetics earlier in life (Figure ). All children presenting with three drivers (5/5) were seen in the NICU within a week of life, and 67% (4/6) of children with two drivers were reassessed within a month of life. The timing of medical genetic reassessment also depended on when phenotypic manifestations were observed. For children with FMH, all reassessments by medical genetics occurred within the first week of life. PPMs were not always observed immediately at birth, with several children presenting for outpatient reassessment between 1 and 6 months of age once phenotype modifications were appreciated. In contrast, most children who did not undergo genetic reassessment showed no clear postnatal drivers for reassessment (69%, 25/36). Cases where drivers were observed without reassessment included VUS (7/36), FMH (2/36), or both a VUS and FMH (2/36). The two children with both VUS and FMH were evaluated by non‐genetic specialists and ultimately both received VACTERL diagnoses. In all cases without genetic reassessment, prenatally identified VUS were considered of low suspicion and neonatal examinations by non‐genetics providers indicated that postnatal findings were concordant with prenatally observed phenotypes. Among the 14 children with multiple prenatal anomalies not reassessed by medical genetics postnatally, 8 had a favourable postnatal presentation, 3 received palliative care or had care withdrawn, and 3 were evaluated by other specialists. pES Reinterpretation Of the children who underwent reassessment by medical genetics, 52% (13/25) were offered pES reinterpretation, 85% (11/13) of which were accepted. The two cases where pES reinterpretation was offered but declined postnatally were both seen during their NICU admissions, one from the isolated cohort at 2 days old and one from the multiple anomalies cohort at 3 days old. Reinterpretation was offered for all children with all three drivers (5/5), 50% of the children with two drivers (3/6), 42% of children with one driver (5/12), and none of the children reassessed with no drivers (n = 2). The driver most often associated with offering reinterpretation was PPM, with 91% (10/11) of children with this driver being offered reinterpretation. For the one case with phenotype modifications where reinterpretation was not offered, the phenotype was determined not to be suggestive of a genetic syndrome. For the other two drivers, reinterpretation was offered to 77% (10/13) of children with FMH and 53% (8/15) of those with VUS. None of the children reassessed with prenatal VUS as their only driver were offered reinterpretation during the interval of this study as all VUS were determined to be of poor clinical fit (Figure ). In all cases where reinterpretation was not offered, reassessment by medical genetics confirmed phenotypes were not of increased suspicion for a genetic syndrome. Clinical contexts of pES reinterpretation. Of the 25 children who received medical genetics reassessments, 13 were offered pES reinterpretation and 12 were not offered. Children are represented by percentages within groups made up of cases with the same number of observed drivers: 3 drivers (n = 5), 2 drivers (n = 6), 1 driver (n = 12), and 0 drivers (n = 2). Drivers include VUS: prenatal identification of a variant of uncertain significance by pES, FMH: prenatal presentations including fetal multisystem structural anomalies or unexplained hydrops, and PPM: postnatal phenotype modification. Subgroups were created based on the number of drivers observed: 0 drivers if none were observed, 1 driver included VUS, FMH, or PPM only; 2 drivers included combinations VUS + FMH or VUS + PPM with no child having FMH + PPM as the only two driver combination; and 3 drivers included combination VUS + FMH + PPM. No children in this study presented with a combination of complex prenatal phenotype and postnatal phenotype modification. Diagnoses In total, postnatal medical genetic reassessment with pES reinterpretation resulted in 4 new postnatal diagnoses. Of these, 3 diagnoses were considered explanatory for the prenatal presentation leading to an overall incremental diagnostic yield of reassessment and selective reinterpretation of 27% (3/11). This equates to 12% (3/25) of those undergoing medical genetics reassessment and 5% (3/61) of the entire liveborn cohort. One of the explanatory postnatal diagnoses was made through clinical variant reinterpretation alone. In this case, a postnatal diagnosis of Fanconi anemia type O was given as the two prenatally identified RAD51C variants of uncertain significance significantly increased in clinical suspicion based on postnatal phenotype modifications and orthogonal evidence from DNA breakage studies (C034, Table ; Table ) []. This case did not undergo formal pES reanalysis or formal variant reclassification. In all other cases that underwent reinterpretation, prenatally identified pES VUS underwent clinical variant reinterpretation and were deemed not to be causative. As suspicion for a genetic etiology of the children's presentations remained, reanalysis of the pES data was undertaken (n = 10). Overall, reanalysis resulted in the identification of novel VUS in 60% of cases (6/10). These newly reprioritized VUSs were then clinically interpreted in the context of the postnatal presentation, a process which resulted in two additional diagnoses (C105 and C113, Table ; Table ). For both cases, a clinical diagnosis was made by the medical geneticists; however, the reporting lab maintained the variants as VUS at the time of diagnosis. Subsequent evidence for case C105, included in a previously published report, supports the MEGF8 variants as pathogenic []. Long‐read genome sequencing established that the maternally inherited missense variant and the de novo splice‐altering variant are in trans, whereas RNA sequencing confirmed the impact of the de novo variant on splicing []. Reanalysis of pES data also resulted in the reprioritization of two pathogenic variants in CD36, allowing for the diagnosis of platelet glycoprotein IV deficiency in a child with a prenatally identified isolated cardiac anomaly. Although this diagnosis explained certain aspects of the postnatal phenotype, such as hematological and cardiovascular complications, it was not considered explanatory for the prenatally identified cardiac defect in this child (C083, Table ; Table ). Including this case, the overall postnatal genetic diagnostic yield was 36% (4/11).

Discussion
Discussion The diagnostic utility of prenatal exome sequencing (pES) in fetal structural anomalies has been established in large prospective cohorts and is reflected in current professional guidance [, , ]. However, despite this established utility, prenatal interpretation of exome data remains constrained by multiple limitations including phenotype‐driven variant prioritization with incomplete or evolving prenatal phenotypes, and knowledge gaps in the fetal presentations of genetic conditions [, ]. Postnatal studies have shown that 32% of children with exome diagnoses present with prenatal features that are uncommon or previously unreported for their underlying conditions [], and up to 68% of postnatal genetic diagnoses could not have been identified through prenatal phenotyping alone due to the absence of specific phenotypic features []. Additionally, approximately 24% of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants identified postnatally would have been classified as VUS if interpreted in the context of the prenatal presentation alone []. In cases of nondiagnostic pES, the value of postnatal reinterpretation is beginning to emerge, but guidance for patient selection and timing of follow‐up by medical genetic providers is lacking. Our study demonstrates that careful case selection for both postnatal reassessment by medical geneticists and pES reinterpretation can meaningfully increase the diagnostic yield. In our cohort, 27% (3/11) of highly selected cases received an explanatory genetic diagnosis for the prenatal phenotype following postnatal pES reinterpretation within 4 months of birth. When including the one additional diagnosis that was not explanatory for the prenatal phenotype, the overall postnatal genetic yield was 36% (4/11). Multiple factors contributed to selection for postnatal medical genetics reassessment and pES reinterpretation in our cohort. The three main clinical drivers identified were postnatal phenotype modifications, fetal multisystem structural anomalies and/or unexplained hydrops, and prenatally identified VUS. At least one of these drivers was present in 92% (23/25) of the children undergoing reassessment. Timing of reassessment occurred earlier in life in cases with an increasing number of drivers, likely reflecting a higher suspicion for a genetic diagnosis. In contrast, most children who did not undergo reassessment were less likely to have identifiable drivers after birth and often had isolated structural anomalies or reassuring postnatal presentations. Postnatal phenotype modifications were observed in 44% (11/25) of reassessed cases, consistent with prior literature [, , , ], and were the key driver of both reassessment and pES reinterpretation. The phenotype modifications included dysmorphisms, limb and genitourinary anomalies, as well as functional and developmental features such as hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay. Many of these features are not assessable prenatally, while others may be variably detected depending on gestational age, fetal position, imaging resolution, and phenotypic subtlety. This likely reflects the evolving nature of phenotypic ascertainment across the perinatal period rather than missed prenatal findings. Importantly, not all postnatal phenotypic modifications prompted pES reinterpretation, as medical genetics reassessment enabled prioritization of clinically relevant features over minor or transient findings. Our postnatal explanatory diagnoses from pES reinterpretation occurred by two complementary mechanisms: (1) clinical variant reinterpretation for previously reported VUS in the context of postnatal phenotype modifications and (2) formal pES reanalysis leading to identification and prioritization of variants not previously reported. In one case, clinical variant reinterpretation in the context of postnatal phenotypic modification and supportive functional studies was sufficient to establish a postnatal diagnosis of Fanconi anemia []. For the remaining three diagnoses, previously unreported variants were identified through reanalysis and were reprioritized for reporting considering the expanded postnatal phenotype modifications. Importantly, these variants were present within the original pES data but were not prioritized for reporting due to insufficient phenotypic overlap. Following postnatal reporting, these variants were interpreted as clinically diagnostic by the medical geneticist despite being classified as VUS by the reporting lab. These cases underscore the limitations of pES variant filtering and interpretation when based on antenatal phenotypic information alone [] and reinforce recent literature emphasizing the importance of careful VUS reporting in the prenatal period and the value of medical genetics involvement in assessing clinical fit [, ]. The proportion of diagnoses identified in our cohort was higher than several previous studies [, , , ]. However, our study population was highly selected for liveborn children with nondiagnostic prenatal genetic investigations in whom a genetic etiology was strongly suspected. In contrast, most prior reports have included more unselected cohorts [, , ]. Our highly selected cohort reflected a two‐step process. First, initial selection by non‐genetic specialists determined which children were re‐referred for postnatal medical genetics reassessment. Second, the offering of pES reinterpretation was guided by medical geneticists following detailed clinical reassessment. This approach enabled prioritization of cases most likely to benefit from pES reinterpretation. Notably, the total number of diagnoses in our highly selected cohort was nearly identical to that reported by Swanson et al., despite performing 20 times fewer reinterpretations (11 vs. 243 cases) []. While unselected reinterpretation remains academically important in assessing the overall diagnostic utility of the approach, our findings demonstrate that careful clinical prioritization can achieve a compatible number of diagnoses in a real‐world practice. The retrospective design of our study allowed inclusion of all cases where pES was offered following the identification of fetal structural anomalies over 6 years, minimizing recruitment bias. However, this study is limited to liveborn children and may not be generalizable to pregnancies ending in termination, fetal demise, or stillbirth, where postmortem evaluation and fetal tissue‐based testing provide alternative diagnostic opportunities. Additional factors, including variable intervals to reassessment and enrichment of the cohort for individuals with ongoing tertiary care, may have enhanced the depth of phenotypic data available for reinterpretation. A key limitation is the inability to determine whether additional explanatory diagnoses have been missed, particularly in younger children whose full phenotypes have yet to emerge. Additionally, current clinical diagnoses based on VUS and concordant postnatal phenotype have not yet been confirmed as causative and may be further refined with additional evidence over time. No standardized recommendations for postnatal medical genetics follow‐up after nondiagnostic pES currently exist, either at our center or in the published literature. Our findings provide insight that may inform the standardization of this practice (Table ). Current prenatal‐focused pES guidelines primarily address indications for testing and only minimally address postnatal reinterpretation, generally suggesting considering reanalysis after approximately 12 months, or in alignment with postnatal exome reanalysis practices [, ]. Overall, our data suggest that earlier reassessment (within the first 6 months of life) may capture clinically relevant findings more promptly than a 12‐month interval, allowing for timely modification of care during a critical developmental period. Newborns with multiple concurrent clinical indications should be prioritized to be seen as soon as possible during the newborn period. Reassessment appears most valuable for children who demonstrate notable postnatal phenotype modification regardless of whether the pES was completed for an isolated anomaly or multiple anomalies. While thorough postnatal assessments are routinely performed by non‐genetic care providers, these evaluations are not conducted from a genetic perspective, highlighting the added value of targeted reassessment by medical genetic specialists [, ]. For cases with isolated anomalies or a prenatal VUS lacking sufficient supporting evidence to explain the postnatal phenotype, our study's findings suggest that reassessment could be deferred unless phenotype modifications are recognized. In resource‐limited healthcare systems, care must balance clinical utility, population needs, and cost‐effectiveness. Universal reinterpretation of pES for all children with prenatally identified anomalies is unlikely to be feasible or necessary. Our findings support systematic postnatal reassessment pathways using a structured, selective approach guided by medical genetic professionals to optimize diagnostic yield while maintaining sustainability.

title: Clinical Application of Long-Read Sequencing for FMR1 Gene Mutation Detection in Populations From Shandong, China.
label_reason: FMR1 long-read method study; prenatal cases without ultrasound phenotype.
abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a common inherited intellectual disability. In this study, long‐read sequencing was used for the FMR1 gene detection. Men with familial inherited intellectual disability and women with indications for FXS screening were defined as high‐risk populations and were included in this study along with non‐high‐risk reproductive‐aged women. PCR‐capillary electrophoresis was used for preliminary screening of non‐high‐risk reproductive‐aged women, and long‐read sequencing was performed on abnormal samples and samples from high‐risk populations. Prenatal diagnosis using long‐read sequencing was performed for pregnant women in need. The prevalence of mutation in high‐risk females was 3.10% (7/226). 3 mutations were detected in male samples, with a mutation ratio of approximately 8.3% (3/36). The three most common CGG repeats were 29, 30, and 36, respectively. Analysis of AGG interruption pattern in 242 samples identified 908 AGG interruptions, involving 67 different patterns. The most frequent AGG interruption pattern was (CGG) 9 AGG(CGG) 9 AGG(CGG) 9 . Furthermore, long‐read sequencing was successfully applied for prenatal diagnosis in two pregnant women, and dynamic mutation of CGG repeat was detected within one family. Long‐read sequencing‐based assay cannot only accurately detect CGG repeat and AGG interruption, but also simultaneously identify other abnormalities of the FMR1 gene. Long‐read sequencing offers a broader detection scope and better characterization of FXS‐related genetic features. Keywords: AGG interruption, CGG repeat, fragile X syndrome, long‐read sequencing

Clinical Application of Long‐Read Sequencing for FMR1 Gene Mutation Detection in Populations From Shandong, China

Introduction
Introduction Fragile X syndrome (FXS; OMIM#300624) is an X‐linked dominant genetic disorder characterized by moderate to severe intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and special facial features, such as long face, large ears and prominent lower jaw. Abnormalities of the FMR1 gene (OMIM#309550) are the primary causes of FXS, and 99% of FXS cases result from the abnormal expansion of CGG repeat of the FMR1 gene. According to the number of repeats, CGG repeat is classified into four categories. (1) Normal type: 5–44 repeats. (2) Intermediate type (gray zone): 45–54 repeats. Individuals with an intermediate allele are phenotypically normal, but their offspring are at risk for premutation. (3) Premutation: 55–200 repeats. Premutation alleles carry a risk of expanding to full mutation during the transmission of female germ cells. The carriers also have an increased risk of developing FXS associated disorders, such as fragile X‐associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), fragile X‐associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI), and fragile X‐associated neuropsychiatric disorders. (4) Full mutation: more than 200 repeats. At this stage, the CpG island in the promoter region of the FMR1 gene is methylated, resulting in the failure of normal expression of its encoded FMRP protein. FMRP plays a crucial role in neural development and synaptic plasticity, and the lack of FMRP can lead to abnormal phenotypes such as intellectual disability (Hou et al. ; Monaghan, Lyon, Spector, erican College of Medical, & Genomics, 2013; Nolin et al. ). Additionally, approximately 1% of FXS patients are caused by mutations or deletions within the FMR1 gene, which also affect the normal expression or function of FMRP (Carroll et al. ). According to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), Southern blot analysis, PCR, next‐generation sequencing, cytogenetic evaluation, and protein analysis can be chosen for fragile X testing (Spector et al. ). However, more than one method is required, as no single method can comprehensively characterize all aspects of FMR1 full mutations. Southern blot can identify FMR1 methylation status, but it has low resolution and requires combination with PCR to accurately determine the number of CGG repeats in premutation (Biancalana et al. ; Filipovic‐Sadic et al. ), and FMR1 methylation status should not be used to predict severity in fetal or newborn cases (Spector et al. ). Conventional PCR can amplify premutation populations, yet it fails to amplify subpopulations carrying full mutation (Spector et al. ). Triplet repeat‐primed PCR (TP‐PCR) has a high analytical sensitivity and specificity for detecting expanded alleles (Spector et al. ). However, TP‐PCR cannot precisely detect FMR1 AGG interruptions in females, single nucleotide variants (SNVs), or deletions. In this study, we used long‐read sequencing to detect the FMR1 gene. This approach can not only detect CGG repeats and AGG interruptions but also identify FMR1 microdeletions, SNVs, and small insertions/deletions (InDels) (Hou et al. ). Men with familial inherited intellectual disability and women with FXS screening indications (‘ACOG Committee Opinion No. 469: Carrier screening for fragile X syndrome,’ ) were defined as high‐risk populations. A total of 262 high‐risk samples were included in this study, comprising 226 female samples and 36 male samples. Additionally, 2472 non‐high‐risk women of reproductive age were recruited. The FMR1 gene was detected in reproductive‐aged women using PCR‐capillary electrophoresis, and abnormal samples were selected. These abnormal samples were then subjected to long‐read sequencing together with high‐risk samples. While providing fertility guidance for reproductive‐aged women, as well as prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling for relevant individuals, we aim to clarify the ratios of various FMR1 genotypes and analyze CGG‐AGG distribution patterns and variation characteristics in populations from Shandong, China, thereby providing a more reliable research basis for precise FXS prevention and control in this region.

Materials and Methods
Materials and Methods Study Subjects Through medical record review and clinical history taking, family history of FMR1 premutation or full mutation was ascertained. Men with familial inherited intellectual disability and women with FXS screening indications were defined as high‐risk populations. The indications for FXS screening were as follows: (1) Family history of unexplained intellectual disability or autism spectrum disorder; (2) Family history of FMR1 premutation or full mutation; (3) History of giving birth to a child with unexplained developmental delay or autism; (4) Unexplained elevated follicle‐stimulating hormone or premature ovarian failure before the age of 40 (‘ACOG Committee Opinion No. 469: Carrier screening for fragile X syndrome,’ ). Additionally, women of reproductive age without the above indications were recruited as a low‐risk population. All participants or their legal guardians provided informed written consent. This study adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Jinan Maternity and Child Care Hospital (Approval No. IRB KY‐23‐59). Sample Collection and DNA Extraction Peripheral blood was collected aseptically from high‐risk individuals and reproductive‐aged women. For individuals requiring prenatal diagnosis, amniotic fluid samples were collected via ultrasound‐guided amniocentesis. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood and amniotic fluid using a genomic DNA extraction kit (Tiangen Biochemical Technology, China). FMR1 Gene Testing in Women of Reproductive Age The FMR1 gene was tested using the Fragile X Syndrome CGG Repeat Number Test Kit (PCR‐capillary electrophoresis method) (Biosan Tech, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The number or range of CGG repeats in the 5′ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene was determined using gene‐specific PCR and triplet repeat‐primed PCR amplification. FXS Genetic Testing by Long‐Read Sequencing After PCR amplification, the genomic DNA was subjected to end repair, adapter ligation, purification, and pooling to prepare a mixed library. The concentration of purified library should be no less than 10 ng/μL, with a total library amount of at least 360 ng. Subsequently, the library was converted into a SMRTbell library using the Sequel Binding Kit 2.0 and Internal Control Kit 1.0 (Pacific Biosciences, USA), and sequenced on the Sequel II platform (Pacific Biosciences, USA) in circular consensus sequencing (CCS) mode. The quality control criteria were as follows: the total number of reads should be ≥ 100 if full mutation was detected in the sample; the total number of reads should be ≥ 200 if premutation was detected in the sample; the total number of reads should be ≥ 500 when neither full mutation nor premutation was present. Sequencing data were aligned to the hg38 reference build using the software suite (smrtlink 10.1.0.119588, Pacific Biosciences). Kernel density estimation was applied to identify peaks of CGG repeat number, and the peaks were associated with different alleles. CGG repeat and AGG interruption were color‐coded and visualized as waterfall plots. Microdeletions in exon 1 of the FMR1gene were identified by aligning flanking sequences of CGG repeat to the reference sequence (Hou et al. ). SNVs and InDels in exon 1 of the FMR1gene were identified using FreeBayes v.1.3.4 (Biomatters, USA).

Results
Results Mutation of FMR1 Gene This study included 226 high‐risk female samples, 36 male samples with familial inherited intellectual disability, and 2472 non‐high‐risk women of reproductive age. Three mosaic alleles with different CGG repeats (29, 369, and 749) were identified in a high‐risk female sample. Among the remaining 225 samples, 6 (6/225, 2.67%) premutation carriers were detected, and no intermediate or full mutation alleles were identified. Among the 36 male patients, three patients with mosaic alleles were identified. Mosaic full mutation alleles with CGG repeats of 280/784 and 289/402/563 were detected in two patients, respectively, and four mosaic alleles with different CGG repeats (105, 249, 423, and 552) were detected in a male patient. The mutation ratio was approximately 8.3% (3/36). Among the 2472 reproductive‐aged women, a total of 17 (17/2472, 0.69%) repeat expansions were detected, including 14 (14/2472, 0.57%) cases with intermediate alleles and 3 (3/2472, 0.12%) cases with premutation alleles. No full mutation alleles were identified (Table ). Distribution of FMR1 CGG Repeat Excluding the mosaic individual, a total of 33 different alleles were identified across 450 X chromosomes from the 225 high‐risk female samples. The CGG repeat number ranged from 10 to 87. The most frequent allele was 29 repeats, accounting for 49.11% (221/450), followed by 30 and 36 repeats, accounting for 25.33% (114/450) and 9.78% (44/450), respectively (Figure , Table ). Among 4944 X chromosomes from the 2472 women of reproductive age, 38 different alleles were identified, with CGG repeats ranging from 11 to 78. The most frequent allele was 29 repeats, accounting for 46.16% (2282/4944), followed by 30 and 36 repeats, accounting for 27.25% (1347/4944) and 9.22% (456/4944), respectively (Figure , Table ). Distribution of FMR1 gene CGG repeat. (A) Distribution of FMR1 gene CGG repeat in high‐risk women. (B) Distribution of FMR1 gene CGG repeat in reproductive‐aged women. FMR1 Gene AGG Interruption Patterns CGG repeat and AGG interruption were color‐coded and visualized as waterfall plots (Figure ). The AGG interruption patterns of 242 samples (14 male samples and 228 female samples) were detected by the long‐read sequencing, and a total of 908 AGG interruptions were identified, involving 67 different distribution patterns. 5 AGG interruptions were detected in intermediate alleles, involving 3 distribution patterns. Among the 8 premutation alleles, only 3 AGG interruptions were identified with three distribution patterns, and no AGG interruptions were detected in the remaining 5 premutation alleles. The most common AGG interruption pattern was (CGG)9AGG(CGG)9AGG(CGG)9 (abbreviated as 9A9A9), with a frequency of approximately 43.62% (205/470). 10A9A9 was the second most common AGG interruption pattern, accounting for 23.83% (112/470) of all X chromosomes. Among the 470 alleles, 2 (0.43%), 50 (10.64%), 342 (72.77%), 66 (14.04%), and 10 (2.13%) alleles carried 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0 AGG interruptions, respectively. Four AGG interruptions were exclusively present in normal alleles. Among the 50 alleles with three AGG interruptions, only one was an intermediate allele; the rest were normal alleles. 2 AGG interruptions were only found in normal alleles (Table ). Display of FMR1 CGG expansions and AGG interruptions by long‐read sequencing for representative samples. (A) Male sample with normal allele. (B) Female sample with normal alleles. (C) Female sample with one normal allele and one premutation allele. (D) Female sample with mosaic normal and full mutation alleles. Clinical Application PCR‐capillary electrophoresis was used to screen the FMR1 gene in the recruited non‐high‐risk women of reproductive age. Abnormal samples were then verified and further analyzed by long‐read sequencing. Long‐read sequencing confirmed 14 intermediate allele carriers and 3 premutation allele carriers, two of whom underwent prenatal diagnosis. Pregnant woman 1 previously gave birth to a boy with autism, who was diagnosed as a full‐mutation patient of the FMR1 gene by testing. In the current pregnancy, amniotic fluid was collected by amniocentesis, and subsequent long‐read sequencing revealed that the male fetus was (CGG)9(AGG)1(CGG)163/(CGG)9(AGG)1(CGG)350/(CGG)9(AGG)1(CGG)636, indicating a full‐mutation status. After comprehensive genetic counseling, the pregnancy was terminated. The clinician provided detailed fertility guidance, recommending prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies. Pregnant woman 2 was a premutation carrier with CGG repeats of 30 and 60. Long‐read sequencing of amniotic fluid revealed the male fetus was (CGG)10(AGG)1(CGG)19. She delivered a healthy male baby at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery. In addition, we identified a female carrier of a premutation allele who exhibited dynamic mutation during reproductive transmission. Her original CGG repeats were 70, which expanded to 369 and 749 upon maternal transmission. This female offspring then underwent another dynamic mutation during the reproductive transmission, resulting in the identification of three mosaic alleles with different CGG repeats (289, 402, and 523) in the third‐generation male offspring.

Discussion
Discussion FXS is a common inherited intellectual disability, with an incidence rate second only to Down syndrome (R. J. Hagerman et al. ). Previous studies have shown that the prevalence rate in South Asian countries ranged from 0.7% to 12.24% (Fazna and Hagerman ). The diagnostic yield of FXS testing in the Hong Kong Chinese population was 0.8% (Au et al. ). By conducting haplotype and linkage disequilibrium analysis on three Asian populations, Chinese, Malay, and Indian, Zhou et al. found that Asian populations exhibited lower diversity in the normal FMR1 CGG repeat length, patterns, and flanking haplotypes compared with Caucasians and African Americans (Zhou et al. ). A meta‐analysis of 54 studies by Hunter et al. concluded that the female prevalence of FXS is approximately 0.0119% (9/75,539), and the female premutation carrier rate is about 0.61% (539/88673) (Hunter et al. ). In this study, 226 females with FXS screening indications (‘ACOG Committee Opinion No. 469: Carrier screening for fragile X syndrome,’ ) and 2472 reproductive‐aged women were tested. The results showed that the female full mutation and premutation rates were 0.04% (1/2698) and 0.33% (9/2698), respectively. These findings differed from Hunter's predicted results, which might be due to differences in sample composition. Hunter's data were from random populations without specific classification. In our study, the proportion of high‐risk women was relatively low, which might have led to a lower mutation rate. Peprah et al. reported that the prevalence of FXS among individuals with intellectual disability varies globally from 0.5% to 9.7% (Peprah ). A study conducted across five cities in China showed that approximately 2.8% of intellectual disability cases were caused by FMR1 full mutations (Zhong et al. ), while one study focusing on the southern Chinese population reported higher proportions of 7.5% (Luo et al. ). In this study, three patients with mutation were detected in 36 men with familial inherited intellectual disability from Shandong, China. The mutation rate was approximately 8.3% (3/36), which was generally consistent with data from southern China. Studies on the distribution of FMR1 CGG repeat vary across populations and regions. Research on four populations in Mexico found 29, 30, and 32 were the three most common CGG repeats (Barros‐Nunez et al. ). An African study reported 29 and 30 were the most frequent CGG repeats (Chiurazzi et al. ). Asian studies showed 29 as the most common CGG repeats in Chinese and Malays, and 30 in Indians (Zhou et al. ). It is reported that the most common CGG repeats in Han Chinese women of reproductive age in Urumqi were 29 and 30. In this study, 2472 reproductive‐aged women were tested. The results showed that the most common CGG repeats in Han Chinese women of reproductive age in Shandong were also 29 and 30, consistent with previous findings, suggesting little geographical variation among Han Chinese women. Both our results and those of Chen et al. (Chen et al. ) indicated a relatively high frequency of 36 CGG repeats in Chinese populations. Similar high frequencies of 36 CGG repeats have been observed in East and Southeast Asian populations (Zhou et al. ), but not in non‐Asian populations (Chen et al. ; Mingroni‐Netto et al. ; Zhou et al. ), suggesting this high frequency is not random but originates from population substructure. SNP analysis suggested 36 CGG repeats were strongly associated with Asian‐specific haplotypes (Zhou et al. ). Previous studies have reported that premutation alleles are highly unstable during transmission through female germ cells, and can expand to full mutation within a single generation. Moreover, the risk of expansion increases with the length of the CGG repeat, reaching nearly 100% when the CGG repeat exceeds 90 (Monaghan et al. ; Nolin et al. ). The smallest repeat reported to undergo dynamic expansion is 59 (Nolin et al. , ). In this study, we identified one case of dynamic mutation. The mother originally had 70 CGG repeats, which expanded to 369 and 749 repeats during germline transmission, resulting in her female offspring being carriers of the full mutation allele. Eichler et al. proposed in 1994 that AGG interruptions within the CGG repeat tract could enhance the stability of CGG repeats (Eichler et al. ). Subsequent studies showed that even a single AGG interruption could significantly reduce the expansion risk when CGG repeats were < 80, with the effect most pronounced for CGG repeats < 70. However, when CGG repeats exceeded 90, AGG interruptions might not mitigate the expansion risk (Nolin et al. ; Yrigollen et al. ). For the dynamic mutation identified in this study, the mother had 70 CGG repeats with no AGG interruptions, which might be the primary cause of the expansion. Therefore, incorporating AGG interruption analysis into FMR1 gene testing can improve risk estimation and genetic counseling for female premutation carriers (Hou et al. ). However, traditional methods can only reliably assess AGG interruption patterns in males and cannot effectively analyze the AGG interruption patterns in females. The long‐read sequencing used in this study sequences the trinucleotide repeat region of the FMR1 gene directly, enabling separation of the two X chromosomes and mosaic alleles in females (Hou et al. ). A total of 14 male samples and 228 female samples were tested by long‐read sequencing in this study, and 67 AGG interruption patterns were identified. Among them, the most frequent pattern was 9A9A9, which was consistent with previous reports (Zhou et al. ). Nolin et al. analyzed AGG interruptions in 1040 alleles from 705 families and found 4 AGG interruptions were present only in intermediate alleles, while 3 AGG interruptions were found exclusively in alleles with < 70 CGG repeats (Nolin et al. ). In this study, we found 4 AGG interruptions only in normal alleles. Among the 50 alleles with 3 AGG interruptions, only one was an intermediate allele, the rest were normal alleles. This may be because most samples analyzed for AGG interruption patterns in this study were from the high‐risk populations. In addition to the instability of CGG repeats, premutation carriers face increased risks for FXS‐associated disorders. It is reported that at least one‐third of male premutation carriers exhibit FXTAS‐related phenotypes after the age of 50 (Jacquemont et al. ); female carriers may also be affected, but with less severe symptoms. It is hypothesized that the FMR1 gene in premutation carriers is transcribed into elevated level mRNA, which binds more RNA‐binding proteins, ultimately leading to RNA toxicity and associated phenotypes (P. J. Hagerman and Hagerman ; Lisik ). Female premutation carriers are also prone to FXPOI, and the length of the CGG repeat affects this process (Sullivan et al. ). For CGG repeats < 80, the age of ovarian decline decreases with increasing repeat length. When CGG repeats are between 80 and 100, the risk of FXPOI increases significantly, likely due to cumulative toxicity of the mRNA in ovarian tissue (Sullivan et al. ). Additionally, premutation carriers have a higher risk for fragile X‐associated neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism (P. J. Hagerman and Hagerman ). Among the premutation carriers identified in this study, only two women were over 40 years old. Clinical examinations were performed on them, and no FXS‐related disorders were detected. Notably, no intermediate alleles were detected in the high‐risk population. Screening of non‐high‐risk women of childbearing age identified 14 carriers of intermediate alleles and 3 carriers of premutation alleles, two of whom underwent prenatal diagnosis. Through accurate detection by long‐read sequencing, we provide prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling for relevant individuals, as well as professional guidance for their subsequent reproductive decisions. In clinical practice, besides CGG repeats and AGG interruptions, variations such as mutations and deletions within the FMR1 gene can also cause FXS. The flanking regions of the CGG repeat in the FMR1 gene are unstable and prone to microdeletions ranging from several to hundreds of base pairs (Coffee et al. ; Wells ). However, in some cases, microdeletions can reduce CGG repeat count, disrupt exon 1 of the FMR1 gene, cause allelic dropout, or alter allele classification by PCR, thus carrying important clinical significance (Hou et al. ). Long‐read sequencing used in this study allows alignment of the flanking sequences of the CGG repeat with the reference sequence, thereby identifying microdeletions in exon 1 of the FMR1 gene (Hou et al. ), which is important clinically. Furthermore, long‐read sequencing can accurately detect mosaic alleles of the FMR1 gene. Previous studies have shown that 12%–41% of male FXS patients are mosaics (Ciaccio et al. ; Peyser et al. ). In this study, long‐read sequencing identified 3 male patients with mosaic alleles. Although the ACMG guidelines state that FMR1 methylation status should not be used to predict severity in fetal or newborn cases, methylation testing remains a key diagnostic feature for full‐mutation characterization in standard testing. Therefore, when using long‐read sequencing for the detection of FXS in adults, it is necessary to combine other detection methods to determine the methylation status. At present, there is a lack of region‐specific FMR1 gene mutation data for the population in Shandong Province, China, accompanied by poor adaptability to local genetic backgrounds and insufficient targeted value for clinical reference. This study constructed the first localized FMR1 gene mutation database for Shandong Province. We systematically integrated data including FMR1 gene polymorphisms, mutation patterns and allelic genotypes from reproductive‐aged women and high‐risk populations within Shandong Province, and characterized the unique mutational features of the local population. This work provided localized data evidence for population screening, clinical diagnosis, genetic counseling, and prognostic evaluation of FXS in this region, and overcame the limitation that universal databases fail to accommodate regional genetic heterogeneity.

Conclusion
Conclusion Long‐read sequencing features long read lengths, high accuracy and no GC bias, and has been applied in genetic testing for diseases such as thalassemia (Liang et al. ), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Liu et al. ) and spinal muscular atrophy (Li et al. ). The long‐fragment ultra‐high GC PCR amplification with Oxford Nanopore sequencing was applied to the detection of the FMR1 gene. The detection results were consistent with those of TP‐PCR and Southern blot (Yang et al. ). Our previous results have shown that compared with traditional PCR methods, long‐read sequencing can not only accurately detect FMR1 CGG repeats and AGG interruptions, but also simultaneously identify other abnormalities including mutations, deletions, and mosaicism (Hou et al. ). Liang et al. also demonstrated that long‐read sequencing enables accurate detection of point mutation, microdeletion and large fragment deletions within the FMR1 gene (Liang et al. ). Long‐read sequencing offers a broader detection scope and better characterization of FXS‐related genetic features, and its testing cost is roughly equivalent to that of conventional PCR methods. However, due to the limited availability of platform, the relatively low popularization, and the long sequencing cycle, for the large‐scale screening, we first used PCR‐capillary electrophoresis for preliminary screening, followed by long‐read sequencing for verification and further analysis of abnormal samples. Although this approach is more economical and rapid for population screening, it may lead to missed diagnoses, especially in cases involving large expansions or low‐level mosaicism, and prolong the overall testing cycle for abnormal samples. It is hoped that with the development and popularization of technology, long‐read sequencing can be applied to large‐scale population screening for FXS at an early date.

title: Prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of sirenomelia: A case report.
label_reason: Sirenomelia ultrasound case, no genetic test.
abstract: Sirenomelia is an extremely rare and almost invariably lethal congenital malformation characterized by variable fusion of the lower limbs and severe associated visceral anomalies. We report a case prenatally diagnosed at 20 weeks of gestation in a 25-year-old nondiabetic, nonconsanguineous woman referred for suspected polymalformative fetal syndrome. Prenatal ultrasound demonstrated severe oligohydramnios, bilateral small hyperechoic kidneys suggestive of renal dysplasia, fused lower limbs, absent external genitalia, and a single umbilical artery, findings strongly supporting the diagnosis of sirenomelia. A suspected conotruncal cardiac anomaly was noted, though limited by the severity of oligohydramnios. Postnatal examination confirmed the prenatal findings; fetal karyotype was normal. Medical termination of pregnancy was performed following multidisciplinary counseling. This case highlights the central role of prenatal ultrasound in the early recognition of sirenomelia, and the importance of careful radiologic description, cautious classification, and multidisciplinary counseling in the management of this rare lethal condition. Keywords: Sirenomelia, Mermaid syndrome, Prenatal diagnosis, Oligohydramnios, Renal dysplasia, Caudal dysgenesis
text:
Prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of sirenomelia: A case report

Introduction
Introduction Sirenomelia, also known as mermaid syndrome, is an uncommon congenital malformation that is usually incompatible with life, defined by different degrees of fusion involving the lower extremities and severe associated visceral anomalies, particularly renal and genitourinary defects []. Early descriptions of sirenomelia date back to the 16th century, notably those of Rocheus in 1542 and Palfyn in 1553. The estimated prevalence is approximately 1 in 100,000 live births []. Due to severe renal agenesis or dysgenesis, which results in oligohydramnios and subsequent pulmonary hypoplasia, the prognosis is usually unfavorable Prenatal ultrasound is essential for early diagnosis, especially when lower limb fusion is associated with severe oligohydramnios, renal abnormalities, abnormal or absent external genitalia, anorectal malformation, and a single umbilical artery []. First-trimester ultrasound can be particularly valuable for early recognition of lower limb fusion, renal anomalies, and abnormal umbilical vascularization. In the second trimester, severe oligohydramnios may limit sonographic visualization making prenatal diagnosis challenging. The etiopathogenesis of sirenomelia remains debated. Several mechanisms have been proposed, including the vascular steal phenomenon, abnormalities of caudal blastogenesis, maternal diabetes, environmental exposures, and possible genetic susceptibility []. We describe a Tunisian case of sirenomelia diagnosed prenatally at 20 weeks of gestation in a 25-year-old woman with no known diabetes or consanguinity. We discuss its clinical, ultrasound, and postnatal features in the context of the current literature.

Case presentation
Case presentation A 25-year-old pregnant woman was referred to our department at 20 weeks of gestation for detailed evaluation of suspected multiple fetal anomalies. Her medical history was unremarkable, with no known diabetes and there was no consanguinity with her 31-year-old partner. No family history of diabetes, congenital anomalies, or genetic disorders was reported. A detailed specialist-performed ultrasound examination at 20 weeks of gestation revealed a viable singleton pregnancy with fetal biometry consistent with gestational age. Severe oligohydramnios was directly visualized and significantly limited the overall anatomical assessment. Lower limb fusion was directly identified, with visualization of a single femur-like long bone (A). and partial visualization of a tibial segment (B), suggestive of a severe form of sirenomelia. Both kidneys appeared small and hyperechoic, with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, suggestive of bilateral renal dysplasia (D). The external genitalia were not visualized. A single umbilical artery was suspected prenatally and confirmed postnatally. Cardiac assessment showed a suspected ventricular septal defect (C). However, evaluation of the outflow tracts was limited by fetal position and severe oligohydramnios, and no definitive conotruncal anomaly could be established. Prenatal ultrasound findings in a fetus with suspected sirenomelia. (A and B) Ultrasound images showing fusion of the lower limbs with visualization of a single femur-like long bone (white arrow) and partial visualization of a tibial segment, suggestive of a severe form of sirenomelia (blue arrow). (C) Fetal cardiac ultrasound showing a suspected discontinuity of the interventricular septum, suggestive of a ventricular septal defect (arrow). (D) Prenatal abdominal ultrasound showing a small hyperechogenic fetal kidney with abnormal parenchymal appearance, suggestive of renal dysplasia (triangles). Fig 1 – dummy alt text Amniocentesis was performed and showed a normal fetal karyotype. Given the severity of the malformations and the unfavorable prognosis, the parents consented to medical termination of pregnancy, resulting in the delivery of a stillborn fetus weighing 350 g. Postnatal examination showed a single umbilical artery, absence of external genitalia and an imperforate anus. The lower limbs were fused from the pelvic region to the knee (). Based on prenatal ultrasound and postnatal palpation, precise skeletal typing could not be established with certainty in the absence of radiographic confirmation. The findings were most suggestive of a severe form of sirenomelia, possibly Stocker type VI or VII, although definitive skeletal classification was not possible without radiographic confirmation. Postnatal macroscopic examination. (A) Lateral view of the fetus showing fusion of the lower limbs (circle), consistent with sirenomelia. (B) Anterior view showing proximal fusion of the lower limbs extending from the pelvic region to the knees (circle). (C) Close-up view showing fused lower limbs forming a single tapered distal extremity (arrow). Fig 2 – dummy alt text Additional investigations, including radiographic evaluation of the lower limbs in the stillborn fetus and maternal laboratory testing for heavy metals and blood glucose, could not be performed because parental consent was not obtained.

Discussion
Discussion Sirenomelia, also known as mermaid syndrome, is an uncommon congenital malformation that is usually incompatible with life, defined by different degrees of fusion involving the lower extremities. It belongs to the spectrum of caudal dysgenesis and is often accompanied by severe genitourinary, gastrointestinal, skeletal, cardiovascular, and vascular anomalies []. The literature reports a male predominance (ratio 2.7:1) and a more frequent association with monozygotic twin pregnancies [, , ]. The diagnosis is usually established based on the presence of lower-limb fusion associated with severe renal anomalies, oligohydramnios, absent or abnormal external genitalia, anorectal malformation, and a single umbilical artery. In 1987, Stocker and Heifetz proposed a 7-type classification of sirenomelia based on the number, arrangement, and degree of fusion of the long bones in the lower limbs []. Type I presents 2 separate femora, tibiae, and fibulae; Type II shows fused femora with separate tibiae and fibulae; Type III includes fused femora and tibiae with separate fibulae; Type IV shows fused femora, tibiae, and fibulae; Type V shows absent femora with fused tibiae and separate fibulae; Type VI shows absent femora with fused tibiae and fibulae; and Type VII represents the most severe form, with absent femora and tibiae and fused fibulae. This classification has prognostic and descriptive value, though radiographic confirmation is required for accurate typing [,]. In the present case, ultrasound examination at 20 weeks of gestation revealed severe oligohydramnios, bilateral renal abnormalities, a suspected cardiac defect, and major lower limb malformations. Postnatal examination confirmed the diagnosis by showing fused lower limbs extending from the pelvis to the knee, absence of external genitalia, imperforate anus, and a single umbilical artery. Prenatal diagnosis can be difficult when severe oligohydramnios limits fetal visualization, particularly in the second trimester. Advances in prenatal ultrasonography have improved the early detection of sirenomelia and other severe congenital malformations. High-resolution 2-dimensional ultrasound enables detailed fetal anatomical assessment from the first trimester, particularly for lower limb fusion, renal anomalies, oligohydramnios, and abnormal umbilical vascularization [,]. Early diagnosis enables timely parental counseling, comprehensive evaluation of associated anomalies, and appropriate use of additional diagnostic investigations when indicated. Doppler assessment of the umbilical vessels and fetal abdominal vasculature may also be useful, as a single umbilical artery and abnormal vascular pattern are frequently reported [,,]. Fetal MRI can be considered as an adjunct to ultrasound in selected cases, particularly when severe oligohydramnios limits sonographic visualization. It may help better delineate associated visceral, spinal, and lower limb anomalies, although prenatal ultrasound remains the primary diagnostic tool for sirenomelia []. The etiopathogenesis of sirenomelia remains controversial. Several mechanisms have been proposed, including maternal diabetes, environmental factors, abnormal caudal blastogenesis, vascular steal phenomenon, and genetic susceptibility [,]. Maternal diabetes has historically been considered a potential risk factor, particularly because caudal developmental defects are more frequent in diabetic pregnancies (10%-15% of affected children are born to diabetic mothers) []. However, maternal diabetes has been reported in only 0.5%-3.7% of sirenomelia cases, indicating that it cannot fully explain the pathogenesis of this malformation suggesting that diabetes alone cannot explain the condition [,]. In our case, maternal diabetes was not known, and there was no personal or family history suggestive of diabetes. The vascular steal hypothesis remains one of the most widely accepted hypotheses. According to this theory, an abnormal large vitelline artery diverts blood flow from the caudal part of the embryo toward the placenta, resulting in hypoperfusion of the caudal mesoderm [,]. This mechanism may explain the association of lower limb fusion, renal agenesis or dysgenesis, anorectal malformations, genital anomalies, and single umbilical artery. However, this theory does not fully explain all associated anomalies, particularly craniofacial and cardiac defects []. Another hypothesis is the defective blastogenesis theory. According to this concept, sirenomelia results from an early developmental disturbance occurring during the third week of embryogenesis, at the end of gastrulation. This early defect may affect multiple caudal structures simultaneously, including the lower limbs, kidneys, genital tract, anorectal region, and vascular system. Other teratogenic factors such as vitamin A, cadmium, and lead have been associated with sirenomelia in animal and human models []. Current understanding suggests that sirenomelia may result from an interaction between vascular abnormalities, early embryonic developmental defects, environmental exposures, and genetic factors [,,]. Sirenomelia is commonly associated with severe renal malformations, including bilateral renal agenesis, renal dysplasia, or hypoplastic kidneys. Renal and urinary tract anomalies frequently impair fetal urine excretion, resulting in severe oligohydramnios. This critical lack of amniotic fluid causes prolonged compression on the fetal chest and prevents essential fluid from expanding the airways, directly leading to pulmonary hypoplasia, one of the main causes of neonatal death [,,]. In the present case, prenatal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral small, hyperechoic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, severe oligohydramnios, complete fusion of the lower limbs, imperforate anus, absent external genitalia, and a single umbilical artery. These findings were highly consistent with sirenomelia. Caudal regression syndrome (CRS) is the main differential diagnosis, as both conditions share caudal developmental defects. However, several features in our case allowed distinction from CRS: complete fusion of the lower limbs into a single structure (whereas lower limbs in CRS are typically hypoplastic but remain separate), the presence of a single umbilical artery (highly characteristic of sirenomelia), and severe bilateral renal dysgenesis/agenesis with consequent oligohydramnios. In contrast, renal involvement in CRS is usually less severe, and lower limb fusion is absent or minimal []. Other differential diagnoses included severe limb-body wall complex and VACTERL association. Limb-body wall complex was excluded due to the absence of abdominal wall defects, thoraco-abdominal involvement, and the presence of a normally inserted umbilical cord. VACTERL association was considered because of the cardiac and anorectal anomalies; however, the complete lower limb fusion and single umbilical artery are not typical features of VACTERL and strongly favored sirenomelia. Postnatal clinical examination, skeletal radiography, and fetopathological assessment, when available, remain essential to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate sirenomelia from other caudal dysgenesis syndromes. The prognosis of sirenomelia is extremely poor. Most affected fetuses die in utero or shortly after birth. Survival is primarily determined by the degree of renal function preservation, as renal agenesis or severe dysplasia leads to oligohydramnios and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia. Fewer than 1% of affected neonates survive beyond the first week of life. Long-term survival is exceptional and depends on the presence of functional renal tissue and the feasibility of complex surgical management []. Once the diagnosis is suspected, multidisciplinary counseling is essential. Parents should be informed about the severity of the condition, the high risk of fetal or neonatal death, the associated malformations, and the available management options. Depending on gestational age, local legislation, and parental wishes, management may include continuation of pregnancy with neonatal palliative care or medical termination of pregnancy [,]. In our case, because of the severity of the malformations and the poor prognosis, medical termination of pregnancy was proposed and accepted by the parents. Unfortunately, additional investigations, including fetal radiography, fetopathological examination, and maternal laboratory testing, could not be performed because parental consent was not obtained. This limited the anatomical and etiological assessment. Clinical significance and contribution This case contributes to the limited North African literature on sirenomelia by documenting a Tunisian case diagnosed after late referral at 20 weeks of gestation. Sirenomelia may be suspected during the first trimester and the absence of early prenatal follow-up delayed diagnosis. This observation emphasizes the public health importance of early antenatal screening and timely referral for fetal anomaly assessment. In addition, the associated cardiac anomaly in our case is notable, as such findings are not consistently reported in sirenomelia and suggest that the pathogenesis may involve more than the vascular steal phenomenon alone, supporting the role of an early blastogenesis defect. Finally, the parental refusal of additional investigations highlights the importance of culturally sensitive counseling in contexts where severe congenital malformations may be associated with misconceptions and stigma. Limitations However, this case has several limitations. First, the absence of fetal radiography prevented precise classification of the skeletal anomalies and the type of lower limb fusion. Second, fetopathological examination was not conducted as parental consent was not obtained. Third, maternal testing for glucose metabolism and heavy metals exposure could not be completed. Finally, genetic testing was unavailable, which limited etiological assessment and recurrence-risk counseling. Although these limitations were present, the association of severe oligohydramnios, renal anomalies, lower limb fusion, imperforate anus, absent external genitalia, and single umbilical artery was strongly suggestive of sirenomelia.

Conclusion
Conclusion Sirenomelia, or mermaid syndrome, is an almost invariably lethal congenital malformation characterized by variable fusion of the lower extremities and severe associated visceral anomalies, particularly renal and genitourinary defects. This case illustrates the crucial role of detailed prenatal ultrasound in the early recognition of sirenomelia, particularly when severe oligohydramnios is accompanied by renal abnormalities, abnormal or absent external genitalia, anorectal malformation, and a single umbilical artery. Early detection permits appropriate multidisciplinary counseling and informed parental choice. While the absence of additional postnatal and maternal investigations limited the etiological assessment, the prenatal and postnatal findings were concordant with a definitive diagnosis of sirenomelia. The present case further revealed the importance of addressing cultural misconceptions surrounding severe congenital malformations in the Tunisian context, and genetic counseling should be considered for couples following such a diagnosis.
