title: Expanding prenatal diagnosis: clinical utility of prenatal whole-exome sequencing in a Romanian case series with fetal anomalies.
label_reason: Ten fetuses with malformations tested by WES.
abstract: The prenatal diagnostic field is rapidly expanding internationally, creating a growing need for guidelines and for a better understanding of the clinical utility of new tests across different clinical settings. This study aimed to investigate the diagnostic yield of prenatal whole exome sequencing (WES) and to assess its clinical utility and impact on outcomes among families with high-risk pregnancies and the multidisciplinary teams supervising the cases. We retrospectively reviewed indications, fetal phenotypes, results, turnaround time, and the clinical impact of WES in 10 pregnancies from the Romanian population, investigated in a private clinical diagnostic laboratory between January 2024 and March 2026. The diagnostic yield of prenatal WES was 50% in this case series of Romanian pregnancies with ultrasound-detected malformations and a previous negative microarray result. Seven out of ten patients opted for medical termination of pregnancy. Our findings are consistent with those of other national and international studies, while highlighting the need for improved clinical pathways and guidelines to support appropriate test selection and prenatal management. The multidisciplinary team considered prenatal WES an efficient tool for prenatal diagnosis, with potential to inform pregnancy management, including the choice of maternity hospital level, delivery planning, and personalized neonatal care.
text:
Expanding prenatal diagnosis: clinical utility of prenatal whole-exome sequencing in a Romanian case series with fetal anomalies

Introduction
Introduction Prenatal diagnostics encompasses a range of tests that use advanced cytogenetic and molecular technologies to evaluate fetal health in utero. Current methods have different indications and can diagnose multiple fetal genetic disorders. These approaches range from classical techniques such as conventional karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and molecular karyotyping to next-generation sequencing panels and comprehensive prenatal tests such as whole-exome sequencing (WES), and medical geneticists may recommend them after consulting with families in prenatal cases []. A prenatal whole-exome sequencing test examines approximately 1–2% of the fetal genome and can achieve a diagnostic yield ranging from 6.2% to 80%, depending on the selected cohort [–]. Prenatal exome testing implementation varies considerably across countries and continents, with discrepancies even within the same continent in turnaround time, cost management, test indications, and result interpretation. Current practice guidelines highlight the importance of using molecular karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) as gold-standard, first-tier tests for pregnancies with ultrasound-detected malformations [,]. This technique has a diagnostic yield of only 30–40% based on international studies [–]. In 2018, the International Society for Prenatal Diagnosis (ISPD), the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM), and the Perinatal Quality Foundation (PQF) presented a joint position statement regarding the use of genome-wide sequencing for fetal diagnosis []. The societies highlighted the importance of next-generation sequencing (NGS) after chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) has been performed and yielded an uninformative result, or its concurrent use in specific cases, while stating that routine sequencing is not sustainable and should not be considered a first-tier test for all genetic conditions []. The objective of the present study was to assess the clinical utility of prenatal whole-exome sequencing in selected patients within Romanian prenatal care, with a particular focus on its diagnostic effectiveness compared with molecular karyotyping, especially in patients with adverse pregnancy outcomes and negative results from standard genetic testing, such as molecular karyotyping. The findings may contribute to the existing literature and support Romanian national authorities in considering WES testing for selected cases, as is currently offered in several countries, including England through the National Health Service (NHS), Israel, the Netherlands, France in academic hospitals, Germany, Belgium, and North America. Currently, prenatal WES is not routinely reimbursed in Eastern European countries such as Romania, limiting access to this testing in many cases. The present study also aimed to compare the diagnostic yield observed in the Romanian cohort with those reported internationally for prenatal WES [–].

Material and Methods
Material and Methods We present a retrospective analysis of indications, genetic testing results (including molecular karyotyping and prenatal WES), and the impact of molecular findings on couples and the multidisciplinary teams involved in their care. The inclusion criteria were: (1) patients of Romanian Caucasian descent; (2) a prenatal sample obtained through an invasive procedure, either amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, or from a product of conception; (3) the fetus presenting with at least one major or two or more structural malformations visible on ultrasound; and (4) testing performed at Synevo Romania between January 2024 and March 2026, representing consecutive cases. The team offered the option to report carrier variants or secondary findings, in accordance with the 2023 recommendations (version 3.2) of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) for reporting secondary findings, only when families provided consent and opted in []. From September 2025, the team incorporated the updated ACMG recommendations (version 3.3) for reporting secondary findings []. Ten consecutive referred cases met the inclusion criteria. None underwent single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-array testing alone; however, SNP-array analysis was performed before WES when clinically indicated. After selecting pregnancies with abnormal ultrasound findings not suggestive of a well-established genetic syndrome, the testing algorithm used molecular karyotyping as the initial test when clinically indicated. In cases with a negative molecular karyotyping result, prenatal WES was subsequently performed. Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA concentration was measured using Qubit fluorometry, and DNA purity was assessed using NanoDrop spectrophotometry. WES Mono (fetus) or Trio (fetus and parents) was performed by massively parallel sequencing of the whole coding region on an Illumina NovaSeq X platform (average coverage >100×; read length 2 × 100 bp). The Twist Human Core Exome kit with the RefSeq and mitochondrial panel (Twist Bioscience, San Francisco, CA, USA) was used for library preparation. Bioinformatic analysis compared the test sample with the human reference sequence (hg38) using Illumina’s DRAGEN Bio-IT and Franklin (Qiagen), together with the OMIM, ClinVar, gnomAD, LOVD, and HGMD databases. Variants with a minor allele frequency <0.01 were prioritized, and interpretation incorporated phenotype-driven filtering using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms. To exclude maternal cell contamination, maternal peripheral blood was tested in parallel. Over 99% of target bases were covered at ≥20× and 97% at ≥30×; the analytical sensitivity for single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) exceeded 99% for regions covered at ≥20× on internal validation. Copy-number variants (CNVs) were assessed from WES data and none were found. As the accredited laboratory had validated these NGS workflows, diagnostic variants were considered high-confidence and did not require routine orthogonal confirmation. Variants were classified according to the ACMG/AMP 2015 guidelines, independently reviewed by two clinical geneticists, and curated by a team of bioinformaticians before interpretation. Testing was performed in an ISO 15189-accredited laboratory that participates in external quality-assessment programs such as GenQA. The turnaround time was under 3 weeks. When the result was ready, the family was scheduled for a medical genetics consultation to understand it and make an informed decision about managing the pregnancy. All families declared no consanguinity. Raw sequencing data have been deposited in a public repository – ClinVar, under submission number SUB16200327. We obtained informed consent from every family after a medical genetics consultation, once we explained the methodology, capabilities, and limitations of the test. Pre-test counseling covered the right not to know, possible adult-onset genetic disorders, and the option to report secondary findings; families could also opt in to receive carrier status, to inform the management of future pregnancies and the testing of at-risk relatives. After the results, a post-test genetic counseling session was held, at which the results were explained, and a written report with recommendations was prepared for the multidisciplinary team caring for the family.

Results
Results Ten cases tested by prenatal WES were included after meeting the criteria above. Microarray was first performed in 8 of the 10 cases with suspected copy number variations and yielded no findings, so the team proceeded with prenatal exome sequencing. The results are shown in and and . Distribution of fetal structural anomalies among the ten pregnancies included in the study Gestational age at testing and WES outcome for each pregnancy The series comprised four cases with central nervous system (CNS) anomalies, three with cardiac malformations, three with severe intrauterine growth restriction, three with skeletal dysplasias, and two with a single umbilical artery. Of the 8 cases with a prior negative SNP array, WES identified a pathogenic variant in four (50% of those previously tested by CMA), and three of these four were primary findings that could explain the phenotype (37.5%). This supports the 2018 position statement of the International Society for Prenatal Diagnosis, the Society for Maternal–Fetal Medicine, and the Perinatal Quality Foundation, which recommends exome sequencing after a non-informative CMA in cases with an ultrasound anomaly. Importantly, the two cases in which WES was used as a first-tier test—Cases 3 and 4, both with suspected skeletal dysplasia and a suggestive phenotype—illustrate that, for certain highly suggestive phenotypes, a direct monogenic approach is both diagnostically and logistically more efficient, consistent with current international recommendations. We considered a case positive when WES identified a primary finding that could explain the phenotype (pathogenic or likely pathogenic); we also counted as positive the case with a second “hot” variant of uncertain significance (VUS) completing a recessive genotype (Case 6). The molecular diagnostic yield was positive for five cases, as primary findings overall, meaning a percentage of 50%, with four cases displaying a Mendelian autosomal dominant disorder and one case showing an autosomal recessive disorder. The yield after a negative SNP array was 37.5% for primary findings, and the yield when WES was used as a first-line test for a highly suggestive monogenic phenotype was 100% (two of two cases; cases 3 and 4). Among our patients, two cases had secondary findings (20%), in one of which we found a homozygous variant in the HFE gene, not the one present in the SF V3.3 ACMG list, as seen in Case 2. Two other fetuses were positive for incidental findings (Cases 4 and 6), representing 20%. Although we followed ACMG guidelines, in cases where the parents decided termination of pregnancy, after this decision, the team agreed to report carrier status of the fetuses for screening purposes and for cascade testing of relatives. One fetus was a carrier of an HJV variant (Case 5). The clinical impact of the prenatal WES test was medical termination of pregnancy (TOP), in Cases 1,2,4,5 and 6 (50% of cases). In two further cases (7 and 8), TOP was conducted based on ultrasound manifestations, as WES yielded negative results. One pregnancy stopped in evolution, and WES couldn’t explain the phenotype; in another case in which WES was negative, the baby was apparently born healthy, so further follow-up is needed. In one positive case (Case 3), the family chose to continue the pregnancy, but WES was very helpful in diagnosis, counseling, and preparing the multidisciplinary team for delivery and pregnancy management. Other important aspects of the clinical impact were genetic counseling and recurrence-risk estimation, based on the known mode of inheritance of each disorder. The team recommended cascade testing of all first-degree relatives in every positive case; at the close of the study, none had undergone segregation analysis except Case 6, whose parents had each been shown previously to carry one of the NBAS variants identified in the fetus. Some products of conception were sent for pathological examination, which confirmed the ultrasound findings — for example, the postaxial polydactyly in Case 5 (). Case 5 — postaxial polydactyly in a fetus with suspected Meckel–Gruber syndrome, confirmed on pathological examination. Published with parental consent.

Discussion
Discussion Managing secondary and incidental findings remains a key component of prenatal genomic testing, with major consequences for informed decision-making and genetic counseling. In our group of patients, thorough pre-test counseling empowered all families to make informed decisions about the disclosure of secondary and incidental findings, and all participants chose to receive these results. Moreover, all families opted to obtain carrier status information after childbirth or medical termination of pregnancy, highlighting the recognized importance of extensive genomic data beyond the initial diagnostic purpose. Our referral pathway, involving gynecologists, obstetricians, medical geneticists, and maternal-fetal medicine specialists, highlights the multidisciplinary nature of prenatal genomic diagnostics and the importance of coordinated clinical assessment to facilitate timely access to testing. A significant challenge in prenatal genomic medicine is the turnaround time (TAT) needed to produce and analyze sequencing outcomes. In alignment with global trends, TAT has steadily improved because of advancements in sequencing technologies, refined laboratory processes, growing proficiency in variant analysis, and the incorporation of AI-driven bioinformatics tools. Nonetheless, further reductions in TAT are crucial in the prenatal context because the therapeutic relevance of genetic testing is inherently connected to the gestational age at diagnosis. This is especially important when fetal structural anomalies are first detected in the second trimester, particularly after 20 weeks of gestation. In numerous European jurisdictions, reproductive options may be significantly restricted by legal restrictions on termination of pregnancy after this gestational age, unless the fetal condition is significantly associated with maternal or neonatal risk. Delays in obtaining a molecular diagnosis may directly influence the range of management options available to prospective parents, as many monogenic disorders exhibit considerable phenotypic variability in the prenatal period and are associated with significant long-term morbidity rather than immediate fetal or maternal compromise. These results underscore the need for early identification of fetal anomalies, prompt referral for genomic evaluation, and rapid access to high-quality prenatal sequencing to optimize the clinical utility of genomic diagnostics and support informed reproductive decision-making. [] Limitations include the small sample size (though important for a country like Romania), the retrospective design, incomplete cascade testing of parents and other first-degree relatives, incomplete postnatal follow-up, and the fact that all data were collected from a single reference laboratory. Given the descriptive nature of this study and the small sample size, we did not perform inferential statistical analyses.

Conclusion
Conclusion In conclusion, prenatal whole-exome sequencing yielded a 50% diagnostic yield in our case series, underscoring its clinical significance for fetuses with structural abnormalities. This diagnostic efficacy aligns with previously published global data and our prior experiences in Romania, reinforcing the consistency of this method across various clinical environments. In addition to providing a molecular diagnosis, prenatal whole-exome sequencing offers clinically relevant insights that enhance genetic counseling, improve recurrence risk evaluation, and support collaborative decision-making about the current pregnancy and future reproductive strategies. Notably, a negative whole-exome sequencing result is not incompatible with an underlying genetic etiology. Some patients may benefit from additional genomic investigations, including epigenetic, transcriptomic, or other advanced molecular analyses, when guided by the clinical phenotype, therefore improving diagnostic precision. Despite variability in the diagnostic yield of prenatal genomic testing influenced by factors such as fetal phenotype, affected organ systems, family history, and case selection, our results contribute to the growing evidence supporting the incorporation of whole-exome sequencing into the diagnostic process for carefully selected pregnancies with fetal structural anomalies. Future multicenter investigations involving larger and more phenotypically varied groups are needed to more accurately delineate the clinical contexts in which prenatal whole-exome sequencing offers the greatest diagnostic and clinical advantages, and to strengthen evidence-based guidelines for its integration into standard prenatal care. The diagnostic yield observed in this cohort may partly reflect referral bias, as only highly selected pregnancies meeting predefined criteria underwent prenatal WES. These preliminary findings support further prospective multicenter studies evaluating prenatal WES in Romanian clinical practice.

title: Fetal Copy Number Variant Detection in Pregnancies with Ultrasound Soft Markers: A Maternal Age-Stratified Retrospective Study.
label_reason: Fetuses with soft markers tested for CNVs.
abstract: Prenatal ultrasound soft markers are common indicators for fetal genetic screening, while the correlation between maternal age and fetal copy number variant (CNV) detection remains controversial. This study aimed to analyze CNV characteristics in fetuses with ultrasound soft marker abnormalities and explore the influence of maternal age on CNV detection. A total of 468 fetuses with abnormal ultrasound soft markers were enrolled and divided into <35 years (n=390) and ≥35 years (n=78) groups based on maternal age. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) was performed for the enrolled fetuses. Fetal pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs and variants of uncertain significance (VUS) were detected and statistically analyzed. The overall detection rates of P/LP CNVs and VUS were 4.1% and 9.0%, respectively. Notably, the P/LP CNVs detection rate was significantly higher in women aged <35 years (4.9%) than in those aged ≥35 years (0%, p =0.047). The CNVs detection rate was 14.0% in fetuses with a single soft marker abnormality and 7.5% in those with ≥2 abnormal soft markers; the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p =0.138). No significant inter-group difference was found in VUS detection rate and CNV detection rates of different types or numbers of soft markers (all p >0.05). In cases with single ultrasound soft marker abnormality, The CNV detection rate was the highest in cases with pyelic separation (n=19), reaching 26.3%; echogenic bowel (n=14) ranked second with a detection rate of 21.4%. As a single‑center retrospective study with underpowered subgroup analyses, our findings suggest that younger pregnant women with ultrasonic soft‑marker abnormalities may still carry risk of fetal pathogenic CNVs. CMA should be considered in pregnancies with ultrasonic soft marker abnormalities after individualized counseling, regardless of maternal age. Keywords: chromosomal microarray analysis, copy number variant, maternal age, prenatal diagnosis, ultrasound soft marker

Fetal Copy Number Variant Detection in Pregnancies with Ultrasound Soft Markers: A Maternal Age-Stratified Retrospective Study

Introduction
Introduction In prenatal diagnosis, ultrasound screening is routinely used to preliminarily assess fetal physical condition and detect potential abnormalities., Prenatal ultrasound soft markers refer to transient and non-specific subtle abnormal imaging manifestations on prenatal ultrasound, without obvious anatomical organic malformations in the fetus. These markers include increased nuchal translucency (NT) thickness, nasal bone hypoplasia, echogenic intracardiac focus, choroid plexus cysts, short long bones, pyelic separation, ventriculomegaly, echogenic bowel, and single umbilical artery, among others. Most of these markers do not have clear pathological significance and may resolve spontaneously with advancing gestational age. However, they are potentially associated with fetal chromosomal aneuploidies, genomic copy number variants (CNVs), and long-term neurodevelopmental abnormalities, serving as crucial ultrasound clues for prenatal genetic risk screening. At present, prenatal clinical practice has regarded ultrasound soft markers as an important auxiliary basis for fetal genetic evaluation. CNV refers to deletions, duplications, insertions, or complex multi-copy alterations of DNA fragments longer than 1 kilobase (kb) in the genome. Widely distributed across the entire human genome, CNV represents a major form of genomic structural variation. CNVs can affect embryonic development and human physiological functions through multiple molecular mechanisms, including altering gene dosage, disrupting the intact structure of genes, and regulating the expression of adjacent genes., They are important genetic causes of hereditary diseases, fetal congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, and a variety of complex disorders., Pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) CNVs are genetic causes of fetal developmental abnormalities, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neonatal congenital diseases., By performing whole-genome scanning, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is capable of identifying CNVs within small chromosomal fragments at a high resolution., With the widespread application of CMA in prenatal diagnosis, an increasing number of subtle fetal CNVs have been identified, greatly improving the detection rate of submicroscopic chromosomal abnormalities that cannot be detected by conventional karyotyping. At present, most existing research primarily evaluates the overall correlation between ultrasound soft markers and fetal CNV abnormalities., Few studies systematically distinguish isolated single soft marker anomalies from multiple soft marker abnormalities, despite their distinct clinical risk implications: multiple soft marker presentations generally confer higher overall chromosomal aberration risk,, while isolated soft markers remain ambiguous in genetic risk stratification across different maternal age cohorts. Additionally, prior studies focusing on maternal age-related genomic risk largely regard advanced maternal age (≥35 years) as the dominant risk factor for fetal genetic aberrations,, with inconsistent conclusions regarding pathogenic CNV prevalence in younger pregnant women presenting ultrasound soft markers., Stratified comparisons of P/LP CNV detection rates between women aged <35 and ≥35 years within soft marker cohorts remain insufficient, and many previous cohorts lack balanced sample distribution across age subgroups, limiting robust clinical inference., Furthermore, few studies have comprehensively stratified CNV detection outcomes by both maternal age and the number of abnormal ultrasound soft markers, nor quantified the varying diagnostic yield of distinct soft marker subtypes across age groups., This study aimed to analyze CNV detection in fetuses with abnormal ultrasonic soft markers. Stratified analyses stratified by maternal age, type of ultrasonic soft markers and the count of abnormal markers were conducted to explore the impact of maternal age on CNVs among these fetuses.

Materials and Methods
Materials and Methods Study Cohort This retrospective observational study consecutively enrolled a total of 468 pregnant women who received prenatal genetic testing due to fetal ultrasonographic soft marker abnormalities in Meizhou People’s Hospital from October 2022 to December 2025. All enrolled participants underwent karyotype analysis and CMA with complete clinical and ultrasonic data. The inclusion criteria are as follows: (1) singleton pregnancy; (2) presence of one or more fetal ultrasound soft marker abnormalities during prenatal ultrasound screening; (3) complete gestational and clinical baseline information; and (4) available fetal genetic detection results. Exclusion criteria: (1) the pregnant woman has a family history of chromosomal abnormalities; (2) fetuses structural malformations, fetal growth restriction, or abnormal amniotic fluid volume; (3) cases confirmed to have chromosomal aneuploidies based on karyotyping; and (4) enrolled pregnant individuals had clear exposure to teratogenic agents including ionizing radiation and chemical toxicants during gestation. All procedures of this research were reviewed and approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Meizhou People’s Hospital. The participant screening and selection process is illustrated in the flowchart (). The flowchart of this study. A flowchart of fetal ultrasound abnormalities and CNVs detection in pregnant women. The flowchart begins with ′Fetuses presented ultrasound abnormalities (n=910)′. It branches to a list: ′Fetuses with Abnormal karyotype (n=50)′, ′Fetal growth restriction (n=68)′, ′Abnormal amniotic fluid volume (n=28)′ and ′Fetuses with structural abnormality (n=296)′. The flow continues to ′Final analysis of fetuses (n=468)′. This splits into two paths: ′Pregnant women aged less than 35 years (n=390)′ and ′Pregnant women aged greater than or equal to 35 years (n=78)′. Both paths lead to ′Overall detection of CNVs′. The flow proceeds to ′CNVs detection rate stratified by different types of abnormal ultrasonic soft markers′, followed by ′Comparison of the detection rates of P/LP CNVs and VUS in fetuses with different types of isolated single abnormal ultrasonic soft markers′. It concludes with ′Comparison of the detection rates of fetal P/LP CNVs and VUS in fetuses of pregnant women aged less than 35 years and greater than or equal to 35 years′. All enrolled fetuses underwent a complete detailed anatomical ultrasound scan performed by certified senior maternal-fetal medicine specialists to comprehensively evaluate organ development and exclude definite fetal structural malformations. The soft marker presentations were categorized into two groups for stratified analysis: isolated single soft marker abnormality (only one type of ultrasound soft marker identified, without additional minor sonographic aberrations or structural defects) and multiple soft marker abnormalities (two or more distinct soft markers detected simultaneously). Sample Collection and Processing Prenatal samples were collected in accordance with standard prenatal sampling protocols, including amniotic fluid, villus, and umbilical cord blood specimens. Sampling gestational age was categorized into three subgroups: first trimester (≤13 weeks), second trimester (14–28 weeks), and third trimester (>28 weeks). All samples were strictly stored, transported, and processed in a standardized laboratory environment to ensure DNA integrity and avoid contamination. Genomic DNA was extracted from fetal specimens using commercial DNA extraction kits, and DNA concentration and purity were detected to meet the requirements of subsequent microarray detection. CNV Detection and Classification Genomic DNA was isolated from fetal specimens and digested with the NspI restriction enzyme to generate short DNA fragments. Following biotin-labeled amplification, the DNA samples were fully blended with hybridization solution and denatured. The processed samples were then loaded onto the Affymetrix Cytoscan 750k chip for hybridization, washing, and staining. Subsequent chip scanning was performed to acquire raw data, which was imported into GenomeStudio software for systematic analysis and result interpretation. All obtained results were aligned with international genomic variation databases. The pathogenicity of identified gene-related CNVs was assessed based on multiple authoritative databases, including the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen), Database of Genomic Variation and Phenotype in Humans using Ensembl Resources (DECIPHER), Database of Genomic Variants (DGV), Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM), and PubMed literature database. In accordance with the guidelines established by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), CNVs were classified into five categories of clinical significance: pathogenic (P), likely pathogenic (LP), variants of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign (LB), and benign (B) CNVs., Statistical Analysis All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS statistical software. Count data were expressed as case numbers and percentages. The differences in the detection rates of P/LP CNVs and VUS between different maternal age groups, different types, and different numbers of ultrasonographic soft markers were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. No prospective sample size power calculation was performed prior to participant enrollment, given the retrospective nature of this clinical cohort. Multiple exploratory subgroup comparisons stratified by maternal age, soft marker category and number of abnormal soft markers were conducted in this study, and correction for multiple testing was not applied. All subgroup comparisons are regarded as exploratory analyses. We attempted multivariable regression adjusting for soft marker type, number of soft markers, gestational age at sampling, and adverse pregnancy history, but model convergence failed due to the limited total number of P/LP CNV positive cases and zero positive events in the advanced maternal age subgroup.

Results
Results Baseline Characteristics of Study Population A total of 468 pregnant women and their fetuses were enrolled in the present study, with comprehensive baseline clinical characteristics summarized in . In terms of maternal age, 390 (83.3%) participants were younger than 35 years, while 78 (16.7%) were aged ≥35 years. A total of 114 cases (24.4%) had a history of adverse pregnancy outcomes, and the remaining 354 cases (75.6%) had no adverse pregnancy history. Regarding the gestational age at sample collection, most samples were obtained during the second trimester: 349 cases (74.6%) were sampled at 14–28 weeks of gestation, followed by 70 cases (15.0%) at ≤13 weeks, and 49 cases (10.5%) at >28 weeks. For fetal sample types, amniotic fluid specimens accounted for the vast majority of samples (398 cases, 85.0%), followed by villus samples (69 cases, 14.7%), with only one case (0.2%) of umbilical cord blood sample collected. Overall Detection Status of CNVs In this study, P/LP CNVs were identified in 19 fetuses (4.1%), and VUS were detected in 42 fetuses (9.0%). No P/LP CNVs or VUS were found in the remaining 407 fetuses (87.0%) (). We further characterized the spectrum of detected P/LP CNVs. The identified pathogenic variants mainly involved classic microdeletion/microduplication syndromes including 15q11.2 deletion syndrome, and X-linked pathogenic copy number alterations. The sizes of these pathogenic fragments ranged from 112 Kb to 46.15 Mb, and each variant contained multiple core dosage-sensitive genes closely associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, congenital malformations and intellectual disability (Supplementary Table 1). Overall detection of CNVs. Abbreviations: CNV, copy number variant; P/LP CNV, Pathogenic/Likely pathogenic CNV; VUS, variants of uncertain significance. A doughnut chart showing CNV detection outcomes, with segments from 4.1 percent to 87.0 percent. Correlation Between Ultrasound Soft Marker Number and CNV Detection Rate Stratified analysis based on the number of abnormal ultrasonic soft markers was performed to explore the variation of CNV detection rates (). The detection rates of total CNVs, P/LP CNVs and VUS exhibited distinct trends with the increase in the number of abnormal ultrasonic items, indicating that the number of abnormal soft markers is closely associated with fetal CNV variation risk. CNV detection rate stratified by the number of ultrasonic soft markers. Abbreviations: CNV, copy number variant; P/LP CNV, Pathogenic/Likely pathogenic CNV; VUS, variants of uncertain significance. Grouped bars compare two CNV result types across one vs multiple ultrasound soft markers. Distribution and CNV Detection Efficiency of Single Ultrasonic Soft Marker Abnormalities Among all cases with a single abnormal ultrasonic soft marker, the constituent ratio of different abnormal markers was further analyzed (). Increased NT thickness was the most prevalent single abnormal ultrasonic soft marker, followed by ventriculomegaly and nasal bone hypoplasia, while other markers including bilateral subependymal cysts, aberrant subclavian artery, and persistent left superior vena cava showed relatively low incidence in the study cohort. Distribution of different types of ultrasonic soft markers in cases with one abnormal ultrasonic soft marker. Abbreviation: NT, nuchal translucency. A donut chart showing ultrasonic soft marker distribution, from 0.2 percent to 35.1 percent. A donut chart illustrates the distribution of various ultrasonic soft markers in cases with one abnormal marker. The slices show the following: Increased NT thickness (151, 35.1%), Ventriculomegaly (76, 17.7%), Nasal bone hypoplasia (61, 14.2%), Choroid plexus cyst (43, 10.0%), Short long bones (30, 7.0%), Pyelic separation (19, 4.4%), Echogenic bowel (14, 3.3%), Tricuspid regurgitation (5, 1.2%), Persistent left superior vena cava (4, 0.9%), Persistent right umbilical vein (3, 0.7%), Aberrant Subclavian Artery (6, 1.4%), Bilateral subependymal cysts (7, 1.6%), Single umbilical artery (8, 1.9%), Increased nuchal fold thickness (1, 0.2%), Small cavum septi pellucidi (1, 0.2%), Echogenic intracardiac focus (1, 0.2%). No axis labels or units are provided. The CNV detection rates varied significantly across different types of single abnormal ultrasonic soft markers (). Specifically, after excluding several types of soft marker abnormalities with small sample sizes (such as tricuspid regurgitation (n=5), persistent right umbilical vein (n=3), and persistent left superior vena cava (n=4))(the blue bars in ), pyelic separation (n=19) yielded the highest CNV detection rate at 26.3%, followed by echogenic bowel (n=14) with a detection rate of 21.4%. In contrast, no CNV were detected in cases with aberrant subclavian artery (n=6) and single umbilical artery (n=8) abnormalities. CNV detection rate across different types of abnormal ultrasonic soft markers. Blue bar chart: The types of ultrasonic soft markers abnormalities in fetuses with P/LP CNVs or VUS and ≤5 cases with these ultrasound soft markers; Red bar chart: The types of ultrasonic soft indicators abnormalities in fetuses with P/LP CNVs or VUS and >5 cases with these ultrasound soft markers. Abbreviation: NT, nuchal translucency. A horizontal bar graph showing CNV detection rate across abnormal ultrasonic soft markers. A horizontal bar graph of CNV detection rate by abnormal ultrasonic soft marker. Horizontal axis label, CNV detection rate, percent, ranging from 0.0 percent to 45.0 percent with ticks at 0.0, 5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 35.0, 40.0, 45.0 percent. Vertical axis lists categories: Tricuspid regurgitation 40.0 percent; Persistent right umbilical vein 33.3 percent; Pyelic separation 26.3 percent; Persistent left superior vena cava 25.0 percent; Echogenic bowel 21.4 percent; Short long bones 16.7 percent; Increased N T thickness 14.6 percent; Bilateral subependymal cysts 14.3 percent; Ventriculomegaly 11.8 percent; Nasal bone hypoplasia 9.8 percent; Choroid plexus cyst 9.3 percent; Small cavum septi pellucidi 0.0 percent; Echogenic intracardiac focus 0.0 percent; Increased nuchal fold left parenthesis N F right parenthesis thickness 0.0 percent; Aberrant Subclavian Artery 0.0 percent; Single umbilical artery 0.0 percent. Stratified Analysis of CNV Detection by Maternal Age and Ultrasonic Abnormality Characteristics To explore the effect of maternal age on fetal CNV detection, all cases were divided into the younger maternal age group (<35 years, n=390) and advanced maternal age group (≥35 years, n=78). The CNV detection rates of different single ultrasound soft marker abnormalities and different numbers of ultrasonic abnormalities were compared between the two groups (). For single ultrasound soft marker abnormalities, subgroup analysis showed no statistically significant differences in the combined detection rates of P/LP CNVs and VUS between the two maternal age groups for all marker types (all p>0.05). Typical single markers including increased NT thickness (14.8% vs 13.0%, p=0.822), ventriculomegaly (11.6% vs 14.3%, p=0.834), and nasal bone hypoplasia (9.4% vs 12.5%, p=0.786) exhibited comparable variant detection rates regardless of maternal age. In addition, no significant age-based differences were observed in cases with choroid plexus cyst, short long bones, pyelic separation, and other rare soft marker abnormalities (all p>0.05). In terms of the number of abnormal ultrasonic items, the detection rate of P/LP CNVs and VUS in cases with single ultrasonic abnormality was 14.8% in the <35 years group and 8.5% in the ≥35 years group, with no statistical difference (p=0.158). For multiple ultrasonic abnormalities, the variant detection rate was 6.5% in the younger maternal age group, while no variants were detected in the advanced age group, and the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.490). Comparison of P/LP CNV and VUS Detection Rates by Maternal Age The overall detection rates of fetal P/LP CNVs and VUS were further compared between the two maternal age groups (). Notably, the detection rate of P/LP CNVs was significantly higher in pregnant women aged <35 years (4.9%, 19/390) than that in women aged ≥35 years (0%, 0/78), and the difference reached statistical significance (p=0.047). In contrast, the VUS detection rate was similar between the younger age group (9.2%, 36/390) and the advanced age group (7.7%, 6/78), with no significant statistical difference (p=0.664).

Discussion
Discussion Ultrasonic soft markers are subtle non-structural fetal abnormalities identified during routine prenatal ultrasound, serving as critical warning signs for potential submicroscopic chromosomal defects and fetal CNVs., Conventional karyotype can only detect macroscopic chromosomal aneuploidies and large structural rearrangements, whereas CMA enables genome-wide detection of microdeletions and microduplications, greatly improving the diagnostic yield of fetal genetic variations in high-risk pregnancies with soft marker anomalies.,, In clinical practice, ultrasound soft markers are frequently encountered in prenatal screening, yet their genetic significance and optimal prenatal diagnostic strategies remain inconsistent across different populations., The present study systematically analyzed fetal P/LP CNVs and VUS in a cohort of 468 pregnant women with fetal ultrasonic soft marker abnormalities, with a particular focus on maternal age stratification, aiming to provide refined clinical evidence for individualized prenatal genetic counseling. In this study, the overall detection rates of fetal P/LP CNVs and VUS were 4.1% and 9.0%, respectively, which aligns with previous studies focusing on prenatal soft marker populations.,, Of course, there are also certain differences from the results of some studies., The vast majority of cases (87.0%) presented no detectable CNV abnormalities, confirming that isolated ultrasonic soft markers are generally benign phenotypic variants with low overall pathogenic genetic risk., Among all ultrasound soft marker subtypes, increased NT thickness, ventriculomegaly, nasal bone hypoplasia, and choroid plexus cyst were the most prevalent anomalies,,, while pyelic separation yielded the highest CNV detection rate at 26.3% followed by echogenic bowel with a detection rate of 21.4%. These findings support the consensus that these ultrasonic markers are more closely correlated with fetal submicroscopic genetic disorders and should be regarded as key indicators triggering further genetic assessment in prenatal clinical practice. The research conducted by Pan et al revealed that the detection rates of P/LP CNVs were high for thickened nuchal fold, single umbilical artery, mild ventriculomegaly, and nasal bone dysplasia. Lu et al reported that CNV was mainly observed in cases of increased NT thickness. The most compelling finding of the current study is the distinct difference in P/LP CNV prevalence between different maternal age groups. Traditionally, advanced maternal age (≥35 years) has been universally recognized as the dominant risk factor for fetal chromosomal abnormalities, while younger pregnant women are generally considered low-risk populations in prenatal genetic evaluation. Clinically, genetic testing is often selectively recommended for advanced-age pregnancies, whereas soft marker anomalies in younger women are frequently underestimated. Larroya et al suggested that the presence of pathogenic CNVs is not associated with paternal age or maternal age. Our stratified analysis demonstrated that the fetal P/LP CNVs detection rate in women aged <35 years reached 4.9%, while no pathogenic CNVs were identified in the advanced maternal age group, and this difference achieved statistical significance (p=0.047). These results indicate that young pregnant women are also at risk of fetal CNV in the presence of abnormal ultrasonic soft markers; therefore, CMA testing may be considered for this group of pregnant women. Of note, the between‑group difference in P/LP CNV detection yielded a borderline p value of 0.047. Coupled with the limited sample size of the advanced‑maternal‑age subgroup, this observation should be regarded as suggestive rather than definitive. It is worth emphasising that, in contrast to chromosomal aneuploidies strongly linked to advancing maternal age,, CNVs represent structural genomic rearrangements whose aetiology is not primarily dependent on maternal age., Therefore, further multicenter and large-sample studies are required to validate these findings. In this study, no significant inter-group difference was observed in VUS detection rates between younger and advanced-age pregnant women (9.2% vs 7.7%, p>0.05). As VUS represent genetic variants with unconfirmed clinical pathogenicity, they cannot directly guide pregnancy outcome judgment or clinical intervention. The consistent VUS distribution across age groups suggests that the elevated pathogenic CNV risk in younger pregnant women is a specific clinical phenomenon rather than a random variation of uncertain genetic alterations. Moreover, further subgroup analysis stratified by the type and number of ultrasound soft markers revealed no significant age-related differences in CNV detection for either single or multiple soft marker abnormalities. These results imply that fetal CNV occurrence associated with ultrasound soft markers is modulated by multifactorial interactions, including genetic polymorphism, embryonic development status, and environmental factors, rather than being simply determined by maternal age. This study provides valuable clinical implications for prenatal genetic counseling and diagnostic strategy optimization. Current clinical guidelines tend to prioritize advanced maternal age as the major indication for invasive genetic testing, potentially leading to insufficient attention and undertesting for younger pregnant women with isolated soft marker abnormalities. Based on our findings, we strongly recommend that CMA detection should be routinely offered to all pregnant individuals with fetal ultrasound soft marker anomalies, regardless of maternal age. Universal genetic screening for such high-risk ultrasound phenotypes can effectively avoid missed diagnosis of pathogenic CNVs in young populations, thereby improving the accuracy of prenatal genetic risk assessment and enabling more precise individualized pregnancy counseling. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, it should also be noted that all participants in this study were referred for invasive prenatal diagnosis owing to fetal ultrasound soft‑marker abnormalities, which introduces a selection bias. The CNV detection rates observed here should be extrapolated to the general obstetric population with great caution selection bias and limit the generalizability of the conclusions. Second, this study only focused on the detection rate of fetal CNV variants and lacked long-term follow-up data on neonatal developmental outcomes, making it impossible to further validate the prognostic value of detected variants. Third, this study has several statistical limitations that deserve acknowledgment. Of note, this higher detection rate of P/LP CNVs among women aged < 35 years was observed specifically within our cohort of pregnancies with fetal ultrasound soft‑marker abnormalities. Given the absence of multivariable adjustment in the present study, we cannot conclude that younger maternal age itself acts as an independent risk factor for pathogenic CNVs; this represents an observed association rather than proven causation. In addition, the zero-rate of P/LP CNVs among the advanced‑maternal‑age subgroup (n = 78) should be interpreted with great caution, as it is likely caused by limited sample size and low statistical power rather than a true absence of pathogenic CNV risk in this population. Moreover, multiple uncorrected subgroup comparisons across soft marker subtypes may increase the risk of type I error; all subgroup findings should be considered exploratory and require external validation in larger cohorts. Future large-sample, multicenter prospective studies with long-term follow-up are warranted to validate our findings, further clarify the age-related genetic risk discrepancies in soft marker pregnancies, and establish more standardized prenatal diagnostic protocols for this specific high-risk population.

Conclusion
Conclusion This study explored fetal CNV features in pregnancies with ultrasound soft marker abnormalities. Notably, younger pregnant women (<35 years) exhibited a significantly higher rate of fetal pathogenic CNVs than advanced-age cases, while VUS detection was comparable between groups. Clinically, abnormal soft markers indicate a potential risk of CNV, which differs from maternal age-related chromosomal aneuploidy, regardless of maternal age. CMA should be considered in pregnancies with ultrasound soft marker abnormalities after individualized counseling, regardless of maternal age, particularly when high-risk marker types are present.

title: Prenatal and Postnatal Identification of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome in a Tertiary Referral Center: A 15-Case Series and Literature Review.
label_reason: Prenatal PMS cases with ultrasound anomalies and SNP array/karyotype/WES.
abstract: Objectives : To characterize the clinical and genetic features of Phelan–McDermid syndrome (PMS) in a Chinese prenatal and postnatal cohort, explore genotype–phenotype correlations, and provide evidence to support prenatal genetic counseling. Methods : G-banded karyotyping, single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays (SNP arrays), copy number variation sequencing, and trio whole-exome sequencing were used for genetic diagnosis. Fifteen patients with PMS (11 prenatal and 4 postnatal) were retrospectively enrolled. Genomic visualization, protein structural prediction, and phenotypic heatmap analyses were conducted to analyze genotype–phenotype associations. Results : The prenatal and postnatal detection rates of PMS were 0.061% and 0.49%, respectively. Only 13.3% of cases were detected by karyotyping, whereas 14 cases were confirmed by SNP array analysis. All 22q13 deletions (69.4 kb–8.5 Mb) involved SHANK3 , and all copy number variants were de novo. A novel SHANK3 frameshift variant, c.3513_3514delCC, was identified and predicted to result in protein truncation leading to intellectual disability. Prenatal cases mainly presented non-specific ultrasound anomalies (63.6%, 7/11), with fetal growth restriction, renal malformations, and cardiovascular defects being the most frequent findings. A notable 36.4% (4/11) of prenatal cases were complicated by missed abortion, whereas postnatal patients showed predominant neurodevelopmental impairments. In our cohort, larger deletions were observed in cases presenting with more extensive multisystem involvement, a pattern that mirrors findings from recent large-cohort studies. central nervous system abnormalities were predominantly linked to SHANK3 haploinsufficiency, while multi-system malformations seemed to correlate with the cumulative loss of multiple genes across the 22q13 region, in keeping with current hypotheses on contiguous gene effects. Conclusions : PMS presents obvious prenatal–postnatal phenotypic heterogeneity. SHANK3 is the core pathogenic gene, and deletion may influence the extent of multisystem involvement. Combined genetic testing can improve the accuracy of prenatal diagnosis and counseling for PMS.
